title: Planning commission to reconsider Lakeside resolution
author: Natalie Jones; njones@chespub.com
content:
Planning commission to reconsider Lakeside resolution

 November 2, 2023 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: Natalie Jones; njones@chespub.com | Page: 3 | Section: News 
 
 418
 Words 

 Read News Document

 EASTON - The Talbot County Planning Commission on Wednesday voted to reconsider an earlier finding of inconsistency on a comprehensive water and sewer plan amendment relating to the Lakeside at Trappe development.Resolution 338, introduced in late February by Talbot County Council member Lynn Mielke, would amend the county's comprehensive water and sewer plan to be consistent with the Maryland Department of the Environment's discharge permit for Lakeside's wastewater treatment plant.The permit, issued in October 2022, is limited to the project's first phase and allows for an annual average flow of 100,000 gallons per day, or roughly 250 gallons per day per equivalent dwelling unit, allowing only 400 residential units to be built.The resolution would mandate that any future expansion of the new wastewater treatment plant require a comprehensive water and sewer plan amendment.In a 3-2 vote in early October, the planning commission found the resolution to be inconsistent with the county's comprehensive water and sewer plan because it referred to a map that needed to be reviewed.However, commissioners endorsed the idea of a phased review and determined its consistency with the comprehensive plan.The maps in need of review are water and sewer service maps for the Town of Trappe.Earlier this year, the Maryland Department of the Environment requested the county submit updated figures for water and sewer service in Trappe with correct classifications for all the town parcels, along with corrected exhibits to Resolution 281 - the original legislation approving water and sewer for Lakeside - to address certain parcels that were inadvertently shown on those maps.At Wednesday's meeting, planning commission member William Boicourt, who initially moved to find the resolution inconsistent with the comprehensive plan at the Oct. 4 meeting, said that while he recognized the issues with the maps, the commission still endorsed the resolution's basic principles.Given that the planning commission would be talking with the county council about other pending Lakeside legislation, Boicourt said he thought it was appropriate to reconsider the resolution's consistency in discussions with the council - a sentiment others agreed with.A joint work session with the county council and county planning commission on all of the Lakeside comprehensive water and sewer plan amendments is scheduled for Monday, Nov. 20 at 4 p.m.The planning commission will hold a special meeting with its attorneys and county staff on Wednesday, Nov. 8, at 9 a.m. to formulate and clarify its questions ahead of the Nov. 20 workshop.

title: Three elected to Greensboro Town Council - Running unopposed David Spencer is mayor-elect
author: Connie Connolly; cconnolly@chespub.com
content:
Three elected to Greensboro Town Council - Running unopposed David Spencer is mayor-elect

 November 8, 2023 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: Connie Connolly; cconnolly@chespub.com | Page: 1A | Section: News

 GREENSBORO - Joining the Greensboro Town Council will be incumbents Bob Harrison and Pete Brelia, and former Mayor Joe Noon.The election was held Tuesday, Nov. 7, in the town hall.Mayor-elect David Spencer, who has served on the town council since his election in 2021, ran unopposed.The Greensboro native was elected mayor in 2007 after serving on the council from 1995 to 2007.Spencer's mayoral run created an extra vacancy on the council to fill the two remaining years of his term. The two candidates with the highest vote counts will serve a fouryear term. Incumbent Harrison received 78 votes and Noon received 71.As the candidate with the third highest count at 67 votes, Brelia will serve a twoyear term.Spencer, who received 97 votes, will be sworn in Nov. 8 at the Caroline County Courthouse. He will swear in the new council members at a future meeting.

title: Easton Town Council passes six-month cannabis moratorium
author: Natalie Jones; njones@chespub.com
content:
Easton Town Council passes six-month cannabis moratorium

 November 8, 2023 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: Natalie Jones; njones@chespub.com | Page: 4 | Section: News 
 
 334
 Words 

 Read News Document

 EASTON - After brief discussion Monday evening, the Easton Town Council passed a revised six-month moratorium for businesses looking to produce or sell cannabis within the town limits.The support for implementing the moratorium comes three weeks after a heated discussion ensued on a decision to delay the vote to wait for further input from the town's planning commission.The moratorium, originally introduced this summer as a nine-month ban on cannabis businesses, will place a pause on applications, approval, construction, expansion, processing or issuance of building permits for a business that grows, processes or sells cannabis within the Easton town limits.The legislation was originally slated for a vote in mid-September, but was postponed to mid-October so all five council members could be present to vote.It will also allow the town to consider and adopt a revised zoning ordinance.Easton's existing zoning ordinance already contains definitions and permitted zoning districts for medical cannabis dispensaries and growing and processing facilities, but does not include language on standards for recreational facilities.At its Oct. 19 meeting, the planning commission began discussing specific items to potentially be included in the zoning ordinance, said Town Attorney Sharon Van Emburgh.Following further discussions this month and in December, the planning commission expects to vote on a set of zoning amendments at its January meeting, according to a letter the commission's chair submitted to the council.The zoning amendments will then need to go through the town council's legislative process, which includes at least one public hearing.Van Emburgh estimated it would take about six months to fully pass the cannabis zoning legislation.That estimation prompted Council President Frank Gunsallus to propose an amendment to shorten the moratorium to six months, which was passed unanimously by the council. A unanimous vote on the amended moratorium followed.The planning commission will continue discussion on the zoning requirements for adult-use cannabis dispensaries at its Thursday, Nov. 16 meeting.

title: 'It felt like we were abandoned' - Management working to address problems at Altair Apartments as residents seek housing elsewhere
author: Maggie Trovato; mtrovato@chespub.com
content:
'It felt like we were abandoned' - Management working to address problems at Altair Apartments as residents seek housing elsewhere

 November 9, 2023 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: Maggie Trovato; mtrovato@chespub.com | Page: 1 | Section: News 
 
 1489
 Words 

 Read News Document

 CAMBRIDGE - In August, everything came to a head at Altair Apartments.Trash piled high outside the apartments on Greenwood Avenue for an entire week. Broken water heaters and air conditioners couldn't be fixed. Even the internet stopped working.Resident Rodaisia Brummell said she felt disgusted."It felt like we were abandoned," Brummell said. "Like they didn't really care about us." The reason for these conditions: its new California-based management company, FPI Management, hadn't been paying all of the bills since taking over the property in April.Property Manager Judkya Murray said that overtime, vendors stopped showing up, causing trash to build up and plumbing to remain broken.She said the problem was all caused by one person at FPI Management, who has since been let go. That one person wasn't paying the bills to keep everything at Altair running. FPI Management could not be reached for comment."I was literally sitting here pulling my hair out because we had no internet," Murray said. "We had no phones. I couldn't call anybody.I couldn't email anybody." At the time, Murray was the assistant property manager acting as the property manager. The previous property manager had left for another opportunity, Murray said.The week the garbage trucks didn't show, Murray remembers the garbage being so plentiful that the building's maintenance worker had to take garbage cans from inside the building to fill with the overflowing trash outside."We were trying to do everything we could possibly do to keep the trash contained somewhere," she said. "It was just too much trash." The building's staff was quitting left and right."Nobody really wanted to leave but it's like, the conditions - you have no choice but to leave," Murray said.Even Murray quit.However, in about three weeks, she was back."The senior director of FPI (Management), she actually reached out to me one day," Murray said. "She was like, 'Can you please come have lunch with me.'" At the lunch, Murray explained why she quit and said the senior director told her they were already working to let go of and replace the the person within the company that hadn't been paying the bills for months.With that conversation, Murray agreed to come back in early October, this time as the official property manager.Having a boss who pays the bills has made Murray's job easier since coming back, she said. But she still has a significant list of to-dos and goals, especially because so many people quit a few months ago.In mid-October, Murray said she has hired a new assistant and interviewed a potential new maintenance worker."And if we hire him, we'll just need one other maintenance guy and we'll be fully staffed," she said. "Once we're fully staffed, everything flows perfectly." Murray also has some big picture goals in the works to increase occupancy and create new community programming.She is working to increase the property's occupancy rate by filling the vacant apartments. Of Altair's 144 total units, Murray said 20 are vacant. She hopes to bring the occupancy rate from 86% to 94% by the end of the year.While the waitlist of applicants is "a mile long," Murray said maintenance has to get the apartments fixed up and ready before new residents can move in.PROBLEMS PROMPT RESIDENTS TO LOOK ELSEWHEREWhile Murray is taking applications to fill apartment vacancies, Millie Lewis and her husband Willie are filling out applications for other apartments in Cambridge. After more than 40 years of living in the Altair Apartments, the Lewises are tired of dealing with the problems.Recently, they dealt with the outcome of a recent water leak, which affected their kitchen, living room and bathroom. In all three rooms, water spilled out from the ceiling. In the kitchen and bathroom, water filled in the ceiling lights.The edges of the carpeting against one wall in the living room has turned from beige to rusted brown.For years, even before the leak, the carpeting in Lewis' bedroom has been coming undone from the floor.Lewis covers these spaces - where pockets of air separate the carpeting and the floor - with small area rugs. She said Altair won't fix this issue, even though she has complained about it.Although the ceilings were patched up by maintenance following the leak, it took weeks and a citation from the city for the mold, which grew from one of those patched up spots in the bathroom, to be removed.Lewis has COPD and asthma, which made her even more concerned about being in a home where there is mold in the bathroom that she and her husband use everyday."I pay my rent every month," she said. "Before I'm supposed to pay it.Why can't the head people do their job? Why can't they pay? Why can't they take care of what's got to be taken care of at these apartments hereft" Lewis isn't the only resident looking to live elsewhere.Tieonna Wisher, who has lived at Altair for three years, said she has already filled out an application for another apartment.She has concerns about how long it takes for management to respond to problems.Wisher has a hole in her wall that she said management hasn't done anything about for months."They keep saying they're going to come in here," she said.Wisher remembers one day when she unplugged a cord from a socket in her home and it sparked and caused half of the lights to go out in her apartment."They told me to call the emergency number," she said. "Call it and nobody answers. Go to the office.Like, nobody wants to do nothing." Brummell, who has lived at Altair for over a year, said she has also started submitting housing applications.In the time that she's lived here, Brummell has experienced a months-long leak in her bathroom and a leaking dishwasher. She said that when her dishwasher was leaking, all maintenance did was drop off a shop vac. She has yet to receive a working dishwasher.It took about three months before Brummell could get someone to fix the leak in her bathroom. She said that gnats are still flying around the apartment because of it.A mother of two young kids, Brummell has noticed her children keep getting sick. She fears it is from the building. The one time she saw mold in her home, a previous property manager told her to spray it with bleach."That's all she told me to do," Brummell said.THE CITY's INVOLVEMENTTo get problems solved, Brummell said she has started reaching out to the City of Cambridge. She said this has been effective because code enforcement can fine Altair for property violations."A couple weeks ago (workers hired by management) came in and painted and fixed my stuff that was supposed to be fixed," she said. "Only because I called the City of Cambridge.Because, if I didn't call them, it wouldn't have been that." Cambridge Assistant City Manager Brandon Hesson said a goal of the city is to solve quality of life issues."That's not always going to be possible from the outside of homes," he said."We need to get people to the point where (residents) trust us and they are contacting us and they're aware of their tenants rights and they're ability to call us about issues they're having with their rental homes and their apartments." Hesson said they have been able to do this at Altair and are "still very present." Since August, Hesson said communication with upper management has been satisfactory. He said they shared an action plan with multiple items they plan to address. As of Nov. 3, Hesson said he was still waiting to see if they are following that plan.Hesson clarified that communication with Altair's on-site management "has always been pretty good." Murray said she is making sure that she stays in communication with the city."I know their biggest thing is nobody was communicating anything back to them," she said about the city. "They just need to know if somebody's on top of (a problem)." With all of the issues at Altair, Brummell said residents are paying rent and not getting the services they should be getting as tenants."Everything's being prolonged," she said. "But ya'll want things from us. You want rent money from us.You want us to go in the house at a certain time. But we're not getting the things that we properly need." 
 
 Caption: TOM MCCALL/STAR DEMOCRAT
 
Judkya Murray, Altair Apartments property manager, was so frustrated with surmounting issues that she quit. Now she is back and trying to get the tenants resources.
 
TOM MCCALL/STAR DEMOCRAT
 
Rodaisia Brummell is looking for another place to live with her husband and two kids. "It felt like we was abandoned," Brummell said about Altair Apartments management. "Like they didn't really care about us."

title: Elections Board audit finds ineligible voters, security issues
author: Tommy Tucker; Capital News Service
content:
Elections Board audit finds ineligible voters, security issues

 November 9, 2023 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: Tommy Tucker; Capital News Service | Page: 11 | Section: News 
 
 398
 Words 

 Read News Document

 ANNAPOLIS - An audit released Friday found that the Maryland Board of Elections did not report for more than a year its findings that people voted or tried to vote more than once in the 2020 general election - well after the results were certified, according to The Office of Legislative Audits.The state elections board identified 134 voters who voted more than once and 1,371 voters who attempted to vote multiple times in the 2020 general election, but it did not report these individuals to the The Office of State Prosecutor until April 2022, the audit said. The audit is part of a routine physical compliance audit of the SBE conducted every three to four years."Definitely the (reports) for the 2020 general election were significantly late and I think they indicated that was due to staff turnover within their office," said Matthew Streett, an assistant director for the Compliance and Performance Audit Division of the OLA. "They reported them after the election results were certified." In the July 2022 primary election, the audit found, the elections board identified four individuals who successfully voted multiple times and 263 voters who attempted to vote multiple times, referring the information to the state prosecutors office in a "timely" manner.Election integrity has become a high-profile issue with former President Donald Trump and his supporters repeatedly challenging the outcome of the 2020 presidential election.The audit also noted that the elections board could enhance its procedures to fully identify deceased or duplicate voters. The audit identified 2,426 "potentially deceased individuals" whose voter registrations were active and 327 individuals with potential duplicate voter registrations."We're just pointing out areas where they can improve," said Streett. "The information they're getting from the Maryland Department of Health was not fully complete and accurate, so they were missing out on a certain pocket of deceased individuals." The Health Department could not be reached for comment on Friday.The audit also found deficiencies with the state elections board's security and control over its information systems, but did not go into detail for security reasons. The department's response to those concerns also was redacted from the report.The elections board did agree to implement the recommendations, but disagreed with several findings.The State Board of Elections could not be reached for comment on Friday.The current Elections Administrator Jared DeMarinis took the helm in June 2023 after longtime administrator Linda Lamone retired.

title: MDOT talks investments in Talbot County
author: Natalie Jones; njones@chespub.com
content:
MDOT talks investments in Talbot County

 November 9, 2023 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: Natalie Jones; njones@chespub.com | Page: 5 | Section: News 
 
 784
 Words 

 Read News Document

 EASTON - State, county and local officials packed the meeting room at the Talbot County Free Library Tuesday afternoon to hear the latest updates on the Maryland Department of Transportation's investments in county projects.The visit to Talbot County capped off another leg of the department's statewide tour discussing its sixyear Draft FY 2024-2029 Consolidated Transportation Program - a $21.2 billion investment into creating a safer, more accessible transportation system.The meeting, hosted by the Talbot County Council, featured Maryland Transportation Secretary Paul J. Wiedefeld and representatives from various state agencies.State Highway Administrator William Pines spoke about his agency's efforts to improve infrastructure and safety at several high-traffic locations within Talbot County.The agency initiated a $1.5 million study of Route 328 to assess safety and capacity improvements along a 1.6-mile stretch between U.S. Route 50 and Black Dog Alley. Delays are seen in this area from turning vehicles and queueing at signalized intersections, and there are limited pedestrian and bicycle facilities, Pines said.A public meeting on the Route 328 project is tentatively scheduled for this winter.Other transportation improvements within Easton include a $600,000 project for new lighting at the intersection of Route 50 and Route 322 (Easton Bypass) to improve visibility and safety, signal improvements and pedestrian upgrades - including a Rails to Trails link - at Route 322 and Glenwood Avenue, and a new signal at Route 50 and Chapel Road that will be activated by the end of November.In 2024, SHA will begin construction on two additional projects: reconstructing the signal at Route 50 and Route 309 and upgrading the flashing signal at Route 331 and Black Dog Alley to a full signal.Two local trail projects are also receiving federal and state grant funding, Pines said.$48,000 will go toward the final design of a 1.25-mile extension of the St. Michaels Nature and Bike Trail, and $30,000 will go toward the study and preliminary design of a rail trail connecting parks in Oxford.Turning to public transit, nearly $1.1 million in operating and capital grants are being allocated to support Delmarva Community Transit.$225,000 of this will fund preventative maintenance and two new small buses, said Travis Johnston, the Maryland Transit Administration's local transit support director.Delmarva Community Services will also receive $123,000 to install a propane filling station for future propane-powered vehicles, enabling DCS to transition to a low-emission fleet.Additionally, $24,000 in highway safety grants were awarded to the Talbot County Sheriff's Office and the Easton Police Department.Turning to the skies, the Easton Airport's runway improvement program is receiving $525,000 from the Maryland Aviation Administration to support the initial phase of construction.THINKING DOWN THE ROADLocal officials also weighed in on a number of priorities and problem areas they hope the transportation agency will address in the future.Discussions on traffic surrounding the proposed new regional medical center site off of Route 50 were top priorities for state legislators, the county and the Town of Easton. Rick Van Emburgh, Easton's town engineer, said he wanted to work with the county and the state on a regional traffic plan to handle the impact on local roads and infrastructure.Cheryl Lewis, Oxford's town manager, raised questions on the agency's response to flooding on the causeway and pedestrian safety in a town with few sidewalks.Queen Anne Mayor Philip Starkey asked if the agency would reevaluate fixing the bridge between the towns of Queen Anne and Hillsboro, which floods every time it rains, he said.Accessibility was raised as an issue in St. Michaels. According to Town Administrator Rob Straebel, all but one of the town's ADA ramps are not in compliance due to poor work from a contractor."I'm not sure what the way forward is, and I'm not here to point fingers or to blame anyone or to place culpability on anyone," he said. "But there really needs to be a sense of urgency to get this project rectified as soon as possible before our tourist season starts in the summer of 2024." Pines said the state was working to develop an "aggressive schedule" to get the project over the finish line.Sen. Johnny Mautz (R-37) further emphasized the need to fix the ramps, noting that Route 33, as the main road running through St. Michaels, doesn't just serve town residents, but residents of Claiborne, McDaniel, Sherwood and Tilghman.Several Royal Oak residents in attendance also raised concerns about the width and safety of Route 329 (Royal Oak Road), asking the transportation officials to lower the speed limit."I wish I could do everything that everyone asked immediately, but we will keep chipping away," Wiedefeld said, closing out the meeting.

State transportation officials take turns sharing updates from their respective agencies on Talbot County projects during a meeting Tuesday, Nov. 7.

title: St. Michaels talks tax rates at commissioners meeting
author: Maggie Trovato; mtrovato@chespub.com
content:
St. Michaels talks tax rates at commissioners meeting

 November 10, 2023 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: Maggie Trovato; mtrovato@chespub.com | Page: 3 | Section: News 
 
 848
 Words 

 Read News Document

 ST. MICHAELS - At a meeting Wednesday, the Commissioners of St. Michaels spoke about gathering stakeholders to discuss the town's tax rates.The discussion followed an issues brief sent to the commissioners from the St. Michaels Historic District Residents Association.The issues brief argues that St. Michaels, "a small tourist town with a tourism economy," is largely supported by its residents, rather than its businesses."The infrastructure needed to support Talbot County's and the town's tourism economy imposes a heavy tax load on St. Michaels homeowners, while those who benefit most are taxed the least, or not at all in the case of the Chesapeake Bay Maritime Museum," the issues brief states.At the meeting, Commission President David Breimhurst said he was glad that the Historic District Residents Association is offering to be part of the solution. He suggested getting all stakeholders from every aspect of the community together to talk and see what they can come up with."I don't think it needs to be 'us against them' or adversarial in any way," he said. "Just to have a calm, adult discussion about where we stand." Dan Spiegel spoke on behalf of the St. Michaels Historic District Residents Association at the meeting Wednesday.He summarized some of the points made in the issues brief and named the four steps the group hopes the commissioners will take:▪ Begin a period of study and assessment of the tax options other towns use to raise revenue from business activities.▪ Engage with the Maritime Museum to urge they make a payment in lieu of taxes to the town.▪ Hold public hearings to discuss any plans that may develop.▪ Look at current residential property rates to determine whether they are "fair and appropriate," in the case that the town raises additional revenue from businesses.Spiegel said that most of the money the town uses to fund services and maintain its infrastructure comes from property taxes.He said that, based on data gathered from the state, there are 81 business structures that pay property taxes in town, compared to 796 homes and non-business structures."In other words, only 9% of the property taxes are paid by businesses," he said.Spiegel said that although Chesapeake Bay Maritime Museum is the "crown jewel" of the town's tourist economy, it is tax exempt and does not make any voluntary payments directly to the town. These types of payments are known as payments in lieu of taxes, or PILOTs."Many universities and colleges pay PILOTs to towns because of their use of the infrastructure and other things that impact the town," he said. "The museum makes no PILOT payments." Spiegel also said money generated by businesses does not stay in the town. He said that 97% of the town's commercial buildings are owned by non-residents and more than 90% of the business operators who rent the buildings are also non-residents."So non-resident landlords, business operators and employees spend their money elsewhere because there are very few normal types of businesses that they can spend money on that would attract their dollars," he said.After Spiegel spoke, Commissioner Tad DuPont said this conversation has already begun."You're stimulating a conversation, but it has started," he said.DuPont said that with the changing tourist economy, St.Michaels needs to change with it and be ahead of it.Commission Treasurer Al Mercier said he could envision multiple areas where the town could generate more revenue, including a tourism tax, an alcohol tax, an accommodations tax and parking meters."These are nine or 10 things that I think we need to put on the agenda going forward," he said.During public comment, Kristen Greenaway, president and CEO of the Chesapeake Bay Maritime Museum, talked about what the museum pays the town, including an annual event fees tax, and what services it offers residents.She said the museum offers free after school and summer programming for local and Talbot County youth, free museum membership for St. Michaels' youth and free entry for locals with passes that can be obtained at the library.Greenaway said the taxes on The Crab Claw restaurant property, which the museum is purchasing, will still be paid, as it will remain zoned as maritime commercial.Spiegel said the Historic District Residents Association is not anti-museum or anti-business."This is an informal group of residents that were organized, that live in the historic district, that are concerned about the future of St. Michaels," he said.John Marrah, a property owner in St. Michaels, said he enjoyed the Historic District Residents Association presentation."It's important that people think they're treated fairly from a taxation standpoint," he said.Marrah added that business and property owners are taxed "with no representation" in St.Michaels. He said that might be something the town should look into."I own properties in town, but since I don't live in town, I can't vote," he said. "I pay property taxes like everybody else."

title: Talbot County is green with gratitude
author: Staff Report
content:
Talbot County is green with gratitude

 November 10, 2023 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: Staff Report | Page: 5 | Section: News 
 
 510
 Words 

 Read News Document

 Operation Green Light for Veterans, hosted nationwide by the National Association for Counties and the National Association of County Veterans Service Officers, invites counties and other government entities to show support for veterans by lighting buildings green each November.While the official time for green lights is Nov. 6 to 12, this year, residents and visitors alike may have noticed that local government buildings have been lit up green for the last few weeks.Talbot County and the Town of Easton chose to start their campaign early, according to officials."Talbot County is home to many veterans, and we appreciate everything that they have done to keep our country safe here and abroad," said Talbot County Council President Chuck Callahan."Operation Green Light allows our community to show its support to veterans in many ways not just lighting up buildings in green, but also sharing resources for veterans, promoting the work of veterans in our community and sharing stories across the Mid-Shore." The county encouraged employee veterans to share their experiences from time in military service as part of the campaign."It's been a humbling experience to be able to read about (our veterans') greatest triumphs as well as challenging moments from their time in service," said Sarah Kilmon, communications manager for the county.The stories will be shared on the Talbot County Government's Facebook page."We are grateful for individuals who chose to serve then and continue to serve now as county employees," said County Manager Clay Stamp. "Veterans have unique skillsets and values, especially in leadership, that makes them important members of our team. They bring different perspectives, and that is invaluable to our efforts to serve our community." At their Oct. 24 Council Meeting, the County thanked Mid-Shore Behavioral Health and local veterans groups for their efforts to help our veterans and officially proclaimed Nov. 6 to 12 as Operation Green Light week. MSBH and Maryland's Commitment to Veterans also highlighted several local resources for Veterans and their families.MSBH connects individuals to mental health services and assists with referrals to behavioral health options for Caroline, Dorchester, Kent, Queen Anne's and Talbot County. They are ready to assist veterans with specific mental health needs and can be reached at 410-770-4801 or info@midshorebehavioralhealth.org.Maryland's Commitment to Veterans connects service members to needs and resources in their area. Veterans can reach out to their hotline to request assistance on services like housing, healthcare and employment at 1-877-770-4801.This week, the groups have been highlighting resources and promoting stories of veterans across the entire Mid-Shore region online, and they encourage businesses and individuals to share the information with the local community.Talbot County businesses, residents and organizations are encouraged by local officials to light their buildings green and share their own resources and stories for veterans on social media using the hashtag #OperationGreenLight.

title: St. Michaels commissioners take action at Wednesday meeting
author: Maggie Trovato; mtrovato@chespub.com
content:
St. Michaels commissioners take action at Wednesday meeting

 November 10, 2023 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: Maggie Trovato; mtrovato@chespub.com | Page: 4 | Section: News 
 
 237
 Words 

 Read News Document

 ST. MICHAELS - The Commissioners of St. Michaels took action on three new items at its meeting on Wednesday.▪ The Commissioners voted unanimously to enter into an agreement between Mid Shore Mediation and the St. Michaels Police Department. SMPD Chief Jeffrey Oswald said the Maryland Police and Correctional Training Commissions recommend the adoption of a police mediation program.▪ The Commissioners agreed to put out a request for proposal for interior and exterior painting of the Environmental Concern building on Boundary Lane. Town Administrator Rob Straebel said proposals are due Nov. 28. He said the RFP will be advertised in the local newspaper and on the town's website.▪ The Commissioners voted unanimously to amend an ordinance to increase the number of Parks and Recreation Advisory Board members from five to seven. Marise Galgano, who is on the board, said they could use "some more hands to get dirty." She said that the board has been working well with Public Works and thinks having more minds would be helpful.▪ The Commissioners did not vote on whether to approve design fees for jail and bathroom improvements at the Police Department. Timothy Crosby of Crosby and Associates shared his design proposal with the commissioners.Commissioner Tad DuPont raised his concerns with the cost of the design, saying that it seemed too high a price. He said he would like to get other estimates on the project before moving forward.

title: Cambridge Harbor closed meeting draws objections - Meeting includes Dorchester County Council and Cambridge City Council
author: Maggie Trovato; mtrovato@chespub.com
content:
Cambridge Harbor closed meeting draws objections - Meeting includes Dorchester County Council and Cambridge City Council

 November 15, 2023 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: Maggie Trovato; mtrovato@chespub.com | Page: 2 | Section: News 
 
 1176
 Words 

 Read News Document

 CAMBRIDGE - Cambridge Waterfront Development Inc. held a closed meeting with stakeholders - including city officials, county officials and development consultants-at the Packing House on Monday.In an interview in late October, CWDI Executive Director Matt Leonard said the purpose of the meeting was "to review in detail, some of the more confidential matters we have going on with the development." The meeting comes about three weeks after a letter, signed by Cambridge City Manager Tom Carroll, expressed City Council's concerns with CWDI's Cambridge Harbor project. The letter said that the Cambridge council does not support CWDI's current plans for the project and that the meeting on Monday was "premature." Before the meeting went into closed session, Dorchester County Council President Lenny Pfeffer said the County Council would be sitting in on the meeting for information purposes only and they would not deliberate.All members of the council were present at the meeting, as well as interim County Manager Jeff Powell.Cambridge City Council voted against going into closed session.Both Commissioner Laurel Atkiss and Commissioner Jameson Harrington voted against going into closed session.Commissioner Brian Roche voted in favor of it.Cambridge Mayor Stephen Rideout, who attended the meeting virtually for the first few minutes, said that one of the three commissioners in attendance would need to leave the meeting so that the council is not in violation of the Maryland Open Meetings Act. Harrington volunteered to leave the meeting.In addition to Atkiss and Roche, Carroll and Cambridge Assistant City Manager Brandon Hesson stayed for the meeting.In an interview, Pfeffer said that according to their county attorney's interpretation of the Maryland Open Meetings Act, there was no concern about violating the act because council members only attended for informational purposes and the meeting outside their "own council." Jim Brady, a reporter with WHCP in Cambridge, objected to the meeting being closed to the public. Jim Johnson, executive editor of the Star Democrat, also objected."This clearly does not fall under any of the exceptions of the closed meeting law and as such, we will be filing a complaint against this meeting," Johnson said.To justify the meeting being closed to the public, CWDI listed two exceptions from the Maryland Open Meetings Act: "to consider a matter that concerns the proposal for a business to locate, expand, or remain" and "to discuss a matter where public discussion would adversely impact the public body's proposal process." In a complaint sent to the state's Open Meetings Compliance Board, the Star Democrat and WHCP alleged nine potential violations of the Open Meetings Act, including that the agenda topics were not consistent with the exceptions CWDI used to justify the closed meeting.In a Nov. 9, Cambridge City Council administrative report, Carroll wrote that it was unclear to him how the meeting complied with Maryland's Open Meeting laws.In response to whether the meeting on Monday stayed on topic, Carroll said, "I didn't accept the topic," as Cambridge City Council didn't go into closed session.Pfeffer said that, to the best of his knowledge, the meeting stayed on topic. He said the County Council did not know exactly what the meeting would be about going into it.Pfeffer said the County Council attended the meeting with the purpose of obtaining all the available information about the project."It's a very dynamic project that has changed multiple times over many years, well before I even was an elected official," he said.Having more information on the project, Pfeffer said, gives the county a better idea of where the project is heading."We want to make sure that if (we're) ever ask to make any decisions regarding (the project), we are well-informed to make those decisions," he said.In an interview, Leonard said he thought the meeting went well. He said that during the meeting, CWDI discussed business deals they are working on."We're working through the strategy in our proposal process to get the next level of development," he said. "And so anything we discussed outside in public would adversely affect that. So we dealt with those aspects of where we're headed on the project." The Cambridge Harbor project will include creating public spaces like a promenade and parks, a boutique hotel that has a restaurant and bar, and residential and mixed-use spaces along the Choptank River. In an interview in September, Leonard said the goal is for the entire project to be complete in somewhere between five and 10 years from now.Leonard said CWDI's proposed tax increment finance district was discussed during the Nov. 13 meeting.In the the City of Cambridge's letter to CWDI, Carroll said this was one of the reasons City Council was concerned about the project. The letter said that the proposed TIF would take too much tax revenue from too large of an area for too long of a time, and the city and county would not receive a "meaningful" tax revenue benefit for decades.In an interview, Harrington said the proposed TIF is one of his biggest concerns with the project."It does not look viable," he said. "In the way it is structured, it seems like it would negatively impact the city as a whole." Harrington said the total new investment would be $113 million in one TIF district and $49 million in a second TIF district.Leonard said that the proposed TIF was discussed in the closed meeting, rather than publicly, because "it could negatively affect the strategy of our proposal for our future developers." He said that the TIF plans will be made a part of the public discussion when it won't "adversely affect our ability to get the best proposals." He expects CWDI to be able to bring all of this information to the public in the first quarter of 2024.Exactly how the TIF plan could adversely affect CWDI's ability to get the best proposals was discussed during the meeting, Leonard said.According to Cambridge City Council documents, the city had engaged outside counsel and received proposals from firms for an independent TIF analysis of the CWDI TIF.Along with the proposed TIF, Harrington said a lack of transparency is one of the biggest concerns with the Cambridge Harbor project."The Cambridge Waterfront Development project is probably one of the biggest deals that's impacted Cambridge," he said."So I think it's important that the public's informed on what's going on. I think Dorchester County and Cambridge itself have a history of a lot of behind the doors deals and that's not the way it should be done." Harrington said he thinks everyone wants a project that redevelops the waterfront and benefits the city and county."As it sits currently," he said, "it doesn't seem like it would do that."

title: County to consider vehicle weight limits on Black Dog Alley
author: Natalie Jones; njones@chespub.com
content:
County to consider vehicle weight limits on Black Dog Alley

 November 16, 2023 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: Natalie Jones; njones@chespub.com | Page: 4 | Section: News 
 
 260
 Words 

 Read News Document

 EASTON - The Talbot County Council on Tuesday introduced a resolution that would establish a vehicle weight limit on Black Dog Alley to reroute some of the road's through traffic.According to Mike Mertaugh, the assistant county engineer, Black Dog Alley has essentially become a bypass around Easton for traffic going to and from southern Caroline County and Dorchester County.That traffic volume, along with heavy trucks, are causing maintenance issues along the roadway, Mertaugh said. Restricting heavy trucks from traveling on the road would extend its lifespan and improve safety on the road.Some parts of the road are narrow, and the southern part of Black Dog Alley does not have a shoulder lane.While the county roads department has worked to keep it maintained, heavy vehicles on the edge of pavement without support can cause the road to "crumble away," Mertaugh said.The restriction wouldn't burden trucks, he said - U.S. Route 50 almost runs parallel to Black Dog Alley, and the highway is designed for that type of traffic.The legislation, if passed, wouldn't impede local traffic or farmers, and exceptions would be made for agricultural businesses and government vehicles.The county already has a similar weight restriction in place on Dover Neck Road, which experienced similar issues.The council unanimously introduced the legislation, known as Resolution 351. A public hearing will be held on Tuesday, Dec. 12, at 6:30 p.m.

title: Changes coming to Oxford finance committee draft resolution
author: Maggie Trovato; mtrovato@chespub.com
content:
Changes coming to Oxford finance committee draft resolution

 November 16, 2023 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: Maggie Trovato; mtrovato@chespub.com | Page: 2 | Section: News 
 
 697
 Words 

 Read News Document

 OXFORD - Before the Commissioners of Oxford decide whether they will create a Financial Advisory Committee, an Investment Advisory Committee or neither, at least one of the drafted resolutions will be receiving some changes.At the town meeting on Tuesday, Commissioner Katrina Greer said that she would like to make changes to the drafted resolution for a Financial Advisory Committee, which she introduced and first discussed in depth at a workshop Oct. 19.Greer's proposed Financial Advisory Committee would be tasked with providing recommendations to the commissioners on issues related to town finances and other financial topics. Specifically, the committee would give advice on short-term and long-term interest rates and types of investments.Commission President Tom Costigan's proposed Investment Advisory Committee would be tasked with reviewing the towns investments quarterly, providing recommendations to the commissioners on investment opportunities, responding to other commissioner requests, and annually reviewing and providing recommendations on the town's investment policy.The committee would receive a packet of documents, which are listed in the proposed resolution, by the town manager. In Greer's proposal, committee members would be able to request information related to town finances that is accessible via the Maryland Public Information Act.Greer's draft resolution will be reposted to the town website once changes have been made so that residents can share any thoughts they have on the proposals before commissioners are expected to vote on them at the Dec. 12 meeting.The first change Greer said she wants to make is to change the membership requirements "to be as inclusive as possible." She said she would like to make it so that voters, residents and property owners can be on the committee.At the Oct. 19 workshop, Costigan said that Greer's original proposed requirement that members must own real property in town was elitist and offensive to renters.In Costigan's proposal, committee members must be registered to vote in Oxford.Greer said she wanted to change another part of the language regarding qualifications."Tom's proposal asks for experience and training in investment policies and implementation," she said."My proposal is much more specific." Greer said she thought they could meet in the middle so that both proposals say: "The members shall have demonstrable, professional experience in finance, such as a financial certification or advanced degree in finance, economics or accounting." Greer also asked that they meet in the middle on the size of the committee.Greer's proposed committee is made up of five members, while Costigan's is made up of three members.Costigan did not say whether he would be amending any of the language in his proposed resolution, but told Town Manager Cheryl Lewis that if he decides to, he will do it as soon as possible.Both Costigan and Greer's drafts were posted online following the Oct. 24 meeting so that residents could compare them and voice their thoughts, either in writing or during the meeting Tuesday.At the meeting, Greer said that the commissioners received a lot of letters."Close to 100," she said. "And that didn't even include duplicate letters." Greer said that 66 of the letters were in support of her proposed committee, four were in support of Costigan's proposed committee and 28 were in support of having no committee at all. Of those 28 letters in support of no committee, Greer said that 15 of them stated that they preferred Costigan's resolution.Commissioner Susan Delean-Botkin reminded residents that neither of the committees need to be created. She said that, according to the town's investment policy, there are only five types of investments the town can make and there is a one year limit on the maximum term of maturity."Restrictions appropriately limit the investment opportunities," she said. "So there is a third option that we do not need other committees for investments or for financial oversight."

title: Cambridge hears presentations about youth services, day shelter
author: Maggie Trovato; mtrovato@chespub.com
content:
Cambridge hears presentations about youth services, day shelter

 November 16, 2023 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: Maggie Trovato; mtrovato@chespub.com | Page: 5 | Section: News 
 
 602
 Words 

 Read News Document

 CAMBRIDGE - Commissioners heard two presentations at a Cambridge City Council meeting on Monday evening.The first was from a Baltimore-based nonprofit, Lead4Life, about a possible partnership with the city. The second was about the need for a day shelter in Cambridge.Jennifer Gauthier, founder and executive director of Lead4Life, spoke about the services which the nonprofit offers and inquired about partnering with the city."Allow us to hire people who can go into the community," Gauthier said. "Allow us to have that peer-to-peer model to be able to spend some of the resources that we have on these two initiatives in your community." Founded in 2008, Lead-4Life aims to lower the number of youth entering the juvenile justice system.According to its website, the nonprofit offers 10 different programs, including alternative placement programming, mentoring and individual and family therapy.At the Council meeting, Gauthier talked about two pilot programs, a gun diversion program and a returning citizens program, which it wants to offer in Cambridge.Gauthier said Lead4Life has the funding to provide these services in Cambridge and "all the way down to the Lower Shore." "We just want to hear any concerns that you have or any opportunity for us that you want to be able to partner (with us)," she said."We're not asking you for money." After Gauthier spoke, Commissioner Sputty Cephas said that he thinks it would be great to partner with Lead4Life and try to expand the program in Cambridge."From everything that I've heard so far, we need you here," he said. "Any way that we can continue to funnel this information and get the word out there about all that you guys are doing, I would love to." Valerie Nwakudo Davis, with Delmarva Community Services, spoke to the Council next about the need for a day shelter in Cambridge."This presentation is not for any agency," she said."It really is on behalf of our homeless population in this city, in this county." Davis said that there is a growing population of homeless people and talked about the importance of having a shelter for people to go to, particularly the aging homeless population."We cannot afford, as a community, to have people sitting on benches when it's 22 degrees outside, or when it's 92 degrees outside," she said.Davis said that although The Salvation Army provides shelter at night, those people in need of service don't have somewhere to go in the day. She said this problem is most apparent on the weekends."Sunday is the most miserable time of the week when you're homeless," she said, adding that places like the library and One Mission Cambridge are closed then.Delmarva Community Services hosted a meeting last week, Davis said. The Overflow Cafe, One Mission Cambridge and The Salvation Army were at the meeting."We talked about what was here already and what we need," she said.To get a day shelter in Cambridge, Davis said support from the local government is needed. She also said support from churches is needed."Because that could be an awesome volunteer segment of this," she said.After Davis spoke, Mayor Stephen Rideout said he had spoken with Davis about this a few weeks ago."I thought it was very important," he said. "It was something that we have not really paid attention to enough. So we're having an ongoing series of meetings with the churches and citizens and agencies to see what we might be able to do here to address this particular issue."

title: County considers changing alcoholic beverage code - If changed, would allow for liquor store to be built in Trappe
author: Natalie Jones; njones@chespub.com
content:
County considers changing alcoholic beverage code - If changed, would allow for liquor store to be built in Trappe

 November 16, 2023 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: Natalie Jones; njones@chespub.com | Page: 2 | Section: News 
 
 343
 Words 

 Read News Document

 EASTON - The Talbot County Council is considering a change to the county's alcoholic beverage code to allow for the development of a liquor store in Trappe.The legislation, introduced by all council members on Tuesday, was spurred by a proposition from residents who hope to open a liquor store within the town.Under the county's current code, there are restrictions on the issuance of off-sale licenses, or a license that allows the sale of alcohol for off-premises consumption, said Patrick Thomas, the county attorney.Every municipality in Talbot County, except for Trappe, has an off-sale license holder.Opening a liquor store would require a Class E license. As of now, new Class E establishments are prohibited from being issued a license or opening within the town due to it not meeting the population requirement of 750 residents.Curtis Snyder, representing the Delmarva Real Estate Management Group, said his company is working to bring more businesses to the town. One thing Trappe residents have asked about, he said, is a beer, wine and liquor store."Just to get a bottle of wine or beeror a bottle of liquor for dinner, the residents have to drive 20 minutes either way to find a beer, wine and liquor store," he said.The town is less than 100 residents away from reaching the minimum population set out in the Class E license requirement, and that doesn't include the recent growth Trappe has started to experience, Snyder said. But still, under current laws, the town can't open a liquor store until the population figures are updated in the 2030 census.Tom Mitchell, Snyder's father-in-law, said they've worked to develop other areas in the town as well, including Momma Maria's and The Coffee Trappe."We're really trying to bring people back to Trappe," he said. "It's such a wonderful town with a tremendous historic record.This would be part of our plan to continue to improve the community." The legislation, known as Bill 1550, is set for a public hearing on Tuesday, Dec. 12, at 6:30 p.m.

title: Easton considering changes to zoning, subdivisions
author: Natalie Jones; njones@chespub.com
content:
Easton considering changes to zoning, subdivisions

 November 17, 2023 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: Natalie Jones; njones@chespub.com | Page: 3 | Section: News 
 
 760
 Words 

 Read News Document

 EASTON - The Easton Town Council is considering amendments and updates to two chapters of the town code concerning zoning and subdivisions.The two ordinances, which separately amend several aspects of the town's zoning code and update its existing subdivision code, were up for public hearings at the council's Monday, Nov. 6, meeting, where a number of town residents opposed some changes.Ordinance 803, which concerns changes to zoning code, drew a number of questions and prompted the council to continue its public hearing to the first meeting in January.The public hearing on Ordinance 804, which would update the town's subdivision code, will be continued at the council's Monday, Nov. 20, meeting.ORDINANCE 803: ZONINGThe town approved and adopted a comprehensive revision of its zoning code in December 2021, but after evaluation and monitoring of the code, the planning commission determined that certain amendments were appropriate to better guide and regulate development activities, according to the text of the ordinance.In response to the evaluation, the planning commission proposed 12 amendments to the zoning code, which were recommended for adoption in March. If passed, Ordinance 803 would enact the amendments.At the Nov. 6 meeting, Town Planner Lynn Thomas characterized a majority of the amendments as "housekeeping." But she noted two more important aspects: changing the ways in which middle housing types are created and changing five of those subtypes from a special exception use to a permitted use in three Easton districts: R-7A, R-10A and central business.Lynn Mielke, a Talbot County Council member who spoke at the meeting only as a resident of the Easton Club neighborhood, raised concerns about the "inadequate" amount of time residents had to read through the 250-page agenda packet and research before attending the meeting to make a comment.Mielke also objected to a revision of the language detailing how quickly planned unit developments must begin construction after final approval and language extending the expiration dates of those projects.The proposed revision extends the length of time owners or developers have to begin construction on a project from two years to three years after final approval. If no action is taken within three years, the site's zoning will revert to its previous classification.Mielke pointed to the proposed Maryland Health Club project within the Easton Club neighborhood as an example, asserting that residents have been "living in limbo and uncertainty" about the development's status.Easton Club resident Pamela Reynolds voiced concern with several housing types currently classified as special exception uses being permitted by right in the R-10A district - a residential area."I find most of them charming names, but they can have a considerable impact on the density (of the) development," she said.Reynolds also questioned if the recently approved and scaled-back neighboring Poplar Hill development could increase its density under the amendment and if the Maryland Health Club's PUD application would be impacted.Speaking on behalf of the East-End Neighborhood Association, president Joseph Minarick expressed worries about trash removal the number of additional cars on the streets if middle housing structures were added in the neighborhood, The association recommended and requested that no change be made to the special exception requirements for all middle housing structures in the three districts in question.Kelly Pezor, who serves on the town's historic district commission, said she and other commissioners were concerned about preserving the area's historic nature and keeping new developments within guidelines.In an Oct. 30 letter to the town council and mayor, the planning commission expressed support for limiting special exceptions to address the town's need for more affordable and diverse housing types. Commissioners also supported revising the expiration of PUD approvals to three years.Council members also raised concerns and questions about the complexity of the proposed amendments.The public record will remain open until the council's first meeting in January.ORDINANCE 804: SUBDIVISIONSSpeaking on revisions to subdivisions within the town code, Thomas said there were not a "tremendous" number of proposed changes.To Thomas, the most significant changes include the elimination of a street hierarchy system, which was dictated by average daily trips; adding new nonresidential street types and standards for commercial and industrial roads; revised standards for residential street types, including street widths; and requiring that at least 50% of park space in a subdivision must be provided in the form of one centrally located neighborhood park.No public comments were shared at the Nov. 6 meeting, though council members voiced positive feedback for the revisions.The two ordinances and details of the proposed changes to the town code can be found on the Town of Easton's website under pending zoning legislation.

title: Commissioners prioritize roads, bridges projects
author: Connie Connolly; cconnolly@chespub.com
content:
Commissioners prioritize roads, bridges projects

 November 22, 2023 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: Connie Connolly; cconnolly@chespub.com | Page: 3A | Section: News 
 
 666
 Words 

 Read News Document

 DENTON - A list of projects to repair and maintain the county's dirt roads and to open closed bridges was presented to the Caroline County Commissioners Oct. 24 by then-Caroline County Director of Public Works Ryan White and Roads Superintendent Bryan North.As of Nov. 8, White was no longer the director, but no further information was available as of press time.The number of houses on the roads determined the priority of attention to them.Applying that standard, Commission President Travis Breeding set aside Alms House, County Farm and Dead End roads east of Denton as low priority.Concerns about the amount of traffic and the distance road crews must travel to maintain the roads were also considered, along with the amount of truck traffic and school bus routes."A truck on a muddy road, it just kills it," White said. "So that's also something we took into account when we figured this out.Breeding and Commissioner Frank Bartz agreed that Mitchell and Wolf roads were priorities because of the number of houses. White said he considered property density rather than the number of houses.Participating remotely, Commission Vice President Larry Porter suggested beginning work on Wolf Road east of Henderson and reaching out to residents for feedback on Mitchell Road south of Denton, who had expressed concerns in the past about increased traffic if the road were tar-and-chipped.Tar-and-chip paving increases the speed on those roads about 10 to 15 miles per hour.Beck Road connecting State Routes 404 and 313 (Federalsburg Highway), Trunkline Road north of Henderson and Jones Corner Road between Concord and American Corner were also considered.Dirt roads are inspected about once a month and scraped as needed, White said.The commissioners determined that Beck and Wolf roads were priorities, which are in line for gravel, then tar-andchip paving, with Mitchell on the list after calls to residents.White said he's reached out to the Maryland State Roads Administration about funding the culvert pipe replacement on River Road.In the meantime, White has "given (SHA) the green light to go ahead and try to get us at least an 80-20 (state and county funding) split on Bloomery Road" north of Federalsburg Road, he said. "That does not sound like it's going to be an issue at all." Issues concerning the approach to the bridge on Long Swamp Road generated some discussion about the extent of the county's ownership of certain rights of way, something County Attorney Stewart Barroll suggested discussing in a closed session."If we can get 100% funding, are we interested in having a discussion about reopening some of the older bridges that have been closed?" Breeding asked. Bartz and Porter agreed.Regarding reopening bridges, property owners will be contacted for their opinions.The attention turned to River Road west of Denton. "I don't think anybody misses that bridge being closed from a traffic standpoint," Porter said."No, but where I'm coming from is the proximity to the high school, the waterfront and the potential for economic growth out there," Breeding said. "It's close to our growth area in the county, it is waterfront property with higher potential property values and it's right in the center of the county as well. If we have a discussion about opening one, i think that one makes sense to talk about.Other closed bridges are on Poplar Neck Road west of Preston, Bloomery Road and Back Landing Road which runs from Preston into Dorchester County. White said he was waiting to hear back from SHA about available funding for reopening the bridge on Gregg Road.According to the county's website, the roads division "is responsible for maintaining over 450 miles of roadway and 39 bridges or crossings in Caroline County." Over 70 miles of those roads are dirt roads.

title: 'We just want to feed 'em' - St. Michaels Community Center gives out turkeys for the holidays
author: Maggie Trovato; mtrovato@chespub.com
content:
'We just want to feed 'em' - St. Michaels Community Center gives out turkeys for the holidays

 November 22, 2023 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: Maggie Trovato; mtrovato@chespub.com | Page: 1 | Section: News 
 
 590
 Words 

 Read News Document

 ST. MICHAELS - A small line formed outside of the St. Michaels Community Center's temporary location on Talbot Street in the late afternoon on Monday.While some people waited to pick up their usual grocery items from the food pantry, others came for a hefty frozen turkey, pie, a sack of potatoes and a large bag of canned and dry items - all the fixings for a delicious and plentiful Thanksgiving dinner.Food Bank Director Amy DeWitt said that the SMCC has been handing out these "Thanksgiving boxes" to people who might not be able to afford a full Thanksgiving dinner for at least six years."(With) the cost of food nowadays, I think a lot of people just can't afford to go out and buy a turkey," DeWitt said. "And I think it's very important for them to have a meal they can prepare at home for their family." From 4 p.m. to 6 p.m. on Monday, DeWitt and her small team handed out all the turkey day classics for residents to cook on Thursday."The boxes are like an addition to what they already have at home," Mark Singleton, DeWitt's assistant, said."So just to push things along, maybe even press the meal for another day or two." In addition to the Thanksgiving boxes, the SMCC is hosting an eat-in community dinner on Wednesday from 11 a.m. to 2 p.m. Walk-ins are welcome. Those in attendance will be served turkey and gravy from Ava's Pizzeria and Wine Bar as well as cornbread stuffing, garlic mashed red skin potatoes, green bean casserole, dinner rolls and homemade apple and pumpkin pies.DeWitt estimated that they will serve between 150 and 175 prepared meals on Wednesday. She said she had around 75 people taking home Thanksgiving boxes this year.One of those people, Theo Bees, is making Thanksgiving dinner for his mom and himself this year."I love to cook," he said.Bees, who was working as a caretaker but is now taking care of his 92-year-old mother, said he plans to cook the entire meal.Bees said he would love it if everybody could celebrate Thanksgiving with their family."People need to be with family," he said, "every holiday." Kerri Clear, executive chef at the SMCC, who is making most of the dishes for Wednesday's community dinner, said the community is very supportive of what the community center does to help residents."We get a lot of donations," Clear said, "a lot of interest from the community." DeWitt said that all of her clients are "very thankful" for the special holiday meals that the SMCC hands out.Singleton said each person appreciates what they do."They show us every time they come in," he said."They're really thankful." And Dewitt, Clear and Singleton are just happy to help out in the community."We just want to feed 'em," DeWitt Said.

 EASTON - The Easton Planning Commission on Thursday, Nov. 16, approved a sketch site plan to redevelop a defunct property on South Washington Street into a live-work building.The project proposes a three-story, 3,800-squarefoot building with commercial space on the first floor and six rental units on the top two levels.Each residential floor will contain three units - two two-bedroom apartments and one one-bedroom apartment.Fifteen parking spaces will be provided on site.The roughly half-acre property, located at 123 South Washington Street, is owned by Henry Capital Easton LLC and is within the town's Central Business Commercial zoning district.In September, the Easton Historical District Commission approved demolition of the defunct, non-contributing structure already on the site and issued a certificate of appropriateness for the new building's proposed architecture.The proposed building is also a reduction of structure coverage on the property and is well under the maximum lot coverage, said Brendan Mullaney, an attorney representing Henry Capital Easton LLC."We believe this is a terrific redevelopment (and) addition to the town on South Washington Street," he said.In discussing the proposal, planning commission members asked about trash and recycling, price points and architectural and landscaping changes.Each residential unit is proposed as a rental, but the property's owner could turn the units into condominiums.Rental prices will be market rate, Mullaney said.Suggestions were also made as to revising the plan to include additional windows in the residential units to bring more light in and increase marketability, along with better defining the structure's base with a different color."I applaud you on this project. This is exactly the kind of project we've been talking about. It really fits in the central business district," said planning commission member Paul Weber.Weber recommended landscaping for the small portion of the property fronting to West Street - a condition that was included as part of the commission's motion to approve the sketch site plan.Mullaney said the developer would also consider the planning commission's comments on windows and defining the base of the building.

title: Landowner wants to build Millington camping retreat
author: Will Bontrager; wbontrager@chespub.com
content:
Landowner wants to build Millington camping retreat

 November 28, 2023 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: Will Bontrager; wbontrager@chespub.com | Page: 1 | Section: News 
 
 864
 Words 

 Read News Document

 CHESTERTOWN - Sandra Donnelly, owner of 32103 Millington Road, presented her plan for the 30-acre property to the Kent County Commissioners on Tuesday, Nov. 14.Accompanied by her attorney, Lance Young, with Bill Mackey the director of the Department of Planning, Housing and Zoning, they discussed Code Home Rule Bill 5-2023; a text amendment making a special exception for "outdoor retreat." Donnelly offered the commissioners an overview of her goals.She said her husband loved the property and since his death, she's looked for effective ways to use it."I'm doing this in his honor," Donnelly said.She took steps to build a camping retreat for outdoor oriented families or small groups. She aims to build 10 to 15 two-room cabins, with a central bathhouse and conduct special events yearround - maximum occupancy of two weeks.It's a simple idea, gaining popularity worldwide, requiring an amendment to a text for the commissioner's approval.Young said when Donnelly presented her idea to him, it didn't fit within the category of a country inn or a bed-and-breakfast or a retreat, so they had to introduce a new idea.Mackey explained the process that brought them before the commissioners.Donnelly's application was reviewed by the Planning Commission on Aug. 3. They gave a favorable recommendation with some added amendments.They suggested Donnelly's project consist of at least 10 acres, set back a minimum of 100 feet from the property line and recommended not to be built in the Village district.Also, the Planning and Zoning commission and Board of Appeals would review events held at the grounds on a case-by-case basis.On Sept. 6, the application worked its way to the Agricultural Advisory Commission.The agricultural commission recommended she not build on land zoned for agriculture, limiting her building to three zones: Rural Character, Rural Residential and Community Residential.Mackey explained why Donnelly's idea required a special exception in the first place."Almost all of our lodging uses are related to some sort of existing building or single structure. But this is a new idea, that there would be a variety of structures and options for people who are looking for a more outdoor experience." However, there have been issues in the region and the country with people abusing their occupancy. In many cases, getting them out has been a problematic, lengthy process.The commissioners' questions for Donnelly and Young revolved around this.Commission member Albert Nickerson asked what would prohibit the retreat from becoming a permanent village.County Attorney Tom Yeager pointed out there have been instances a seasonal campground evolved into one year-round."How would the two-week time period be enforced other than by the honor system?" he asked.Donnelly replied it's no different than someone overstaying their time in a hotel. She would call the police if that were to happen.In this case, enforcement would fall under Mackey's department as a zoning infraction.Price said enforcement, like providing an eviction notice to a tenant, is a 45-to 60-day process in most cases, and he'd prefer to prevent that.Price said, "If there's a solution or a clause we can put in to protect you and the county, I think this is an appropriate time to consider it." Donnelly agreed.Since this was a public hearing, Janet Christensen-Lewis voiced her concern over this text amendment.As the only person to sign the testimony log, she began by saying she has nothing against Donnelly but urged the commissioners to reject the text amendment.Christensen-Lewis said, "Whatever she (Donnelly) wants to do, you don't know what other people in the county are going to do, or how responsible they'll be." She echoed the commissioners sentiments, adding that enforcement policy, getting an uncooperative tenant out, is driven by complaints.If the property owner doesn't complain, or the temporary tenants don't, then how would the county know it's happening?Further, she said the county is stretched thin and does not have the resources to deal with existing zoning codes.She urged the commissioners to consider the property may soon be annexed by Millington, and hookups to water lines could pose a problem.In her closing statements, she said there are some fundamental parameters that needed consideration: the total footprint of all buildings, the determination for acreage for activities, and the definition of adequate landscaping.Donnelly addressed Christensen-Lewis' comments.She said she's willing to hook up or not hook up to certain water mains. She said that whatever taxes she needs to pay for a commercial property, she's willing.And she said that many of the things brought up in opposition to her application are worst-case scenarios.Since all events held there will be on a case-by-case basis, Donnelly doesn't see how the text amendment could be abused either.Young said Donnelly's vision fits with the county's comprehensive plan of maintaining a rural, small town character. He said the plan places an emphasis on increasing tourism and economy, supports existing businesses and aims to feature year-round attractions.All things the outdoor retreat would do, in his opinion.Fithian, although having similar questions, saw some of the potential problems brought to light were issues any business would have.The commissioners will have a third hearing during their legislative session on Dec. 19.

Sandra Donnelly and her attorney Lance Young discuss a proposed text amendment to allow for building a retreat in Millington.

title: County Council member talks boat insurance at marinas
author: Maggie Trovato; mtrovato@chespub.com
content:
County Council member talks boat insurance at marinas

 November 30, 2023 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: Maggie Trovato; mtrovato@chespub.com | Page: 5 | Section: News 
 
 393
 Words 

 Read News Document

 CAMBRIDGE - During a Dorchester County Council meeting Nov. 21, Council Vice President Mike Detmer said it is time the Council discuss whether the county should require boat insurance for anyone that rents a boat slip at a county marina."We had talked before about the expediency or the need of having insurance for our boats in marinas," Detmer said. "As we get towards our thinking about next year - which is essentially now - we should really think about having that requirement."Detmer said he thinks it is the responsibility of the Council to consider the insurance requirement "as a protection" for everyone."Insurance isn't free, but it is attainable, and in this instance I think it's needed," he said.Detmer said that having this conversation earlier is better because it will give boat owners more time to figure out where to get the insurance, what the insurance will cost and when they will need the insurance by."So it's not a surprise," he said.Council President Lenny Pfeffer said that from an insurance perspective, this requirement could be beneficial."I mean we are a member of a pooled trust," he said. "So by us being diligent with that, we're helping the pooled trust for ourself, our own rates, as well as all the other members in the pooled trust."County Attorney Chip MacLeod said it is fair that "anybody that brings risk to county property has some coverage.""If it was the boat owner's fault for not maintaining the boat and it catches fire and burns down one of our piers, we're going to fix our pier and everything else," he said. "But then our insurance company should be able to go back to somebody else that might have been responsible and get their insurance company."MacLeod said the policy would be helpful."You want to just shift the risk where it should be shifted when it's fair," he said. "From a legal aspect, it certainly is best practice."The Council previously discussed the possibility of this requirement at at a meeting in June.At that meeting, Pfeffer said there is concern over how the potential insurance requirements would affect the "more senior boats" that have difficulty getting insurance other than general liability insurance. Detmer said if the council decides to put an insurance requirement in place, the county should give people a year's notice before it begins asking for proof of insurance.
