title: Doverbrook Apartments redevelopment project begins
author: Maggie Trovato; mtrovato@chespub.com
content:
Doverbrook Apartments redevelopment project begins

 December 21, 2023 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: Maggie Trovato; mtrovato@chespub.com | Page: A3 | Section: News 
 
 641
 Words 

 Read News Document

 EASTON - Work is underway at the Dover brook Apartments, located off Dover Street in Easton.Last week, the apartment complex officially closed its doors to residents for the redevelopment project to begin. When complete, the property's seven buildings will be torn down and replaced with five new buildings.
Although there will be two fewer buildings when complete, there will be an increase in 14 units, bringing the total to 64 units, confirmed Don Bibb, director of the Talbot Housing Commission.
"We're beginning the remediation," he said about where they are in the project.
"Probably in January they'll start tearing buildings down." Rather than a public housing program, the new units will be a part of a housing choice voucher program known as Section 8 housing.
"Both programs are structured such that a program participant pays no more than 30% of their adjusted household income toward the rent," Bibb said about the public housing and voucher programs.
Along with new, energy-efficient units, the redevelopment project will create a playground in the center of the community. Bibb said he believes the basketball court that is already on the property will stay there.
The Easton Housing Authority building located on the property will receive a facelift to create a better space for the community as well as new office space. An addition of 1,000 square feet will be constructed on the back of the building.
Bibb said that it was time for these renovations.
"I mean, this property's close to 51, 52 years old," he said. "It's been fairly well maintained, but it's outlived it's lifetime. So it's time to give something back to the community and the residents." The project, which will take about 14 months (barring any delays, Bibb said), is estimated to cost close to $25 million. Bibb said somewhere around $24 million has been raised so far.
Last year, the Easton Town Council and Talbot County Council each voted to award the project $250,000 - totaling $500,000.
Last Wednesday, Gov. Wes Moore announced $63.7 million in awards through Maryland Department of Housing and Community Development programs, including $400,000 to the Dover brook Apartments project through the department's Community Legacy program.
"To win the decade, we must be intentional about building sustainable, vibrant communities that lift all Marylanders," Moore said in a news release. "These investments will support local and county leaders in their vital work to drive economic growth and create stronger pathways to prosperity in all parts of the state.
Together, we will continue to revitalize our communities and reveal Maryland's full potential." Bibb said the award from the state was great.
"We had that small gap (between cost and money raised), and that's why we applied to the state for that legacy," he said.
Since work on the apartments began last week, some residents have been moved to Housing-Commission-owned properties in St.
Michaels. Bibb said a few of the units in St. Michaels are still being worked on, and so some Doverbrook residents are being put up in a hotel until those renovations are finished.
The Housing Commission of Talbot hired a relocation specialty company to help find Doverbrook's residents relocation units. Bibb said that those who didn't get relocated to the Housing Commission's properties in St. Michaels were given vouchers for other properties.
"It's been tough with the relocation because the rental market is so tight," he said.
"But we did get everyone relocated." Those living at the apartments before renovations will have first right of refusal to come back.
Adding 14 more affordable housing units in Easton is significant, Bibb said.
"There's always a high demand for affordable housing," he said. "Nationwide, it's a problem I mean we could build another 200 (units), and it still wouldn't meet the need."

title: NEWS Rural council reflects on 2024 challenges - 'Pathways to Prosperity' Summit caps another successful year
author: CONTRIBUTED
content:
NEWS Rural council reflects on 2024 challenges - 'Pathways to Prosperity' Summit caps another successful year

 December 22, 2023 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: CONTRIBUTED | Page: 2 | Section: News 
 
 726
 Words 

 Read News Document

 ANNAPOLIS. When more than 200 rural community leaders and other stakeholders came together for the Rural Maryland Council's recent Pathways to Prosperity summit, there was one clear message. rural communities have an inherent ability to pivot, respond and recover during hard times.The breakout sessions focused on this ability to dig deep and come up with creative solutions, a quality that rural communities can share with its suburban and urban counterparts so that all of Maryland can tackle the tough issues and come out the other end more resilient and sustainable, the council said in a press release.
"Housing is an economic development issue," said Andy Bauer, vice president and Baltimore Branch of the Federal Reserve Bank of Richmond, during the lunch plenary. "The housing issue is something that's going to be with us for a while. It's going to take a lot of innovation in order to provide or make it easier for more supply to come online in either the form of greater density and more single family units." "It's going to have to be intentional," he added. "At the end of the day everybody in those communities are going to have to be onboard." Finding balance and leveraging challenges for the better was the message that Maryland Secretary of Agriculture Kevin Atticks delivered to summit attendees.
"Agriculture has to be profitable," he said. "Our farmers and our agricultural land are under so much pressure from development and from our clean energy goals." He didn't stop there, adding a message about resource conservation.
"We are farming in the context of the Bay. That's a pressure. We need to protect the land, preserve the land, and make sure the land is working for the Bay, not just being profitable," he said.
The summit closed with a message of hope and encouragement to tackle the challenges that lie ahead and to continue to break barriers from Maryland's first woman comptroller Brooke Lierman.
"We are focused on a new vision under our new leadership, and that is to be a partner in creating a state that is more equitable, more resilient and more prosperous so that every Marylander can reach their full potential," Lierman said. "There are still barriers to break, but by working together we can keep breaking them." The summit was just one of the key accomplishments for the Rural Maryland Council this year, the press release said. The Council received historic funding of the Rural Maryland Prosperity Investment Fund in the amount $9,050,000, along with the Maryland Agricultural Education and Rural Development Assistance Fund (MAERDAF), which received an additional $118,485. The funding enabled RMC to provide grants to the state's five rural regional councils as well as 84 RMPIF grants totaling $8,369,629 and 47 MAERDAF grants totaling $1,153,203.
Other 2023 RMC achievements include monitoring 135 bills, writing 60 position statements, passing three bills and hosting seven legislative committee meetings as well as co-hosting the 2023 Regional Rural Broadband Forum with the USDA Rural Development on June 21.
Looking to the coming year's legislative session, RMC has established several key priorities including: ¡ Level funding of $9 million in the fiscal year 2025 operating budget for Rural Maryland Prosperity Investment Fund.
¡ Efforts to address affordable housing issues such as efforts to repair and weatherize homes to keep seniors aging in their homes as well as the creation of additional workforce housing units to serve public service and moderate income workers.
¡ $1,000,000 for the Wood Products Industry Equity Investment Fund to reach renewable energy goals and support upgrades in electric infrastructure.
¡ Establishing programs and policies to sustain and enhance agricultural production and agri-tourism and efforts to address food security.
"As we close this year, we'll take a moment to appreciate our successes, and then quickly roll up our sleeves as we know that the challenges facing our rural communities continue to be numerous and complex," RMC Chair Susan O'Neill said. "We encourage all our stakeholders to join us and draw on their resilience and ability to innovate so together we can build a stronger future for all Marylanders." Founded in 1994, the Rural Maryland Council operates under the direction of a 40-member executive board in a nonpartisan and nondiscriminatory manner.
For more information on the Rural Maryland Council or to get involved, visit rural. maryland.gov or contact RMC at 410-841-5772 or rmc.mda@maryland.gov.

 OXFORD - The Town of Oxford is seeking a person to fill its planning and zoning coordinator position.According to the job description, posted on the town website, the planning and zoning coordinator will be tasked with reviewing, verifying and approving permits for construction, subdivision and shoreline work; advising applicants, boards and commissions; coordinating review with other departments and agencies and providing assistance in support of commissions and boards, among other tasks.
Oxford's Commission President Tom Costigan said that in Oxford, improvements and maintenance are made to houses often.

The coordinator position was posted on Dec. 28. According to the job description, the salary range for the position will fall between $50,000 to $70,000 per year, depending on experience.
Town Manager Cheryl Lewis said this position is not a new one. The person hired will be filling the role of town planner.
Lewis said the name change was made to more clearly describe the role.
The position was previously held by Maria Brophy, Lewis' daughter. Lewis said Brophy has taken a position elsewhere and said she could not further comment on personnel matters.

"While she was here, (Brophy) was just an absolutely wonderful employee," he said. "She was very helpful working with the boards and whatnot. We will miss her, and we look forward to whoever the next person is that we bring on to doing a great job as well."

author: Connie Connolly; cconnolly@chespub.com
content:
A spacious and welcoming place - Central branch reopens main floor following a year of renovations

 January 3, 2024 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: Connie Connolly; cconnolly@chespub.com | Page: 11 | Section: News 
 
 986
 Words 

 Read News Document

 DENTON - Following a year of renovating and redesigning, the central branch of the Caroline County Public Library at 100 Market Street in the county seat reopened its first floor space Dec. 18.The soft reopening is designed to help staff fine tune details as they welcome patrons and visitors. A grand opening celebration is planned when the new elevator is finished in spring 2024.
New carpet, neutral walls, fresh shelving and new furniture create welcoming decor in the more open spaces of the library's main floor. The main desk is bigger and moved away from the wall, making it easier for staff members to see most of the library's interior.
Bennett said she wanted people to experience the library as "bright, open and inviting."
"This is perfect," customer Romont Fletcher of Denton said Dec. 20 as he set up his laptop on the desk attached to an upholstered chair. He had not been in the library for a year and was surprised when he walked in. "This is a great renovation," he said.
"This is good space, and it's flexible space," Executive Director Debby Bennett said. "It's a well-built library." Bennett, who has been with the library since 1983, will retire in June 2024.
"In 1983, people came in, got their books and checked them out and went home," Bennett said. "Now people come to stay, whether it's work on our computer, hang out with their friends in the Teen Zone, a family comes in and spends time looking for materials and just spending time here, small meetings in the study room, research in the Maryland room."
The $2.1 million renovation project began Jan. 2, 2023. Bennett, the Caroline County Board of Library Trustees and library staff met their goal of reopening the first floor to the public before Christmas.
The central branch has experienced many changes in its 62-year history. Card catalogs and hand-stamping due dates have been computerized. Circulating books are still a staple, but today library card holders can check out a Cricut machine, sewing machines and even fishing poles.
The central branch has 13,739 card holders who can check out materials, but visitors can obtain guest passes to use the public computers.
As if to illustrate the changes, two days after reopening, four teenaged young men checked out software to play games on library Xboxes in the Teen Zone.
The renovation was funded mainly by two "highly competitive" State Library Capital Grants, Bennett said.
In addition to replacing the roof slates on the library's 1995 addition, the building underwent extensive first floor renovations.
Phase 2 includes improving the elevator in 2024.
The Phase 1 grant in fiscal year 2023 financed 79%, or $917,000 of the project.
The library board provided the local match of $244,000 from their John Hargreaves fund.
This phase included replacing three HVAC units at the end of their useful life, improving lighting, upgrading the emergency fire alarm system and phone system, enhancing electrical capacity for increased technology, removing the wall dividing the two children's rooms, providing a family bathroom adjacent to the children's areas, increasing seating capacity, improving sight lines and creating quiet areas. The improvements brought the library into compliance with ADA requirements.
The cost didn't include shelving, furniture and other additional costs that were incurred throughout the renovation, about $335,236. The library paid for those costs, except for $78,000 raised by the Friends of the Library for shelving for the adult, young adult and Maryland Room collections.
Phase 2 is being funded by a fiscal year 2024 State Library Capital Grant that pays for 78%, or $467,000, of the project, with the remaining $132,000 provided by the Caroline County Commissioners.
This phase includes replacing the elevator, which is "at the end of its useful life," Bennett said.
The new elevator will comply with ADA requirements and current codes.
The phase also includes replacing the addition's 4,000 square foot roof with artificial slate, which had deteriorated and become a "serious safety hazard," Bennett said.
The elevator provides access to public space, administrative offices and the third floor attic storage area.
"The (two-sided) main service desk is going to work a lot better for staff to both answer basic questions and check out items, and also to be able to work with people with more complex reference questions," Bennett said. "And also we have so much better visibility of the other desks and more areas of library to see who might need help (and) for security."
"Back in 1995 when we renovated and added on, we didn't have cell phones and laptops and iPads," Bennett said, adding that the internet was fairly new then.
"The MakerSpace used to be our reference area in 1995 with 7-foot shelves of reference books. Now, all the reference materials are online."
More square footage not taken up by books "frees up more people space," she said.
There's a lot to figure out," Bennett said. "Half our staff are new and didn't work down here. And for all the staff, it's a new layout. So it's a matter of figuring out procedures and ironing out all the little extra things. So opening like this without a big fanfare - and this is a quiet time of the year anyway - is giving us time to figure a lot so that things go smoothly for staff and customers."
"I've seen a lot of changes, but this library has always been innovative," Bennett said. "It's always been forward-thinking and also thinking: What does the community need? What does community need that they don't even know they need?"

title: Easton Town Council approves changes to bicycle code
author: Natalie Jones; njones@chespub.com
content:
Easton Town Council approves changes to bicycle code

 January 4, 2024 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: Natalie Jones; njones@chespub.com | Page: 1 | Section: News 
 
 439
 Words 

 Read News Document

 EASTON - The Easton Town Council unanimously passed legislation Tuesday updating the town's code on bicycles, skateboards and scooters.Ordinance 802, first introduced in November, deletes outdated provisions of the town code relating to bicycles, skateboards and scooters and updates language on prohibited riding areas and enforcement.
The most significant change to this part of the town code concerns who is allowed to ride bicycles on sidewalks within town limits.
Under the existing code, all residents are prohibited from riding bicycles on the sidewalks. A newly added exception, which will go into effect within three weeks, allows children under 13 years old to ride on the sidewalk.
Prior to the ordinance passing, Heather Grant, the executive director of Talbot Thrive, a local nonprofit dedicated to promoting healthy and safe outdoor mobility within the county, requested a revision to allow for all those under 18 years old to ride on sidewalks.
"This age-appropriate exception allows schoolchildren to ride their bikes where they feel safest, whether on the sidewalk, a trail or a town street, and goes hand-in-hand with our organization's mission to get more kids on bikes and more kids riding them to school," she said.
An idea for a dismount district - an area where bike, skateboard and scooter riders would need to walk instead - in downtown Easton was initially floated around by Ward 1 Council Member Maureen Curry, but ultimately was not enacted.
Language on lawful bicycle riding was also updated in the new ordinance.
It includes provisions on maintaining safe operation and control of the bike, riders considering the safety of others, and yielding right of way to pedestrians.
The code update additionally makes riding skateboards and scooters on streets, sidewalks, parking lots and other public property lawful.
The use of both devices in those spaces was prohibited under a town ordinance passed in 1988.
Today, skaters can flex their skills at Easton's recently opened skate park and pump track in North Easton Park.
Language allowing roller skating was added to the code for the first time through the new ordinance.
Provisions of the bicycle ordinance will be enforced by the Easton Police Department. Violations are municipal infractions.
If police see a child operating a bicycle, skateboard or scooter in an unsafe or dangerous way, they can impound the vehicle, whether or not a citation is issued from the violation.
Grant called on police to also enforce existing laws, including the three-foot buffer between cyclists and cars and requiring cars to stop for pedestrians at all crosswalks.
Provisions on town bicycle inspections and licensing will be deleted through the new ordinance.

 EASTON - The Easton Town Council approved a supplemental growth allocation Tuesday to reclassify just over eight acres of land within the county's critical area on a lot at Talbot Commerce Park.The council granting the supplemental growth allocation is a step in redesignating the lot from a resource conservation area to an intensely developed area - a change in classification for land within the state's critical area, or land within 1,000 feet of tidal waters and tidal wetlands.
However, it is not approval for future development site plans.
Additional reviews will be done by the planning commission and town staff.
Applicant Thomas R. Cohee first requested the growth allocation for the two lots off of Mary's Court in 2020. The lots are zoned agricultural and business commercial, and office buildings already exist on one of the lots.
Several other developments, though residential, have gone through the supplemental growth allocation process since the state's critical area law was passed in 1984, including Easton Club, Cooke's Hope, Easton Village and Londonderry, said Town Attorney Sharon Van Emburgh.
After the critical area law passed, local jurisdictions, including Talbot County, established critical area programs.
The county provided a portion of its growth allocation to Easton, but the town has already used all of its 155 acres originally allotted, meaning that any new growth allocation must come from Talbot County.
Cohee's request was reviewed by both the town and county planning commissions.
Proposed development for the commerce park lots includes an addition to the existing office building, several new office buildings, a mixed use office and warehouse building and stormwater management infrastructure.
Although the property's stream buffer, non-tidal wetlands and wetland buffers are being designated as intensely developed areas with the allocation, no development activity will occur in those areas, said Ryan Showalter, an attorney representing Cohee.
The project received a favorable recommendation from the town's planning commission, though its conditions included rezoning the critical area lot to a zoning district permitting the proposed uses.

 Work has begun on what will be a years-long modernization and improvement project at the Easton Airport.Last week, crews began constructing a security and containment fence, designating areas that will soon see the project's impacts.
"The purpose of the fencing is to define the construction area and maintain security for aircraft operations throughout the implementation of the Airfield Modernization Program," said a release from the airport. title: Comptroller highlights changes during tour of Queen Anne's County
author: DOUG BISHOP dbishop@chespub.com
content:
Comptroller highlights changes during tour of Queen Anne's County

 January 6, 2024 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: DOUG BISHOP dbishop@chespub.com | Section: Local News 
 
 607
 Words 

 Read News Document

 CENTREVILLE — Maryland Comptroller Brooke Lierman visited four establishments in Queen Anne's County on Dec. 20: the newly opened YMCA in Centreville, Everside Health Center also in Centreville, and two local businesses on Kent Island, both located in the Chesapeake Bay Business Park — Italberco, a growing sweet-tooth business working with the food industry providing dessert ingredients and Queen Anne's County's largest employer, Paul Reed Smith Guitars.Her visit began at the YMCA, where she met with YMCA Mid-Shore Region Executive Director Robbie Gill; two Queen Anne's County commissioners, Chris Corchiarino and Jack Wilson; Queen Anne's County Administrator Todd Mohn; county Economic Development and Tourism Director Heather Tinelli; and Queen Anne's Community Services Director Cathy Willis. The meeting was "a working lunch" served at the Y.
During the lunch, Lierman spoke about the changes made within the comptroller's office in the past year. Several new positions have been created, including a chief information officer. She said that the Comptroller's Office is striving for "more transparency."
Beginning in February, for the first time ever, businesses will be able to pay their taxes online.
"We are also preparing, in the Comptroller's Office, a designed plan for future prosperity for the state," Lierman said, "not a plan for just the next four years, but far beyond that."
Lierman has been visiting each of Maryland's 23 counties over the past year, sharing a similar message.
She expressed concern in an interview with the Bay Times and Record Observer that the state deficit is mounting, beginning with the 2024 state budget. Former Maryland Gov. Larry Hogan left the state with a surplus. However, that surplus has since disappeared.
Before the Hogan administration left office, the General Assembly passed massive legislation for new state funding for public schools, which will kick-in in 2024.
She said, "The governor and I will need to speak about what we're going to do. It will be either to cut state services, or find new sources of revenue."
She didn't mention anything about raising taxes when mentioning "new sources of revenue."
Wilson spoke about efforts in Queen Anne's County to help restore the Chesapeake Bay and suggested Lierman come back to go out with some watermen to witness oyster seeding that is helping cleanse the bay waters. He also spoke about concerns with local farmers on the issue of solar panels being erected near preservation farmlands within the county.
Wilson praised the newly established Everside Health program, which is now covering all county government and public school employees. Queen Anne's is the first county in Maryland to become part of the Everside Health benefits. It was mentioned that Everside is about to cover six other Maryland counties.
Wilson spoke about the Queen Anne's Chamber of Commerce looking into Everside covering local small businesses within the county to help with health care benefits for their employees.
Corchiarino spoke briefly about the issues concerning the Chesapeake Bay Bridge. He said, "The effects of bridge traffic are crippling to Queen Anne's County."
Lierman said, "As of Jan. 3, there will be a published 'State of the Economy' report presented to the public, providing residents with both good and bad outlooks for the state going forward."
She mentioned that there are 12 comptroller offices within the state. The Eastern Shore office is located in Salisbury. The closest office to Queen Anne's County is in Annapolis.
Lierman was elected the state's first female comptroller in November 2022. She was a state delegate previously for eight years, representing part of Baltimore City. She is the mother of two children, a boy, 11, and girl, 6. Lierman grew-up in Montgomery County.
After the meeting at the Y, Lierman visited and toured the other three facilities, gathering information about their business successes.

title: Maryland lawmakers return to Annapolis for 446th General Assembly
author: Natalie Jones
content:
Maryland lawmakers return to Annapolis for 446th General Assembly

 January 10, 2024 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: Natalie Jones | Section: General Assembly 
 
 512
 Words 

 Read News Document

 ANNAPOLIS — Despite flooding in downtown Annapolis and a maze of construction surrounding the State House, Maryland lawmakers were eager to get back to work as the 446th General Assembly kicked off Wednesday.Over 500 bills were prefiled ahead of the session's Wednesday start, with conversations about public safety, budgetary concerns, health care, climate change and housing expected to dominate the 90-day legislative session.
Although national change is on the horizon with primary and general elections, the General Assembly is returning to normalcy after the past few sessions saddled lawmakers with a number of challenges and adjustments, including the pandemic, redistricting and a new Democratic administration.
Senate President Bill Ferguson, a Baltimore Democrat heading into his fifth year at the helm of the Senate, acknowledged the settling pace in his address to state senators.
"The good news is we're back to governing," Ferguson said. "We are in a place where we are normalizing the world; we're back to where we've always been, and we got to focus on the things that matter the most."
To Ferguson, the top priority is balancing the state budget, he said, but making investments in education, health care, public safety and the environment are also key to making Maryland safer and stronger.
Gov. Wes Moore (D) must submit his budget proposal to the legislature by next week.
Ferguson and President Pro Tem Malcolm Augustine, a Democrat from Prince George's County, were unanimously nominated to reassume their positions, maintaining consistency in the Senate's leadership.
Similar priorities were echoed in the House of Delegates by House Speaker Adrienne Jones, a Democrat from Baltimore County who was nominated to lead the House as speaker for a fifth full session. She first assumed the role in May 2019.
In spite of the alignment in priorities, a significant change was seen in the chamber as Del. Sheree Sample-Hughes (D-Dorchester, Wicomico) was ousted as the House speaker pro tem.
Del. Dana Stein, a Baltimore County Democrat, was Jones' choice as the next speaker pro tem — a nomination that was echoed and affirmed across the chamber.
Though Jones did not speak to the change in leadership on the floor Wednesday, she acknowledged the significant challenges the state is facing: difficult fiscal realities, an "untenable situation" around juvenile crime and efforts to maintain the state's transportation system, among others.
Numerous bills tackling juvenile justice reforms were filed prior to the session.
This year, the legislature will fund the state trauma system, increase the availability of workforce housing and keep its commitment to the Blueprint, Jones said.
The speaker also plans to promote a set of bills she called "the decency agenda" — legislation to put safeguards and best practices in place to prevent intolerance and hate from taking root in the state.
But overall, Jones wants lawmakers to remember that shared values are more powerful than what divides them.
"We will do this work with civility and with expediency, we will talk and then listen to each other. We'll keep an open mind to ideas and opinions that differ from our own," she said. "We'll do this work together, united as public servants working for the people of Maryland."

title: Caroline Zoning Appeals board denies Hartland Holdings grain silo variance
author: Connie Connolly
content:
Caroline Zoning Appeals board denies Hartland Holdings grain silo variance

 January 10, 2024 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: Connie Connolly | Section: Local News 
 
 1365
 Words 

 Read News Document

 DENTON — Over the course of two meetings and four hours of testimony and deliberation, the Caroline County Board of Zoning Appeals voted against granting a zoning variance to a agricultural operation near Greensboro.Benjamin Flahart of Quarryville, Pennsylvania, whose Hartland Holdings LLC owns the 160-acre farm in question, was denied a 43-foot variance for already-constructed grain silos at 14010 River Road.
His attorney, Brendan Mullaney of McAllister, DeTar, Showalter & Walker in Easton and Brett Ewing of Lane Engineering represented him at the Board's Nov. 19 meeting and attended the Dec. 19 meeting with Flahart. Both meetings were held at the Health and Public Services Building in Denton and were attended by about a dozen Caroline residents.
Board of Zoning Appeals Chair Karen Hardy, Vice Chair Ben Butler and Member Kevin Parks voted unanimously to deny the variance, claiming that Flahart knew, or should have known, that setting up grain bins within the county's 500-foot road setback requirement was a violation of the county code.
"It's the principle to me," Hardy said at the Nov. 14 meeting. "If … we just say, 'Okay, no problem, come on into Caroline County, put up what you want, and then whenever it doesn't go your way, just come on and bring your attorneys and … we'll give you your variance' — I don't want that to be something that happens here."
Several times during the course of both meetings, Hardy said Flahart had "created his own hardship."
Butler said he felt "the same way," although moving the grain bins would cost "a lot of money."
"But I really feel like he created this situation, and I just feel like he should have to move it," Butler said.
Flahart bought grain bins from Mountaire in Greensboro and moved them to the River Road location. Three of the bins are located within the setback limit. At the Dec. 19 meeting Flahart estimated demolishing and relocating the three bins would be "close to $1 million."
"I know that the financial hardship is severe, and I do understand that, but it is somewhat self-created," Hardy said after the unanimous vote. "I don't feel good about that decision. Unfortunately, we could not do it any other way."
The Board of Zoning Appeals considered two items related to Flahart's River Road operation. The first item considered at the Nov. 14 meeting involved a public hearing and an extended debate addressing Hartland Holdings LLC's application for a special use exception in accordance with the Caroline County Code.
Flahart's operation, permitted in 2019 to store his own grain, evolved into an "agricultural products processing plant" when it began storing grain from other farms and selling it, which required a special use exception.
Mullaney explained Hartland Holdings LLC "owns a significant amount of land" on the Eastern Shore — "1,000 acres in Cecil County, over 2,000 acres in Dorchester and over 1,500 acres in Caroline."
He added that "in Pennsylvania and many other counties, you don't have to permit things like grain silos and agricultural barns."
Despite the additional structures' being added to the grain operation without permission, Mullaney said he believed all the variance criteria were satisfied. He said he and Ewing had worked together to submit permit applications "to get all this stuff cleaned up with Planning and Codes, the building permitting department and the Office of Health."
According to Matt Kaczynski, assistant director of development review for Caroline County, in 2019 Flahart hired engineering company Red Barn Consulting, which, in turn reached out to the planning department for the requirements to establish an agricultural products processing facility.
Kaczynski said the timeline required by the county prompted the Red Barn engineer to scale back the operation "to basically one grain tank."
"It was our understanding … that (Flayhart) would come back later for an expansion," he said. "Fast forward to now … What was constructed and what is shown on the site plan now was not what was reviewed and approved as part of the building permit process, so we had received some complaints from neighbors in the area about what was going on onsite."
Kaczynski said Flahart may not have been aware of Red Barn's process, as Flahart maintained during the Dec. 19 meeting.
However, Hardy said on Nov. 14 Flahart should have been aware "to some degree what's happening. … At the end of the day, it just makes me question the integrity of the man who's moving into this."
She brought up briefly "the elephant in the room" that wasn't under consideration: Flahart's dissolved air flotation, or DAF, pit, which has been a source of controversy and was a concern addressed at the Dec. 12 Caroline County Commission meeting.
Several people spoke up during the public hearing.
Local farmer James Lewis, who is the extension agent for Caroline County, said he has hauled his grain to the River Road facility the last couple of years. He said the operation benefited the community and that he was concerned about the carbon footprint involved with tearing down and moving the bins 43 additional feet from the road.
Caroline County farmer John Saathoff said he was "mainly concerned about the precedent" that would be set, although he liked "the option of having another grain facility."
In 2019 Flahart didn't own 1,500 acres in the county, Saathoff said. "He owned one farm, and that one bin was able to accommodate that farm."
"Everybody knows initially his plan all along was to go commercial," but "it was going to take too long." Because Flahart had also erected a scale and scale house, "that was clear evidence, in my opinion, of his original intention."
"Those of us down here in the trenches (who) have been here all this time — we're bound by the law," Saathoff said. "Those of us who have been here for generations, every time we want to do something, we come in your office and we apply for a permit, and we do what we're supposed to do. And these people who hire their attorneys, they get to do whatever they want. I don't think that's how we want this county to be."
Brett Meyers, a farmer who lives next door to Flahart's River Road property, said the permitting process is "not negotiable."
"I find it hard to believe a man with enough wherewithal to buy all these farms (and) put these grain tanks up wouldn't have understood that there was a permitting process involved to build what he wanted to build and to have to adhere to a site plan," Meyers said.
Although the 43 feet was not "going to make too much of a difference," Meyers said, "I feel like you're going to open Pandora's box. Where does it stop with the grain and the tanks. How big is it going to get? … If you okay this, how far is it going to get?"
Mike and Suellen Woodward, whose property adjoins the operation, voiced several concerns, including the increased heavy truck traffic and the lack of communication to neighbors that would allow them to present concerns earlier about the operation's expansion.
"We've seen this happen from the beginning," Mike Woodward said. "I don't understand how he got all those grain bins up with no permit at all. I don't care about the grain operation. That doesn't bother me at all. But the part of the permitting process — something was skipped somewhere, whether he didn't follow through or somebody else didn't follow through."
"And that happens all the time," Kaczynski said. "More often than you would want to know. We issue building permits. We go out onsite to do final inspections, and we find that they've constructed various other things without permits."
The board considered the benefits to local farmers hauling their grain to a nearby facility, but noted Flahart's business expansion that ventured beyond the approved site plan.
After almost two hours of testimony and discussion Nov. 14 the board deliberated, voting unanimously to approve a special use exception with the conditions that the applicant receive final site plan approval from the planning director or commission prior to issuing a permit and/or zoning certificate.
A further condition required the applicant and county entering into a development rights and responsibilities agreement to work with the Department of Public Works to address wear and tear on county roads affected by Hartland Holdings LLC's truck traffic.

title: Odor lingers as Centreville addresses cannabis facility
author: HANNAH COMBS hcombs@chespub.com
content:
Odor lingers as Centreville addresses cannabis facility

 January 10, 2024 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: HANNAH COMBS hcombs@chespub.com | Section: Local News 
 
 735
 Words 

 Read News Document

 CENTREVILLE — An acrid smell has been lingering in the air over Centreville, and residents affected haven't been afraid to raise a stink. The unpleasant, to some, odor has been the topic of several town council meetings, the latest on Jan. 4.Although there is no ordinance governing odor control — as noted by council member Dan Worth — what was stirring the pot was the proposed ordinance to amend the Town's zoning to only allow indoor agriculture as a permitted use in the Planned Business District.
Ordinance 05-2023, if passed, would potentially restrict Centreville's largest private employer, Green Thumb Industries from expanding their outdoor grow facility in the business park. Council ultimately withdrew the ordinance, following a motion made by member Jeff Kiel and seconded by Eric Johnson.
Green Thumb Industries appeared before council in September of last year to address how those odors could be mitigated.
Speaking on behalf of the cannabis grower, at the Jan. 4 meeting, Jeremy Kacuba, told council they had met with residents of Symphony Village, the largest contingent of residents affected by the odors, last month. A third party firm was recruited by Green Thumb to offer potential solutions to the emanating odors.
Those concerns brought forth by the community are real and have been identified by engineers, Kacuba said, as concentrated processes within the facility. There are some lab processes for the extraction of cannabis oils and further processing, those are the "predominant sources," he said, but the outdoor grow in and of itself is "insignificant" in terms of contribution of odor into the community.
Kacuba noted, there is one concentrated process within the outdoor grow that was identified and is a part of their proposed mitigation solution where plants are brought down during the harvest time and dried to allow for further processing. There is a significant concentration in those drying trailers that can be easily mitigated with the engineering solution Green Thumb Industries has come up with, he said.
The solution recommended by Green Thumb's engineers is not inexpensive, Kacuba said, and would require an initial upfront investment associated with ongoing operational and testing expenses. "(We're) ready to move forward with that solution...a cost we're willing to bear to be a good neighbor to Centreville."
Rebecca Brown, senior management with Green Thumb Industries, told Council they are committed to hearing concerns and being able to address them.
"Filtration systems and molecular atomizers...are not cheap...we've allocated the capital. We've taken this to the strictest regulations in the municipalities we already operate in," Brown said.
Regardless of the council's vote on Ordinance 05-2023, Green Thumb representatives assured the Town they would be moving forward with odor control with a target goal of "elimination."
Kacuba said the company was prepared to "execute the initial capital solution" within approximately two months and then move towards monitoring, with the intent to have odor control systems fully operational in June; noting late summer and fall is when the largest potential of emission related to the outdoor grow process could occur.
There are approximately 200 employees at the Centreville site, established in 2016, responsible for growing, harvesting and processing cannabis. Their operations are run much like an FDA food processing facility would be required, Kabuca said.
Kacuba addressed monitoring and outlined a strategy where samples would be collected based on the recommendation of the engineering specialists. Then lab testing by the third party will track those metrics, and that information will be shared with the town.
During the public comment portion of the meeting, residents again voiced their concerns.
Pat Fox of Symphony Village said she had noticed a lot of strong odor lately and asked if any attempts had been made to mitigate the odor to date.
Another Symphony Village resident, Joe Sikes, said, "not meant to be rude, another source of smell has been the smell of the clothing on the workers."
Mark Emerson of Cloverfields suggested data is how decisions should be made and requested "Council set rigorous standards" for those testing measures.
Addressing Council directly, Symphony Village resident Julie Seymour asked if the town could implement a reporting system similar to the toll-free number used in Delaware for poultry farms.
Council President Ashley Kaiser encouraged those calls to be "politely" reported to Town Hall.
Also addressing Council, Joe Brown, Symphony Village resident, said "We seem very quickly to have gotten this solution" — a solution he was cautious was real.
Kaiser said she thinks complaints drove the solution, but she is hopeful that it will resolve the issue.

title: St. Michaels Commissioners choose Boundary Lane park master plan
author: Maggie Trovato
content:
St. Michaels Commissioners choose Boundary Lane park master plan

 January 12, 2024 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: Maggie Trovato | Section: Local News 
 
 711
 Words 

 Read News Document

 ST. MICHAELS — With time ticking to submit a grant application to the state, the Commissioners of St. Michaels concluded a nearly three-hour meeting Wednesday with a vote to move forward with a master plan for a new park on Boundary Lane.The master plan for the park that town staff recommend be named San Domingo Creek Park — as the 7.6-acre property is adjacent to the creek — includes nature trails, expanded wetlands, a living shoreline, a fishing pier, a comfort station and a pollinator meadow.
The property was purchased by the town in September for $2.9 million. Formerly owned by nonprofit Environmental Concern, the property has an existing administrative building, which the town plans to use for a new town office.
At the meeting, Town Planner Steve Ball told commissioners that the town intends to submit a grant application to the state for Program Open Space funds in order to offset the cost of the park.
With the grant application due Feb. 10, he said the commissioners would need to decide if any changes need to be made to the master plan at the Jan. 11 meeting so the plan can be brought back for final adoption at the Jan. 24 meeting and then submitted to the state.
After Ball spoke, Scott Scarfone, an associate principal at Mahan Rykiel Associates, gave a presentation on two master plan options.
Following the presentation, commissioners discussed aspects of both plans and whether certain parts should be included. They considered the possibilities of including a dog park and a viewing mound as well as different parking options.
Commissioner Tad DuPont said the town has spent a large chunk of its savings to purchase the land and that the town should maximize the amount of open space in the plan to get as much grant money as possible.
"It's my feeling that the town has this one shot to maximize as much open space, unencumbered as possible, to be able to be able to get the most money we can from Program Open Space to cover our costs," he said, causing residents at the meeting to applaud.
Program Open Space is a state program under the Department of Natural Resources that administers funding for open and recreational space in local communities.
DuPont said he didn't think the dog park was appropriate on the land and didn't like the viewing mound — a 10-foot hill with an ADA-accessible path that visitors could walk up to get a view of the creek from above.
The inclusion of a dog park has been a point of contention when it comes to proposed plans for the park.
In February, town commissioners passed a resolution supporting a dog park location within the town, though no location was specified.
At a joint meeting in December between the St. Michaels Planning Commission and the town's Parks and Recreation Advisory Board, Ball said the inclusion of a dog park would not be consistent with the open space funding program.
DuPont also voiced his concerns with the plans for a parking lot off Boundary Lane. He said that 12 parking spaces outside the town office building would be enough — eight spots for employees, two spots for visitors and two handicap spots.
During public comment, resident Langley Shook said if there is no dog park on the property, there is no need for more parking. He said adding more parking could affect how much funding the town gets from the state.
"All the parking would do would be to draw people who would have to drive at a distance," he said. "Which I think you generally don't want."
Shook made a suggestion to not include the additional parking lot to the plan, and if there is a need for more parking down the line, it can be added to the park later on.
Commission President David Breimhurst said not everyone who uses the park is going to be able-bodied.
"We'll have senior citizens and others who are not going to enjoy (the walk to get to the park)," he said. "They're going to want to be able to park, maybe walk to one of the pavilions and sit and enjoy the view."
Ultimately, the commissioners voted to not include the dog park or viewing mound in the master plan.
The master plan they voted on does include the parking lot off Boundary Lane.

title: New Year ushers in single-use plastic bag ban in Town of Centreville

New Year ushers in single-use plastic bag ban in Town of Centreville

 Author/Byline: Staff Writer | Section: Local News 
 
 489

 Read News Document

 The town of Centreville instituted a single-use plastic bag ban that went into effect on Jan. 1.Centreville joins Anne Arundel and Prince George's counties and the City of Frederick whose plastic bag bans also started the first of the year. According to the Maryland Retailer's Alliance, more than 70% of Marylanders now live in jurisdictions with carry out bag policies in place.
On July 20, 2023, Centreville Town Council passed the ordinance to ban single-use plastic carry out bags within Centreville town limits.
For Town Council President Ashley Kaiser while the ban addresses single-use plastic bags the spirit of the ordinance is to encourage the use of reusable bags and eliminate the reliance on plastic bags, many of which end up polluting our highways and waterways.
"Consumers have an opportunity to play a significant role in the implementation of this bill. I don't think that anyone who is shopping at a local business wants to burden a local business, but instead wants to support them. If a paper bag fee is going to be a problem for you, decline the bag," says Kaiser. "There are things people can do to change their behavior like making a point to remember to always carry reusable bags with them," she adds.
Following that philosophy, the Town of Centreville launched a "Bring Your Own Bag" campaign in October in coordination with Plastic Free QAC. The campaign included specially designed reusable bags with a rack card featuring information on the bag ban as well as tips for how to remember to bring your bag to your next shopping trip.
Bags were handed out at Centreville Day in October and at the Centreville Farmers' Market Heck with the Malls market day in December and were made available at Town Hall. A limited supply of Town reusable bags and vintage farmers' market reusable bags are currently available for consumers to pick up at Centreville Town Hall from 9 a.m. to 4:30 p.m. Monday through Friday.
The Centreville single-use plastic bag ordinance stipulates that retail establishments with the exception of food service facilities "shall charge, collect and retain at least 10 cents for each paper carry out bag that it provides to a customer."
Exceptions to the ordinance includes, but are not limited to:
Nonprofit fraternal, civic, war veterans, religious, or charitable organizations and fire companies can still use plastic carry out bags.
Due to cross contamination concerns restaurants may not allow customers to use their own reusable bags. Restaurants will provide paper bags, but will not charge a paper bag fee.
The Centreville Market's Market and cottage food businesses can continue to use plastic.
Pharmacies and opticians will not charge a paper bag fee for prescription items.
Consumers and business owners who want to read the full text of the ordinance and frequently asked questions can visit townofcentreville.org and type "plastic bag ban" in the search window. For more information, please contact Carol D'Agostino, mainstreet@townofcentreville.org or 410-758-1180, ext. 17.

title: Queen Anne's County fairgrounds undergoing facelift

Queen Anne's County fairgrounds undergoing facelift

 CENTREVILLE — Since October, demolition of old barns at the 4-H Park in Centreville and immediate new construction of barns to replace them have been underway.Construction was made possible by funds directed by the Queen Anne's County Economic Development & Tourism Office with grant funding from the Rural Maryland Economic Development Fund provided by Upper Shore Regional Council and the Maryland Department of Commerce.
The 4-H Park capital improvements were provided $1.2 million. They include not only replacing the old barns, which have stood for more than 80 years, but improvements to electricity, plumbing and stormwater management on the fairgrounds.
For as long as anyone can remember, stormwater has flooded the fairgrounds many times, with excess water standing on the grounds for days after heavy rain storms.
Incremental work had been done on storm management over the years, with some improvements, however, this storm water management project will make substantial improvements in that area going forward.
"Before leaving office, Governor Larry Hogan provided funds for rural counties that had been impacted by the COVID pandemic," said Economic and Tourism Development Director Heather Tinelli. "All the rural counties in Maryland received funds for projects to help strengthen our agricultural communities in our state. Governor Hogan provided $50 million total for all the rural counties. QA received $2.9 million for 11 different projects. The improvements at the 4-H Park is the largest project of them all in our county."
"Our 4-H Park reflects the importance of our agricultural community, as well as how popular our annual county fair is to us," she added.
It's been noted that the Queen Anne's County Fair is by far the largest social gathering of people in the county each year. No other event comes close, with an annual paid attendance of 25,000 people over six days.
Those numbers were true before the pandemic began, and the fair numbers have returned since the pandemic ended.
Park Board member Berl Jastram is the Buildings and Grounds chairman. He has worked closely with Tinelli with the 4-H Park receiving the grant funds for the improvements and overseeing the work that has been done thus far.
It is expected improvements will be completed sometime this spring, long before the county fair arrives in August.

title: Caroline Commissioners clarify aims of Jan. 23 DAF hearing
author: Connie Connolly
content:
Caroline Commissioners clarify aims of Jan. 23 DAF hearing

 January 17, 2024 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: Connie Connolly | Section: Local News 
 
 854
 Words 

 Read News Document

 DENTON — With the DAF storage moratorium attracting attention among residents, the Caroline County Commissioners clarified the purpose of the Jan. 23 public hearing towards the close of their weekly meeting Tuesday, Jan. 16.Commission President Travis Breeding said he noticed there was "some misinformation and uproar going around" the town of Ridgely about the hearing.
A flyer distributed to Ridgely residents alleged that the "Holding Company that purchased the Hanover property on Peaviner Road plans to start DAF processing in various ravines located on the property." The flyer author said the same holding company owned property on River Road and "have already started processing this sludge."
The author urged residents to attend the public hearing and sign an online petition created by Nancy Boone. By press time Jan. 16, the petition had garnered 138 signatures.
The purpose of the 6 p.m. public hearing Tuesday, Jan. 23, is to "receive comments on the storage of dissolved air flotation, or DAF, in Caroline County that was brought to our attention several weeks ago," he said.
The hearing will be held at the Health and Public Services Building, 403 S. 7th St., Denton.
Breeding said the commissioners would issue a formal statement, but stated several points he wanted the public to know "to bring everybody up to date."
The commissioners learned "that the livestock manure storage facilities — essentially manure storage pits from dairy or beef cattle operations — had been repurposed for and (were) being used for the storage of DAF. The storage was causing a nuisance to neighbors, so the county put a moratorium into effect. County officials have used the past few weeks to gather information about DAF," Breeding said as he read from his draft statement.
"This was brought to our attention by the fact that it was being used by someone who did not go through the permitting and approval process, and we're dealing with that as well," Porter said.
While "it seems evident that the state only regulates the product, the production and the application of DAF, … it is the county's responsibility to regulate the storage," he said.
"In my opinion, the state kind of dropped the ball here and left it up to us without even notifying us that this was going on. And naturally, the producers and then the haulers and the appliers didn't come and ask us for permission, so we were totally oblivious to what was going on. So essentially, the county is ready to create those regulations, and it's seeking public input into that process," Breeding said.
The objective of the hearing is to for the public to share comments, but the commissioners cautioned that the county was focused on DAF open pit storage, not the application of DAF as a soil amendment nor fertilizing with manure, both of which are legal agricultural practices.
Breeding said he's learned in his relatively short tenure as a county commissioner "that if regulatory territory is occupied by the federal government or the state, we are preempted, and therefore we don't have the ability to change those requirements. But what we have found is that this is totally the Wild West," he said. "It is up to us to come up with a reasonable storage solution here."
"I believe that I do not want any open air storage, and I want it only in the I-2 Industrial Area, because I believe it's an industrial product," Breeding said.
"We have to be really careful about banning it and not making a reasonable accommodation, either, and setting reasonable rules, so we don't get challenged," he said.
"I think I agree with that," Porter said. "I think I would even like to say that even if it does go into a zoning classification … I still want there to be public hearings."
I don't want anybody walking out of that meeting thinking that this is going to be some kind of a magic wand — that they're not going to smell anything again," Porter said. "This stuff has been used in fields for a long time. … It is a soil amendment that is beneficial to farmers. … We are only talking about the storage of this material."
Breeding said he was "fine" with a provision that DAF could be stored "for a maximum of 45 days on a property that it is actively being applied to, … but otherwise, (it) needs to be in a closed container and in the I-2 Industrial Areas of the county. So that's my position right now, and that's what I want to present to the public on Jan. 23."
"This is the ironic part," Breeding said. "The town of Ridgely and residents over there would have no idea that this was even a possibility had we not brought it up. So, we are actively trying to address this issue by even letting them know, 'Hey, this is a possibility of something that could happen out there.'"
"So, we're trying to get ahead of it. The firestorm was created by us and now we're the ones getting burned by it," he said.
Porter said Ridgely officials had been proactive, as well, because they are aware of the potential DAF storage problem "and the complications."

 EASTON — The Talbot County Council on Tuesday approved a change to the county's alcoholic beverage code, paving the way for a liquor store to be considered and established in Trappe.The bill, first introduced in November, came after a request from several Trappe residents hoping to develop a liquor store within the town.
The existing county code included certain restrictions on the issuance of off-sale licenses, or licenses that allow the sale of alcohol for off-premises consumption.
According to Patrick Thomas, the county attorney, a formula limits the number of off-sale licenses that can be issued.
Thomas said Trappe does have some off-sales licenses, but the town does not have a Class E license, which is required to open a liquor store. It's the only municipality in Talbot County that does not have one.

Town residents currently have to drive to Easton or Cambridge to shop at a liquor store.
Council Vice President Pete Lesher emphasized that the council does not issue liquor licenses — the county liquor board does — but the bill enables that the board to be able to review one for the town.
"Without this legislation, a new business would not be possible," he said. "So this is enabling legislation for sure."
The bill was approved unanimously.

title: Tense discussion precedes Easton Town Council approval for Pride festival
author: Natalie Jones
content:
Tense discussion precedes Easton Town Council approval for Pride festival

 January 18, 2024 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: Natalie Jones | Section: Local News 
 
 1010
 Words 

 Read News Document

 EASTON — A request to approve a public assembly permit for the Delmarva Pride Center's annual Pride festival, though approved in a 3-2 vote, elicited strong concerns from some Easton Town Council members.Though the Delmarva Pride Festival is heading into its third year in Easton, one council member's uneasiness with the contents of the festival stirred up a multi-pronged discussion on Town Council precedents and the council's responsibilities and scope in reviewing events meant to benefit the community good.
This year's Delmarva Pride Festival is set for Saturday, June 15, from 11 a.m. to 4 p.m. It's planned as a celebration of the Delmarva LGBTQ+ community and its allies during Pride Month.
The previous two Pride festivals held in Easton featured a variety of food trucks, live music, local vendors and performances. Residents and pets alike donned rainbow clothing and accessories as they celebrated in the heart of downtown Easton.
Festival organizers expect about 2,000 people to attend the 2024 festival.
COUNCIL CONTENTIONS
After the introduction of the festival's public assembly permit at Tuesday's town council meeting, Ward 3 Council Member David Montgomery raised a flag about the festival's activities in previous years.
He cited a video he'd seen that reportedly showed "overtly sexualized performances and behavior" and voiced concern about harm to children exposed to those displays.
"For these reasons, I don't believe this event as it was constituted in the past serves the common good of our town," Montgomery said.
The Ward 3 council member said he wanted to see what could be done to find a "more appropriate" location and about festival organizers' efforts to prevent similar behavior, adding that the displays were "not ones that many people want to see in this town."
Montgomery suggested postponing Delmarva Pride Center's application to a later meeting for a more thorough discussion.
Town Council President Frank Gunsallus said the council should extend the privilege of waiting to Montgomery, citing the council's precedent of tabling discussions based on members seeking more information or a deeper understanding prior to voting.
Ward 4 council member the Rev. Elmer Davis Jr. disagreed, calling it "quite unfair" to change the Pride festival's location or timing.
"I respect my colleagues, but I don't respect their opinion on this issue and this concern," he said. "I think the date and time is here and available to us, and I think we should vote on it."
Davis honed in on Montgomery's mention of young children in the context of the event, pointing out that parents had brought them to the festival.
"We are not in a position to be parental guidance for anyone; that's the parents' responsibility. We don't have oversight," he said, eliciting some claps from residents in the gallery.
Montgomery countered, saying he thought the council did have a responsibility to look at the content of festivals proposed to occur in the town. He re-emphasized his concerns about opening the festival up to minors and potentially harmful content.
Easton Mayor Megan Cook pointed out the festival's success over the last two years and a lack of complaints.
"The only complaint I ever heard was that it was such a lovely event, and it's shared with Juneteenth — he wished it was actually extended into two weekends," she said before Gunsallus began speaking over her.
"We've had an outpouring of people raising concerns in the past week," he said.
"We've also had an outpouring of support on this," Cook said, being echoed by Ward 1 Council Member Maureen Curry.
"You're right, and that's fine," Gunsallus said. "But we also have to serve everyone that has voted and put us in this position as a broader community."
Montgomery's motion to table approving the festival's permit was put to a vote, with Gunsallus seconding it. But before a roll call could be taken, Ward 2 council member Don Abbatiello chimed in.
"While I wholeheartedly disagree with waiting, and I have every intention, when we do vote on this, to vote in favor of allowing the public assembly permit to go through — if there is a member of this council who would like to wait, even if I disagree with it ... then we should wait," he said.
Though Abbatiello supported waiting because of the precedent set by the council before, he emphasized strongly that he would be voting in favor of the assembly permit as soon as possible.
Curry and Davis also emphasized their intentions to support the permit's approval, but they said they would honor Montgomery's request to wait.
VIDEO
A video of a performer from a previous festival was shown at the meeting, though it was not the same video that put Montgomery on edge. That video reportedly involved children coming up to a dancer, watching the dancer's crotch and handing money to them, he said later.
Tina Jones, a co-founder and treasurer of Delmarva Pride Center, approached the podium to try to allay the concerns voiced by some council members, tackling the questions sparked by the video.
"These are dancers, these are performers — if you decided they're something else, that's the decision you're making, but these are professionals," she said. "They are no different than a ballet dancer or somebody in a musical, and I bet you would have no problem letting a child come up with them and present flowers."
No one was "scantily clothed" either, Jones said.
Montgomery said he only asked for assurances that there would be no exhibitions like the ones reportedly in the video he referred to.
"We are not trying to groom anybody, we are not trying to change anybody's mind about who they are or what they want to be," Jones said. "We're just trying to say to folks who feel different, who feel like they don't have a place, that they do have a place, and I would love for that place to be the place where I grew up."
Montgomery later conceded to the council moving to vote, saying he doubted the council would hear anything different.
Curry initiated the motion to approve the assembly permit for the Pride festival, which was supported with resounding "ayes" from Abbatiello and Davis.
Montgomery and Gunsallus voted against approving the permit for the Pride festival, resulting in a 3-2 approval.

title: Long-awaited Easton dog park officially opens
author: Natalie Jones
content:
Long-awaited Easton dog park officially opens

 January 19, 2024 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: Natalie Jones | Section: Local News 
 
 467
 Words

 EASTON — Not even sub-freezing temperatures and bits of ice laying on the turf grass Thursday morning could stop over a dozen dogs — and their owners — from celebrating the grand opening of Easton's long-awaited dog park.Dogs of all ages, sizes and breeds were pulling at their leashes with energetic anticipation, waiting for the ceremonial red ribbon to be cut by Easton Mayor Megan Cook.
Thursday's ribbon cutting was a welcome sight for local dog owners and dog lovers, many of whom had waited years for the project to come to fruition.
A voiced interest in a dog park first came seven or eight years ago, said Rick Van Emburgh, the town engineer.
But in 2019, Easton residents David Ferraris and Noah Matten restarted the efforts, working with Rauch Inc., a local engineering firm, to prepare concept plans for a dog park near the downtown area.
And in fall 2020, the town received $7 million in bond funding, a majority of which was required to be allocated to parks.
Almost three years later, in March 2023, the Easton Town Council voted to fully fund the dog park on Brewers Lane and to add a restroom there, Van Emburgh said.
With the legislative work completed, construction of the dog park required a true group effort from the town's public works, parks and recreation, IT, buildings and finance departments.
Willow Construction, Easton Utilities and Chester River Landscaping also lent a hand with a number of other efforts to make the park a reality.
"I believe this is a wonderful example of teamwork," Van Emburgh said. "I believe it's a wonderful example of our community working together to build something beautiful for our town residents and our dogs."
Cook kept her comments brief, acknowledging a number of excitedly yapping dogs waiting to enter the park and play.
"I really want to give an extra shoutout to all the departments," the mayor said. "Pretty much every department in the Town of Easton played a role in getting this park up and running."
Once the ribbon was cut, the dogs were unleashed and off to play.
The new park, open dawn to dusk, includes two separate play areas for the pups based on weight, with a larger area allocated to dogs over 35 pounds.
A turf grass layer on top makes for a comfortable surface for dogs to run, jump and roll around, and underneath, there's an anti-microbial infill material and an irrigation system for cooling the turf.
It was clear that the dogs were excited as they raced in circles and made new friends, and the smiles on owners' faces told a similar story.
Easton resident Scott Cohen, who stopped by the park with his two Australian Shepherd-poodle mixes Scruffy, 4, and Casey, 3, said the dogs had a great time playing Thursday morning.
"I think it's a terrific add to the community," he said.

title: Michaelmas, a forgotten local holiday, and a resident's journey to bring it back
author: Maggie Trovato
content:
Michaelmas, a forgotten local holiday, and a resident's journey to bring it back

 January 21, 2024 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: Maggie Trovato | Section: Local News 
 
 1311
 Words 

 Read News Document

 ST. MICHAELS — Although a relatively new resident, "occult detective" Jon Nelson has spent months working on a project that proves his love for his new town."I met my wife here," Nelson, who moved to St. Michaels in October, said at a Commissioners of St. Michaels meeting Jan. 10. "The best gift I could think to give back to the (town) is to say here's a reminder that this used to be very important to you."
That gift is a three-month research project that delves into a forgotten, centuries-old local holiday, Michaelmas.
Nelson enjoys uncovering forgotten history in his free time. Most recently, he worked on a project with St. Michaels Police Chief Jeffrey Oswald to discover who the first policeman of St. Michaels was, when the department was founded and what the department's original badges looked like.
At the Commissioners of St. Michaels meeting in early January, Nelson gave a presentation on the history of Michaelmas, also known as St. Michaels Day, and asked commissioners to pass a resolution that acknowledges the holiday once existed.
So what was Michaelmas? And why isn't it celebrated anymore? The story, which goes all the way back to the 1600s and ends with a group of teenagers mooning an audience in the 1970s, is a winding one, jam-packed with local history.
A COUNTY FEAST
When Nelson picked up the second volume of "History of Talbot County, Maryland" by Oswald Tilghman from the library in an effort to learn more about the history of the area, a list of important dates for St. Michaels caught his eye.
"The very first thing that (it) said was that every Sept. 29, St. Michaels holds a party for the entire county of Talbot," Nelson said at the meeting. "And I though that was cool, except that it was Oct. 1, and I was so disappointed."
Nelson had missed the holiday by just a few days.
This is what started Nelson's deep dive into all things Michaelmas, an event celebrated in St. Michaels from the 1600s into the 1800s, and then again for a brief period in the 1970s.
It took Nelson about three months of combing through old records, books and newspapers to find as many first- and second-hand accounts of the forgotten local celebration as he could.
The date, he discovered, had to do with taxes. Nelson said that St. Michaels was not part of a British colony, which meant that the town had to invent its own laws and customs.
Because St. Michaels didn't have a form of currency, on Sept. 29, residents would bring harvested tobacco or seafood to Christ Church, a quasi-governmental authority at the time, in order to pay taxes to the town.
"Because the church was one of the most prominent locations and it was really easy to get to, everybody would show up," Nelson said, "every single year."
As soon as everyone had paid their taxes, "the Feast of St. Michael and All Angels" would commence.
BIGGER THAN ST. MICHAELS
Although the holiday became unique to St. Michaels in the United States, Michaelmas has European roots that go back to the Middle Ages.
According to Encyclopedia Britannica, Michaelmas, which is still celebrated in Western churches on Sept. 29, was a "great religious feast" during the Middle Ages that coincided with the harvest in Western Europe.
In the Anglican Church, the holiday's proper name is the Feast of St. Michael and All Angels. In the Catholic Church, Michaelmas has come to be known as the the Feast of Saints Michael, Gabriel and Raphael, the archangels.
Nelson said that for the Town of St. Michaels, the name and date of the holiday were "imported from England."
"But overtime people stopped calling it Michaelmas," he said. "They started calling it St. Michaels Day because that's an easier thing to say. And pretty soon they started calling it St. Michaels Day, the day that we would all go to St. Michaels to pay our taxes and have that festival."
Nelson said that in St. Michaels, it had become a nondenominational holiday.
END OF AN ERA
Following the War of 1812, an economic depression in St. Michaels led to the end of St. Michaels Day, Nelson said.
During the war, shipbuilders in St. Michaels were hard at work building small and fast sailing ships called Baltimore Clippers.
"But as soon as 1820 hit, we had a whole lot of boats and nobody to sell boats to," Nelson said. "So people just moved. They got out of town. There was a big economic depression."
The last celebration of St. Michaels Day Nelson was able to find was in 1824, 200 years ago.
"And it slowly just fell out of public memory," he said.
A BRIEF RETURN
After more than 100 years of a town tradition abandoned, Nelson said St. Michaels Day was brought back — as St. Michaels Days — in 1971.
The town continued to hold the celebration annually on the second to last weekend in September through 1977.
For those handful of years, organizations all over town were involved. The event drew people from around the county and beyond.
"There were house tours and museum tours and walking tours and boat races and horse shows and parades and dancing," Nelson said.
St. Michaels High School would put on a play each year.
"But they had to get permission from the high school administrators and the town council before they were allowed to put on the play," Nelson said. "It was such a big deal that they were worried about being embarrassed."
St. Michaels Days had become so popular that in 1976, the town received a letter from U.S. President Gerald Ford asking that the high school band play in the capital for St. Michaels Day.
While the band and the adults in charge were in Washington, D.C. for St. Michaels Day that year, high school students who remained in Talbot County were left to put on the annual play themselves, Nelson said. The commissioners and school administrators didn't review the script that year, saying they trusted the students to put on the play.
"But they apparently left the not-so-good-kids behind," Nelson said. "So the play (that) year was about how their parents were old and they didn't understand the way the world was."
The play ended with a real surprise: the students mooned the audience.
In big, white letters, "ST. MICHAELS" was spelled out across the students' bloomers as they faced away from the audience.
As a result, kids were no longer allowed to attend St. Michaels Days after that year, Nelson said.
During his presentation, Nelson read from a Star Democrat article from 1978 with the headline "Lack of interest threatens St. Michaels Days."
The article included comments from those involved with the event's organization. It cited competition with the Baltimore City Fair, lack of enthusiasm from school bands and businesses not making enough money from the festival as reasons why the organizers said they didn't want to put the event on again.
Nelson said he thinks the the fact that kids were no longer allowed at the event is the reason the town stopped putting it on nearly 50 years ago.
"They said no kids are allowed," he said in an interview. "And it turns out that's the easiest way to kill a celebration."
NEXT STEPS
In an interview Jan. 18, Nelson said the reason he only asked commissioners to pass a resolution that acknowledges that the celebration once existed is because he didn't think they would be interested in holding the event again.
Nelson said that since giving his presentation to commissioners, he has talked with Town Manager Rob Straebel.
"The meet-in-the-middle piece we've come to is (that) I'll go brief the St. Michaels Business Association," Nelson said.
If the Business Association agrees to hold the event and is willing to send a letter of support to the commissioners, Nelson said the commissioners will make a proclamation for St. Michaels Day, rather than just passing a resolution.
"We've kind of handshake promised," Nelson said. "As long as we get all of our paperwork in before that, we could get it proclaimed."
