title: Letter had no good reasoning
author: Staff Writer
content:
Letter had no good reasoning

 January 21, 2024 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: Staff Writer | Section: Editors Inbox 
 
 397
 Words 

 Read News Document

 Sometimes you publish letters to the editor that contain strong political views that are based on false information or bad logic or both.When a political view is based on good reasoning, I don't feel the need to respond. But I do feel the need to respond when a writer gets published with no good reasoning. Such is the case with Mr. Adrian's letter "Gone down a dark road," in Sunday's 14 January edition.
His letter is filled with false statements. For example, he claims that Democrats control elections to push some kind of agenda. There is no evidence for that. Quite the contrary. Mr. Adrian somehow completely missed the well-known information that Republicans are involved in managing elections. There are hundreds, if not thousands, of examples.
Even the head Republican, Donald Trump, knew that when he called the Republicans who control elections asking them to alter votes in 2020. As another example, Mr. Adrian seems to claim that harvesting crops in the fall leads to harvesting ballots. I don't think there is any evidence for that.
But what really gets me is the use of questions for arguments. This illogical method of argument is a tool of conspiracy theorists and despots for thousands of years. "When did you stop beating your spouse?" is the classic retort to that entire form of reasoning.
Mr. Adrian received a document about mail-in ballots and points out he could print it. "What could possibly go wrong?" he writes as if that question is a legitimate argument against the entire process. Without evidence, the question makes no sense, any more than me asking Mr. Adrian when he stopped beating people. Mr. Adrian should read about how the Arizona Republican Party spent millions of tax dollars on a month's-long audit of ballots that only showed Mr. Biden's votes were undercounted. Georgia audited their elections three times by hand counting ballots and found no fraud. These are just two facts out of hundreds of examples that belie the assumption underlying Mr. Adrian's question.
Mr. Adrian poses many other questions that assume evidence where none exists. And he ends his letter with the question, "Which political party controls the Board of Elections anyway?" as if that is a reason for everyone to doubt elections. It is not.
All available evidence is that elections in Maryland are fair and honest. People should appreciate that and take the time to vote.
MICHAEL DAVIS
Easton

title: Chestertown commission — appointments for life
author: STEVEN MITCHELL
content:
Chestertown commission — appointments for life

 January 21, 2024 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: STEVEN MITCHELL | Section: Columns 
 
 565
 Words 

 Read News Document

 I was dismayed when a small group turned out last Tuesday night to support the candidacy of long-term resident, Cherilyn Widell, to what we thought was an open position on the Historic District Commission (HDC) due to the ending of a three-year term for one of the seven commissioner seats.Ms. Widell has impeccable credentials to serve on the HDC including once serving as the highest-ranking historic officer in the state of California — an appointment made by then governor Pete Wilson. She even received the Calvert Prize, which is the highest award for Historic Preservation in Maryland. I thought her 45 years of historic preservation activities would make her a shoo-in for the position on our HDC.
I was wrong.
It turns out that Chestertown has a little-known and unwritten policy that allows anyone serving on a committee, commission, etc. to ask for reappointment and that will be granted regardless of the expertise of the incumbent or anyone else seeking appointment to that position. In the case of the HDC, each commissioner is appointed to a three-year term — or maybe it is a lifetime term? That is because at the end of the three-year term, if you ask for reappointment, you will automatically be granted a new term. You either have to decline the appointment or die to relinquish it. Why have term limits at all? Just let people serve as long as they like and don't mislead the town by posting that the positions have term limits, because they don't.
I don't have to give you examples of why this isn't the best approach to making the most of the existing talent in our town, nor for long-term town management. The purpose of term limits after all is to encourage greater citizen participation by ensuring regular turnover in key positions such as our HDC.
The mayor and Town Council have done Chestertown a disservice by not appointing to the HDC someone whose credentials in historic preservation are beyond reproach. The current HDC does not currently meet the certified local government (CLG) criteria mandated by the federal government and the state of Maryland.
They have not complied with this since Ed Minch passed away in 2021 and have not filed the required paperwork since 2020. Having CLG certification allows the town to receive grants that are reserved only for CLG towns — grants that conserve our tax dollars. We risk losing that ability with the continued blind appointment of incumbents. The HDC could have used Ms. Widell's expertise to address this, and at the same time, our town would reap the benefits from her 45 years of experience in historic preservation.
Will this be the same approach to other positions across Chestertown? I'm afraid it looks that way. If this doesn't seem right to you, please write to the mayor and Town Council and let them know that you believe that committee term limits ensure new ideas and new perspectives are infused into the decision-making process while at the same time help avoid the perpetual concentration of power within a small group of people.
The best path forward for Chestertown involves using the extensive talent, commitment and skills available to support all of our committees and commissions and leave the term limits in place to help support this.
Steven Mitchell is a licensed professional engineer with more than 40 years experience in environmental, safety and facility management. He lives in Chestertown.

title: A lifetime of accomplishments in Easton
author: Staff Writer
content:
A lifetime of accomplishments in Easton

 January 21, 2024 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: Staff Writer | Section: Editorials 
 
 806
 Words 

 Read News Document

 Last weekend, hundreds of friends gathered to wish former Easton Mayor Bob Willey a happy retirement.It was a forced retirement. Willey lost two elections last year, first in the mayoral race in May and then in the race for Town Council president in September.
Those elections ended 32 years in elected office in the town, first as a councilman on the Town Council for six years, followed by six years as Town Council president and then a 20-year run as mayor.
But those electoral losses should not overshadow a lifetime of accomplishments.
His list of accomplishments during those 32 years is long, just as the list of dignitaries gathered to honor him Jan. 13 was long — a proclamation from the Talbot County Council, a proclamation and shadowbox from the Town of Easton, a framed plaque of recognition from Easton Utilities and citations from state Del. Chris Adams and state Sen. Johnny Mautz.
"It's heartening to see Mayor Willey get recognition for all he's done for our town and region," Mayor Megan Cook said. "Knowing him and many of the dignitaries that have come to present, it's easy to see the positive impact and impression he's made to each of them, from the local fire department to the Senate floor."
There were honors recognizing a lifetime of devotion to Easton.
Those walking the Rails to Trails will soon see a plaque on a boulder honoring Willey for his leadership in building the well-used trail system throughout the town. A concept for the monument was shown at the retirement reception.
Easton Volunteer Fire Department dedicated its new fire engine, Engine 63, to Willey, including a plaque affixed to the side of the engine. That honor recognized 60 years of service with the volunteer fire department.
Willey joined the fire department two years after marrying Betsy Lee Thompson from Oxford on Sept. 2, 1961. The couple raised three children in Easton. That family now includes four grandchildren and two great-grandchildren.
Willey was employed by Waverly Press for 41 years until retiring in March 2002.
Bob Willey was not one to boast of his accomplishments — and there were many over the years. Typical were his comments at the opening of another branch of the Rails to Trails in April last year.
"Our teams have been consistently making improvements to the beauty of the trail, while also making it more usable and safe," Willey said at the ribbon-cutting. "It will be nice to show off some of that hard work and to share it with the community."
Every day hundreds walk, run and bike along the trails through the city, which were developed under his leadership.
Perhaps it is not the trails that are his greatest accomplishment over those many years in public office. One of his lasting legacies is the unseen strong financial position of the Town of Easton.
That was not the case when Willey first became mayor in 2003.
Easton's economy was in shambles when Willey first became mayor. The town was deeply in debt. Under his fiscally conservative leadership, that dire situation turned around. Easton has not had a tax increase since 2007.
After a lifetime of accomplishments in Easton, Willey was visibly moved by the outpouring of love and support at the Jan. 13 reception.
"It means a lot," he said. "It's more than I ever could've hoped for. I'm really glad to see everyone out here enjoying themselves and having a good time. ... It really was a surprise."
There is more to do. Willey left office with some unfinished business. Others will need to pick up the mantle and complete these projects.
Affordable housing continues to be a difficult problem. In 2007, the then mayor created the Affordable Housing Commission and a low-cost home repair loan program which met with some success.
"We need to achieve more," he said last year.
And there is the new Easton hospital, which moved closer to becoming a reality last week with the state's approval of the certificate of need and the governor including $100 million in his budget proposal to make the plans happen.
Yet when the new hospital is built, the current buildings will be vacant. We like one of Willey's ideas to turn that property into a Veterans Administration facility to serve the many veterans on the Eastern Shore.
It's a great idea. It will be up to the next generation of town leaders to turn that idea — or another idea — into a workable plan.
They would be wise to look to Bob Willey's leadership over the past decades for examples of how to make that happen.
His philosophy was hidden in a comment he made at the ribbon-cutting ceremony for the Rails to Trails segment.
"This is just another step forward," Willey said referring to the added trail. "It's going to get better."
That is a philosophy for success in leading a town — keep taking steps forward and believe that it's going to get better.

title: Talbot County seeking housing coordinator to create workforce housing program
author: Natalie Jones
content:
Talbot County seeking housing coordinator to create workforce housing program

 January 24, 2024 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: Natalie Jones | Section: Local News 
 
 670
 Words 

 Read News Document

 EASTON — In an effort to address housing needs in the community, Talbot County is seeking a housing coordinator within the county's planning and zoning department.The housing coordinator, who would report to the county's assistant planning officer, would be responsible for creating a critical workforce housing program for individuals seeking safe and affordable housing, according to the job description.
The county-funded role is not a new one. It was a full-time position prior to 2020, with the job focusing on providing technical and administrative assistance to the county related to development and implementation of housing initiatives, said Bryce Yelton, the county's assistant planning officer.
Previous responsibilities included assisting county residents with access to applicable housing services and grant opportunities, along with preparing grant applications, reports and coordinating with federal, state and local housing programs and commissions, Yelton said.
Former housing coordinators also assisted the public with housing program applications as needed.
The role was filled "briefly" in 2020 in a part-time capacity, Yelton said. That year, the county saw widespread housing insecurity due to the COVID-19 pandemic.
But after a period of vacancy in 2020 and 2021, the housing coordinator role was removed and restructured into other positions within the county's department of planning and zoning.
A "pressing need" for housing still exists within Talbot County today, Yelton said, though its effects are not as severe as they were during the pandemic.
Efforts to alleviate housing needs in the county aren't only falling on the planning and zoning department — Talbot County Council Member Keasha Haythe has played a significant part in revitalizing the position into a full-time role.
Haythe, who's just over a year into her first term on the council, advocated for the need for the position to fellow council members at the start of last year's budget cycle.
Having worked with housing coordinators in her previous economic development roles, Haythe was familiar with the job's functions and responsibilities, and she drafted the job description for Talbot County's position.
The role was approved as a full-time position in the county's fiscal year 2024 budget cycle.
While Haythe's career experience aided in her knowledge of the need for the role in the county, prioritizing the search for a housing coordinator also comes from a personal place.
When she was looking into buying her first house in Talbot County 15 years ago, Haythe took advantage of the services offered by a previous county housing coordinator.
Haythe was able to purchase her first home with the help of the United States Department of Agriculture's direct home loan program, which provides a path to homeownership for low-income families in eligible rural areas, including Talbot County.
"Having used those resources before I purchased my home, when I was running for county council, that was the one thing that I said that I wanted to make a priority … to have that housing coordinator position come back, and expand it a little bit to stand up some type of housing program, not only for the purchase of a home, but some type of program that helps with rentals as well," she said.
The lack of affordable housing is affecting all demographics in the county, Haythe said, from younger residents looking to purchase their first home to older individuals on fixed incomes looking for affordable homes to rent.
But for residents in need, ensuring resources like the USDA program are communicated is another key step in addressing housing issues, she said.
Haythe's ultimate goal is for the county to eventually enter a public-private partnership to help with affordable housing and ensure that housing isn't more than 30% of a person's income — a solution she called the "real" and "true" way to achieve affordable housing.
"Home ownership may not be a fit for everyone," Haythe said. "However, if that is the American dream, if that is your dream, we want to make sure that, specifically for Talbot County, that we put tools and resources in place to get people to their dreams of homeownership."
The county is still seeking applicants for the position. The full job description can be found online at talbotcountymd.gov/job_openings.

title: League of Women Voters holds training for election info website
author: TOM MCCALL
content:
League of Women Voters holds training for election info website

 January 24, 2024 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: TOM MCCALL | Section: News 
 
 469
 Words 

 Read News Document

 CENTREVILLE — A group of women came together to get trained on how to run a spin-free election information portal called Vote 411. They came with laptops from as far as Frederick and St. Mary's counties to be ready for this year's primary election on May 14.This exacting and meticulous training is what the nonprofit the League of Women Voters is all about. They hold the power to vote as sacred and nonpartisan information about that vote to be integral.
"The goal is to provide training for the people that are going to be doing the voters guide and inputting information in the Vote 411 website," said the president of the Queen Anne's County League of Women Voters, Elizabeth Hammond.
"This is it for in-person training. There will be an online training on Saturday, Jan. 20. I think it is a good idea to do both of them," Hammond said.
She said the organization gets donations to do this work and create the voters guide both online and in print.
"We insert it in the Record Observer and then order about 500 extra copies and distribute them to towns and post offices and various other public places to pick up and get information to make intelligent decisions about what they want to vote for," Hammond said.
She is clear about the big picture of voting rights.
"Voting is one of the freedoms that we absolutely cherish. You want to be able to make a responsible decision and vote for the candidate that you think can do the best job. That is what we try to do with the voter's guide — to give the voters the best information possible in a nonpartisan way," Hammond said.
She said this primary election will be smaller than the general election, which will have a more involved voter's guide.
The state Board of Elections is the ultimate authority for the League of Women Voters.
"It amazing what the state Board does. What the election boards do is amazing, and they really deserve all the support we can give them and their thanks. That's why you watch the candidate listings on the state board, because that is what is going to show up, and then the proof comes when they send out the individual ballots for each county. The hard thing is you have to look through each one of those ballots. It is like 200 pages long," said Jeanne Halpin of the League of Women Voters of Maryland.
She led the training that took place at the Queen Anne's County Public Library in Centreville.
She tried to be less daunting to all the volunteers that showed up across the state.
"This is just a great learning opportunity. Don't get stressed, don't go crazy. The political parties are nominating candidates. They are asking people to run. In both the primary and the general," Halpin said.

title: Greensboro may get funds to move pump station, restore site of old wastewater treatment plant
author: Connie Connolly
content:
Greensboro may get funds to move pump station, restore site of old wastewater treatment plant

 January 24, 2024 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: Connie Connolly | Section: Local News 
 
 655
 Words 

 Read News Document

 DENTON — Though she wasn't on the agenda, Caroline County Assistant Director of Planning Leslie Grunden reported a positive development in protecting a stream flowing into the Choptank River north of Greensboro.Leading off the Jan. 23 meeting of the Caroline County Commission, Grunden said state funding was available to shore up "erosion at the town's pump station at the site of the old treatment plant located on a small tributary that feeds directly to the Choptank River," she said.
Greensboro Director of Public Works Brandon Cunningham alerted Commission President Travis Breeding about the "severe erosion" after recent significant rainfall.
"When he called me, and I went to look at it, I was like, 'Oh, yeah, this is a big deal,'" Breeding said.
Grunden said Cunningham told her he noticed "some erosion had been increasing" over the past several months.
"I think that was part of the old outfall for the old treatment plant, but the sides and the bottom are lined all the way down to the river — under the overpass into the river," Grunden said. "And over time, because it was probably put it in in the '60s, … it's broken up and starting to collapse and that's exacerbating the erosion."
A short-term solution in the form of an emergency grant was already in the works to add rocks and rebar and help hold the bank in place "while we went looking for funding for the long-term solution," to move the pump station farther uphill, Grunden said.
The aim is to remove the infrastructure and convert the stream location to a natural floodplain.
"Bringing the pump station up the hill (on town property) keeps it out of harm's way from erosion but also from eventual rising water from the Choptank," she said.
"This pump station takes flow from the town to the plant, so for that to be in jeopardy kind of keeps me up at night," Grunden said. The north county wastewater treatment plant is located on State Route 313, just north of Greensboro Volunteer Fire Company's community hall.
Grunden said her usual funding sources could support either the infrastructure or stream and floodplain restoration but not both. "So, I kind of put the word out saying we need money for both," she said.
However, the Maryland Department of the Environment gave her a call a week or two ago, "essentially (saying), 'We think we found the money to do both,' which is … almost a miracle," Grunden said.
MDE had "actually never done this grant. It's a grant they get from EPA that they've never had interest in," she said. "They would actually be the recipient, and then the county would be the sub-recipient. (MDE) would actually have to do all the reporting up to EPA, and I would provide them status reports and invoices."
She is currently putting together a project budget. Preliminary estimates put the pump station relocation at $1.3 million, and Grunden's guess is removing the structures would be half a million, with stream and floodplain restoration another half a million.
"And then I always have a contingency plan because nothing ever goes the way you want," she said. "So, we're at about $2.4 million. (The Department of Natural Resources) has reached out to say they'd be interested in helping with the stream and floodplain component, which would give us more money if we need more to deal with on the pump station side."
Grunden said she was "pretty confident" that enough funding would be available for the two-phase project, "where the first phase would be moving the pump station and demo-ing the old buildings, and the second phase would be going in and doing the stream and the floodplain restoration."
Although the project is "not a sure thing," she said MDE reaching out to her was "a really good sign that they're serious about providing the funding."
"I can't think of a better move that we can make there environmentally other than to get that stuff out of the floodplain," Breeding said.

title: Oxford introduces ordinance to establish cannabis business regulations
author: Maggie Trovato
content:
Oxford introduces ordinance to establish cannabis business regulations

 January 25, 2024 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: Maggie Trovato | Section: Local News 
 
 486
 Words 

 Read News Document

 OXFORD — With a nine-month cannabis moratorium set to end in Oxford at the end of February, the Commissioners of Oxford introduced an ordinance that would establish regulations for cannabis businesses at a town meeting on Tuesday.A resolution establishing the moratorium — which temporarily blocked applications, site plans, permits, construction, processing and approval for businesses looking to manufacture or sell recreational or medicinal cannabis in Oxford — was passed May 9, two months before adult use of recreational cannabis was legalized in Maryland.
The ordinance that commissioners introduced at the town meeting on Tuesday would amend the Oxford Zoning Ordinance.
Specifically, the proposed ordinance would permit cannabis dispensaries and processing facilities as a special exception in Oxford's general commercial zoning districts (C-2).
Town Attorney Lyndsey Ryan said that general commercial zoning districts already include greenhouses and retail as special exception uses, so dispensaries and processing facilities are consistent with those uses.
The ordinance would also permit growing facilities as a special exception in Oxford's commercial industrial district. Ryan said this zoning district includes other uses for growing crops.
It also includes the provision that "a particular use may not create excessive noise, smoke, odor and glare." An applicant has to prove this when they to get the special exception with the Board of Appeals."
The proposed ordinance would not allow for on-site consumption of cannabis, like smoke lounges. Ryan said that penalties would be applicable to a property owner if they were to operate an on-site consumption business.
The Oxford Planning Commission recommended the Commissioners of Oxford introduce and adopt the ordinance.
Ryan said that she and Oxford's former Town Planner Maria Brophy had worked with the Planning Commission to draft the ordinance. They based the ordinance on applicable regulations in the Maryland Alcoholic Beverages article in the Code of Maryland Regulations.
A public hearing on the proposed ordinance is set for the beginning of the next Commissioners of Oxford meeting on Feb. 13.
Before voting to introduce the ordinance, Commission President Tom Costigan asked where Oxford was in comparison to other nearby towns regarding cannabis moratoriums.
Ryan said many local municipalities had issued a year-long moratorium. She said she believed Oxford was the only municipality to be drafting an ordinance on cannabis businesses at the moment.
Commissioner Katrina Greer asked if Ryan had heard anything about locations for dispensaries, micro-processing facilities and processing facilities in the county.
Ryan said she hadn't heard anything yet. She said licenses are supposed to roll out in the next few months.
According to the Maryland Cannabis Administration, there are two standard dispensary licenses available in Talbot County.
There are also four standard growers, six micro-growers, eight standard processors and six micro-processors licenses available in the Eastern Region of the state, which includes Caroline, Dorchester, Kent, Queen Anne's, Somerset, Talbot, Wicomico and Worcester counties.
According to a breakdown of business license applications submitted to the Maryland Cannabis Administration, there were 25 applications submitted in Talbot County for standard dispensaries.
Reporter Natalie Jones Contributed to this article.

title: Oxford audit brings question of how to strengthen internal controls in small town
author: Maggie Trovato
content:
Oxford audit brings question of how to strengthen internal controls in small town

 January 25, 2024 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: Maggie Trovato | Section: Local News 
 
 512
 Words 

 Read News Document

 OXFORD — After a presentation on the Town of Oxford's fiscal year 2023 audit, commissioners received suggestions on how the town could address a material weakness for its segregation of duties.During a Commissioners of Oxford meeting Tuesday evening, Roy Geiser, a partner at the accounting firm UHY, went through the highlights of the financial report. For fiscal year 2023, Oxford received an unmodified opinion, the highest level of assurance that can be given by an auditor.
"And what that means is (that) these financials as presented, in our opinion, are free of any material misstatements," Geiser said.
Toward the end of his presentation, Geiser detailed a material weakness that was found regarding the town's segregation of duties — meaning that there aren't enough town employees to separate financial duties.
"A lot of towns your size have this exact comment," Geiser said about the finding.
There are three levels of of control deficiencies that auditors can find, Geiser said. These are: a deficiency, a significant deficiency or a material weakness.
Geiser said that material weakness is the most severe of these deficiencies. If found, a material weakness needs to be communicated by the auditor via a letter.
This is not the first year the Town of Oxford has received this comment about the lack of internal controls in its audit. According to the financial reports posted on the town website, this has been a finding in town audits going back to 2016.
Geiser suggested that commissioners ask questions if they ever notice something "out of line" when it comes to town finances.
After Geiser's presentation, Commissioner Katrina Greer asked him how other towns handle this material weakness issue.
Geiser said that while some towns don't do anything, others use a third-party consultant.
"They maybe bring them in quarterly just to have another set of eyes looking around," he said.
Some other towns, Geiser said, will have council member involved or set up an audit committee. He said an audit committee is "very rare" for a town the size of Oxford.
Greer said this is something the commissioners will be talking about more in the future.
At the previous town meeting on Jan. 11, Greer said she would like to discuss the possibility of hiring someone with a finance or accounting background to take on some of the town's financial duties in order to address this issue with internal controls.
"This would take some burden off the manager and enable us to comply with the audit recommendation of having multiple people performing financial roles," she said at the meeting.
Town Manager Cheryl Lewis said she had shared originally this idea with the commissioners because hiring more employees is the way to solve this problem.
"Admittedly most towns our size can't afford more staff," Lewis said at the Jan. 11 meeting. "Oxford is not in that situation, per se."
At the meeting Tuesday, one resident asked Geiser if hiring a part-time employee could solve the issue.
"In a perfect world, you want at least three people in your accounting function," Geiser said. "There are ways to get around it with other checks and balances. So a part-time person could help that situation."

title: Second amendment introduced for Lakeside unit resolution
author: Natalie Jones
content:
Second amendment introduced for Lakeside unit resolution

 January 26, 2024 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: Natalie Jones | Section: Environment 
 
 764
 Words 

 Read News Document

 EASTON — A second amendment to previously introduced legislation relating to the number of equivalent dwelling units in each phase of development at Lakeside at Trappe was introduced Tuesday by two Talbot County Council members.The amendment, requested by council Vice President Pete Lesher and introduced by him and council member Lynn Mielke, would modify the still-pending Resolution 347 to incorporate provisions of separate, but related, Lakeside legislation — Resolution 338 and its amendment — into its language.
The original version of Resolution 347, first introduced last September, would amend the county's comprehensive plan to include the number of equivalent dwelling units for each phase of development at Lakeside, though the numbers for Phases 2 through 6 are estimated.
It also provides the current water and sewer classifications for each phase. A total of 2,874 equivalent dwelling units are planned at Lakeside.
The language to be incorporated from Resolution 338 proposes amending the county's comprehensive water and sewer plan to be consistent with the Maryland Department of the Environment's discharge permit for Lakeside's wastewater treatment plant.
The permit, issued in October 2022, is limited to the project's first phase and allows for an annual average flow of 100,000 gallons per day, or roughly 250 gallons per day per equivalent dwelling unit, only allowing for roughly 400 residential units to be built.
A major permit modification approved by the Maryland Department of the Environment is required for any future expansion of the wastewater treatment plant.
Resolution 338's provisions also would mandate any future expansion of the new plant to require a comprehensive water and sewer plan amendment.
The resolution's amendment, introduced in November, adds language requiring a certification from the Talbot County Planning Commission of the amendment's consistency with the county's comprehensive plan.
At Tuesday's council meeting, Lesher emphasized that none of the language proposed to be added to Resolution 347 via its second amendment is new. It's a different way to help the county's Planning Commission come to a finding of consistency, he said.
Resolution 347, though considered in a multi-hour Planning Commission meeting last October, has yet to receive any final determination of consistency, which is required when amending the county's comprehensive water and sewer plan.
Multiple postponements of discussion on the legislation have lengthened the process, though the amended language of Resolution 338 was found consistent by the Planning Commission in December.
"This simply gives an alternative for the Planning Commission to say, 'Yes, with this language, if you combine it, we can find this consistent,'" Lesher said. "They may find Resolution 347 consistent without this amendment, they may find it consistent both without and with this amendment. If we get those alternatives, we then have that option to act at the council level."
The need for Resolution 347 stems from a request from the Maryland Department of the Environment last spring.
The agency asked the county to submit updated phase information and figures for water and sewer services with corrected classifications for all parcels within Trappe, including Lakeside, in a comprehensive water and sewer plan amendment.
Related legislation, Resolution 348, addresses the incorrect water and sewer classifications of parcels shown in two exhibits to Resolution 281, the original legislation approving a wastewater treatment plant for Lakeside under a draft discharge permit.
"Without that finding of consistency though, this resolution doesn't reach our desk," Lesher added, "and we don't have that way of bringing closure to the outstanding issues from MDE that will allow us to finish that Report of the Review."
Council Member Keasha Haythe questioned the need to add language from Resolution 338 into Resolution 347, saying the addition seemed to be the opposite of what the Maryland Department of the Environment requested.
The Town of Trappe is not on the same page as the county regarding the resolutions, she pointed out. Later, Haythe confirmed that the initial resolutions proposed were in line with what the agency wanted from the county.
The county's Planning Commission and the Public Works Advisory Board are set to discuss the two pending resolutions and amendments in a joint meeting on Wednesday, Feb. 7, at 11 a.m.
A public hearing on all three Lakeside resolutions and amendments will be held at 6:30 p.m. at the Tuesday, Feb. 13, County Council meeting.
Following Tuesday's meeting, council President Chuck Callahan issued a statement on the pending legislation.
"We understand that the resolutions regarding the county's comprehensive water and sewer plan and the Town of Trappe can be difficult to follow. It is a complicated matter with a lengthy history," he said in the statement. "The council looks forward to addressing this matter on Feb. 13, 2024, and resolving the concerns raised by the Maryland Department of the Environment."

title: Caroline Commissioners hear from record crowd on DAF storage
author: Connie Connolly
content:
Caroline Commissioners hear from record crowd on DAF storage

 January 27, 2024 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: Connie Connolly | Section: Local News 
 
 1976
 Words 

 Read News Document

 DENTON — "Are we the Green Garden County?" Tolbert Rowe asked rhetorically, alluding to Caroline County's longtime nickname.The Caroline County native, businessman and well-known leader wrapped up an hour and a half of public comments to cheers and applause: "At some point, we're going to have to sue somebody, and I say do it, because we're tired of people coming and pooping in our yard and not cleaning up after themselves."
The Caroline County Commissioners heard from Rowe and some two dozen of the more than 150 county residents and visitors who attended a public hearing on DAF residual storage from 6 to 8 p.m. Tuesday, Jan. 23, in the conference room of the Health and Public Services Building in Denton.
Commission Vice President Larry Porter said it was the largest attendance for a public hearing he had seen during his 14-year tenure.
{p class="p1"}The DAF storage issue and how to deal with it began when the commissioners, at their Dec. 12 meeting, heard from property owners who complained about odor and flies believed to be emanating from a DAF residuals storage pit on River Road near Greensboro.
As a result, the commissioners adopted Resolution 2023-025 as a "temporary moratorium on certain use of land or structures for storage of food processing residual and/or DAF residuals in Caroline County" for 60 days, starting Dec. 19.
The moratorium doesn't apply to structures or land used for storage of those residuals prior to Jan. 1, 2023.
Many at the hearing fear the same type of operation is gearing up on the outskirts of Ridgely.
While the standing room only crowd at the public hearing was concerned, upset and seeking answers, they were civil and appreciative of those who testified and the commissioners' efforts to study the issue and decide how to regulate it.
Since that time, the commissioners enacted a 60-day moratorium on new DAF residual storage while they research the issue and decide how to regulate it.
A diverse crowd of farmers and environmentalists, outdoor enthusiasts and parents, business owners and civic leaders, as well as officials from the Maryland Departments and Agriculture and Environment attended the hearing, many of whom filled the hallway outside the conference room.
Deputy County Administrator Daniel Fox narrated a slide show describing the purpose and scope of the hearing and defining the terms.
DAF RESIDUALS DEFINEDDAF, or dissolved air flotation, "is a method used to process wastewater that comes from any food processing plant in which dissolved air is injected into the wastewater. These air bubbles attach to particles, causing them to float to the surface where they can then be removed by a skimming device," Fox read.
However, "DAF Residuals is the semi-solid slurry of small particles of fats, proteins and other fibrous materials that were removed from the skimming process." Much of this material is generated from poultry processing plants on Delmarva, and some comes from industrial and wastewater treatment sludge.
It is DAF residuals and the responsible handling of the byproduct, which comes from outside the county, that prompted many to share their concerns, knowledge and experiences.
Caroline County Commission President Travis Breeding opened the hearing.
"I want to be clear: The county has received no formal applications for the storage of DAF," he said. "All storage that has been occurring in the county so far has been undisclosed to us, and it has largely been in repurposed facilities around the county — either former dairy cattle manure bins or other structures that have been repurposed. … It's just been done without our knowledge."
Breeding said the commissioners' intention is "to have a workshop with Maryland Department of Agriculture, Maryland Department of Environment and industry representatives to generate some type of regulations to control the storage, so it doesn't have a negative impact on the county.
"Once those regulations are generated, it will go through the legislative process, which does include public hearings again, so there will be another opportunity for the residents of the county to comment on whatever final decision or final proposal the commissioners come up with."
The commissioners stated public comments will be accepted during the legislative process.
CONCERNS AIREDWhile not naming anyone in particular, several referred to a "bad actor" they wanted held accountable, and they appealed to the commissioners to extend the 60-day moratorium.
Nearly 50 people signed up to testify, but about half said their concerns had been addressed by others who were asked to limit their remarks to three minutes.
Most speaking were concerned with their health — breathing the "stench" emitted from stored DAF residuals, pathogens possibly leeching into well water and waterways, and the increase of flying insects and the possibility of their carrying diseases.
Jean Meyer of Greensboro said she lives adjacent to one of the several farms owned by the "individual that we're talking about tonight" who "got a permit for nothing that he's done."
"We all have shallow wells; (DAF residuals) could contaminate the water," Meyer said. "Who's gonna put in a new well, who's gonna pay for my medical bills, if I should become sick from the runoff?"
An electrician and a former worker in the nuclear field both said they would be cited for noncompliance.
"I work in the nuclear field and … if you blatantly disregard rules and regulations, you get the hammer dropped on you," said Dan Marron of Greensboro.
A case was made by Ridgely Town Commissioner Anthony Casey, who focused primarily on the former Hanover Foods property and "a proposed DAF site a half-mile away from the town limits (that) will affect the entire population of the town, currently at 1,870."
Casey listed how DAF residual storage near the town would have a "crippling effect on the town's culture and economy," including the possible relocation of the Cow Barn Athletic Complex. Also adversely affected would be "every business," Ridgely Elementary School, Ridgely Memorial Park, the Rails to Trails path, Martin Sutton Park and the Caroline Humane Society, among others.
Events such as Ridgely's Winter Festival, the Lions Club's annual Strawberry Festival and the annual district Little League All-Star tournaments would be marred by the odor and increased number of flies, Casey said.
"The town of Ridgely is 100% against DAF storage of any kind," he said, speaking on behalf of the town commissioners, town staff and residents. He urged the county commissioners to "not only approve resolution 2023-025" but to "shut this operation down entirely."
Debbie Bostic, who lives on Peaviner Road across from "the pit where the sludge is supposed to be dumped" on the former Hanover Foods property, said she was worried about the increased heavy truck traffic and pollution of nearby waterways. "We will no longer be able to enjoy the great outdoors," she said.
The 400-member Tuckahoe Equestrian Club was represented by several members, and two running groups who use Tuckahoe State Park for events expressed their concerns.
STATE VS. COUNTY ROLESThe county commissioners and staff distinguished the county's role in regulating DAF residual storage from the state of Maryland's authority.
"Caroline County has no authority to prohibit the application of DAF to farmland," Fox told the audience. However, "MDA and MDE do not regulate the storage of DAF residuals; therefore, Caroline County is not preempted by the State regarding the storage of DAF residuals."
While both Delaware and Virginia require permits for DAF residual storage, Maryland does not, prompting its being trucked into Eastern Shore counties.
"It's a dumping ground, and it's got to stop," Alan Girard said following the meeting. The Eastern Shore director of the Chesapeake Bay Foundation said, "The state needs to step up. The General Assembly has the power to charge (MDE and MDA) to safely regulate this material. And that's what they should do."
Girard and Matt Pluta, Choptank Riverkeeper with ShoreRivers drew attention to the environmental impacts, their remarks eliciting applause and cheers from the audience, composed mostly of rural residents and farmers.
Girard cited examples of DAF residual storage complaints CBF has fielded from other Maryland counties, as well as steps the foundation has taken to get answers from state agencies.
He referred to a University of Maryland report issued in September in which "they say there's no comprehensive public database to track DAF generation, shipment and composition."
Girard said once a year state chemists test "material …. generated from these industrial rendering facilities — I know people have concern with that term; I don't use it lightly."
"So, when it gets in the storage facilities and comingles, and farmers are trying to abide by their nutrient management regs and receive a load of this stuff, what's in it? Nobody knows," he said. "And there's good farmers in the room behind me that are trying to do the right thing. … They try to apply it safely."
Pluta said DAF residuals are "an industrial waste product. … It is generated by facilities that hold discharge permits, but the loophole in the state is that once it's turned over to a hauler or somebody to use on their farm it becomes a soil amendment."
Citing pathogens researchers have found in DAF material, Pluta questioned why DAF isn't regulated by the state. "They have regulations for poultry manure. They even make you register your beehives. Why can't we register DAF?" he said. "Why is the state pushing this on to the counties to manage, when they certainly have the tools to manage it at a state level?"
Girard made a distinction between responsible farmers and those who skirt permitting requirements and regulations.
"We need to make sure that we're backing our farming community, making sure that the bad actors are held accountable, and we can allow agriculture to continue on the Delmarva Peninsula," Girard said.
CALLS FOR CAUTIONDenton resident Holly Porter is executive director of the Delmarva Chicken Association, a trade organization representing the $5 billion industry. She pointed out the "three-legged stool" of the chicken companies, and the chicken growers and grain farmers, many of whom in Caroline County, who use soil amendments.
She said it appeared the county was dealing with a "bad actor."
"We've heard that (DAF residuals) are a registered soil amendment by the Maryland Department of Agriculture and by the state chemists. These are ag products," she said.
Disputing the representation of DAF residuals as "industrial" products, she asked, "What other industrial item is stored? That would be called commercial fertilizer, which is also made in an industrial site, is an ag product and is used on farm fields as well."
Cow Barn Events owner Marty Collison is also a poultry farmer.
"This DAF operation would put me out of business," he said. His venue hosts indoor and outdoor events, including weddings. However, he suggested to the commissioners that science equals solutions.
Collison advised against "knee jerk reactions. Do your homework. Get the data. Know what is out there, what they're spreading. Is it really dangerous? And then make an informed decision, and it may have to be some compromise between the ag community and the events venue community."
Girard advised the commissioners to "pass the moratorium and wait for the state to act, and if they don't act … keep the moratorium in place. We need a statewide solution."
The commissioners stated, "Any property that the County is aware of that is in violation of the moratorium has been issued a cease-and-desist order."
"We are we are working through the court system," Breeding said. "We don't have the ability to just go out and put somebody in handcuffs. It's got to go through the court system, so we're working through that."
The loudest round of applause and cheering followed a brief statement by Steve Fleegle, who can see the Hartland Holdings River Road operation from his home. "I have not heard one positive thing out of this whole hearing tonight, and we've been here for almost an hour."
"All we're doing is enriching people from out of state with these chicken plants," Fleegle said. "I implore you guys to shut this thing down as soon as you can, because it's not fair to us. We were here first. We didn't ask for this, and we don't deserve this." 

 © Copyright © 2024 Star Democrat, Chesapeake Publishing Group (Adams Publishing/APGMedia). All rights reserved.

Environmental and agricultural concerns are discussed, but the primary focus is the governmental process.

title: Harris: No offshore wind turbines
author: Connie Connolly
content:
Harris: No offshore wind turbines

 January 27, 2024 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: Connie Connolly | Section: Local News 
 
 1914
 Words 

 Read News Document

 OCEAN CITY — Outside the doors of the Roland E. Powell Convention Center in Ocean City, two masked protestors stood quietly with posters criticizing U.S. Rep. Andy Harris (R-Md.).Just inside, two volunteers handed out postcards stating, "Stop Offshore Wind" and "Join Facebook group 'Protect Ocean City.'"
In the auditorium, Worcester County residents slowly filed in. At least 300 people came out in below freezing temperatures Saturday afternoon, Jan. 20, for a congressional hearing held on their sandy turf.
Warning of dire consequences if offshore wind industrialization is allowed off Maryland's Atlantic coast, three legislators called on experts to bolster their call to halt construction of wind turbines off the mid-Atlantic coast. Harris was joined by New Jersey Congressmen Jeff Van Drew (R) and Chris Smith (R).
EXPERTS WARN OF DANGERS
Six experts testified and answered questions from the legislators. whose districts "are directly impacted" by "offshore wind industrialization," according to news releases issued by the congressmen's offices.
The panel of experts focused on the negative impacts of offshore wind energy to the fishing industry, environment and energy policy, national security, tourism, the local economy — including the Mid-Shore counties — and even the medical value of horseshoe crabs.
While the general economic impact of offshore wind development was explored, Harris told The Star Democrat following the hearing that allowing wind turbines off the coast of Ocean City to generate power would increase energy costs for all Eastern Shore residents.
Harris doubted that "the average person would be willing to pay the extra taxes and extra rates in order to develop a source of energy that … is roughly four times as expensive as what your current source of energy is," he said. "That impacts everyone whether or not you live on the Shore."
Harris lives in Dorchester County.
"Most people I know who open their electric bills this year say, 'Wow, I can't believe it's that much higher than it was last year," Harris said. "It will get even higher if we insist on producing very high-cost sources of energy."
"We might be willing to bear the costs, but are we ready to industrialize the ocean floor?" he said.
One of those costs is the increase in deaths of whales and dolphins, which the legislators attributed to the construction of wind turbines. Smith called them the "canaries in the coalmine" and blamed the Biden administration and New Jersey Gov. Phil Murphy for their "(refusal) to even listen to the numerous warnings from local leaders, mayors and state senators" and "continuing with false promises."
Smith said the construction of 3,400 offshore wind turbines across 2.4 million acres was being "fast-tracked."
Lisa Linowes is executive director of WindAction Group, which studies and provides information on "the potential harmful impacts of large-scale wind energy facilities on wildlife and the natural environment."
Although Linowes has been concerned about the dangers posed to marine life, She expressed concerns about maritime safety, and the Biden Administration's relaxing of regulations designed to protect baleen, right and humpback whales, sentiments echoed by others on the panel.
For instance, radar interference, physical obstacles and turbulence caused by wind turbines pose dangers to aircraft, according to the Coast Guard and Air Force, she said, and no "comprehensive assessment" has been conducted.
Other panelists agreed with Linowes' assessment of the dangers, and Harris said radar interference constituted a national security concern.
Meghan Lapp of Seafreeze, a Rhode Island commercial fishing company, said offshore wind turbines would interfere with "all classes of U.S. radar."
In December 2023, a new series of leases were proposed farther off the Maryland coast, Harris said, but were "withdrawn from consideration by the Bureau of Ocean Energy Management because of protests from the Department of Defense and from NASA, who said that those leasing areas would adversely affect our ability to maintain national security and, in the case of NASA, … interfere with the Wallops Flight Center."
In addition to maritime safety concerns, Linowes said the "discrepancy between federal treatment of ocean industries is staggering," citing federal agencies' downplaying correlations between "last year's surge of large baleen whale deaths on the East Coast coinciding with unprecedented offshore wind seismic surveys."
"Had the whale deaths coincided with oil and gas surveys instead of offshore wind surveys, the pause and investigation requested by the congressmen would have been standard procedure," she said.
Robert Rand of Rand Acoustics LLC in Brunswick, Maine, said underwater testing and sonar surveys by offshore wind development was damaging the hearing of marine mammals, which is vital to their survival.
"I know how to measure sound," Rand said. "More than that, I care about whales."
His independent surveys of whale populations off the coasts of Hawaii and Cape Cod revealed stark contrasts in their communication patterns, suggesting that, even with NOAA's noise mitigation requirements, whales were adversely affected by high decibel sounds associated with offshore wind development, he said.
Panelist Travis Fisher is the director of energy and environmental policy studies at the Cato Institute. With wind turbine power, he said Marylanders would end up paying more for wind, in addition to a backup source of power, hitting lower income residents harder.
Observing the results of California and Germany's green energy policies has been instructive, he said.
"Both places have chosen to embrace intermittent energy at the expense of reliable energy," he said. "Germany's energy transition has caused its residents to pay three times more for electricity than we pay in the United States. California has higher electricity prices than any other state in the lower 48."
"It's not too late to recognize the folly of a forced energy transition," Fisher said. "There is no justification for an off-shore wind mandate."
Also testifying was Bonnie Brady of the Long Island Commercial Fishing Association.
LOCAL LEADERS UNIFY
Although Danish company Ørsted canceled two off-shore wind projects in fall 2023, it was continuing to develop Skipjack Wind 20 miles off the Maryland coast.
However, on Jan. 25, Ørsted announced it had "withdrawn from the Maryland Public Service Commission orders approving the Skipjack 1 and 2 projects" following "consultation with the State of Maryland" and "an extensive review of the orders." It cited "challenging market conditions, including inflation, high interest rates and supply chain constraints" as reasons for the decision.
The company "intends to continue advancing development and permitting for the combined project, including submission of its updated Construction and Operations Plan to the Bureau of Ocean Energy Management," according to a press release.
Harris said another company besides Ørsted holds a Maryland offshore lease, a "cleverly named U.S. Wind, which is a wholly owned subsidiary of an Italian company."
The project doesn't sit well with Worcester County and Ocean City's leaders, four of whom spoke during the hearing.
"The Bureau of Ocean Energy Management's own environmental impact statement study further convinced me that the potential negative impacts of offshore wind industrialization off Maryland's Coast outweighs the many promised benefits by European-based offshore wind developers," said state Sen. Mary Beth Carozza (R-Somerset, Wicomico, Worcester).
"With my prior work experience at the Pentagon and the U.S. Senate Homeland Security Committee, I especially am sensitive to the security and safety concerns raised by the Department of Defense, including the detrimental effect of wind turbines on existing radar systems by false alarms and missed detection of real targets," Carozza said.
Mainly concerned with tourism, they warned of potential hazards caused by strong storms, and even the health of the horseshoe crab population.
Del. Wayne Hartman (R-Wicomico, Worcester) said the "vast majority" of constituents who had contacted him were "adamantly opposed to the implementation of offshore wind projects."
"According to a study from North Carolina State University, 55% of vacation renters would not return to the vacation destination if turbines were visible," he said. "This is very concerning for the future of economic development in Ocean City as tourism accounts for the largest percentage of the local economy."
"We have a horseshoe crab harvest here critical for the safety of injectable medications, yet there were plans to put turbines right in horseshoe sanctuary areas," Pat Shrawder of said. She is district representative for state Sen. Mary Beth Carozza (R-Somerset, Wicomico, Worcester).
"My understanding is that the horseshoe crab industry is centered in the mid-Atlantic here," Harris said. "As a physician I'll tell you, a lot of people don't know when you get an intravenous medication of any kind — something that comes out of a sterile intravenous vial — that batch has been tested against a derivative of horseshoe crabs to make sure it doesn't have bacterial endotoxin — something that would kill you."
Electromagnetic fields and underwater cables would also interfere with horseshoe crabs' migration paths.
The effect of strong storms on wind turbines has not been adequately studied, Harris said.
"Our residents are fearful of the effect of hurricane force winds on wind turbulence," Schrawder said. "Ocean City is subject to strong northeasters or hurricanes. Even the EIS (Enterprise Infrastructure Solutions of the U.S. General Services Administration) report states that a hurricane could result in the loss of a blade and or turbine collapse. We worry about a football field-sized blade hurtling (sic) through the air."
Ocean City Mayor Rick Meehan, a Republican who has served as mayor since 2006, galvanized the mostly local audience. He said he represented 26,000 property owners, residents and a million visitors who stand in "total opposition to the proposed U.S. Wind project."
"The discussion on wind turbines off the coast of Ocean City goes back as far as 2010," Meehan said. "Yet this is the first time a committee from the federal government has actually held a hearing here in Ocean City."
Meehan said the wind turbines would mar the resort's vista. "The sunrise over the Atlantic would look like a backdrop from Star Wars," he said.
"The first time I saw the renderings of what U.S. Wind was proposing — and at the time, those were four megawatt or possibly six megawatt turbines approximately 450 feet tall — I had stated our opposition to the size and locations of those turbines at that time seven years ago. Our concerns fell on deaf ears," Meehan said. "Today, those same turbines are now 18 megawatt turbines at … maybe 1,065 feet in height, and they're proposing the same locations. Our concerns continue to fall on deaf ears."
"What has also been ignored is the revenue that Ocean City sends: Millions of dollars to both the state and the federal government each year," Meehan said. "We only have one industry in Ocean City, and that's tourism. Why would the state or the federal government want to unnecessarily jeopardize our future?"
"What I can assure you is that the Town of Ocean City will not back down from our opposition to these projects and to our future here in Ocean City," Meehan said as the audience applauded and cheered.
FIGHT CONTINUES
U.S. Wind, the Bureau of Ocean Energy Management and the National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration were invited to attend the hearing. U.S. Wind did not respond and the federal agencies "declined to attend," Harris said.
Smith said "calls for an honest review of offshore wind industrialization has left unaddressed and unanswered so many questions; so much so, that in March of last year, Andy Harris, Jeff Van Drew and I offered an amendment that passed 244 to 189 to have the watchdog of Congress, the Government Accountability Office, investigate the impacts of wind turbines, and their audit will be coming out very soon."
The bottom line for Harris: "I believe it's time to reconsider whether offshore wind is the right approach for Maryland."
Van Drew was more pointed. "We have a war to win," he said. "Do not succumb, do not be weak, and we will prevail."
To watch the entire hearing, go to www.youtube.com/watch?v=1ThWS1FT1Qo

title: Community involvement critical to government
author: Staff Writer
content:
Community involvement critical to government

 January 28, 2024 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: Staff Writer | Section: Columns 
 
 568
 Words 

 Read News Document

 Community involvement is critical to the effective and ongoing improvement of local government. We have seen what difference it made in Talbot County in the multiple efforts to address the Lakeside issues and in Dorchester County in the successful lawsuit by Shore Rivers and The Dorchester Citizens for Planned Growth against Valley Proteins that still needs community oversight.Jim Brady and WHCP Radio have brought important information to the community about Dorchester County audits and the differences of opinion with regard to the development of Cambridge Harbor.
Another instance of community engagement was the effort by the Dorchester Citizens for Better Government to collect signatures on petitions to amend the county charter. While unsuccessful, it prompted the current county council to reestablish their Charter Commission that is working to propose charter amendments for vote in November 2024.
Maryland is made up of 23 counties and over 150 cities and towns, each with its own elected leadership. Just because we go and vote for these candidates does not mean that our job is over as citizens. Those who are elected, whether we voted for them or not, need to be encouraged about and watched with regard to the issues of governance put before them.
Those decisions impact our lives as well as the lives of everyone in our communities. Bad decisions can impact communities for years and can take a great deal of effort and money to overcome.
Now, getting involved is not an easy task. Our lives today are as busy as ever and asking a few people to do all of the watching, even in a small town, is just not reasonable. However, leaving elected officials to act without scrutiny is not a formula for good government.
In Cambridge, our city manager always tries to provide the community with the opportunity to meet and learn about important proposals and provide their opinions. The City Council for proposed ordinances including our budget have second readings and public hearings to hear from the community. Too often, those meetings are not well attended. One reason could be that the proposal is a good one and the community is fine with it. Another could be that the community is just not interested.
In Cambridge, we are fortunate to have the Cambridge Association of Neighborhoods (CAN). It started as a small group of citizens that felt that an existing neighborhood organization was not doing enough. CAN continues to grow and spread across the city in numbers and has people who regularly attend some of the important meetings involving the city, county, and school board to inform the community as to what is happening.
Could there be other neighborhood associations doing the same thing here in Cambridge?
Certainly, but creating new neighborhood associations rather than creating smaller neighborhood groups as part of CAN for different parts of the city would be more work than is necessary, but more of the city needs to be heard from in order to address the multiple challenges that face our community.
If you think that more needs to be done, reach out to CAN and learn more about what it does and how you might be able to help. We are having City Council elections this year and helping the community to know who is running for what position and what their qualifications are is important for the welfare of our community and improvement of the place where we live.
Stephen Rideout is the mayor in Cambridge.

title: Federalsurg water lines go dry as pump fails
author: TOM MCCALL
content:
Federalsurg water lines go dry as pump fails

 January 29, 2024 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: TOM MCCALL | Section: Local News 
 
 353
 Words 

 Read News Document

 FEDERALSBURG — The Town of Federalsburg remains without running water Monday morning despite efforts to fix a failed well and restore pressure.The problem began Friday night after a power outage at the town's water and sewage plant. The power outage depleted water in the system and left air in the lines.
Mayor Kim Abner said an alert system did not go off Friday night when one of the town's water pumps failed to work. She said currently all three pumps are working and that they are pumping 600,000 gallons to fill the system. She said Department of Emergency Services was distributing water to people.
Abner said Monday morning that she expects the water to be back soon. Abner said an investigation will be undertaken to figure out why this happened so it can be avoided in the future.
She said the town staff and council members have been pitching in to help people get water.
The latest Facebook post reported progress at 9:30 a.m. Monday.
"Staff will be delivering meals. Meals will be at fire department. All three wells are back online and pressure is coming up," the post read. "We are now pumping 500 gallons a minute, but we need to fill the water towers and lines that were empty. It will take time, but we are making progress."
Bottled water for pick up is available at Federalsburg Volunteer Fire Department Company at noon.
Abner is telling people not to turn on their faucets yet to allow pressure to build up in the pipes.
A Facebook statement from the mayor, council and staff said, "Water conditions have not improved like they should have. We have called in a well specialist for assistance. In the meantime, we are working on sourcing drinking water for our residents. Once we have a distribution location, we will let you know. We sincerely apologize for any inconvenience and appreciate your understanding. Staff worked tirelessly yesterday (Sunday) to try to restore services and truly thought time would have allowed the lines to fill and restore pressure."
Abner said some people have been calm and some have been agitated on Facebook, but that solutions are in progress.

title: Federalsburg works to resolve water, sewer issues
author: Connie Connolly
content:
Federalsburg works to resolve water, sewer issues

 January 30, 2024 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: Connie Connolly | Section: Local News 
 
 472
 Words 

 Read News Document

 FEDERALSBURG — Following a water shutdown that began Friday, Jan. 26, the town of Federalsburg announced Tuesday evening that water service was restored.However, another difficulty challenged town officials before 1 p.m. Tuesday when a sinkhole developed on Maple Avenue, caused by "an issue with the sewer main," according to the town's official Facebook page.
"Further details to be determined once the water is drained and the pipe can actually be observed," the post stated. "The crew is working on the repair as we speak and no services to residents will be affected." The 300 block of Maple Ave will be closed until the repairs are complete.
One resident commented on the post: "It's OK. We can't drink the water so we don't need the toilet. All good."
As for water service, the "system continues to replenish itself," the town announced on Facebook. Residents were asked to conserve water and to be aware of air bubbles or cloudiness in the water. "This is normal and will return to normal once all air is out of the line," the post stated.
The water problem began Friday night after a power outage at the town's water and sewage plant. The outage caused the town's water pumps to fail, depleting the water in the system and leaving air in the lines.
Mayor Kim Abner said an alert system did not go off Friday night when one of the town's water pumps failed to work. She said Monday that all three pumps were up and running, pumping 600,000 gallons to fill the system.
The Maryland Department of the Environment recommended Monday afternoon that the mayor and town council post that "regular and bacterial testing is in process and results will be posted as soon as this info is available."
Bottled water was available at the Federalsburg Fire House until 7 p.m. Tuesday, Jan. 30. The Maryland National Guard also provided a tank of water for residents to fill their own containers.
Town staff delivered meals at Federalsburg Volunteer Fire Company, as well as bottled water available for pick up. Caroline County Public Schools provided bottled water to Federalsburg Elementary School and the Judy Center.
On Monday morning, the town had posted on its Facebook page, "All three wells are back online and pressure is coming up. We are now pumping 500 gallons a minute, but we need to fill the water towers and lines that were empty. It will take time, but we are making progress."
In a Tuesday afternoon text message to The Star Democrat, Abner said town officials "will be having a debrief on the event with staff and external entities as to how we can prevent something like this from happening again if there is another power outage."
"We want to thank all of the neighboring Towns and agencies for their assistance," Abner's text message said.
Star Democrat reporter Tom McCall contributed to this story.

title: Sewage overflows in Cambridge, city prioritizing improvements
author: MAGGIE TROVATO mtrovato@chespub.com
content:
Sewage overflows in Cambridge, city prioritizing improvements

 January 31, 2024 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: MAGGIE TROVATO mtrovato@chespub.com | Section: Local News 
 
 779
 Words 

 Read News Document

 CAMBRIDGE — Harford County resident Jayne Ash saw more than she expected on Jan. 13 when she brought a group of people to Cambridge to look at birds.The end of Oakley Street, near the Choptank River, was flooded that day, Ash said.
"And the overflow was not draining," she said.
The group began to notice a white residue on the sidewalks, which seemed to have been left by the water, now below the curb but still flooding the street.
"The longer we stood there and the longer we looked, we just realized that this was just really nasty sewage water," Ash said, adding that she saw what looked like human feces floating in the water.
As the group was leaving the area, Ash said she could see a leak "coming out of the street," bubbling up six to eight inches.
The entire experience worried Ash.
"We figured we probably shouldn't be walking in the water," she said. "So we were kind of tiptoeing around the edges of where we normally would have gone."
Ash said the city should have roped off the area, posted signs and pumped up the flooded water to transport it elsewhere.
"It's just so many things that they could have done, but I guess they weren't keeping aware of it," she said.
According to the Code of Maryland Regulations, the owner or operator of any sewer system is required to report any overflow — defined as a loss of wastewater or discharge from a sewer system — to the Maryland Department of the Environment and local health department. This report must be made no later than 24 hours after the owner or operator becomes aware of the overflow.
COMAR also states that unless advised otherwise by the state or local health department, the owner or operator of the sewer system must notify the public no later than 24 hours after they become aware of the overflow if it enters shellfish harvesting waters, drinking water sources, waters used as public beaches or waters used for public recreation.
They must also notify the public if the state or local health department has reason to believe the overflow is a public health risk
The public must be notified via a public service announcement or paid advertising in a daily newspaper, radio station, or television station. According to COMAR, if appropriate, the public should be notified of larger overflows with potential environmental or health impacts through posted signage, as well as through the media.
On Jan. 17, the city submitted a telephone report to MDE. In a letter attached to the report, signed by Cambridge City Engineer Carl "Bucky" Jackson, Jackson said that high tides caused the sewage overflow event on Jan. 13.
According to the report, the city was informed of the overflow by MDE on Jan. 17 following a complaint from a resident. No personnel from the city observed the overflow.
Jackson said in the report that based on the National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration's Cambridge tide gauge, the overflow is estimated to have begun at 8 a.m. and stopped around 11:59 p.m on Jan. 13.
Jackson wrote that discharge from the overflow wasn't observed, but paper products were discovered around around the manhole where the overflow occurred. Once notified, the street and storm drains were cleaned and disinfected.
In an interview, Jackson said signage notifying residents and visitors of the overflow were placed at the location of the event within four hours of the city learning about it.
Jackson said it was surprising that high tide was the sole cause of this incident. He said that, usually, the cause is a mix of high tide and heavy rains.
Water and sewer infrastructure improvements are one of the city's priorities this year.
Cambridge City Council has set out a $20 million capital program over the next five years for water and sewer infrastructure. The city has budgeted $8 million for fiscal year 2024.
During a meeting between Cambridge City Council, city staff and local state legislators last Monday, Jan. 22, City Manager Tom Carroll said Cambridge annually gets fined for violating the Clean Water Act.
"We are focused on fixing the sewer issues and reducing or eliminating overflows," he said at the meeting.
Earlier this month, the City Council awarded a contract bid to replace the West End sewer, located in the lowest lying area of the city at Water Street and Hambrooks Boulevard.
"Routinely, we have elicit discharges when we have wet weather events," Carroll said. "We have sewage overflows. And we're hoping that this project will fix that."
Jackson said the West End sewer replacement will benefit Oakley Street near the river.
Carroll said there are three other major sewer projects planned that are in "various stages of design" as well as a water booster station to accommodate new development.
