title: Rideout, Harrington not running for reelection
author: MAGGIE TROVATO mtrovato@chespub.com
content:
Rideout, Harrington not running for reelection

 June 5, 2024 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: MAGGIE TROVATO mtrovato@chespub.com | Section: Local News 
 
 745
 Words 

 Read News Document

 CAMBRIDGE — Come October, Cambridge voters will not see the names Stephen Rideout or Jameson Harrington on their ballots.The mayor and commissioner, respectively, have said they will not be seeking reelection for when their terms are up in 2025.
For Rideout, who is turning 81 this summer, this has always been the plan. He said when he ran in 2022, he only intended to fill the remainder of former Mayor Andrew Bradshaw's term.
Bradshaw resigned in January 2022 after being charged with 50 counts of distributing revenge porn on Reddit. In April 2022, Bradshaw pleaded guilty to five counts of distributing revenge porn.
In a June 3 interview with the Star Democrat, Rideout said part of the reason he ran was to help Cambridge see what a "weak mayor" should do. In a "weak mayor" government system, the mayor's power is limited.
Harrington, who was sworn into office in January 2021, said he made his decision not to run again about two years ago. He said he likes to volunteer and help, but politics is "just not my forte."
"I want to work with people that their only goal is to make Cambridge a better place to live for all," he said in a June 3 interview with the Star Democrat. "And unfortunately in politics, I've dealt with a lot of people that want to make it a better place to live only for themselves."
In his nearly four years as a commissioner, Harrington is proud of a lot of what the City Council has done. Three standouts, he said, are when former City Manager Tom Carroll was hired, when the town purchased a ladder truck for Rescue Fire Company and when the council passed legislation to establish the Land Bank Authority of Cambridge, which can take on, manage and sell vacant land in order to stabilize neighborhoods and encourage redevelopment.
Harrington said the creation of the land bank authority is something he had been hoping for since he took office.
"I wanted to see it through," he said.
One of the most important goals for the city moving forward, Harrington said, is hiring Cambridge's next city manager. Carroll announced in March that he would be resigning from the city manager position. His last day was May 3.
"You've got to have a certain background to be able to handle a city like Cambridge," Harrington said about the city manager position. "You're not coming in where everything's already in place, and you're just filling a slot. There's actual work to be done."
When it comes to the mayor's seat, Rideout said that the city's next mayor should determine what the community's needs are and encourage support or changes to get those needs met. He said that as mayor, he has worked to address gun violence and children's issues, like juvenile justice reform. Rideout said he has been working with the state to find a better funding stream system for children's programs in rural or less wealthy communities.
He said homelessness is one issue that still needs to be addressed.
"We need to do more to find solutions for them," he said about Cambridge's unhoused population.
Rideout said he is most proud of the successes accomplished by others in Cambridge. He mentioned nonprofits New Beginnings Youth and Family Services, MidShore Meals Til Monday, the Cambridge Empowerment Center and ALL4LOVE.
"All of those programs have really taken off because of what they're doing and because of the vision that their leadership had, (which) we've been able to support it one way or another," he said. "That's what's important. Not what I've done."
Rideout brought up the "positive" direction that Dorchester County Public Schools is headed in.
Five years from now, Rideout hopes Cambridge will have better housing, more jobs available for adults and teens and more high school graduates who want to stay in Cambridge or return after college.
Harrington said he hopes that five years from now, Cambridge will still be "on the up and up," even if that progress is slow.
"Just in my time in Cambridge over the past 12 years, I've seen a lot of good things happen," he said. "It's not in the same place as it was when I moved here. It's in a better place, and I hope it continues on that trend."
Harrington said progress will come from the city having a good city manager and a council that supports the city manager.
"I love Cambridge," he said. "It's a great town full of great people despite some of the issues. And I know there's a bright future ahead."

Easton residents look to jumpstart discussion of soon-to-be vacant lot

 EASTON — Two Easton residents are seeking feedback on the prospects of a soon-to-be vacant one-acre lot on South Hanson St, which will be left when the Talbot County Health Department moves to a new location on Cadmus Lane later this month.Residents Greg Zimmerman and Joyce DeLaurentis created a survey to collect opinions of town residents on what the space could turn into. In the survey, it states that "with community support, there may be an opportunity for the Town of Easton to acquire this property" from the county.
Zimmerman, who has a background in business development and has lived in Easton for six years, feels this is a chance for community members to "lead on an issue rather than react to something later."
"The survey gives the community members a voice in the decision making process," Zimmerman said. "It'll also help the public officials understand community priorities."
The survey includes a list of multiple-choice questions measuring respondents' thoughts on potential uses for the space, such as a community pocket park, housing and small business startups. It also has open feedback questions for residents to fill out.
Thus far, Zimmerman has noticed many responses indicating residents would support a new community center, a multi-use park or a courtyard with small shops.Throughout his time in Easton, he also has noticed that the public's opinions are not always known, adding that the survey can "create a conduit between residents and public officials."
"When I have attended some of the meetings, I'm always wondering, 'What does the majority of the population feel about this?' Zimmerman said. "I don't know. And I don't really know if the town officials know either."
The property, which is owned by the county, is still operational and will be through most of June. County Manager Clay Stamp said the council will discuss the future prospects of the building and surrounding land "in the coming months."
"It's going to be a process that the County Council goes through," Stamp said. "I'm sure it's going to be a fairly open process. I'm sure they're going to be interested in getting input … That's going to be on their agenda in the coming months."
Stamp said the primary focus will be on moving the department into its new building, which will better house the department that has outgrown its current location.
"We're laser-focused on trying to get them into their new building, where they'll be able to better serve the community," Stamp said.
Talbot County Health Department spokesperson Justin Beall said a ribbon-cutting is set for the end of this month. The department's goal is to re-open at the new location by early July.
Results of the survey will be presented to Easton Town Council and Talbot County Council once county discussions concerning the property begin, according to Zimmerman. However, the survey will remain open for the foreseeable future to gather "as many responses as possible."
"We're not advocating for a specific outcome or on behalf of any interest group," Zimmerman said. "This is a grassroots effort to promote a process that encourages public input. Tell us what you think and we'll help amplify the collective voice of the community."
Residents can fill out the survey by emailing {span}eastoncommunitysurveys@gmail.com and filling out the anonymous form.

title: Easton Town Council holds off on annexation vote
author: Maggie Trovato
content:
Easton Town Council holds off on annexation vote

 June 5, 2024 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: Maggie Trovato | Section: Local News 
 
 717
 Words 

 Read News Document

 EASTON — Although the Easton Planning Commission recommended the annexation of land on the east side of Ocean Gateway for a potential affordable multifamily housing development project, the Easton Town Council was not ready to make a move on the recommended legislation at its meeting Monday evening.At the meeting, Zach Smith spoke on behalf Corrigan & Trippe Ventures, the company proposing the project. Smith said the company would like the Town of Easton to annex about 17 acres of Talbot County land.
The now-vacant property lies east of U.S. Route 50, between the Royal Farms and Unitarian Universalist Fellowship at Easton. It is designated as a priority one growth area in the town's comprehensive plan, which means the land is most likely "deemed appropriate for consideration for annexation," according to the plan.
Before Smith spoke, Town Planner Lynn Thomas said that after two meetings, the Easton Planning Commission voted to recommend the annexation request be approved, finding it consistent with the Comprehensive Plan. Thomas said the commission also recommended the Town Council apply the R10A zoning classification to the property, which is for medium-density residential use, according to the town zoning code.
Thomas said the Maryland Department of Planning believes a zoning waiver from the county will be necessary because of the difference in the proposed and existing zoning. Currently, the property is zoned as town conservation, according to the county website.
Although annexation is the only thing on the table right now, Smith went over rough plans for the project, making the argument that it will address Easton's need for more affordable housing.
While there is no definitive plan for the project, the drafted annexation agreement states that, at a minimum, the project will need to have at least 25% affordable housing for any developers that end up taking over the annexed property.
Smith said the company is committed to making 100% of the units affordable housing units.
During the meeting, Ward 4 Council Member the Rev. Elmer Davis Jr. asked Smith what affordable housing means to him.
"We have a lot of people that come before us and say that this is affordable housing," he said. "And I'm not quite sure anyone has fully defined what affordable housing is."
Smith said he believes affordable housing is making units available to people who make 50% to 60% of the community's median household income at a rent that does not exceed 30% of their income.
During a public hearing on the proposed legislation, Tom Alspach, who spoke on behalf of the Talbot Preservation Alliance, said that if they really wanted an estimated 240 affordable units, it should be explicitly written in the annexation agreement. He said that without those "definitive terms," all they have is hopes and plans.
"Hopes and plans are not enforceable," he said. "Hopes and plans change all the time."
Alspach also brought up the project's consistency with the town's comprehensive plan, saying that the comprehensive plan calls for the area to be a commercial developed area, not residential.
Ward 1 Council Member Maureen Curry asked Smith if Corrigan & Trippe Ventures would consider increasing the project's minimum percentage of affordable housing up from 25%. Smith said he thought they would.
"But no matter what, if that fails, any development there, if we build four houses, one of them has to be affordable," he said.
Easton resident Becky Allen, who lives right next to the vacant property, said there are better places in town for this kind of housing project. She said the proposed location is isolated from the town.
"Affordable housing has vulnerable residents," she said. "A lot of times they need pedestrian walkways, they need areas for public transportation."
Allen also brought up congestion. She said that a lot of vehicles driving onto Route 50, which is already "heavily congested" would just be difficult.
Town growth rate was also brought up during the meeting. Ward 2 Council Member Don Abbatiello said he is in favor of affordable housing but, considering the town has a set amount of resources, more than 200 new units seems like "an awful lot."
Ward 3 Council Member David Montgomery pointed out that a project like this could bring more affordable housing to Easton than an inclusive zoning ordinance could. He said that he would like the council to try to vote on this legislation at the next council meeting.
Reporter Veronica Fernandez-Alvarado contributed to this article.

title: QAC opposes recreational rockfish restrictions with letter
author: ANDREA GRABENSTEIN agrabenstein@chespub.com
content:
QAC opposes recreational rockfish restrictions with letter

 June 5, 2024 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: ANDREA GRABENSTEIN agrabenstein@chespub.com | Section: Local News 
 
 230
 Words 

 Read News Document

 CENTREVILLE — At its May 28 meeting, the Queen Anne's County Commissioners approved signing a letter in opposition of new measures from the Atlantic State Marine Fisheries Commission limiting the number of rockfish caught recreationally.A letter to Gov. Wes Moore outlined the commissioners' opposition to the measures passed earlier this year, which limit the Atlantic striped bass bag limits from two fish to one.
"Everybody is only allowed one fish, and it has to be a slot fish, between 19 and 25 inches," Commissioner President Jim Moran said.
The economic fallout from the reduction and adverse effects will be seen on charter boat captains, county restaurants, hotels and local business, and the overall local tourism industry, Commissioner Phil Dumenil said.
The reduction of fish that can be kept has resulted in far fewer charter trips booked, he said.
"People aren't going to come down from Philly or Washington or Baltimore to spend a day out on the Bay fishing for rockfish and get to keep one," Dumenil said.
With the letter, the commissioners hope to get some traction and ultimately a reversal on the decision, Dumenil said.
Agreeing with the letter of opposition, Moran also noted on the other side of the matter, the Maryland fishery was in trouble and needed help.
The commissioners noted appreciation of Moore's previous visit with the agricultural industry and extended an invitation to visit local watermen for the same treatment.

title: Council introduces one-cent resolution question for 2024 ballot
author: Veronica Fernandez-Alvarado
content:
Council introduces one-cent resolution question for 2024 ballot

 June 6, 2024 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: Veronica Fernandez-Alvarado | Section: News 
 
 427
 Words 

 Read News Document

 EASTON — Five years ago, Talbot County residents had the opportunity to vote on a one-cent resolution that would increase residents' taxes for public safety over five years. Last week, Talbot County Council members introduced the same resolution to appear on the 2024 general election ballot.During a May 28 meeting, the council unanimously introduced a resolution to place a question on the ballot at the 2024 general election to amend section 614 of the charter of Talbot County to allow the council to add up to one cent per $100 of assessed value above the revenue cap for an additional five years beginning July 1, 2026.
According to the resolution document, the original resolution was adopted by a 5-0 vote of the Talbot County Council on July 21, 2020. The resolution was approved by the majority of Talbot County voters at the 2020 general election.
This resolution would "allow but not require" the Talbot County Council to add up to one cent per one hundred dollars of assessed value above the revenue cap for an additional five years.
Talbot County Attorney Patrick Thomas said that as of July 1, 2021, revenues derived from property taxes included in the constant yield tax rate certification shall not increase more than 2% from the previous year.
This increase has helped offset the county's costs of maintaining public safety, officials said.
Clay Stamp, the county manager of Talbot County, said he was a public supporter of the resolution when it was initially introduced because it would assist in providing quicker services for the residents of Talbot County.
Over the last fiscal year, the one-cent initiative has provided about $200,000 for the county to offset the public safety budget, which includes law enforcement, fire departments and other emergency services.
When reintroduced in May, Council Member Dave Stepp said over half of Talbot County voters supported this resolution in 2020. The funds generated from this resolution have solved many problems Stepp has seen in neighboring counties, he said.
"It would benefit our public services here in Talbot County," Stepp said. "The names of the departments that would make it to the ballot question would be the Sheriff's department, Department of Emergency Services as well as the Department of Corrections. We've seen a lot of positive things that have happened in those departments over the years."
Stepp asked his fellow council members to support the resolution and allow residents to decide whether or not they would like to see it implemented for the following five years.
The council unanimously voted to introduce the resolution. A public hearing will be on Tuesday, June 25.

title: Galena passes budget while starting first time investment
author: WILL BONTRAGER wbontrager@chespub.com
content:
Galena passes budget while starting first time investment

 June 6, 2024 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: WILL BONTRAGER wbontrager@chespub.com | Section: News 
 
 622
 Words 

 Read News Document

 GALENA — After a public hearing for the budget where no members of the public attended, Mayor John Carroll and the Galena Town Council on Monday night passed the ordinance to their fiscal year 2025 budget.The total allocations divided between fund categories: General, $553,250; Sewer, $342,246; and Water, $173,675 — for a combined total of $1,069,171 matched their total income for a balanced budget.
The town budget includes a tax revenue of $258,000, alongside $76,678 in receivables for utilities.
The property tax rate, Carroll said, remains set at .0222 per $100 of assessed value. There was no increase in taxes, no increase for additional fees, water or in trash and recycling.
Town Attorney Tom Yeager reminded the council they were passing the ordinance to pass the budget.
Ultimately, they approved of ordinance 2024-01FY-25 Budget.
Also during this budget session, the town embarked for the first time in investing. They decided to take some money out of their savings and place it in an interest bearing certificate of deposit account.
Financial and Administrative Clerk Marisa Pisapia, while bringing up various line items, got the attention of the council about this. Once they scoured places to invest they chose to secure their investment with PNC Bank for eight months at a 4.65% interest rate.
Council member Sarah Merrell made it official.
"I make a motion to authorize doing a CD out of our water savings account," she said.
The motion passed unanimously.
Carroll detailed the next step in the process. Right before they leave for the Maryland Municipal League June 23 — 26 in Ocean City, they'll meet with someone from PNC Bank. From there they'll set up an account to get things in motion.
As a first, reiterated Carroll, "we're dipping our toes in it."
In other financial matters, Grants Coordinator and Tech Support Grant Audrey Erschen talked about the various grants she's been working on.
She received notification their Teen Play Area was included in the State of Maryland's FY2025 Budget, and must be approved by the Maryland Board of Public Works. The grant was for climbing equipment and installation.
They were not awarded this year on their No Gym, Think Outside Application, but she'll try again next year.
And in the tech department, she was informed they would not have to replace their Quick Books until 2026 — a relief for the council.
Maintenance and Facilities Coordinator Warren Walters had updates of his own particularly concerning the wastewater treatment plant. They had removed 42.55 tons of sludge in 2024, with a total cost of $2,957.24. Total effluent gallons (liquid waste or sewage discharged) discharged were 3,873,000 and daily average effluent gallons were 25,463.
Carroll who wanted to get a general idea, said, "It looks like we're averaging 25,000 gallons or so. That's what I wanted to see, where we're truly at. I want to know what our capacity is always. And when it fluctuates during a certain point of time."
Walters, working with Erschen, said his goal going ahead is in mitigation procedures, aiming to reduce the production of methane and leachate that can contaminate surface waters. This process involves managing wastewater at its source, which can include water conservation and recycling.
Walters is in conversations with the Environmental Protection Agency, so the town possibly won't have to spend money on the mitigation process. Carroll thought that a good idea, and mentioned that he's been talking with the University of Maryland Finance Center too. The idea is once they have their survey complete, they'll open up the conversation even more.
"We can attack it from both angles," Carroll said, "state and federal."
After hearing updates on all departments, Yeager commended the council on their work.
Carroll noted the completion of the budget was a team effort.
The Galena Town Council's next meeting will be on Monday, July 1. See more information at townofgalena.com.

title: FEMA grants Cambridge $1.7 million for flood mitigation project
author: STAFF REPORT
content:
FEMA grants Cambridge $1.7 million for flood mitigation project

 June 7, 2024 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: STAFF REPORT | Section: Local News 
 
 321
 Words 

 Read News Document

 CAMBRIDGE — The Federal Emergency Management Agency has awarded the City of Cambridge $1.7 million for a flood mitigation project along the shore of the Choptank River.According to a news release from the city, the "Make Cambridge Resilient Flood Mitigation Project" will stretch from west of city limits, near Gerry Boyle Park at Great Marsh, to the mouth of Cambridge Creek.
The project will create a flood barrier along the river that is integrated with a nature-based living shoreline. Along with the living shoreline, a stormwater management system will be put in place to reduce flood risk, according to the news release.
The project will have two phases: design and permitting, and construction. The first phase, which scientists from the University of Maryland Center for Environmental Science at Horn Point will assist with, will include gathering and analyzing data, completing a detailed design and obtaining the permitting needed for construction.
The week of June 3, field surveyors began conducting a hydrographic survey by boat to measure tidal information and other physical features along the shore of the Choptank.
Along with the $1.7 million awarded for the first phase of the project, FEMA is reserving $16 million for the second phase of the project, the news release states. The total $17.7 million in grant money is being awarded through FEMA's Hazard Mitigation Assistance grant.
The city is committing 10.5% of funds for both phases of the project through a grant from the Maryland Department of Natural Resources, the Resilient Maryland Revolving Loan Fund and city budget funds.
"The City of Cambridge is committed to the 'Make Cambridge Resilient Initiative' and views this project as a major step forward," the press release states.
In terms of timeline, phase one of the project will extend through 2025. Public outreach will be scheduled throughout the first phase of the project, according to the news release. It says the city will directly coordinate with affected property owners for concerns and property assessment.

title: Willingness to understand
author: Staff Writer
content:
Willingness to understand

 June 9, 2024 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: Staff Writer | Section: Editors Inbox 
 
 359
 Words 

 Read News Document

 Misunderstanding, preconceptions and lack of awareness. That's what I was left with after listening to members of the Easton Town Council on June 3. What began as a purported "budgetary issue" quickly revealed itself to be a thinly veiled attempt to shutter our LGBTQ+ community. It was also a rather clumsy but obvious nudge toward a small-minded political agenda.If fiscal responsibility was the concern, the council would have recognized that the minor expense of printing banners for any community event is dwarfed by the significant revenue potential of nurturing a thriving diverse tourist demographic.
What shortsighted local government would actively choose to send a message of exclusion to potential tourism demographics, effectively hanging a "closed for business" sign on our community? The actions of a few specific council members reek of political posturing, not financial prudence.
The Pride banners send a powerful and important message to all of our residents and visitors — that our community is willing to grow into a place of belonging, safety and inclusion for all. Period.
During both council meetings this simple message was lost amid a tirade of inaccurate fear-mongering and the inappropriate insertion of personal lifestyle and medical choices into a conversation where they had no place. To foster greater understanding and inclusivity, we must be brave enough to ask and actively listen with respect for our fellow humans.
Understanding our neighbors does not mean we must adopt their personal choices or even agree with them. It simply means having the human decency to listen and learn from one another and respect the differences. Only through open and honest communication can we work to grow a community of true inclusivity.
To our LGBTQ+ community members: Your experiences and perspectives are valued. Many of us are committed to creating a community where you feel welcomed, respected and supported.
Kudos to the community members who spoke to the issue at hand at the June 3 council meeting. It's time we move beyond political posturing, stop assuming that we "know" what our neighbors' lives are and start having real conversations. All of our neighbors deserve nothing less than our full support in the form of our willingness to understand.
KATE RICHARDS
Tilghman

title: Be suspicious of motives
author: Staff Writer
content:
Be suspicious of motives

 June 9, 2024 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: Staff Writer | Section: Editors Inbox 
 
 314
 Words 

 Read News Document

 This Sunday morning started as it usually does, for me. Early wake up, turn on the coffee pot and let our dog out to do his morning business, then serve his breakfast, which quickly disappears. Then comes our walk, which we both enjoy, followed by posting of the American flag and picking up the morning edition of the Star, to read with breakfast. That is a normal Sunday morning for me and for many other newspaper readers, I hope.As I turned to the editorial articles and letters to the editor in this week's edition, I was struck, and disheartened, by the divisive nature of the thoughts and words that appear there, for all to read. I have no need, or desire, to repeat them. To do so, would only serve to elevate the practice of denigrating the ideals and beliefs of others, who may not share my political leanings. What I would like to do is to encourage those who choose to participate in our election processes to be honest, civil, and well informed.
Listen to the words, ideas and ideals that the candidates themselves speak and stand for. Be suspicious of partisan operatives that attempt to steer you, and others, to their candidates, by assigning derogatory labels on those "others" or with deceptive accounts of what opposition candidates have actually done, or stand for.
At the end of the day, or more appropriately, the election cycle, we are all God's children, aren't we? We will share the same earth, going forward, regardless of who is elected. We will prosper, or suffer, as a result of our collective decisions on who we elect to serve and lead us, in this grand experiment we call democracy. I say again, be suspicious of the motives of those who attempt to steer you to one candidate or another.
Their interests and values may not be what they seem.
WILLIAM KEPPEN
Easton

title: Easton budget projects more than $100K saved in overtime pay
author: KONNER METZ kmetz@chespub.com
content:
Easton budget projects more than $100K saved in overtime pay

 June 9, 2024 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: KONNER METZ kmetz@chespub.com | Section: Local News 
 
 604
 Words 

 Read News Document

 EASTON — In what was a difficult process, Easton officials worked all spring to finalize the $28 million fiscal year 2025 budget, which included a sizable decrease in overtime pay, an area of much discussion in previous council meetings.According to figures provided by Town Manager Donald Richardson, the town is budgeted to save $127,250 in overtime pay to employees in FY25.
The decrease comes after Mayor Megan Cook reworked the budget, which was approved at a June 3 Town Council meeting, to switch the status of 13 department heads from non-exempt to exempt. Exempt employees do not receive overtime pay.
"It was a lot of negotiation, because it's not an easy transition," Ward 1 Council Member Maureen Curry said. "But in my opinion, it was the right thing to do."
While $430,320 was budgeted for overtime in FY24, Richardson said the current expenditures are about $498,000 as the July 1 fiscal year end approaches. FY25's budget allots $303,070 for overtime pay.
Notably, there is no overtime budgeted in FY25 for the town manager, building inspections and engineering departments. Those three areas combined for a total of more than $90,000 in projected overtime in FY24's budget, with engineering coming in second-highest overall at $72,000.
The highest department in overtime budgeting was police patrol, which will decrease from $256,700 in FY24 to a projected $209,000 in FY25, still the highest amount.
IT, police administration and parks and recreation will all receive overtime decreases compared to last year's budget. Police special operations, meanwhile, is budgeted for an increase of more than $25,000 in FY25 overtime pay.
"Shifting select administrative staff to exempt status has reduced overtime costs and aims to prevent potential budget overruns," Council President Frank Gunsallus wrote in a statement. "... I commend everyone involved in this budget process for their hard work to ensure financial responsibility and transparency."
The Town Council held a workshop in April to discuss shifting department heads to exempt status. Cook presented a plan of action, including a 3% salary increase for those moving to exempt status to offset the losses in overtime pay.
Council members expressed concern with this increase during the workshop, and those increases were reduced by the time the final budget was passed early June.
In June 7 interviews with the Star Democrat, Curry and Ward 2 Council Member Don Abbatiello both praised the mayor for working to reduce those increases during the budget process.
"She came back, and many of those increases that we thought were a little excessive were reduced by the mayor to make it a little bit more palatable for the council to accept," Abbatiello said.
Cook and Chief Human Resource Officer Rick Farr vouched during the April workshop that this was a much-needed change for the town. While council members largely agreed, it took some tinkering and adjustments.
Abbatiello is pleased with the status change for select employees and sees it continuing for years to come.
"We're talking about department heads," Abbatiello said. "We're not talking about the guys who work outside in public works. We're not talking about the office staff."
While Abbatiello and Curry each expressed satisfaction with this year's budget, next year's will be no easy task.
Both mentioned that federal funds from the American Rescue Plan Act will run dry. Abbatiello noted the council must keep its eye on the balance of the budget's allocation toward salaries and benefits versus capital projects
"You do not want salaries and benefits far (exceeding) operations and capital projects, because then you're not going to get anything accomplished around town," he said.
"Next year is going to be even more of a challenge," Curry said. "And some belt-tightening may be in order."
Maggie Trovato contributed reporting to this story.

title: Why is charter change needed?
author: Staff Writer
content:
Why is charter change needed?

 June 9, 2024 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: Staff Writer | Section: Editors Inbox 
 
 461
 Words 

 Read News Document

 On June 18, Oxford citizens will vote to elect a new town commissioner. Norm Bell and Josh Coder are the two candidates for the open seat on the commission. Candidate Bell has lived in Oxford for 12 years. Candidate Bell is a member and is now the chairman of the Oxford Planning and Zoning Commission and past president of the Board of Trustees for the Oxford Community Center.Candidate Coder has lived in Oxford 3½ years. Candidate Coder is an EMT and volunteer firefighter in the Oxford Volunteer Fire Department. Each candidate has a website that states their platform and what each expects to accomplish if elected.
There is, however, one significant distinction in their appeal to the Oxford voters. Candidate Bell accepted the invitation from the League of Women Voters to participate in a candidate forum giving Oxford voters the opportunity to ask questions about each candidate's platform and qualifications. Candidate Coder declined to take part in the League of Women Voters candidate forum. This declination to stand before the Oxford voters and answer any questions about Candidate Coder's qualifications and platform is not consistent with Candidate Coder's campaign focus on transparency in government.
If Candidate Coder had not declined to take part in the candidate forum, he could have answered many questions including, "Why is a charter amendment needed to require a referendum on annexation as the town's comprehensive plan prohibits annexations excepting certain named built properties?"
In the spring of 2023 ,the Oxford Planning Commission began the required review of the Town's comprehensive plan first focusing on future growth areas and the extension of water and sewer services through annexation. After several Planning Commission meetings and two public workshops revised sewer and water maps were presented to the public. The citizens overwhelming approved the proposed new water and sewer map known as Map 4, which prohibits any future annexations excepting built properties along Laing's Landing and at the tip of Bachelors Point.
On June 29, 2023, the town's commissioners approved, after a public workshop to consider public comments, Map 4.The named properties have septic systems and an owner may ask for annexation. Section 14 of the town code would govern these applications for annexation.
Under Maryland law annexations must be consistent with the town's comprehensive plan. As the town's comprehensive plan now prohibits any annexations other than certain named properties, future annexations of any other properties is a moot point. Why is a charter amendment needed?
Candidate Coder's campaign advises voters that they have a choice in the June 18 election. Candidate Bell is the candidate with 12 years of residency in the town, community service in government and non-government positions, demonstrated leadership in those roles and the willingness to be fully transparent to the voter. Candidate Bell is the voters' best choice.
ED MILLER
Oxford

title: Commissioners of Oxford candidate forum will not take place
author: Maggie Trovato
content:
Commissioners of Oxford candidate forum will not take place

 June 12, 2024 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: Maggie Trovato | Section: Local News 
 
 408

 OXFORD — With only one candidate accepting the invitation, the League of Women Voters of the Mid-Shore will not be hosting a candidate forum for the open Oxford commissioner seat before the town's June 18 election.Candidates Norm Bell and Josh Coder are running to fill Commissioner Susan Delean-Botkin's seat. Delean-Botkin, whose term is expiring, did not seek re-election. Delean-Botkin was appointed to the commission seat in June 2023 following the resignation of former Commissioner Brian Wells, who moved to Easton.
Coder and Bell, who are running for the three-year term, were both invited to participate in a candidate forum hosted by the Mid-Shore chapter of the League of Women Voters. Kathi Bangert from the Mid-Shore League said in an email that Bell accepted the invitation and Coder said he wasn't available.
Bangert said that the league was unable to officially schedule the forum because of this.
"According to league rules, at least two candidates must attend for a forum to be held," she said.
Candidate forums are a way to give voters the opportunity to learn about candidates' views on issues that are important to the community, Bangert said. During the forums, candidates are asked the same questions by a moderator. Those questions are submitted to the moderator by audience members.
"This enables voters to compare and evaluate responses from candidates," Bangert said.
Bell said he got a notification from the league that Coder had declined to participate.
"To me, the forum is not for the candidates, it's for the voters," Bell said.
Bell compared the election process to applying for a job.
"To me, the forum is part of the interview process," he said. "It's the ability to stand there, both of us, side-by-side, answering the same questions from the audience and from the League of Women Voters."
Bell said he didn't know if the cancelation of the forum would have an effect on voter turnout or the election results, but said it could. He said that he has heard comments that some people would have liked there to be a forum.
"And I've heard comments that that may change some votes," he said. "How it will impact the election, I can't say."
Bell called the situation "a lost opportunity."
"I think it's for the voters," Bell said about the forum. "It's not for me. It's not for Josh. It's something that I think we should have done, and I'm not happy that we're not doing it."

title: CWDI, YMCA say there is no Cambridge Harbor deal after email hints at YMCA move
author: Maggie Trovato
content:
CWDI, YMCA say there is no Cambridge Harbor deal after email hints at YMCA move

 June 12, 2024 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: Maggie Trovato | Section: Local News 
 
 882
 Words 

 Read News Document

 CAMBRIDGE — Although a June 7 email sent by the YMCA of the Chesapeake made people think the organization had reached a deal with Cambridge Waterfront Development Inc. to build a new YMCA on the Cambridge Harbor site, both CWDI Executive Director Matt Leonard and YMCA of the Chesapeake CEO Robbie Gill confirmed Tuesday that there is no deal."There has not been talk of a deal with the YMCA," Leonard said in an interview with the Star Democrat, adding that the two groups do have conversations from time to time about the YMCA's interest in being a part of the project to develop space along the Choptank River.
Leonard said CWDI has had those kinds of conversations with multiple respondents of a July 2022 request for proposals. The YMCA was one of the respondents of that request.
The June 7 email the YMCA sent out included a "facility update" about banners the organization is replacing at its current Cambridge location on Talbot Avenue.
"As we work to highlight all the positives that come with building a new Robbins Family Y at Cambridge Harbor, we wanted to give you a sneak peak of the new banners," the email reads.
After the email was sent out, people on social media shared concerns about the YMCA's plans. Cambridge Association of Neighborhoods President Chuck McFadden said in an interview that when he saw the email, he was "taken aback," and he said the news was "buried" in an email about banners.
Gill, who has received emails and phone calls from concerned residents since the email went out, said the YMCA is advocating the need to build a new YMCA. He said the existing site is not sustainable over the next two decades and can't provide certain programs, amenities and services.
"We are trying to help frame a narrative because, right now, you have other people that are framing narratives that are just wrong," he said.
Gill said the emails and phone calls expressing concerns with the YMCA's hopes to move to Cambridge Harbor have not made him reconsider those plans. He said the YMCA had a market study completed, which tested three sites for a new YMCA in Dorchester County, and Cambridge Harbor tested as the strongest site.
"We're trying to help people understand that if you did build a YMCA in the right location, that it could serve up to 7,000 people and 1,000 people a day," he said.
FUTURE PLANS
CWDI plans to issue another request for proposals in the fall for the second phase of the Cambridge Harbor project. Leonard said CWDI has made it clear to the respondents of the 2022 request for proposals that it will be issuing the new request in the fall.
"And if they're interested in having a place at Cambridge Harbor, they need to respond to that RFP," Leonard said.
Leonard said the YMCA "to some extent" fits the goal of having Cambridge Harbor benefit the community through offering things for the public to enjoy, like activity spaces.
"But we also understand there may be others," Leonard said about potential site partners.
The fate of the Cambridge YMCA has been a topic of conversation in the community for nearly a year. In July, Gill said that the YMCA began considering moving the facility following its market study. In late August, CWDI included a design for a new YMCA facility at the Cambridge Harbor site in its 2023 mid-year report, which sparked concerns from residents.
In October, the city council passed three ordinances that essentially limit institutional uses on the the YMCA's 201 Talbot Ave property in the event the YMCA were to move.
Gill and Leonard have both repeatedly said that there is no deal between CWDI and the YMCA to move the Cambridge facility to Cambridge Harbor. At a CWDI community update meeting April 18, Leonard said CWDI was not currently negotiating with the YMCA, and Gill said in an interview at the same event that there were no new developments with the Cambridge YMCA.
Although Leonard and Gill say there is no deal, Leonard said that CWDI paid for design plans to be drawn up of the YMCA's Talbot Avenue property if the YMCA were to move. He said that CWDI was asked by "some members of the community" what it would do with the Talbot Avenue property if CWDI received it. Leonard said CWDI would propose infill residential development to match the neighborhood.
"While we were having some of the Cambridge Harbor project design, we had our designer do a quick sketch of what that might look like," he said.
Though the Talbot Avenue property is not on the Cambridge Harbor site and CWDI's mission is to develop Cambridge Harbor, Leonard said CWDI is allowed to make deals to develop Cambridge Harbor "that sometimes might include other properties" per its charter.
Gill, who has seen CWDI's design plans, said the YMCA has not had any conversations with the city or potential developers about the redevelopment of the Talbot Avenue property.
"We just believe, based on the size of the site, it could be redeveloped to generate tax revenue that could be helpful," he said.
Gill said the YMCA will host Triangle2, the firm that completed the YMCA's market study, at its Cambridge location at 5 p.m. on June 18 to present data from the market study. The meeting will be open to Cambridge YMCA members.

title: Trappe council, developers address questions
author: Veronica Fernandez-Alvarado
content:
Trappe council, developers address questions

 June 13, 2024 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: Veronica Fernandez-Alvarado | Section: Local News 
 
 806
 Words 

 Read News Document

 TRAPPE — Trappe residents recently used a Town Council meeting to voice concerns over fee increases.In the public comments during the meeting, town officials said residents offered misinformation about Lakeside that the council and Lakeside developers attempted to clear up.
The public hearing was held during a June 5 meeting on Ordinance 3-2024, an ordinance to increase the monthly water and sewer fees. Many residents asked why there was a fee increase for the residents of Trappe and why the Lakeside development hasn't offset the cost of living in Trappe.
Brian Schmidt, Trappe council president, told residents that the rise in sewer and water fees has nothing to do with Lakeside but rather with the rise in the cost of living in the area as a whole.
Schmidt reminded residents that in 2017, the town was almost bankrupt, and it couldn't sustain itself without increasing water bills. Additionally, the cost of chemicals and the cost of running the plant as a whole has risen. He said he was confused as to why residents saw a correlation between the rise in water and sewer fees and the Lakeside development.
"We haven't put out a single dime for the Lakeside's treatment plant," Schmidt said. "We are responsible for ours (treatment plant) and the water tower that we have over here also servicing Lakeside, and they (Lakeside residents) are paying toward that water bill, that water bill that Lakeside is paying towards our treatment, toward our water tower."
In a separate interview, Schmidt mentioned that the developer of Lakeside is investing in Trappe and has made plans to continue to invest in Trappe, including a new town hall, water system expansion and funding for the fire department.
"The volunteer fire department is close to receiving a $450,000 check from the developer," Schmidt said. "Each one of those houses is responsible for a $100 donation to the fire department as well. So, at this point, it is $1,200 from the 120 homes."
In a separate interview, Robert Rauch, Lakeside's engineer, explained the economic benefits the development brings to not only the town but the region as a whole.
"The planning, design, studies, permitting and construction have supported dozens of local companies and hundreds of people employed by the companies that have worked on the project for over 20 years," Rauch said. "Taxes, impact fees, and developer contributions have and will continue to benefit town and county residents."
Rauch said the Gov. Wes Moore and the state of Maryland have publicly recognized the housing shortage in Maryland. The Lakeside development will provide a wide range of housing types and price points to help address the housing needs. Lakeside provides a regional growth center that will ease the pressure of sprawl development on other areas in the county.
Rauch mentioned that the residents of Lakeside will support local restaurants and businesses, use locally provided services and support the many local charities, non-profit organizations and arts and entertainment venues.
For Rauch, there are people who misunderstand that the approved Lakeside Planned Neighborhood is a large development of 2,501 residential units with a mix of commercial use on the property. However, it has had a slow start to growth in a way that many surrounding communities have not.
"Over the 20-plus years since Lakeside was approved, fewer than 150 homes have been built in Lakeside, while more than 1,900 homes were approved or built in Easton," Rauch said.
Schmidt told residents at that Wednesday evening meeting that the benefits and profits from the development would come later when the Lakeside development has grown more.
Eventually, the Lakeside wastewater treatment plant will be transferred to Trappe. Agreements for this transfer were mentioned at Wednesday's meeting and tabled for a future meeting.
Ryan Showalter, attorney for Lakeside, explained the developer's responsibilities after the plant is transferred.
"The developer is responsible for providing all of the wastewater collection and treatment infrastructure necessary to serve the full build-out of the Lakeside project," Showalter said in a separate interview. "Once the initial phase of the wastewater treatment plant is complete and turned over to the town, the developer remains responsible for any deficiencies between the costs of operation and maintenance and the sewer revenues collected by the town from Lakeside residents."
Additionally, once the transfer is completed, the developer remains responsible for incrementally expanding the wastewater treatment plant as the capacity is utilized.
Toward the end of the meeting, the council unanimously voted to adopt Ordinance 3-2024. Council member Rosalee Potter commented to the residents of Trappe prior to the vote.
"It's hard for you, but it's also hard for us because whatever we do, it affects you, but it also affects our pocketbooks as well," Potter said. "We're not doing these things because we want to, but we do these things because we have to, in order to see that the town itself continues to thrive, continues to operate, continues to be a town of Trappe."

title: Oxford commissioners thank Lewis before her retirement as town manager
author: Maggie Trovato
content:
Oxford commissioners thank Lewis before her retirement as town manager

 June 13, 2024 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: Maggie Trovato | Section: Local News 
 
 505
 Words 

 Read News Document

 OXFORD — Applause broke out more than once in the meeting room of the Oxford Community Services Building Tuesday night as the Commissioners of Oxford thanked outgoing Town Manager Cheryl Lewis for her 12 years of service to the town.Lewis, who is retiring, was hired as town clerk in 2012 and was later promoted to town manager. June 30 will be her last day as a Town of Oxford employee.
"I love this job," Lewis said after being handed an official citation from the Maryland General Assembly, a proclamation from the town and a painting to remind her of what she considers one of her proudest achievements as town manager. "It's been a wonderful 12 years. This is a wonderful town, and I hope everybody here understands what a wonderful gift they've got living here. So thank you very much."
Former Oxford Commissioner and retired Judge Sidney Campen Jr. presented Lewis with a citation from the Maryland General Assembly. After reading the citation, Campen thanked Cheryl for her dedication, hard work and the accomplishments she made as town manager.
Campen brought up architect Christopher Wren, whose epitaph, which is in Latin, translates to "If you would seek my monument, look around you.''
"What I say to the people of Oxford, look around at what Cheryl has done for this town," he said. "Thank you, Cheryl."
After presenting a proclamation from the town, Commission President Tom Costigan thanked Lewis and told her it had been a privilege and honor to serve with her.
"As you sail off into the sunset at the end of this month, we wanted to give you something to remind you of your time in Oxford," he said before the commissioners presented her with a painting of El Galeón, a ship that Lewis, with the help of others, brought to Oxford for a few days.
Commissioner Susan Delean-Botkin choked up as she thanked Lewis for her work in the town.
"She'll be greatly missed but remembered for how her vision makes Oxford a better place now and in the future," Delean-Botkin said. "It was a great 12 years."
Commissioner Katrina Greer thanked Lewis for her work ethic and professionalism.
"I don't think I could say it any better than my colleagues have said," Greer said.
While many attendees of the meeting on Tuesday stood up to clap as Lewis was thanked by current and former commissioners, others remained seated, highlighting a divide in residents' feelings on how the town is run.
In the last year, transparency has been a recurring topic during public comment at town meetings. Much of this was spurred by the abrupt retirement of former Police Chief Patrick Maxwell in February 2023. According to previous Star Democrat reporting, following the news of Maxwell's retirement, residents showed up to a town meeting to ask questions about the circumstances of Maxwell's retirement as well as transparency with the town's finances and hiring practices.
In an interview Wednesday, Lewis said the town is still in the process of hiring its next town manager, but expects to hire someone by the end of the month.

title: Two candidates run for Oxford commission seat
author: Maggie Trovato
content:
Two candidates run for Oxford commission seat

 June 13, 2024 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: Maggie Trovato | Section: Local News 
 
 665
 Words 

 Read News Document

 OXFORD — Two candidates will vie for the open Commissioners of Oxford seat in the town's election on June 18.Candidates Norm Bell and Josh Coder are running to fill the seat of Commissioner Susan Delean-Botkin's, whose term is expiring. Delean-Botkin, who did not seek re-election, was appointed to the commission seat in June 2023 following the resignation of former Commissioner Brian Wells.
The person elected to the position will serve a three-year term. On June 18, between 8 a.m. and 8 p.m., Oxford voters can head to the Oxford Community Services Building at 101 Market St. to cast their vote.
NORMAN BELLOxford resident Norman Bell, 79, is retired from a 45-year career at DuPont. He has municipal government experience through volunteerism, including being chair of the Oxford Planning Commission, president of the Oxford Community Center, chair of the Oxford Hiring Procedures Ad Hoc Committee, and member of the Sea Level Rise and Stormwater Steering Team. Bell has a wife, Paula, two sons and two granddaughters.
Why are you running?
"We need to calm the divisive atmosphere that is keeping us from moving forward. The people of Oxford have a history of working together to make significant accomplishments. I believe that every resident wants to continue this history of success. I have developed a skillset, through my professional and volunteer experiences, that can help to make this happen. I want to partner with the people of Oxford, in whom I believe, to plan and build for a successful future."
What will you bring to the commission?
"I began volunteering in Oxford after moving here 12 years ago. I have experience working with town government committees and nonprofit organizations. During my 45-year career with DuPont, I developed skills managing teams, and the ability to encourage people to work toward consensus. I found these skills very helpful in my work as chair of the Oxford Planning Commission, president of the Oxford Community Center, chair of the Oxford Hiring Practices Policy Committee, and as a member of the Sea Level Rise and Stormwater Steering Team. Those responsibilities required full time commitment. As commissioner, I will be equally devoted to my responsibilities."
What would you say is the most pressing issue facing Oxford and how do you think the commissioners need to address it?
"As of July 1 , five of the 11 town employees, including hopefully a new town manager, will have less than six months of experience as Oxford town employees. This is the most pressing short-term issue. Our attention to the professional development of these new employees will ensure the continuation of services to our residents. Our most long-term pressing issue is sea level rise. The commissioners need to address it by empowering citizens to be engaged in helping to find solutions."
Do you feel that the town and commissioners have done a good job of addressing sea level rise and flooding in Oxford? Why or why not?
"The town has been addressing the flooding issue. A comprehensive flood plan was developed, priorities set and grant funding obtained. Detailed engineering studies, necessary to begin the actual design and implementation work, were just approved. Could it have been done in a more expeditious manner? Starting the work depended upon grant funding availability.
Sea level rise is a longer-term issue. As a good first step, the town commissioned a study to assess the future impact of sea level rise on Oxford and its residents. The next step is to empower already engaged citizens in helping to find solutions to this long-term issue. I am a part of the steering team, which is developing that process."
JOSHUA CODERCoder is a Oxford volunteer firefighter and EMT. According to his campaign website, Joshua Coder has a degree in international affairs and economics and a master's degree in geology. His website says he has experience with permitting, environmental compliance, construction, water management, managing budgets and managing audit documentation and financial disclosures. It says he is an Army veteran.
Coder declined to respond to the Star Democrat's questions and instead directed the newspaper to his website.

title: Talbot County Council balks at Route 662 closure
author: KONNER METZ kmetz@chespub.com
content:
Talbot County Council balks at Route 662 closure

 June 13, 2024 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: KONNER METZ kmetz@chespub.com | Section: Local News 
 
 785
 Words 

 Read News Document

 EASTON — The Talbot County Council advanced the prospects of a new hospital in Easton during its meeting Tuesday, passing a resolution to amend a development rights and responsibilities agreement.The University of Maryland Shore Regional Health is preparing to build a new regional medical center off Longwoods Road, next to U.S. Route 50 and just north of the Easton Airport. However, as construction nears, the council heard for the first time of what could be a major road closure.
Designs of the hospital have part of the building right on top of where Route 662 is currently. UM Shore Regional Health Attorney Ryan Showalter discussed the possibility of temporarily closing Route 662 for reconstruction while construction on the hospital begins.
Showalter told the council that the timing of the construction could be delayed by eight months if Shore Regional Health cannot construct the building and the new route simultaneously.
"One thing that became very apparent is that the construction of the hospital and the completion of the hospital would be materially delayed if we can't begin work on the hospital foundation while we're constructing new 662," Showalter said.
"What that means is we will be before you maybe as early as your next meeting with proposed amendments to an existing bill."
That existing legislation is Bill 1231, which dates back to 2013. It "conditions the transfer" of the old route to Shore Regional Health on the completion of the new road, Showalter said.
Showalter told the council that road construction could start as soon as August or September if all the necessary permits pass through. He said it will be completed before beach traffic picks up next spring.
Shore Regional Health would work with the State Highway Administration on reconstruction and detouring traffic to Route 50. Showalter said construction would be six days a week, with a team working from both the south and the north ends.
COUNCIL CONCERNED
While the resolution to adjust the outdated development rights and responsibilities agreement did not include redlined items such as the Route 662 reconstruction, the council spent much of the public hearing in open discussion.
"This amendment mainly updates outdated provisions of the existing DRRA and moves the public works-related language into the public works agreement," County Attorney Patrick Thomas said, noting that the sewer route is being evaluated, as well as other "housekeeping items" in the amendment.
Still, multiple council members shared concerns of a potential closure of the road.
"Knowing how busy that road is, knowing how important that road is to our agricultural community, (I think) that we look at every possible alternative to closing 662," council member Paul Lesher said.
"We've considered a wide range of alternatives," Showalter responded. "This is the alternative that is functional."
"I'd like to understand why the building didn't take into consideration its original design," council member Lynn Mielke asked. "Having this teeny part that was going to cause us to have to change the … highway. Why couldn't it have been oriented a little bit differently to avoid this whole situation?"
"It always was very close to 662," Showalter said. "The slight change in growth in the building occurred after virtually everything else was designed. So shifting the building and shifting that design would've added six months or nine months."
Showalter added that the change was made around 10 years ago, and that "those decisions were not revisited in an effort to keep this project moving."
Council President Chuck Callahan vouched for the forward movement of the hospital and its development rights and responsibilities agreement, adding that it's been around 15 years coming.
"At the end of the day, I don't want it to feel like we're the problem, because it's [the state's] road," Callahan said.
Council member Dave Stepp was hesitant, asking if the vote on the resolution could be delayed until council member Keasha Hythe — who was out Tuesday — was present. Mielke shared similar thoughts, hoping to address the resolution at hand at the same time as the Route 662 issue.
Showalter stated that the Shore Regional Health had board votes Wednesday and Friday to authorize funding, and preferred to respond to all questions during Tuesday night's public hearing and "reach a conclusion."
"Any of the items that would raise possible concerns have all been redlined out of this piece of the agreement," Lesher said. "This has been stripped down to bare bones to items that I don't think should raise any concerns for this council."
"I haven't independently made that decision," Mielke responded.
Callahan, Lesher and Stepp all voted to pass the resolution, while Mielke abstained. At the meeting's end, Callahan said he understood Mielke's vote while reaffirming the council's support for the project.
"We're definitely 100% behind this hospital," Callahan said. "… but we have to be cautious on how we handle this, too. 

 © Copyright © 2024 Star Democrat, Chesapeake Publishing Group (Adams Publishing/APGMedia). All rights reserved.

title: Oxford commissioners recommend livestream of election
author: Maggie Trovato
content:
Oxford commissioners recommend livestream of election

 June 13, 2024 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: Maggie Trovato | Section: Local News 
 
 440
 Words 

 Read News Document

 OXFORD — The Commissioners of Oxford voted unanimously at a town meeting Tuesday to recommend livestreaming of the town's June 18 election.The recommendation will be made to the Oxford Board of Supervisors of Election, which has the power to make this decision. It is in response to a request from resident Josh Coder for poll watchers to be present during the election for a commissioner next week.
Coder is one of two candidates running to fill the commission seat that Commissioner Susan Delean-Botkin currently holds. Delean-Botkin, whose term is expiring, did not seek reelection. Resident Norm Bell is the other candidate running in the election.
At the meeting Tuesday, Town Manager Cheryl Lewis said that because the town charter is silent on poll watchers in elections, the commissioners would need to pass an emergency ordinance before election day to meet Coder's request.
Lewis said that Town Attorney Lyndsey Ryan suggested the election be livestreamed instead, so that anyone can watch the election process as it's happening. Lewis said this was what the Talbot County Board of Elections did during the COVID-19 pandemic.
Under this arrangement, viewers of the livestream would be able to watch voters enter the room, get signed up, receive their ballot and then drop their ballot in the ballot box. The video would not show residents filling out their ballots. Lewis said there would be no sound.
After the polls close at 8 p.m., the sound could be turned on and viewers could watch the election board count votes.
"This would provide everyone the opportunity to watch the polls without interfering," Lewis said. "And the reason it won't be interfering with the election is we're not permitting individuals that currently are not allowed to be in this room to enter the room."
Lewis called this option a compromise.
"It shows willingness that we're attempting to figure out how to make this work for everybody," she said.
Commissioner Katrina Greer said it is important for the commissioners to take time to examine the town's voting processes.
"It's also only a week before the election, so we should take our time and examine some of the processes and other parts of our charter in terms of chain of custody for absentee ballots, voter registration and all those issues," she said. "But we should take our time and not do it in an emergency ordinance."
Delean-Botkin said she agreed with Greer. She mentioned that the election is four business days away.
"That's really too short for something this important," she said.
Voting in the election to fill the commission seat will take place between 8 a.m. and 8 p.m. at the Oxford Community Services Building at 101 Market St on June 18.

title: Imagined grievances
author: Staff Writer
content:
Imagined grievances

 June 16, 2024 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: Staff Writer | Section: Editors Inbox 
 
 379
 Words 

 Read News Document

 Imagined grievancesI live in Oxford, one of the safest towns in America. I was therefore confused when Josh Coder, who is running for town commissioner, made safety part of his platform. The town recently concluded a search for a new police chief and completing due diligence can take time. It was a typical hiring process during which time I never felt any danger to myself or my property.
Why create a fear concerning the lack of safety?
Another issue revolved around the fear of financial impropriety in the town office. Mr. Coder started his campaign stating the need for a forensic audit, otherwise known as a fraud audit, even though there was no evidence. I'm glad to see he has now taken this off his website. Why create fear and put our town in such a negative light to begin with?
Two other issues on Mr. Coder's platform are the fear of annexation and the town not doing anything about flooding issues. Mr. Coder was at the town meeting on May 28 when it was clearly explained why annexation is not an issue. He also attended the Sea Level Rise meeting on June 5 when the purpose of the town's 2016 flooding study was explained along with the town efforts and obstacles, such as a lack of available grant money it has needed. Yet he still perpetuates the myth that annexation is a problem, and the town has been irresponsible in the mitigation of flooding.
I would have enjoyed talking to Mr. Coder about these issues in an effort to understand his platform. However, the only appearances he's made have been through private parties. Twice, I directly asked to be invited to one but never received an invitation.
Now the new fear is election fraud; Josh Coder stating that poll watchers are needed. I don't always share the same viewpoint as all of my neighbors, but I have never felt any of them to be dishonest human beings. It is sad that Mr. Coder has mistrust of his fellow citizens, the ones he wants to represent.
Creating fear and mistrust does not build community — it tears it down. What I fear is that if Mr. Coder is elected, we will have three more years of imagined grievances and neighbors not trusting neighbors.

Oxford

title: Gov. Moore: 'The Shore must be able to live up to all of its promise'
author: KONNER METZ kmetz@chespub.com
content:
Gov. Moore: 'The Shore must be able to live up to all of its promise'

 June 16, 2024 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: KONNER METZ kmetz@chespub.com | Section: Local News 
 
 503
 Words 

 Read News Document

 RIDGELY — Gov. Wes Moore spent Friday afternoon on the Eastern Shore, meeting with local officials as well as nonprofit and agricultural leaders."It's great being back here, it's the 18th time that we've been on the Shore since I've been the governor," Moore said. "... I believe deeply that if this is going to be Maryland's decade, it means that the Shore must also be able to live up to all of its promise."
He made his first stop at the Caroline County Sheriff's Office for a tour of the facility that opened in 2021. Sheriff Donald Baker showed the governor everything from the department's inventory of supplies to its men and women working daily to protect residents.
"We absolutely treat our citizens the way they should be treated," Baker said to the governor.
The two talked about low homicide rates in Caroline County, collaboration between neighboring police and the task of policing in such a large state where policies are different county-by-county. Moore asked about the county's approach to other forms of policing and community safety.
"We definitely believe in community policing," the sheriff said.
Moore took the short ride from Denton to Ridgely to visit Martin's House & Barn, a homeless shelter that provides a food pantry and thrift shop for those in need.
He met with staff and board members of the organization, lauding the work they do for the homeless population.
"We've prioritized everything from funding going toward the Shore, health care … but also organizations like this one that are doing remarkable work," Moore said.
Moore donned a baseball cap for his final stop of the day at Twin Maple Farm in Ridgely. Dave Tribbett Jr. introduced the governor to his team and the farm's planting of miscanthus grass, an environmentally friendly product that can be used for bedding in chicken houses and the creation of biodegradable to-go containers.
Visibly impressed by the environmental benefits of miscanthus grass, Moore asked about building infrastructure to process the grass, as well as the challenges of growing it.
The governor didn't mind getting up close, walking through the farm's fields and getting a close look at the water filtration system and the ground beneath the crops.
Representatives and members from the Maryland Department of Agriculture, Mountaire Farms and USDA were present for Moore's last stop. Travis Hedrick, CEO of North Carolina-based AGgrow Tech, provided Moore insight into the benefits of miscanthus.
Hedrick said miscanthus is especially great for small farmers since it doesn't require equipment to replant it every year. There are around 3,000 acres of the crop on the Shore, he said.
If sent to other farms in the area, Hedrick and others emphasized it could create a mini-industry of growing and processing jobs.
"You had me at jobs," Moore said.
Before his three-stop tour, Moore's team held a cabinet meeting with the Caroline County commissioners.
"I just told the commissioners — and as they've seen — our belief in them and our commitment to their success is real and this is an administration that believes deeply in making sure the Shore succeeds," Moore said.

title: Norm Bell narrowly wins Oxford commissioner race
author: STAFF REPORT
content:
Norm Bell narrowly wins Oxford commissioner race

 June 18, 2024 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: STAFF REPORT | Section: Local News 
 
 138
 Words 

 Read News Document

 Norm Bell narrowly defeated his opponent, Joshua Coder, in a race for the open Commissioners of Oxford seat Tuesday.Bell received 224 total votes, and Coder received 212 votes, according to Town Manager Cheryl Lewis.
Bell and Coder ran to fill the seat of Commissioner Susan Delean-Botkin's, whose term is expiring. Delean-Botkin, who did not seek re-election, was appointed to the commission seat in June 2023 following the resignation of former Commissioner Brian Wells.
Bell, 79, is retired from a 45-year career at DuPont. He has municipal government experience through volunteerism, including being chair of the Oxford Planning Commission, president of the Oxford Community Center, chair of the Oxford Hiring Procedures Ad Hoc Committee, and member of the Sea Level Rise and Stormwater Steering Team. Bell has a wife, Paula, two sons and two granddaughters.
He will serve a three-year term.

title: Easton Town Council hears support, pushback in aftermath of Pride festival
author: KONNER METZ kmetz@chespub.com
content:
Easton Town Council hears support, pushback in aftermath of Pride festival

 June 19, 2024 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: KONNER METZ kmetz@chespub.com | Section: Local News 
 
 589
 Words 

 Read News Document

 EASTON — In the wake of the Delmarva Pride Center's third annual Pride festival last Saturday, the Easton Town Council saw a full chamber June 17.For a second consecutive meeting, many attendees spoke out in support of Pride initiatives and the festival, including Tina Jones, a board member of the Delmarva Pride Center.
"Those four days were a time of love and joy, of music and dance," Jones said of the festival. "Everyone could be themselves, love themselves and share their love with others."
The June 3 meeting saw significant pushback on council President Frank Gunsallus for questioning whether the town funds should support downtown Pride banners at a council meeting in May.
"I think it is safe to say that the economic return to the Town of Easton more than offset the cost of a few banners and a handful of street lights," Jones said on June 17.
Some who attended the festival thanked council members they saw Saturday, including Gunsallus, Curry and Davis.
Resident Jen Voshell spoke during public comment to Gunsallus, "wondering if (he) would consider retracting (his) previous opposition" and "support the permitting (of the festival) in 2025." In January, Gunsallus and Ward 3 council member David Montgomery voted against issuing the permit to hold the annual event.
At the end of Monday's meeting, Gunsallus said he "(appreciated) the meaningful conversations with members of the community" and was "glad that everyone had a good time" at the festival.
Others spoke to express displeasure with the council's approval of the festival's permit.
Resident Gary Judy called out the council members who approved the festival's permit in January by a 3-2 vote — Maureen Curry, Don Abbatiello and the Rev. Elmer Davis. "You three will be remembered for opening this door," he said, adding that other groups may now have the ability to obtain festival permits.
Shari Wilcoxon, who wrote to the council in the winter asking for the festival to be held on West Street instead of South Harrison Street, called Monday evening for the council to be "apolitical."
"Would you fully support … a Moms for Liberty parade?" Wilcoxon asked. "Would you pay for banners?"
MONTGOMERY COMMENTS
Meanwhile, other meeting attendees addressed Montgomery's comments from the June 3 meeting, which included a claim of "danger to our community from promotion of (the) transexual ideology."
"By saying that Pride, the Pride flag or any section of our LGBT community is merely an ideology overlooks what the essence of Pride is: a celebration of human rights and the recognition of inherent dignity of all individuals regardless of their (sexual) orientation or gender identity," Mayor Megan Cook said at the outset of Monday's meeting.
Montgomery responded, saying he "did not appreciate being chastised" by Cook. The mayor said they will likely not ever "see eye-to-eye on social issues," but that she hopes everyone can keep an "open mind."
"What I'm trying to do is to be helpful to those who are being misled by what I think is clearly an ideology, and it's demonstrated by the way my comments were received last month," Montgomery said. "Shouting someone down in an effort of de-platforming simply proves we are dealing with an ideology and a political movement."
Jen Wagner, a St. Michaels resident who owns a business in Easton, took to the podium to call for the resignation of Gunsallus and Montgomery, to which the Town Council president said "that's too far."
"I will not prolong this debate tonight on facts or their interpretation," Montgomery said at the meeting's end. "I will object to personal attacks, which exclusively came from the audience directed in this direction."

title: Maryland stories: Legion, firefighters retire U.S. flags
author: Michael Reid mreid@somdnews.com
content:
Maryland stories: Legion, firefighters retire U.S. flags

 June 19, 2024 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: Michael Reid mreid@somdnews.com | Section: News 
 
 379
 Words 

 Read News Document

 St. Mary's held a retirement ceremony of sorts during its 38th annual National Flag Day event on June 14 in Leonardtown.A total of 906 flags were burned.
The event marks the date in 1777 when the Continental Congress approved the design of a national flag, according to the Library of Congress. Flag Day became official in 1916 when President Woodrow Wilson issued a presidential proclamation to honor the Stars and Stripes every year on June 14, and in 1949 President Harry S. Trueman signed an Act of Congress designating a national Flag Day.
"I actually love this ceremony. It's humbling and it's patriotic and I absolutely love it," said Rep. Matt Morgan (R-St. Mary's), who added the event was the largest in the state. "I was reminded by how important ceremonies like this are when I was doing some research ... and a poll said that only 18% of young people were extremely proud of the country, and that's huge indictment on our nation's education system and social media. ... You look around and it's hard to believe but America's history is, although not perfect, if you're comparing it to perfection it's still pretty unique and special."
Commissioner Mike Hewitt (R) served as emcee for last week's event, which featured a procession of St. Mary's County color guards, remarks from dignitaries and the hanging of the POW flag by Paul Thorn of St. Mary's County ABATE of Maryland.
American Legion Post 221 of Avenue held a flag retirement ceremony, while Elks Lodge 2092 of California gave a history of the American flag.
"Flag Day to me means to preserve the flag, take care of the flag and when it's in disarray then we do the honor ceremony," said American Legion Post 221 Color Guard Capt. Rick Jennings, who added he thinks "a lot of people know about [Flag Day] but let it go to the wayside."
The cast from the St. Mary's Summerstock production of "Cinderella" performed the national anthem and the county song, and refreshments were provided by the Seventh District Optimist Club.
Residents can drop off unserviceable flags at the three St. Mary's County senior centers, three public libraries, the ACE Hardware stores in Charlotte Hall and Leonardtown or at the American Legion Post 221 at 21690 Colton's Point Road in Avenue.
