title: Hogan Visits Port Street
author: Tom McCall
content:
Hogan Visits Port Street

 October 18, 2024 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: Tom McCall | Section: Local News 
 
 358
 Words 

 Read News Document

 EASTON — Port Street got a distinguished visitor at the Neighborhood Service Center. Former Gov. Larry Hogan is running for the open U.S. Senate seat and stopped in Easton Friday to talk with people at the service center.He visited the facility on 126 Port Street and asked questions.
The Responsible Father Initiative, founded by Corey Pack and co-facilitated by Lou Dorsey, is an outreach program to help men become better fathers. It is a nonprofit and is all confidential. It provides food, clothing and first month's rent to people in need. These men gave Hogan the tour of the center.
Pack spoke to the governor about what they teach.
"We go over what is called the three E's. Emotion, energy and expression. And we talk about effective listening skills," Pack said. "We run through the 7/38/55 rule. 7% of the way we communicate is verbally. 38% is with our tone and 55% is with our body language."
The governor listened closely.
"I did not realize that," Hogan said. "That is an important lesson for me to learn."
He listened to more about the program.
"We try to develop more nurturing and caring fathers in this program. Most of the guys grew up in a home without a father. Some have been incarcerated with no contact with their children. It is great for them to see their children and establish a relationship with their children," Dorsey said.
Hogan recognized that a lot of men needed these services and saluted their dedication to helping these men flourish.
"It sounds like you guys are doing really important work here," Hogan said.
One of the Neighborhood Service Center workers asked Hogan to run for president. He smiled.
Hogan toured spaces intended for children. Then he went into the kitchen and in another room saw where they store clothes to give away.
At the end of tour, he was give two T-shirts and a coffee mug that touted the Neighborhood Service Center.
After his visit he stopped to do an interview in the parking lot. Hogan said his campaign is focused on the economy and crime.
"We are meeting voters every day," he said. "The people of Maryland know me after eight years of being governor."

title: Talbot not alone facing criticism on elections
author: CALEY FOX SHANNON and MORGAN LEASON Capital News Service
content:
Talbot not alone facing criticism on elections

 October 19, 2024 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: CALEY FOX SHANNON and MORGAN LEASON Capital News Service | Section: Local News 
 
 1225
 Words 

 Read News Document

 ANNAPOLIS — As local election boards work around the clock to recruit and train workers before early voting starts next week, some Maryland counties are facing pressure to hire more Republican election judges.Elections officials across the state told Capital News Service they are still working through the challenge of hiring an equal number of Republican and Democratic election judges, who administer the vote and then count ballots.
"Parity is something we always aspire to," David Garreis, Anne Arundel County election director, told CNS. "But frequently what you're gonna find is that the participation rates between the parties are very different."
By Maryland law, local boards of elections must make every effort to staff polling places with an equal number of judges who are registered Democrats and Republicans. That's what Garreis and other local election officials tell CNS they are working on now.
But officials in some counties aren't offering their recruitment numbers or providing updates to the public — even in the face of concerns from local Republicans who say they'd like to volunteer but can't seem to get a foot in the door.
"I think they're not being fair with me, and they're not being transparent about the situation," said Shawn Poulson, a Kent County Republican and former local party official who says his application to serve as a judge was sidelined by his local board.
CNS spoke with non-partisan election officials, party leaders and would-be Republican judges in multiple counties to understand this issue, which has elevated the conversation about election integrity in Maryland.
TALBOT COUNTYIn an Oct. 1 letter to the local board of elections, Talbot County Sheriff Joseph Gamble said he had received 25 complaints from residents over the uneven party distribution of election judges.
Among those complaints, Gamble said, were several Republicans who wanted to serve but were instead placed on standby and told that there were no vacancies at the time. Elections aren't under Gamble's purview as sheriff, but he told CNS he was weighing in due to the high volume of complaints he had received.
Jared DeMarinis, the state administrator of elections, quickly tried to reassure the public in a press release following Gamble's letter.
"An election judge's partisan affiliation does not impact or determine the outcome of the election," he wrote. "Voters decide the outcomes of elections."
The head of the local board said the numbers are getting pretty close to even.
Tammy Stafford, Talbot County's election director, told CNS this week that she has hired 124 election judges, including 61 Democrats, 53 Republicans and 10 unaffiliated judges. She emphasized that these numbers are subject to change.
Stafford said that 106 of the election judges in her county are returning after having worked in the primary. She said her office continues to take applications from interested voters, but as of now, the 10 polling places across Talbot County are fully staffed.
KENT COUNTYPoulson, 47, of Worton, told CNS that he applied to be a Republican election judge in Kent County and was placed on a standby list instead of being assigned to a polling place.
Poulson previously served as an election judge and was chair of the Kent County Republican Central Committee. After stepping down from the committee this spring, Poulson said he immediately applied to be an election judge. He said he wanted to be a chief judge — one of the two judges who run a polling place and manage other judges.
Instead, Poulson was disappointed to receive a letter last month stating he was assigned as a standby judge. Poulson said he is not aware of an update from Kent County Election Director Cheemoandia Blake.
Blake declined to speak with CNS or provide an update on the number of election judges hired in Kent County by party.
ANNE ARUNDEL COUNTYGarreis said his team is working tirelessly to recruit judges through events at churches and schools as well as by direct mail and social media. These efforts include partnership with both the Democratic and Republican Central Committees in Anne Arundel County.
"With our election judges, usually the first qualification is, do you have a pulse?" Garreis said. "Because it's usually very hard to find election judges. The only reason that we would really turn someone away is if they are at a precinct, and we've already filled all the spots at the precinct."
Garreis said he has hired more than 2,100 judges so far and needs to hire roughly 400 more. Of those judges, more than half are Democrats, just over a quarter are Republicans, and the rest are unaffiliated.
Registered voters need to attend a three-hour training session in person before they can serve as an election judge.
CALVERT COUNTYKristen Scott, deputy elections administrator in Calvert County, told CNS she has recruited 368 election judges: 181 Democrats, 140 Republicans and 47 unaffiliated. She said the uneven party split should not be of concern to voters.
"The one thing that we really do stress to our election judges is that this is a nonpartisan position," Scott said. "When you're in that polling place, there's no political talk. It's very nonpartisan, and you're there to serve the voter, whatever party it is."
Like Garreis, Scott said she doesn't immediately turn away judges but places them on a standby list. In the event that someone cannot serve, she can replace those individuals with Republicans on standby. She said she prioritizes parity on a precinct level.
Scott said that voters can also be poll watchers. Watchers, sometimes called "challengers," register with their party and are approved to be onsite at precincts to watch election judges. Watchers are unpaid and do not interact with voters or make decisions regarding the vote, but they can report misconduct or other concerns.
CECIL COUNTYGary Holmes, Cecil County's election director, told CNS he has fully staffed his precincts, hiring approximately 150 Republicans, 140 Democrats and 46 judges who are unaffiliated or third-party.
Although President Joe Biden won Maryland in the 2020 general election, voters in Cecil County overwhelmingly favored Donald Trump.
Holmes said that when he attends training sessions, he tells prospective election judges, "You're not here to be political. You're not here to express an opinion."
Holmes said that his team is proactively fighting misinformation about the election, sharing proper links through social media and directing voters to the state's election rumor-tracking page.
Holmes said that the state's rigorous system of checks and balances ensures that the vote is secure.
"We don't care who you vote for as long as you get the chance to vote, and we can assure you that we're very particular about how these records are being kept," he said.
MONTGOMERY COUNTYGilberto Zelaya, public relations officer at the Montgomery County Board of Elections, told CNS that he couldn't say how parity is shaping up between Democrats and Republicans because his team is still in the thick of recruiting.
To hire between 3,500 and 4,000 election judges, Zelaya said, his team holds an average of 500 events annually. Zelaya said he works closely with both parties and has held at least four meet-and-greet events this year at the local GOP office in Rockville.
Stacey Sauter, vice chair of the Montgomery County GOP, also plays a role in voter education and election judge recruitment.
"It's an overwhelming task for the Board of Elections," Sauter told CNS. "And what I have witnessed so far is what they do is very fair and balanced, but they are the apparatus. You cannot control what happens with the people when they go to work at the polls."

title: Cambridge election results in, mayoral race goes to runoff
author: Maggie Trovato
content:
Cambridge election results in, mayoral race goes to runoff

 October 19, 2024 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: Maggie Trovato | Section: Local News 
 
 1017
 Words 

 Read News Document

 CAMBRIDGE — Throughout Saturday, Cambridge residents visited 447 Race Street to cast their votes in the city's election for a mayor and commissioners.A total of 14 candidates ran to fill the city's mayoral and five commissioner seats. The mayoral race will go to a runoff election in December.
A total of 1,543 Cambridge residents showed up to the polls Saturday. Cambridge Assistant City Manager Brandon Hesson said there are 8,982 active registered voters in Cambridge.
Hesson said the number of registered voters in Cambridge is an "incredible amount." He said it is important they vote for their preferred candidates.
"Every other Monday is a council meeting where important decisions are made," he said. "And the residents are going to want people in those seats that represent them and their thoughts on where this community should and shouldn't be going."
MAYORAL RACECambridge Commission President Lajan Cephas and former Cambridge Mayor Andrew Bradshaw will go head to head in a runoff election to determine the city's next mayor.
Cephas received 637 votes Saturday, or 42.52% of the vote. Bradshaw received 614 votes, or 40.99% of the vote.
Cephas said the results tell her that residents have faith in the city's current leadership.
"They're saying that we would like for you to do this another four years," she said. "So that's how I feel. It's a good feeling to know we are going in the right direction."
Cephas said now it is a matter of making reconnections with voters.
Bradshaw said he is confident going into the runoff, but he knows Cephas is a "very solid candidate as well." He said that now, the voters will be able to directly compare him and Cephas.
"We can talk about policy versus a lack of policy direction," he said. "And we're in a position where we can now contrast the candidates for people in a really direct way."
Former Cambridge Commissioner La-Shon Foster, who also ran in the race, received 247 votes, or 16.49% of the vote.
The run-off election will be held on Dec. 3 at 447 Race Street. The candidate that secures the most votes in the run-off election will take Mayor Stephen Rideout's seat.
In June, Rideout said he would not be running for reelection. He told the Star Democrat that when he ran in 2022, he only intended to fill the remainder of the term of Bradshaw, who resigned in January 2022 after being charged for distributing revenge porn on Reddit.
WARD 1Brett Summers won the Ward 1 commissioner race with 293 votes, or 54.56% of the vote.
Incumbent Commissioner Laurel Atkiss received 244 votes, or 45.44% of the vote. Atkiss was elected in June 2023 in a special election to finish the unexpired term of then Ward 1 Commissioner Brian Roche.
Summers said he is looking forward to working to implement the ideas he ran on including advocating to hire a commercial real estate broker for the Cambridge Harbor project, hiring a tenant advocate, building a dog park and returning the Cambridge Police Department to a 25-step pay scale.
"I'm eager to work with my other city council members and see if we can implement some new things that make Cambridge better," he said.
WARD 2Shay Lewis-Sisco won the Ward 2 commissioner race with 106 votes, or 50.96% of the vote.
Nancy Jackson received 66 votes, or 31.73% of the vote. Jermaine Anderson received 20 votes, or or 9.62% of the vote. Jenna LeCompte received 16 votes, or 7.69% of the vote.
Lewis-Sisco said she anticipated the race would go to a runoff and said she is overwhelmed and excited.
"I'm absolutely looking forward to serving the community, representing Ward 2 to the best of my ability, engaging the community leaders to be a part of the process, to be able to work collaboratively (and) to be responsive to community," she said. "I'm also super excited to serve with the other commissioners that were elected tonight."
Currently, Lajan Cephas is the Ward 2 commissioner.
WARD 3Frank Stout was voted in as the city's Ward 3 commissioner. Stout received 191 votes, or 73.46% of the vote.
Gary Gordy received 69 votes, or 26.54% of the vote.
Stout said he is "very thankful" for the support he's received and he is looking forward to representing Ward 3 and the city to his "fullest and best ability." He said he's also looking forward to serving with the other elected commissioners.
"I'm really thankful for the total outcome," he said about the election. "I think there's a great group to work with."
Jameson Harrington is the current Ward 3 commissioner. In June, Harrington told the Star Democrat that he would not be seeking reelection. He said he likes to volunteer and help, but politics is "just not my forte."
WARD 4Incumbent Commissioner Sputty Cephas took the city's Ward 4 commissioner seat. Cephas received 144 votes, or 54.14% of the vote. Sputty Cephas has served as commissioner since 2021.
Sputty Cephas said he's excited to be able to "continue forward" as commissioner of Ward 4.
"I definitely felt that my work wasn't complete," he said. "And I'm grateful to the citizens and constituents of the fourth ward that they agreed and that they have reelected me for another term."
He said he's looking forward to continuing to engage the city's youth, continuing to move the city forward and continuing to unify the city.
Former Commissioner Dave Cannon received 122 votes, or 45.86% of the vote.
WARD 5With no other candidates on the ballot, incumbent Commissioner Brian Roche will keep his Ward 5 commission seat. Roche received 158 votes.
In a text, Roche said moving into the next term, he hopes the newly elected mayor and commissioners will understand "how to truly raise the quality of life" for Cambridge's underserved.
"I've seen first hand how Cambridge has become so dependent on government transfer payments to survive... we often fail to put these programs through the filter of 'will this lift us out of poverty' or 'will it finally empower our citizens to build generational wealth?'" he said.
Roche was elected as commissioner of the ward in June 2023 in a special election to finish the unexpired term of former Commissioner Chad Malkus. Before that, Roche served as commissioner of Ward 1, which he was sworn into in 2021.

title: Talbot County election equipment certified by accuracy tests
author: KONNER METZ kmetz@chespub.com
content:
Talbot County election equipment certified by accuracy tests

 October 19, 2024 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: KONNER METZ kmetz@chespub.com | Section: Local News 
 
 269
 Words 

 Read News Document

 EASTON — Documentation of last month's logic and accuracy testing for the Talbot County Board of Elections was available for public inspection on Friday morning.The logic and accuracy testing was officially certified on Oct. 2 following a lengthy testing process from Sept. 4 to Sept. 24. Election equipment was confirmed as properly functioning and accurate by this testing, election officials say.
Every piece of Talbot County election equipment went through a checklist and was "tested separately," said Fred Gleockler, an IT specialist for the Talbot County Board of Elections. Gleockler, along with two others, conducted the certification.
Certified were the voting machines voters will use at polling places, as well as the scanner and tabulator machines. Gleockler said the logic and accuracy testing gets "more detailed every year."
"I'm proud that we do a great job on (logic) and (accuracy)," Gleockler said.
Talbot County Election Director Tammy Stafford said the logic and accuracy certification is "just the beginning of the process."
"There's a lot of reconciliation and comparison of numbers," Stafford said. This includes canvassing of mail-in ballots, along with a manual audit and comprehensive audit.
Stafford said the comprehensive audit at the end of the election is conducted by the Maryland State Board of Elections and a third party, Clear Ballot, a Boston-based elections technology company.
Clear Ballot's online portal shows a comparison of its independent tabulation of ballots and the results of the voting system's tabulation. If discrepancy between the two is above 0.5%, further auditing will be done.
Gleockler said the state's comprehensive audit process with Clear Ballot is the "best thing Maryland ever did."
"We can't have a difference of one," Gleockler said.

title: Some Oxford residents call for change, creating rift in town
author: Maggie Trovato
content:
Some Oxford residents call for change, creating rift in town

 October 19, 2024 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: Maggie Trovato | Section: Local News 
 
 1820
 Words 

 Read News Document

 OXFORD — When Tom Costigan was first elected to the Commissioners of Oxford in 2022, somewhere between six and 10 people would sit in the audience during most town meetings."Including my wife," he said.
Today, getting a seat at Oxford's meetings, held every other Tuesday evening, can be a challenge.
Usually by the 6 p.m. start time, most, if not all of the seats, are filled. Sometimes, it's standing room only. In late July, the town office learned that a resident had reported town meetings to the Office of the State Fire Marshal for being overcrowded.
Many residents say the community's heightened involvement in Oxford's government started with former Police Chief Patrick Maxwell's abrupt retirement in February 2023, for which the town never provided a reason.
Since then, residents have continued to show up for meetings. Many of them seek more transparency from the town's government, which some residents think is more of a concern than others.
Town Commissioner Katrina Greer said she thinks Maxwell's departure was a wake-up call for the town.
"There were things that came to light about salaries and jobs and things that were not completely transparent to the public," Greer said. "And so that's when I decided to run for office, that March."
At the Feb. 28, 2023, town meeting, over 100 residents packed the Oxford Community Center, many voicing concerns about the circumstances of Maxwell's retirement and transparency in the town's government.
Commission President Norm Bell said Maxwell's departure resulted in "contentious meetings."
"My belief is that the tension was always under the surface," he said about residents' concerns. "This opened it up and let it explode."
CHANGE IN ATMOSPHEREWhen Costigan and his wife bought their house in Oxford in 2000, there were multiple things he loved about the town. He loved the many volunteer opportunities, the "tremendous sense of community" and the normalcy of saying hello to a passing stranger on the street.
"It just seemed like Valhalla," he said.
Twenty-four years later, Costigan thinks the town is different, but the "important vestiges" of what he loved still remain.
He said he's noticed a change in the atmosphere at town meetings.
"When you've got people sitting there that you know are just waiting to pounce on you, it's really hard to do a meeting like that," he said.
Bell characterized town meetings these days as vocal and, to some extent, tense.
Recently, the town passed — and then repealed and replaced — a resolution establishing general rules and procedures regarding public participation at town meetings. When Bell introduced the original resolution in early September, he said it was developed as a result of "disruptive behavior" at a previous town meeting in August.
During that August meeting, yelling broke out after resident Scott Rensberger asked to sit down with Bell at a later date to discuss a public letter Bell wrote in April. The letter mentioned videos made by Rensberger about government transparency in Oxford. One of the videos detailed concerns with decisions made by former Town Manager Cheryl Lewis.
In the time since Maxwell's departure from the police department, residents have brought up concerns with some of the town practices and asked for more transparency regarding town finances, salaries and hiring practices.
Before Lewis — who some of the transparency concerns were directed toward — retired in June, the town announced her role would be filled by Michael Calvert, who was previously a city administrator in Liberty, South Carolina.
Just three days after the announcement, it was announced that the town and Calvert had "mutually agreed to part ways."
The commission did not comment on why the decision was made. Former Liberty City Council member Peggy Edwards said she resigned from the council due to issues with Calvert and the city's mayor. She said that when Calvert was in the position, there was a lack of transparency and mismanagement of money.
Rensberger said it didn't take him long to find out that "there were a lot of problems" in Liberty and took the information he found to Oxford's town attorney.
SPECTRUM OF VIEWSThe yelling incident at the August meeting caused resident Tom Campbell to say that he has a hard time recognizing the town anymore.
"This can't be every town meeting," Campbell said. "We're getting nowhere, and it's making it hard for me to cheer on my community anymore."
Rensberger said in an email that he thinks town meetings are "just fine." He said people are entitled to their opinions and should raise their hands to speak. He said he is against interruptions and name calling.
Greer said there have been very few incidents during town meetings that were "even a small problem." She said sharing different viewpoints is essential to coming to the best possible decision.
"You'll have people in the same room that are ultra-conservative, and you'll have people that worked for Nancy Pelosi," she said. "And they're ignited, and they care about open government and professionalism and having things be transparent."
Greer said this is what makes commissioners better. She said commissioners shouldn't necessarily agree all the time, either. "It should not be a rubber stamp of ideas," she said.
Not every resident in town is on the same page about whether what is happening at town meetings is for the better.
Deborah Pulzone, who has lived in Oxford for almost 30 years, said things have gotten "too divisive and ugly" in the last year. She said she is trying to maintain a "center ground."
"There have been so many times I've bitten my tongue, I almost have a hole in it," she said.
For Pulzone, division in Oxford is a microcosm of what's happening in the country.
"There is a lot of divide in the country," she said. "And people are seeing it and hearing it, and they're feeling it here."
Resident Karen Wayland, who moved to Oxford two years ago, but grew up in a small town, said there might be some division in the town, but it's no different from other places.
"I just think it's uncomfortable for people who have had a certain way of doing things and now are being asked to justify their decisions more than they had to in the past," she said.
Wayland said that's what being in government is all about. "Being able to articulate why you're doing something to everyone who has a right to know," she said.
Greer thinks the sustained involvement and interest in town government from residents is amazing. She sees it as a reflection of the post-COVID-19 world.
"People are paying attention," she said. "We have a particularly engaged and intelligent citizen community that often works together on many different nonprofits and commissions. And so they're paying attention."
TAKING STEPS FORWARDRuss Gray, who has lived in Oxford for almost 22 years, said everyone in town wants the same thing: faith and trust in their government and open communication with their government.
He thinks there is a faction of the town that "is pretty much talking about everything that's wrong with Oxford."
To overcome division, Gray thinks the Oxford community needs to figure out how to get back to engaging in a friendly way and listening to each other, even when they disagree.
"Everyone needs to put effort in it," he said. "We cannot pick sides. Period."
Rensberger, who bought a home in Oxford eight years ago, said the town is "completely torn apart." He said on one side, there are the people who control the town and its various boards and commissions, and on the other, there are people with no control.
"Right now, the two commissioners that run the town are doing their best to keep my side from even asking questions," he said in an email.
Rensberger called Oxford the least transparent town he's ever seen. He thinks a forensic audit would bring clarity to multiple issues, but said he doesn't think all of the commissioners want that.
"Oxford's only about 40 simple questions away from becoming the perfect town," he said.
Gray said there is a need for transparency, "but not where you think it would be."
At a town meeting on Sept. 24, Gray brought up an informal meeting Greer held days before for residents to share their thoughts on the process for interacting with commissioners and qualities they want in a town manager.
The email, which the Star Democrat obtained, was sent to a list of undisclosed recipients. One of those recipients was Commission President Bell. If Bell had attended, it could have been considered a quorum, the minimum number of commissioners needed to conduct business.
At a town meeting on Oct. 8, Town Attorney Lyndsey Ryan said that if two commissioners had been present at the informal meeting, it could have been a violation of the Maryland Open Meetings Act, but since Bell was not there, it was not a violation.
In an interview, Gray said Greer's actions could have resulted in an Open Meetings Act violation and said there are ways to get word out to the entire public, not just to select residents.
Greer said meeting individually with residents is one of the best things you can do as a commissioner. She said the email did go to Bell, but Bell and Costigan are "smart enough to know" what they can and can't do when it comes to the Open Meetings Act.
Greer said she didn't send the email to everyone because she doesn't have everyone's email. She said she doesn't normally post on social media.
Wayland said improving public notice and getting better at sharing public documents are important steps toward improving residents' transparency concerns.
"If you operate with a commitment to transparency, people are more likely to take your word for what you say rather than trying to FOIA everything," she said. "I think, unfortunately, there's a lot of mistrust in the town and it's going to take a real commitment to openness and transparency before the commissioners are going to get a lot of breathing room."
Greer said there are many things she thinks the commissioners will need to address, but for right now, they need to address staffing issues.
Oxford's town office is currently without a town manager or a planning and zoning coordinator. At the end of the month, it will also be without an assistant clerk. Costigan said he thinks the shelf life of employees is getting shorter, not just in Oxford, but all over.
As they address staffing, Greer said the commissioners need to move toward a more transparent government.
Bell said he thinks there are people in town that are satisfied with the transparency of town government and those that want more of it.
"I'm not arguing with that," he said about those who want more transparency. "They're right."
Bell said the commissioners are taking those steps toward increased transparency, it's just a matter of how they go about it and timing.
Greer said there are some people who have been involved with Oxford's government for many years that have had difficulty accepting change.
"And I'm sensitive to that," she said. "But it doesn't mean, as an organization, that we shouldn't inspect ourselves and try to be better. It's not a criticism of the past, it is a wish for the future."

title: Oxford needs to resolve rift dividing the town
author: Staff Writer
content:
Oxford needs to resolve rift dividing the town

 October 19, 2024 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: Staff Writer | Section: Editorials 
 
 692
 Words 

 Read News Document

 There is trouble brewing in Oxford.Actually, it has been brewing for quite some time.
Star Democrat reporter Maggie Trovato did an excellent job providing the background on the rift in Oxford. Her story appears on the front page of today's weekend edition.
Trovato's reporting provides the background on how we got to where we are today. It does not, however, offer solutions.
Solutions need to come from Oxford town leaders and the residents.
We hope they find those solutions quickly.
Over the years, Oxford has maintained its quaint, historical charm. The tree-line streets. The downtown shops. The Robert Morris Inn. The Scotitsh Highland Creamery.
James Michner penned his classic novel "Chesapeake" while staying in town.
Yet the image that draws thousands of tourists each year does not carry over to town meetings, which have become packed with angry residents, shouting at each other but not always listening to what others are saying.
Many residents say the community's rift in Oxford's government started with former Police Chief Patrick Maxwell's abrupt retirement in February 2023, for which the town never provided a reason.
Since then, residents have packed town commission meetings. Many of them seek more transparency from the town's government, which some residents think is more of a concern than others.
Commission President Norm Bell said Maxwell's departure resulted in "contentious meetings."
"My belief is that the tension was always under the surface," he said about residents' concerns. "This opened it up and let it explode."
Residents began asking questions and did not always get answers.
One of those residents is Scott Rensberger. Rensberger rubs some people the wrong way. This is too bad because he has been asking questions that deserve answers.
The questions started with the salary for Town Manager Cheryl Lewis, a salary that was not easily found in the town's budget.
That's a problem. Residents should know what town officials are paid. The town budget should be easy to follow, clearly showing where money is going.
After Lewis announced her retirement, the town commissioners hired Michael Calvert, who was previously city administrator in Liberty, South Carolina.
That hire lasted just three days. Questions were raised about Calvert's history, which a former Liberty council member said lacked transparency and included accusations of mismanagement of money.
The commission never commented on what led to the quick decision to mutually agree to part ways with Calvert.
We think an explanation from the commission would go a long way to begin healing the rift in town. The explanation could be as simple as: "We made a mistake and did not take enough time checking candidates' background. We are moving forward and have established a plan to avoid those mistakes as we look for a new town manager."
The commission needs to pledge to strive for transparency in its actions. A good start would be conducting interviews with town manager finalists in open session.
Likewise, the yelling from the audience needs to stop. Having resident involvement in meetings is the foundation of a democracy, but that involvement needs to be civil.
A yelling incident at an August Commissioners of Oxford meeting caused resident Tom Campbell to say that he has a hard time recognizing the town anymore.
"This can't be every town meeting," Campbell said. "We're getting nowhere, and it's making it hard for me to cheer on my community anymore."
Russ Gray, who has lived in Oxford for almost 22 years, said everyone in town wants the same thing: faith and trust in their government and open communication with their government.
He thinks there is a faction of the town that "is pretty much talking about everything that's wrong with Oxford."
To overcome division, Gray thinks the Oxford community needs to figure out how to get back to engaging in a friendly way and listening to each other, even when they disagree.
"Everyone needs to put effort in it," he said. "We cannot pick sides. Period."
Russ Gray is an astute observer of Oxford politics. We think Oxford town meetings need to be more like a Norman Rockwell image and less like an episode of "The Jerry Springer Show."
Oxford has the people to make this happen. Let's hope they decide to work together to make town government more resemble the image that draws thousands of tourists to Oxford each year.

title: Despite split opinions, Easton Planning Commission approves Silo Square townhomes
author: KONNER METZ kmetz@chespub.com
content:
Despite split opinions, Easton Planning Commission approves Silo Square townhomes

 October 19, 2024 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: KONNER METZ kmetz@chespub.com | Section: Local News 
 
 656
 Words 

 Read News Document

 EASTON — Amid resident pushback and design concerns, the Easton Planning Commission unanimously voted to approve a 28-unit townhouse development at the site of a former Perdue AgriBusiness operation in Easton.The Silo Square development is led by Chesapeake Community Development, a subsidiary of The Arc Central Chesapeake Region. It is a mixed-income housing project on a 2.36-acre lot at 410 Needwood Avenue, within the East End area that the town is aiming to revitalize.
An updated site plan was presented at Thursday's Planning Commission meeting, along with a traffic study that was requested when developers weren't granted approval last month. The project is set to include 16 three-story townhomes and 12 two-story townhomes.
The 10 grain bins currently on the lot, often referred to by community members as silos, would be demolished.
Residents that live near the site spoke during public comment on Thursday, largely in opposition to the design of the townhomes. Developers have stated the architecture is intended to "pay homage" to the Perdue site and fit in the surrounding industrial area.
"This is the core of Easton," resident Tom Ledvina said. "The code and the (comprehensive) plan say it has to look, it has to be compatible with that historic look that makes Easton special. And this just doesn't."
Zach Smith, an attorney representing the developers, asked that the commission look toward the town staff's review and analysis of the project, which noted it does fit within Easton's comprehensive plan.
"We don't have to get the consensus of the neighbors in order to move forward," Smith said. "What we have to do is to comply with the town's requirements."
Resident Maury Schlesinger spoke in disapproval of how the project faces inward toward the parking lot, with its back to the street. He said it will be "distinct" and "separate" compared to the nearby residential designs.
"Is this how we want our economically challenged people to live?" Schlesinger asked the commission. "Is this how we build an inclusive community? And is the desire to approve more housing right now so great that concern for (developers') budgets and timetable overcomes the need to protect the character of the town?
"I'm all for affordable housing, but it shouldn't look like this."
COMMISSION SPLITCommission members Victoria McAndrews and William Ryall, who were not present at the September meeting, expressed their own concerns about the project. McAndrews and fellow member Thomas Klein said they didn't like the design.
"This to me, has an incredibly suburban subdivision feel, as opposed to being an integrated part of the neighborhood," McAndrews said. "And I'm just wondering what is the rationale for not following the existing framework of how the neighborhood is laid out."
Commission Chairperson Philip Toussaint and Vice Chairperson Michael Ports complimented the design of the townhomes and pushed for approval.
Smith did the same, noting that developers fulfilled the requests made by the commission last month to include a traffic study — which revealed no significant impacts — and remove a section of fencing.
"We left this meeting last month with a clear direction that we needed to address the fence and we needed … a traffic study," Smith said. "We've done both of those things, and now we're at a point where we're facing having to come back yet again. This is how workforce housing projects die."
Ryall, who said he liked the design but was "torn" over whether it fit within the surrounding residential area, joined Toussaint and Ports in supporting approval.
"I don't want to let perfection get in the way of the good," Ryall said. "So I'm willing to vote in favor of it."
Ports moved for approval, seconded by Toussaint. All members voted yes, though McAndrews and Klein did so reluctantly, emphasizing their disagreement with the design.
Since the proposal came in the town's planned redevelopment overlay district, it will not require approval from the Easton Town Council. Thursday's vote was passed on the conditions that developers make minor adjustments to the site plan and approval is granted by town staff.

title: Equal means equal
author: Staff Writer
content:
Equal means equal

 October 19, 2024 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: Staff Writer | Section: Editors Inbox 
 
 321
 Words 

 Read News Document

 There has been a great deal of consternation lately concerning election judges in Talbot County. In fact, many people have complained to Sheriff Gamble since Maryland election law is being violated. As a good citizen and duly elected law enforcement officer, the sheriff wrote a letter to the election director questioning the intent of violating the law.For months, the election director has been dodging questions made by the public and apparently has been manipulating the law; however, this issue of flagrant abuse of the law has gone national. As anticipated, our Maryland state attorney general finally decided to weigh in. The Attorney General sent a letter to duly elected Sheriff reminding him that, as sheriff, he has nothing to do with enforcing election law.
Of course, we citizens of all political parties have a responsibility to ensure fair and safe elections, and the sheriff, unlike the attorney general, was properly amplifying the disbelief of concerned citizens.
Intentionally breaking the law? Are you really?
After the slap, the attorney general quoted the law, which states each polling place shall have an equal number of election judges from Democrat and Republican parties. He then says that, although that is true at each polling place, the total number of judges need not be equal between the two parties. What? Where are these unequal judges on duty if not at a polling place?
In past years, the people of Talbot County were told by the director of the Board of Elections that there weren't enough Republicans who signed up to be election judges. Nonsense.
If judge totals must be equal at every polling place, then the totals across the county will be equal. There are now 61 Democrats, 53 Republicans and 10 "other."
In our 10 precincts, only four abide by the law. It appears that information has been withheld from Talbot voters.
What part of equal does the election director Tammy Stafford and the Talbot election board not understand?
MARYANN JUDY
Easton

title: State officials, County Council discuss Talbot transportation projects
author: KONNER METZ kmetz@chespub.com
content:
State officials, County Council discuss Talbot transportation projects

 October 23, 2024 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: KONNER METZ kmetz@chespub.com | Section: Local News 
 
 602
 Words 

 Read News Document

 EASTON — State transportation leaders and officials filled the chamber of the Talbot County Council on Tuesday afternoon to discuss local transportation projects and a tightening state budget.Paul Wiedefeld, secretary of the Maryland Department of Transportation, explained the "significant budgetary challenges" his department is facing, due in part to the state's economy, increasing material costs and lower than expected revenue.
Wiedefeld noted that MDOT's Consolidated Transportation Program for fiscal years 2025 to 2030 — which has an $18.9 billion balanced plan — experienced a $1.3 billion reduction compared to last year's program.
He and Will Pines, administrator of the State Highway Administration, emphasized safety as the state's top priority.
"While we must live within our budget, we'll continue to do big things to support projects and programs throughout the county," Pines said.
Pines noted a bevy of improvements, which included higher visibility at Maryland 322 and U.S. Route 50 intersections, traffic signal improvements at Route 50 and Airport Road, a new signal at Black Dog Alley and Dover Road, and resurfacing on Matthewstown Road.
He also thanked the St. Michaels community for its patience as the state worked on sidewalk reconstruction.
Representatives from the state's Transportation Authority, Motor Vehicle Administration, Aviation Administration and Port Administration provided updates to the council.
Ashish Solanki, director of the Office of Regional Aviation Assistance, told council members about the $1.4 billion in "economic activity" generated from the state's 34 public airports.
"We recognize that certainly (Easton Airport) is one of those strong contributors to that economic impact," Solanki said. He stated upwards of 500 jobs and more than $91 million in business revenue stems from the Easton Airport.
He added that the state is providing $560,000 in grant assistance to Easton Airport this year.
After thanking state officials for their updates and assistance to the county, Council Vice President Pete Lesher asked Pines about improvements at Route 322 and Glenwood Avenue in Easton. That project was listed for potential deferral by the state.
"I know that our partners at Easton are looking forward to that project as part of the rail-trail safety," Lesher said. " … I just wanted to ask about the likelihood of that and whether that might be reconsidered."
Pines said that the state is "evaluating" that project and others to see if they fit within the Federal Highway Administration's Highway Safety Improvement Program. If so, federal funding could be unlocked, but if not, that Glenwood Avenue project would have to "compete it out against many other projects that need the state funding," Pines said.
"This very well could be a great candidate, it just has to go through the more detailed evaluation for us to confirm," he said.
Council President Chuck Callahan thanked Wiedefeld, Pines and District 2 Engineer Ken Fender for their help in improving safety at the airport and its surrounding roads. "It's those little things that mean a lot to us, and we really appreciate it," Callahan said.
Callahan added that he's grateful for the state's partnership in facilitating the temporary closure of a portion of Route 662, which is allowing construction of the University of Maryland Shore Regional Health's new hospital. Route 662's partial closure began earlier this month. The road will reopen in May.
Sen. Johnny Mautz (R-Caroline, Dorchester, Talbot, Wicomico) was in attendance, and echoed the same about the hospital, saying it's going to "have a huge impact on transportation in the county." Mautz encouraged the County Council to stay on top of transportation challenges in the coming year.
"I think we're going to have some challenges," Mautz said, "and I just would urge the council and the town to communicate with MDOT and hopefully MDOT will be looking for that communication."

title: Branson and Perez vie for Denton council seat
author: Tom McCall
content:
Branson and Perez vie for Denton council seat

 October 23, 2024 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: Tom McCall | Section: Local News 
 
 915
 Words 

 Read News Document

 DENTON — Two candidates have qualified to run in Denton's upcoming Town Council election. They are Lester L. Branson and Angel L. Perez.Branson is 82 and Perez is 38. Perez is the program and events manager for the Chesapeake Culinary Center and the CEO and founder of Caroline Pride. Branson is an optometrist on Market Street.
The winner will serve a five-year term. The election will be held the same day as the general election, Nov. 5, at the Denton Town Office, located at 4 N. Second St. The polls will be open from 7 a.m. to 8 p.m.
The Star Democrat spoke to both candidates ahead of the election. Their answers to the paper's questions can be found below.
WHAT IS YOUR POLITICAL EXPERIENCE?Perez: "Here on the Shore, I served as community outreach/Main Street coordinator for the Town of Greensboro. I presented best practices at statewide Maryland Municipal League Conference in my talk titled, 'Partnering for Progress: Municipalities and Community Organizations Working Together,' where elected officials and municipal staff learned about developing partnerships between municipalities and community organizations is critical to providing quality services to a shared constituency. In addition to this Maryland political experience, I also bring fresh ideas from serving as district assistant for a city council in Massachusetts. We created a communication bridge between residents and the City Council and community programs."
Perez went on to list leadership positions he has held with 19 boards and organizations on the Eastern Shore in the past 10 years.
Branson: "I have been mayor five times and on the board for 38 years. So I know everything you want to know."
WHAT MAKES YOU THE BEST CANDIDATE FOR THE POSITION?Branson: "The biggest thing is I have been doing this for 38 years and I know the ins and outs of everything."
Perez: "Over the past 10 years I have dedicated myself to working tirelessly to be part of the solution. I come to run as a candidate to bring people together, connecting with our community and impacting it in a positive way, especially through the creation of different local programs for youth and families. Having the ability to make decisions based on knowledge and data not assumptions, making decisions that benefit everyone in our town. Direct contact with all the different kinds of residents in Denton and knowledge of the situations that our community has, especially our elderly, youth and small business owners. Being able to bring new ideas and perspectives and new ways to help our town grow."
WHY ARE YOU RUNNING?Branson: "I am running because there is a lot of things I'd like to get done. And the five of us, right now, for the last few years, we work so sweetly together, and there is no rift or anything like that. We really get things done for the town of Denton and the citizens of Denton. I am hoping to keep that going."
Perez: "My home, the Town of Denton, has always had a special place in my heart, and I can serve better our community as part of the Town Council. I want to continue to work for my community in a respectful and equitable manner and help our town move towards the future with strong economic growth while maintaining our small town charm."
WHAT CHANGE WOULD YOU LIKE TO SEE IN THE NEXT FIVE YEARS?Perez: "I will actively listen to small business owners to develop solutions together. Also, I will provide support and assistance to the downtown Main Street office to combine efforts to protect and preserve our local businesses. We should keep property taxes low and water costs affordable for all... Our town is full of history and art. The Town Council can create collaborations with organizations that showcase art and history in our town is essential to expand, promote, and highlight the arts and history district in our town by providing them with the necessary support. Thus, making our town, art and history enjoyed by visitors and citizens... For the past 10 years, my work has been focused on seeking the well-being and impacting our youth in a positive way through different programs and community services. As a council member, I will seek to create collaborations and build bridges of communication with different organizations to create, promote and expand programs that help our young people reach their full potential."
Branson: "See the change from the social service building. I really want to see the road to nowhere from Walmart over to 404 is going to be called Commerce Drive. It has gone from $1 million to $3 million to build the road. I really want us to cut taxes again this year. I hope there is a way to get this road money to help with the taxes and not have to double tax the people in town. I am looking for any way that we can make it better for affordable housing for people in Denton... Another big thing is that we are looking with the county, they are going to have to build another middle school. There is a possibility that where Caroline County High School is that there is land to do that out there. In the future, are they going to keep the middle school there or put it somewhere else in Denton or are they going to go out to North Caroline and put it there? ... Another thing is to build water and sewer out in west Denton. There are a lot of houses where their septic systems are going out."

title: Easton outlines plan to use excess ARPA funds
author: KONNER METZ kmetz@chespub.com
content:
Easton outlines plan to use excess ARPA funds

 October 23, 2024 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: KONNER METZ kmetz@chespub.com | Section: Local News 
 
 390
 Words 

 Read News Document

 EASTON — As the deadline to obligate pandemic-era federal funds nears, the Town of Easton is moving toward an agreement that will allow for flexibility in allocating that money to different public works projects.The Easton Town Council held a workshop Monday to discuss a memorandum of understanding that will allocate up to $735,270 of American Rescue Plan Act funds to the town's public works department. The American Rescue Plan Act of 2021 awarded funds to local governments in the wake of the pandemic.
Funds must be obligated by Dec. 31 and spent by the end of next year.
There are currently $664,350 in ARPA dollars that still need to be obligated. In that total, the council previously approved the reallocation of $225,000 for Rails to Trails work on Port Street.
Town Attorney Sharon VanEmburgh said the U.S. treasury department allows for interagency agreements in obligating the ARPA funds, such as the one drafted for Easton.
Town Engineer Rick Van Emburgh said the MOU, which would be between Mayor Megan Cook and the public works department, will provide flexibility in making sure excess funds are used.
"To the dollar is hard to predict," Van Emburgh said of the fluctuating costs of projects. "And so that's why we are asking for the flexibility of having the MOU."
In addition to the Port Street trails, projects around town that may receive this funding include: impervious surface removal at Easton Point Park, sidewalk accessibility improvements, storm drain work on Harrison Street and East Avenue, and traffic signal intersection improvements.
A schedule of project timelines was shared with council members on Monday. Interim Town Manager Alan Lowrey said the town is aiming to complete projects by September, 2026 in order to have a "three-month buffer" with the Dec, 31, 2026 deadline.
"It's investments in hard infrastructure improvements in the town that we need and will have to be paid for at some point to be done, which I think is great," Lowrey said. "If we can knock some of this stuff that we need to do with these residual dollars and not give money back to the federal government, that's a win-win."
An ordinance to amend the ARPA budget and make the memorandum of understanding possible was introduced at Easton Town Council later Monday evening. A public hearing for that ordinance will be held at the town's next council meeting on Nov. 4.

title: Transportation departments share projects during Caroline County meeting

Transportation departments share projects during Caroline County meeting

 DENTON — On Tuesday morning, the Caroline County Commissioners gathered to discuss the state's Consolidated Transportation Program. Members of the Maryland Department of Transportation shared an annual presentation that included various infrastructure projects and funding challenges.Representatives from MDOT, Maryland Aviation Administration, Maryland Motor Vehicle Administration, Maryland Transit Administration, Maryland Department of Transportation State Highway Administration and Maryland Transportation Authority shared information affecting local transportation as well as statewide transportation.
LOCALWill Pines, administrator for the State Highway Administration, shared various transportation projects in Caroline County, both pending and completed.
"We understand the fiscal challenges Maryland is facing," Pines said. "However, I want to assure you of two things. First, SHA will continue to do big things moving forward, multimodal projects that improve safety, and accessibility and equity. And second, safety will always be our highest priority."
According to Pines, the newly constructed bridge on Maryland 16 over Mill Creek was reopened to traffic in September.
Additionally, Pines said two county priorities are the focal point of the fall. The first is the construction of pavement widening and signalization upgrades to provide a dedicated left turn lane from Maryland 328 to Maryland 404. This $2.1 million project is anticipated to be completed near the end of 2025.
The second is the conversion of the flashing signals at Maryland 313 and Maryland 317 to full color signals. This improvement will facilitate safer traffic movements at the intersection.
SHA hosted the second public meeting for the Maryland 404 Planning and Environmental Linkage Study. The meeting was well attended, according to Pines, and the study is anticipated to be completed by the end of the year. Once completed, SHA will work with Caroline County to identify potential breakout projects along the corridor, pending available funding.
SHA has begun a pipe replacement project on Maryland 328, near Salisbury Road. Construction crews will work daytime hours this week for site preparation, then switch to overnight hours to minimize the impacts to traffic.
Travis Johnston, local transit support director for Maryland Transit Administration, said MTA provides nearly $1 million in operating and capital grants to support local transit operations provided by Delmarva Community Transit in conjunction with Kent and Talbot counties. In addition to continued preventative maintenance, the funds will also provide one new small bus.
Earlier this month, Gov. Wes Moore announced additional grant funding to the county aimed at helping the Caroline County Sheriff's Office and the Denton Police Department address speed impairment and aggressive driving.

title: Easton Utilities to join electric utility alliance
author: KONNER METZ kmetz@chespub.com
content:
Easton Utilities to join electric utility alliance

 October 23, 2024 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: KONNER METZ kmetz@chespub.com | Section: Local News 
 
 393
 Words 

 Read News Document

 EASTON — Easton Utilities is positioning to join a municipal alliance with four other electric utility agencies across the state following support from the Easton Town Council on Monday evening.Councilmembers unanimously approved a resolution authorizing Easton Utilities to join in forming the Maryland Municipal Electric Utility Alliance. The other municipalities are Berlin, Hagerstown, Thurmont and Williamsport.
Easton Utilities, a not-for-profit utility and telecommunications company, provides electric, natural gas, water, internet and more to residents of the town ans surrounding areas. Company leaders say the alliance will facilitate a shared voice between the five members on "legislative and regulatory matters."
John Hines, vice president of electric operations and special projects at Easton Utilities, spoke to the Town Council on Monday.
"Formalizing an alliance of these shared interests will strengthen our collective positions in Annapolis during the General Assembly's legislative session," Hines said, "at a time when energy issues continue to be at the forefront of policymakers' agendas."
The alliance's articles of incorporation had already been signed by the mayors of Berlin and Thurmont prior to Monday's approval. Representatives from all five municipalities, including Mayor Megan Cook, gathered in Berlin for a workgroup session to discuss the potential alliance.
"How do you anticipate navigating a vote amongst the alliance that is unfavorable to Easton Utilities and the Town of Easton?" Council President Frank Gunsallus asked Hines.
"There may be issues that don't necessarily help us, but don't hurt us," Hines responded. "And so, at the end of the day, the broader organization and the power that comes from five bodies really will create a bigger impact."
Hines added that Easton Utilities can withdraw from the alliance at any time, and that "it still gives each local government the ability to act autonomously.
Gunsallus called it a "great idea," and all four councilmembers present voted to approve the resolution.
HOSPITAL UTILITIESThe Town Council approved a second resolution Monday evening involving Easton Utilities. Resolution 6201 authorizes the utility company to extend service to what will be Shore Regional Health's new medical center on Longwoods Road in Easton.
The medical center, which held a groundbreaking earlier Monday, is under construction and projected to open in the summer of 2028. It is replacing the current hospital on South Washington Street.
Since Easton Utilities' electric, water and wastewater services to support the project will exceed $2 million, a resolution was necessary. All four councilmembers present voted to approve the resolution.

title: Dorchester County talks road projects with MDOT
author: MAGGIE TROVATO mtrovato@chespub.com
content:
Dorchester County talks road projects with MDOT

 October 24, 2024 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: MAGGIE TROVATO mtrovato@chespub.com | Section: Local News 
 
 702
 Words 

 Read News Document

 CAMBRIDGE — During an annual transportation meeting, the Dorchester County Council pushed Maryland Department of Transportation officials on two issues: the current paving project on U.S. Route 50 and the intersection at Maryland routes 14 and 392.At the outset of the meeting, Deputy Secretary of Transportation Samantha Biddle acknowledged the department's budgetary challenges. She said the $18.9 billion Consolidated Transportation Program for fiscal years 2025 to 2030 has $1.3 billion less than the last program.
"But even with these reductions, we are committed to using those resources to advance the state's priorities," Biddle said. "And that number one priority that you always hear from us is safety."
County Council member Ricky Travers questioned the department's commitment to safety after hearing about an intersection project whose timeline is being stretched due to the budget.
"You stood up and you said your number one priority for MDOT was safety," he said to the officials. "It's not there."
INTERSECTION PROJECTState Highway Administration District Engineer Mark Crampton told the council at the meeting that the timeline to put in a roundabout at the intersection of Maryland Route 14 and Route 392 in East New Market will need to be stretched for budgetary reasons.
Crampton said the survey for the project has been completed, and a 30% plan is scheduled for January. He said the final design for the project isn't expected until fiscal year 2028 due to the extended timeline.
After Crampton spoke, Council President Lenny Pfeffer introduced the MDOT officials to Dawn Stanley, who was in an accident at the intersection last year.
"We want to put a human element to this," Pfeffer said. "I know that you aren't the ones deciding about the budget here, but we need you to be able to take these stories back with you."
Stanley said she was on a motorcycle when she collided with a car that didn't see her. She said the accident caused seven breaks in her back, two breaks in her shoulder, eight broken ribs and a broken finger. A retired EMT, Stanley said she has also "cleaned up many" people off that intersection since the '80s.
"This place needs to be fixed, and it needs to be fixed now before someone gets killed," she said. "Or is it going to take the family member of a higher up to get killed for the state to do something?"
After Stanley spoke, Crampton said he was sorry for what happened to her.
Travers told Crampton it is frustrating that the council has presented the need for the project many times and the issue hasn't been fixed yet.
"We've been through the study, we've done all this stuff," Travers said. "And then you stand up here tonight and say, 'well we're looking at 2028 or ...' It's unacceptable."
PAVING PROJECTMDOT is in the midst of a project to resurface Route 50 between Bucktown Road and the Frederick C. Malkus Jr. Bridge. Because the asphalt mix used for the project requires the temperature be at least 50 degree Fahrenheit to place it, there have been some days where MDOT has had to do work on the project in the daytime, which has caused significant traffic.
Travers said that along with increased traffic, there were accidents. He said more consideration should have gone into what time of the year to do this project.
"Nothing against the job," he said. "It's needed, and we thank you for that. But we got to figure out a better way to do this."
State Highway Administration Administrator Will Pines said that due to beach traffic in the summer, SHA had a tight window for the project. He said the project should be complete by the end of the year, weather permitting.
Pines said the westbound part of the project, which has not yet begun, could be postponed until the spring, but that could affect funding. He said if they begin other projects before finishing this one, the funding for this project could be used for other projects if there are change orders.
Council Vice President Mike Detmer said there needs to be more communication when it comes to this project.
Biddle said they will work on getting the word out better when it comes to communication and will look into short-term solutions for increasing visibility at the East New Market intersection.

title: Oxford commission approves changes to floodplain management
author: Veronica Fernandez-Alvarado
content:
Oxford commission approves changes to floodplain management

 October 24, 2024 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: Veronica Fernandez-Alvarado | Section: News 
 
 333
 Words 

 Read News Document

 OXFORD — The Commissioners of Oxford approved an ordinance to amend the town's floodplain management ordinance. The changes would loosen requirements for residents seeking to make significant improvements to buildings.Commission President Norm Bell opened the public hearing for Ordinance 2416 and shared additional information on the changes made.
Previously for buildings in Oxford, owners were required to track and calculate the costs of any construction made since July 1, 2013 prior to making changes to the structures.
If all those improvement costs equal or exceed 50% of the market value of a building prior to the start of the construction, it would require the building to be up to code and raised in elevation.
The amended ordinance revises the definition of "substantial improvement," removing the 2013 date and substituting "the previous five (5) years."
Bell said the revision allows for a lean way for owners to make improvements on their buildings.
"What this is saying is we're only going to go back five years, or 1,825 days," Bell said. "So it's shortening the period that you can take a look at the 50% requirement. It's liberalizing it."
An additional change in the ordinance was the revision of the "agreement to submit an elevation certificate."
An elevation certificate is a form on which applicants for a permit to construct a building or structure show compliance with floodplain management legislation.
Previously people looking to make substantial improvements to buildings would need to submit an elevation certificate with a building permit application upon the construction of the foundation and prior to further vertical construction; and prior to the final inspection and moving in.
The revision removes the requirement of submitting the form prior to placement of the foundation and further vertical construction.
According to Bell, the changes would make it cheaper for owners to have engineers/surveyors certify that the floor of buildings seeking improvements is above the mean high water mark and it lowers costs of the certification by a "couple of hundred dollars."
After answering clarifying questions from the public, commissioners unanimously approved the ordinance.

title: Lower Shore delegation visits Dorchester County Council
author: MAGGIE TROVATO mtrovato@chespub.com
content:
Lower Shore delegation visits Dorchester County Council

 October 25, 2024 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: MAGGIE TROVATO mtrovato@chespub.com | Section: Local News 
 
 674
 Words 

 Read News Document

 CAMBRIDGE — As the 447th session of the Maryland General Assembly draws near, legislators of the Lower Shore delegation met with the Dorchester County Council to talk about issues important to the council, including juvenile crime and solar energy.Sen. Johnny Mautz (R-Caroline, Dorchester, Talbot, Wicomico), Del. Sheree Sample-Hughes (D-Dorchester, Wicomico), Del. Christopher Adams (R-Dorchester, Talbot, Wicomico) and Del. Tom Hutchinson (R-Caroline, Dorchester, Talbot, Wicomico) sat in the first row at a Dorchester County Council meeting Oct. 22 to talk with the council about some of the things the council hopes are addressed during the upcoming legislative session.
JUVENILE CRIMEThe County Council requested the delegation consider creating legislation to address juvenile crime. In 2022, state legislators passed bills to limit what charges children under the age of 13 face.
Council member Rob Kramer talked about being the victim of juvenile crime. According to a news release from the Cambridge Police Department, on Oct. 6, four people reportedly robbed REK Firearms, which Kramer owns, using a stolen vehicle. A 16-year-old boy from Cambridge was arrested.
Kramer said he was told that because the person arrested was a teen, nothing could be done.
"How is that fair to me?" Kramer asked.
Sample-Hughes said juvenile crime has been a "challenging subject" and she doesn't think the General Assembly understands the severity of the situation and the importance of making "specific changes." She said it would be beneficial for the legislators if the council wrote a letter detailing day-to-day operations when it comes to juvenile justice.
Adams questioned how the state is protecting its children with the current laws in place.
"We are a civil society," He said. "It's a free society. But there have to be consequences for behavior."
Hutchinson said a juvenile reform bill passed during the last legislative session will not go into effect until Nov. 1, and he doesn't expect his "friends on the other side" to want to pass more legislation until it is clear what the effects of that bill are.
Council President Lenny Pfeffer brought up concerns with the county's ability to house teens in the Dorchester County Detention Center. Pfeffer said detention center Warden Don Satterfield has said laws require underage detainees to neither see nor hear adult detainees.
Pfeffer said this has become a financial and logistical burden, as eight people under 18 have been sent to the detention center in less than a year.
Sample-Hughes said looking into technical assistance from the Maryland Commission on Correctional Standards could be helpful in determining what can be done to address this issue.
SOLAR ENERGY Council Vice President Mike Detmer brought up solar energy during the meeting. He said the county is trying to "hone in" on the decommissioning aspect of solar legislation.
Detmer said he thinks it's crucial to have legislation deterring solar companies from leaving solar equipment on a site when the company leaves. He said that if a solar company uses recyclable materials, the company shouldn't get credit for it until after the equipment has been taken down so that the county isn't left to remove it.
Detmer also talked about the importance of having a percentage cap on total solar acreage in a county. He said 72% of Dorchester County land isn't developable and the county has to "shoehorn" growth and agriculture.
Adams said the Eastern Shore Delegation is planning to have a Zoom meeting with the Maryland Public Service Commission, Maryland Energy Administration and Maryland Department of Agriculture to gather more information on plans for solar energy.
"We need to understand what it is the state's trying to do to our rural farmland," he said.
DETENTION CENTER MEDICAL COSTSThe council asked about whether there has been talk at the state level about specialty medical care costs for detention center detainees. Pfeffer said the county has detainees that require $20,000 or $40,000 per month of specialty medical care.
"I don't know whether there could be a carve-out in these situations," he said. "We understand it's our responsibility to take care of our detainees. But in these extreme situations, it has put a complete burden on our budgets for those departments. It just immediately drains it."

title: On the ballot: What is Question 1 or the Right to Reproductive Freedom Amendment?
author: Veronica Fernandez-Alvarado
content:
On the ballot: What is Question 1 or the Right to Reproductive Freedom Amendment?

 October 26, 2024 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: Veronica Fernandez-Alvarado | Section: News 
 
 565
 Words 

 Read News Document

 EASTON — Reproductive healthcare access is up for vote in Maryland. Voters will have the chance to decide state protections on abortion access and whether or not to codify it into the state constitution.During the 2023 General Assembly, state lawmakers passed an amendment that would enshrine the right to an abortion and "reproductive freedom," in Maryland's constitution.
The United States Supreme Court overturned Roe v. Wade in June of 2022, with a 5-4 vote indicating there is no constitutional right to abortion. Since that summer, the topic of abortion has been a hot-button issue across the nation.
States have weighed establishing constitutional amendments declaring protection over the right to abortion, and constitutional amendments have been approved by voters in California, Vermont and Michigan.
States such as Tennessee, Alabama and West Virginia have passed amendments declaring that the state's constitution does not secure or protect a person's right to abortion.
Currently, abortion is legal in Maryland until viability and abortion is legal after viability if the woman's life or health is endangered or there is a fetal anomaly.
What is on the ballot?Question 1, or the Right to Reproductive Freedom Amendment, would amend the Declaration of Rights in the Maryland Constitution to add a new section that guarantees a right to "reproductive freedom." According to the referendum, the term "reproductive freedom" includes include "the ability to make and effectuate decisions to prevent, continue or end one's own pregnancy.
If the amendment is approved by voters, it would prohibit the constitutional right of abortion access from being denied or infringed unless there is a compelling state interest, which would need to be achieved using the least restrictive means.
Erin Bradley, board chair of Freedom in Reproductive Maryland, has been advocating for passing the referendum.
"What this legislation does is it protects (abortion) at the highest level possible," Bradley said during an event in August. "It's very easy to change statutes in any state's constitutional amendments. As you see, I need all of you here to go vote for it. So we would need to do that every time we try to change the constitution. So this is the highest legal protection we can offer in the state of Maryland."
The referendum is endorsed by Gov. Wes Moore, Maryland State Education Association and Pro-Choice Maryland.
Opponents of the referendum include the Maryland Catholic Conference, Maryland Right to Life PAC and Maryland Family Institute.
Frank Arlinghause, a Maryland doctor opposing the referendum, described the then Maryland Senate bill as "extreme."
"Amending the Maryland Constitution is an unusual and extreme measure, and this bill would take an extreme position on abortion, restricting the legislature's opportunities to pass reasonable restrictions on abortion in late pregnancy or to restrict it as other healthcare," Arlinghause said.
Understanding Question 1:The amendment was introduced as Senate Bill 798 on Feb. 6, 2023 and was passed by the Maryland Senate with a 32-15 vote. On March 30 of that year, the Maryland House passed the bill by a 98-38 vote, with three absent or no voting.
A yes vote supports adding a new article to the Maryland Constitution's Declaration of Rights establishing a right to reproductive freedom, defined to include "the ability to make and effectuate decisions to prevent, continue, or end one's own pregnancy."
A "no" vote opposes amending the state constitution to establish a right to reproductive freedom.
Early voting locations will be open from 7 a.m. to 8 p.m. until October 31. Election day is Tuesday November 5.
