title: Cambridge elects strong, capable commissioners
author: STEPHEN RIDEOUT
content:
Cambridge elects strong, capable commissioners

 October 26, 2024 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: STEPHEN RIDEOUT | Section: Columns 
 
 596
 Words 

 Read News Document

 So, the votes are in from the Oct. 19 Cambridge city election, and all of the races, except for the mayor, are decided.Congratulations to those who won and thank you to all of the candidates for their willingness to run and offer to be representatives for our community.
While the numbers of people who voted continue to trouble me, because there were so few in some races, the only way for an engaged community to go is up.
The Dorchester Star reported that 1,543 residents voted out of 8,982 registered voters. That is a little over 17% of the total registered voters that voted.
I know that the citizens of Cambridge can do better than that. How does the community find ways to do better? Maybe the next City Council should consider allowing people to vote who have second homes here or own a business in the city but live in the county.
They have an interest in the city and who runs it and might be offered the opportunity to vote here.
As the five wards have approximately the same number of registered voters, the average would be 1,796 eligible voters in each ward. When you look at the results from the different wards and compare the total votes to the eligible voters in each ward for the commissioner races, the numbers are surprising.
Ward 1: 537Ward 2: 208 (4 candidates)Ward 3: 260Ward 4: 266Ward 5: 158 (uncontested)
Despite the low turnout, Cambridge will have a strong and capable group of commissioners for the upcoming term. People who have served before. People who are and have been actively engaged in the community in their work and their volunteerism. People who want to see the city do more for the youth who live here.
With the race for mayor, the total votes cast were 1,498. That vote total was just under 17% of the total registered voters in Cambridge. In watching the vote count on the evening of the 19th, I noticed that there were a few voters that did not vote for any of the mayoral candidates.
As with prior mayoral races, neither of the two finalists have a lock on winning the runoff on Dec. 3. If you can vote in this election, whether or not you voted on Oct. 19, you need to learn more about both candidates and make your voice heard by casting your vote.
As our local system of government is what is known as a "weak mayor" system, having knowledgeable and engaged commissioners is critically important as the city continues the improvements that have been taking place since the city council-city manager form of government was established in 2015. Having a qualified and respected mayor is important for our community and how we are seen by the rest of the state.
The other critical piece for continuing improvement here is having a good and solid city manager to run the day-to-day operations. We have that now in Glenn Steckman. The City Council needs to allow him to do his work and lead city staff to address the challenges of local government while they address the policy issues and pass needed legislation. It is clear that Mr. Steckman is the right person for Cambridge at a critical time in our continuing growth.
Even though the city vote is almost completed, please remember to vote on Nov. 5 for that other election; and in particular please vote in favor of the six proposed county charter amendments that will help our county to be run more effectively and efficiently. These affect you just as much as does your vote in the city elections.

title: Be a voter
author: Staff Writer
content:
Be a voter

 October 26, 2024 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: Staff Writer | Section: Editors Inbox 
 
 431
 Words 

 Read News Document

 In the 2020 election, Talbot County's outcome was decided by just 116 votes out of over 22,000 cast. In communities like ours, your vote — your individual voice — carries significant weight.While much of the focus in this election cycle is naturally on the presidential and congressional races, Talbot County also has three important school board elections, several judicial candidates, and two critical ballot measures to consider.
In an election cycle flooded with misleading mailers and interference from a nationwide, Republican-leaning PAC attempting to sway the outcome, I encourage all voters to take a close, thoughtful look at each candidate and their positions.
Regardless of your party affiliation, it would serve us well to vote for the candidates who are the most curious and driven for common-sense solutions, the ones who are both passionate and compassionate. Vote for the people with experience and objective professionalism and vote as if the future of Talbot County depends on your voice. Because it does.
There are several convenient ways to cast your vote — by mail, early voting at the Easton Fire Hall or on Election Day itself. The key is to start by making your voting plan. Ask yourself: Am I registered to vote? Where and when should I vote? Do I need a ride, or can I bring a friend or family member along? Will I need time off work or child care arrangements? These are important considerations to address ahead of time, so you're not caught off guard by travel plans, a child's event, or a late work shift on Election Day. Voting has never been easier, more efficient, or more secure.
We have put together an informative and accessible resource page – TalbotDems.org/VOTE – that provides voter information links, election dates and candidate information. Even if you do not agree with our positions, you might find the information provided useful.
In the final days of this election, I hope we can take a moment to reflect upon and appreciate the incredible personal and professional sacrifices of our friends and neighbors managing our local elections and running for office. We should rise to their example and be active participants in the democratic process.
The first step toward coming back together as a nation is participating in the democracy that generations of Americans have fought for, marched for, sat in for and walked out for, cried and cheered for, and sacrificed and died for.
Voting is more than a civic right. It is a fundamental responsibility of every American embedded into the DNA of our nation. Election day is Nov. 5. Be an American. Be a voter.
PATRICK FIRTH
Trappe

title: Sewer connection was illegal
author: Staff Writer
content:
Sewer connection was illegal

 October 26, 2024 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: Staff Writer | Section: Editors Inbox 
 
 378
 Words 

 Read News Document

 (The following is an abbreviated version of a communication sent to the Talbot County Council on Wednesday.)You'll be interested to learn that an illegal sewer connection in Trappe occurred right under your noses. You'll not be surprised that it involves Lakeside. Nor surprised that the illegal connection turns out to have been a linchpin to getting that malign venture under way.
The Lakeside developer had to somehow connect Lakeside to the existing Trappe wastewater treatment plant. To do that he arranged an easement across a 20-acre parcel that is not part of Lakeside. The line was then installed in that easement and extended to an existing line under the highway. The issue is that the 20-acre parcel was then connected to the line illegally.
In a February 2022 email, Talbot Integrity Projected specifically alerted you to the risk that that that 20-acre parcel could be connected to the sewer line without your knowledge, and that doing so would be illegal. I cited the fact that the 20-acre parcel in question only appeared to be eligible for a connection due to the county's admittedly erroneous maps attached to Resolution 281. I flagged specifically that that parcel had never been reclassified from "unprogrammed."
It is just now that we learn sewerage from that 20-acre parcel does discharge into the Lakeside line, disregarding the legally required county approval. The developer's lawyer, Ryan Showalter, drafted the easement agreement. The developer's engineer, Rauch Inc., designed the system. Trappe's attorney was involved— and her legal fees were paid by the developer. Evidence suggests that the county engineer or someone in county government was also well aware of this illegal connection.
Maryland law says: "Unless they conform to the county plan or revision or amendment of the county plan, the following systems and facilities may not be installed or extended … sewerage system." Evidence shows that the developer's and town's lawyers and engineers, and apparently the county engineer, knew about this, but it seems the illegal connection was a necessary quid pro quo for Lakeside to hookup, and so it was arranged.
Effluent from the industrial operation on the 20-acre parcel is discharging into La Trappe Creek today, as it has been for 2½ years.
A thorough investigation of these matters by a completely independent party is obviously warranted.
DAN WATSON
Easton

title: Easton workshop comes to close as East End plans move forward
author: KONNER METZ kmetz@chespub.com
content:
Easton workshop comes to close as East End plans move forward

 October 30, 2024 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: KONNER METZ kmetz@chespub.com | Section: Local News 
 
 495
 Words 

 Read News Document

 EASTON — More than 50 residents and town employees gathered Monday night to get a closer look at the East End Small Area Plan being developed by the town's planning and zoning department.The town hosted a final presentation of its five-day interactive workshop at the Easton Church of God on Monday. Consultants presented renderings and potential redevelopment options for Easton's East End plan, which will update the town's current plan that dates back to 1997.
Planning and Zoning Director Miguel Salinas thanked attendees for participating in multiple public sessions over the weekend and stressed that the opportunity for public participation did not end Monday.
"This is not the final opportunity for public input," Salinas said, pointing out that the plan will go through refinement and then hit the desks of the town's Planning Commission and Town Council before final approval.
Seth Harry, principal architect of Frederick-based Seth Harry & Associates, and Dave Ager, principal of Clarksville-based Townscape Design, are each on the town's consultant team. They explained shared with residents some of the main goals in their East End designs: open space, walkability, connectivity and local employment opportunities.
A rendering of a redesigned Dover Street and Dover Road intersection was shown, with "civic open space" occupying the "triangle" formed when the two roads meet. Ager said the open space could be the "heart of the overall area."
"The entire Dover Road or Dover Street north side is really ideal for commercial, and the south side is really ideal for residential," Ager said.
"It was an opportunity hidden in plain sight, and we just needed to reveal that potential," Harry said.
East towards U.S. Route 50, Ager and Harry discussed adding on-street parking and "enhanced" pedestrian crossings to slow down traffic near the Doverbrook Apartments. They also detailed plans to extend Easton's downtown with small commercial opportunities.
"The incubator and commercial space works to change the character of the street," Harry said. "So the idea again is bringing more of the downtown core farther out."
"... It's essentially unfettered all the way to (Route) 50, and it doesn't feel like you're in a community or a … walkable neighborhood," he continued. "So, the drivers drive accordingly."
Resident Maury Schlesinger asked if the Dover Triangle and commercial plans would interfere with the success of the rest of the downtown. Harry said the downtown's primary competition comes from retail on Route 50.
"The retail here in Dover Triangle is positioned to complement and not compete with the downtown shopping," Harry said. "It should actually enhance your regional capture and make your downtown more of a destination."
During the weekend, town planners and consultants also worked to create renderings of small "pocket neighborhoods" that could address housing needs at the Brookletts Avenue and Rails to Trails intersection.
It was discussed that the area could provide workspaces for local artists as well.
The East End Area, according to the town, is just under one-half square mile and is home to more than 2,000 residents.
Residents can visit eastend.eastonmd.gov/charrette to view renderings and learn more.

title: Turnout strong at Talbot County early voting location
author: Tom McCall
content:
Turnout strong at Talbot County early voting location

 October 30, 2024 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: Tom McCall | Section: Local News 
 
 579
 Words 

 Read News Document

 EASTON — Early voting was running smoothly at the Easton Volunteer Fire Department, according to poll workers staffing the early voting location Wednesday, the day before Maryland's early voting period closes for the 2024 general election.Voting numbers as of Wednesday afternoon indicated strong turnout. Over 500 ballots had been cast so far that day, according to poll workers.
"Our first day was 1,945, and we had 1,100 yesterday," said Edward Forte, an election judge. "Today we have 459 at 1 pm. By 8 tonight we should be pretty close to 1,000."
As of Tuesday evening, 7,145 Talbot County voters had voted during early voting, or about 25% of the county's registered voters. Early voting closes on Oct. 31.
"There is no rhyme or reason. We will be sitting here, and there will be nobody in here, then 10 people show up at 2:30. I think people drive here and see a lot of cars. They go home, then drive by again when they are doing errands — see nobody is here and park," Forte said.
Forte said there have been a lot of celebratory announcements for first-time voters during the early voting period.
"We have a lot of first time voters. At least a dozen a day. It is good," he said.
The fire station and other polling locations around the state are open for 13 hours a day during early voting, which means long hours for election judges and volunteers.
Roshanda Roberts, Democratic chief judge, said, "Early voting has been steady, pretty full. Everything has been running smoothly. It is a very long day. It starts at quarter of six until about a little after 8 p.m."
She said her job is, "To make sure that this election for early voting runs smoothly, without any hiccups."
Outside the calm interior of the voting chamber, there is a riot of colorful signs for senate hopefuls, school board seats and presidential candidates. There are two tents right next to each other amid all the signs, one for each major political party.
Mary Pellicano, a volunteer for the Talbot Democrats, said, "The mood is pretty positive. We have a lot of energy behind Harris and Walz, and especially Question 1 on the ballot. People are very energized. People want their vote to count."
Pellicana also had a Democratic voter guide to help voters with the judges on the ballot. She said not all candidates are clearly identified by party on the ballot.
"Early voting makes voting easier, and that is very supportive of democracy. The more people who have a voice, the more representative our government is," Pellicano said.
Republican Catherine Nobles said early voting helps voters ensure they can cast their ballots. "Early voting is a good thing, because it gives people time to get in," she said. "Don't wait until the last minute. God knows what could happen. It is kind of a very angry place right now. I said to my husband 'it is stressful now because it is just so angry.' I was called a Nazi yesterday. Hopefully we are all for the country, right?"
The Maryland Board of Elections was reporting high voter turnout for in-person early voting statewide, though as of Tuesday, these numbers were lower than they were for the general election in 2020.
According to the state Board of Elections, 695,432 Marylanders had early voted as of Tuesday evening, compared to 780,694 as of the sixth day of early voting in 2020. Statewide turnout numbers were higher than those for the same early voting period in 2016.

title: Easton Club East resident requests court to order delay of HOA election
author: KONNER METZ kmetz@chespub.com
content:
Easton Club East resident requests court to order delay of HOA election

 October 31, 2024 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: KONNER METZ kmetz@chespub.com | Section: Local News 
 
 368

 EASTON — A resident of Easton Club East has filed a complaint requesting an injunction against the Easton Club East Community Association's board election after his candidacy was rejected.Jerome Wade, represented by attorney Lyndsey Ryan, filed the complaint on Oct. 21, according to Talbot County Circuit Court records. It outlines why he is "challenging the unlawful rejection of his nomination" and his claims that the association exceeded its authority and violated its bylaws.
Easton Club East, a single-family home neighborhood located off of Dutchmans Lane, is home to more than 800 residents, according to its website. Its Board of Directors, made up of three to seven members, sought nomination forms for three expiring positions on Sept. 16, according to the complaint.
Election voting takes place from Oct. 23 to Nov. 6. Wade is requesting the Circuit Court issue an injunction to prevent Easton Club East from holding its election until the court issues a judgment.
In Wade's filing, which also requests a declaratory judgment and temporary restraining order, he stated that residents wanting to be board candidates were "asked" to answer a list of questions in 100 words or less for each question.
After submitting the candidate nomination form on Sept. 30 — the deadline day — to Easton Club East Community Manager Rhonda Bennett, Wade says he was asked shorten his answers to be within the 100-word limit and given until the next morning to do so.
The complaint states that Wade sent a revised form on Oct. 1. Later that day, the association's nominating committee informed Wade his nomination submission was rejected "due to noncompliance" with Easton Club East guidelines.
Four other candidates submitted nomination forms that were accepted, three of which included responses more than 100 words, the complaint states.
"The unequal treatment of the Plaintiff led to the denial of his nomination and preclusion from participating in what should be a democratic process," the complaint reads.
The association's bylaws prescribe a nominating committee to collect written candidacy submissions "within the timeframe and in the format established by the Board of Directors."
Bennett declined to provide comment when reached by the Star Democrat Wednesday.
A hearing for the injunction originally scheduled for Wednesday was postponed. As of Wednesday, no replacement date had been set.

title: County discusses regulation enforcement on short term rentals
author: Veronica Fernandez-Alvarado
content:
County discusses regulation enforcement on short term rentals

 October 31, 2024 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: Veronica Fernandez-Alvarado | Section: News 
 
 430
 Words 

 Read News Document

 EASTON — At a Tuesday evening meeting between the Talbot County Council and incorporated towns within the county, concerns were raised over the enforcement of the county's accommodation tax on short-term rentals.Martha Darling Sparks, finance director for Talbot County, shared future plans to better regulate short-term rentals with a platform already used by the county called Granicus. Granicus owns a software called Host Compliance, which uses artificial intelligence and machine learning to provide data on short-term rentals and track them as they appear online.
The software will be able to help towns know of unlicensed rentals in their area so local officials can better enforce rental regulations.
Currently, enforcement of the accommodation tax on short-term rentals relies on what Sparks describes as an "honor system."
Sparks said the law requires owners of short-term rentals to collect an accommodations tax from patrons. Owners are then required to remit the funds to the county on a monthly basis. Then, on a quarterly basis, the county remits 95% of the tax collected back to the towns and keeps 5% as an administrative fee.
According to Sparks, because the tax requirement not more strictly enforced, there are rentals operating in Talbot County that may not adhering to the regulations.
Alfred Mercier, St. Michaels commission president, said short-term rentals have become a challenge to the town. Mercier said on a monthly basis there could be 30 different Airbnbs in operation but that they are hard to track because the rentals can be open one weekend and closed the next.
Sparks said if towns have a permitting process or an approval process for these rentals, it is important to emphasize to owners that short-term rentals are subject to the accommodation tax in Talbot County.
According to Sparks, historically, the county does not involve itself in regulation or the monitoring of the towns because that is done through planning and zoning committees to make sure that short-term rentals are properly licensed.
Sparks said that when the county moves toward this new system of collecting accommodation tax online, there is a request from the county to see the number of short-term rentals in towns.
Sparks plans to discuss with Bryce Yelton, assistant planning officer of Talbot County, about a new process where the county communicates with the towns when new unlicensed rentals appear online.
"We were going to talk about a process where we'd like to communicate with the towns when something comes up on our radar, to pass it along to (towns), because we already have that software," Sparks said. "So it might be a good way for us to partner and (give an) information exchange."

title: Cambridge mayor planning to leave before term is up, looks back on term
author: MAGGIE TROVATO mtrovato@chespub.com
content:
Cambridge mayor planning to leave before term is up, looks back on term

 October 31, 2024 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: MAGGIE TROVATO mtrovato@chespub.com | Section: Local News 
 
 765
 Words 

 Read News Document

 CAMBRIDGE — Cambridge Mayor Stephen Rideout is planning to step down as mayor a few weeks before his term ends.In an interview with the Star Democrat, Rideout said he and his wife are planning to move to a continuing care retirement community in Frederick. He is planning to resign sometime in early December as a result.
"Our children are in Alexandria or in North Carolina, and so we wanted to get closer to them," he said.
Rideout said although he hasn't made a formal announcement, he has advised multiple people of his plan to resign, including City Manager Glenn Steckman and City Council President Lajan Cephas.
Steckman said that when Rideout leaves, it will be up to the commissioners how they fill the open seat.
The last time the seat was made vacant — when former Cambridge Mayor Andrew Bradshaw resigned in January 2022 after being charged for distributing revenge porn on Reddit — Cephas took on the duties of mayor until Rideout took the helm.
Cephas and Bradshaw are currently vying to be mayor in the next term. The two candidates will go head to head in a runoff election on Dec. 3.
'PROGRESS IS BEING MADE'Looking back on his time as mayor, Rideout said his goals in office centered around crime and kids, two areas he felt the community most wanted addressed.
He talked about the importance of reducing criminal behavior and delinquency and finding ways to effectively divert children into programming.
Rideout said a challenge of the Eastern Shore and Cambridge is that there aren't enough strong nonprofits. He mentioned New Beginnings Youth and Family Services, the Cambridge Empowerment Center and MidShore Meals til Monday as nonprofits that have "really stepped up" and made significant progress over the last few years.
Rideout also talked about the Portia Johnson-Ennels Youth Internship Program, a summer program for Cambridge residents between the ages of 16 and 23 that are interested in local government.
"That's the kind of thing that I think we need to do," Rideout said.
Rideout thinks "progress is being made," in Cambridge but doesn't see that improvement as his or the City Council's accomplishment. He credits past city managers, city staff and staff leadership.
"We need to strengthen the existing programs so they can expand," he said. "And we need to find other people that have great ideas who want to bring another resource to the community for the kids."
One of the things Rideout is most proud of during his time in office are the recent changes in management and ownership at the Bradford House Apartments, which offers multifamily, subsidized housing for low-income individuals who are elderly or have special needs.
Over the past year and a half, residents have expressed concerns about the safety of the building, from bed bug infestations to call-for-aid systems not working to a lack of security.
Rideout said the city was able to get the U.S. Department of Housing and Urban Development, Sen. Ben Cardin (D-Md.), Sen. Chris Van Hollen (D-Md.) and the local state delegation involved, and city staff put in "so much work" to get the issues at Bradford House addressed.
"The changes now are happening," Rideout said. "And that to me is how government can work, should work."
Rideout said he decided to run for mayor after striking out on trying to find someone else for the job. He said he went to different people in Cambridge who he thought would make a good mayor and none of those people were interested in running to fill Bradshaw's seat.
"I felt it was important to have a calming voice during what I anticipated and expected would be a transition until this election," Rideout said. "Because I was only going to do it for the two years."
Cephas said Rideout "brought stability back to Cambridge" following Bradshaw's resignation. She said he also brought "steady decision making."
"He was extremely thoughtful of everyone on both sides," Cephas said. "It's something that I learned from him being the commission president while he was the mayor."
Rideout's main piece of advice to the next mayor of Cambridge is to listen.
"And listen again," he said.
He said the mayor should match their ideas to what the community wants and make sure the community knows they've been heard.
A decade from now, Rideout hopes Cambridge will be a place where students excel in schools, early childhood education programs are teaching kids how to read and write, and new businesses are moving in. He said focusing on the future generations is an important element of making progress in Cambridge.
"Because we aren't going to get businesses who come here who have employees who have children until our school system is improving," he said.

title: Trappe's Post Office reopens after 2-year closure
author: Veronica Fernandez-Alvarado
content:
Trappe's Post Office reopens after 2-year closure

 November 1, 2024 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: Veronica Fernandez-Alvarado | Section: News

 Words 

 Read News Document

 TRAPPE — Residents of Trappe celebrated the reopening of the town's post office this week after it had been under construction for two years.In Oct. 2022, the Trappe Post Office was forced to close due to a burst pipe. Mark Wahl, strategic communications specialist for the U.S. Postal Service, said construction had to be extended due to complications with the removal of asbestos.
According to Trappe Town Council President Brian Schmidt, the closure of the post office caused significant inconvenience to residents of the town.
Schmidt noted many residents had to travel to Cambridge to pick up their mail since there were many homes in Trappe that could not have mail delivered directly.
"All those people, including the town hall, had to drive to Cambridge every day to pick up mail," Schmidt said. "So the fact that we can now get our mail a lot closer is nice. And the services that (the post office) offers, not just for the town, but for the people outside of the town as well."
According to Schmidt the construction process was slow and disorganized and lacked good communication with town leadership. Schmidt said the town had a hard time communicating with anybody who knew anything about the post office and its ongoing progress.
Schmidt said many of Trappe's residents were pushed to be creative when it came to obtaining their mail. Older constituents of the town could not easily drive to the post office in Cambridge.
Schmidt said he knew of one resident who changed her address to one of her neighbor's. According to Schmidt, the resident was also caring for her husband whose health was failing, and the closure of the post office created another burden for her.
Ann Frock, a resident of Trappe, said before the closing of the post office she had maintained the same P.O. Box for 28 years. She had to find new arrangements to get mail after the office's closure. Frock said she would drive to Cambridge to retrieve her mail and her friend's mail.
"We're really glad that it reopened, and we're sorry that it took so long," Frock said. "And the whole community wishes that we would have been more informed about what was going on. But we're just really glad to have it back open again."

title: Public hearing discusses short term rental regulations
author: ANDREA GRABENSTEIN agrabenstein@chespub.com
content:
Public hearing discusses short term rental regulations

 November 1, 2024 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: ANDREA GRABENSTEIN agrabenstein@chespub.com | Section: News 
 
 499
 Words 

 Read News Document

 CENTREVILLE — Following favorable recommendation by the Queen Anne's County Planning Commission, the County Commissioners held a public hearing to discuss a proposed ordinance regulating short-term rentals in the county Oct. 22.The intent of the ordinance is to address short-term rentals in the county with a focus on protecting existing neighborhoods and addressing enforcement, according to Stephanie Jones, senior planner.
As of the summer, Queen Anne's County has a total of 181 short-term rentals, she said.
Proposed ordinance regulations include the owner or property manager must be within 25 miles of the property as well as occupancy and guest capacity limits. Guests who are not overnight occupants must vacate by 11 p.m., outdoor amplified music must be discontinued by 8 p.m., and all parking must be on site, Jones said.
Short-term property owners must receive a zoning certificate annually and additional special events approval is separate conditional use, she said.
Short-term rentals must register with the finance office who will collect the hotel tax, Jones said. The proposed ordinance would make short term rental permitted in all county zoning districts and dwelling units and would not supersede any Homeowners Association enforceability.
The planning department is currently working with consultant Granicus and its Host Compliance software to address after hour and weekend response scenarios such as noise, according to Jones. Disturbances will be able to be addressed by calling or filling out an online application for Granicus to contact the property owner directly, she said.
Violations and complaints will be tracked and kept record of, according to Jones.
At public comment, neighbors of Love Point voiced in favor of the proposed ordinance to regulate short term rentals, which they expressed as bringing an increase of traffic hazards and noise complaints to the area.
A key to rental is property management, according to Commissioner Patrick McLaughlin who cited his own experience as a short-term rental owner in Garrett County. In the event of a disturbance, the sheriff's department there has a list of property managers to contact, he said.
In order for a property representative to mitigate a situation as quickly as possible, instead of a 25 mile radius, Commissioner Jack Wilson suggested a qualified agent live in the county, noting the possibility of Bay Bridge traffic backup, "Our citizens shouldn't be inconvenienced by that," he said.
This is the commissioners first stab at a short-term rental ordinance and they can return at a later date to discuss and tweak it as necessary, Commission President Jim Moran said.
"We're not casting a net to stop short-term rentals, we're casting a net to stop those who are abusing the short term rentals to the point where they're disrupting all the homeowners and the citizens of Queen Anne's County," he said.
Moran noted a change in the times, with more property owners coming across the Chesapeake Bay Bridge to buy homes for investments, the quality of life for those already living there should not diminish.
Comments are available to be made before the commissioners vote at the next regular meeting Nov. 12 at 5:30 p.m.

title: Community survey, town workshop jumpstart discussion on health department lot in Easton
author: KONNER METZ kmetz@chespub.com
content:
Community survey, town workshop jumpstart discussion on health department lot in Easton

 Author/Byline: KONNER METZ kmetz@chespub.com | Section: Local News 
 
 552

 Read News Document

 EASTON — Around 200 county residents participated in a community-led survey regarding potential next steps for a one-acre lot in Easton that used to house the Talbot County Health Department.The department moved from 100 S Hanson St. to its new location, 510 Cadmus Ln., in July. Easton residents Greg Zimmerman and Joyce DeLaurentis created a survey intended to gather opinions from residents on what they would like to see replace the old Health Department building.
Zimmerman took time to analyze the results of the survey, which received 203 responses, some from residents that live near the building and others from county residents outside of town.
"For me, the two most revealing takeaways were that there was very strong support for the town to take a leadership role," Zimmerman said, "and that there was strong support for some type of green space and either indoor or outdoor gathering venue."
According to survey results, around 77% of respondents answered it was "important" the town "(coordinate) the redevelopment" of the property, with 6% answering that it was not. The property is currently owned by the county, which could choose to sell or transfer it to the town.
Nearly 50% of respondents answered in support of a community pocket park or gathering space, with around 24% in opposition. Many of the other alternatives posed in the survey — splitting the lot between housing and open space, renovating for small businesses and garden apartments — received similar levels of support and opposition.
A question asking if residents would support single-family homes at the lot had around 22% of respondents answer yes and 53% answer no.
Zimmerman said the survey served its purpose of getting residents involved and having their voices heard prior to a decision being made about the property.
"I think the survey is successful in revealing what people think so that there's better alignment between the public and policymakers," Zimmerman said.
The lot is included in Easton's East End Small Area Plan, an initiative to redevelop and improve a one-half square mile area in town.
Last week, town planners and consultants led a five-day workshop to move forward with that plan, including opportunities for public input. Seth Harry, principal architect for Frederick-based Seth & Harry Associates, said there was substantial feedback on the Health Department site.
At the workshop's final presentation on Oct. 28, Harry and Dave Ager, of Clarksville-based Townscape Design, presented five potential ways the lot could be used. Some would necessitate the removal of the building, while other options repurpose or resize the current building.
These alternatives included: a garden space, an outdoor pavilion with open space, open space on the perimeter with the existing building, adding onto the existing building and keeping green space, and a redesigned building with an outdoor event lawn.
"It was our goal and our direction to come up with ideas," Ager said. "These are ideas to be contemplated and discussed by the community."
Zimmerman believes the outreach done to the community has served as a "conduit" between residents and policymakers, as well as increasing public participation.
"In some cases, people even living … right around the health department property didn't even know that the Health Department was moving," Zimmerman said.
To view the survey results, send an email to eastoncommunitysurveys@gmail.com. To view the Town of Easton's East End presentation and the included alternatives for the health department lot, visit eastend.eastonmd.gov/charrette.

title: When can Marylanders expect election results?
author: Aidan Hughes and Shaela Foster Capital News Service
content:
When can Marylanders expect election results?

 November 5, 2024 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: Aidan Hughes and Shaela Foster Capital News Service | Section: Local News 
 
 575
 Words 

 Read News Document

 Even before Election Day, the 2024 election generated immense enthusiasm in Maryland, with nearly 1 million people having voted early in-person and over 600,000 more voters casting their ballots by mail as of Tuesday morning.In the past, counting votes in the state has been a slow process. Only about 8% of votes cast in Maryland were reported by midnight on Election Day 2020, and The New York Times has reported that officials expect this year's pace to match 2020 and 2022.
Katherine Berry, deputy administrator of the State Board of Elections, said in an emailed statement to CNS that "results will be released after all polling locations statewide do not have lines and are able to begin tabulating election day results."
Updates will be available on the State Board of Elections website as results are released.
"The first sets of results will be the mail-in ballots canvassed so far and the early voting results followed by election day," Berry said, adding that results will be refreshed every 10 minutes.
In most counties, canvassing mail-in ballots began on Oct. 15.
Three counties — Cecil, Dorchester, and Somerset — won't begin canvassing mail-in ballots at all until Nov. 7.
Mail-in ballots can also be postmarked or placed in drop boxes until 8 p.m. on Election Day and arrive as late as Nov. 15, meaning some ballots — for example, from some military and overseas voters — won't be canvassed until days after polls close.
Provisional ballots aren't counted in Maryland until Nov. 13, according to Berry. Over 78,000 provisional ballots were cast in 2016, and more than 112,000 were cast in 2020.
Because results from election officials can take a while to release, media outlets are usually the first to declare the winners of elections. These calls are unofficial and have no power to determine who actually won.
Major news organizations rely on "decision desks" composed of experts that attempt to determine when a race is clear enough to announce a victor.
Those decision desks rely on a wealth of data, like voter surveys or exit polls, historical trends and incoming vote returns on election night. When a decision desk believes one candidate has an insurmountable lead, the outlet will call the race.
In some instances though, decision desks will declare a winner before most — or any — results are reported by election officials.
This was the case in Maryland during the last presidential election. As soon as polls closed at 8 p.m., the Associated Press declared Biden won the state in 2020, even though the first votes weren't reported by election officials until 8:55 p.m.
The state was similarly called for Hillary Clinton at 8 p.m. in 2016 and for Barack Obama at 8:01 p.m in 2012.
According to an explainer from AP, the outlet doesn't declare the outcome of races considered competitive until enough votes are counted to make clear who won.
Although most decision desks take a cautious approach to calling races and are generally reliable, that doesn't mean they're infallible.
The Associated Press and other outlets had to retract incorrect calls for a California House race in 2018, and in 2020 some critics suggested that Fox News irresponsibly called Arizona for Joe Biden before they could have been sufficiently certain of the winner.
Marylanders shouldn't be surprised if outlets call the state's presidential choice on a similarly quick timeline again this year. If other down-ballot races — such as closely-watched contests for the Senate and House — are more competitive, it's possible that those calls would come later.

title: Easton Club East restarts HOA election, reaches settlement with resident
author: KONNER METZ kmetz@chespub.com
content:
Easton Club East restarts HOA election, reaches settlement with resident

 November 5, 2024 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: KONNER METZ kmetz@chespub.com | Section: Local News 
 
 475
 Words 

 Read News Document

 EASTON — The retirement neighborhood Easton Club East has restarted its board election following the settlement of a lawsuit in which a resident alleged his nomination was unlawfully rejected.On Oct. 21, Jerry Wade filed a complaint in the Talbot County Circuit Court claiming the Easton Club East Community Association violated its bylaws and exceeded its authority when it rejected his application to run for a board position.
Easton Club East is located off of Dutchmans Lane and is home to more than 800 residents, according to its website. The homeowners association's election began Oct. 23, with voting scheduled to close Wednesday.
Four candidates, three of whom were incumbents, were originally accepted on the ballot to vie for three open spots.
However, a settlement reached Oct. 31 between Wade and Easton Club East will restart the election beginning this Thursday, permitting Wade's candidacy. All votes already cast are "null and void," the association wrote in a notice sent to residents on Oct. 31.
Wade initial's filing, which requested an injunction be granted by the court, centered around the 100-word requirements for answers on the open nomination form that candidates completed. Wade claimed Easton Club East's nominating committee denied his nomination "due to noncompliance" despite other accepted nominees also having answers above the 100-word limit to the candidate questions.
"The unequal treatment of the Plaintiff led to the denial of his nomination and preclusion from participating in what should be a democratic process," the complaint read.
In an email to residents, the current Easton Club East Board of Directors stated the reason for the delay of the election was Wade's complaint. The email stated the board "takes any allegation of a violation of the Bylaws extremely seriously."
"The Board believes that this resolution is the best path forward for a timely completion of the election process in accordance with the Bylaws and applicable law," the email reads. "The Board also does not wish to engage in costly litigation with any Member of the Community."
In an interview, Wade said the settlement process was "quite business-like" and "in no way uncordial."
Wes Hagood is the only non-incumbent running other than Wade. He says he was the only candidate to initially adhere to the nomination requirements, noting that Easton Club East didn't enforce the 100-word requirement when reviewing nomination forms from the incumbent board members.
"I think they've treated Jerry (Wade) very unfairly," Hagood said. "I think they've treated me unfairly."
Hagood says in his discussions with neighborhood residents, "this is not the first time this has occurred."
"They don't want it to be open and democratic," he said.
Easton Club East Community Manager Rhonda Bennett did not immediately respond to request for comment Tuesday afternoon.
The Easton Club East Community Association will hold a meeting Wednesday evening to distribute candidate bios and accept any further nominations for the open board positions. Voting in the election begins Thursday and closes Nov. 13.

title: Cambridge officials talk city election turnout, new council
author: MAGGIE TROVATO mtrovato@chespub.com
content:
Cambridge officials talk city election turnout, new council

 November 5, 2024 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: MAGGIE TROVATO mtrovato@chespub.com | Section: Local News 
 
 938
 Words 

 Read News Document

 CAMBRIDGE — Voter turnout for Cambridge's election for city commissioners and a mayor on Oct. 19 was at 17%. Cambridge City Manager Glenn Steckman said that although this is a disappointing percentage, the polls were busy throughout the day on Oct. 19."And at points we had people lined out the door and around side the building," he said.
During a Cambridge City Council meeting on Oct. 28, Commissioner Jameson Harrington, who did not run for reelection, said he hopes there is better voter turnout in the future.
"If you don't vote, there's no democracy," he said.
Commission President Lajan Cephas — who ran for mayor in the election and will be in a runoff election for the position in December — said in an interview with the Star Democrat that she didn't want to complain about voter turnout because there are residents in Cambridge who are busy with "their own personal situations and dilemmas." She said those people don't need to be blamed.
"I think it's more of a situation of the city needs to find other ways of being more engaging so we can alert residents to make them aware," she said, adding that she appreciates everyone that voted.
Cephas' opponent in the mayoral election, former Cambridge Mayor Andrew Bradshaw, said that while 17% is low, it's in line with the city's past elections.
Cambridge Mayor Stephen Rideout, who did not run for reelection, said the turnout was consistent, but he was disappointed.
"I think if we are going to change and our community is going to begin to trust us, the voters have to step into and step up to the plate and learn about the candidates and come out and vote," he said.
Rideout said garnering more trust in local government from residents is something that will take time, but it is important. Rideout said he believes that trust will contribute to increased voter turnout rates.
"With trust, people become engaged," he said. "And with engagement, there are people coming to the meetings (and) when there are commissioners out in the community, they're approaching them and telling them what's going on and what's right and what's wrong."
A FEW NEW FACes
The Oct. 19 election resulted in two brand new faces on the council and three returning faces. One of those returning commissioners, Ward 3's Frank Stout, hasn't been on the council since 2012. The other two returning commissioners, Ward 4 Commissioner Sputty Cephas and Ward 5 Commissioner Brian Roche, are currently on the council.
Rideout said he thinks this next City Council will be "very strong."
Talking about the new faces on the council, Rideout said Ward 2 Commissioner-elect Shay Lewis-Sisco is a "quick study" who has been very involved in the community. He said that although he didn't support Ward 1 Commissioner-elect Brett Summers in the race, he thinks Summers is "a smart guy" with a "great business sense" who will bring new ideas to the Cambridge Harbor project.
Steckman said he intends to meet with the new council members individually before they are sworn in. He said the city plans to coordinate a workshop where the new council members can meet with department heads and learn about what city staff is working on. Steckman said that once the next term has begun, there needs to be a discussion over the council's goals and objectives for the term so that city staff can ensure those goals are reflected in the budget.
Bradshaw said he thinks the newly-elected group of commissioners is a talented one.
"I think that there's a lot of potential for success for Cambridge and that's my hope that I'm going to be able to work with them and move the city forward," he said.
Cephas said she feels confident in the city's newly-elected leadership and does not think there will be a learning curve.
"If it were up to me to pick the next upcoming council, it's everyone that was elected," she said. "It's good spirits, great vibes (and) experience."
RUNOFF ELECTION
The city's next mayor has yet to be determined. On Dec. 3, there will be a runoff election for residents to decide who should take Rideout's seat for the next term.
With none of the three mayoral candidates — Cephas, Bradshaw and former Cambridge Commissioner La-Shon Foster — securing more than 50% of the vote in the Oct. 19 election, Cephas and Bradshaw, the top two candidates, will go head to head in the runoff election. The election will be held at 447 Race St. Polls will be open from 7 a.m. to 7 p.m.
Steckman said he doesn't know what to expect in terms of voter turnout in the runoff election. He isn't sure if it will be better or worse than turnout on Oct. 19.
Rideout told the Star Democrat he is voting for Cephas in the runoff election.
"She picked up and led during a difficult time between May of 2021 and my election in September of '22 when Mayor Bradshaw should have resigned soon after his admission to the police that he had committed to the offenses," he said. "She has reached out through other avenues to connect the city with the Department of Housing and Urban Development that resulted in our grant writer submitting a successful application that resulted in $1.8 million grant to the city, which has the potential for even more funding."
Bradshaw said people have the right to vote for who they would like to and he respects that.
"They have the opportunity to reach out and I'd be happy to have a conversation to discuss where I see things for myself and for the city," he said. "But if they choose not to do so, that's well within their rights and I'll respect that."

title: Talbot County Democrats marked election night with celebration of campaign efforts
author: Veronica Fernandez-Alvarado
content:
Talbot County Democrats marked election night with celebration of campaign efforts

 November 6, 2024 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: Veronica Fernandez-Alvarado | Section: News 
 
 691
 Words 

 Read News Document

 EASTON — Cheers filled the BAAM Center on election night as dozens of local Democrats watched votes roll in for the 2024 general election and celebrated the end of a highly divisive election campaign.To be in community among like-minded residents, Talbot Democrats hosted an election watch party filled with food, drinks, guests dressed in their best campaign gear and deep discussion about hopes and fears for the future.
Patrick Firth, chair of the Talbot County Democratic Central Committee, said this celebration was needed for the community on the Shore. Firth said the people gathered on Tuesday are the heartbeat of the Democratic community and more than anything deserved a celebration and to feel appreciated for all their work.
"We had a record of over 200 individual volunteers helping us throughout the election, from greeting voters to canvassing, to phone banking," Firth said. "Talbot led the Eastern Shore this past weekend in canvassing, knocking on over 1000 doors in Talbot County."
Lined around the room were political signs showing support for Vice President Kamala Harris, Maryland Senate candidate Angela Alsobrooks and Talbot County candidate for Board of Education Candace Henry.
Kathy Hostetter, resident of Wye Mills, said she was feeling hopeful Tuesday night though she understood the presidential race would be close. Hostetter shared her enthusiasm for Alsobrooks, who hours later would win a U.S. Senate Seat in Maryland.
"Talbot County is one of the most beautiful places," Hostetter said. "We have a great state here in Maryland, we've got a great blue state. So tonight, we're very hopeful, and we want to keep it blue."
Hours after the party ended, former president Donald Trump triumphed over Democratic opponent Kamala Harris. Though initially expected to be a close race, Trump flipped several swing states in his favor and won the popular vote for the first time as a candidate.
Election night was a mix of triumphs and defeats for Democrats in Maryland. Alsobrooks claimed victory over incumbent Republican former Gov. Larry Hogan. Additionally, Maryland voters overwhelmingly supported an amendment to Maryland's constitution for reproductive freedom.
Michele Dappert, president of the Talbot County Democrat Party, said though Maryland is a famously blue state, this year's election has divided voters, especially in Talbot County.
According to the State Board of Elections' unofficial 2024 General Election Results for Talbot County, over half of voters chose former President Donald Trump as their presidential candidate and an overwhelming number of residents voted for Republican candidate Larry Hogan for U.S. Senate.
Dappert said though there is political separation among those on the Eastern Shore, all voters have essentially the same end goal: to have their values understood, heard and put into practice.
"Look, I get it, politics can be contentious, but when you meet people locally at the door, most of us are just trying to get by, and we're just trying to send our kids to school, have clean water, be able to walk outside and feel safe no matter what you look like and who you are," Dappert said. "And those are all very universal values, so I find it very important to defend them."
Sitting next to Dappert in a Kamala Harris camo cap and a blue shirt, which showed "CLXXVII Minutes" on the front and "11,780 Votes" on the back, was her father George Dappert. George Dappert explained the meaning behind his shirt.
The front represented, in roman numerals, the 186 minutes Trump watched TV during the Jan. 6 insurrection. The back represented the number of votes Trump was trying to find in Georgia to turn the state in his favor during the 2020 Presidential Election.
George Dappert said the Democratic Party has done everything they could in terms of getting out to vote, talking to people and getting the message out there for others to vote. For him, practicing the political right of voting is essential to democracy and he urges everyone to continue to be politically active regardless of major elections.
"It is what generations of our forefathers and foremothers have fought for, bled for, marched for, done everything that they could," George Dappert said. "To willfully not vote is an abdication of your responsibility and what they have given from their past to our future."

title: 'It's an honor': American Legion Post 77 Hometown Heroes project takes off
author: KONNER METZ kmetz@chespub.com
content:
'It's an honor': American Legion Post 77 Hometown Heroes project takes off

 November 7, 2024 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: KONNER METZ kmetz@chespub.com | Section: Local News 
 
 454
 Words 

 Read News Document

 EASTON — The American Legion Blake-Blackston Post 77 and the Town of Easton are working to line downtown streets with banners honoring veterans in the community ahead of Veterans Day.The joint effort began Nov. 1, when town public works employees erected the first banners on telephone poles at Glenwood Avenue, across from the Post 77 headquarters. Those included banners for the post's founders, Nelson Blake and John Blackston, both U.S. Army veterans.
William Griffin, current Post 77 commander, reflected on the project as the initial banners were hung. His banner was included in the first order as well, recognizing his service in the Army during the Cold War.
"It's an honor," Griffin said. "It's just an honor where, when I'm dead and gone, my grandkids can ride down this street and see their pop-pop."
This is the first year the banners have been hung in Easton. Joan Harris-Brooks helped organize the ordering and erection of the banners. The first two orders contained 13 banners each. A third order was on its way, she said.
The Hometown Heroes Banner program began in 2006 in Harrisburg, Pennsylvania. Today, Mid-Shore towns including Federalsburg, Hurlock and Preston showcase banners honoring past and present veterans, part of the motivation to bring the initiative to Easton.
Harris-Brooks' father was a life member at Post 77, bringing that much more meaning to the project's culmination, she said. She hopes the banners bring awareness of all local veterans and first responders have done to better the Easton community.
"Not only did they serve in the country, but they served this community, which is very dear to all of us," Harris-Brooks said.
Easton Mayor Megan Cook, Town Council President Frank Gunsallus and Ward 4 Councilmember the Rev. Elmer Davis all stopped by on Nov. 1 to witness some of the first banners go up. Gunsallus' father will be on one of the banners.
Griffin encourages people to stop by Blake-Blackston Post 77 to learn the stories behind the faces on the banners. He pointed out Harry Dobson, Post 77's first commander, and Robert Poney Sr., a talented musician remembered by any current members of the post.
"You may look at the picture, but you don't have a story behind it," he said.
With banners planned for streets such as Glenwood Avenue, Port Street and West Street, Harris-Brooks hopes the Hometown Heroes banners expand to other areas within town. So far, there's been "overwhelming support," she says.
"This is something that should've been done years ago," Griffin said. " … There's so many people who should (be) recognized. The old saying, 'You may be gone, but you're not forgotten.' And the only way you don't forget them is by putting something up like this, to remember those who paved the way before I did."

title: Dorchester County Council passes solar legislation, says more may be coming
author: MAGGIE TROVATO mtrovato@chespub.com
content:
Dorchester County Council passes solar legislation, says more may be coming

 November 8, 2024 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: MAGGIE TROVATO mtrovato@chespub.com | Section: Local News 
 
 680
 Words 

 Read News Document

 CAMBRIDGE — In a 3-2 vote, the Dorchester County Council passed a bill that addresses setbacks and buffers, ownership, and decommissioning plans for accessory, small scale and utility scale solar energy systems.After the bill was passed at a meeting on Nov. 4, Council President Lenny Pfeffer said this is a start for solar legislation in the county.
"Laws can be amended and modified," he said. "But if we don't do something now, before the start of the General Assembly, we could be facing much worse without any safeguards in place."
Council members Rob Kramer and William Nichols voted against the bill. Council member Ricky Travers, Council Vice President Mike Detmer and Pfeffer voted in favor of it.
Under the new bill, solar developments located off scenic byways will need to be set back 100 feet from all property lines, and developments that are not located off of scenic byways will need to be set back 75 feet. Requirements regarding vegetative buffers, perimeter fencing, topsoil and site plans are also in the legislation.
The bill defines who the owners of a solar site are. Pfeffer said in an interview with the Star Democrat in September that the owners of the property and the operator of the solar development would both be considered the owner.
The bill was reintroduced in September after getting tabled in March. In the reintroduced bill, a section was added regarding decommissioning solar projects. Per the legislation, a decommissioning plan will need to be submitted and approved by the county prior to the building permit application.
In the September interview, Pfeffer said the bill was tabled so the council could wait for state solar legislation to go into affect and make sure the county was in line with it.
At the meeting Nov. 4, residents thanked the council for their efforts and shared concerns that the county bill doesn't do enough to restrict solar development.
The reintroduced bill left out a section in the original proposed bill that put a cap on how many aggregate acres of the county can house utility-scale solar energy systems.
Beth Hill said although she feels the bill is a step in the right direction, she thinks there needs to be a cap on the number of acres in the county that can be used for solar development.
"Other counties around us do have caps," she said, mentioning Caroline County, which has a 2,000-acre cap on total rural land available for solar development.
Tracy Whitby-Fairall, who attended a town hall on the subject that Detmer hosted the previous week, said she recognized the county's efforts. She called the bill a "good foundation for a strong framework" for the county.
"I think there are some things that could be improved," she said, later adding, "I hope this isn't the end of the legislation. I hope this is the beginning."
Erick Windsor, who asked the council to vote against the bill, talked about the county's history of thriving tomato, dairy and lumber industries, which are now gone. He said that large solar operations take land away from grain farming.
"And this is going to affect all the other industries in this county that work around grain farming, like chicken farming," he said. "So you hurt the chicken farmers and you're going to hurt the industry in Hurlock that processes all this stuff."
Windsor said more restrictions need to be put on solar so it doesn't "decimate" the north part of the county.
Detmer said the bill — especially the decommissioning component — is "crucial" to have at the county level before the Maryland General Assembly session begins in January. He talked about the possibility of additional legislation coming down from the state.
"The Wild West of solar that we are in right now, I'm very bothered by it," he said. "I think we have to plant our flag here in this place that we're ready to go right now. If we don't act tonight, the law's not going to be in place when the session starts."
Detmer said this isn't the end of creating legislation around solar, but action needs to be taken now.
"We've got to put the seatbelt on," he said.

title: ‘A gem’: State and local leaders celebrate Port Street Commons project
author: KONNER METZ kmetz@chespub.com
content:
‘A gem’: State and local leaders celebrate Port Street Commons project

 November 8, 2024 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: KONNER METZ kmetz@chespub.com | Section: Local News 
 
 596
 Words 

 Read News Document

 EASTON — A multi-use property bringing affordable housing and behavioral health services to Easton is officially complete.Port Street Commons, a 24,000-square-foot project led by The Arc Central Chesapeake Region, celebrated the end of construction with a ribbon-cutting ceremony that included local and state officials. The space houses nine apartment units as well as a headquarters for The Arc, complete with offices and a behavioral health suite.
Speaking to more than 100 attendees Thursday morning, The Arc President and CEO Jonathon Rondeau said the organization is "building a future where equity and inclusion are the norm."
"There will be people whose lives change within these walls because of the services they receive, the connections they make, the housing they can afford," Rondeau said.
The $11 million project, financed through a capital campaign, received $2.5 million in investment from the state and $750,000 in federal funding, Rondeau said. Chesapeake Neighbors, a housing subsidiary of The Arc, held a lottery in September for potential tenants that fell within the income requirements, with more than 250 people entering.
There are seven two-bedroom units and two three-bedroom units, all of them featuring free Wi-Fi and appliances. Two of the first-floor units are tailored to accommodate tenants with disabilities.
Members of the Easton Town Council and Talbot County Council, along with Sen. Johnny Mautz (R-Caroline, Dorchester, Talbot, Wicomico) and Del. Tom Hutchinson (R-Caroline, Dorchester, Talbot, Wicomico), attended Thursday's ceremony.
Easton Mayor Megan Cook said the project is a fit for the town's goal to revitalize the area next to the Tred Avon River. She noted Port Street Commons is the first project to fall under the town's mixed-use waterfront zoning.
"We're eager to encourage mixed-use facilities such as this, allowing for exciting new businesses in tandem with more affordable housing, both of which are critical for growth in our community," she said.
The site at 480 Port Street was identified in July 2021, and construction began just under two years later. In an interview, Rondeau said the quick timeline helps The Arc fulfill the community's immediate housing needs, adding that the town was a crucial partner.
"There's a lot of development happening here in Easton," Rondeau said. "It's a small town, only so many inspectors and things like that. The town has been great. They've really worked with us to help meet those timelines when we had a problem."
Rondeau said four families who were randomly drawn have been confirmed, with the first of those moving in Dec. 2. All nine apartments should be occupied by March, he said.
Julia Glanz, deputy secretary of the Maryland Department of Housing & Community Development, and Carol Beatty, secretary of the Maryland Department of Disabilities, both complimented the housing project during the ceremony.
Beatty said the apartments tackle "one of the most common concerns" she hears from Marylanders with disabilities — a lack of accessible housing that is also affordable.
Glanz was excited about the project and hopes it can be an example for other mixed-use housing endeavors.
"It is, I think, a gem across the state," Glanz said in an interview. " … From what I've seen in the last year and a half, this is very unique. And it's bringing so many different facets of life into one space."
The deputy secretary noted that the House Expansion and Affordability Act of 2024, which encourages higher-density affordable housing projects, reduces government barriers. However, Port Street Commons completed most of its three-and-a-half year turnaround before that act was passed.
"The Arc being able to do that without that legislation … is a testament to the community effort here in Easton and Talbot County, which we don't see everywhere," Glanz said.

title: Easton considers ordinance to crack down on seafood processing odors
author: KONNER METZ kmetz@chespub.com
content:
Easton considers ordinance to crack down on seafood processing odors

 November 8, 2024 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: KONNER METZ kmetz@chespub.com | Section: Local News 
 
 811
 Words 

 Read News Document

 EASTON — Amid resident concerns, the Easton Town Council is considering an ordinance to adjust zoning and place restrictions on seafood processors.The legislation, sent to the council for review following approval from the Planning Commission, was created in response to odor complaints from residents living near the business Chesapeake Brand Seafood on Maryland Avenue.
At Monday's Town Council meeting, councilmembers heard mixed reviews on the ordinance from residents and business owners, opting to leave the public hearing open and explore options such as moving the business out of a residential area.
Under the ordinance's proposed definition, seafood processing would be defined as "harvested seafood" being "cleaned, cut, eviscerated or otherwise prepared or cooked for sale in bulk, with a resulting by-product."
If approved, seafood processing would remain permitted in the industrial zoning district but only allowed in business commercial through a special exception. That exception would require that by-products are "stored within a closed or refrigerated vehicle," with operators required to install "odor control technology" so "no odor from any product or by-product can be detected outside the building."
Ward 4 Councilmember the Rev. Elmer Davis, who said he's heard the complaints from many of his constituents, took issue with the fact that the proposed ordinance requires existing businesses to comply by Jan. 1, 2026 instead of sooner.
"I don't think it's fair for the individuals who live in that area to have to go through another summer dealing with the odor," Davis said. "It's unfair. So I'm going to advocate that it be six months."
Davis added he doesn't think seafood processing should be allowed in business commercial zoning at all. Ward 2 Councilmember Don Abbatiello agreed with Davis' perspective but asked that the council consider the legislation's potential impacts on other seafood businesses.
"My only concern would be that we have several other seafood facilities in town who don't have these issues," Abbatiello said. "And I would hate to see them get caught up in a similar scenario, where they're getting, for lack of a better term, punished."
Council President Frank Gunsallus asked if the town had a plan to aid smaller seafood businesses if they're forced to comply with the costly odor mitigation requirements.
"If we're going to be potentially imposing regulations on businesses that have significant financial impact to the point which some have claimed would put them out of business, I think we should take pause with that," Gunsallus said.
"I'm not quite concerned about that, personally," Davis responded. "I'm more concerned about the constituents in the neighborhood. … What you're just saying (makes) it seem like it's a hardship on the business when they probably haven't even tried."
Zach Smith, attorney for Chesapeake Brand Seafood owner/operator Mitchell Hughes, provided a letter to the council to be read aloud during the public hearing on the ordinance.
If passed, the ordinance "will put Mitchell out of business and will cause significant economic harm to him, his families, his employees and the local watermen that he supports," Smith wrote.
The attorney said Hughes has taken "reasonable steps" to mitigate the impact on residents as they have brought up concerns. However, he says buying new equipment isn't doable.
"While Mitchell has tried to be a good neighbor, he cannot reasonably install equipment that prohibits any smell from being detected outside of his building," Smith wrote. "Mitchell has looked into what will be necessary to satisfy this proposed regulation, and such technology is not feasible and will be extremely cost prohibitive."
RESIDENT CONCERNSDuring the public hearing, many residents voiced impacts Hughes' business has had on their quality of life. Resident Philip Bernot said he's lived next to grain processors, metal fabricators and plumbers at the site since 2001, never before experiencing any issue that brought him to a town meeting.
"Not a single one of these businesses has ever brought me up here to complain," Bernot said. "Not a single one of these businesses has repeatedly caused a gut-wrenching stench to take over the entire neighborhood."
A representative for Sea Watch International said the business on Glebe Park Drive would be "swept up into new legislation." Bruce Cole, owner of Cole's Seafood House & Deli, echoed this, saying the ordinance would negatively impact his operation on North Washington Street.
"(The) impact that he has is going to impact me," Cole said, noting equipment may cost around $100,000. " … I don't have any complaints."
Following the public hearing, Ward 1 Councilmember Maureen Curry asked the council to pause on taking action. She emphasized the operation of the business under scrutiny is different from businesses like Cole's.
"They're not doing it for retail, they're doing it for wholesale and to push out a product," Curry said. The council left the public hearing open for the Nov. 18 meeting.
Curry added that she hopes the council can work toward a "best case scenario" in which Chesapeake Brand Seafood moves out of its current location to a more appropriate one away from residents.

title: 4 of 6 charter amendments pass in Dorchester County
author: STAFF REPORT
content:
4 of 6 charter amendments pass in Dorchester County

 November 8, 2024 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: STAFF REPORT | Section: Local News 
 
 514
 Words 

 Read News Document

 Voters in Dorchester County this general election were posed with six questions asking residents whether or not certain changes should be made to the county charter.Four of six proposed charter amendments were passed by Dorchester County voters, according to unofficial results from the Maryland Board of Elections.
As of Friday afternoon, Dorchester County election workers still had about 1,100 mail-in and provisional ballots left to canvas. This is not enough votes to alter the outcomes of these amendments, but exact vote totals may change in the coming days.
QUESTION AThe first question on the ballot for Dorchester County residents asked whether the county charter should be amended to say that the review of administrative structure be conducted within the first fiscal year of each Dorchester County Council term.
Currently, the charter says a review of administrative structure should take place at least every four years, but it does not state when in that four years it should take place.
Nearly 90% of Dorchester County voters chose to approve the amendment as of totals posted Friday.
QUESTION BThe second question on the ballot asked whether budget-related due dates should be pushed back 15 days in the county charter.
The first due date is for when the county must prepare the budget by. The ballot question asked if that due date should be changed to May 15 from May 1. The question also asked if the county council's budget adoption due date should be changed to June 15 from May 31.
About 76% of ballots counted by Friday voted to approve the change.
QUESTION CThe third question asked whether the county charter should be amended to remove the residency requirement for the county manager position.
Currently, the charter states the county manager does not have to reside in the county at the time they are appointed but must become a resident within six months. It states that the county manager needs to retain residency in the county for the duration of their time in that position.
About 61% of county voters chose to retain the requirements, according to totals posted Friday.
QUESTION DThe fourth question on the ballot asked whether the charter should be amended to clarify certain responsibilities of the county manager, including day-to-day operations, and establish procedures for certain vacancies.
Currently, the charter has procedures in place for council member and treasurer vacancies, as well as certain board and commission vacancies.
More than 87% of Dorchester County voters had chosen to approve the amendment as of Friday.
QUESTION EThe fifth question asked whether the county charter should be amended to remove the residency requirement for the finance director position.
Currently, the charter states the finance director must become a resident of the county within six months of appointment and stay a resident.
Just under 60% of county voters had chosen not to approve the change as of Friday.
QUESTION FThe final question on the ballot asked whether the charter should be amended to include language to ensure transparency of governmental functions as well as access to open meetings and public records.
Dorchester County voters overwhelmingly supported the amendment, which had received approval from almost 93% of the electorate as of Friday.

Dorchester County to put pickleball courts on Glasgow Street

 CAMBRIDGE — After a decision to resurface the Glasgow Tennis Courts left pickleball players high and dry, pickleball courts are coming to Glasgow Street.At a Dorchester County Council meeting Nov. 4, the council voted unanimously to move forward with the acquisition of property behind the Judy Center on Glasgow Street, which will allow for the creation of six new pickleball courts.

Trieu said the county would be able to create pickleball courts behind the Judy Center next to the Glasgow Tennis Courts and offer youth and adult pickleball programming.
At the Nov. 4 County Council meeting, Council President Lenny Pfeffer thanked Trieu for his efforts to make this happen and told those watching the meeting to spread the word about the plan for new courts.
