title: New Cambridge solar ordinance will have 'immediate effect'
author: MAGGIE TROVATO mtrovato@chespub.com
content:
New Cambridge solar ordinance will have 'immediate effect'

 December 12, 2024 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: MAGGIE TROVATO mtrovato@chespub.com | Section: Local News 
 
 561
 Words 

 Read News Document

 CAMBRIDGE — Along with passing an ordinance regarding solar energy systems on wooded lots, the Cambridge City Council has directed city staff to look into removing community solar from a 350-acre maximum on solar permitted in the city.During a City Council meeting on Dec. 9, the council unanimously approved an ordinance amending the city's Unified Development Code for solar energy systems on wooded lots. Specifically, the amendment allows small-scale solar and community solar on wooded lots as long as the solar project complies with the city's Forest Conservation Ordinance or the state's Model Forest Conservation Ordinance.
Before the ordinance was passed, Cambridge Planning and Zoning Director Brian Herrmann said it was consistent with the city's comprehensive plan and the Planning and Zoning Commission had approved it in early November.
Herrmann said the ordinance would apply to sites that are at least 40,000 square feet. He said requirements of the ordinance include that the area cleared on the wooded lot cannot exceed 10 acres and impacted trees must be replanted at a 2-to-1 ratio or a fee be paid in lieu.
Small-scale solar energy systems are typically located on a homeowner's property, Herrmann said.
"It's essentially generating electricity where it is used," he said.
Community solar energy systems provide power to the residents of a community. Herrmann said that in Maryland, 40% of the output of a community solar system must serve low- to moderate-income residents.
During the meeting, Tony Kupersmith, a lawyer representing a renewable energy company, said the company he represents has a community solar project on Leonards Lane and this ordinance is "critical" for that project.
"So I get to let you know that what you do tonight would have an immediate effect for an actual project that is ready to go forward, that wants to go forward, and the only issue right now holding us up is the wooded lot issue," Kupersmith said before requesting the council adopt the ordinance.
Herrmann told the council that the city's 350-acre solar maximum — which it is close to reaching — limits the impact of this ordinance.
"We have two projects in the final stages of the development review process," he said. "If those two are to go through, we're going to be at 325 acres. So there's only about 25 acres left before we actually hit this amount. So I guess you can see we're not talking about a lot of solar systems that are going to be built even if this does pass."
Commissioner Brian Roche asked why community solar is included in that 350-acre maximum that also includes medium- and large-scale solar energy systems. He said it should be excluded.
"We don't want to see our entire land base covered with solar panel projects, but the way I understand community solar is really it is to the benefit of people that cannot either put it on their roof (and) they want to collaborate ... or they otherwise may not be able to have it," he said. "To me, I would strike that out from that maximum."
Roche asked that only medium- and large-scale solar energy systems be included in the 350-acre maximum and not community solar energy systems.
City Attorney Patrick Thomas said that because Roche's request goes "beyond the scope" of the ordinance on the table, it would need to go through a separate text amendment process. He said a separate ordinance to address the maximum could be prepared.

title: Talbot County Council denies raise in accommodation tax
author: Veronica Fernandez-Alvarado
content:
Talbot County Council denies raise in accommodation tax

 December 12, 2024 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: Veronica Fernandez-Alvarado | Section: Local News 
 
 879
 Words 

 Read News Document

 EASTON — A controversial proposal to raise the accommodation tax was voted down by the the Talbot County Council Tuesday.During an impromptu public comment period, lodge owners and community members expressed concerns over the increase in the accommodation tax saying it would hurt profits and tourism in the county. Additional comments concerning a lack of information were shared resulting in the proposal not passing.
The rise of the accommodation tax was presented by Cassandra Vanhooser, director of the department of Economic Development and Tourism, on Tuesday who gave an overview of the steps taken by her department to get a proposal in front of the council including approval for the Tourism Board of Talbot County and receiving support from Easton, Oxford, St. Michaels and Trappe.
"(Talbot County Council is) being called on to balance the effects on tourism businesses with the benefits to the towns and the county," Vanhooser said. "The Tourism Board has weighed the evidence, and they believe that the benefits outweigh the disadvantages."
Talbot County's current public accommodations tax rate, or hotel tax rate, is 4%, the lowest of any county in the state. The tax is levied on those staying in hotels and short-term rentals, collected by the business and then paid to either the county or to the towns.
Easton, Oxford and St. Michaels collect revenues from such properties within one mile outside town limits. The county collects revenue from all other properties.
A potential increase to 6%, which would raise annual revenue by around $1 million, requires approval from lawmakers in Annapolis.
Despite voting down an increase, the council voted to strengthen the existing accommodation tax.
Martha Sparks, financial director for Talbot County, suggested removing the 120-day grace period for owners of short-term rentals to provide accommodation tax collected to the county before the county can impose a 10% penalty. Sparks proposed that the council approve a request to the legislature to reduce that period of time.
The council unanimously approved the proposal.
Prior to voting on a letter of support for the accommodation tax increase, several people began to raise their hands in order to get their opinions on record. Commission President Chuck Callahan opened the floor for public comment.
PUBLIC COMMENTDuring public comment, business owner Scott Wagner expressed concern on raising taxes saying that though the accommodation tax has not been raised in 20 years, prices of rooms for rentals have, which in turn provides more funds from accommodation tax.
Wagner said room rates have "ridden the wave of inflation" and described raising the accommodation tax to "feeding the monster."
"This is feeding the monster, and the monster is asking for a million dollars more next year, so when the monster is going to get fatter. I've never seen the tax go down, quite frankly."
In contrast, Jessica Bellis, a member of the Talbot County Tourism Board, expressed concern over the negative connotation with the accommodation tax.
"We can use words like the monster that you're feeding, but the monster is making sure that we do have the roads and the infrastructure and the police department and the marketing to be able to promote and sustain tourism, which is a major industry in Talbot County," Bellis said.
Included in public comment were concerns over information. Kevin Hartmann, Easton resident, said lodging providers were not asked for comment at the time of the town's vote. He said the towns were "significantly under-educated as to the ramifications."
According to Hartmann, two surveys were conducted to gather the opinions of lodging operators. One was done by the Talbot County Tourism Board and the other was conducted by Hartmann. The board's survey, he said, showed 75% of operators did not support the increase in tax. For the survey done by Hartmann it was over 84%.
The survey by the tourism board was released on Dec. 5 and the last town to vote on supporting the raise was on Dec. 4.
"You have in your package, letters from your five towns of Talbot County, each one of those voted for the increase," Hartmann said. "But the significant difference is this: None of those towns heard what you're hearing tonight, none of those towns have the results of the survey at the time of their vote. None of those towns held a public hearing on the matter."
After hearing the comment given by Hartmann, Easton Council President Frank Gunsallus, spoke and shared his thoughts on the information provided.
"Our vote already occurred, but after hearing all the testimonies tonight, and especially Mr. Hartmann's … perhaps we could have been better educated before we voted," Gunsallus said. "I believe that people reserve the right to change their mind, and I know our votes were cast, but I am, on your record, withdrawing my support for this accommodation tax."
After much deliberation from the council, the motion was denied in a 3-2 vote with Councilmembers Pete Lesher and Keasha Haythe voting in support of the proposal.
Vanhooser, director of Economic Development and Tourism, said Wednesday that the proposal failed and will not move forward this state legislature period.
"The Tourism Board obviously supports this, because they see it as a way to fund my department and tourism marketing and promotion, and the towns, you know, were in favor, despite what was said last night, because it raises their revenue, which they need for the various things they spend the money on."

Dorchester County Council stresses need for conservative budget in FY2026

 CAMBRIDGE — As Dorchester County begins preparing for budget season, "conservative" is the name of the game.During a Dorchester County Council meeting on Dec. 3, council members stressed the importance of the county being conservative and efficient with how it spends its money in the upcoming fiscal year.
In response to County Manager Jerry Jones' question of whether the council has any priorities for the fiscal year 2026 budget, Council Member Ricky Travers said he wants to "hold the status quo" without raising taxes.
"My goal would be to be very conservative because we don't know where we're going to be at, what money we're going to have to spend," he said.
Council President Lenny Pfeffer brought up the budget deficit facing the state.
"With the state facing a $2.7 billion deficit, we're not sure exactly what the governor's going to cut," Pfeffer said. "So I think we're going to have to be very dynamic and make changes on the go as we go through this next budget cycle."
According to Dorchester County's budget adoption schedule, the County Council will begin holding budget work sessions in late February. Following public hearings, the adoption of the budget is scheduled for June 10.
The county's fiscal year 2025 budget, which included a 5% raise across the board for county employees, totaled $86.52 million. The operating budget increased by about $2.5 million, or roughly 3%, compared to fiscal year 2024, and the capital budget decreased by about $6.3 million, which is roughly 58%.
During the meeting on Dec. 3, Council Member William Nichols and Council Vice President Mike Detmer both agreed that not raising taxes — particularly for seniors — is important.
"It would be the last thing I would do," Nichols said about taxing seniors.
Detmer said he values the county manager and county staff for being consistent and increasing efficiency in county government. He said that along with being conservative and consistent, the county should also make sure it remains creative when it comes to the budget.
"We can't just be in shutdown mode, you know?" he said. "There's low-hanging fruit out there that we've got to be able to convert little things and enrich the life here."
Pfeffer said that the county's budget goals will be discussed more during the upcoming budget workshops.
"We're going to hear from all our department heads and see what the real needs versus wants are going to be from the county," he said.

title: Shore residents share mixed views on new Chesapeake Bay Bridge
author: ANDREA GRABENSTEIN agrabenstein@chespub.com
content:
Shore residents share mixed views on new Chesapeake Bay Bridge

 December 13, 2024 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: ANDREA GRABENSTEIN agrabenstein@chespub.com | Section: Local News 
 
 1059
 Words 

 Read News Document

 STEVENSVILLE — Informational displays lined the walls of Kent Island High School's cafeteria Wednesday, laying out narrowed-down options for a new Bay Bridge.The self-paced open house welcomed the community to gather information and submit feedback as the Maryland Transportation Authority conducts Tier 2 of the Chesapeake Bay Crossing Study. The study, launched in 2017, seeks to examine the state's options when it comes to the aging bridge.
Melissa Williams, Maryland Transportation Authority director of the division of planning and program development, said the team that developed the various plans for the new bridge went through in-depth analysis on the traffic data gathered throughout the year. It has developed seven proposed alternatives to the current Bay Bridge, with one alternative being a no-build option.
"We are proposing to remove both existing Bay Bridge spans due to the substantial cost of future maintenance and repair the impact to the traveling public associated with those repairs," Williams said.
Bridge spans, full tunnels, bridge tunnels and double decker bridge options were evaluated during the study. Bridge spans were recommended as construction would have fewer environmental impacts and a lower cost compared to other options. Additionally, the bridge spans would allow for greater flexibility in maintaining traffic during maintenance and emergency response situations.
The proposed alternatives include either a new eight-lane or 10-lane bridge consisting of two spans constructed north or south of the existing bridge.
The proposed alternatives consider bus service improvements, part-time shoulder use, interchange consolidation, park and ride facilities, congestion pricing, and pedestrian and bicycle shared use.
The Kent Island open house marks the third total, and second in-person, open house held by the Chesapeake Bay Crossing Tier 2 Study. On the Dec. 11, 129 attended the meeting. An in-person open house was also hosted at Broadneck High School in Annapolis Dec. 9, with 192 in attendance. In-person open houses followed a virtual open house on Dec. 4, in which 435 individuals logged on.
According to Williams, the open houses provided a transparent view of the project to the community.
"It's great to show lines on paper, " she said.
Patty Baker, of Kent Island, remembers the construction of the westbound span of the Bay Bridge. "It was impressive to watch," she said.
Baker attended several of the study's open houses last year and was interested to see how progress and updates have developed. "I couldn't have dreamed what would happen," she said, noting now the once rural area has become more and more part of a freeway and for so long summer beach traffic has detected weekend activities for locals. With the potential for roadway widening, Baker voiced concerns about areas so close to Route 50 including the Stevensville Cemetery, where her own family plots are. She said she appreciated the open house's layout and staff clarification to questions, particularly as to why the new bridges cannot be placed in different corridors.
"They are doing the best they can with what they are working with," she said.
Attending the project's last open house a year ago, Martin Gleason, of Grasonville, was interested in continual aspects of the project and found it to be very informative in regards to the "when, where, and how."
An area resident of 47 years, Brian H. of Kent Island, considered the potential new bridge "long overdue" and found the study thoroughly researched. He was enthusiastic about how the potential lane widening change would improve traffic flow.
Tom Helfenbein, of Kent Island, found the open house informative and offered suggestions of widening certain merging areas and moving chokepoints down to Route 404. "All consideration seems to stop at the (Queenstown) Outlets," he said.
Despite opportunities for public comment, Jennifer Laird, of Chester, claimed she didn't feel like the opinion of locals was being considered and did not approve of any aspect of the project, stating, "It's going to change everything," including bringing in more people from the western shore. Laird claimed the infrastructure was unequipped to handle the traffic and strongly preferred the new bridge be placed elsewhere.
Cheryl Gover, of Queenstown, voiced concerns of bottlenecking, traffic congestion impacts, and was worried how the proposed bridge shared use path would affect jumpers. Gover also recommended finding ways to create alternative routes off the bridge for locals.
Working in Glen Burnie, Jay Diepenbrock, of Centreville, takes a round trip over the Bay Bridge at least twice a week and knows personally how bad traffic can be. Noting it gets worse before it gets better, Diepenbrock was a little disappointed by the the projected timeline, with scheduled construction completion no sooner than about 2035.
"It will probably happen when I'm too old to be driving," he said. Nonetheless, Diepenbrock was optimistic it would be a much needed improvement for future generations.
Heather Lowe, project manager for the Bay Crossing Tier 2 Study, said a multi-use path for bicycles and pedestrians would be separated from travel lanes by a physical barrier across the more than four-mile bridge.
December open houses serve as formal scoping meetings to hear comments on the issues that will be evaluated in an environmental impact statement, according to Andrew Bing, virtual open house facilitator. Included in the areas of environmental considerations are impacts to natural resources, impacts to parks and recreation areas and impacts on historic properties and archaeological sites.
The Environmental Impact Study will focus on socioeconomic resources and land use, and minority and low income population. After time to consider and evaluate public feedback, a draft impact study is anticipated to be published in November 2025, followed by additional public hearings.
A final environmental impact study and record of decisions are anticipated for fall 2026, along with identified selected alternatives.
The Transportation Authority is anticipating finishing the current phase of the Chesapeake Bay Crossing Study in 2026. Five years of design and permitting would follow with construction anticipated for 2032, Bing said.
Anyone unable to attend the open houses still has time to submit comments through the Chesapeake Bay Crossing Study website. Comments received by Jan. 13 will be part of the study's summarization, Williams said, and comments will continue to be received after this date. "We want to hear what you have to say," she said.
Following the data collection, the study is expected to return with additional open houses next year.
Viewing of the virtual open house is available online. More information, as well as feedback submissions and public comments with personal information redacted are available for viewing at baycrossingstudy.com.
Reporter Veronica Fernandez-Alvarado contributed to this story.

title: St. Michaels raises penalties for 6 town code violations
author: Veronica Fernandez-Alvarado
content:
St. Michaels raises penalties for 6 town code violations

 December 13, 2024 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: Veronica Fernandez-Alvarado | Section: News 
 
 290
 Words 

 Read News Document

 ST. MICHAELS — Significant increases in fines for various violations of town codes were approved by the St. Michaels commissions on Wednesday evening.The increases were made on six different town codes and included including raises in fines for short-term rental, transient vendors and leash animal control violations. The fines for some infractions increased by more than 10 times.
Violation fines for short-term rentals operating without permission from the town doubled from $250 to $500.
Condemnation, otherwise known as "housing standards," increased from a steady $100 to $250 for a first violation, $300 for a second violation and $500 for a third violation.
Addressing non-compliance currently has a violation fine of $25. It has been increased to $150. This means that any owner of a building or premises that is not posted with the official street number within 30 days after said owner receives notice of the official street number shall be punishable by a fine of $150. Each day that the owner fails to display the official street number will constitute a separate offense.
Fines for violations relating to transient vendors, or vendors who sell produce or seafood at a roadside or a temporary location, were increased from $25 to $250.
Public urination fines were increased from $25 to $250, and public defecation fines went from $50 to $500.
Finally, leash animal control violation fines doubled from $50 to $100.
Commissioner David Wojciechowski asked if code enforcement officers would issue a warning first prior to issuing fines on the violations. Officer Jeffrey Oswald said on most of the violations there will be warnings prior to the penalties. This would not be the case for public urination and defecation.
After Commissioner Alfred Mercier opened a quiet public hearing on the increases, the commission unanimously approved the fine raises.

title: Legislators hear Cambridge's priorities before General Assembly session begins
author: MAGGIE TROVATO mtrovato@chespub.com
content:
Legislators hear Cambridge's priorities before General Assembly session begins

 December 13, 2024 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: MAGGIE TROVATO mtrovato@chespub.com | Section: Local News 
 
 580
 Words 

 Read News Document

 CAMBRIDGE — Before the regularly scheduled Cambridge City Council meeting on Dec. 9, the council and city staff shared their priorities with state legislators, who are preparing to go back to Annapolis for the 447th session of the Maryland General Assembly.During the legislative delegation work session, Cambridge City Manager Glenn Steckman acknowledged getting state funding this year will be difficult and asked that the Lower Shore delegation notify the city if they come across anything during session that could benefit Cambridge.
Steckman said the city doesn't have a list of laws or law changes that it wants enacted by the General Assembly.
"We're not here to try to make laws and recommend the law changes, but to show you what the issues that the elected leadership here is dealing with and the appointed staff is dealing with," he said. "We're looking for your help and guidance on the legislative level."
The six priorities — which Steckman detailed during the meeting and said are in no particular order — are to:
Preserve and renovate Cambridge's historic City Hall on Gay Street.Continue to move the Cambridge Harbor project forward.Improve housing and revitalize the Pine Street neighborhood.Make enhancements and improvements to city youth services.Update and improve the city's water and sewer infrastructure.Provide local workforce development programs and opportunities.
Steckman said when it comes to workforce development, it can be difficult for residents without transportation who are seeking employment or training opportunities in other counties.
"Obviously, if we want to grow the industrial part of the economy or (the) commercial (part), we need more job training to prepare, not only our existing workforce, but our workforce coming up through the school system," he said.
After Steckman discussed the city's priorities, Del. Tom Hutchinson (R-Caroline, Dorchester, Talbot, Wicomico), Del. Sheree Sample-Hughes (D-Dorchester, Wicomico), Del. Chris Adams (R-Caroline, Dorchester, Talbot, Wicomico) and Sen. Johnny Mautz (R-Caroline, Dorchester, Talbot, Wicomico) all chimed in.
Hutchinson said he sees improving youth services as a very important priority, referencing a local teen who had been detained by the Department of Juvenile Services for stealing a car.
"This is a really serious issue," Hutchinson said. "If we have children who are saying, 'I'm bored and it's fine,' then we really need to work on that and correct that."
Sample-Hughes said that some of the bills on rentals and housing that didn't get passed during last year's session could come back to the General Assembly this year. She said it would be useful for the city to keep in touch as the legislators hear these bills brought back.
"I think your on the ground insight is very beneficial to what we have to do when it comes to the policy work and not only just the financial side of things," she said.
Adams told the council this year will be a "budget year." The state faces a predicted $2.7 billion budget deficit in fiscal year 2026.
"We know that this is going to be a tough year," Adams said. "So legislative requests that revolve around funding capital projects are going to be tough. There is always bond money, and we as a delegation will surely do our part ... in submitting those requests."
Mautz asked that the council stay in touch with the Lower Shore delegation throughout the upcoming legislative session. He said that when the governor's budget comes out, the city should make sure there aren't cuts that will negatively affect the city.
"If there's an actual cut that's going to affect something in the City of Cambridge, somebody needs to call (us)," he said.

title: Developers host 3rd community meeting for Easton Crossing project
author: KONNER METZ kmetz@chespub.com
content:
Developers host 3rd community meeting for Easton Crossing project

 December 13, 2024 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: KONNER METZ kmetz@chespub.com | Section: Local News 
 
 591
 Words 

 Read News Document

 EASTON — Developers and residents gathered Wednesday evening for a third community meeting concerning a planned mixed-use development on Brookletts Avenue.Chesapeake Community Development, a subsidiary of The Arc Central Chesapeake Region, hosted the meeting to update neighbors on its draft site plans and facilitate community feedback.
The Easton Crossing infill project is expected to add around 120 units where a former Perdue AgriBusiness operation used to sit. Additionally, there are significant plans for commercial use and open areas.
Renderings show six buildings planned for the 6.5-acre site. Ross Benincasa, senior vice president of community development at Chesapeake Community Development, said the first building, which will have 15 residential units, is projected to open in December 2027.
Benincasa emphasized the mixed-income aspect of the project on Wednesday. Some units will be at market rate, and others down to where people "will be paying $500 to $600 a month for a new apartment."
"Unlike most developers, we don't build affordable units and market-rate units," Benincasa said. "We build the same unit across the site, and we just have specific ratio goals that we hit for that site. If I'm living in an affordable unit and Joe is in a market-rate unit, and I go over to … Joe's apartment one night, I will have no idea who pays what."
Based on previous feedback, developers and architects are looking into using bricks that are darker in color to match surrounding buildings. They also touched on other topics that were raised at previous community meetings this year, such as lighting, open space and plantings.
"You're going to be seeing a mix of pedestrian (lights) and some larger lights in the areas of the parking lot," Benincasa said. "But those larger lights, from a sizing perspective, are going to feel more like downtown Easton."
There will be a focus on maintaining open space at the property, as well as around 70% native plantings. Benincasa added that once finished, there will be "around four to 10 shrubs or trees per 50 feet."
All parking spots will be screened, some by shrubs and trees and others by buildings. While Benincasa said South Street will be a "secondary" exit and entrance for residents, developers "fully anticipate" most drivers to use Brookletts Avenue.
"But we don't want them on Brookletts. That's the point," resident Harriett Page said.
Benincasa said a traffic study was completed by Lenart Traffic Consulting last week, which did not signify worries about the traffic increase around the site. An increase of around 20 cars during peak hour on Brookletts Avenue is projected.
Resident Joe Minarick said "with Brookletts being the main thoroughclear and the main import" for the site, those projections "(seemed) a little funny."
"Brookletts might be the front of the project, but it is not the only way that people are going to go in and out," Benincasa said. Those heading east toward Caroline County may use Kemp Lane to access Dover Road, he said.
As for the commercial aspect of the site, Benincasa said developers aren't expecting national businesses. In fact, Chesapeake Community Development is looking for local businesses "emotionally invested in their success."
Developers may also encourage businesses to hire people with disabilities, a segment of the population that The Arc strives to serve.
"We have had discussions about if a business wants to hire people with disabilities, then there would be, sort of, credits for that," said Jonathon Rondeau, president and CEO of The Arc. "Or for hiring local as well."
"That will be coming in 2026, 2027," he continued, "as we think about what those incentives are as we begin to market the commercial spaces."

title: St. Michaels commissioners approve updates to docking infractions
author: Veronica Fernandez-Alvarado
content:
St. Michaels commissioners approve updates to docking infractions

 December 14, 2024 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: Veronica Fernandez-Alvarado | Section: News 
 
 359
 Words 

 Read News Document

 ST. MICHAELS — On Wednesday evening, the Commissioners of St. Michaels voted to give police authority to cite docking infractions and approve bids for trash and recycling services.Amendments were made to town Boats and Boating code regarding town-owned slips. A public discussion was held on a proposed amendment to provide police authority to cite docking infractions, as well as measures to correct grammar errors, change language for uniformity and remove a "problematic provision" that references judgment liens of personal prosperity.
The amendments were unanimously approved.
PROPERTY MAINTENANCEA proposed amendment to a town ordinance concerning property maintenance and littering was brought before the commissioners. The requested amendment would remove duplicative language, increase penalties for littering and provide certain authorities to cite for littering and weed control violations.
Prior to the amendment, the ordinance stated that "no owner of property within the town" can cause, permit or maintain the existence of weeds higher than 12 inches on the property. The new amendment it added "or occupant" to provide accountability on rentals as well.
Additionally, it adds that a violation of this article is subject to a fine of $200 for first offense and that the property owner and occupant of the property may each be separately cited. Repeat violations would be subject to a fine of $300.
The amendment was unanimously approved by the commissioners.
TRASH COLLECTION SERVICESA bid was approved for a three-year contract with Republic Services for trash and recycling services. The proposed contract states costs for the town would be $239,001.91. In comparison, during fiscal year 2023 the town spent $191,000 for recycling and trash collection.
St. Michaels' staff reached out to other trash and recycle businesses for new bids but only Republic Services sent in a bid. Ultimately, the commissioners approved the three year contract with Republic Services.
TOWN MANAGER RECRUITMENTFinally, a bid was approved for the Mercer Group Associates as the firm to lead recruitment of the next Town Administrator. The firm's bid was for $24,000 to provide services including position analysis, recruitment process, resume review, candidate screening and interview process.
Mercer Group will also assist in the negotiation of an employment contract after completing the roughly 100-day recruitment process.
Commissioners unanimously approved the bid.

title: Wreaths Across America honors veterans graves
author: Lilly Howard lhoward@chespub.com
content:
Wreaths Across America honors veterans graves

 December 17, 2024 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: Lilly Howard lhoward@chespub.com | Section: State News 
 
 396
 Words 

 Read News Document

 Cecil County organizers partnered with gas station chain Sheetz helped facilitate deliveries of holiday wreathes to various cemeteries in Cecil County, including Rosebank and St. Mary Anne's, last week to be used in Wreaths Across America across the county. Wreaths Across America is an annual tribute to our nation's veterans, honoring those who served by placing a wreath on their graves around the holidays.Julia Swoboda initiated the first Wreaths Across America event in Cecil County nine years ago at St. Mary Anne's, after she attended the annual Arlington National Cemetery wreath ceremony in 2016 — where the initiative first began in 1992, and where nearly 400,000 veterans and their families are buried.
"After that, I was really inspired to come back to Cecil County and start our event," Swoboda said. "I think anyone who's done that [gone to Arlington's ceremony] really understands the impact that makes on you and then just inspires you really to see what you can do in your community."
Once Swoboda brought the initiative to St. Mary Anne's in North East, it spread across the county to other cemeteries, such as Rosebank in Rising Sun.
"It's really been a way for me to kind of stay connected to honoring the sacrifices that our community members have made," Swoboda said.
This year's Wreaths Across America theme is "live with purpose," which Swoboda says encapsulates the event perfectly for her.
"When you're there you see the people coming are not only honoring the people who have lived with purpose in our community, but they're also finding a way to be involved and honor those and integrate it in their purpose of their life," Swoboda said. "And that's something really beautiful to see in our community, especially at a time where things are really divisive. This event is something that seems to bring everyone together."
All the wreaths were placed on veterans' graves across Cecil County Saturday, Dec. 14.
"We have so many veterans who continue to worship at our church, plus those whose family members who are interred here, and those who've come before us," said St. Mary Anne's Pastor John Schaeffer.
He pointed out that the historic church cemetery holds graves of veterans who served in the Spanish American War and the Revolutionary War all the way up to the more recent Iraq War and Afghanistan War. This initiative honors all veterans throughout time, ensuring their service is never forgotten.

title: Groundbreaking of Millington Senior Village attended by Secretary Day
author: WILL BONTRAGER wbontrager@chespub.com
content:
Groundbreaking of Millington Senior Village attended by Secretary Day

 December 18, 2024 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: WILL BONTRAGER wbontrager@chespub.com | Section: News 
 
 564
 Words 

 Read News Document

 MILLINGTON — "I am proud of what we achieved and am looking forward to this project coming to life and bearing fruit," Millington Mayor Kevin Hemstock told an audience of stakeholders and community leaders on Dec. 3, about the new senior housing center being built. The new facility will be located at 172 Sassafras Street — the site of the former Millington Elementary School.He along with Maryland Department of Housing and Community Development (DHCD) Secretary Jake Day, Chair of Home Partnership Inc. Phil Wohlfort and Kent County Commissioners Ron Fithian, John Price and Albert Nickerson, tossed out the first shovelfuls of dirt.
"As we break ground today, it's not just the beginning of a building project, I think this is going to be important for a lot of people in Millington," Hemstock said.
Earlier, inside the building of the school, in a spacious room with walls that still had paintings of emblematic characters from childhood, Clifford the Big Red Dog, The Wizard of Oz, Winnie the Pooh and Bambi, Hemstock pointed out the irony that the senior center will be built there.
"This is a magical moment," Hemstock said, adding that 100 years ago the location was a farm. Then in 1974 the school was built. He said it is interesting to think the first students at the school may benefit in the near-future from what is being built.
2005 was the first mention of a senior housing center in the Town.
Since then, the concept has grown significantly, he stated, plans altering from building a senior center across the street to this location.
Jamie Williams, director of Kent County Economic and Tourism Development traced the history of the property after the school closed in 2017.
The property officially transitioned to the County in May of 2019, she said, then the approximate 24 acres and 36,000 sq ft. building and property were purchased by the Town of Millington in 2022 for $1.
Williams, who told the audience the project speaks to the power of community, collaboration and vision, highlighted the partnerships involved.
The Upper Shore Regional Council provided $50,000 for a preliminary architectural feasibility report.
The Rural Maryland council approved $100,000 for design and engineering cost of the roof and fire suppression system.
The Town of Millington invested $1.4 million for repairs, maintenance, utility cost, staff time, permit fees and submitted a $500,000 community legacy grant application to the DHCD for the construction of the roof and fire suppression system.
Home Partnership Inc. committed over $630,000 towards reconstructing 2200 square ft. for senior-focused spaces.
With all that effort, Williams acknowledged, challenges still remain, estimating the overall cost is projected to be $1.5 million.
She recognized that also includes creating walking trails, a community garden, and creating other enriching open spaces. That takes partnerships, to "build a brighter future for Kent County," she expressed.
After introductions, Secretary Day spoke, expressing the need for this center in an aging population.
"Housing is critical, particularly when we have failed to build housing from 2018 until now," Day said.
Housing costs are high and not likely to decline, he added.
With supply chain interest and expensive labor costs, as all the developers, builders and government officials could attest to, it can be challenging, Day noted.
Day emphasized that with local government all-in, and the developers and community all-in, he knows that Governor Wes Moore would want the DHCD to be all-in, as well.
"We're not at the finish line yet but we are 100% committed," Day reiterated.

title: Oxford names next town manager, announces clerk-treasurer will stay with town
author: Maggie Trovato
content:
Oxford names next town manager, announces clerk-treasurer will stay with town

 December 18, 2024 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: Maggie Trovato | Section: Local News 
 
 603
 Words 

 Read News Document

 OXFORD — After nearly half a year without a town manager and a controversial hire that never actually made it into the Oxford Town Office, the Commissioners of Oxford have found a new town manager.Holly Wahl, currently the Chesapeake Beach Town Administrator, will begin the role on Jan. 6
During a Commissioners of Oxford meeting Tuesday, Commissioner Katrina Greer read the news to residents.
The commissioners also announced at the meeting that the town's Clerk-Treasurer Vickie Sharp will be staying in her position and will not leave the town for other employment at the end of the year, which Sharp had told the Star Democrat in late November.
"I think we all want to thank Vickie for the work she did in the last month and a half with nobody in the office to talk to except herself," Commission President Norm Bell said.
Residents in the audience of the meeting clapped upon hearing the news, and at the end of the meeting, one resident reacted to the news and the tone of the meeting by saying it felt like the best Christmas present.
According to a news release from Oxford, Wahl has served Chesapeake Beach as its town administrator for the last eight years. In that time, she helped reduce town taxes more than 17% while increasing services to citizens and businesses, reduce liabilities by $9.44 million, increase the town's net position by over $21 million and improve the town's fund balance by over $15 million, the news release said.
Wahl attributes those improvements in Chesapeake Beach to fiscal accountability, the acquisition of grant funding, the implementation of organizational changes, the application of technology and the alignment of staff with mission-critical activities to eliminate inefficiency, according to the news release.
During the meeting, Greer said the commissioners are "delighted" that Wahl will be joining the town.
"I mean, we think this woman is going to knock it out of the park," she said.
In the news release, the commissioners said they think Wahl's experience in procurement and in managing larger projects will bring the town "cost savings with better management."
"Ms. Wahl has experience applying for and managing grant monies, coordinating with state and local agencies and has worked with the Army Corps of Engineers on major waterways projects such as the $3 million federal dredging of Fishing Creek Channel," the release said.
Along with town management, Wahl's experience includes operations director roles in both the private and nonprofit sectors. According to the news release, Wahl holds business administration degrees from the University of Maryland and Johns Hopkins University. Wahl is currently finalizing her dissertation to obtain a doctorate in public administration and public policy from George Washington University.
At the meeting on Tuesday, Bell acknowledged the months-long search it took to find a new town manager.
"It was a learning experience," he said. "And I think we wound up with a very good pick."
In late June, Michael Calvert — a former city administrator in Liberty, South Carolina — was hired to fill the role of town manager, which former Town Manager Cheryl Lewis was retiring from. But just three days after the commissioners announced the hire, they announced that the town and Calvert had "mutually agreed to part ways."
The commission did not comment on why the decision was made. Former Liberty City Council Member Peggy Edwards said she resigned from the council due to issues with Calvert and the city's mayor. She said that when Calvert was in the position, there was a lack of transparency and mismanagement of money.
The situation led to the commissioners choosing a search firm to assist in the search for the next town manager, which led to Wahl's hiring.

title: Cambridge receives clean audit despite Finance Department changes
author: MAGGIE TROVATO mtrovato@chespub.com
content:
Cambridge receives clean audit despite Finance Department changes

 December 19, 2024 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: MAGGIE TROVATO mtrovato@chespub.com | Section: Local News 
 
 498
 Words

 CAMBRIDGE — Although unexpected staff changes whirled through Cambridge's Finance Department this past year, the city has received the highest level of assurance for its fiscal year 2024 financial audit.During a Cambridge City Council work session on Dec. 16, accounting firm PKS & Company's manager, Ryan Taylor, said the city received a clean opinion on its fiscal year 2024 audit.
"This is the highest level of assurance that we can give as CPAs," he said. Taylor said PKS did not identify any noncompliance or material weaknesses in the Cambridge audit, either.
A "significant deficiency issue" related to month-end close was identified, however, Taylor said.
Month-end close is an accounting process to finalize the financial report of the previous month. Taylor said the deficiency issue was due to "extenuating circumstances" this past year, mentioning the deaths of city Finance Department staff members.
In late December 2023, the city's previous Finance Director Deborah Cooper died. In July, accounting clerk Lisa Herbert died.
Taylor said these deaths caused a "shakeup" in the department and things fell behind.
"But I'm happy to say that we met with (Finance Director Perry Peregoy) and (Finance Manager Vicky Simmons), and they've kind of developed a correction action plan with steps that have already been put into place to fix some of these issues," Taylor said. "So I think we're in a pretty good spot with that moving into this next fiscal year."
After PKS's presentation, Commissioner Sputty Cephas thanked the city's Finance Department, acknowledging the losses of Cooper and Herbert.
"We're coming up on a year that Ms. Deborah passed away," he said. "That was a tremendous shock — I would say detriment — to my life."
Cephas called it admirable that the Finance Department staff has been able to receive these audit results with all of this change.
"So thank you all for what you do to continue (getting) the results that we're receiving," he said.
Current Cambridge Finance Director Perry Peregoy thanked the accounting firm for the work they've done.
"They came into a challenged environment, and they have assisted us greatly in giving us a clean slate to carry on from the hard work that Ms. Deborah had done in the past," he said. "And we greatly appreciate the guidance that they have provided for us."
Peregoy also thanked Finance Manager Vicky Simmons for her work in the city's Finance Department. He said that when Herbert became ill, Simmons stepped up. Once the city was able to hire someone to fill Herbert's role, Simmons was tasked with assisting PKS staff so they could complete the financial audit, Peregoy said.
"And she worked tirelessly through the last four or five months, preparing documents, responding to requests and really providing an incredible leadership role to some members of staff who had never gone through an exercise like an audit of the type we go through here," he said about Simmons. "So I just want to draw attention to what Vicky has done and thank her very much for everything she's done for the city over the years."

title: Samaritan Group and Good Neighbor Fund call for support
author: WILL BONTRAGER wbontrager@chespub.com
content:
Samaritan Group and Good Neighbor Fund call for support

 December 19, 2024 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: WILL BONTRAGER wbontrager@chespub.com | Section: News 
 
 589
 Words 

 Read News Document

 CHESTERTOWN — James Diggs, board chair of the Samaritan Group of Kent County, a nonprofit addressing homelessness, understands it is a multi-faceted issue.The Samaritan Group is preparing to open its three-month cold weather shelter to homeless individuals starting Jan. 1.
But the cold weather shelter is not all they do.
Partnering with the Good Neighbor Fund, a nonprofit with similar goals, the Samaritan Group has been meeting weekly with individuals referred by the Kent County Department of Social Services.
Diggs said, "We help people in unfortunate circumstances with electric bills, rent, utilities, provide short term shelter and a range of other services, with the goal to keep them from becoming homeless in the first place."
This could make all the difference, Diggs emphasized, keeping the lights on to get them through the difficult winter months.
For Diggs and Good Neighbor Fund, both housed with the Chester Valley Ministers Association, bringing someone back from the "verge of homelessness," is more than half the battle in addressing the growing issue.
"The increased need for outreach services over the last year has been staggering. Since the Covid pandemic, the increased need has been steadily rising, but this year the need has grown at an unsettling rate," said Laurie Loveless of Good Neighbor Fund in a November press release.
"Both organizations have observed a significant increase in demand for outreach services over the last three years, with the average amount spent from 2022-2023 doubling from the average spent in 2019-2021. The Samaritan Group annual budget dedicated a little over $35,000 for outreach services in 2024 and as of the end of September over $40,000 has been spent to support community members. The Good Neighbor Fund spent $31,665 in 2023 and spent over $40,000 so far in 2024."
"Combined, over $80,000 was spent so far this year between the Samaritan Group and the Good Neighbor Fund helping over 200 households in Kent County with 247 adults and 166 children."
Unfortunately these two organizations have exhausted their funds.
With three months left in the year, 2024 surpassed the budgeted dollars for the "outreach services" that are provided by the Samaritan Group of Kent County and Good Neighbor Fund. Both were forced to temporarily suspend their outreach until more funds can be raised.
Diggs said, "An assessment that seeks to better understand our community's need for low-income housing, short-term financial assistance, permanent supportive housing for senior and differently abled community members, and other solutions for people who are unhoused, is the necessary next step for homelessness action in Kent County."
But, Diggs, doing this ministry and work for as long as he has, knows the homeless are as varied as any other resident, each situation requiring a variety of different services a shelter does not always address.
For the ones who need the cold weather shelter, they welcome them with wide open arms. Often times the police have brought people to the shelter, entrusting them to their care, Diggs noted.
The January shelter will be located at the Chestertown Church of the Nazarene. In February, the shelter will be at First United Methodist Church. It will be at the Presbyterian Church of Chestertown in March.
Starting in January, those who need it get a home-cooked meal around 6 p.m., a place to shower, clean sheets, a bed, and all-night supervision by paid overnight staff and one sleeper (a person on-site in case of any emergencies).
At 8 a.m., they awake and are given a breakfast and a lunch to-go. In those morning hours they are encouraged to go to the various warming stations in town like the Kent County Public Library.

title: Oxford Commissioners tackle Strand project issues with meeting
author: Maggie Trovato
content:
Oxford Commissioners tackle Strand project issues with meeting

 December 20, 2024 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: Maggie Trovato | Section: Local News 
 
 527
 Words 

 Read News Document

 OXFORD — During a Commissioners of Oxford meeting Tuesday, the commissioners talked about the Strand Beach project, acknowledging its bumpy path toward completion."Many of you have asked me (if) the project on the Strand — the beach part of the project — (was) completed," Commissioner Katrina Greer said to residents at the meeting. "And no, it wasn't completed."
Greer said that although contractor Underwood and Associates was paid to create a living shoreline on Oxford's waterfront, the project was not finished to the specifications that Underwood and Associates had originally presented.
The project plan was to create a berm, place hooks along the east and west areas of the Strand to bring in sand, create small islands in the water to reduce waves coming onto the beach and plant low marsh grasses on those islands.
Greer said that to date, not all of the grasses have been planted on the islands and the islands are two feet higher in elevation than they're supposed to be. She said previous Town Manager Cheryl Lewis signed off on the project in June.
"Now we did pay the contractor in June," Greer said. "And so we needed to bring some leverage to the table to be able to have the contractor bring the project back in line with what had been permitted and what we had been owed."
Greer said she made some phone calls and brought together compliance and permitting staff within the Maryland Department of the Environment and the U.S. Army Corps of Engineers, as well as the organizations that funded the project and the contractor. The meeting with the different groups was held Dec. 10.
"And I will say we came away with exactly what we wanted," Greer said.
Out of the meeting, the town was able to ensure that — at no cost to the town — Underwood and Associates will bring down the elevation of the islands to the U.S. Army Corps of Engineers' specs and take out the sand that goes out to the headlands, which was part of the U.S. Army Corps of Engineers' permitting.
"For us to leave the sand there was a permitting noncompliance issue," Greer said. "It's a very strong word in front of this contractor. He is sitting there looking at his future permitting, his future funding, and they all told him pretty resoundingly that this needed to be done and that the deviation from the permit was unacceptable."
Greer said Underwood and Associates also agreed to put all of the plantings in. The group will need to address all of these issues before April 19, which is the end of the period for installation, to keep the project in compliance.
"So the pressure's on," Commission President Norm Bell said.
Greer said she was glad they were able to have the meeting and she hopes that in the future, the town won't have to do this with other projects.
Commissioner Tom Costigan expressed hope that it will be smooth sailing going forward.
"There's going to be good discussion after the meeting too, between the actual contractor and the compliance people," he said. "So hopefully there's communication between the two of them and any sort of problems won't rear their ugly heads again."

content:
Trappe commission approves building permit process for new Lakeside homes

 December 20, 2024 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: Veronica Fernandez-Alvarado | Section: News 
 
 528
 Words 

 Read News Document

 TRAPPE — On Tuesday evening, the Trappe Planning Commission heard and approved several new building plans for the further construction of the Lakeside at Trappe residential development.Representatives from Lennar and Brookfield, two separate construction companies, presented plans for new residential buildings to be added to the existing Lakeside development. including townhouses and more cost-effective single-family homes.
Kilber Arrington, product development manager for Lennar, said he manages all the architectural efforts for Lennar's Maryland division, which also spans into Delaware and parts of Pennsylvania. Arrington said the Lennar team looks forward to starting its new development plans with the town.
"We're excited to come down here to Trappe," Arrington said. "We've been looking for places to put our product in and let it get to market, and we think that this is a really good place for this product to succeed. What we introduced were a total of seven single-family homes and two townhomes."
In his presentation, Arrington said the single-family homes range in square footage from just under 1,400 square feet to just under 2,000 square feet. According to Arrington, this particular lineup is designed specifically for the "move down buyers." Arrington defined the "move down buyers" as those who want to downsize a bit from previous large homes.
Arrington said the designs also work for young families and couples who are moving out of townhomes and want to get an affordable single family home.
Next, Arrington presented the townhouses, which are three stories high and range between 1,600 square feet and 2,200 square feet. Arrington said these townhouses are designed for first-time buyers and young families.
After the presentation, the floor was open for questions and commissioners asked clarifying questions on design, color schemes and price ranges for the entry-level single family homes, which Arrington said he is reluctant to say because they are still being worked out.
Nick Higgins, production manager for Brookfield, presented designs next. He showed three product designs with two products that were "evolutions" of products already built in Lakeside. The idea of the two designs was to make them more cost effective.
Additionally, Higgins presented a third product that he described as a "huge success" for the company across the Washington, Maryland and Virginia area.
"We think it's a fantastic, esthetically very livable, and it's one of our also one of our most kind of cost-effective products that we built," Higgins said. "We thought these three products would fit really well into here to address some of the affordability concerns given the rates that have gone up significantly since the start of this project."
Commissioners asked similar questions about design of the products as they did of the other company's designs.
Robert Rauch, owner of Rauch Inc., Lakeside's developer, said his company has worked with Lennar and Brookfield to make sure that their designs and plans follow all regulations and requirements for the Lakeside properties.
"In our role, we prepare the actual building permit application package, and part of that is an extensive checklist that we go through to verify and confirm that the proposed plans are consistent with both the guidelines of the Lakeside and your (project management) plan," Rauch said.
The council unanimously approved the building permit processes for Lennar and Brookfields.

title: As pressures to increase solar mount, Caroline County examines options to hold its ground
author: AHMAD GARNETT agarnett@chespub.com
content:
As pressures to increase solar mount, Caroline County examines options to hold its ground

 December 20, 2024 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: AHMAD GARNETT agarnett@chespub.com | Section: Local News 
 
 770
 Words 

 Read News Document

 DENTON — During a discussion of solar policy Tuesday morning, the Caroline County commissioners concluded that legal action might be necessary to get the state and the county to see eye-to-eye."I don't know if there's going to be any other avenue that we're going to go except to go to court," Caroline County Commissioner Vice President Larry Porter said. "I think that's probably where we're going to end up."
These comments were made during a discussion on the Hobbs Road solar project, a 15-acre project proposed by Nexamp Solar LLC to put solar panels on a field that is no longer usable for farming. The commissioners approved a measure Tuesday that gives Nexamp the option to lease the land, which was formerly used as a landfill.
But the commissioners were clear that despite the approval of this project, their general stance on solar development in the area had not changed.
"We know there's been a lot of concern and conversation in the community about solar projects, and we want to make it clear that the Commissioners hear you," The Caroline County government stated in a Facebook post prior to the meeting.
"They do not want to see our county overrun with solar farms. However, they also have to follow state regulations that require a certain amount of land to be used for renewable energy production," the post said. "By allowing this solar project on the Hobbs Road site, the Commissioners have actually preserved 15 acres of prime agricultural land that could have been used for this project instead."
After the commissioner's vote, Porter addressed concerns voiced by residents in the comment section of the county's post.
"There's been a good amount of discussion on Facebook about our participation in this," Porter said. "We've been called sell-outs and everything else because people for some reason think that we're in favor of this. I don't think there's just been any county that's fought harder against covering farmland with solar panels than Carolina County."
THE COUNTY'S STANCEThe county has a 2,000-acre moratorium for solar development in place, which is facing pressure as the state looks to expand solar energy use in the coming years to meet 100% clean energy goals by 2040.
In the past, the commissioners have voiced concerns that solar development threatens the area's rural nature and takes available land away from agricultural practices.
Porter mentioned throughout the Tuesday meeting that farmers receive offers from solar companies in their mail weekly offering large sums of money to use their land to place solar panels.
"I think the dilemma that we find ourselves in, I know everyone has the right of the farmer to do with his land what he wants," Porter said. "When someone comes in and says, 'we're going to make you this offer, and you have an opportunity to make money on your own land.' It's very difficult for us to sit up here and say, 'No, you can't.'"
Steve Kline, president and CEO of Eastern Shore Land Conservancy, attended the meeting on Tuesday and spoke with the commissioners on a plan that Talbot and Queen Anne's counties follow that he said could be beneficial to Caroline County.
"What ESLC encourages Caroline County to adopt is a per-acre mitigation fee," Kline said. "... In Talbot, the mitigation fee is based on Maryland ag land preservation foundation fair market appraisal averages. In Queen Anne's County, the system assesses a half percent transfer tax on projects converting farmland to solar, and all of those funds are allocated for land preservation projects.
"... While both counties have adopted a different approach, both counties use substantially all of their fees on land conservation. The ESLC strongly believes the best way to protect agricultural land against all the threats it faces is permanent conservations like the ones we write," Kline said.
Del. Jeff Ghrist (R-Kent, Queen Anne's, Cecil, Caroline) made a suggestion that all nine Eastern Shore counties fight together instead of separately to get communities on board with their plans to limit solar development. This, he said, will lend itself to a better outcome when it's time for legal action.
"Talbot County is going to host a meeting with all nine counties to talk about, and I think ahead of this meeting, we need to make sure that all nine counties are sharing whatever zoning laws that you all have already passed, and hopefully intend on enforcing. If there's some consistency with a lot of our zoning, as consistent we can possibly be, it's gonna be a lot easier to enforce it. It's gotta be a lot easier to message it to the public. And if you guys do it, it'll be easier to defend in court."

title: CWDI breaks ground on Cambridge Harbor promenade
author: MAGGIE TROVATO mtrovato@chespub.com
content:
CWDI breaks ground on Cambridge Harbor promenade

 December 21, 2024 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: MAGGIE TROVATO mtrovato@chespub.com | Section: Local News 
 
 555
 Words 

 Read News Document

 CAMBRIDGE — After a tumultuous year — complete with a lawsuit and mediation with the City of Cambridge — Cambridge Waterfront Development Inc. has taken a significant step forward in bringing life to the city's waterfront.Thursday, CWDI and the Dorchester Chamber of Commerce, held a groundbreaking ceremony for the Cambridge Harbor promenade. Once complete, the project will extend the existing promenade along the wharf, next to Yacht Maintenance, so that it stretches around what is known as Lookout Point and to the Franklin Street boat ramp.
For CWDI Board Secretary-Treasurer Frank Narr, who has been involved with the Cambridge Harbor project for almost 32 years, it felt "unbelievable" to witness the ground breaking.
"You know, it's funny, 32 years ago Gov. Schaefer said we're going to get this done in three or four years," he said. "But the reality is — as political climate changes, as things like the hospital, changes in health care, things like that — you start to realize these things take time and you have to have patience."
Narr said passion has kept him involved with the project for all these years.
"I'm just passionate about making sure what we do here is right for the community," he said. "Because you only get one chance to do it right."
Although the groundbreaking was held Thursday, the work to extend the promenade has already started. Narr said CWDI expects the project to be finished by the end of June.
Once the promenade project is complete, CWDI plans to put out a request for proposals for Cambridge Harbor's developable parcels. Narr said the community will have the opportunity to offer input once CWDI has received proposals.
The ground breaking on Thursday brought together a variety of local and state representatives, including members of the Cambridge City Council.
In the last year and a half, tensions between the city and CWDI bubbled to the surface, culminating in a lawsuit filed against CWDI by the city regarding a transfer agreement. In August, the groups settled the lawsuit, with both city officials and CWDI board members expressing hopes for a stronger relationship moving forward.
During the groundbreaking, Cambridge Commission President and Mayor-elect Lajan Cephas acknowledged the hard work of CWDI's board.
"They've experienced a lot of abuse over the last couple years," she said, adding that it's important trust is rebuilt.
"So I think this is a wonderful opportunity for us to take the next step forward," she said about the promenade. "The best step forward."
CWDI Board President Angie Hengst said the board hopes this promenade will be enjoyed by the entire community and "will be just the beginning of creating a waterfront area and experience that is accessible to all."
Dorchester County Council President Lenny Pfeffer called Thursday "a great day" for the community.
"This is a clear canvas now that we're going to start building up from," he said. "And this is a great project to start with."
Chesapeake Conservancy's President and CEO Joel Dunn, called the day "bittersweet." He said it's his second to last day at the Chesapeake Conservancy, which is a project partner of Cambridge Harbor.
"I've helped create a national wildlife refuge, a national park, two national monuments, expand Blackwater Refuge, create local parks, state parks," Dunn said about his time with the organization. "But I've got to tell you, this is one of my favorite parks that I've ever been a part of."

title: Oxford's next town manager faces controversies on western shore
author: Maggie Trovato
content:
Oxford's next town manager faces controversies on western shore

 December 21, 2024 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: Maggie Trovato | Section: Local News 
 
 835
 Words 

 Read News Document

 OXFORD — As Oxford prepares to welcome Holly Wahl as its next town manager, controversy is swirling in the town where she was previously employed.Wahl announced her resignation as Chesapeake Beach's town administrator on Dec. 4, amid some turmoil in the western shore town.
Bruce Wahl, who had served as mayor of Chesapeake Beach from 2008 to 2016, ran for the position again earlier this year and was elected mayor on Nov. 5.
Prior to Election Day, in social media posts, Bruce Wahl said that if elected, the "persecution of town citizens" by "the current town administration will completely cease."
His comments were related to complaints from residents who claimed their water and sewer bills have recently risen dramatically.
Holly Wahl and Bruce Wahl are not related.
In interviews with the Star Democrat on Friday, the Commissioners of Oxford said they were aware of and not concerned about the controversy in Chesapeake Beach.
"We're confident that we hired the right person," Oxford Commission President Norm Bell said. "We were delighted to talk to her. We're very comfortable in her experiences and how they can help the town. And that's what we based the decision (on)."
Bell said his understanding of the water and sewer bill issue is that people weren't paying annual water and sewer bill connection fees. He said that when Wahl took on her position in Chesapeake Beach, she saw that as a problem and made sure the town started collecting that money.
During a Chesapeake Beach Town Council work session in early September, Wahl said audits revealed "significant underpayment of connection fees" by commercial properties and said the delinquent payments amounted to a $6 million loss to the town.
In an email, Wahl told the Star Democrat: "My record of contributions to the Town of Chesapeake Beach, MD, is publicly available on the Town's website, along with meeting minutes and recordings. I am very much looking forward to working with the Commissioners, staff, citizens, and businesses of the Town of Oxford."
Oxford Commissioner Katrina Greer said Friday that Wahl is a "highly qualified and ethical manager" who was "wringing out corruption" in the connection fees issue.
"And it only made me feel stronger about hiring her," Greer said.
Oxford Commissioner Tom Costigan said Wahl was carefully vetted by the hiring search firm Baker Tilly. He said the information coming out about Wahl is not something the commissioners are worried about.
"We interviewed a lot of candidates," he said. "We narrowed it down to four. She was by far the strongest of the four, and we are optimistic about her future performance here in Oxford."
Oxford hired Baker Tilly to do the search after the town announced the hire of — and then three days later announced they would be parting ways with — Michael Calvert as the next town manager.
Shortly after the news of Calvert's hire, some Oxford residents expressed concerns about the town's candidate vetting process. The week the town announced the decision to part ways with Calvert, Peggy Edwards, a former council member from the town where Calvert was previously employed, told the Star Democrat she resigned from the council due to issues with Calvert and the city's mayor. She said that when Calvert was in the position, there was a lack of transparency and mismanagement of money.
SEVERANCE PACKAGE CONCERNS
On the same day Wahl announced her resignation, the outgoing mayor and the Chesapeake Beach Town Council met for what was labeled an "emergency meeting" to consider for approval of an "emergency ordinance" approving a severance package for Wahl. The town's previous Mayor Pat "Irish" Mahoney said the severance package was reasonable.
The ordinance, which was unanimously approved by the current council, gives Wahl a severance of six months' salary and all accrued vacation time. Southern Maryland News, which is owned and operated by the same company as the Star Democrat, has filed a Freedom of Information Act request for the dollar amount of Wahl's compensation package.
The approved ordinance states that Wahl will receive the compensation "in a lump sum with one payment paid prior to Dec. 18, 2024, based upon her wage rate on the date of her resignation."
In addition to the compensation, the ordinance stipulates that "the town agrees to hold Holly Wahl harmless in any future actions including all indemnification and attorneys' fees for any action that may be pursued against her."
During the public comment portion of the Dec. 4 meeting, a few citizens spoke out against the pending action. Daniel Duvall, who lost the race for a Chesapeake Beach Town Council seat by three votes, said approving a severance package "is not an emergency" and was "a questionable use of taxpayer funds."
Another Chesapeake Beach resident, Deborah Buckingham, reiterated the ordinance did not "meet the criteria of an emergency." She added, "Holly Wahl doesn't deserve any severance."
There was plenty of praise for the town administrator at the meeting, too.
"She's fantastic. I've never seen so much communication in the last eight years," Randy Getman, the town's election administrator, said. "I have no issue with Bruce Wahl wanting to pick his own town administrator."

 The Town of Greensboro conducted its Town Council meeting on Thursday via Zoom discussing many issues on the agenda, as well as some raise by members of the audience.A Greensboro resident, who did not identify herself during the meeting, suggested a YouTube channel be created for residents who can't attend the Town Council meetings, which at this time are only offered online via Zoom call. title: Emergency bill drafted for cannabis, alcohol tax dollars
author: AHMAD GARNETT agarnett@chespub.com
content:
Emergency bill drafted for cannabis, alcohol tax dollars

 December 24, 2024 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: AHMAD GARNETT agarnett@chespub.com | Section: Local News 
 
 296
 Words 

 Read News Document

 DENTON — The Caroline County Commissioners moved an emergency bill on for its third reading Tuesday to establish the Caroline County Community Reinvestment and Repair Fund.The tax sales of alcoholic beverages and cannabis will go to the fund, which will benefit low-income communities in Caroline county.
The emergency bill is being proposed by the county to comply with the Maryland Alcoholic Beverages and Cannabis Article, which allows the sales tax of these items to be used for the county's benefit. The state mandated each county create its own version of this fund.
According to the draft bill, "The revenue paid into the CCCRRF shall be used only for funding community-based initiatives intended to benefit low-income communities, and community-based initiatives that serve disproportionately impacted areas, as defined in 36-101 of the Alcoholic Beverages and Cannabis Article of the State Code, and any related administrative expenses."
The Caroline County Commissioners are hoping to have exact answers for how this funding will be allocated before the third and final reading of the bill Jan. 7.
"An Allegheny County commissioner said that it was to be self-determined," Caroline County Commission Vice President Larry Porter said about allocating funds. "I think our decision is that we don't like doing self-determined things that might come back. So I would suggest that we either wait for confirmation on what areas or what zip codes the money can be spent, or we get confirmation verifying that it's self-determined and there will be no repercussions on where we spend the money."
The emergency bill's third reading and potential enactment will take place in a closed meeting Jan. 7. As an emergency bill, the bill would become effective on the day of enactment.
Public comments or concerns regarding the emergency bill should be emailed to info@caroline.org by Jan. 1 for review.
