title: Legislators, local officials differ on unhoused individuals bill
author: Konner Metz
content:
Legislators, local officials differ on unhoused individuals bill

 February 19, 2025 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: Konner Metz | Section: Local News 
 
 686
 Words 

 Read News Document

 EASTON — A bill filed in Annapolis to enshrine rights for homeless individuals is drawing differing opinions from advocates and local officials.House Bill 487, and its paired Senate Bill 484, would protect the ability of homeless individuals to partake in "life-sustaining activities" such as sleeping, eating or drinking, in public places so long as traffic is not obstructed.
If passed, any civil or criminal punishment against an unhoused individual who is on public land without an "adequate alternative indoor" space would be considered cruel and unusual punishment.
According to the U.S. Department of Housing and Urban Development's most recent data, Maryland's homeless population in 2023 was 5,865 individuals, both sheltered and unsheltered.
Del. Bernice Mireku North (D-Montgomery), the bill's sponsor, and other advocates say the proposed legislation comes in response to a Supreme Court decision last June that ruled it was not cruel and unusual punishment for local governments to civilly and criminally penalize homeless people for setting up encampments on public land.
Mireku-North wrote in a statement to The Star Democrat that the proposed bill has "brought to light the heart-led efforts" of local governments to support unhoused individuals. An emphasis of the bill is to prevent immediate arrests, she said.
"At a minimum, we are asking law enforcement to prioritize inquiring whether an alternative indoor space exists for unhoused people engaging in life-sustaining activities before resorting to arrest," Mireku-North wrote.
The delegate said legislators are "committed" to working with local officials and stakeholders on the bill.
Allie Post, director of development and communications for The Women's Law Center of Maryland, said the bill would be a measure in which the state "(stands) up for folks proactively" following the June Supreme Court ruling.
"Especially for survivors (of domestic violence) and survivors of color, homelessness is often a price of leaving an abuser," Post said. "And folks who have less financial means and less flexibility in those means are really put between a rock and a hard place, and this is an opportunity for Maryland to step up and start taking seriously the homelessness problem that we have."
While advocates say it's a needed step forward in the path to address Maryland's homelessness crisis, some Easton and Talbot County officials say the bill is endangering the efforts already being taken.
Talbot County Sheriff Joe Gamble and the Sheriff's Office released a video on Facebook last month depicting what they believe a potential encounter could look like with a homeless individual if the bill is passed.
"If these were to pass, we could have homeless encampments in Idlewild Park, (the) courthouse," Gamble said in a separate video the department shared. " … You literally could set up a tent on the 50-yard-line at Easton High School before an Easton football game and call it your home, and we would not be able to move those people."
Gamble said the homelessness issue is serious in Talbot County and that he's not against addressing it. However, he believes the bill as written will strip away authority of locally elected officials.
"They will not be able to follow the zoning laws that they've put into place to make downtown Easton the place it is, or downtown St. Michaels or downtown Oxford to be those nice places that people want to come to visit and spend their hard-earned money," Gamble said in an interview. "They will have absolutely no control over it."
Easton Mayor Megan Cook addressed the Senate Judicial Proceedings Committee in a Feb. 5 letter opposing the bill.
Cook wrote that the bill "would supersede local ordinance and policies that have been carefully crafted to address the needs of both unhoused individuals and the broader community."
"By prohibiting local and state officials from enforcing reasonable regulations on the use of public spaces, the bill could lead to unintended consequences that compromise public safety, hinder economic development, and create significant enforcement challenges," Cook wrote.
In her letter, Cook asked legislators to instead focus on policies that would provide funding for housing assistance, mental health and job programs.
"Our community is committed to addressing homelessness with dignity and care—through outreach, support services, and housing initiatives—while also ensuring that public spaces remain accessible and safe for all," Cook wrote.

title: Demolition begins as developers wait for Easton Crossing project approval
author: Maggie Trovato
content:
Demolition begins as developers wait for Easton Crossing project approval

 February 19, 2025 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: Maggie Trovato | Section: Local News 
 
 442
 Words 

 Read News Document

 EASTON — Demolition of the abandoned silos and storage buildings on Brookletts Avenue is underway.The tearing down of the former Perdue AgriBusiness operation is one step in The Arc Central Chesapeake Region's plan to build Easton Crossing, a mixed-use development, on about 6.29 acres between Brookletts Avenue and South Street.
Ross Benincasa, who is senior vice president of community development at Chesapeake Community Development, a subsidiary of The Arc Central Chesapeake Region, said the demolition will take six months. He said some of the material from the silos will be salvaged for potential future use.
Although demolition has begun, the project still requires site plan approval from the Easton Planning Commission. It is scheduled to go before the Planning Commission on Thursday. Following site plan approval, the project will need standard grading and building permits.
Easton resident Maury Schlesinger was walking his dog Monday when he noticed demolition was underway. Although he has some concerns with future plans for the site, Schlesinger said he thinks the demolition is "appropriate."
"Something has to happen there," he said.
According to the draft site plan for Easton Crossing, if approved, the development would create 123 multi-family units, including 29 affordable apartments priced below the market rate. It would also bring parking, stormwater management and landscaping to the property.
The property would have six buildings, with some buildings that include commercial spaces. The first building, which would have 15 units, is expected to open in December 2027 if the plan is approved.
Benincasa said project plans "emphasize public green spaces."
"We want the community as well as our tenants to enjoy the space, which is why nearly 30% of the property will be open public space," he said.
According to Planning Commission documents, town staff would like the developers to address scale and consistency concerns with one of the proposed buildings.
Schlesinger also has concerns with that building. He said it would bring too much density to one area of the property.
"I think it needs to be relooked at," he said.
Schlesinger brought up concerns with traffic and the need for traffic improvements.
"I'm not opposed to a redevelopment project on that site, and I think that there's some really good stuff they're trying to do here," he said. "It just could be moved from being a good project to a really great project that the town could be really proud of and could show off as good, small-town urban redevelopment."
Benincasa said community feedback has been helpful. He said feedback helped the developers define what types of units are wanted in the area as well as determine which materials are "more reflective" of the town's historic architecture.
Schlesinger said he hopes the Planning Commission "does the right thing."

title: Easton OKs outdoor party at Hummingbird Inn for Pride Festival weekend
author: Konner Metz
content:
Easton OKs outdoor party at Hummingbird Inn for Pride Festival weekend

 February 20, 2025 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: Konner Metz | Section: Local News 
 
 627
 Words 

 Read News Document

 EASTON — The Town Council approved its first extension of Easton's new noise ordinance, granting the Hummingbird Inn permission to host an outdoor dance party the night after the Delmarva Pride Festival this summer.A zoning certificate was passed by councilmembers in a 3-1 vote during a Monday meeting. Ward 1 Councilmember Maureen Curry was absent from the meeting.
The exception will allow the Hummingbird Inn to host a party June 14 until 11:30 p.m., a 90-minute extension of the town's normal limit for outdoor music.
The 10 p.m. cutoff was established last July following resident concerns of music at night. The council instituted a noise ordinance, which required businesses or groups seek special approval to play amplified outdoor music past 10 p.m.
Eric Levinson, owner of the Hummingbird Inn, said he was happy and relieved when the council approved the inn's zoning certificate.
"What I appreciated was the fact that they didn't just assume it was going to be a problem and deny it," Levinson said in an interview, "and that they said, 'Let's see how it goes. And then if there's a problem, then we'll deal with it at that time.'"
Before Monday's Town Council meeting, Levinson gained signatures from surrounding neighbors in support of the extended dance party. Last year, around 70 people attended. Easton police noted no complaints were made.
Levinson expects 100 to 120 people at the event this year. The later end time will allow for a better atmosphere, he said.
"The problem was at that time of year it doesn't really get dark until later, so we had people hanging around and stuff, but nobody was actually doing anything until it was dark," Levinson said of 2024's party. "It just didn't set the right mood."
Monday, councilmembers thanked Levinson for reaching out to neighbors well in advance. However, Ward 3 Councilmember David Montgomery voted against the extension.
Montgomery said approving the request would set a "very dangerous precedent," and that there are many other one-time events that could seek similar exemptions.
"I don't see how to differentiate this request for a special exemption from one that might come from the Tidewater Inn if they have a couple with 100 guests, a man and woman who are being married and they want to have Christian gospel music until 11:30 at night," Montgomery said. "I think we would have to approve that request equally well."
Ward 2 Councilmember Don Abbatiello, who voted in favor, acknowledged Montgomery's concerns as valid. But he said the dance party being an annual event versus a weekly one made a difference in his opinion.
"I was going to give them the benefit of the doubt with the idea that if there are complaints … then I'm fine with not approving it in the future," Abbatiello added.
Ward 4 Councilmember the Rev. Elmer Davis said he's not "overly concerned," though this approval will set a precedent and that the town will be monitoring if complaints are made.
Levinson said Town Council President Frank Gunsallus helped the business navigate the request for the extension, a first for the town as well. Gunsallus made the motion for its approval Monday.
"Given everything that you've done to go through this the right way and do your due diligence, and the fact that this is a once-a-year thing, I think that it is completely acceptable," Gunsallus said.
Considering tense discussions and split votes surrounding the Delmarva Pride Festival and its place in Easton in recent years, Levinson says he's glad the town is following through on its promises to be both inclusive and neighborly.
"It is good to see that they're following that, standing by that, and putting their own personal preferences or opinions aside," Levinson said. "Because that's the way it should be. It's not based on what they like or dislike. It's what's good for the community."

title: ESLC talks land values at Dorchester County Council meeting
author: Maggie Trovato
content:
ESLC talks land values at Dorchester County Council meeting

 February 20, 2025 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: Maggie Trovato | Section: Local News 
 
 608
 Words 

 Read News Document

 CAMBRIDGE — When it comes to acreage and land value, Dorchester County is expected to be one of the most affected counties by sea level rise and storm surge in the year 2100, according to the Eastern Shore Land Conservancy.During a Dorchester County Council meeting Feb. 18, Eastern Shore Land Conservancy Land Use and Policy Director Owen Bailey presented data on land value throughout the Eastern Shore. Bailey said the data was acquired with the help of Urban3.
The land trust estimates that an average of three feet of sea level rise in 2100 would mean the loss of 270,000 acres of the Eastern Shore and $2 billion in property tax values.
"And then when you add in storm surge, then that really puts into perspective the financial distress that our communities are going to face in the future with the loss of properties and property tax revenues," Bailey said.
After Bailey showed a map that accounted for storm surge in 2100, County Council President Lenny Pfeffer pointed out that more than half of Dorchester County's land is projected to be gone.
Bailey said Cambridge alone is projected to lose 280 acres and $63 million in value by 2100.
Throughout his presentation, Bailey advocated for concentrated development on the Shore to increase property value. At the same time, he spoke about the importance of maintaining the value that could be loss to sea level rise.
Bailey said the efficiency of land use can be measured by looking at value per acre.
"You take the appraised value of each parcel and you divide it by how many acres it sits on," he said.
When the Eastern Shore Land Conservancy applied this to the Eastern Shore, it noticed historic downtowns are "much more productive than the more suburban, car-focused development" that has been popular since the 1950s. This means that those downtowns, which often are more vulnerable to sea level rise, bring in more property tax revenue per acre than more sprawling areas of the Eastern Shore.
Bailey said that before the Bay Bridge was built in 1952, only 10,000 acres of land — valued at approximately $560,000 per acre — had been developed on the Shore. An additional 163,000 has been developed at less than half of that value since.
With the additional developed land, there has been a need for more sprawling infrastructure, he said.
"So we've built all this infrastructure," Bailey said. "But we haven't really built the value to help us with the maintenance of that infrastructure, which is why a lot of our jurisdictions, pretty much all of our jurisdictions, are struggling with how to keep up with that kind of maintenance."
Bailey said many historic communities on the Shore, which bring more value per acre, are built on waterfronts, meaning sea level rise will most likely affect them.
"So we're encouraging every town to think about how are you going to account for that," he said. "How can you either move that property, protect it or replace that value somewhere else in our community?"
Along with concentrating development, Bailey recommended the county look at zoning restricting the county from allowing value to grow.
"This is something we're encouraging every jurisdiction to take a look at," he said. "It's not our job to tell you what to do. We just want to provide the data and perspective. ... Use your land wisely."
At the end of the presentation Dorchester County Council Vice President Mike Detmer asked if the land trust had any recommendations specific to Dorchester County zoning ordinances.
Bailey said they have been focusing on municipalities, looking at zoning in historic districts.
"And how can we ease up on that zoning just to allow that historic pattern to continue," he said.

title: Planning Commission approves majority of 123-unit Easton Crossing development
author: Konner Metz
content:
Planning Commission approves majority of 123-unit Easton Crossing development

 February 22, 2025 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: Konner Metz | Section: Local News 
 
 641
 Words 

 Read News Document

 EASTON — A mixed-use project on Brookletts Avenue at the site of the former Perdue AgriBusiness operation received a stamp of approval, though not a full one.The Easton Planning Commission voted Thursday to approve 67 of the 123 units planned for Easton Crossing, a joint commercial and residential development. But Building 409, the project's largest structure, and the 56 units that come along with it are still under consideration.
Commission members and residents alike expressed concerns about the five-story building that includes around 10,000 square feet of retail space. Developers from The Arc Central Chesapeake Region, the project's developer, agreed to work on alternative options for the unapproved building and return to the commission at a future date.
Largely, the commission applauded developers for their advanced outreach to the community, as well as what they called an attractive project aimed at addressing Easton's lack of affordable housing.
"I love the project," commission chair Philip Toussaint said. "I think the positive aspects of it far outweigh any negative aspects. We have to take that into account when we're making a decision."
Toussaint joined vice chair Michael Ports, William Ryall and Victoria McAndrews in approving the project with the exception of Building 409. Thomas Klein was the sole vote against, citing his concerns that the plan's 217 off-street parking spots won't suffice once the units are occupied and commercial tenants move in.
The proposal noted 49 on-street parking spaces along Brookletts Avenue are mostly unused right now and would provide additional parking once renters and businesses move into Easton Crossing.
Klein said only 217 dedicated spaces for a 229-bedroom development did not seem sufficient, particularly if the backup plan is parking on Brookletts.
"If people from the development start to go and park in those areas, the tenants that live there now are not going to have any place to park," Klein said.
Ross Benincasa, senior vice president of Chesapeake Community Development, presented the site plan at Thursday's meeting. It calls for 30% of the rental units to be affordably priced, with others at workforce and market-rate levels.
Demolition of the Perdue grain bins and storage buildings currently on the lot began this month. Apartments are expected to be available beginning in 2027.
Speaking to the commission Thursday, Benincasa said the nonprofit developers felt a "necessary duty" to make a dent in Easton's affordable housing crisis with the infill project.
"We really felt kind of a need to make sure that if this was going to be developed, that we thought of it more inclusively," Benincasa said, "and more geared around making sure there was housing provided for all income levels, including people with disabilities."
BLENDING INWhile many complimented the project's cohesion with the intersecting Rails to Trails, worries centered around the fact that the structures don't integrate into the neighboring historic community.
Talbot County Council Member Lynn Mielke, speaking for herself and not the council, said the project is "incompatible" and its architecture ignores the nearby residential buildings.
Toussaint pushed Benincasa on if it was appropriate for the project to face away from The Hill, one of the first free African American neighborhoods in the country. The commission chair said that's been a significant source of public input.
"It appears to me that you've turned your back on the existing community, The Hill district," Toussaint said. "And you focus on Rails to Trails, and did a wonderful job of that."
Benincasa said The Arc doesn't own a lot of land in The Hill community to be able to integrate with it and that he disagrees with sentiments that the project doesn't fit into the surrounding fabric.
"We are not necessarily in that community here, and I would go as far to say as I think that doing duplexes here or mimicking that in some way would kind of really negatively offset what we could do in terms of usable units," Benincasa said. "It's never been a serious consideration."

title: Tensions rise as Cambridge City Council discusses HR position
author: MAGGIE TROVATO mtrovato@chespub.com
content:
Tensions rise as Cambridge City Council discusses HR position

 February 26, 2025 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: MAGGIE TROVATO mtrovato@chespub.com | Section: Local News 
 
 622
 Words

 CAMBRIDGE — A motion to adopt a job description for the addition of a human resource generalist position to City of Cambridge staff resulted in significant discussion and caused some tension at a Cambridge City Council meeting Feb. 24.During the meeting, City Manager Glenn Steckman recommended creating the additional staff position. He said there is currently only one employee in the department who has "a tremendous amount of responsibility under her job title."
Steckman said that the city advertised for the position in house and currently has a candidate within city staff. The position would require a budget amendment and could be discussed further at an upcoming meeting, he said.
Commission President Sputty Cephas said he would like to see the process started sooner rather than later and made a motion to adopt a job description for the role.
The motion was ultimately voted down, with Cephas voting for it, Commissioner Shay Lewis-Sisco abstaining from the vote and the three remaining commissioners voting against the motion.
During discussion, Lewis-Sisco said she had concerns with the city's hiring process. At the end of the meeting she said she abstained from the vote not because she doesn't understand why the council needed to take an action when the city seems to have started the hiring process.
Commissioner Brian Roche, who voted against the motion, said he didn't think the city's vision moving forward was "articulated well." He said he thinks the city needs a more comprehensive view of how human resources should function and should look for ways to set the director of administrative services up for better success.
Commissioner Frank Stout said he voted against the motion because he wasn't prepared to make a decision. He said his vote was not because he was opposed to the idea.
"I was just a little taken back, I think, for something that does require a budget amendment of this nature," he said.
During discussion, Steckman said the budget amendment would only be for three and a half months of salary and said he expects the city will have a "substantial" surplus this fiscal year.
Cephas, who said the request had been five years in the making, said by voting no, a commissioner is saying they are against the idea. He called for the commissioners to display more support of city departments.
"If (city staff) presents something to us, we have a responsibility to support them as long as it makes sense," he said. "And to not support this tonight, yeah, that's a problem."
As commissioners made comments on the issue at the end of the meeting, Steckman interjected to say his intention was to introduce the position. He said he was planning on bringing a formal resolution to a later meeting.
"A little discussion kind of got a little out of control tonight," he said. "There is a process that I have, and we will continue that process forward."
Mayor Lajan Cephas cut discussion short, saying it was already approaching 8:46 p.m. and talking about the issue "over and over again" wasn't getting the council anywhere. When Commissioner Frank Stout tried to talk, she said she had closed discussion and the commissioners would need to take a vote.
"It's getting late, right?" Cephas said. "If this fails and you have additional questions, you can make an appointment with the city manager and go to the city manager's office."
Before the meeting was adjourned, Lajan Cephas asked that everyone be patient as the new group of commissioners settles in and finds its stride. The commissioners were sworn into their seats in January. Two of the five commissioners have no prior experience on the council, and one commissioner, Stout, served as a Cambridge commissioner from 2008 through 2012.
This article has been updated to correctly state the experience of the the commissioners.

title: Caroline County holds first FY26 budget workshop
author: AHMAD GARNETT agarnett@chespub.com
content:
Caroline County holds first FY26 budget workshop

 February 26, 2025 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: AHMAD GARNETT agarnett@chespub.com | Section: News 
 
 480
 Words 

 Read News Document

 DENTON — On Tuesday, the Caroline County Commissioners held their fiscal year 2026 budget roundtable with all internal and external county agencies.While agencies need more money for salary raises and equipment repairs and replacements, the commissioners are facing tight budget constraints.
At the Caroline County Commissioners meeting last week, the draft FY 2026 budget presented showed Caroline County could be facing around a $900,000 shortfall this budget season.
Caroline County Deputy Administrator Daniel Fox presented projected operating requests and revenues for the upcoming fiscal year during the last week's meeting.
Fox acknowledged while the entire budget is fluid, the current requests total $79.7 million and the revenues total $78.8 million, up from the fiscal year 2024 operating budget, which was balanced at $72.3 million.
Some of those fluid items include income tax cuts proposed by Gov. Wes Moore and potential cuts to The Blueprint for Maryland's Future, the state's education funding initiative.
The County Commissioners are concerned that the Blueprint cuts will leave the county in a bad financial predicament.
"There is no leadership at the top. There no leadership in the state," Commission Vice President Larry Porter said Tuesday. "We don't have anyone who is willing to stand up and say this Blueprint policy is a mistake."
On Tuesday, all internal and external county agencies presented their FY26 budget requests.
"We just want to take input from from all the agencies that are asking here straight from them," Commission President Travis Breeding said. "Learn what their priorities are ... to help us educate ourselves and make informed decisions on what they need."
The majority of the agencies experienced some of the same issues. Their fiscal year budgets were rising for multiple reasons.
Employee pay, overtime, and general equipment and technology updates were needed for many agencies.
"One of biggest challenges is hiring and retaining employees. It's getting increasingly difficult for us," Executive Director of Caroline County Public Library Jonah Owens said. "Queen Anne's County typically offers salaries 20 to 25% above ours, Anne Arundel County sometimes 50 to 100% higher salaries than what we offer for similar positions. We have become a farm team, as have all our agencies have."
For many agencies, every five to 10 years, equipment needs upgrades. Some upgrades fall on this fiscal year. Others will come in the following years.
But facing a budget shortfall, the commissioners are aware of potential cuts they will have to make and how honoring these requests from agencies will be difficult.
"We can't go out and and find any more money," Breeding said. "Our tax rates are as high, I think, as as we feel comfortable having them. I don't want to entertain any rate increases.
"I think the only thing we can do is search for efficiencies inside our existing budget and make sure we spend it as efficiently as we can, and prioritize spending in the areas that actually need additional funding."
Star Democrat Reporter Konner Metz contributed to this report.

content:
Ghrist, Caroline County push bill allowing small businesses and non-profits to serve liquor

 February 26, 2025 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 DENTON — On Del. Jefferson Ghrist (R-Kent, Queen Anne's, Cecil, Caroline) list of priorities for the 2025 Maryland General Assembly is a bill aimed at making alcohol more available to rural event venues in Caroline County."Each year our County Delegation is proud to work closely with the Caroline County Government to bring their legislative requests to the General Assembly," Ghrist stated in a press release.
This year, the Caroline County Government requested HB 1335, a delegation bill to create a beer, wine and liquor license for rural special event venues.
According to Caroline County Commissioner President Travis Breeding, the proposed bill will allow two things. The proposed bill will expand the venue license to nonprofit organizations to allow those nonprofit organizations the opportunity to serve beer, wine and liquor on their properties. It will also extend that opportunity to event venues that would want to get that license if they are properly zoned to hold events.
"Right now, you could go and get a license to serve for one event," Breeding said. "The problem that these nonprofits are running into at the end of each one of those events, they have to dispose of any leftover alcohol.
"It's a very it's a tough projection to make when you organize these events, or you plan them, because you don't want to run out. So this would give them ability, these nonprofits, the ability to lock up any excess alcohol and store it until the next event that they would have."
According to Breeding, this proposed bill is important because it gives local businesses and nonprofit organizations a chance to flow in another revenue stream.
"Right now, the event venues would have to hire a alcohol catering company," Breeding said, "which would come in and cater the event essentially. We don't have anybody that I'm aware of, or we don't have many in-county businesses that provide that service, so this would be an opportunity to allow local businesses to fill that that role, give them another revenue stream to help make their business ventures viable and more profitable."

title: Oxford residents share thoughts on who should be allowed to vote in town elections
author: Maggie Trovato
content:
Oxford residents share thoughts on who should be allowed to vote in town elections

 February 27, 2025 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: Maggie Trovato | Section: Local News 
 
 731
 Words 

 Read News Document

 OXFORD — At a Commissioners of Oxford public hearing Tuesday evening, it all boiled down to the question of who should have the right to vote in town elections.The public hearing was held for a resolution that would amend the town's charter to clarify a person must register with the Talbot County Board of Elections to qualify as a voter in the town. This means a resident would not be able to vote in Oxford town elections if they aren't registered with the county board.
The commissioners opted not to vote on the resolution during the meeting.
"Listening to this conversation, it seems like we're putting the cart before the horse," Resident Warren Davis said during the public hearing. "What we really want to do is figure out who we want to vote in our elections."
Oxford Town Attorney Lyndsey Ryan said registering with the Talbot County Board of Elections means an Oxford resident is declaring their home in Oxford as their domicile, or primary residence. She said that when a person registers in Talbot County, they are removed from any voting registry they may have been on elsewhere.
Currently, the town charter states a person should register in the town office. The charter says it is the duty of Oxford's Election Board to keep registration lists up to date.
When it comes to eligibility, the charter states a person is able to vote if they are a U.S. citizen, are at least 18 and have resided in the town for at least 30 days prior to any town election.
At the outset of the public hearing, Ryan said the commissioners could choose to take a different path than the resolution presented.
Commissioner Katrina Greer brought up her concern that the list of registered voters in Talbot County is not always updated.
"As residents in a very small town, I know who lives here, I know who died this year," she said. "And so it's much easier for our own board of elections to clean up those voter logs."
Residents who spoke at the public hearing brought up scenarios and shared thoughts on who should and shouldn't be able to vote in town elections.
After confirming Oxford commissioners serve all proprietors and renters in town, Dan Kordell said anyone who owns or rents property in town should have a say in who is serving them.
"It's about representation," he said.
Jim Wilcox asked the commissioners to focus on who should vote based on "who has skin in the game." He said property owners and people with leases for more than 30 days should be able to vote in town elections.
"I would say somebody who has maybe a six-month lease," he said. "Something that shows a substantial term commitment to Oxford rather than just landing here for 30 days."
Warren Davis brought up that there are multiple residents in town with more than one residence. He included himself in the category, saying he usually goes to Maine in the summer.
"Should I be allowed to vote in Oxford because I'm not here for 30 days before the election?" he asked.
Multiple residents spoke to the issue of whether residents away at college should be able to vote in town elections. David Donovan said he doesn't think these students should be able to vote in town elections.
"They don't have any skin in the game," he said. "They don't have any intention to move back here. ... So I don't think those people should be allowed to vote here."
Chris Maynard said that could be considered disenfranchisement.
"We should keep in mind that 18-year-olds, we're referring to them as children, but they're really adults," she said, later adding, "It's not that the parents drive them over to the voting place and tell them what to do."
Donovan said he has an alternative to the town's proposed resolution. He proposed the town instead amend the voting eligibility section in the charter to say that voters should be physically present in their Oxford residence 30 days prior to the election unless they are absent due to vacation or circumstances beyond their control.
He said residents absent from town for those 30 days due to "voluntary enrollment in any education program" should not be considered eligible to vote.
Donovan said the town should add an application for absentee voting that requires absentee voters to affirm they are eligible to vote.
After the public hearing, the commissioners agreed to schedule a work session to discuss the issue further.

title: Oxford hires full-time town clerk, seeks treasurer
author: Maggie Trovato

Oxford hires full-time town clerk, seeks treasurer

 February 27, 2025 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: Maggie Trovato | Section: Local News 
 
 362
 Words

 OXFORD — The Town of Oxford has a new full-time employee.During a Commissioners of Oxford meeting Tuesday, Town Manager Holly Wahl announced the addition of Ashley Samonisky as town clerk. Wahl said Samonisky has worked with the town on a temporary basis since November, "a time when the town was significantly backlogged on permit applications," Wahl said.
"And she's done a great job of cleaning up that process and helping support those on the Planning Commission and the Historic Commission," she said. "And she's also worked very closely with me as a town manager in terms of working through the town's operational processes."
Samonisky will now serve in the town clerk position full time.
"In this capacity, Ashley will continue to coordinate permit applications, she will continue to provide support to the Historic Commission and the Planning Commission, and she will now also provide support to the commissioners," Wahl said.
In the announcement, Wahl said Samonisky has more than 10 years of experience at the federal, state and local level — as well as with private and nonprofit agencies — in continuity of operations, hazard mitigation, emergency management, stakeholder engagement, communications, social media and public outreach.
"So we're very, very happy to have Ashley," Wahl said.
With the move to hire Samonisky as town clerk, the town is separating the previous position of clerk-treasurer in two. Later in the meeting, the commissioners voted unanimously to post a job description for the role of town treasurer.
During a meeting on Feb. 19, Commission President Norm Bell said Vickie Sharp, who had been the town's clerk-treasurer since April, was "no longer employed" by the town "due to violations of some policies."
Sharp told the Star Democrat on Feb. 20 that she did not wish to comment, and Wahl told the Star Democrat the same day that she could not provide more information about why the position was open.
Tuesday, Wahl called the commissioners' move to separate the clerk and treasurer functions "really important."
"They are two very separate functions," she said. "And so we need to be sure that we're tracking our record keeping properly. And Ashley will do that as the clerk in support of all the governmental functions of the town."

title: Residents challenge solar project over zoning, health risks
author: WILL BONTRAGER wbontrager@chespub.com
content:
Residents challenge solar project over zoning, health risks

 February 28, 2025 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: WILL BONTRAGER wbontrager@chespub.com | Section: Local News 
 
 548
 Words 

 Read News Document

 The Maryland Public Service Commission heard residents' concerns Tuesday over a proposed community solar project on 41 acres of a 199-acre property at 10066 Peacock Corner Road in Millington, owned by David Chance.The project, designated TPE MD KE51, is being developed by Turning Point Energy (TPE), a renewable energy firm that has spearheaded several solar initiatives in Maryland, including a second proposal in Kennedyville. According to company information, Turning Point focuses on sustainable, ground-mounted solar projects designed to expand clean energy access in the region.
More than a dozen residents gathered at Galena Elementary School at 7 p.m. for the PSC hearing, moderated by Chief Public Utility Law Judge Chuck McLean. In addition to Turning Point representatives, legal counsel, and project managers, officials from the Maryland Department of Natural Resources, Kent County Attorney Tom Yeager and Planning, Housing and Zoning deputy Carla Gerber were in attendance.
After brief introductions by Turning Point's team, Yeager and Gerber outlined the county's position. Yeager noted that local zoning restricts solar projects in this agriculture district to five acres and contended that Turning Point should have applied for a special exception. Project manager Frances Yuhas said the company was aware of the five‐acre limit for utility-scale solar in the district and chose not to seek an exception, adding that final approval lies with the Public Service Commission under state preemption.
Resident Darryl Calloway expressed his concern, saying, "I would love someone to address the health concerns I have such as microwaves. Anyone who lives near these arrays, what happens to them?"
Certified solar thermal engineer Dick Durham raised additional issues about panel efficiency and recycling challenges, noting that the panels contain materials such as lead and cadmium telluride. He also warned that pending legislation, Senate Bill 0931, could reshape land-use controls in ways reminiscent of eminent domain.
When asked about the origin of the panels, Yuhas said production could occur in the United States but noted that international manufacturing — including in Mexico or China —remains a possibility. Maryland Department of Natural Resources official Ginny Rogers addressed environmental risk concerns, stating, "From what we see there is no risk at all involved," and outlined plans to plant native, pollinator-friendly ground cover to boost biodiversity.
Kennedyville resident Judi Gifford questioned the economic benefits of the array, asking, "Are there any savings for residents at all?" Yuhas replied that subscribers to the power would be guaranteed a 5 to 10 percent discount over a 25-year subscription. Gerber added that the county would likely reclassify the property as commercial rather than agricultural, potentially increasing tax revenue.
At the hearing, Turning Point announced they committed to a $52,000 donation to Kent County's agricultural preservation program — a request based on state law calculations of agricultural value. Representatives from the company stayed afterward to discuss next steps pending a PSC decision on their certificate of public convenience and necessity.
When asked how they felt the county received their project proposal, TPE representative, Attorney Margaret Witherup of Witherup Allen Law admitted, "It's hard to tell. Each site is different."
No other comment were received from Turning Point legal counsel, Attorney Witherup, or from representatives at Kimley-Horn and Associates, Inc. Kent County officials said they will continue to monitor developments in the project. More details can be found under Case No. 9742 at the Maryland PSC website.

title: St. Michaels discuss ordinance for leaf blowers
author: AHMAD GARNETT agarnett@chespub.com
content:
St. Michaels discuss ordinance for leaf blowers

 February 28, 2025 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: AHMAD GARNETT agarnett@chespub.com | Section: News 
 
 340
 Words

 ST. MICHAELS — On Wednesday, St. Michaels officials held their third discussion of Noise Ordnance 567, which deals with gasoline-powered leaf blowers.Residents have voiced their concerns about gas leaf blowers being very loud and being used at especially early or late hours, concerns the new ordinance aims to address.
"So I think the main challenge from a policy standpoint is the impacts on local commercial lawn care companies by requiring electric leaf blowers," Town Administrator Rob Straebel said. "But for non commercial users such as residents and property owners, this could be a fairly easy transition."
The conversation surrounding limiting leaf blowers was first brought up on Oct. 25, 2023 but stopped after commercial landscape operators said they couldn't do their job properly with electric leaf blowers. The conversation was brought back up on Jan. 22, this time aimed at just gas-powered leaf blowers, which are usually noisier.
The commissioners would take into the consideration that residents would need to purchase electric leaf blowers, they said, by ensuring it does not go into effect for another year or two. Noise levels for electric or battery leaf blowers will have to be limited to 65 decibels.
Contractors and St. Michaels public works officials argued that gas leaf blowers makes their jobs easier. Electric or battery powered leaf blowers must be charged, which takes time. They also argued that gas-powered leaf blowers are more powerful and help them accomplish their jobs faster.
Commissioner Alex Roiter argued that the contractors and workers are wasting time by just blowing a couple of leafs with the gas blower.
Public Works Operational Manager Brian Thompson pushed back and explained that "most contractors are not going to waste time. They want to get in and get out because it's money flow."
Thompson said he is not against electric leaf blowers but that there are certain times when gas-powered equipment is needed.
After back-and-forth, the officials decided the ordinance needed some work because it did not properly explain what equipment can be used and by whom.
The commissioners decided to table the conversation for another meeting.

title: St. Michaels hears presentation on houseboat vacation rentals
author: AHMAD GARNETT agarnett@chespub.com
content:
St. Michaels hears presentation on houseboat vacation rentals

 February 28, 2025 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: AHMAD GARNETT agarnett@chespub.com | Section: News 
 
 575
 Words 

 Read News Document

 ST.MICHAELS — Flohom, a company that provides vacationers the chance to stay on houseboats, presented the company's plans for St. Michaels to government officials.Flohom and St. Michaels Marina owner Michael Morgan have discussed putting one or two Flohoms in the marina.
"I run a strict place. Everyone knows my style," Morgan told the town's commissioners at a meeting Wednesday. "I was timid at first, but then a heard their rules and the type of clientele that they have. If I thought this would displease my customer base, I wouldn't even have entertained it. I think it's a neat concept."
The Flohom presentation showed how the boats are built, how the company was started, and what types of rules and regulations are enforced within the company.
Customers are not permitted or allowed to drive the Flohom boats at all, so they remain docked in the same place.
To eliminate excessive noise, Flohom monitors the sound of anyone that stays in the houseboats. If the sound gets too loud, the guest will receive a text message asking them to lower their noise level. Noise monitors do not listen or record conversation but monitor the sound decibels in the home.
Flohom staff members look to dock in places where guests can walk or drive a short distance to get breakfast or lunch and attend different town events.
"I'm new to this as well," Morgan said. "I'm willing to take the chance on it because I think it would be a unique thing for the town, it would be another option for people to come and stay and do something in St. Michaels. Not to mention the accommodation tax"
Commissioners and town residents had multiple questions for the company and for Morgan.
Commissioner David Wojiechowski questioned if Flohom would have to pay accommodation tax, and if so, if all other boats or yacht should pay the same accommodation tax if they stay overnight.
"It is an overnight rental competing against our hotel rooms," Wjiechowski said. "So if this gets approved and pays an accommodation tax, then all 200 slips that are overnight should pay an accommodation tax."
Morgan said that other slips would not be subject to accommodation tax.
Flohom staff confirmed the company does have a plan to bring business to St. Michaels after going through the proper protocols. But the company has an interest in exploring the town and gauging reception first.
"This is just an initial presentation," Jerry South Co-Founder of Flohom said. "Were not sure if this is something that requires a vote. We wanted to be very proactive and come in and say, 'hey, this is what we are doing.'"
Flohom doesn't need a approval from the town council just yet. The company first must go in front of the town's Planning Commission to ensure plans abide by the town's zoning policies.
"The use that they are proposing tonight would not be allowed with our current codes," Town Administrator Rob Straebel said. "So it would require a zoning change that would most likely go in front of the Planning Commission, then come back to the commissioners for discussion.
"So the presentation is just to see if there is enough support to move forward with consideration of a zoning change to potentially allow this."
St. Michaels residents also wanted to know if Flohom can give the houseboat model an historic look instead of a "business look."
Flohom officials confirmed they can remodel the boats to give them a historic look.
This report was updated to clarify how accommodation tax could be applied.

title: Trappe, Talbot County Council discuss contentious sewer connection
author: Konner Metz
content:
Trappe, Talbot County Council discuss contentious sewer connection

 February 28, 2025 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: Konner Metz | Section: Local News 
 
 542
 Words 

 Read News Document

 EASTON — Trappe and Talbot County officials held a back-and-forth discussion at Tuesday's County Council meeting regarding an industrial property's sewer connection to Trappe's wastewater treatment plant.The discussion centered around whether the connection of Paris Foods Corporation to the treatment plant was done properly. The connection was approved in 2021 and became active in 2022, according to Trappe officials.
Lyndsey Ryan, Trappe's attorney, said the town approved that connection with the understanding that Paris Foods sat on a parcel classified as S-1, meaning the connection did not require county approval.
But that understanding was based on what officials say were "erroneous maps" attached to Resolution 281, a piece of county legislation.
"Recently, it's been brought to Trappe's attention that … the Paris Foods property was actually unprogrammed," Ryan said Tuesday.
First introduced in 2019, Resolution 281 amended the county's comprehensive plan to reclassify certain portions of Lakeside — an ongoing 2,501-home development east of U.S. Route 50 in Trappe — for immediate priority for water and sewer service.
The resolution's attached maps showed properties not part of the Lakeside development to have incorrect water and sewer classifications. Paris Foods sits on the same side of Route 50 as Lakeside, just south of Lakeside's already-built homes.
The map errors came to light in the fall of 2021, county and town officials say. The maps incorrectly showed Paris Foods as S-1, while the resolution's text included correct classifications.
As Paris Foods and Trappe now work toward applying for an amendment to the county's comprehensive water and sewer plan to designate Paris Foods as S-1, County Council Vice President Pete Lesher pushed for answers on why it wasn't done sooner.
"You were aware that the maps were erroneous, by that time, by November of 2021?" Lesher asked.
"I don't believe that it was really brought to our attention," Ryan responded. "I know that there was speculation to the maps being erroneous. But again, at the time, we were focused on Lakeside and the other properties."
Ryan emphasized that at the time Trappe approved Paris Foods' connection, there had been "no discussion about the maps of (Resolution) 281 being incorrect."
"Certainly, had we been aware of that and looked into the issue, we wouldn't have approved the connection," she said.
Lesher later asked Ryan when the town became "aware of this illegal connection."
"From our opinion, the connection was not illegal, or there was not an act from the town to make it illegal," Ryan said.
Ryan said the town realized last fall that Paris Foods never went through the process to amend the county's comprehensive water and sewer plan. The town informed the county of the Paris Foods situation in December via a letter.
Lesher said his main concern was the "long gap between when the erroneous maps came to light in November of 2021 and this report to the county in December of 2024."
"We are apologetic for that," Ryan said.
"I know that you're a very sharp attorney," Lesher said. "I hope that you'll not disappoint your client next time, and not rely on mere maps and take a sharper look at the text."
Council Member Keasha Haythe asked if moving forward, the town and county could better communicate regarding any water and sewer connections. Trappe Town Council President Brian Schmidt said Trappe will "absolutely" work to better that communication.

title: MACo officials say cost shifts from state to counties are ‘absurd,’ unfair
author: Konner Metz
content:
MACo officials say cost shifts from state to counties are ‘absurd,’ unfair

 March 1, 2025 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: Konner Metz | Section: Local News 
 
 647
 Words 

 Read News Document

 Representatives from the Maryland Association of Counties minced no words when speaking to the Eastern Shore's state legislators Friday morning about the expected cost burdens being placed on counties this budget cycle."Shifting these costs onto counties at this point is absurd," said Kevin Kinnally, the association's legislative director.
Earlier this month, the Department of Legislative Services told the Eastern Shore Delegation that local governments across the state may have to pick up around $144 million in costs as the state legislature and Gov. Wes Moore grapple with tackling a near $3 billion deficit.
The governor's proposed fiscal year 2026 budget would shift costs in a number of areas, including teacher pensions and property assessments, according to MACo officials.
In Caroline and Talbot counties, projected local cost shifts are in the $700,000 range, per legislative services projections. Dorchester County is at $830,000, while Queen Anne's County leads the pack for the Mid-Shore at $970,000. Kent is the lowest of the five counties with a $300,000 projection.
Friday at the Eastern Shore Delegation meeting, Kinnally said the Shore's poorer counties, like Caroline and Dorchester, are being "railroaded."
Kinnally claims the state budget leaves counties with no choice but to raise property tax rates, going so far as to deem it a "state-mandated property tax increase."
"Two-thirds of Marylanders live in counties at the maximum local income tax rate, so the only place to go is to the property tax," Kinnally said. "Which is regressive, which everybody hates. But they're pushing us into a corner here, and that's not fair."
Michael Sanderson, executive director of MACo, said the organization took a closer look at how cost shifts would impact Dorchester County's fiscal situation.
After running the numbers, Sanderson said he believes Dorchester County may have to raise property taxes, a result he called "absolutely bonkers."
"I have no idea how Dorchester County manages this year's budget," Sanderson said.
SOLAR COMPROMISEAs legislators and industry leaders have eyes on a joint hearing Friday regarding the state's solar legislation, MACo is opposing Senate Bill 931 and its paired House bill.
The legislation is designed to expand solar energy across the state, a measure intended to work toward accomplishing Moore's clean energy goals for Maryland. If passed, the bill would give the state authority to approve solar energy projects — a significant harm to local siting authority, critics say.
Dominic Butchko, MACo's intergovernmental relations director, said the association opposes the legislation based on five impacted areas: safety, livability of rural areas, concerns for local taxpayers, affordable housing opportunities being stripped and inefficiencies in the legislation's requirements.
Butchko said the legislation strays from compromises MACo thought it reached last November.
But through recent discussions with solar industry leaders and environmental advocates, Butchko still sees a path to compromise.
"Those efforts have started to yield some fruit," Butchko said. "We believe we actually have amendments that revert the legislation back to where we were at or pretty close to where we were at in November."
MUNICIPAL LEAGUE
Friday, the Eastern Shore Delegation heard a brief update from the Maryland Municipal League, an organization representing local municipal governments.
The group has two legislative priorities this session: Senate Bill 390, which would allow local governments to have trained civilians issue speed camera citations instead of police officers; and House Bill 991, which would allow local governments to institute food and beverage fees.
Justin Fiore, the league's deputy director of advocacy and public affairs, said House Bill 991 could give flexibility to governments that are "heavily dependent on property taxes as (their) only revenue."
"We have 43 million visitors annually to the state of Maryland, and while they do pay a hotel tax if they stay, we really don't capture revenue from the services that they utilize," Fiore said.
The food and beverage fee bill is still waiting committee review and House approval before it moves to the Senate, while the speed camera citation bill was passed by the Senate earlier this month and currently sits in the House.

title: Dorchester County and DCPS working to reduce FY26 budget deficits
author: Maggie Trovato
content:
Dorchester County and DCPS working to reduce FY26 budget deficits

 March 1, 2025 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: Maggie Trovato | Section: Local News 
 
 573
 Words 

 Read News Document

 CAMBRIDGE — Dorchester County Manager Jerry Jones considers the fiscal year 2026 budget a moving target."There are a lot of things that are changing," he said about predicted state funding during a Dorchester County Council budget work session Thursday. "This is not a weekly thing, but almost a daily thing. ... We just don't know how this is going to unfold."
County staff has been going through the operating and capital budgets line by line to find efficiencies, Jones said.
"We are constantly working on solutions," he said. "We're finding those efficiencies. We have made substantial changes already."
During the work session, Jones detailed estimated revenue and expenditures for fiscal year 2026. According to Jones' presentation, preliminary projections for the budget show a deficit of $6.2 million, with $87.7 million in estimated revenue and $93.9 million in estimated expenditures.
Jones outlined a list of mandates from the state that contribute to the county's deficit. These include reductions in grant funding, losses from proposed property tax deductions, an increase in state education maintenance of effort costs and increased financial responsibilities for things like teacher retirement.
Both Jones and County Council members said the budget would look a lot different without these mandates. Jones said that without the mandates, the county would not be facing a deficit. He said he county would instead have had $200,812 more in revenue than expenditures.
The council and county manager also talked about significant budget cuts made two years ago. Council Vice President Mike Detmer said the fat had already been trimmed from the budget at that time.
"At this point, we're trying to keep the ship from sinking," he said.
Council President Lenny Pfeffer said he and Detmer have plans to go to Annapolis to testify in front of the Maryland General Assembly on legislation that would negatively affect the county's budget.
EDUCATION FUNDING
Detmer said the decrease in state funding and increase in the county's fiscal responsibility is largely driven by the state's goal to meet its financial obligation to the Blueprint for Maryland's Future, a state plan that aims to improve student outcomes and the quality of education.
Dorchester County Public Schools, which has its own budget separate from the county, also is facing a deficit. The deficit, which was estimated to be $10.19 million in January, is now estimated to be $5.59 million.
During a Dorchester County Board of Education budget work session also held Thursday, Dorchester County Public Schools Superintendent Jymil Thompson shared refinements the district has made to the budget since the board's work session in January.
He said the $4.6 million in additional cuts to to reduce the deficit were made through reductions to alternative education programming, supplies costs, travel costs, contracted services and fixed charges as well as expanding the district's understanding of Blueprint guidance to better match funding with expenses.
"We are taking it serious, and we are trying to make the changes we can to reduce our budget in a smart way," Thompson said.
At the County Council work session, council member Ricky Travers said other counties are having the same budget problems.
"Rural Maryland is the worst right now because the bigger counties, you just add another zero to it, but they've got a little bit more ability to garnish more money per penny (on taxes)," he said. "But this big number is astronomical."
Jones said the county will play it by ear on when it holds its next budget work session. He said when it is held will be announced to the public.

title: Talbot County OKs funding for Easton High auditorium lights, other projects
author: Konner Metz
content:
Talbot County OKs funding for Easton High auditorium lights, other projects

 March 1, 2025 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: Konner Metz | Section: Local News 
 
 238
 Words 

 Read News Document

 EASTON — Funding to replace Easton High School's auditorium lights was approved by the Talbot County Council at its Tuesday meeting.The auditorium's current lights date back to the school's renovation in 1997. County officials say they've heard for years about the need for new lights.
The project will cost $817,000, just over half of a total $1.5 million to be pulled from the county's capital projects fund. Talbot County's fiscal year 2025 budget has already accounted for the costs.
"That's huge for the auditorium," County Council President Chuck Callahan said. "So I'm glad that went through. That's going to be big for the school."
Council members also unanimously approved $556,000 for light replacements at St. Michaels Middle High School and $116,000 for athletic field improvements across the district.
Following those approvals, the County Council passed a bill permitting the county's sale of bonds to borrow $26.9 million for Chapel District Elementary School renovations. That funding from the county spans both fiscal years 2025 and 2026.
The renovation project, which broke ground last August, will upgrade the existing building and add on an additional 16,000 square feet. Chapel Elementary was last renovated in 1994.
Callahan said Talbot County Public Schools Director of Operations Kevin Shafer has done a "phenomenal job" leading renovation efforts.
"You've done excellent keeping us up to speed and everything, and trying to keep everything on budget," Callahan said. "We really, really appreciate it. It's huge for the community down there too."

title: Eastern Shore renters face challenges with affordable housing
author: Maggie Trovato
content:
Eastern Shore renters face challenges with affordable housing

 March 1, 2025 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: Maggie Trovato | Section: Local News 
 
 1987
 Words 

 Read News Document

 CAMBRIDGE — Bradford House Apartments resident Linda Johnson doesn't carry mace on her keychain anymore.She doesn't feel the need to use a key or a cell phone instead of her finger to tap the buttons of the apartment's elevator.
After years of asking apartment management to address resident safety concerns, from mold and bug infestations to a lack of security, Johnson and other Bradford House residents finally feel safe.
"I feel better every day," said Johnson, who has lived at Bradford House on Race Street in Cambridge for nearly 25 years. "I'm not angry no more."
The complex — which offers multifamily, subsidized housing for low-income individuals who are elderly or have special needs — came under new management with a new principal owner in the fall, and residents started to see changes they had requested for years be made.
But as housing problems across the Eastern Shore persist, others have not been as lucky.
A SHORE PROBLEM
With a lack of affordable housing options on the Eastern Shore and a need for better enforcement over housing standards, renters living in poor conditions often feel stuck.
In the eyes of Larry Rooths, the head of the Public Safety and Intelligence Committee for the Eastern Shore branch of the Caucus of African American Leaders, the lack of affordable housing is a national issue.
"But it seems a lot worse down here because there's so little housing," he said, "and there's no infrastructure in place for emergency services, emergency shelters."
Rooths said he's noticed landlords don't feel like they have to do much for tenants because there aren't many other places those tenants can go.
"And then the residents feel like that also," he said. "They don't want to stir up too much trouble because they know if somebody comes in and shuts the building down, where are they going?"
Rooths sees a need for housing legislation with more enforcement power so landlords address the issues residents face. He said the Shore also needs more housing infrastructure.
"If you create a situation where there's enough housing, then the landlords lose control," he said. "...If you don't like the place you're living in, you get up and move. But if there's no place to move or you can't move to another apartment building close to where you work, then it gets difficult."
The caucus is working to get tenants to form groups, which Rooths said would help them know their rights and push elected officials to make change.
"Unless there's some change in legislation or there's some increased funding to create a bigger pool of housing, this problem is going to be the same," he said.
In October, the Tenant Safety Act of 2024 went into effect in Maryland. The act, which places responsibility on landlords to provide safe dwelling for tenants, guarantees tenants can form groups.
Shore Legal Access Executive Director Meredith Girard considers Bradford House's tenant association a critical piece of its success in getting new management.
"I think the tenant association was critical to really letting the management and the court know what the issues were and how widespread it was," Girard said. "And that prompted some really important changes so that now the building is managed by a new company."
Girard said rural counties don't always have enough resources to support a rental inspection and licensing system. She said it would be great if counties on the Eastern Shore could pool their resources to form a regional housing commission.
"Where you could set some basic standards for habitability to make sure that if you're renting a unit, that the oven works, that the heat works, that the plumbing works, that the roof isn't leaking," she said.
Girard acknowledged rural landlords may also be strapped for resources. She said in some cases, landlords might not have the resources to make needed repairs.
"Which then becomes this really problematic cycle," she said.
At Bradford House, previous management said the property had been neglected before they took over in 2022.
In an April 2024 statement to The Star Democrat, Millennia Housing Management, the previous management at the complex, said it had invested more than $300,000 into the maintenance and enhancement of the "severely distressed property."
Girard said that when problems in complexes are fixed, tenants are often scared to complain about the conditions because they don't have anywhere else to go.
"And they don't want to upset their landlords," she said. "But at the same time, they need landlords to fix the things that need to be fixed."
Maryland Legal Aid Advocacy Director for the Human Right to Housing Zafar Shah said further protections against evictions are needed so tenants aren't reluctant to use the Tenant Safety Act of 2024. He said the Maryland legislature is considering a good cause eviction bill "that would protect tenants from lease non-renewal without a good reason."
"This is the big priority for renters in Maryland," he said.
NO WHERE TO GO
De'Auntte Clark came to Cambridge for peace.
In 2016, her 14-year-old son was killed after being hit by a car in Anne Arundel County. Four years later, her husband died from COVID-19.
In September 2022, Clark brought her family to the Eastern Shore for a fresh start. But since moving here, Clark has found anything but the peace she was seeking.
"I'm so numb, I can't cry," she said.
With concerns about the safety of her apartment at Calvin Mowbray Park and Stephen Camper Park in Cambridge and nowhere else to go, Clark spent more than a month living out of a van with her family.
A few days after her family moved into the complex, Clark noticed what seemed like mold in the cabinets along one of the walls in the kitchen.
Maintenance came to clean the cabinets out, but as the weather outside got colder and she turned the heat on, Clark said she started to see black spots pop up on the walls.
In December 2023, Clark's son, Keith Dezurn — who has a medical history of severe, persistent asthma — was airlifted to the University of Maryland Children's Hospital because he was struggling to breathe. He stayed in intensive care for five days, Clark said, displaying symptoms consistent with mold exposure.
Clark said on the way to the hospital in Baltimore, she could barely see anything and was crying.
"I don't want to lose another child," she said.
Ed Cafasso, a spokesperson for the property that is managed by WinnResidential, said on Jan. 15 that the health and safety of residents is WinnResidential's number one priority.
"Any time a household reports a moisture-related issue, it is treated as an emergency and remediated immediately by a professional, licensed specialist," he said.
Cafasso said over the past year, there have been seven instances at the complex that required professional mold remediation. He said there were zero reported cases of mold at the 190-apartment community as of January.
Before Clark and her family could move into a new unit at the complex this past fall, the unit was condemned. Cambridge Assistant City Manager Brandon Hesson said that in condemning the unit, the city ordered mold and moisture testing be done.
An inspection report obtained by The Star Democrat from the city showed an early November analysis found aspergillus and penicillium spore counts in the unit that were "significantly higher than the baseline count and probably indicates a source of contamination."
The unit was later removed from the city's list of condemned properties after a report by Simple Mold Solutions, which was based on the analysis, found the numbers "indicated a normal fungal environment with no elevated concentrations of airborne mold spores." The report recommended the HVAC system be cleaned to prevent mold spores from circulating.
But Clark's son's health scare was enough to make her seek housing elsewhere. The search proved to be no easy feat.
Limited affordable housing options on the Eastern Shore and across the state have made it difficult for Clark to find somewhere new to settle.
Clark said she went to multiple shelters in Howard County, where her children are currently enrolled in school, but all of them were full. She said the places she did find that had space required she live in the county for six months, which she had not.
Moving from place to place hasn't been easy on Clark's kids. She said they are scared to go back to the complex.
"They don't want to go back there, and I don't know what to do," Clark told The Star Democrat while they were living out of a van. "But at the same time, I know we can't keep living like this."
In mid-December, Clark and her family were able to secure a hotel room after living out of a van for more than a month. On Valentine's Day, they moved into a townhouse on the western shore.
"It's much better," she said. "No mold."
ZOOMING IN ON THE PROBLEM
Clark's story isn't an uncommon one when it comes to tenants of affordable housing on the Eastern Shore.
Residential issues at affordable housing complexes in Cambridge have come to a head more than once in the last two years.
In an attempt to attack the bigger issue at the local level, Cambridge has beefed up its Code Enforcement Department and is working on projects intended to increase and improve the city's housing stock.
Hesson said although the issues at housing facilities are all unique, there are common themes among them.
"There have been failures by agencies at the local, state and federal level to hold up the standards we've set for housing providers here," he said. "It's not my place to point fingers, because it isn't going to fix anything. The city is part of that structure, and we're committed to being better."
Hesson said building "strong relationships" with the governing authorities for the different housing facilities has helped achieve "significant progress."
"We've been able to draw attention to where these systems and processes have fallen short, and residents are seeing some of the early results of those efforts," he said.
PROGRESS
For Linda Johnson, those results are clear.
On Feb. 13, Johnson moved into a new unit within Bradford House Apartments. The move is not just a win for Johnson, who has been a loud and consistent voice of the Bradford House community, but proof of a new era for the apartment complex and its residents.
For years Bradford House residents expressed concerns about the safety of the building. In September 2023, the property — which was then managed by Millennia — received a U.S. Department of Housing and Urban Development inspection score that indicated health and safety deficiencies.
Three months later, Millennia received a debarment order from HUD, preventing the company from participating in any new business with the department.
In October, it was announced that Nuveen, an asset manager and subsidiary of financial planning firm TIAA, had been made principal owner of the apartment complex. Paths Management Services, a subsidiary of Nuveen, would manage the property.
Johnson's new digs, complete with a brand new, updated kitchen and laminate wood flooring, are a stark contrast from her previous unit.
When The Star Democrat visited some residents' homes last year, residents pointed out things like holes in ceilings, possible mold and problems with stoves. At that time, multiple residents had active rent escrow cases, where tenants pay their rent to a court, rather than to their landlord, until property issues are addressed.
The change at Bradford House isn't just visible in individual apartment units. The hallways have new flooring, the stairways are consistently clean, there is better lighting and new cameras and the community room has been renovated. Johnson said management is fixing the elevator that's been broken for more than a year.
"It's been wonderful," Johnson said. "I mean Paths came in here, they didn't talk, they worked."
Johnson is the president of the complex's tenant association, which was formed with guidance from Shore Legal Access.
"Just because we're low income people doesn't mean we have to live like that," she said.
Johnson said other renters going through housing issues should fight for what they believe in, adding that tenants have the right to withhold rent and form tenant associations.
"Your voice matters," she said.
Star Democrat reporter Konner Metz contributed to this report.

title: VFW plans parade to welcome Vietnam veterans home 50 years after end of war
author: WENDY WEITZEL wweitzel@chespub.com
content:
VFW plans parade to welcome Vietnam veterans home 50 years after end of war

 March 1, 2025 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: WENDY WEITZEL wweitzel@chespub.com | Section: Local News 
 
 374
 Words 

 Read News Document

 EASTON — When Kenley Timms returned home from the Vietnam War, he did not receive a warm welcome."I was never spit on, never thrown trash at, but when I landed at National Airport in Washington, I walked into the airport, and there was a lady and her child, probably 5, 7 years old, and I spoke to the child, and that woman picked that child up like I was the devil," Timms said.
Other returning soldiers faced even more hostile receptions upon returning to a country where political tides had turned and the Vietnam War, unbeknownst to those deployed, had become deeply unpopular.
"And at the time, I didn't know about it because when I was in Vietnam, I didn't know what was happening back in the United States," Timms said.
Now, 50 years after the war ended, Timms, the commander of VFW Post 5118, and a collection of other veterans at the post in Easton are seeking to give their fellow service members the welcome home they never got.
On March 30, the VFW post plans to hold a wreath laying ceremony before a parade through downtown Easton and a short program in honor of Vietnam veterans.
"I'm hoping that we'll have a couple thousand people standing in the streets, waving to us," Timms said. "You'll see a lot of veterans walking or riding, ones that are able to walk, tears rolling down their face."
The parade route, which has already been approved by the Town of Easton, will begin at the intersection of Dover and Washington streets, then make its way down Washington Street and Glebe Road to the VFW. Event organizers plan to distribute American flags for spectators to wave.
But beyond event attendance, the Vietnam veterans behind the event are hoping to gather parade participants and gain assistance with transportation for veterans who are unable to walk the parade route.
"We need transportation, but we don't want a bus. We want something where people can see them, the public can wave to them," Timms said.
"What we're looking for is people to participate," added Wayne Hall, president of the VFW's Vietnam Veterans Chapter. "If anybody has any military vehicles, the collectors, we'd be glad to have them."
Those who wish to be involved in the event can contact 410-310-5748.
