title: A stranger gets a proper burial
author: MARTY MADDEN mmadden@somdnews.com
content:
A stranger gets a proper burial

 March 3, 2025 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: MARTY MADDEN mmadden@somdnews.com | Section: News 
 
 453
 Words 

 Read News Document

 Considering no one present knew the departed, the modest turnout last week for a burial in a Lusby cemetery was remarkable.The Feb. 27 service at Middleham and St. Peter's Cemetery was drawn from the Book of Common Prayer, which was used often during the last quarter of the 19th century. That may have been the time when remains interred was part of a live person.
"I believe it was from somebody's private cemetery when the cliffs used to be way, way out," George Oliver told Southern Maryland News.
Oliver, who resides in Chesapeake Ranch Estates, frequently visits beach areas at the base of the cliffs, mostly in search of sharks' teeth and other fossils.
The Alabama native recalled the discovery of what turned out to be a coffin containing human remains at the edge of the Chesapeake Bay.
"I found it in November and discovered there was a skeleton in it," Oliver said. "I had been seeing it for months. It was sitting up out of the water. I just thought it was wood filled with sand."
Oliver said he contacted local law enforcement and was told of his find, "You can have it. There's nothing there."
Notifications were made to Calvert Marine Museum and the Calvert County Historical Society.
"Our parish was contacted several weeks ago by the county historic planner, Christopher Sperling," Hugh Davies, a parishioner at Middleham and St. Peter's, said. "He informed us that the county had received the remains of an unknown person and asked if they might be reinterred in the Middleham cemetery. The church had provided such a reinterment over 10 years ago."
Oliver also had been involved with that discovery.
"In 2008, we found a leg," Oliver said, adding that he had hoped the leg was missing from the remains he had found in late last year. However, remains of two legs were identified from that find.
Other information provided by the church stated the best estimate of the time of the coffin and remains is the late 19th century.
Church officials reported that a general conclusion reached is that the person "was likely a Christian" and that reinterment was needed. The Lusby church was deemed the most appropriate place for the interment, in part since Middleham Chapel is the oldest church building in Calvert County, dating back to 1684.
Pastor Erin Betz Shank, priest in charge at the parish, recited the service drawn from the Book of Common Prayer.
A white cloth bag containing the bones located within the coffin was re-placed in the coffin and attendees were invited to deposit handfuls of earth into the grave.
"We therefore commit their body to the ground, earth to earth, ashes to ashes, dust to dust," Shank recited during the service, which included the reciting of the Lord's Prayer.

title: Easton considers tightening zoning regulations amid council concerns
author: Konner Metz
content:
Easton considers tightening zoning regulations amid council concerns

 March 4, 2025 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: Konner Metz | Section: Local News 
 
 522
 Words 

 Read News Document

 EASTON — At a workshop Monday, town planners presented potential changes to Easton's planned redevelopment overlay, a district which aims to facilitate revitalization of industrial areas or older, dilapidated parts of town.The discussion comes as the Easton Town Council is seeking more say in large housing projects, particularly following the approval last month of most of Easton Crossing, a 123-unit mixed-use development on Brookletts Avenue.
Since that project sits in the planned redevelopment overlay district, the Planning Commission granted final approval rather than the Town Council.
"If I'm going to be the head coach, I want to call the play," Ward 4 Councilmember the Rev. Elmer Davis said Monday. "Because the only person they get rid of is the head coach."
Town Planner Lynn Thomas brought two main options to give councilmembers more oversight. The overlay district could be deleted, sending projects through a planned unit development application (which requires Town Council approval). Or the town could introduce limits to what can be done through the planned redevelopment overlay district, such as a cap on the number of units or overall size of the project.
If limits were instituted, developers looking to build in the overlay district above those caps would go through the planned unit development process, and thus the council.
Thomas said town staff lean toward revising the planned redevelopment instead of eliminating it entirely. Councilmembers largely agreed.
Ward 2 Councilmember Don Abbatiello said his main concern lies with "large-scale projects" not coming before the council.
"I think the residents would probably appreciate another opportunity to speak up (at Town Council meetings) on a development of that size," Abbatiello added, referencing the Easton Crossing project.
Town Attorney Sharon VanEmburgh said based on council feedback, she and town staff will return at a later date with specific options for the limits that could be placed on the planned redevelopment overlay district.
Thomas, a longtime town employee, noted that since the redevelopment overlay was introduced in 1993, part of its intent has been to incentivize developers to locate in those parts of town. Results have been mixed, he said.
"I think we've seen some (reinvestment) but probably not as much as we envisioned when enacted," Thomas said.
The overlay district accounts for 155 acres, around 2% of the town's total area. Recent projects in the overlay include Easton Crossing, the 28-unit Silo Square project on Needwood Avenue, and Building African American Minds' new academic center on Jowite Street.
Other recommendations provided Monday included establishing regular planning and zoning reports to the council and holding joint workshops between the council and Planning Commission.
Council President Frank Gunsallus said a mix of those reports and workshops would be beneficial. Davis pushed on why those aren't already occurring.
"That's low-hanging fruit. Tell me why we're not doing that now," Davis asked Miguel Salinas, the town's planning and zoning director.
Salinas replied, "It is low-hanging fruit, and I think it's a good tool for communication."
Planning Commission Chair Philip Toussaint spoke at the end of Monday's workshop, expressing desire to work closely with the Town Council moving forward.
"I think any enhanced model of communication that we can put together, I'm all for that," Toussaint said. "I think that's a fantastic idea."

title: Caroline County emergency cannabis bill moved to introduction
author: AHMAD GARNETT agarnett@chespub.com
content:
Caroline County emergency cannabis bill moved to introduction

 March 5, 2025 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: AHMAD GARNETT agarnett@chespub.com | Section: News 
 
 384
 Words 

 Read News Document

 DENTON — At their Tuesday meeting, the Caroline County Commissioners discussed an emergency cannabis bill that would allow the county to set zoning regulations for cannabis facilities.The emergency bill is proposed to allow Caroline County to get on track with regulations and requirements of from the state.
It would also create parameters for dispensaries, growers and processors and where they can grow, process and sell cannabis in the county.
The adjustments are being made as a result of House Bill 805, a 2024 bill that established zoning requirements for cannabis businesses that are more restrictive than some that existed prior to the legalization of recreational cannabis in the state.
The state regulation mandates that cannabis dispensaries cannot be located within 500 feet of schools, child care center, programs, recreation centers, libraries, public parks or churches. Dispensaries will also not be allowed to be within 1,000 feet of another dispensary.
All state regulations are upheld in Caroline County's proposed emergency bill.
For cannabis growers and processors, Caroline County's proposed emergency bill will mandate growers and processors to be in the I2 industrial district of Caroline County.
The regulations will also mandate that growers and processors not be located within 1,200 feet of schools, religious facilities, public or nonprofit parks, recreation areas, playgrounds, civic centers, club, libraries, registered family daycares and group daycares. They also can't be within 300 feet of a residence.
Caroline County Commissioners Vice President Larry Porter questioned if the distance in feet of the dispensaries, growers and processors could be increased to a further distance from the places the state suggested.
Caroline County Director of Planning and Codes Crystal Dadds responded, "For the processors and growers the distances, yes they can be increased, but for the dispensaries, no, they are covered by state law."
Porter made another suggestion that Caroline County make a color-coded map of the county to indicate areas where dispensaries, growers and processors can be located for when businesses put in an application.
"Yes, we can put something together to give a better visual where those areas are and what the setbacks look like," Dadds said.
The licensing of cannabis sales will be handled by the state. The counties have no control of applications, only the zoning of where dispensaries, growers and processors can be located.
The Caroline County Commissioners decided to move the emergency cannabis bill forward for introduction.

title: Southern Dorchester residents share thoughts on town incorporation
author: Maggie Trovato
content:
Southern Dorchester residents share thoughts on town incorporation

 March 5, 2025 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: Maggie Trovato | Section: Local News 
 
 646
 Words 

 Read News Document

 WINGATE — Lifelong Dorchester County resident Dick Dawson thought the Lakes and Straits Volunteer Fire Company hall in Wingate on March 3 was busier than he's seen in 45 years, apart from luncheons and dinners."That tells you something," he said at the outset of a meeting at the fire hall to discuss efforts to incorporate a new town in the southern part of the county.
Dawson, his 17-year-old grandson Drew Dawson and Elijah's General Store owner David Beverley are working to incorporate Blackwater, a new town, in an effort to protect southern Dorchester County communities from disappearing due to sea level rise and state critical area regulations.
The communities included in the plan for Blackwater are Andrews, Robbins, Wesley, Lakesville, Crapo, Wingate, Toddville, Bishops Head and Crocheron. Each community would still exist within the new town. The planners believe incorporation would give the area a better chance of receiving funding from government agencies.
March 3, the planners shared their vision and heard from residents of the communities that Blackwater would encompass. Residents raised concerns about taxes, money management, residency requirements and the incorporation process. With multiple residents in the room opposed to the idea, tension ebbed and flowed throughout the meeting.
During a tense portion, with some residents visibly upset and yelling, Chuckie Hayward said he was tired of the "bickering." He said although he's against the idea to incorporate, he came to listen.
"I'm here because I want to hear everything out first before I really make a decision," he said.
Many residents shared concerns with having to pay taxes to the town. The Dawsons and Beverley have said the town would not impose new taxes.
Drew Dawson said 60% of residents would have to vote in favor of being taxed in order for the town to impose taxes. He said he doesn't see that happening.
County resident Matt Ritter said taxes often arise when communities experience growth.
"Once you allow building and allow all this excess to happen, growth comes down here and this becomes just like Cambridge," he said. "And then you've got all these city folk down here trying to change things up. And they always raise their hand to raise the taxes."
Former Cambridge Mayor Andrew Bradshaw, who shared his understanding of municipalities at the meeting, said the town would be able to secure federal and state funding that is only open to municipalities.
"If you all can get the kind of representation this would provide, it gives a force behind the effort that just doesn't exist right now," Bradshaw said.
In order for Blackwater to get incorporated, the planners need to gather signatures on a petition, then go to the county to submit the drafted town charter for review. If the county accepts the charter, the decision will go to the registered voters within the area that Blackwater would encompass.
Resident Scott Hughes spoke about the importance of forming the town the right way and having a "bulletproof" charter. He said he expects the push to create Blackwater will be a success.
"But let's make it happen so that nobody can take advantage of it," he said.
Lindsay Wheatley said she sees three options for the communities: Sell all the land to sika deer hunters who want to strip away houses and put up deer stands, stay and not do anything as roads and the area's heritage crumble, or fight.
"This might be our only opportunity ever," she said. "We're dwindling. Look around, right? I chose to come back here because I love it, and all of you love it too. I'm going to fight. I'm going to sign it. I'm going to do everything that I can do with integrity and honesty to protect this area for as long as I can."
Drew Dawson said he and the other planners will discuss the ideas raised during the meeting and decide how to amend the draft charter.
"I think there are some pretty good ideas," he said.

title: Dorchester County ballot questions will not take effect due to 'administrative error'
author: Maggie Trovato
content:
Dorchester County ballot questions will not take effect due to 'administrative error'

 March 5, 2025 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: Maggie Trovato | Section: Local News 
 
 454
 Words 

 Read News Document

 CAMBRIDGE — Although Dorchester County voters who took to the polls in November voted on whether changes should be made to the county charter, those changes will not be made this year.During a Dorchester County Council meeting on March 4, Council President Lenny Pfeffer announced the county had made an "administrative error" by not advertising the referendum questions for five consecutive weeks after the council approved them.
"With it not being advertised correctly per state law, it would not make those referendum questions valid to change the charter," Pfeffer said.
The error in advertising was an accident, Pfeffer said, and he apologized to county residents.
"As far as blame for this, this entire (council) and Dorchester County takes general responsibility for this mistake," he said.
Pfeffer said the error was discovered in the process of reclaiming the county's sanitary district. He said that during the bond review process, legal counsel for the bond review discovered the oversight.
Pfeffer said the county waited for additional legal review before telling the public.
In an interview with the Star Democrat March 5, Pfeffer said the council was notified of the error a little over a month ago. He said the county had previously been trying to have the amendments made to the charter by spring.
In November, county residents voted to amend four parts of the county charter. The changes amended the charter to:
Have the review of administrative structure be conducted within the first fiscal year of each Dorchester County Council term. Currently, the charter says a review of administrative structure should take place at least every four years, but it does not state when in that four years it should take place.Push back budget-related due dates 15 days.Clarify responsibilities of the county manager, including day-to-day operations, and establish procedures for certain vacancies. Currently, the charter has procedures in place for council member and treasurer vacancies, as well as certain board and commission vacancies.Include language to ensure transparency of governmental functions as well as access to open meetings and public records.
Pfeffer said although these amendments cannot be made to the charter now, they could be voted on again in future elections.
"So it will be up to the wishes of the Charter Review Commission and the council before the next election on if any one, all of, or whatever list of referendum questions could get placed on the ballot next time," he said.
Dorchester County Attorney Chip MacLeod said the county is looking into whether the ballot questions that were approved by voters could be addressed through county code or policy changes.
MacLeod called the situation "unfortunate," but made it clear other opportunities might exist.
"One way or another, the county's going to be impacted by those charter amendments, even though they're not technically valid," he said.

title: Caroline County worried solar concerns will grow bigger if proposed bills are passed
author: AHMAD GARNETT agarnett@chespub.com
content:
Caroline County worried solar concerns will grow bigger if proposed bills are passed

 March 5, 2025 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: AHMAD GARNETT agarnett@chespub.com | Section: News

 DENTON — Proposed House Bill 1036 and Senate Bill 931 have been a discussion for Caroline County Commissioners since the state's legislative session began in January.According to Maryland General Assembly website, the proposed bills state, "Altering the factors the Public Service Commission must consider before taking final action on a certificate of public convenience and necessity; establishing certain requirements for the construction of a certain solar energy generating station or energy storage device."
While at legislative sessions last week, Caroline County Commissioners President Travis Breeding and Vice President Larry Porter spoke to oppose the proposed bills, stating they did not provide enough authority over solar development to local jurisdictions.
"I think there were some valuable testimonies on both sides," Porter said. "Since some that time, we have received proposed amendments to the bill. My guess is we will receive some relief in some taxation and commissioning area, but I'm not sure they are going to give up siting authority."
The state has been pushing renewable energy in all counties in the state. To maintain some local autonomy over the effort, counties have created acre moratoriums and location ordinances for solar development.
Caroline County currently has a 2,000-acre moratorium in place.
The commissioners' concern about the proposed bill is the lack of control in the siting of solar in the county.
"I'm gonna break some news here, I think they drafted this bill with a total give away to the solar companies," Breeding said. "To shift the starting point completely in the favor of the solar companies, that's just speculation on my part."
"I think we going to get hosed, and we are getting hosed actively right now with the amendments," he said. "We're gonna walk away thinking we've gotten something out of the deal, but we still are gonna get preempted by the state as far as siting."
Caroline County has personally experienced an issue with siting regulations for a solar company wanting to set up a solar facility in an area in the county where solar is not allowed.
Chaberton Solar requested to put solar panels down in a residentially zoned area, where such developments are prohibited by the county.
The applicant was informed by the county prior to submitting its application that it did not have a complete site plan and had omitted some necessary details from the application in addition to the zoning violation, Barroll said.
The county filed an intervention with a public utility law judge in December stating the application was not complete as a result of these factors, but other entities attested that Chaberton met all the requirements to construct the planned solar facility.
The Power Plant Research Program of the state's Department of Natural Resources filed a paper that said it had reviewed the application and the application was complete. In December, the public utility judge pushed the application through to the next stage.
The county has since taken this solar case to court to block the planting of solar in the restricted area.
The county is concerned if proposed house bill 1036 and senate bill 931 are filed, they will face similar issues with siting as they face with Chaberton Solar.
"Everyone that was in that hearing room testifying against that bill was saying 'Do not stripe the counties of local zoning authority' and that message fell on deaf ears."

title: Chaberton Solar case provides first public hearing
author: AHMAD GARNETT agarnett@chespub.com
content:
Chaberton Solar case provides first public hearing

 March 5, 2025 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: AHMAD GARNETT agarnett@chespub.com | Section: News 
 
 481
 Words 

 Read News Document

 DENTON — Caroline County's newest battle with renewable energy has been over Chaberton Solar.A virtual public hearing was held Monday on the Chaberton Solar case, in which Caroline County is fighting a permit it alleges was issued in violation of local zoning laws.
According to Caroline County Attorney Steve Barroll, an application for a 3.0 milliwatt solar facility near Federalsburg, filed by Chaberton Solar Pahar LLC, did not meet requirements laid out by the county.
The company requested to put solar panels down in a residentially zoned area where such developments are prohibited by the county.
The applicant was informed by the county prior to submitting the application back in December that it did not have a complete site plan and had omitted some necessary details from the application in addition to the zoning violation, Barroll said.
The county filed an intervention with a public utility law judge in December stating the application was not complete as a result of these factors but other entities attested that Chaberton met all the requirements to construct the planned solar facility.
The Power Plant Research Program of the state's Department of Natural Resources filed a paper that said it had reviewed the application and the application was complete. In December, the public utility judge pushed the application through to the next stage.
According to Lauren Barchi, community engagement manager for Chamberton Solar, the proposed solar facility will cover 42 acres parcel, and 20 acres will be used for the placement of solar panels.
Chaberton also plans to create an access road off the project location. The project's access to the site will be controlled via a locked gate with a seven-foot agricultural style fence around the perimeter.
Public hearings, including the hearing Monday, need to be held before the project can receive final approval.
While no public comment was presented at the hearing Monday evening, Caroline County Commissioners President Travis Breeding spoke on Caroline County's stance against the proposed solar field.
"I should express that Caroline County respectfully opposes this application because it is R1 residential zone property," Breeding said. "It's directly contrary to the county zoning code in our comprehensive plan."
"The county spends a significant amount of time and resources to review and analyze its zone code and comprehensive plan. And it shouldn't be disregarded by solar developers or the state.
"This property in particular is inappropriate for solar because it borders the town of Federalsburg and has access to infrastructure such as water and sewer."
Barchi spoke in favor of Chaberton facility in Federalsburg, stating the benefits of the project proceeding in Caroline County.
"In total over a dozen neighbors and landowners have been spoken to with no opposition to the project," Barchi said. "This community solar project will benefit the local community in many ways, including tax revenue to the state and county."
A second public hearing will be held in person on June 12. The location will be determined at a later date.

title: Proposed tax breaks could mean service cuts in lower-income counties
author: PAUL KIEFER Capital News Service
content:
Proposed tax breaks could mean service cuts in lower-income counties

 March 6, 2025 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: PAUL KIEFER Capital News Service | Section: State News 
 
 963
 Words 

 Read News Document

 ANNAPOLIS — Gov. Wes Moore plans to change how Marylanders take deductions on their state income taxes, but officials in some of the state's poorest counties say that plan could force them to cut services."You mentioned that the federal government is creating chaos for our state government in an effort to balance their budget," Del. Jefferson Ghrist, a Republican representing Caroline, Cecil, Kent and Queen Anne's Counties, told Gov. Moore in a recent budget hearing. "It appears that your budget does sort of the same thing to our county governments."
Moore's administration, however, contends that the reforms will provide tax relief to a majority of Marylanders — including residents of lower-income counties — even if those county governments face a revenue loss.
"This proposal leaves more cash in the pockets of the majority of Maryland's households," said Budget and Management Secretary Helene Grady.
Lawmakers in Annapolis are weighing a two-pronged approach to tax reform intended to shift the scales in favor of low- and middle-income households.
Moore's proposal to double the state's standard deduction would provide a tax break to Marylanders who opt not to itemize their income tax deductions — many of them low- and middle-income. To account for the resulting revenue loss, the governor's office proposes ending the practice of itemized deductions, which would mean a larger income tax bill for many high-income Marylanders.
But county governments also collect income taxes, and a tax break for lower-income Marylanders would deal a blow to some counties' budgets.
Representatives from Allegany County appeared in Annapolis last week to ask lawmakers to soften that blow.
"Governor Moore discussed the idea that no Marylanders should be left behind," Allegany County Attorney T. Lee Beeman told lawmakers on Friday. "Ultimately, his proposal this year will do exactly that in Allegany County. It will leave Allegany County behind."
If the General Assembly moves forward with doubling the standard deduction, Allegany County would stand to lose $3.2 million in revenue next year, according to Maryland's Board of Revenue Estimates.
While the vast majority of county residents would receive a tax cut, "we'll be looking at probably cutting potentially each and every service we have," said Allegany County Administrator Jason Bennett. "We're pretty slim as it is."
Last year, the county laid off emergency services staff and scaled back employee health insurance in response to a $13 million deficit. Additional cuts could mean scaling back snow clearance operations in the winter, public transit service and support for the county's library service, he told Capital News Service.
If Allegany County raised local income taxes to the maximum rate allowed under Maryland law, he added, the county could only make up for half of the projected losses created by doubling the standard deduction.
Allegany County is not alone. Del. Malcolm Ruff, a Democrat representing Baltimore City, noted that doubling the standard deduction could undercut services in his district.
"Baltimore City would lose approximately $40 million over the next five years based on those changes," Ruff said.
The Board of Revenue Estimates projects that half of Maryland's counties and county equivalents would lose income tax revenue if the state moves forward with the proposed changes to deductions. Those include all but one of the 10 poorest Maryland counties as of the Census Bureau's 2023 American Community Survey.
"Contrast that with our friends in the beltway corridor," said Beeman. "Montgomery County stands to gain $300 million in income tax revenue over the next five years. It's a shocking contrast."
Meanwhile, some members of the Legislative Black Caucus of Maryland have expressed concerns that eliminating itemized deductions would have a disproportionate impact on majority-Black districts in the Washington suburbs.
Residents of Charles and Prince George's Counties itemize their deductions at higher rates than residents of any other Maryland counties. That presents a political challenge for someone like Sen. Michael Jackson, a Democrat representing parts of Calvert, Charles and Prince George's Counties. Residents in those districts are more likely than other Marylanders to see their tax bills increase under Moore's plan.
Jackson told CNS that he and other caucus members representing those counties are in talks with the governor to address their concerns.
But Moore's current proposals drew praise from some outside observers.
"Itemized deductions are regressive," said Miles Trinidad, a state policy analyst with the Institute on Taxation and Economic Policy, a nonpartisan think tank. "These policies offer the largest benefits to higher income taxpayers and little if any benefits to low- and middle-income families."
Grady, meanwhile, notes that the governor's tax reforms would offer a tax cut to a majority of Marylanders, and that aid to local governments accounts for a third of general fund expenses in the proposed 2026 budget — aid that would support both public school systems and county governments.
The governor's office also underscores that Maryland's standard deduction is only a third of Virginia's, meaning that some poor and working-class residents who would pay no income tax in Virginia make enough to pay income tax in Maryland.
While Moore's proposal would still leave Maryland's standard deduction lower than those in Virginia and Washington, his office argues the change is in the interest of fairness.
However, given the dire state of Maryland's budget and the prospect of dwindling federal support, Grady also noted that the state may not be in a position to simultaneously offer tax cuts to most Marylanders and shield counties from the statewide budget crunch.
"Given the general fund challenge, it would be very difficult to insulate counties entirely from impacts," she said.
Senate President Bill Ferguson, a Democrat representing Baltimore City, echoed Grady's sentiment.
"I appreciate [the governor's] approach of bringing forth a proposal that attempted to balance state needs, local needs and our business climate," he said. "But we're dealing with an unprecedented situation, and so just as the state is having to tighten the belt. I think local jurisdictions are going to be in a similar place this upcoming year."

title: Town Council holds off on confirming County Council vice president to utilities commission
author: Konner Metz
content:
Town Council holds off on confirming County Council vice president to utilities commission

 March 6, 2025 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: Konner Metz | Section: Local News 
 
 597
 Words 

 Read News Document

 EASTON — While board and commission appointments typically pass by the Easton Town Council with little to no discussion, such was not the case at Monday's meeting.Some councilmembers raised concerns over Mayor Megan Cook's appointment of Pete Lesher to the Easton Utilities Commission, ultimately deciding to hold off on confirming that appointment. Lesher is the vice president of the Talbot County Council.
Town Council President Frank Gunsallus asked Cook if her appointment went through staff review. Cook said it went through a review process with Easton Utilities and she met with John Horner, the nonprofit's president and CEO.
Gunsallus asked if Lesher would step down from his county seat. "I do not believe so," Cook responded.
"He swore an oath to the county, and sometimes we have competing interests," Gunsallus later said. "And he can't have two masters. I think there will be a conflict when land needs to be resumed for solar, as is currently in the legislature. So I think that that is something that we should be considering."
Lesher was appointed to fill the role of current commission member Buck Duncan, whose term expires this May.
Town Attorney Sharon VanEmburgh said at Monday's meeting it wasn't fully clear whether there were legal issues with Lesher being on the County Council and potentially the Easton Utilities Commission.
VanEmburgh said the state's constitution doesn't allow someone to hold two "trust and profit" offices. The question in need of answering is whether the commission post would be considered such.
"I think we would probably get to the conclusion that it is not a second office of trust and profit," VanEmburgh said. "But I just don't know."
Gunsallus suggested the appointment go through both the town and county's ethics commissions. Ward 1 Councilmember Maureen Curry said if VanEmburgh returns with an opinion that supports the appointment as legal, she sees "no need for an ethics review on a local basis."
Ward 4 Councilmember the Rev. Elmer Davis said it's "vital and important" for the town to ensure it's "on the right side of the law." Councilmembers agreed to address Lesher's appointment at the town's next meeting once legal advice is obtained.
"As always, we respect the Mayor and support the members of the Town Council and their decisions," Horner wrote in a statement Wednesday. "The appointment and confirmation of an Easton Utilities' Commissioner is an essential step in ensuring the efficient and effective management of our operations."
OTHER APPOINTMENTS
During the discussion, Ward 3 Councilmember David Montgomery said he feels appointments are already a "rubber stamp" by the time they hit the council's desk.
"I would really like to have an opportunity to have some discussion with the mayor … in an executive session," Montgomery said, "just to hear your thoughts about different candidates rather than always having one candidate put in front of us."
Cook said during appointment processes, there's a "lot of thought" that goes into candidates and resumes.
"It's not something that we take lightly," Cook said.
Montgomery said he hopes the opportunity for such conversations will be afforded to the council during interviews for the town manager role. Cook said the council will have chances to meet candidates, adding that there will be full-day interviews.
It's been seven months since the town parted with its most recent full-time manager, Don Richardson, on Aug. 5, 2024. Police Chief Alan Lowrey has served in an interim capacity since.
Last December, Easton announced it opened a search for a new town manager. The town secured the services of the professional recruitment agency Sumter Local Government Consulting.
Wednesday, Cook told The Star Democrat that the town has narrowed its search down to a group of semifinalists.

title: Talbot County provides first look at draft budget for FY26
author: Konner Metz
content:
Talbot County provides first look at draft budget for FY26

 March 7, 2025 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: Konner Metz | Section: Local News 
 
 474
 Words 

 Read News Document

 EASTON — Talbot County Manager Clay Stamp said one aspect was clear when drafting the county's fiscal year 2026 budget: it needed to remain flat.Speaking with the Talbot County Council at a workshop Tuesday, county employees presented a balanced draft budget coming in at $163.3 million. It comes in slightly below last year's budget of $163.8 million.
The county's total budget has ballooned in recent years. In fiscal year 2023, it was $112 million, and one year later, it rose to $128 million. It took a sharper jump to the $163 million mark last year.
Stamp said the increases were for good cause. "You've made incredible and important investments in public safety and education," he told council members.
But Stamp emphasized that given federal uncertainties, state cost shifts and recurring county costs, it is important to curb that recent upward trend.
"That was a mandate as we put this budget together," Stamp said of the belt-tightening.
Stamp said the draft fiscal year 2026 budget currently proposes no additional job positions. The county's capital improvement plan is also trimmed back, he said. He hopes the county can focus on finishing projects already underway, such as Chapel District Elementary School renovations and a new EMS station in Cordova.
When drafting the budget, Stamp and Finance Director Martha Sparks said they initially came in $6 million over their target. To remedy that, they're proposing delayed payments for postemployment benefits and correctional officers' retirements, respectively — the latter of which is to be expected to be included in fiscal year 2027.
Sparks mentioned that tax hikes proposed at the state level for wealthy individuals may have an impact on Talbot County revenues. Sparks said last time a similar tax increase was levied in 2009, it made a significant dent, partly due to the recession.
"We had an exodus of the wealthy in our county as a result of that," Sparks said. "And it took us approximately 10 years to recover."
Sparks added, however, that the county looks OK for fiscal year 2026 in terms of those tax proposals. She said she's "not sure what that will look like for us moving forward."
As for policy and funding shifts at the federal level, Stamp said "it's reasonable" to expect impacts will trickle down to Talbot County.
"We are cognizant of that," Stamp said. "Radars are up, antennas are up. We're watching closely."
The draft budget shows $55 million in funding for the Talbot Board of Education. Stamp said the county must contribute that mark since it's required by state funding formulas. Any additional education funding is left for the County Council to consider in the coming weeks.
Council members and staff will hold a number of workshops this month and in April before a budget proposal is officially introduced April 15.
Public budget hearings are scheduled for May 6, and the County Council is expected to enact a budget ordinance May 27.

title: Hundreds protest Rep. Harris, Trump outside Tidewater Inn in Easton
author: Konner Metz
content:
Hundreds protest Rep. Harris, Trump outside Tidewater Inn in Easton

 March 7, 2025 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: Konner Metz | Section: Local News 
 
 437
 Words 

 Read News Document

 EASTON — Hundreds lined Dover and Harrison streets Thursday evening, protesting Rep. Andy Harris (R-Md., 1st) and the Trump administration outside a fundraiser hosted by Harris at the Tidewater Inn.By 5 p.m., a large crowd gathered outside the Talbot County Democratic Party headquarters and began walking down sidewalks and past the Tidewater.
They repeated chants of "Andy Harris has got to go" and "fire Andy Harris." Some called for the congressman, who represents the Eastern Shore of Maryland, to host a town hall.
Phil Jackson, chair of the Talbot Democratic Central Committee, said Harris is "absolutely failing to represent Talbot County."
"Andy Harris has historically done very little for the Eastern Shore," Jackson said. "... I think this is indicative of a very strong desire for new leadership."
By 6:30 p.m., Harris' event inside the inn continued and most of the crowd had dispersed. The large crowd did not appear to encounter Harris at any point Thursday evening.
Following his event, Harris told The Star Democrat that the Eastern Shore elected him and President Donald Trump, and that he's "delivering on President Trump's agenda."
Among the president's agenda items raised by protesters Thursday was the Department of Government Efficiency, Elon Musk and mass firings of federal workers. Many of the more than 300 protesters held signs opposing DOGE.
"I think folks have had enough with the current administration and the overreach and behavior we're seeing right now," Jackson said.
Harris, meanwhile, said the cuts are necessary due to a federal deficit nearing $2 trillion.
"If they want to help us with some way to make the government more efficient — other than actually letting go of people whose jobs are probably not contributing to government efficiency — I'm all ears," Harris said of those who oppose the firings. "But they're not offering solutions."
"I feel bad for anyone who's losing a job, but I'm hoping with the economic growth we have, we're going to provide plenty of private sector jobs for those leaving the federal government," he added.
Harris, who chairs the House Freedom Caucus, met with Trump at the White House Wednesday. He said people at his fundraiser Thursday were excited to hear about what's going on in Washington, D.C.
"I told them some of what it's like to be sitting next to the leader of the free world," Harris said.
Outside the Tidewater, the tenor from protesters was much different. The crowd of hundreds loudly cheered as cars drove by and honked in support of the protest.
Jackson was pleased with the large turnout and says the protest was a "tipping point."
"It's really reached an egregious point," Jackson said. "And I think people are really upset about it."

title: 'A milestone': Demolition of Talbot County Business Center a big step for Easton Airport
author: Konner Metz
content:
'A milestone': Demolition of Talbot County Business Center a big step for Easton Airport

 March 7, 2025 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: Konner Metz | Section: Local News 
 
 308
 Words 

 Read News Document

 EASTON — Wednesday morning, the Town of Easton granted Reynolds Excavating Inc. a demolition permit to begin work on the former Talbot County Business Center.Later that day, demolition had already begun.
The clearing of the property is part of the second phase of Easton Airport's airfield modernization project, a long-term effort to improve the airport's safety and operations.
Micah Risher, Easton Airport's manager, said the demolition is a major step in the modernization efforts, which began in 2006.
"This is a milestone," Risher said. "We've been waiting for 20 years to get to this point."
Once cleared, the site will become a runway protection zone, meant to improve safety in case of an aircraft crash or extended landing.
The business center, previously a Black & Decker facility, saw its tenants move out in 2023 and 2024, all of whom successfully relocated.
Thursday, significant work on the building's southwest end nearest to Glebe Road was underway. The building's exterior and roof were in the process of being torn down.
Risher noted that an environmental report was completed to ensure demolition is handled properly. Testing and mitigation measures were taken to abide by state and federal regulations.
Risher said the site will mostly be made up of open, green space, along with airfield lighting.
"It's a big environmental improvement project," Risher said.
Additionally, scrap materials from the building will be reused, Risher said. Asphalt and concrete will be crushed and repurposed for the new airfield, while aluminum will be recycled by Reynolds Excavating.
Easton Airport will continue operations during demolition. The building is expected to be mostly demolished later this spring, with site work and recycling continuing throughout the year.
Risher expressed excitement that the demolition is underway. He said it's a step forward in swapping one economic driver, the former business center, for a new one, the runway zone and overall airfield upgrade.
"The reality is it's being transformed," Risher said.

title: State says no to granite curbs in Maryland town
author: Jane Bellmyer jbellmyer@cecilwhig.com

State says no to granite curbs in Maryland town

 In the struggle between historic sidewalks in Port Deposit and the Americans with Disabilities Act, the ADA wins, according to the Maryland State Highway Administration.SHA has two projects in progress in Port Deposit; one to remediate flooding and the second to make stretches of sidewalk handicapped accessible. This will mean either leveling heaving granite stones or removing them entirely.
Vicky Rinkerman, town administrator, said that in this early phase SHA engineers have reported that the town's existing historic granite sidewalks and curbing are central to the study.
"Their intent is to keep as much granite as possible," Rinkerman said. "However, they are looking for the most ADA compliant sidewalks."
That, she said, will mean a loss of granite curbing in areas where that ADA compliance will come into play. She added that the engineers offered no suggestions to the town on how to preserve what is not part of the project scope.
"We may look at other towns," she said.
One section of sidewalk on the north end of town will likely shift to skirt a utility pole. While many homes along Port Deposit's Main Street come right up to the sidewalk, Rinkerman said 145 North Main has some wiggle room. That will allow for a wider sidewalk in that area.
Meanwhile, the SHA's drainage remediation study is also early in its process but town officials are voicing concern. Rinkerman will meet with SHA March 20.
"We will be asking about the culverts," she told the mayor and town council. "We want to confirm their exact plan designs for the drain in Vannort Drive."
Questions to be answered by the SHA include whether or not there would there be a flap gate to prevent back flow, and if the catch basin and the drain pipe need to be enlarged.
Rinkerman said the town has time to prove its case with SHA since the state agency won't begin any physical work until 2027 at the earliest.

title: Federal layoffs come home to Oxford
author: Maggie Trovato
content:
Federal layoffs come home to Oxford

 March 8, 2025 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: Maggie Trovato | Section: Local News 
 
 926
 Words 

 Read News Document

 OXFORD — Marine scientist Sierra Hildebrandt had about 30 minutes on Feb. 27 before her government computer and access to her email were revoked at the Cooperative Oxford Laboratory.Hildebrandt had just learned that she'd been terminated from her dream job with the National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration.
"I cried," she said about learning the news.
Hildebrandt was one of two NOAA scientists fired from the Oxford lab that day. The two represented a 15% reduction of the lab's total workforce, both state and federal.
"We're already a small lab," Hildebrandt said. She said with the two terminations, there are only two remaining federal employees and one federal government contractor at the Oxford lab who do field work.
Hildebrandt and environmental scientist Jake Shaner, who also was fired from his position at the Oxford lab, were not alone. At least 800 employees across NOAA have lost their jobs since Feb. 27, part of the Trump administration's move to reduce the size of the government. According to the Associated Press, President Donald Trump has called the size of the federal government "bloated."
In an email to The Star Democrat, NOAA public affairs specialist Jasmine Blackwell said she could not discuss "internal personnel and management matters." She said NOAA remains dedicated to its mission of "providing timely information, research and resources that serve the American public and ensure our nation's environmental and economic resilience."
THE IMPACT ON OXFORDAlthough NOAA is known for gathering weather data, the agency does more than that.
At the Cooperative Oxford Laboratory, scientists monitor water quality, tides and the presence of vibrio, which can cause fatal food poisonings, in oyster populations. The lab — which is Oxford's largest employer — works on an array of projects, from oyster restoration to evaluating nature-based solutions like living shorelines.
At the time that Hildebrandt and Shaner were let go, they were implementing a water quality monitoring station in Oxford with another scientist. Shaner said the monitoring station gathers tide data, helping Oxford determine when flooding is likely.
"So that falls off immediately," Shaner said, explaining that leaving one scientist to maintain the station alone would be difficult.
Hildebrandt and Shaner were the only two scientists at the lab working with the Town of Oxford to evaluate the Strand Beach project, a project to create a living shoreline on Oxford's waterfront. Hildebrandt said their job was to understand how the already implemented shoreline was providing coastal protection and additional ecosystem benefits.
Oxford Town Manager Holly Wahl said the loss of Shaner and Hildebrandt from the lab is having an impact on the completion of that project. She said the lab is engrained in the town and surrounding areas.
"When we have the largest employer in town facing terminations, I think that directly will absolutely impact the town from an economic standpoint," Wahl said. "As well as just the economic standpoint of having that innovation and research directly accessible to the town to continue to make improvements to protect property, to protect vital critical resources that we're providing to citizens."
Oxford Commission President Norm Bell said this situation shows Oxford and the Eastern Shore are not isolated from the rest of the country.
"We're really starting to grapple with what do we do longer term so that we can survive as sea levels rise (and) storm water levels rise," he said.
Bell said the work Hildebrandt and Shaner were doing in Oxford was helping the town address those water-related concerns.
THE BIG PICTUREShaner had been working at the Cooperative Oxford Laboratory — which is utilized by NOAA, the Maryland Department of Natural Resources and the U.S. Coast Guard — since 2016. Although Shaner had about nine years under his belt at the lab, eight of them were spent as a state employee. At the time of his termination, Shaner was considered a probationary federal employee.
St. Michaels resident and deep-sea ecologist Andrew Thaler works with NOAA scientists and uses the agency's data. He said that when employees are hired, they are put on a period of probation before they can receive tenure. He said the probation period repeats when someone switches jobs within the federal government.
"So if you get promoted to a management level position, your probation block starts over," he said. "So many people were fired who were senior in the administration."
At the U.S. Department of Agriculture, more than 5,000 probationary employees were temporarily reinstated to their positions via a federal board ruling Wednesday after the employees had been terminated in February. The ruling was determined based on "reasonable grounds" to believe the agency "committed a prohibited personnel practice."
According to the Congressional Research Service, factors that should be taken into account with reductions in force include tenure of employment, military preference, length of service and efficiency or performance ratings. The service states agencies are "generally required" to provide written notice to affected employees 60 days in advance of the date of release.
Hildebrandt said she understands layoffs occur, but she said her and Shaner were well-performing employees.
"I think I wouldn't be as heartbroken if this was done the correct way," she said. "And if both of us were not performing very well in our jobs."
WHAT'S NEXT?"A NOAA job is a dream job for a lot of marine scientists," Thaler said.
Both Hildebrandt and Shaner have filled out forms to volunteer at the lab so they can continue to work on the projects they had been working on in a volunteer capacity.
Shaner said the terminations at the Oxford lab are a resource lost for the community.
"You're losing skilled people that live here, care about the Eastern Shore and the Chesapeake Bay and want to fix problems," he said.

title: After heated meeting, Talbot County retains DEI statement by 3-2 vote
author: Konner Metz
content:
After heated meeting, Talbot County retains DEI statement by 3-2 vote

 March 12, 2025 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: Konner Metz | Section: Local News 
 
 995
 Words 

 Read News Document

 EASTON — During a charged meeting that saw council members exchange remarks and three members of the public asked to leave for speaking out of turn, the Talbot County Council rejected a resolution to repeal the county's DEI statement.Although tensions eased by the meeting's end Tuesday night, council members had heated back-and-forth before voting 3-2 against the resolution sponsored by Dave Stepp.
Council President Chuck Callahan joined Stepp in favoring the resolution. Vice President Pete Lesher and council members Keasha Haythe and Lynn Mielke opposed.
Stepp contends the resolution will protect Talbot County's federal funding after a Jan. 20 executive order from the Trump administration to end all diversity, equity and inclusion policies and programs in the federal government.
Stepp said he's heard from many county employees that want the diversity statement repealed. He called it a "political stunt" for the measure to be voted down.
"You simply choose to go against the oath of office you took when you took this office," Stepp said of the three council members who voted against.
Haythe, Lesher and Mielke contested Stepp's claims.
"We really were not going to go there tonight because all five of us have agreed to sit here and tell the truth, the whole truth and nothing but the truth," Haythe said. "And in some of those statements, the truth was not told."
She said she hasn't heard from any county employees who want the statement removed.
"What we are not going to do as this council is stand here and accept the lies that are pushed down from the federal government to our local community," Haythe said. "We are not doing that."
The failed resolution would have repealed two 2020 resolutions — the first developed the county's diversity statement found in the employee handbook, and the second implemented an annual report of diversity training offered to staff.
Stepp said that an email to the council from Talbot County Sheriff Joe Gamble, a Republican, stated a grant for police work in Trappe is at risk due to the county's DEI statement.
Lesher disagreed, stating that Trump's executive order "does not deprive federal funds for our airport modernization, for rural development or for policing."
"Those funds are not in peril," Lesher said.
"So you're saying the sheriff is lying?" Stepp responded.
Prior to the vote, Haythe added her support for diversity training, saying it helps people identify their underlying biases, including herself.
"Council members should go through diversity training as well," Haythe said. "We all should, because there is bias. There's bias on this council. I've received it."
SPLIT PUBLIC
At the council's Feb. 26 meeting during which the matter was tabled, more than 100 residents attended, most speaking against Stepp's resolution. Tuesday, public opinion was split.
At one point, Stepp motioned to move public comment so it occurred before the council's vote. Callahan seconded, but the rest of the council disagreed.
Some residents expressed displeasure the vote would be held before their comments. Stepp said "the three council members didn't want those to speak in the audience."
Haythe responded, pointing out that the council did not move up public comment at its last meeting.
"We had public comment in the same order at our last meeting, and we did not move anything to the front," Haythe said.
Many residents opposing DEI attended Tuesday's meeting. Lori Stepp, chair of the Talbot County Republican Central Committee and Dave Stepp's wife, said the DEI statement including equity and inclusion doesn't line up with the original 2020 resolution that only mentioned diversity in its text.
"That's not what the original council voted on," she said in an interview. "So unfortunately, I'm not sure how the equity and inclusion piece got thrown in there for the county employees."
Easton resident Brandi Whiting said DEI is "here for a reason" and that she's seen it make a positive impact in her experiences hiring for different companies.
"If you want to sell your morals for money, you go right ahead," Whiting said during public comment. "But I'm glad that at least three of our council people did not."
Resident Shari Wilcoxon called out Haythe, Lesher and Mielke for voting against Stepp's resolution.
"If we do indeed lose these funds that you have now put in jeopardy, it is on the three of you ... who rolled the dice for all Talbot County citizens," Wilcoxon said.
Following her comments, Wilcoxon and another resident expressed disagreement from their seats with Haythe while Callahan and a third resident went back and forth. "You've been a problem all night," Callahan told the third resident.
After Callahan initially requested only the third resident leave the room, Haythe said to him that the others who spoke from their seats out of turn should be asked to leave as well.
Callahan then asked the other two residents to leave. While deputies escorted the third resident out, the other two left on their own.
MOVING ON
Rhetoric toned down once public comment closed, as council members ensured they will continue to work together in the future.
"I don't think any minds got changed, but I appreciate the public engagement," Lesher said.
Stepp said he still wished public comment was moved up. "But I thank those who did stick around to make sure that those comments, you were able to get them out," he said.
Haythe and Callahan said the council will move on as a unified group.
"Once we take a vote, we're done and we move on. That's it," Haythe said. "And we still continue to be friends."
Callahan thanked county staff for supporting the council during the controversial last two weeks and expressed appreciation for fellow council members.
"I really appreciate you putting your thoughts together," Callahan told Stepp. "It takes a lot of bravery to do that. It really, really does. And Keasha, the same way with you.
"But at the end of the day, it's over, we've made a decision and we all move on."
This story has been updated to clarify that three residents were asked to leave during the public comment portion of the meeting for speaking out of turn. Police escorted one person while the other two left on their own.

title: Cambridge shares progress on Douglas Street houses
author: Maggie Trovato
content:
Cambridge shares progress on Douglas Street houses

 March 12, 2025 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: Maggie Trovato | Section: Local News

 CAMBRIDGE — Those walking down Douglas Street this summer might see new homeowners sitting on spacious porches, looking out onto Cornish Park as kids run around and play.A city project to build four homes on Douglas Street in Cambridge's historic Pine Street neighborhood has been underway since September. Cambridge Housing Program Manager Ed Crosby said the city expects construction on all four houses to be complete by June 30.
These custom houses will be energy efficient and have features that make them feel like home, from oak staircases to crown molding.
"We wanted folks to take a sense of pride," Crosby said.
This project is one way the city is improving its housing stock, uplifting the community and fostering a culture where residents want to stay in Cambridge.
The houses on Douglas Street will be sold at 80% of area median income to people who qualify based on income and standards by the U.S. Department of Housing and Urban Development. Crosby said prospective buyers will have to complete homebuyer education training.
Three of the four homes getting built on Douglas Street will have three bedrooms. The fourth home will have four bedrooms and follow accessibility guidelines from the Americans with Disabilities Act, including having a ramp.
In all of the houses, features include electric fireplaces and washer and dryer units. Each house will have backyard space with a shed.
Crosby said the homes will be listed in the low $200,000s, with the most expensive home possibly reaching $250,000 in price. In February, the median selling price for homes in Cambridge was $276,000, according to Realtor.com.
On March 4, those working on the houses were putting up drywall. Gregory Beard, the general contractor for the project, said the next steps will be painting, putting in flooring, installing trim and bringing in subcontractors to install fixtures, hardware and plumbing.
"Things are coming together great," Beard said. "Fantastic build. It's a fun project."
Crosby hopes the city will have the property listed online this month.
"There's an excitement brewing that we're just ready to move forward with this," he said.
Although the properties could be purchased by people who don't live in Cambridge, Crosby said the city has made an "intentional effort" to market the homes to city residents before listing them. He said there are at least 30 Cambridge residents who have shown interest in the homes and have applied to buy one.
In late February, the city gave tours to show the construction progress to the Cambridge City Council and the Maryland Department of Housing and Community Development. Crosby said the tours gave attendees an opportunity to learn more about the project from the developer, architect, engineers and contractors.
During the tours, some commissioners gave the city ideas on how to ensure the homes are not flipped or purchased by landlords to turn into rentals, Crosby said.
"You can actually write that into the deed where there's a requirement that the city could get what is called the right of first sale," he said. "So if it comes to a point and the homeowner's interested in selling, the city would have the opportunity to actually purchase the property back and then keep it under that 80% of AMI program so that we can continue to have it available as affordable housing."
After the city finishes building the Douglas Street houses, it plans to build at least 10 more homes on Chesapeake Court and School House Lane. Crosby said this project will help inform the city on how to go about building more houses.
"And from this blueprint, we'll learn how the next set of homes will be," he said.

title: Emergency cannabis bill discussed at Caroline commissioners meeting
author: AHMAD GARNETT agarnett@chespub.com
content:
Emergency cannabis bill discussed at Caroline commissioners meeting

 March 12, 2025 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: AHMAD GARNETT agarnett@chespub.com | Section: News 
 
 522
 Words 

 Read News Document

 DENTON — The Caroline County Commissioners held the first reading of an emergency cannabis legislative bill and the introduction of permit zoning on property legislative bill at Tuesday's meeting.The emergency cannabis bill is proposed to allow Caroline County to get on track with regulations and requirements of from the state.
The adjustments are being made as a result of House Bill 805, a 2024 bill that established zoning requirements for cannabis businesses that are more restrictive than some that existed prior to the legalization of recreational cannabis in the state.
The state regulation mandates that cannabis dispensaries cannot be located within 500 feet of schools, child care center, programs, recreation centers, libraries, public parks or churches.
At last week's meeting, Commissioners Vice President Larry Porter suggested a zoning map be created to show the zoning locations for the proposed emergency cannabis bill.
While Caroline County Director of Planning and Codes Crystal Dadds is still working on the zoning map, Porter made a suggestion on increasing the distance for dispensaries from schools.
"My concern is the dispensaries, I don't think 500 feet is enough," Porter said. "Im particularly concerned about the schools."
The 500 feet distance of schools, child care center, programs, recreation centers, libraries, public parks or churches is mandated by the state.
While dispensaries will only be allowed to be located in C1 and C2 commercial zoning districts, some schools in Caroline County are close to commercial zoning districts.
"I don't think we will ever run into a situation where a dispensary is that close to a school," County Commissioners President Travis Breeding said, "but to Commissioner Porter's point, 500 feet is not enough."
The county could be at legal liability if they decide to mandate that the buffer between cannabis businesses and schools will be bigger.
"So what will happen if you enact an ordinance with a greater distance and someone applies within the 500 feet and they are denied, it would be an appeal by the judge to rule in favor of the applicant," County Attorney Stewart Barroll said. "Or somebody can file suit against the county stating their ordinance is invalid."
The officials will discuss all avenues of the proposed bills and make some revisions before making a final decision.
The county commissioners also discussed a new section to denials of a zoning legislative bill. The new section will allow the Department of Planning and Codes to deny applications if an applicant is not within code or zoning compliance of the county on that same property.
"If you had a violation on your property, let's say you put a pool in without a permit and it's unresolved," Batts said, "now you come in and you want to seek a permit for something else, we would not grant that permit until you updated or gotten your proper permits for the other structure."
If a resident comes into fix a violation, the county will permit to allow the resolution of the violation.
Also covered in the proposed bill if an applicant has multiple properties they can apply for permits on one property and not be denied because of a violation on another property.
Both proposed bills will move on for the first and second reading.

title: Rally held in Cambridge demanding Harris hold town hall

 CAMBRIDGE — Chants of "Where is Andy?" and "AWOL Andy" sounded outside the Hyatt Regency Chesapeake Bay Golf Resort, Spa and Marina Thursday evening as people lined the sidewalks with signs.Cambridge Indivisible — a chapter of a national organization that aims to elect progressive leaders — held a rally outside the entrance of the Hyatt to demand Rep. Andy Harris (R-Md. 1st) hold a town hall.
The rally was held before Harris was set to take the stage at the Hyatt as the keynote speaker for the 79th annual Dorchester Chamber of Commerce Business Meeting and Dinner.
Cambridge Indivisible Founder and Chair Michelle Fowle said Harris' constituents "just want answers."
"Andy Harris refuses to meet with us for a town hall," she said. "He's locked us out of his office. He won't talk to us."
Myra Orme Frost, who held a sign on the sidewalk as cars honked their horns, said her concern is that Harris' agenda is more aligned with Department of Government Efficiency head Elon Musk than with his constituents.
Those at the rally voiced concerns over veterans affairs and mass firings of federal workers.
Charles Breitschwerdt, a Republican, had not participated in political rallies before this year. He expressed concerns with the information coming from the Trump administration, calling it lies.
This is not the first rally that has been held on the Mid-Shore this month to criticize Harris. Last week, hundreds lined Dover and Harrison streets in Easton protesting Harris and the Trump administration outside a fundraiser hosted by Harris at the Tidewater Inn.
Fowle said Harris' "inaction" will only increase their action.
"They're just waiting for us to throw up our hands and say there's nothing that we can do," she said. "But there's a lot that we can do. And it's to show up, it's to call him out, it's to speak truth to power. And we are not going to stop until all of this ends."
Before the rally, Cambridge Police Chief Justin Todd said the Cambridge Police Department was aware of plans for the rally and were in communication with the Hyatt. Todd said the department wanted to ensure everyone's safety, including those attending the rally and those attending the Dorchester Chamber event.
Speaking to members of the media after the chamber dinner, Harris said he didn't believe many of the people at the rally were his constituents. He said he believed the protesters were paid and brought in by buses.
Harris said he will be holding a virtual town hall on March 25 so he can communicate with constituents from all over his district.
"If these protesters want to call in, if they want to get on my town hall, I will answer that question on my town hall," he said. "But I'm not going to hold a town hall for 100 people when I could hold a town hall and reach out to 5,000 people who don't have to leave their homes, get bused in by some entity paying for that bus."

 OXFORD — In an effort to address flooding caused by rainy day events, Oxford is looking into setting up portable stormwater pump stations across town.During a Commissioners of Oxford meeting Tuesday, engineer Wayne Newton presented plans to install four temporary, portable pump stations in three locations in town: Two stations near the causeway, one station at Bank Street and one station at Mill Street.
Newton is the president of Messick & Associates, an engineering firm the town has a contract with. He said he expects the pump stations will relieve moderate flooding, which he defined as anything less than storm surge.
"A storm surge comes in, it comes over the bulkhead, it comes over the causeway, that's not what we're planning for here," he said. "We're just planning for rainy day events."
Oxford Wastewater Superintendent Matt Ozman, who has been working closely with Newton, said the pumps will allow the town to drain water faster.
"It's the plan of moving the water where it's not going to take us days, it'll be hours," Ozman said.
Oxford Commission President Norm Bell said the town is trying to take a step back, look at what it would like to see in the future and determine what is needed today in order to build toward that.
"So this is more of a holistic viewpoint than what we've been looking at previously," he said.
Commissioner Tom Costigan said the portable pump stations are more flexible than permanent pump stations in the ground.
"You can take our solution and move it to where the problem is instead of having a problem and saying, 'Oh, well we've got this really neat pump station eight blocks away,'" he said.
Along with placing portable pump stations in the low-lying areas Newton identified, Newton also outlined plans to address the existing drain system on Mill Street that runs through the marina. He said he would like to re-grade and rebuild some of the drain system so water drains toward the water tower and the pump station can be moved to that area.
"We'd prefer (the pump station) to be down there," Newton said about the area where the water tower is. "There's more room for it down there."
Newton said over the next month, his office plans to work on designs and cost estimates for the project that he can bring back to the commissioners for review. He said his goal is to have the project complete by the end of 2025.
The project will be funded using American Rescue Plan Act funds.
Ozman considers this project to be laying the foundation when it comes to addressing flooding issues. He said the town can hone in on these three areas first, then address flooding in other areas.
"We're trying to do the best that we can with the money that's available at the time without having to spend millions on something that can't be moved, can't be touched, can't be retrofitted," he said.

 DENTON — On Tuesday evening, the Caroline County Commissioners held the first public hearing for the county's fiscal year 2026 budget.At the workshop, agencies presented their needs for more money for salary raises and equipment repairs and replacements. But the commissioners are facing tight budget constraints.
"We just want to take input from from all the agencies that are asking here straight from them," Commission President Travis Breeding said. "Learn what their priorities are ... to help us educate ourselves and make informed decisions on what they need."
At a Caroline County Commissioners meeting in February, the draft FY 2026 budget presented showed the county could be facing around a $900,000 shortfall this budget season.
After the first FY26 budget roundtable, that number has increased. The county is expected to bring in $77 million in revenue, while the proposed fiscal year budget is projected to be $79 million, leaving a $2 million shortfall.
"We gotta find $2 million in cuts somewhere basically," Caroline County Commissioners President Travis Breeding said. "We still have tough decisions to make, well evaluate everyone's testimony and well do what we think is best."
While majority of the public comment Tuesday was thanking the commissioners for their work, the commissioners offered some insight on property tax rates.
"I don't think the property tax rate has been raised in nine years," Larry Porter Caroline County Commissioners Vice President said. "For the people who say my taxes go up every year, your taxes go up because of the assessment, we don't control assessments."
"The only number we control up here is the property tax rate and we have held the line for nine years, and my guess is we will hold it this year."
Residents may still have to pay more in property taxes regardless if the rate remains the same because if the assessment values have risen the rate is applied to those values.
While the property tax rate may not go up the commissioners understand that many changes must be made to keep up with the states requirements for the counties.
"Sooner or later I don't know if its reasonable to think planning, budgeting and looking at cost is gonna be enough, if the state keeps shoving expenses and cost down the line to us," Porter said.

title: Commissioners of Oxford table voting resolution
author: Maggie Trovato
content:
Commissioners of Oxford table voting resolution

 March 13, 2025 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: Maggie Trovato | Section: Local News 
 
 426
 Words 

 Read News Document

 OXFORD — Although at the start of a Commissioners of Oxford discussion Tuesday Commission President Norm Bell recommended the commissioners vote that evening on a resolution to clarify the town's voting registration requirements, the commissioners tabled the resolution in a two to one vote."In order to get this right, I think we need more time," Commissioner Katrina Greer said. "I think it would be better to do nothing and write some rules for the election committee, which we can do without a charter change."
The now tabled resolution would amend the town's charter to clarify a person must register with the Talbot County Board of Elections to qualify as a voter in the town. This means a resident would not be able to vote in Oxford town elections if they aren't registered with the county board.
Before the vote was taken, Bell expressed concern that if the resolution is not voted on at the meeting, it could be delayed to the point where, if the resolution is passed, it is not in effect for the town's upcoming election in June when Commissioner Tom Costigan's term is set to expire.
But Bell, who ultimately voted in favor of tabling the resolution, acknowledged the commissioners should not rush into making amendments to the charter regarding voting.
At a public hearing for the resolution Feb. 25, residents shared thoughts on who should and shouldn't be considered eligible to vote in town elections. The discussion, which opened the doors to potential additional charter amendments, led commissioners to hold a work session March 5.
Greer said the work session brought a lot of input, and she said there were still a lot of questions.
"I do not want to pass this in a rush tonight," she said Tuesday.
Costigan, the only commissioner to vote against tabling the resolution, said he felt the resolution addressed a "flaw" in the charter's verbiage.
"All that it did was recognize that the Talbot County system was the most logical way to assure that people are eligible and can vote," he said, adding that the concerns around who is eligible to vote would need to be addressed in another section of the charter.
After the resolution was tabled, Town Attorney Lyndsey Ryan suggested the commissioners write rules for the Oxford Election Board regarding registration, absentee ballots and poll watching.
"The last election we had a livestream for individuals to watch," she said. "If you're going to follow that process again, we should have something established."
Greer said they should hold a work session on the matter, and Bell agreed that a work session should be scheduled.
