Wahl said Underwood and Associates is required to complete this phase of the project by April 19.
In December, the Commissioners of Oxford announced that although the Strand Beach project was signed off on in June by previous Town Manager Cheryl Lewis, the project had not been completed to the specifications that Underwood and Associates had originally presented.
The plan for the project was to create a berm, place hooks along the east and west areas of the Strand to bring in sand, create small islands in the water to reduce waves coming onto the beach and plant low marsh grasses on those islands. During the commissioners meeting in December, Commissioner Katrina Greer said not all the grasses had been planted on the islands and the islands were two feet higher in elevation than they were supposed to be.
That month, Greer brought together the Maryland Department of the Environment, the U.S. Army Corps of Engineers, Underwood and Associates and the organizations that funded the project to ensure Underwood and Associates would bring down the elevation of the islands and take out the sand that goes out to the headlands at no cost to the town.

title: Cambridge mayor aims to reach 'every pocket' of city with new committee
author: Maggie Trovato
content:
Cambridge mayor aims to reach 'every pocket' of city with new committee

 April 3, 2025 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: Maggie Trovato | Section: Local News 
 
 585
 Words 

 Read News Document

 CAMBRIDGE — Cambridge Mayor Lajan Cephas wants to make sure she is hearing from an array of voices in her community."I want to make sure I understand the perspective of everyone in this community," Cephas told The Star Democrat. "It's very difficult being one person doing that."
To make that goal a more achievable one, Cephas is creating a Mayor's Accessibility Committee that she envisions will bring residents with different experiences to one table. She said she believes the committee will help ensure voices from every part of the community are heard.
"So that's the sole purpose," Cephas said. "It's just to make sure that we provide a space and equal opportunity for all in this community so they have a seat at this table."
At a Cambridge City Council meeting in late January, Cephas shared her intentions to create the Mayor's Office of Initiatives. She said she envisions the office made up of volunteers who "operate in support of the mayor."
In January, Cephas said she envisioned having roughly four different committees to ensure different voices in the community are heard. March 25, Cephas told the Star Democrat she now would like to focus on executing the Mayor's Accessibility Committee.
She said if the need for another committee is determined later on, the Accessibility Committee can make a recommendation to the Cambridge City Council to form that committee.
On March 24, the City Council passed a resolution to adopt the Mayor's Accessibility Committee with an amendment to ensure the committee does not incur costs to the city.
According to council documents, the committee will be tasked with providing recommendations to city commissioners and the city manager on how the city can make its communications more accessible to residents with "limited to no English proficiency." The committee will also be tasked with making recommendations on how the city can improve access to its facilities for people with disabilities.
According to council documents, the committee will consist of seven members — the mayor and six city residents. The residents will be appointed by the mayor and will need to be approved by the city's commissioners.
Cephas said the committee will be subject to the Maryland Open Meetings Act. She said meeting minutes will be forwarded to the city to be posted on the city's website.
Cephas believes this committee will help her "be the best mayor" she can be for "every pocket of the city."
In an interview, Cephas said she doesn't have certain people in mind for the committee, but she does have certain specialties and skills in mind.
Along with residents who have translation skills, she mentioned residents who have experience with economic and workforce development and residents who have knowledge about mental health. She also mentioned having a high school student on the committee who can share the perspective of the city's young residents.
Before the City Council voted in favor of the measure unanimously, multiple commissioners agreed there is a need for the committee. Commissioner Shay Lewis-Sisco talked about the need for translating council information for residents who are more proficient in languages other than English.
"I definitely think the direction of what you're proposing here is needed in terms of engaging the community at large in these conversations," Lewis-Sisco said.
Those interested in joining the committee should look for updates at choosecambridge.com/. Cephas said the city will be adding a place on its website where residents can apply. She said in the meantime, residents can email her at mayor@choosecambridge.com and she will forward the link to the posting on the website when it becomes available.

title: Talbot Planning Commission sends DAF legislation to County Council
author: Konner Metz
content:
Talbot Planning Commission sends DAF legislation to County Council

 April 4, 2025 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: Konner Metz | Section: Local News 
 
 380
 Words 

 Read News Document

 EASTON — The Talbot County Council will soon be considering new restrictions on the storage of food processing residuals.Wednesday, the Talbot County Planning Commission unanimously voted to send a piece of legislation up to the council, deeming it consistent with the county's comprehensive plan.
The legislation aims to help Talbot County fall in line with neighboring counties on restricting the residuals, which are animal waste from food processing that are often applied to farmland as fertilizer.
Under state law, the residuals cannot be applied to land between Dec. 15 and March 1, requiring them to be stored during the winter months.
Last year, Caroline County restricted storage of food processing residuals, often referred to as dissolved air flotation, or DAF, residuals. It came amid significant resident complaints of the noxious odors and bugs that stemmed from farming operations keeping the product in open storage tanks.
Talbot's legislation would ban open-top storage of DAF or food processing residuals. Closed-top storage would be permitted provided it follows the following conditions, among others:
The storage applicant receives site plan approval from the county.The applicant has an approved nutrient management plan from the state.The applicant has at least a 500-foot setback from residential properties, or at least a 200-foot setback if all affected property owners consent.The applicant applies the materials on the same property where they are being stored.The applicant stores and applies the materials in a permitted zoning district.
The legislation would not ban storage of food processing residuals in a temporary storage unit — such as a "mobile, closed container" — near where they are being applied. Such temporary storage would be capped at 90 days.
Before the commission approved the legislation, the body set forth a few minor conditions to be amended.
"The one thing that we do want to make sure is that we exempt food processing residuals that are used for livestock feed," commission member Chip Councell said.
Bryce Yelton, assistant planning officer, said that would be an easy amendment to make, simply by adjusting the definition for food processing residuals in the legislation.
Councell added that the county discussed the DAF legislation with the Talbot County Farm Bureau last August. The farm bureau was supportive, he said.
While the commission is recommending approval to the County Council, the bill will still require a council vote to be enacted.

title: 'You are all God’s gift': Volunteers honored for dedication, service to seniors
author: WILL BONTRAGER wbontrager@chespub.com
content:
'You are all God’s gift': Volunteers honored for dedication, service to seniors

 April 4, 2025 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: WILL BONTRAGER wbontrager@chespub.com | Section: Seniors 
 
 550
 Words 

 Read News Document

 Susan Higgs of Upper Shore Aging Inc. showed appreciation for the many volunteers dedicated to serving the Retired and Senior Volunteer Program, RSVP, of which she is project director."We're a team and I can't say enough. You are all God's gift and I thank you," Higgs said at their annual recognition event on Friday at the Amy Lynn Ferris Adult Activity Center on 200 Schauber Rd.
Upper Shore Aging, Inc., a non-profit organization, is a designated Area Agency on Aging by the State of Maryland, serving over 31,000 seniors in Caroline, Kent and Talbot counties. Over a catered dinner from Out of the Ordinary Catering, run by Robert Yalley, Upper Shore celebrated 50 years of service.
Higgs, using a PowerPoint presentation, showed that when they first began the Retired and Senior Volunteer Program there were only a few cells of busy bees.
But over the years, Kent County has produced more than 100 volunteers, who this year already put in more than 7,000 hours.
Each volunteer agency is called a station with a station manager. The Kent Association of Riding Therapy's (KART) station manager is Sue Caswell. Her volunteering duties involve walking with the horses and helping children with disabilities with them. She said it is an extremely rewarding experience.
Another station is the Museums of Kent, and with 11 museums, it can be a busy one, run by station manager Carolyn Sorge.
The list of Program stations is long in the county and getting longer, Higgs pointed out. Their goal as stations, volunteers or busy bees, is to produce honey, a sweetness to the community — to establish and build connections creating a better quality of life for everyone.
As they do this this year, they face some challenges.
Upper Shore Executive Director Herb Cain pointed out their funding comes from the Maryland Department of Aging, which may be facing federal and state cuts. Cuts to that department means potential cuts to Upper Shore, which may fall to county government to support some programs in their jurisdiction.
Cain has already visited the Kent County Commissioners and expressed his concerns, and so far, all the counties have been supportive, he noted.
But there is a level of uncertainty, he acknowledged, especially in the federal funding.
In this financially unstable environment, Higgs said, volunteers are needed more than ever. Having professional, knowledgeable seniors active and involved benefits the community. Placing older adults in these high-quality positions improves their quality of life as well.
Higgs said with 10,000 baby boomers retiring since COVID-19, isolation and loneliness can set in. Volunteering provides purpose, decreases loneliness and adds a sense of fulfillment.
Higgs' positive energy and optimism is an example of the benefits of volunteering, and she encouraged residents to reach out to them if interested at shiggs@uppershoreaging.org.
Upper Shore Aging's website for the Retired Seniors Volunteer Program, volunteersontheshore.org, is a centralized place for anyone seeking a volunteer opportunity in Kent, Caroline or Talbot counties. The site includes information on the enrollment process and a listing under each county of volunteer opportunities.
In Kent County, a handful of these organizations include the Chester River Hospital Center Auxiliary, Amy Lynn Ferris Adult Activity Center, Meals on Wheels, Kent Association of Riding Therapy (KART) and many more.
"To me this is a very special program. We're still here and making things happen and living life. Look at us now!" Higgs said.

title: Maryland officials worry about 'chaos' to come
author: EMMA TUFO and JACK BOWMAN Capital News Service
content:
Maryland officials worry about 'chaos' to come

 April 8, 2025 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: EMMA TUFO and JACK BOWMAN Capital News Service | Section: State News 
 
 353
 Words 

 Read News Document

 ANNAPOLIS — The Maryland General Assembly just concluded its scheduled spring session, but Democratic leaders are already looking ahead to an uncertain future driven by President Donald Trump's "chaos."In comments to reporters, Gov. Wes Moore boasted about the legislature's accomplishments — stressing that Trump's shadow still looms.
"You cannot talk about those things without acknowledging the chaos that is taking place in Washington, D.C.," Moore told reporters.
Maryland could potentially lose the new FBI building it was supposed to get, while also facing stock market volatility and a tariff policy Moore described as a "national sales tax."
"While I'm thankful for the progress we've made in this session, we know that protecting Marylanders, and caring for Marylanders and defending Marylanders does not happen over 90 days," Moore said.
Lawmakers in the waning hours of the session announced the formation of a Joint Federal Action Oversight Committee, a bipartisan group will be tasked with monitoring the ripple effects of the federal government on Maryland.
Senate President Bill Ferguson (D-Baltimore City) told reporters lawmakers have spent this session bracing for external threats.
"We have been working this year to protect the state of Maryland against the draconian slash and burn actions of the Trump administration," Ferguson said. "And with Elon Musk, who has been talking about efficiency, but really destroying Marylanders' lives."
Fear of Trump and Musk's plans also loomed large in the minds of Democrats on the Senate floor, as debate heated up in advance of Monday's midnight deadline for adjournment.
In a conversation about how to help laid-off federal workers, Sen. Jim Rosapepe argued that it's hard to work out cost estimates in the current political climate.
"It's hard to estimate this because we don't know how much damage Mr. Musk and his merry band are going to do," said Rosapepe (D-Prince George's, Anne Arundel).
Senate Republican Leader Stephen Hershey (R-Kent, Queen Anne's, Cecil, Caroline) interrupted to say, "I know, you've said that a few times."
Rosapepe raised his voice.
"That's the important point here," he said. "It's unclear what these people in Washington are doing to our state."
"We know it's bad," he said, "but we don't know how bad it's going to be."

title: Caroline County enacts cannabis and permit emergency bills
author: AHMAD GARNETT agarnett@chespub.com
content:
Caroline County enacts cannabis and permit emergency bills

 April 8, 2025 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: AHMAD GARNETT agarnett@chespub.com | Section: News 
 
 305
 Words 

 Read News Document

 DENTON — The Caroline County Commissioners held the third reading for emergency legislative bills on cannabis facilities and permit denials. Both emergency bills were enacted.The emergency cannabis bill was proposed to allow Caroline County to get on track with regulations and requirements of from the state.
Adjustments were required to county legislation as a result of House Bill 805, a 2024 state bill establishing zoning requirements for cannabis businesses that are more restrictive than some that existed prior to the legalization of recreational cannabis in the state.
The state regulation mandates cannabis dispensaries cannot be located within 500 feet of schools, child care center programs, recreation centers, libraries, public parks or churches.
The county commissioners discussed potentially increasing the distance mandates further than 500 feet.
Commission Vice President Larry Porter brought attention to the distance because of the close proximity to schools in the county.
All dispensaries are required to be in the C2 district of the county, which leaves two schools in close proximity of the district.
"The only two areas we found was in Denton close to Lockerman Middle School. It is outside that 500 feet setback requirement," Caroline County Director of Planning and Codes Crystal Dadds said. "Then over by Denton Elementary school, but still outside the 500 feet setback requirement."
In response, the commissioners decided to keep the 500 foot mandate.
Permit Denials
The second emergency bill passed at the meeting added a new section to county legislation that will allow the Department of Planning and Codes to deny applications for new work if an applicant is not within code or zoning compliance on that same property.
If a resident comes into fix a violation, the county will permit to allow the resolution of the violation.
If an applicant has multiple properties, they can apply for permits on one property and not be denied because of a violation on another property.

title: Maryland session concludes with balanced budget
author: Marissa Yelenik and Sofia Appolonio Capital News Service
content:
Maryland session concludes with balanced budget

 April 8, 2025 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: Marissa Yelenik and Sofia Appolonio Capital News Service | Section: State News 
 
 1120
 Words 

 Read News Document

 ANNAPOLIS — Maryland lawmakers passed a budget on Monday, concluding their spring session after months of grappling with a tough fiscal reality and new federal policies.The end-of-session agreement hikes taxes and cuts programs to balance the spending plan for the 2026 fiscal year, assuming the federal funding picture does not change radically in the months to come.
Lawmakers made the budget work partly by trimming back the Blueprint for Maryland's Future, the ambitious 2021 education reform plan meant to improve public schools. Architects of the deal said the changes will preserve the Blueprint's priorities.
"We present a budget that puts Maryland in a strong fiscal position and faces the challenges ahead while protecting our shared values and priorities," said Senate Budget and Taxation Chair Guy Guzzone. (D-Howard).
But House Minority Whip Del. Jesse Pippy (R-Frederick, Carroll) argued that the plan unnecessarily burdens taxpayers.
"A majority of my colleagues feel very strongly that we could have balanced the budget without raising taxes," Pippy said. "I don't think the direction of the state is the direction that most Marylanders want to go in."
Republicans made their mark on legislative work in the opening months of the new presidential administration, which helped give rise to the newly formed Maryland Freedom Caucus.
Still, the Democrat-controlled legislature generally opposed President Donald Trump's policies.
The state — home to the most federal workers in the country outside of Washington, D.C. — likely faces continuing challenges with the Trump administration's mass government layoffs. At present, one Democratic leader said, the number of fired workers in Maryland stands at about 11,000.
"We expect that number to climb to 30,000, and there are many more contractors, probably at least double that amount," said Sen. Katie Fry Hester (D-Howard, Montgomery).
The legislature might have to reconvene at some point this year to cope with unemployment and changes in federal policy affecting Maryland. For now, though, the General Assembly has settled a range of issues.
BUDGET
The $67 billion spending plan addresses a significant deficit through approximately $2 billion in spending cuts and $1.6 billion in tax changes.
The budget raises income taxes on the state's higher earners, extends the sales tax to certain technology services and introduces a $5 tire fee. It includes two new tax brackets, increases the standard deduction, phases out itemized deductions for those in higher tax brackets and includes tax hikes on individual goods and services.
Many lawmakers celebrated its passage, but some said increasing the standard deduction would lead to service cuts in lower-income counties that rely on the income tax of low- and middle-income residents. The finalized plan will now go to Moore for consideration.
ENERGY
Energy was a hot topic this session as lawmakers worked to address high energy prices. They passed a three-bill package on Monday.
The package focuses on new in-state energy generation, ratepayer protections and reforms, solar siting and permitting and the creation of a state energy planning office. It outlines procurement processes for nuclear, battery storage and dispatchable energy, and removes trash incineration from the state's Renewable Portfolio Standard.
"I think, on balance, it's a good package," said Sen. Brian Feldman (D-Montgomery), chair of the Senate Education, Energy and the Environment committee.
The package initially drew criticism from environmental advocates, who were concerned one of the bills would lead to new natural gas development in the state. But the Chesapeake Climate Action Network Action Fund praised the bill as passed, saying in a statement that it "will likely reduce the chance of new gas plant construction in the state and … will advance a host of clean energy priorities," including battery storage.
Republican critics worry that the package doesn't do enough to help ratepayers.
EDUCATION
Blueprint funding was the subject of debate during the legislative session. In January, Moore proposed short-term cuts to mitigate the cost of the massive education plan, pushing back and pausing funding for different programs.
The education budget came under even more scrutiny late in the session when an expected $418 million in federal funds was suddenly in jeopardy. U.S. Secretary of Education Linda McMahon announced the end of a pandemic-era fund for state educational spending.
As it stands, state lawmakers agreed to postpone the Blueprint requirement that teachers receive a set amount of planning every school week, delaying it for three years. Additional Blueprint funding was decreased through freezes and cuts.
JUSTICE SYSTEM
Lawmakers passed a bill to let prisoners access medical or geriatric parole more easily by allowing them to prove they are no longer a threat to others. It would not apply to those serving life sentences without parole or those on the sex offender registry. Geriatric parole would only be available to those over 65 who have served at least 20 years of their sentence.
Lawmakers also approved the Maryland Second Look Act, which aimed to reduce the sentences of some inmates with good behavior credits.
A proposal to scale back the state's practice of automatically sentencing teen offenders as adults in violent crimes stalled in committee. The bill faced pushback from law enforcement over concerns that the Department of Juvenile Services couldn't accommodate juveniles with "complex problems."
PRIVACY
Concerns over the Trump administration's immigration policy encouraged some lawmakers to propose the Maryland Data Privacy Act to prevent law enforcement and other local officials from sharing sensitive data with immigration officers. The bill failed to receive enough support.
Despite concerns about unregulated police drones, lawmakers decided not to advance a proposal to set guidelines for law enforcement uses of aerial surveillance.
DISABILITIES
Lawmakers passed Eric's ID Law — a measure allowing individuals with invisible disabilities to include a sticker on the bottom of their license, identification or moped operator's permit. The notation is meant to improve interactions and communication with law enforcement.
REPARATIONS
Maryland lawmakers approved the creation of a commission to study the impact of slavery after years of debate and consideration. The Maryland Reparations Commission would make recommendations to the state legislature, providing guidance on what, if any, benefits should be given to those impacted by historical inequality by November 2027.
SEX ABUSE
After emotional deliberation, lawmakers voted to downsize the monetary compensation the state can provide for sexual abuse lawsuits, amending the amount survivors can file for under the 2023 Child Victims Act.
GENDER-AFFIRMING CARE
Republicans introduced a bill that would have made it a felony for a healthcare provider to give hormone replacement therapy to any minor, but the measure did not pass.
If passed, the Fairness in Girls' Sports Act would have required both public schools and the nonpublic schools that compete against them to separate sports teams based on the team members' sex assigned at birth. Similar legislation has been introduced since 2022.
The General Assembly turned away a bill to allow "X" as a sex designation on birth certificates for transgender and nonbinary individuals.
CNS reporters Rachel McCrea, Emma Tufo, Sasha Allen, Paul Kiefer, Adriana Navarro and Jack Bowman also contributed to this piece.

 EASTON — With less than 30 days until Easton's election, candidates for Town Council president are racking up endorsements, including from fellow council members and local officials.Incumbent Frank Gunsallus is squaring off against Don Abbatiello, the current Ward 2 representative. The election, which is nonpartisan, is set for May 6.
Abbatiello has received endorsements from council members Maureen Curry and David Montgomery, the latter coming as a surprise to some residents. Gunsallus has been endorsed by Talbot County Sheriff Joe Gamble.
Montgomery, Ward 3 representative, told The Star Democrat on Monday that he believes Abbatiello is the "best leader" for the town's future.
"Don and I have not always agreed on everything or voted the same way," Montgomery said. "But he has always been willing to sit down to listen to my reasons for my position, to talk about his reasons for his position and to try to work out something that is satisfactory to both of us."
Montgomery has previously voted alongside Gunsallus against items such as a permit for the Delmarva Pride Festival and a paper bag fee, though Gunsallus most recently voted in favor of the Pride Festival permit for 2025.
But Montgomery says he is more closely aligned with Abbatiello on most issues, including the need to slow "excessive growth" and an inclusionary zoning ordinance that council has debated but not voted on.
"I think neither of us sees the inclusive zoning ordinance as the best way of going out and providing affordable housing," Montgomery said.
In a statement, Curry said Abbatiello "has the skill set, the maturity, commitment and level thinking abilities needed to guide the council."
Meanwhile, Gamble announced his endorsement of Gunsallus last month, citing the current president's "unwavering commitment to both his family and this town."
"I am confident in Frank's ability to continue leading Easton in the right direction," Gamble wrote in his endorsement. "… I trust that he will continue to serve our community with the care, thoughtfulness, and dedication that has defined his service over the years."
Abbatiello has been endorsed by former Mayor Bob Willey and former Easton fire chief Sonny Jones. Abbatiello is a longtime member of the Easton fire department.
The town's election will take place May 6 from 7 a.m. to 8 p.m. at the Easton Volunteer Fire Department on Leonard Rieck Drive.

title: Easton accepts transfer of Easton Village roads, hears resident concerns
author: Konner Metz
content:
Easton accepts transfer of Easton Village roads, hears resident concerns

 April 9, 2025 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: Konner Metz | Section: Local News 
 
 502
 Words 

 Read News Document

 EASTON — The Easton Town Council accepted ownership Monday of roads in the Easton Village development, though the transfer of the roads was met with safety concerns from residents.Located off of Easton Parkway and Saint Michaels Road, the neighborhood sits adjacent to the Tred Avon River. Council members unanimously agreed to take on ownership of 28 roads, alleys and rights-of-way, as well as nearly nine acres of open and park space located in the development.
The town will assume responsibility for upkeep of the roads. Town attorney Sharon VanEmburgh said the town is working on a memorandum of understanding to outline how the town and homeowners association will split park maintenance duties.
The conveyance was contingent on the developers, Easton Village LLC, completing a list of work, such as sidewalk, street lights and land restoration improvements. Town officials said most of that work has been done.
But most of Monday's discussion — as well as back-and-forth at a town meeting last month — centered around safety concerns from residents at two Easton Village homes and why a shared driveway between their homes isn't designated as an alley.
Resident Marc Ebersberger said since the lane next to his residence is designated as a shared driveway, his home isn't easily located on GPS systems. He and his neighbors said there have been multiple health emergencies during which response was delayed or they flagged down responders who could not locate the home.
"Twenty minutes could be the difference between permanent disability or recovery, or between life and death," Ebersberger said.
Ebersberger said by sifting through meeting minutes he found the Planning Commission voted not to allow shared driveways to move forward in Easton Village in 2016.
Ryan Showalter, an attorney representing Easton Village LLC, said the two lots and their shared driveway was recorded on a plat in 2015 before the Planning Commission held any discussion of shared driveways.
Town attorney Sharon VanEmburgh said Monday the town believed the issue with Ebersberger was resolved in 2023. She said town staff isn't looking for the shared driveway designation to be changed since "it's not set up to be an alley."
She said shared driveways are still allowed per subdivision regulations.
Town Council members agreed the safety concerns are imminent, though they largely emphasized that approving the road and park transfers was a separate issue from residents' requests.
Ward 4 Councilmember the Rev. Elmer Davis asked to move forward with the conveyances while noting residents "need to be heard."
"It sounds like to me the can has been kicked down the road and it's been kicked down a little too long," Davis said.
"If we're talking about a life safety issue, this should be a no-brainer," Ward 1 Councilmember Maureen Curry said.
After approving the road and park transfers, the council passed a motion for town engineers to install a street sign and light near the homes in question in the next 60 days. Mayor Megan Cook added she would reach out to Talbot County Emergency Services to discuss how dispatchers can improve response times to the Easton Village homes.

title: Neighborhood Service Center in $300,000 hole amid federal funding uncertainty
author: Konner Metz
content:
Neighborhood Service Center in $300,000 hole amid federal funding uncertainty

 April 12, 2025 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: Konner Metz | Section: Local News 
 
 686
 Words 

 Read News Document

 EASTON — In her 15 years at the Neighborhood Service Center, Marilyn Neal has never faced a financial obstacle like the one the nonprofit is up against now.A delayed grant reimbursement is leaving the organization $300,000 in the hole. The center's leaders say the financial uncertainty has caused panic, sleepless nights and fear.
"Fear that we close the doors and our staff can't work," Neal said, "fear that we can't give food to a family."
Located on Port Street, the Neighborhood Service Center is a go-to for low-income residents, seniors and families. It lends emergency financial support on electric and rent bills. Staff run a daily food pantry and mobile food pantry. The nonprofit provides case managers to work directly with the county's most vulnerable populations.
The center is designated as Talbot County's community action agency, meaning its most consistent federal funding comes from a Community Services Block Grant.
That grant is administered by the federal Administration for Children & Families, a division of Health and Human Services, along with the Maryland Department of Housing and Community Development at the state level.
Neighborhood Service Center leaders say they've been working around that "fully executed grant," which hasn't been reimbursed yet. They expected to start receiving funds for this year's first two quarters by the end of December. That didn't happen.
In a statement Friday, the Department of Housing and Community Development said it received payment from the federal government this week for its first and second quarter block grants. First quarter funds were delayed, and payments to local agencies are in the process of approval. Second quarter funds will be on time, DHCD stated.
In the meantime, the service center says the holdup is leaving it $302,000 short, forcing it to pull from contingency funds.
Sitting across from one another late Thursday morning, Neal and fiscal officer Kathy Taylor discussed which cost-saving strategies are being implemented and the additional belt-tightening that might be on the way.
The nonprofit's 13-member staff is already trimming its hours. Full-time staff are down from 40-hour to 32-hour weeks, and part-time stuff have cut back from five to two days a week.
There's been discussion around how the nonprofit would operate with only three staff members and whether after-school offerings or programs for formerly incarcerated fathers have to shut down.
"Everything we do stabilizes a household," Neal said. "And when we don't have those funds and we don't have the Neighborhood Service Center in Talbot County, I don't know what this county looks like."
ASKING FOR HELP
Earlier this week, Neal, Taylor and many staff members attended a Talbot County Council meeting to request $150,000 in county assistance to fill the gaps presented by the reimbursement delay.
"The money's tightening down now," County Manager Clay Stamp said. "But the need is not tightening down. They run everything on a shoestring."
Council members were largely supportive of the center's work, but they remained steadfast in keeping fiscal responsibility at top of mind. Council members Keasha Haythe and Lynn Mielke preferred the council hold off on any promises until it came to understand how town governments may be helping the center financially.
Haythe asked if the center has a long-term sustainability plan or money in savings. Neal said the center operates by drawing on its available funds to help families in poverty at any given moment, making it hard to save a specific amount.
"We're scaling back," Council President Chuck Callahan, who also serves as chairman of the service center's board, said at the meeting. " … I think we also need a plan for the future on how we stabilize the Neighborhood Service Center."
The council partially fulfilled Neal's request, giving the center $50,000, which won't put the county's budget in any danger, Stamp noted.
Despite the shortened hours and growing uncertainty, Neighborhood Service Center staff have remained dedicated to their work.
To Neal, it all starts with the staff members and how their compassion spreads into the community. Taylor feels that now more than ever.
"We struggle with that balance of, 'OK should we leave?'" Taylor said. "But we don't want to because we love what we do and the impact on the community that we have."
To learn more, visit https://nsctalbotmd.org/.

title: Sample-Hughes: profile in courage in Annapolis
author: DAVID REEL
content:
Sample-Hughes: profile in courage in Annapolis

 April 12, 2025 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: DAVID REEL | Section: Columns 
 
 813
 Words 

 Read News Document

 Shortly after the Maryland General Assembly convened in January for their 2025 session, I wrote a commentary with the title — "Doing the right thing and consequences in Annapolis."My example of doing the right thing was Democratic state Del. Sheree Sample-Hughes refusing late in the 2023 legislative session to vote for legislation in the House of Delegates favored by the House Democratic leadership.
When asked why she did so, she said simply that she was being respectful of and responsive to the views of her constituents who opposed that legislation.
My example of consequences for doing the right thing was Del. Sample-Hughes being replaced on the first day of the 2024 session as the speaker pro tempore in the House of Delegates, the second highest leadership position for a member of the majority party.
It did not matter that she was eminently qualified for her former leadership position.
After serving two terms as a member of the Wicomico County Council, she has represented Dorchester and Wicomico counties in the House of Delegates since Jan. 14, 2015.
In the House, she has served as a member of following key committees — Economic Matters, Judiciary, Rules and Executive Nominations, Health and Government Operations, Spending Affordability and the Joint Committee on Administrative, Executive and Legislative Review.
She also has served as the House of Delegates representative to the Rural Maryland Council. This council focuses on bringing together citizens, community-based organizations, federal, state, county and municipal government officials, as well as representatives of the for-profit and non-profit sectors to collectively address the unique needs of rural Maryland communities.
This council also provides a venue for members of agriculture and natural resource-based industries, health care facilities, educational institutions, economic and community development organizations, for-profit and non-profit corporations and government agencies to cross traditional boundaries, share information and address in a more holistic way the special needs and opportunities in rural Maryland.
When asked how she felt about her abrupt dismissal as speaker pro tempore, Delegate Sample-Hughes said, "Where we are today, is that I stood by my convictions and stood up for my constituents. The phone calls and the emails that I received last session on three bills that were, you know, top bills in the state, but I still had to vote my district."
Adding insult to injury, Del. Sample-Hughes' replacement as speaker pro tempore was and is a delegate from a district in Baltimore.
Last week, Del. Sample-Hughes again stood up for the two counties of her Eastern Shore district as well as for all of the Eastern Shore.
In a floor speech described by one observer as passionate and fiery, she spoke against the House version of a $67 billion state budget, in part because the current version of the bill needs a wide range of new taxes, tax increases, new fees, fee increases and budget cuts to meet the state constitutional mandate that the state budget be balanced.
In her remarks, Del. Sample-Hughes challenged a once oft-stated guiding principle in Annapolis — always do what is best for everybody in Maryland. She said bluntly, "This institution is not for everybody. This proposed budget will disproportionately impact rural counties, like those on the Eastern Shore."
As one example she noted the Dorchester County Public Schools has cut summer school programs in order to fund state mandates to implement the Blueprint for Maryland's Future, often referred to as the Kirwan plan.
Del. Sample-Hughes did more than speak against a budget crafted and embraced by the Democratic leadership in the House of Delegates.
She "walked her talk."
She was one of only three Democratic members in the House of Delegates to join all the House Republican House members in voting no on the House version of a state budget.
In a media interview following her speech, she was asked if she feared retaliation for again voting against legislation crafted and supported by her party's leadership.
She replied with a blend of disheartening realism, resignation and defiance to those who choose to punish, rather than respect her commitment to listen and respond to the concerns and opinions of her constituents. She reiterated her belief expressed earlier in her floor speech.
"History repeats itself. I'm sure there will be [retaliation], but at the end of the day, I'm going to be fine. I'm going to continue to be me. I'm not going to change who I am."
We can hope she will never change who she is.
The battle on state budget matters is finally over. A compromise version of a state budget and funding sources for was approved by the General Assembly on Monday, April 7.
That is not the end of the story.
Next year and into future years the General Assembly and the governor will very likely need to address significant state budget deficits.
Now more than ever, we need to support Del. Sample-Hughes and like-minded colleagues on both sides of the aisle in Annapolis for their unwavering commitments to do the right thing despite the potential for consequences.

title: As Easton election nears, campaign finance transparency discussion sparks
author: Maggie Trovato
content:
As Easton election nears, campaign finance transparency discussion sparks

 April 15, 2025 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: Maggie Trovato | Section: Local News 
 
 621
 Words 

 Read News Document

 EASTON — With a little less than a month until Easton residents elect their next council president, incumbent Frank Gunsallus said he is voluntarily reporting his campaign finances.Gunsallus' announcement came after Easton Mayor Megan Cook and Councilmember David Montgomery shared their efforts to draft a town ordinance related to campaign finances.
The ordinance would require campaign contributions be reported and would limit the amount someone can contribute to a campaign. The town doesn't currently have any campaign finance-related laws in place.
In an interview with The Star Democrat Monday, Cook said they hope to introduce a draft ordinance at the next Easton Town Council meeting April 21.
"We've been receiving questions from residents and neighbors," Cook said, "and here's a way that we can move forward and better the election process for the community."
Although Cook said this effort is an attempt to address an "overall general concern" that isn't specific to any one campaign, Montgomery raised concerns with the upcoming town election, which is set for May 6.
"In my opinion, the elections before this have largely been financed by the candidates themselves," he said. "The candidates have gotten out knocking on doors, sometimes through media, frequently in forums that are put on. ... Nobody before this has tried to flood the town and the roads all over the county with signs and other ways of publicizing their name."
"We don't want that to determine who wins," he said.
GUNSALLUS' STATEMENT
Gunsallus' statement, which he sent to The Star Democrat Monday afternoon, says he "agrees with and joins hands with" Cook and Montgomery in their efforts to ensure there is more transparency surrounding campaign finances.
"Transparency builds trust, and that's why I have made the conscious decision to voluntarily report my campaign finances annually through the Maryland Campaign Reporting Information System (MDCRIS)," the statement says. "All citizens are welcome to go to this public website at (https://campaignfinance.maryland.gov/Public/ViewCommittees) and review all elected officials' financial reporting. Open, consistent financial disclosure is essential to maintaining public confidence in our local government."
Gunsallus said he has been reporting campaign finance information on the website for years.
As of early Monday evening, the Friends of Frank Gunsallus page showed campaign activity from Jan. 11, 2024, through Jan. 8, 2025. Gunsallus announced his reelection campaign in December.
As of Jan. 8, the committee had paid $639 to APG Chesapeake, which owns The Star Democrat, for political advertising. The website showed only two contributions, each under $50, from individuals.
Current Ward 2 Councilmember Don Abbatiello, who is running against Gunsallus for the council president seat, said he thinks transparency with campaign finances is important at every level of government.
"I think it's important that the residents, the voters know exactly who's donating to the candidates that they're thinking about voting for," he said.
Abbatiello said he wouldn't have a problem sharing his campaign finances with the public.
"I don't have any political party support in this race or any kind of political action committee," he said, "so it's all been from individuals donating to the campaign."
Abbatiello said he hasn't heard concerns from voters specific to campaign finances in the town's upcoming election.
"I know there were some people questioning about the number of signs around town," he said. "But nobody questioning specifically, 'Where'd the money come from?'"
Along with the council president seat, candidates are vying for Ward 2 and Ward 4 council seats. In Ward 2, Lynnette D. Keefe and Robert J. Rankin will go head to head. In Ward 4, the race is between incumbent the Rev. Elmer Davis, Moonyene S. Jackson-Amis and Cameron Keefe.
If the council votes to introduce a campaign finance ordinance, a public hearing will need to be scheduled before the council can pass it. As a result, it is unlikely to take effect before the May 6 election.

title: Proposed resolution sets off tense discussion at Cambridge meeting
author: Maggie Trovato
content:
Proposed resolution sets off tense discussion at Cambridge meeting

 April 16, 2025 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: Maggie Trovato | Section: Local News 
 
 470
 Words 

 Read News Document

 CAMBRIDGE — Tensions flared at the April 14 Cambridge City Council meeting over a proposed resolution directing the city manager to analyze the city's human resources capabilities and follow a specific process when hiring staff.The resolution was ultimately tabled.
Commissioner Frank Stout, who brought the resolution to the council, said he saw the resolution as a way to standardize the hiring process and ensure the city completes a broad search for job candidates, citing previous meeting discussions on the topic.
City Manager Glenn Steckman said he was not consulted about the resolution before it was sent to him. He said much of what is outlined in the resolution is already part of the city's process.
"I will tell you, I'm not real happy about this," he said. "It has bothered me through the weekend. And I appreciate the commissioners that hired me. They know about my experience."
Steckman was hired prior to the city's November election, after which several new faces were added to the council.
Bringing up part of the resolution that encourages the city manager to "expand recruitment efforts beyond internal applicants to include external candidates," Steckman said he's heard from city staff that they think the council wants to take opportunities away from them.
He said with most organizations, including the city, there is a five-day window where employees can apply to a job posting before the posting is made public. After the five days, management can make a decision about whether to expand the search externally, Steckman said.
"I'm not exactly sure why I need a resolution to tell me what I already know how to do," he said.
Stout said he sees the resolution as a way to "put words around" what the council had discussed in previous meetings.
"I don't want there to be anything misconstrued that I don't have full faith and confidence in city staff," he said.
Commissioner Brian Roche agreed with Stout's resolution, saying none of the language was "detrimental" and it just put into words what the council said it wanted to see.
Before calling on the commissioners to make a motion to table the resolution indefinitely, Mayor Lajan Cephas cut off discussion and spoke about the value of city employees.
As she spoke, Stout asked her to "please" not "steer" the discussion "in a different direction," and Cephas responded, "I didn't interrupt you when you were speaking, so can you please provide me the same respect?"
After talking about the importance of having opportunities for promotion in a workplace, Cephas said although she doesn't have a vote in council matters, she has a voice.
"I'm going to stand up for city employees every single time," she said.
Not long after Cephas' comments, the council opted in a 3-2 vote to table the resolution until after June 30, which will mark the end of the budget process. Stout and Roche voted against the motion.

title: DON ABBATIELLO
author: Konner Metz
content:
DON ABBATIELLO

 April 16, 2025 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: Konner Metz | Section: Don Abbatiello 
 
 713

 Email: don.m.abbatiello@gmail.comAge: 48
Family: Married 23 years/ Son 19 years old/ Daughter 16 years old
Education: Bachelor's degree in education from Salisbury University, masters degree in history from Salisbury University
Occupation: Public school teacher for 27 years
Previous political experience: Six years as Easton Town Council Ward 2 representative
1. Why are you running for Easton Town Council president?
I'm running for council president because elections should be about options, not just be a coronation. It's important to offer voters a choice.
I want to bring a collaborative, consensus-building leadership style to the council and to be a leader who listens. Good leadership is about teamwork — no matter how strong your ideas are, they won't move forward without support from your fellow council members. I believe I can lead with respect and cooperation to help guide thoughtful decisions that reflect the needs of our residents.
2. What issues will you prioritize if elected?
My priorities are smart development, public safety and fiscal responsibility. Easton is growing fast, and we need to manage that growth and avoid unnecessary development.
I support limiting annexation until we ensure infrastructure can support our current development. For large redevelopment projects, the Town Council needs to be included in the decision making.
I'll prioritize support for our police and fire departments — funding, staffing and equipment must be maintained to support first-class service. Health care access is another major concern. I want to work with medical partners to attract more doctors.
I will ensure we continue balanced budgets, prioritizing services residents rely on without wasting taxpayers' money.
3. While the town has grown, affordable housing remains a challenge for residents. How should the town build more housing, in particular affordable housing?
There's no one-size-fits-all solution to affordable housing, but we must be proactive. I'd work closely with partners like the Affordable Housing Board and Habitat for Humanity to explore opportunities for creating starter homes. Zoning tools, incentives for developers and creative use of town-owned properties could also play a role. We need to support a mix of housing types to serve working families, young professionals and seniors. It's important to balance affordability with quality in the community.
4. The town has seen increased development in its downtown core as well as on Route 50. How should the town prepare for the impacts of such growth?
To prepare for Easton's growth, we need a strong, forward-thinking plan that addresses traffic, infrastructure and public services. New development should not outpace our ability to support it. Council members must be actively involved in major project decisions, particularly those with large impacts. Developers should be responsible for mitigating traffic and parking issues their projects may cause. Infrastructure improvements should be timed with development, not after. Transparency, community input and smart land-use policies are key to guiding growth in a way that keeps Easton a livable, vibrant town and preserves our way of life.
5. What are your plans for public safety in Easton? What can be improved?
Strong public safety services are essential to maintaining Easton as a safe and welcoming place for families, businesses and visitors.
I support increasing the presence of police on the rail trails, in parks and at community events to ensure safety and visibility. I support expanding our public camera system to deter crime and aid investigations. Our police need competitive benefits, including improved pensions, to attract and retain top talent.
Our volunteer fire department needs to be supported with the best equipment. I'm incredibly proud of the Easton Volunteer Fire Department's regional training campus that will better prepare our emergency responders and reduce training costs.
6. What have you accomplished during your time on the council thus far? How will you seek to continue those efforts?
During my time on the council, I've supported initiatives that improve quality of life and promote responsible government. I've worked to expand walkability, including sidewalk and crosswalk improvements. I've brought new playgrounds and improved old ones in my ward. We've passed balanced budgets every year without raising the property tax rate. I helped implement the take-home car program for Easton Police, an important recruitment and retention tool. I've focused on community-based policies that are practical and sustainable.

title: Talbot County introduces $161M budget with a focus on conservatism
author: Konner Metz
content:
Talbot County introduces $161M budget with a focus on conservatism

 April 16, 2025 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: Konner Metz | Section: Local News 
 
 718
 Words 

 Read News Document

 EASTON — Talbot County officials introduced a $161 million budget proposal Tuesday, emphasizing their intention to flatten spending after multiple years of significant increases.Tuesday's proposal is balanced at around $2 million below last year's total budget.
"This year, you are introducing a budget that is flat from last year at this point in time, which was a hard task, and I commend you for doing that," County Manager Clay Stamp told County Council members.
Three fiscal years ago, the county's budget was $112 million before it rose to $128 million one year later and $163 million last year. The county is continuing to focus on building a stable fund reserve, an effort that has peaked in the last three years, Stamp said.
In addition to smoothing out recent hikes, Stamp said this year's budget considers threats it faces from federal and state government spending cuts.
"There's some severe federal policy shifts going on right now," Stamp said. "The state of Maryland is passing funding obligations down to (county) governments."
One obligation Talbot County will assume, pending an amendment to the proposed budget, is $440,000 in teachers' pension payments. Finance Director Martha Sparks noted the county worked with state legislators to add language to the law "in the eleventh hour" during this year's General Assembly.
Talbot County would cover that $440,000 through an education supplement tax. The supplement to the property tax would be less than half a cent per $100 of assessed value.
Overall, the real property tax rate is proposed at 79 cents per $100 of assessed value, nearly even with last year's total rate. The tax bill on a home valued at $300,000 would increase by $4.80 from last year, county officials said.
The county will bring in a projected $67 million in property tax revenue in fiscal year 2026, up from $60 million last year (not including the education supplement tax). That's a 12.3% increase, which stems from rising property value reassessments.
"As undesirable as it is to raise taxes, our tax increases by our charter's design are moderate increases and are reflected in our standing as the county with the lowest property tax rate in the state of Maryland," Sparks said.
The proposed budget includes $55 million in funding for Talbot County Public Schools, a mark required by the state's funding plans in its expansive education initiative, The Blueprint for Maryland's Future.
The county did not include the district's request for $5.7 million in additional funding to help with teacher salary increases and new positions, among other requests. Vice President Pete Lesher urged the council to do so at a previous workshop, but the rest of the council opted to hold off. The budget ordinance could be amended to include some or all of that request.
Stamp said despite the flattened budget, capital upgrades aren't stalling. He pointed to projects such as the St. Michaels library branch upgrade, moving the county's public safety complex and continuing renovations at Chapel District Elementary School.
Sparks noted the county is in a "healthy financial position" thanks to fiscal year 2025 revenues exceeding projections by around $8 million. The added revenue is largely due to income tax distributions from the state coming in higher than expected, Sparks said.
A similar situation with the income tax revenue isn't a guarantee for next fiscal year, she said.
Tax hikes to the state's most wealthy, part of Gov. Wes Moore's plan to close an over $3 billion state budget deficit, were enacted by the General Assembly this month. Those increases could drive wealthy residents out of Talbot County to surrounding states and reduce income tax revenue, county officials say.
"The last time this type of tax was implemented, Talbot County's income tax revenues decreased by 40% within one year," Sparks said.
Amid looming uncertainty, County Council members thanked Stamp and the financial staff for their work to present a balanced budget ordinance Tuesday.
"Clearly we've still got some storm clouds on the horizon, both from the federal and state budgets (and) impacts on local budgeting." Lesher said. "… We're going into this, as you outlined, in a strong position. I think that this is a sound approach."
Public budget hearings will be held May 6 at 2 p.m. in the Talbot County Courthouse Bradley Meeting Room and 7 p.m. in the Easton High School Cafeteria. The final budget is expected to be passed by the County Council May 27.

title: FRANK GUNSALLUS
author: Konner Metz
content:
FRANK GUNSALLUS

 April 16, 2025 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: Konner Metz | Section: Frank Gunsallus 
 
 772
 Words 

 Read News Document

 Email: fgunsallus@eastonmd.govAge: 36
Family: Wife, Iryna, and daughter, Maria.
Education: Salisbury University and Easton High School
Occupation: Account Manager
Previous political experience: Current Easton Town Council President since 2023. Served on the Talbot County Chamber of Commerce Government Affairs Committee and Mid-Shore Board of Realtors Government Affairs Committee
1. Why are you running for Easton Town Council president?
My core reason for seeking reelection as Easton Town Council president is my inherent and unwavering dedication to serving the community. I believe service to one's fellow citizens is an exceptionally important calling and a fundamental responsibility to make a positive difference.
I am running for reelection because Easton is at a critical point. We are facing serious decisions about housing, growth, infrastructure and public safety that will impact our town's future. I've served the council with a focus on results, not rhetoric. I will continue to provide steady, common-sense leadership that respects the taxpayer, protects our neighborhoods and moves Easton forward.
2. What issues will you prioritize if elected?
I will prioritize four primary issues: defeating the proposed inclusionary zoning ordinance, enhancing public safety, improving infrastructure and increasing government transparency.
The inclusionary zoning ordinance would drive up costs for home builders, discourage investment in our community and negatively impact home values.
I will ensure the police and fire departments receive the necessary funding and support to effectively serve the community.
As we see more development, we need to consider investing in areas like roads, utilities and stormwater management to improve infrastructure.
We must ensure Easton's residents have an in-depth understanding of issues and proposals and why decisions are reached. I will strongly encourage more direct community engagement.
3. While the town has grown, affordable housing remains a challenge for residents. How should the town build more housing, in particular affordable housing?
Inclusionary zoning is not the answer. It restricts supply and raises costs for builders and homebuyers through the redistribution of losses imposed on market-rate units to offset the cost of below-market rate requirements.
Over time this type of legislation can create a deflationary effect, reducing the market value of comparable homes. The town should instead encourage workforce housing by streamlining permitting, offering targeted incentives and considering the removal or deferral of upfront costs when specific housing products are being delivered. I served on the Attainable Housing Task Force, and there are more effective ways to expand workforce housing by collaborating with private and nonprofit partners — without penalizing those who already live here.
4. The town has seen increased development in its downtown core as well as on Route 50. How should the town prepare for the impacts of such growth?
We need to get ahead of the growth, not react to it after the fact. That starts with infrastructure: roads, traffic flow, sewer capacity and stormwater systems all need investment. We also need to be clear-eyed about the fiscal impact of development and make sure projects pay their fair share toward the infrastructure they require. Growth must be managed, which includes enforcing our comprehensive plan and making sure development fits the character and capacity of the area.
5. What are your plans for public safety in Easton? What can be improved?
Public safety is non-negotiable. As Easton grows, the demands on our police and volunteer fire departments grow too. We need to ensure these departments are fully staffed, have modern equipment and receive the training they need. I support data-driven policing and community-based approaches, but that only works if the departments are adequately resourced.
I will lead efforts to explore various options to support our first responders financially, including improving retirement benefits for our public safety personnel by increasing contribution percentages or by exploring enrollment in alternative programs such as Law Enforcement Officers' Pension System, which could strengthen lateral recruitment efforts.
6. What have you accomplished during your time on the council thus far? How will you seek to continue those efforts?
I've supported freedom, family values, public safety, key infrastructure investments and capital improvements. I've worked to improve communication between the town and residents. I've advocated for fiscal responsibility and accountability. I led the effort for the council to formally oppose a bill that would restrict the abilities of law enforcement agencies. I testified publicly in Annapolis against tax increases. I took the initiative to rewrite the council's rules and procedures.
I'll continue asking questions, doing research and making decisions based on what's best for Easton. My primary focus remains on the four items I have prioritized herein and on delivering the best results for the people of Easton.

title: Caroline County discusses Capital Transportation Priorities request
author: AHMAD GARNETT agarnett@chespub.com
content:
Caroline County discusses Capital Transportation Priorities request

 April 16, 2025 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: AHMAD GARNETT agarnett@chespub.com | Section: News 
 
 368
 Words

 DENTON — The Caroline County Commissioners discussed their Capital Transportation Priorities list and drafted a letter to send to the state at their April 15 meeting.The priority list is presented to the state every year to receive funding for road work projects within the county that the commissioners and town officials believes are a priority.
The state will ultimately determine which projects it funds.
PRIORITY A
Priority A for Caroline County is maintaining and improving existing infrastructure. The county asked for a comprehensive resurfacing of Route 313 from Route 404 to Federalsburg, including repairs to pavement, shoulders and stormwater infrastructure.
Next is the completion of the resurfacing project on Route 16 from Lake Drive to Route 404.
Lastly, Caroline County asked for general resurfacing, shoulder repair, drainage improvement and signage upgrades across Caroline County's state road network. Timely investment in these areas will help avoid further deterioration, reduce maintenance costs and significantly improve travel conditions for our residents and businesses, the county said.
PRIORITY B
The county requested Route 404 be widened from Harmony Road to Route 16 East.
Previous phases of this project have led to improved traffic flow and reduced accidents, demonstrating the importance of completing the corridor, the county said in its priorities list.
PRIORITY CCaroline County requested help with rebuilding and resurfacing Route 454 (Crownstone Road) from Marydel to Templeville.
Route 454 is a vital connector for residents in the western part of the county and serves as a gateway to Queen Anne's County. This route has seen substantial wear and requires resurfacing and structural upgrades to ensure safe and dependable travel, the county said.
PRIORITY DThe county requested state assistance with rebuilding and resurfacing Route 313 from Greensboro to Goldsboro.
This is a major north-south route within the county and is essential for local mobility and emergency response, the county said. It added resurfacing and drainage improvements are necessary to restore safe travel conditions and extend the life of the corridor.
PRIORITY ERounding out the county's priority list is an effort to restripe Route 317 and add a right turn lane.
"We propose restriping MD 317 (Burnsville Road) at the intersection of MD 313 to add a right turn lane. This improvement will help enhance traffic flow and improve safety for all drivers," the county said.

While commission President Travis Breeding discussed leaving the definition at "or" instead of "and," the commissioners decided to change the definition to "and" to ensure a facility accomplishes all of these tasks.

title: Dorchester County proposes tax increases to balance FY26 budget
author: Maggie Trovato
content:
Dorchester County proposes tax increases to balance FY26 budget

 April 17, 2025 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: Maggie Trovato | Section: Local News 
 
 633
 Words 

 Read News Document

 CAMBRIDGE — In an effort to address a $6.2 million deficit, the Dorchester County Council introduced a draft fiscal year 2026 budget that raised taxes.The $91.96 million proposed operating budget presented Tuesday includes proposals to increase property taxes, remove the municipal tax differential, increase local income tax and eliminate tax rebates offered to municipalities.
The council will consider these proposals through the remainder of the budget process, which concludes May 20.
The balanced draft budget comes after months of work by county staff to eliminate an estimated $6.2 million operating budget deficit, which the county has said was brought on by cost shifts from the state.
"These are painful decisions," County Manager Jerry Jones said in an interview with The Star Democrat. "But at the end of the day, given the climate and what's being pushed down from the state for us to absorb, sadly it's one of those things we have to do."
GETTING INTO THE NUMBERS
In the draft operating budget, the county is proposing an increase of the real property tax by 3 cents so county residents would pay a rate of $1.03 per $100 of assessed valuation of property.
The proposal to remove the tax differential, or lower property tax rate, for municipalities would mean Cambridge and Hurlock residents would have to pay the full tax rate of $1.03 per $100 of assessed valuation of property.
In the current fiscal year, Cambridge residents pay the county $0.9267 per $100 of assessed valuation of property and Hurlock residents pay $0.9179 per $100 of assessed value.
On properties with a semi-annual tax payment option, the proposal would add a service charge based on a rate of 0.02% applied to unpaid real property taxes due in December.
With the proposed property tax changes to the budget, the county expects to bring in an additional $2.15 million.
The proposed budget would raise the county's income tax rate from 3.2% to 3.3%, generating $600,000 more in revenue.
In another effort to increase revenue, the county voted April 15 to increase its 911 fee to $4.25 per month. This is the second time the rate has been raised this year.
In early March, the council passed a resolution to increase the county fee that residents pay on their cell phone lines from $1.50 to $2 per month. Council Vice President Mike Detmer said in March that he introduced the legislation to increase the fee to $4.25 as a potential way to reduce a budget deficit.
To alleviate the tax and fee increases' impact on seniors, the county is considering expanding its senior tax credit, which offers a 5% deduction on the county tax bill for those who are at least 70 years old and receive the Homeowners' Property Tax Credit. If passed, the expansion would increase that deduction to 10% and expand eligibility to Homeowners' Property Tax Credit recipients who are at least 67 years old.
Proposed expenditure increases include 3% salary increases for airport, solid waste, water and wastewater, courthouse maintenance, courthouse security and Eastern Shore Innovation Center personnel and an increase in spending on the county's 14 volunteer fire companies. The proposed $35,000 total increase to fire companies would add to the county's $1.22 million expenditure on fire companies and advanced life support services.
Proposed cuts to expenditures include the delaying or eliminating funding to nonprofits that request money from the county.
According to the draft grants budget, the county expects to receive a total of $9.78 million in state and federal grants.
At the end of the council meeting April 15, Detmer encouraged residents to come to council meetings or reach out to council members and make their voices and concerns about the budget heard. He said he is available to discuss the budget or just listen.
"It's your budget too," he said.
The first public budget hearing, as well as a meeting with municipalities, will be held May 6.

title: Easton Planning Commission approves Zaxbys on Route 50
author: Konner Metz
content:
Easton Planning Commission approves Zaxbys on Route 50

 April 18, 2025 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: Konner Metz | Section: Local News 
 
 493
 Words 

 Read News Document

 EASTON — The Easton Planning Commission approved a plan to build a Zaxbys restaurant on Route 50 Thursday.Developers for the restaurant largely quelled concerns expressed last month when commission members tabled architectural approval. Those concerns centered on the bright red and blue colors in design renderings.
Thursday, franchise co-owner and Delmarva Real Estate Management Group attorney Curtis Snyder presented colored renderings of an updated design, which includes additional brick around the 2,000-square-foot building. The new renderings were less "cartoonish" in color and more accurately reflect what the building will look like, Snyder said.
Most commission members felt the updated design was an improvement.
"There are some existing businesses that have blues that are much brighter than this," commission member Laurie Forster said. "… I don't think it's unacceptable, and I do think it could be a great addition to the restaurant scene."
The Georgia-based franchise has hundreds of restaurants nationwide and is known for its chicken fingers, wings and signature sauces.
Commission member Tom Klein said the Easton Zaxbys will bring jobs to town and serve as an upgrade to the "eyesore" that is the empty Wendy's building.
"If this went down in flames, I don't know how long it would be before something else came along," Klein said. "So it could be sitting for quite some time like a lot of other empty lots on 50."
Snyder said the Zaxbys building will be smaller than the former Wendy's, allowing for two drive-thru lanes that can accommodate 26 cars at once. "We're confident in getting people in and out," Snyder said in response to a question of whether lines may spill onto the highway.
PUSHBACK
During Thursday's meeting, member Victoria McAndrews criticized the design, saying it's "very garish" compared to other Zaxbys restaurants in the country.
"I'm just not looking at this as an improvement over what was not satisfactory to begin with," McAndrews said.
Snyder said corporate isn't willing to budge on the blue and red colors, part of the company's branding efforts.
McAndrews said the commission is not doing its job by accepting designs pushed down from the corporate level.
"That's in direct conflict with what the (comprehensive) plan says for Easton that we're supposed to strive for, which is not making it look like Anywhere, USA," she said.
"I'm still getting blowback from corporate over this design," Snyder responded. "They do not want this brick on their building. … This is an extreme deviation in their mind."
Following Forster and Klein's comments, commission Chair Philip Toussaint and member William Ryall indicated their satisfaction with the updated Zaxbys application. Ryall made the motion for approval, and McAndrews joined the rest of the commission in voting yes despite her concerns.
"I think it's an improvement," Ryall said. "It's not perfect, but nothing ever is."
The Easton Zaxbys is one of three locations developers are pursuing as part of the restaurant's Maryland debut, with the others in Cambridge and Berlin.
The Easton location is projected to open in late 2025 or early 2026, Snyder told The Star Democrat last month.

title: Counties approve Chesapeake College budget request, shift cost of tech center
author: Maggie Trovato
content:
Counties approve Chesapeake College budget request, shift cost of tech center

 April 19, 2025 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: Maggie Trovato | Section: Local News 
 
 526
 Words 

 Read News Document

 WYE MILLS — In a joint meeting Thursday, officials across Caroline, Dorchester, Kent, Queen Anne's and Talbot counties approved a shift in county cost shares for Chesapeake College's new technical building.During the meeting, which was held at the college's main campus in Queen Anne's County, the five counties approved a total $9.02 million budget request made by the college for fiscal year 2026. The school's budget is $1.31 million higher than its fiscal year 2025 budget.
Part of the $9.02 million budget request included a $952,560 request for the design of a new technical building. Chesapeake College Vice President for Administrative Services Karen Smith said the new building will have areas for a variety of programs, including agriculture, electrical, welding and fabrication, construction trades and advanced manufacturing. She said the cost for the design phase could be lower depending on state approval.
Although the five counties approved the request for funding for the design, the decision came with a shift in contributions toward the project.
Dorchester County's share of costs for the design phase will be taken on by Queen Anne's County. This means Queen Anne's County's responsibility for the project will jump from 28.9%, or an estimated $275,290, to 47.8%, or an estimated $455,324.
During the meeting, Dorchester County Council President Lenny Pfeffer and Vice President Mike Detmer outlined their council's concerns regarding paying for the project.
Although other counties hope to use the new technical building for career and technical education at the high school level, Dorchester County has a career and technology center it is still paying off, they said.
Through its budget process, Dorchester County has struggled to eliminate an estimated $6.2 million deficit.
Pfeffer said Dorchester County takes in about $45 million in property and income taxes and will have to give Dorchester County Public Schools $26.6 million for fiscal year 2026.
"So we're trying to run the rest of the county on half of that," he said. "So while in conceptual context, we believe in the project, fiscally our citizens and our staff are saying we don't know how we're going to be able to participate."
At the Chesapeake College meeting, Queen Anne's County Commissioner Jack Wilson Jr. shared his county's decision to cover Dorchester County for the project design costs.
"We all know what happens if we let this money go back to the state," Wilson said. "It's going to go somewhere else in this state, and it's not going to be here. We got this far. And Lenny, listen, I feel for you guys. I know what you're going through. But I think we just need to keep it on the rails at least through the design phase and see what the state's going to help with."
According to documents from the meeting, the state will support 75% of project costs, and the counties will support the remaining 25%.
After the counties voted to approve the amended capital budget, Kent County Commission President Ron Fithian said he understands the position Dorchester County is in, mentioning the Blueprint for Maryland's Future and "unfunded mandates" by the state.
"I think we all understand any one of us could be in your same position very easily," Fithian told the Dorchester County Council members.

title: Civility on Easton Town Council
author: Staff Writer
content:

The applicant is proposing to combine three parcels at 336 Romancoke Road (Route 8) in Stevensville for a 5,154-square-foot convenience store, six gasoline fuel islands with 12 fueling positions, and a 1,248-square-foot car wash located at the rear of the convenience store.
The Queen Anne's County Planning Commission previously tabled a decision on the concept plan for another Royal Farms convenience store on Kent Island in December 2022.
The county received extensive public input regarding the project, according to Planning Director Amy Moredock. The room was packed with concerned citizens and surrounding business owners Wednesday.
Major concerns the board continued to address with the developers included traffic impact on Maryland Route 8, entrance and exit access, and architectural issues.
The proposal is not before the County Commissioners for a vote, and due to subsequent comments from the planning commission that must be addressed, the Royal Farms project is not expected to be placed on an agenda for some time, Moredock said.
Bay Bridge Cove residents and members of the Homeowners Association there plan to seek information about a potential county ordinance to prevent gas stations within 500 feet of a day care center, Tamburrino said.

title: 70 children attend flashlight Easter egg hunt in Caroline County

70 children attend flashlight Easter egg hunt in Caroline County

 April 20, 2025 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: AHMAD GARNETT | Section: News 
 
 336
