title: Political mailers stir discourse; mayor says Gunsallus claims are 'flat-out false'
author: Konner Metz
content:
Political mailers stir discourse; mayor says Gunsallus claims are 'flat-out false'

 May 2, 2025 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: Konner Metz | Section: Local News 
 
 764
 Words 

 Read News Document

 EASTON — Two political mailers from Town Council President Frank Gunsallus and the local Republican committee are stirring discourse, including from Mayor Megan Cook, who said claims made on the flyers are "flat-out false" and insulting.The mailers, which many residents received Thursday, list the Talbot County Republican Central Committee on the authority line. The committee has endorsed Gunsallus in his race against Don Abbatiello for president, as well as candidates Lynn and Cameron Keefe in the Ward 2 and Ward 4 races, respectively.
Both Gunsallus flyers call out the mayor, one stating, "Don't let our out-of-town Mayor and her supporters change the character of Easton." They home in on draft inclusionary zoning legislation — which Cook and town planners have advocated for and Gunsallus opposes — that has not yet been introduced as an ordinance.
Cook told The Star Democrat Friday that multiple statements made by the Gunsallus campaign are false, including the claim Cook recruited three candidates to run in Tuesday's election. Cook said she did not recruit anyone.
"I just think all the claims are ridiculous," Cook said. "They're all misleading or flat-out false."
One sentence states that Cook "and her staff quietly usher in new developments—with little to no public input." The mayor disputed that assertion.
"It's an insult to our staff, who are excellent, and the many volunteers that we have serving on boards and commissions," she said.
Neither Gunsallus nor the Republican Central Committee responded to The Star Democrat's requests for interviews.
This year's council president race is the second in a row during which mailers were sent to residents. In 2023, during a four-person race for the seat, mailers targeted former mayor and then-candidate Bob Willey.
Flyers during that campaign were paid for by Scott R. Wagner, a former Pennsylvania state senator and Talbot County business owner. One featured an image of a diaper and said both politicians and diapers need to be changed.
In an interview Thursday, Abbatiello said this year's flyers are "full of misstatements."
"They are meant to instill fear in residents," Abbatiello said. "They are meant to divide the community. All so that they can win an election."
INCLUSIONARY ZONING
In Thursday's flyers — as well as flyers sent to Ward 4 mail boxes this week by Cameron Keefe and the Republican committee — inclusionary zoning is prominent.
Presented to the Town Council at a February workshop, draft legislation would require residential developers to allocate 15% of their units as affordable. For ownership developments, the legislation would require inclusionary units meet an affordable price for households making up to 100% of area median income.
The legislation would grant developers that provide inclusionary units on the same site as market-rate units with a 20% density bonus. But the ordinance hasn't been formally introduced. Its next step is a potential recommendation to the council from the town's housing task force.
In an interview earlier this week before the flyers were received, Republican Central Committee Vice Chair Shari Wilcoxon said inclusionary zoning is the "number one thing in this whole race." She said if passed, it could hurt property values.
"In my opinion, every single person who owns property in this town, Republican or Democrat, ought to be concerned," she said.
"I am of the full belief that the mayor, it's her bill," Wilcoxon said. "She tried to get it through before, but didn't have the votes, so it somehow got tabled until after the election."
Gunsallus has made clear his opposition to inclusionary zoning. In an interview with The Star Democrat's editorial board last week, he said defeating inclusionary zoning is one of his top three priorities.
Regarding the legislation, a Gunsallus mailer reads: "I am the only Councilmember who has vocally opposed the current Inclusionary Zoning bill, which will allow (and effectively require) high-density housing in each and every neighborhood."
In a fact check post on the town's website Friday afternoon, the town clarified the bill would only affect new developments or redeveloped properties with seven or more residential units. It also addressed other claims made by candidates during this election cycle.
Councilmember David Montgomery has also expressed his opposition publicly. Montgomery has endorsed Abbatiello and cited Abbatiello's concerns over the legislation as a reason for supporting him.
"I think neither of us sees the inclusive zoning ordinance as the best way of going out and providing affordable housing," Montgomery said last month.
Abbatiello, who was questioned at a candidate town hall Tuesday about his unclear stance on inclusionary zoning, said Thursday he doesn't think it's the answer.
"I think there's other things that we can do, and I've said that repeatedly," he said. "But again, I wasn't going to make a decision without hearing all the information."

title: Poor judgment, lack of transparency

Poor judgment, lack of transparency

 If one needed further proof of Frank Gunsallus' lack of fitness for reelection to the presidency of the Town Council, view online his performance at the April 21 council meeting.I'm referring to his handling of a vote for discussion of a draft ordinance regarding future campaign finance regulations. He refused adding it the agenda because of his unfounded belief that it would affect this year's election, even though the town attorney had repeatedly corrected him. Gunsallus continued to badger the attorney to get the answer he wanted, adding he would not put the matter on the agenda until he received a response to his letter to the attorney general's office on the appropriateness of moving forward.
Once, again the town attorney schooled him by advising that the AG has no jurisdiction over municipal elections, and therefore, his opinion was not germane. Fortunately, four council members overrode his objection.
His next gambit was to suggest that council members may have ethical violations, if allowed to vote since two were running for reelection. The attorney further advised him that an ordinance, if passed, would only affect future elections and discussion was not a vote negating any possible violation.
Mr. Gunsallus so far has not shared current donation information despite his and his surrogates' repeated assertions that he has done so because he contributed to a state database on previous year's donations. While publishing such information is voluntary, contrast this with Mr. Abbatiello who has provided a list of donors to town authorities to make it available to the public.
You can determine how to characterize this behavior, but to me it illustrates, poor judgment, lack of transparency and manipulation or misstatement of facts. Not the character of a person we need to lead the Easton Town Council.
PAMELA McCLOUD
Easton

title: Rankin and Davis: The Star Democrat's picks for Wards 2 and 4
author: Staff Writer
content:
Rankin and Davis: The Star Democrat's picks for Wards 2 and 4

 May 3, 2025 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: Staff Writer | Section: Editorials 
 
 681
 Words 

 Read News Document

 The Star Democrat recommends votes for Robert Rankin in the Ward 2 Easton Town Council Election and for the Rev. Elmer Davis in Ward 4.ROBERT RANKIN
Robert Rankin is a newcomer to Easton politics, yet he displayed a firm grasp of the issues facing the town.
We liked his stands on issues, and most importantly, we liked that he admitted when he needed more information before voicing a conclusive opinion on issues we asked about.
Rankin's professionalism was evident. He called for a multi-faceted approach to increasing affordable housing in Easton, stressing the need to get more housing that is affordable for young families. His suggestions included working with developers to provide incentives, looking for more projects with townhomes and apartments, and redeveloping existing properties. It was a thoughtful answer.
Rankin also talked about his concerns on how new residential developments impact traffic, parking, schools and public safety. He wants an emphasis on a more strategic approach to approving future projects.
He wants to see more pedestrian-friendly and traffic calming features throughout the town. One suggestion included more crosswalks and sidewalks to better support pedestrian safety.
He was the only candidate to talk about increasing recreational opportunities on the east side of Route 50 where the majority of Ward 2 is located.
He suggested looking at retirement packages to assist in recruiting and retaining police officers in Easton.
One last note: Rankin has managed trade associations during his career. He knows what it is like to build consensus among many competing interests. Those will be valuable skills on the council.
THE REV. ELMER DAVIS
The Rev. Elmer Davis has long been a voice for people in the 4th Ward. He is also a voice of reason in the city during council meetings. Davis is not afraid to speak his mind, but his background as a preacher and pastor helps him look for common ground.
Davis noted his position on the Town Council dais. As the Ward 4 council member, he is the last one called to voice an opinion on discussion topics. This gives him a chance to hear all of the other council members. Often his message is one of finding consensus in disparate views.
"I aim to continue bridging the gap between the council and the people I represent, ensuring every voice is heard and valued," he said.
Davis was prophetic when he asked the question in our interview: "What do we want Easton to be?"
His multi-part answer is a walkable community with sufficient traffic infrastructure to keep the town moving. He suggested a bus service from hotels to downtown to get visitors to the shops that make Easton special. He was solution oriented.
Davis called for ensuring that first responders have the equipment and resources to respond to any incident.
He offered the best option we have heard for building affordable housing in the community — having the town purchase land and then partnering with organizations such as Habitat for Humanity to build the homes, involving the future homeowner in the process.
He said the town needs affordable housing "that people working at WaWa and McDonald's can afford."
He wants the council involved in approving housing projects in Easton. The Planning Commission, he said, should be making recommendations, not granting approvals.
One of his two opponents, Moonyene Jackson-Amis, would be our pick if Davis had not been doing such a fine job during his five years on the council. She is a former council member, an attorney and a community leader with multiple college degrees. She spoke passionately in our conversations about underrepresented communities in Easton. She continues to be a foundational rock in our town.
But Davis is our pick to continue his work on the council. He has done well these past five years, and he has become the face of Ward 4 with deep connections throughout the community.
Davis has experience, civility and strong ties to the community. He talks about his close-knit connection to his roots in the community shaping his values.
"I believe there is still much work to be done to enhance the quality of life for our residents," Davis said. We agree, and the reverend is the person to do that.

title: Easton election cycle has been charged, political in nature
author: Konner Metz
content:
Easton election cycle has been charged, political in nature

 May 3, 2025 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: Konner Metz | Section: Local News 
 
 869
 Words 

 Read News Document

 EASTON — Easton saw a heated election the last time the council president seat was up for grabs. This year's race is no different.Since campaigns for the three open Town Council seats began this winter, there have been stolen and vandalized campaign signs, tense debates on campaign finance transparency and, most recently, political mailers from Republican-endorsed candidates calling out Mayor Megan Cook.
The tenor of the election cycle — which culminates with voting Tuesday — is largely influenced by the race for Town Council president between incumbent Frank Gunsallus and current Ward 2 representative Don Abbatiello.
At a town hall Tuesday, both candidates offered thoughts on civility.
"In the past two years, the council members overall, have been almost always conducting themselves in a civil manner," said Gunsallus. "There are times where debate may get heated. That is the nature of democracy."
"Arguing is fine, I get it. Disagreements occur," Abbatiello said. "But it needs to be done in a respectful manner."
Ward 1 Councilmember Maureen Curry, who has endorsed Abbatiello, said the charged nature of this election isn't normal for Easton. And it's hurting the town, she says.
"Anytime you create an environment based on animosity, it becomes counterproductive, fairly quickly," Curry said. "And I think that's sort of where we are today."
Talbot County Republican Central Committee vice chair Shari Wilcoxon believes a reason the race is so intense is that it's a fight to preserve Easton's charm.
"People love our little town. It's a jewel," she said. "And we had a lot of people move here during COVID because they wanted to get out of the crud to come to this little town. A lot of us want to preserve that."
ENDORSEMENTS
As Gunsallus and Abbatiello square off, they have racked up endorsements from local politicians and even fellow council members.
Abbatiello received endorsements from Curry and, in a surprise to some, Ward 3's David Montgomery, who had sided with Gunsallus on several contentious matters discussed by the council in the past year.
"It would be very hard for us to move forward productively for the next four years under that kind of leadership," Montgomery said of Gunsallus.
Curry says Abbatiello's experience and knowledge make him the best candidate. "He has the right temperament," she said.
Meanwhile, Gunsallus' main endorsements come from Republican leaders — the Republican Central Committee, Sheriff Joe Gamble, Sen. Johnny Mautz and Dels. Chris Adams and Tom Hutchinson.
Wilcoxon said the committee looked at values — not necessarily party affiliation — when endorsing Gunsallus and mother-and-son newcomers Lynn and Cameron Keefe, who are running in Wards 2 and 4, respectively.
"To me he's a phenomenal leader," Wilcoxon said of Gunsallus, citing his thoughtfulness and transparency.
"He's not afraid to ask questions," Mautz said. " ... Sometimes, the questions may seem silly. And other times, they may reveal things that most people aren't aware of."
Abbatiello and his supporters have denounced the involvement of political parties in the town's election, which is nonpartisan and doesn't list candidates alongside a party.
"I do not think that the Republican Party platform has anything to do with the issues that we face here in Easton, and so I don't understand why the party has decided to intervene so strongly in a local election," Montgomery, a Republican, said.
Mautz said while the election is performed as nonpartisan, it is political in nature. "Every election has got politics baked into it," he said.
"I think that everybody fools themselves if they say it's nonpartisan," Wilcoxon said. "Everybody knows. Everybody knows everybody's party. We can just cut the pretending, right?"
Flavio Hickel, an associate professor of political science at Washington College, sees both sides of the argument.
"Broadly speaking, I don't think it's a good idea to allow for local party endorsements or to make nonpartisan elections partisan, because you are allowing partisanship to interfere in local town government," Hickel said.
However, Hickel said knowing which parties candidates align with is informative for voters, especially at a local level.
"Most voters probably aren't familiar with the candidates running," he said. " ... What party identity does at all levels of elections is it provides a very quick information shortcut for voters."
Curry and Montgomery's endorsements have raised questions, too.
Wilcoxon said she views Montgomery's opposition to Gunsallus as personal and said she believes Montgomery and Cook's sponsorship of a campaign finance ordinance was "100%" an attack on Gunsallus' campaign.
At the town hall Tuesday, Gunsallus spoke of council endorsements: "I would not want an endorsement from a fellow council member because I believe that that is out of bounds," he said. Then he made a remark seemingly concerning Montgomery.
"And especially one of them, I would not accept it."

title: Gunsallus campaign flyer is misleading, outright false
author: MEGAN COOK
content:
Gunsallus campaign flyer is misleading, outright false

 May 3, 2025 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: MEGAN COOK | Section: Columns 
 
 719
 Words 

 Read News Document

 As someone who has worked hard to serve this community with honesty and transparency, I've always believed that facts should guide our public conversations, especially during an election. That's why I feel compelled to address several misleading and outright false claims circulating in recent campaign materials.When falsehoods are left unchallenged, it risks becoming accepted as fact. Our community deserves better. These tactics are part of an effort not to inform or unite us but to stir fear and falsely influence voters. That's not who we are in the Town of Easton, and it's not how we should conduct ourselves.
One candidate, Frank Gunsallus, has claimed he is the only council member in 30 years to have gone "line by line" through the town budget. That statement isn't just misleading, it's false and is a disservice to the many council members, past and present, who have worked diligently every year to ensure taxpayer dollars are spent wisely. Every budget season involves careful review, discussion and difficult decisions. Suggesting otherwise dismisses the thoughtful and responsible work of others who have taken that duty seriously, including myself when I served on the council from 2009-2023.
The inclusionary zoning bill is still a work in progress, and no final version has been drafted. Since 2022, there have been numerous meetings and workshops with both the Town Council and Planning Commission. A dedicated task force, made up of volunteers who spent countless hours reviewing Easton's housing needs, was appointed to offer thoughtful recommendations. That group is still finalizing its report.
To claim the bill mandates high-density housing in every neighborhood is simply false and undermines the work of dozens of people trying in good faith to address a real challenge. The goal is simple: to make it possible for teachers, nurses, police officers and others who serve our town to actually live here. If an officer has sworn to protect and serve our town, they ought to be able to call it home.
The same flyer accuses the mayor and staff of quietly ushering in development with little or no public input. That's not only untrue, it's an insult to the hardworking staff, Planning Commission and community members involved in every step of our public planning process. Nothing is being "snuck in." Transparency and community input are cornerstones of how we operate. Claims to the contrary are simply false.
It's also been claimed that I "recruited" three pro-mayor, pro-development candidates to run for Town Council. That's false. Two of the implied candidates are already serving on the council. One of them is running against Mr. Gunsallus not because of ideology, but out of concern over how meetings are managed, the lack of respect shown and civility and communication breakdowns among council members.
Mischaracterizing the motives of individuals who Mr. Gunsallus opposes is unfair and misleading. Voters should look for leadership that is respectful, collaborative and able to work with others, especially when navigating difficult issues. That's the kind of leadership Easton deserves.
It's also been suggested that because I wasn't born in Easton, I somehow care less or am less committed to this community. That's not only wrong, it's also deeply disrespectful. My husband and I moved to Easton 22 years ago for his job as a pediatrician and to be closer to his family. My work as mayor, as a former council member and my involvement in projects like Project Idlewild, CarePacks, coaching sports and serving on local boards and clubs, has always been about giving back to the place my husband and I chose to raise our family.
And I'm far from alone. Many of the people who make meaningful contributions to Easton each day weren't born here. What matters is not where someone started, but the heart and effort they bring to serving this town.
Easton is a town worth fighting for, not with fear or falsehoods, but with integrity, respect and a commitment to the truth. Elections should be about ideas, accountability, and the future we want to build together, not personal attacks or misleading claims. I will continue to stand up for the facts, for our hardworking staff and volunteers and for a community where we listen to each other even when we disagree. I encourage every voter to look past the lies, ask thoughtful questions and choose leaders who value collaboration, honesty and real public service.

title: Two potential dispensaries compete to open in Easton
author: AHMAD GARNETT agarnett@chespub.com
content:
Two potential dispensaries compete to open in Easton

 May 3, 2025 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: AHMAD GARNETT agarnett@chespub.com | Section: News 
 
 295
 Words 

 Read News Document

 EASTON — Two potential cannabis dispensaries are racing to secure final approvals from the Easton planners, but only one will be able to be built, at least in the location the business plans.Both potential locations sit near each other in the former bank locations near the Giant and Walmart on Elliott Road. State law will require one of the two dispensaries to find another spot.
"It was described at our hearing as something of a race to the finish at this point," said Lynn Thomas, town planner, in an interview. "The one issue that is at play for both of them is part of the state law requires minimum separation between other cannabis dispensaries.
"They obviously are right across the street from one another, so whoever gets their final approval first is going to prevent the other from opening at that location."
According to the Maryland Cannabis Administration, dispensaries are required to be 1,000 feet away from each other.
The applicant for 8223 Elliott Road is BGFY LLC and the applicant for 8171 Elliott Road is Driller Ventures LLC, Thomas said in an email.
Both business were approved for special exception by the town on different dates.
According to the town planner, BGFY LLC received its special exception on Dec. 17. A subdivision application for this property is currently under review, which would create a new parking lot surrounding the dispensary. Following the completion of the subdivision, the business will also need to submit applications for building permits.
According to Thomas, Driller Ventures LLC received a special exception on Jan. 25. The business' next step in the process is to apply for building permits.
The town planner states, "to my knowledge, we have not yet received any such applications."
The Star Democrat could not reach Driller Ventures LLC or BGFY LLC for comment.

title: Critical component of democracy

 On May 6, Easton residents will decide who they want to represent them on the Town Council for the next four years.Participation in local government is a critical component of democracy and a responsibility that should not be taken lightly.
Town elections are smaller than state and national elections and typically candidates are known within the community absent of political party. Town issues are also very different from federal and state issues and impact a larger percentage of the electorate.
As a result, town elections should be nonpartisan and focus on individual candidates and their ideas for the future.
Running for local office is not easy. It requires time, commitment and resources to be successful. Serving is no less difficult and demands the ability to research issues, gather input from a wide range of stakeholders and make decisions that are in the best interest of the whole.
Good leaders listen, build consensus and look to unite, not divide. This cannot happen when political parties exert influence on local elections through contributions and slanderous talking points.
As the campaigns wind down, it is now time for the voters to decide who they want representing them. I continue to pledge to serve Easton and all of its residents through honesty, hard work, integrity and respect.
I call on all residents to be engaged, seek the truth and hold your leaders accountable for their actions. And I humbly ask for your vote on May 6.

title: Easton hires town manager
author: STAFF REPORT
content:
Easton hires town manager

 May 5, 2025 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: STAFF REPORT | Section: Local News 
 
 501

 Read News Document

 Andrew "Andy" Kitzrow has been named the Easton town manager.The appointment by the mayor was announced at the Town Council meeting Monday evening.
Kitzrow comes to Easton after serving as the Salisbury city administrator since 2023 and as the deputy city administrator since 2017.
As Easton town manager, he will be responsible for overseeing all town operations, acting as a leader to personnel and serving as a key point of contact for the mayor, town leadership, Town Council and residents of Easton.
"I'm looking forward to working alongside you to make Easton the best place on the Eastern Shore," Kitzrow told council members and residents Monday.
Kitzrow brings a wealth of experience and knowledge to the role with 19 years in local government, including seven years in executive leadership roles.
After obtaining his bachelor's degree at University of North Carolina at Chapel Hill in 2005, Kitzrow began a career in community administration by serving as a recreation program director and later a recreation superintendent for Wicomico County before landing his role as deputy city administrator for the Salisbury in 2017.
In his roles as Salisbury deputy city administrator and city administrator, Kitzrow championed many projects and initiatives, including:
The establishment of the Arts, Business and Culture Department, promoting tourism, revitalization and economic growth.The introduction of THRIVE, an employee health and wellness plan designed to holistically improve the physical, mental and emotional well-being of city staff.The launching of two youth community centers, which now serve hundreds of youths while fostering growth and community engagement.The recruitment of top talent in numerous critical roles throughout the organization, including police chief and fire chief.Overseeing teams that secured over $25 million in state and federal grants.
Mayor Megan Cook said the town partnered with a local government consulting firm during the hiring process, which began last fall. Around 50 applicants were narrowed to 10 semifinalists and then four finalists, she said.
The four finalists participated in full-day, in-person interviews and met with council members.
"Andy brings with him a deep understanding of municipal operations and brings a steady, informed perspective to the role," Cook said. She added that Kitzrow has strong budgeting and capital improvement planning experience.
Easton Police Chief Alan Lowrey has been filling in as acting town manager since the town parted ways with former town manager Don Richardson in August 2024. Cook and council members thanked Lowrey for stepping up and serving in the important role.
"We've been lucky to have his leadership and his guidance — and his sense of humor — the last several months," Cook said.
Kitzrow's appointment was made by Cook and approved by the Town Council at its meeting on Monday. He is scheduled to begin serving as Easton town manager on July 7.
"Every new beginning comes from the courage to let go of the familiar," Kitzrow said in a news release from the town. "As I step into the role of town manager for Easton, I do so with great excitement for the opportunities that lie ahead."
This story has been updated with details from the Monday night council meeting.

 EASTON — A record number of residents voted in Easton's election Tuesday.There are 3,001 votes and counting in the council president race, which saw Don Abbatiello defeat incumbent Frank Gunsallus. Tuesday night, Abbatiello held a decisive 2,025- to 976-vote lead.
The previous record for voter turnout in a municipal election came in the 2023 mayoral contest, according to town officials. In that election, 2,578 residents cast a vote in the competitive mayoral race, which was won by current Mayor Megan Cook.
Around 230 absentee ballots remain to be counted Wednesday, election supervisor Ed Forte said.
In Ward 2, Robert Rankin won the seat being vacated by Abbatiello. Rankin earned 493 votes Tuesday, a decisive lead over opponent Lynn Keefe's 228.
In Ward 4, incumbent the Rev. Elmer Davis has a sizable lead. Davis has 253 votes, with Cameron Keefe in second with 128 and Moonyene Jackson-Amis third with 103.
Residents began coming out to the Easton Volunteer Fire Department once polls opened at 7 a.m, and the steady pace continued through much of the day.
The town's Board of Canvassers will tally absentee ballots Wednesday and then formally certify the election.
Both in the morning and afternoon, the line for residents from Ward 3 stretched to outside the voting hall.
At one point early Tuesday afternoon, the line for voters went past the indoor lobby all the way to the outside doors of the building.
Tuesday evening, the turnout continued to be steady as many residents navigated a crowded parking lot to perform their civic duty.
Inside the fire hall, Forte and election judges swiftly assisted voters who were unsure of which wards they live in. Election judge Mariana Lesher called it a "crazy" good turnout.

title: Residents soon will move in to renovated Doverbrook Apartments
author: Konner Metz
content:
Residents soon will move in to renovated Doverbrook Apartments

 May 6, 2025 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 339

 EASTON — The revitalized Doverbrook Apartments were shown off to state, county and town leaders last week as final touches are completed before residents move in.Don Bibb, executive director of the Housing Commission of Talbot, said the 64-unit redevelopment project will benefit the community.
"You can see the tremendous improvement this has made to the community and the opportunity for much improved, long-term sustainable housing for the program participants that we have that are going to be living here," Bibb said April 30 during a tour of the complex.
Bibb said Thursday that move-in for returning residents is imminent and is likely to begin within seven to 10 days.
The commission and construction company Pennrose began redevelopment of the Doverbrook Apartments in late 2023. The $26 million project replaced the apartment complex's seven old buildings with five new buildings, adding 14 units to its original 50-unit setup.
"It's good utilization of open space that provides the opportunity for the growth to add more units in," Bibb said.
Located on Dover Street, the complex will accommodate households earning between 30% and 80% of the area median income, or between $21,000 and $58,000 for one-person households.
It includes one-, two-, three- and four-bedroom apartments. Project leaders said the complex was designed to bring original residents — who were assisted in finding temporary housing during construction — back once completed.
Bibb said of the original 50 tenants, around 30 will return — a relatively high percentage for a redevelopment project during which residents move elsewhere temporarily.
Maryland Department of Housing and Community Development Secretary Jake Day toured the apartment complex April 30. He applauded the redevelopment efforts and lightheartedly pointed out how close residents will be to Rise Up Coffee across the street.
"Do your marketing materials for the remaining (units) talk about how many steps it is to the Rise Up?" Day said with a smile.
Bibb praised the public-private aspect of the project, which included state and local funding and low-income housing tax credits for the 14 new units.
"It was well worth the blood, sweat and tears," Bibb said.

title: Program Open Space bill is 'a success,' county says

content:
Program Open Space bill is 'a success,' county says

 Author/Byline: AHMAD GARNETT agarnett@chespub.com | Section: News 
 
 383
 Words 

 Read News Document

 DENTON — Bruce Bereano and Steve Wise, Caroline County's lobbyists, presented their 2025 legislative session wrap-up at the Caroline County Commissioners meeting Tuesday.Bereano and Wise spoke about House Bill 717, a bill that was passed this session regarding Program Open Space, a state program that allocates funding from transfer tax collections.
"This was a success," Wise said. "We were able to get all counties in the state to use that capital money for operating, upgrades and improvements."
House Bill 717 originally started as a departmental bill, spearheaded by the Department of Natural Resources. Caroline County Commissioners President Travis Breeding testified on a panel to support the bill with Secretary of the Department of Natural Resources Josh Kurtz.
Breeding originally sent a request to Maryland Association of Counties and the counties' lobbyist to have Program Open Space changed to allow the counties to use acquisition funds for park improvements, he said.
The association then suggested "instead of making the bill a standalone bill let's see if Secretary Kurtz is willing to include it in their department bill," Breeding said. Kurtz agreed and then included it in DNR's bill.
The bill states, "altering and repealing certain provisions of law regarding the use of Program Open Space local funding"
"We got it put in, and it made its way through the legislature and passed. It hasn't been signed yet," Breeding said. "What it's going to do, it'll allow Caroline County to use 25% of the money it gets in Program Open Space and additional 25 towards building park infrastructure. Whereas before, roughly 25% of the money allocated to the county from the state had to be used to purchase property."
According to Breeding, projects like the Sharp Road Park project and the North County Park project could see improvements from this bill.
"It does make more money available for us to do the improvements at Sharp Road Park and North County Park and various other parks around the county," Breeding said. "So, it does give us more state funds to work with to make improvements."
The county's lobbyists credit Kurtz for help with getting the Program Open Space into the bill.
"Really very thankful to the secretary for being so flexible, and open-minded and accepting, and throughout all of it, he was very insistent on having that as a part of the bill," Bereano said.

title: Piscataway Conoy Tribe receives land donation
author: Matt Wynn mwynn@somdnews.com
content:
Piscataway Conoy Tribe receives land donation

 May 7, 2025 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: Matt Wynn mwynn@somdnews.com | Section: News 
 
 581
 Words 

 Read News Document

 After a long process, it's official — a property on Country Lane in Waldorf will be donated to the Piscataway Conoy Tribe.The donation did not come easily, as tensions rose between a split tribe, with a number coming out to oppose it.
Charles County first received notification about the land donation request in January 2020 and sent correspondence about the process on Feb. 5, 2020.
On July 29, 2020, the county sent the first of four lease renewal documents between then and March 16, 2022. Despite several attempts at communication between the county and the tribe, the two sides were unable to come to a formal agreement.
A letter said the plot of land had been a center for indigenous culture with biannual pow-wows from 1982 through 2014, as well as school field trips and other public events.
The letter also stated that the Cedarville Band was required to jump through "numerous bureaucratic hoops," including paying $10,000 for a land survey.
The American Civil Liberties Union requested the county stop a planned eviction and work toward a long-term solution to donate the land to the Cedarville Band of Piscataway Indians.
"Returning the land would affirmatively recognize and show appreciation for the people who have been preserving American history and Indigenous American culture on this land," the ACLU letter stated.
The site is divided with approximately 9.5 acres in Charles County and 7 acres in Prince George's County.
"The property being proposed for transfer is located in both Prince George's and Charles counties. The property is owned entirely by Charles County, and so there is no approval needed from Prince George's County in order to complete the transfer," Danielle Mitchell, an attorney with Charles County government, told Southern Maryland News earlier this year.
During a public hearing last month, a large number of the Piscataway were split on what to do with the land.
From the 1950s through the 1970s, the property was owned by the U.S. Army and used as a Nike Battery site.
Rosanna Swann, the first speaker of the hearing, said at the time she opposed the land donation because of a court case between Jesse James Swann Jr. and Francis Gray, who both lead different portions of the Piscataway people.
Rosanna Swann also pointed to the site as a potential "environmental disaster" due to its military history and said that the area was contaminated and could cost anywhere from $4 to $10 million to clean up.
Gray, the chairman of the Piscataway Conoy Tribe, said, "We the Piscataway Conoy people welcome this opportunity as it will finally provide a much needed home base. … It runs deeper than that. It will provide a means for the preservation of our identity."
Later in the night, Acting County Administrator Deborah Hall said that the federal government covers the cleanup of the contaminated land.
Many others came up and supported the donation, citing the importance of giving the Piscataway people a land base so other tribes can find them.
County attorneys reported that there were well over 200 written comments on the matter, and that sentiments were very split on if the land should be donated.
On May 6, it was time to put it to a vote.
Commissioner Gilbert "BJ" Bowling (D) told tribe members in attendance that he would be abstaining from the vote.
"I don't feel it's appropriate for me to get in the middle of it," Bowling said, citing disagreement between sects of the tribe and the ongoing legal dispute.
The other four commissioners voted yes, passing the resolution and giving the tribe a land base.

title: Record voter turnout, margins of victory highlight Easton election
author: Konner Metz
content:
Record voter turnout, margins of victory highlight Easton election

 May 7, 2025 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: Konner Metz | Section: Local News 
 
 727
 Words 

 Read News Document

 EASTON — In an election with record voter turnout, two of every three Easton voters cast ballots for current Ward 2 Councilmember Don Abbatiello, giving him a landslide victory over incumbent Frank Gunsallus in the race for Town Council president.Easton also elected Robert Rankin to fill Abbatiello's Ward 2 seat and reelected incumbent the Rev. Elmer Davis in Ward 4.
More than 3,200 residents cast ballots, a record high for a municipal election, according to town officials. Abbatiello earned 2,215 votes, or 69%, to Gunsallus' 1,012.
Abbatiello said he was "amazed" and "grateful" when the results were announced.
"To get over 2,000 of those 3,000 votes was amazing and humbling," Abbatiello said. "But then it very quickly set in, over 2,000 people have put a lot of faith in me to make sure that I do the right things for the town. So there's that as well in the back of your mind."
Abbatiello said Gunsallus congratulated him when the results were announced Tuesday night and that the two shook hands.
In a statement Wednesday, Gunsallus thanked his supporters and said he "will always be grateful for the opportunity" to serve the community. Gunsallus' term ends after less than two years on the council, as he won a special election in September 2023.
"While this election didn't go our way, I'm incredibly proud of the honest and transparent campaign we ran — and deeply thankful to those who stood beside our team throughout it," Gunsallus wrote.
"My hope moving forward is that the Easton Town Council listens closely to all voices in our community, and that we continue building a future rooted in respect and shared purpose," he later added.
The election cycle was heated and political, especially the Abbatiello and Gunsallus contest. Republican-endorsed candidates sent mailers calling out Mayor Megan Cook. Campaign signs were stolen and vandalized. And council held tense debates over campaign finance transparency.
Wednesday morning, Abbatiello said his goal during the campaign was to be nonpartisan. He thinks the vote outcome shows Easton residents agree.
"I think that that's what that vote yesterday showed, is that the residents of Easton want the town to remain nonpartisan, to focus on town issues first," he said.
Rankin shared a similar sentiment.
"A lot of resources were put into a lot of billboards and mailers and robocalls, and I think some of the turnout was due to folks who saw through some of that and don't want big party politics in local elections," Rankin said.
"I think that stood out yesterday and the town of Easton, the people of Easton, had their chance to speak and they did so with a resounding voice."
Once absentee ballots were counted Wednesday, Rankin held a 528-237 advantage over opponent Lynn Keefe. Rankin, winning 69% of the vote, said the result was humbling.
"Local government works best when the community is engaged and involved, and to have so many people from the town of Easton participate in the election is just so important and so rewarding," Rankin said.
In a statement, Keefe said the campaign cycle was an experience she won't forget. "I pray that the Lord will lead the newly election to do the right thing for all the citizens of the town," she wrote.
In Ward 4, incumbent the Rev. Elmer Davis earned 54% of the vote 287 ballots cast for him. Cameron Keefe was second with 129 and Moonyene Jackson-Amis third with 117.
Davis said it was a challenge to run a successful campaign in the crowded Ward 4 field.
"It's one thing to have one opponent, but it's another thing to have two opponents," Davis said. "In my mind, I had to do double the work."
In a statement, Cameron Keefe wished Davis the best, and added: "It was an absolute blast running and I urge the people of Easton to keep those on the council in our prayers."
Moonyene Jackson-Amis thanked her supporters for voting for values such as affordable housing and cultural offerings.
"In less than two weeks of campaigning, Elmer Davis and his supporters got their wake-up call," she wrote in a statement. "Yes, he won the election, but my team and I won the victory. Over 100 voters stood up for values that matter."
The Board of Canvassers certified the election results Wednesday. The elected council members will be sworn in at the Town Council's next meeting on May 19.

title: Denton approves budget with lower tax rate
author: AHMAD GARNETT agarnett@chespub.com
content:
Denton approves budget with lower tax rate

 May 7, 2025 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: AHMAD GARNETT agarnett@chespub.com | Section: News 
 
 530
 Words 

 Read News Document

 DENTON — The Denton Town Council presented and approved its fiscal year 2026 general fund budget and appropriations with a 2% lower property tax rate."We were able to lower the tax rate 3 cents," said Dallas Lister, a Town Council member, "which is a commitment that we've been trying to make each year, is to try to be as efficient as possible and not let the taxes increase where we can. This has been a lot of work on the staff, we really didn't have a lot of hard lift this year. We just set some priorities and staff made it happen, so it's spectacular."
The tax rate decreases from 69 cents per $100 of assessed value to 66 cents per $100 of assessed value on properties taxed within the boundaries of Denton. Town officials credit increased property values in Denton for being able to lower the rate.
"Because our property rates were higher, if we had stayed the same, people would have had the same tax rate but they would have been paying more money because of the percentage," McNinch said. "That's when when we decide to go down, the impact is, $40,000 roughly on our budget."
According to McNinch, the officials understand that some fees might increase, but they felt lowering the tax rate was the best decision for the town residents and for the council.
"We're aware that other taxes and fees might increase, but we need to hold our line ... we want to make sure we're providing the best services to our public and other things that might go up are county, state, utilities, that we don't have control over," McNinch said. "But with us trying to reduce and trying to put these things in place. We understand it's tough out there right now. It is for us too."
Denton tax revenues will increase by close to $150,000, while license and agencies revenues will decrease next fiscal year, according to the approved budget.
While a majority of the expenditures saw minor increases and decreases, Park and Recreation received the biggest decrease, dropping by $60,000.
"We've gotten things done," McNinch said. "We've gotten the Fourth Street Park done, we're partnering with the county, and the Sharp Road Park looks different. We've had park plans in place and and we've been able to get things done. So yes, that impacts the budget positively."
Tourism Visitor Center received a $14,000 increase, and Main Street received about a $4,000 increase in the budget. According to Mayor McNinch, Denton being named the first American Discovery Trail Town has an "impact on the decision."
"We want our visitor center open as much as possible," McNinch said. "We've been able to help support that a little bit more over the course of the last couple of years. We see the benefit of tourism for economic development.
"Things like the American Heritage Trail, we do see an increase in visitation to our visitor center. Those things are important, and we also increased the Main Street budget a little bit, because again that all works in trying to provide a community that people want to visit and want to live."

title: In packed meeting, short-term rental owners speak out against proposed regulations
author: Konner Metz
content:
In packed meeting, short-term rental owners speak out against proposed regulations

 May 8, 2025 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: Konner Metz | Section: Local News 
 
 764
 Words 

 Read News Document

 EASTON — Over 40 people filled the room for Wednesday's Talbot County Planning Commission meeting, an unusually large turnout for the 9 a.m. event.Many of those in the crowd were property owners who came to oppose potential new regulations on short-term rentals.
In legislation drafted by Talbot County Council members Lynn Mielke and Pete Lesher and subsequently referred to the Planning Commission, new restrictions would be placed on short-term rental operations and licenses.
Mielke says the proposed revisions come as there's a "proliferation" of short-term rentals that are hurting neighbors and communities. But owners argue some of the proposals will derail short-term rental businesses.
One change would mandate a seven-night minimum stay for short-term lease holders in some districts, while the other districts would maintain the current rule of a three-night minimum.
"That is absolutely a killer," said Bill Morrison, who operates a rental in St. Michaels. "It will drive business away."
Property owners called the potential revisions government overreach and a breach of privacy. Kathleen Schamel called the legislation a "non-starter."
Mielke, along with a handful of residents who spoke in support of the draft regulations, disagreed.
Tilghman Island resident Leslie Steen said short-term rentals "diminish the sense of community."
"Concentration is an issue," she said. "Four short-term rentals within 1,000 feet is too many. There's a domino effect. My neighbor goes short-term rental, I'm out of here. Then my house, guess what? It'll sell as a short-term rental."
THE LEGISLATION
In order to obtain a short-term rental license, property owners in Talbot County must go through the Short Term Rental Review Board. Most license requests are granted. The properties are often listed on sites such as Airbnb or Vrbo and leased out to tenants.
Once an initial license is approved, property owners must obtain renewal from the board one year later, and then every two years after the one-year mark.
Cindy Reichart, vice chair of the board, spoke in opposition to Mielke's proposed regulations Wednesday. Reichart noted the number of licenses hasn't significantly increased in recent years — there were 157 in 2018 and 164 in 2024, she said.
"I'm scratching my head trying to understand why all these changes are requested," Reichart said.
In addition to the seven-night minimum, the proposed revisions would:
Split licenses into two classes. Class A for properties that are the applicant's primary residence and Class B for properties that aren't the applicant's primary residence.
Limit Class B licenses to one per 500 feet or one per 1,000 feet, depending on the zoning district.
Require that short-term rentals install landlines.
Require that license renewal applications include detailed logs of when the rental was occupied by tenants, family members and the owner.
Some short-term rental owners said having to provide logs of when family or friends stay will infringe on privacy or become an extra burden.
"Our renewal process is already plenty burdensome," said Steve Goldberg.
Mielke noted that the purpose of the revisions is to "strike a balance between residents and short-term rental owners." She said many residents moved into communities such as Bentley Hay and Rio Vista not expecting much of the neighborhood to be flooded with short-term rental houses.
WHAT'S NEXT
The proposed revisions were introduced by the County Council April 18, then referred to the Planning Commission. A second version of the revisions — which added wording on the seven-night minimum stay — was created between April 18 and Wednesday's meeting.
Some property owners and representatives said the edited legislation should've never been reviewed by the commission since County Council didn't introduce it as edited.
"Councilwoman Mielke picked and chose what she wanted and presented it without council approval," said Martha Suss, a former Short Term Rental Review Board member.
The legislation would have to make its way back to the County Council's desk in order to be voted into law. Once the Planning Commission makes a recommendation on the revisions, they will likely appear on the council's agenda for approval.
The Planning Commission received over 70 written testimonies regarding the proposed changes. Wednesday, it held public comment for over 90 minutes, including remarks from commission member Ed Heikes, who recused himself from the dais to speak against the legislation.
Commission members agreed to leave written public comment open. The proposal will return when the commission and County Council host a joint workshop Tuesday, June 10, at 2:30 p.m.
Keith Watts, chair of the STR Review Board, said Wednesday the revisions shouldn't make it out of the commission.
"This should die a quiet and dignified death somewhere," Watts said.
But St. Michaels resident Monica Otte felt the proposal is an adequate effort to provide balance.
"Balance between the interests and rights of the short-term rental owners, and the neighbors, the full-time resident neighbors," Otte said.

title: Caroline County retains tax differentials, at least for this year
author: AHMAD GARNETT agarnett@chespub.com
content:
Caroline County retains tax differentials, at least for this year

 May 8, 2025 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: AHMAD GARNETT agarnett@chespub.com | Section: News 
 
 546
 Words 

 Read News Document

 DENTON — The Caroline County Commissioners held their last fiscal year 2026 public budget hearing Tuesday evening.While the commissioners received multiple recognitions for balancing the budget, municipalities brought questions about property tax rates and real property tax differential rates.
Ridgely Commissioner Brad Sears asked the county commissioners what the extended outlook was for municipal tax differentials.
"Just in terms of looking forward from my town's perspective, I would like to get your overall sense of where this might be headed, if that's appropriate," Sears said.
In Caroline County's proposed budget, the property tax rate sits at 98 cents per $100 of assessed value. For towns incorporated within the county, tax rates can sit between one cents to six cents lower than the county's rate.
The differentials were put in place to keep resident of towns from being taxed twice for services provided to these residents by the municipality instead of the county.
"This is something that was in play when I came into office, and it's been a real subject that I battle with over the years," County Commissioners Vice President Larry Porter said. "What this means is it does not affect the town's budget, it affects the money the county collects in their county property tax rate.
"I will say tonight that this will be the last year I would support the property tax differential, I know its gonna be a very controversial subject... In this year's budget, we did not collect about $600,000 in the property tax differential. We're able to balance the budget this year. Going forward, I don't have a clue."
Porter advocated for eliminating the differentials in coming years, pointing to cost shifts from the state that he says will make it more difficult for the county to balance future budgets.
"We will not be able to forgo $600,000 revenue in the next year, I don't think we will," Porter said. "I see nothing but cost being shifted every year, the Blueprint number just keeps exponentially going up every year... I'm not sure where the road is going to take us."
The situation is similar to one being seen in Dorchester County this fiscal year.
In an effort to address a $6.2 million deficit, Dorchester County has proposed multiple tax increases in its draft fiscal year 2026 budget, including the removal of tax differentials for Cambridge and Hurlock residents.
The Cambridge City Council has voiced opposition to the county's elimination of the differentials. In a unanimous vote Monday, the City Council voted to adopt a resolution that requests the Dorchester County Council "develop and implement an annual tax differential or rebate model" to address the "tax burden" of county property taxes on Cambridge residents.
While Caroline County Commissioners President Travis Breeding does not fully agree with Porter, he said he understands Porter's point.
"My position is a little different than Commissioner Porter. I believe that there are redundant services that are provided by the municipalities," Breeding said. "I know the formula that generated the tax differential was generated for police protection.
"....I don't know what the fiscal situation is going to be next year, we may find ourselves in the same dilemma that Dorchester county is in this year, I don't think we will…. I am still at the maintain point, but I certainly understand Commissioner Porter's position. That's where I'm at right now."

title: Cambridge Indivisible aims to teach members about civics, cofounder says
author: Maggie Trovato
content:
Cambridge Indivisible aims to teach members about civics, cofounder says

 May 9, 2025 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: Maggie Trovato | Section: Local News 
 
 645
 Words 

 Read News Document

 CAMBRIDGE — For Cambridge Indivisible cofounder and Cochair Michelle Fowle, it's about understanding the power you have."I think the really important thing is for people to understand the power that they actually hold," she said. "So that's kind of my focus. And I'm doing that here."
When Fowle moved to Cambridge from California with her husband, Andy, in September, the two hit the ground running to form Cambridge Indivisible, which is a chapter of a national organization that aims to elect progressive leaders.
Fowle said the overarching goal of the group is to give people a place to build community and learn about civics. She said everyone is welcome.
"We have Republicans who are showing up now at our protests, asking how they can help," she said. "And I embrace them."
Mentioning health care and housing, Fowle said there are issues that people on both sides of the aisle can unite on. She said that for her, the organization isn't about identity politics.
"We don't have to agree," she said. "In fact, we shouldn't agree. And it's healthy to have that conversation. I'm not trying to make you be me."
There was a time when Fowle knew very little about politics.
"They say that there's two days that are critical in your life," she said. "It's the day you're born and the day you find out why. And in November 2016, I found out why."
Fowle said the 2016 general election results thrust her into a world of activism after not paying close attention to politics for many years. While living in California, Fowle learned from other organizers, helped put on rallies and marches, and built relationships with elected officials.
"For somebody who didn't know anything, I can teach it now," she said.
MAKING WAVES
In recent months, Cambridge Indivisible has garnered attention over events it has hosted around town. During one event in March, the chapter hosted Rep. Jamie Raskin (D-Md.) for a town hall.
The chapter also has hosted multiple rallies to criticize elected federal leadership. That criticism has been largely directed toward Rep. Andy Harris (R-Md.) for not holding in-person town halls for his constituents. Harris hosted multiple virtual town halls in the past two months.
Fowle said the Cambridge chapter of Indivisible has more than 1,000 members from across the Eastern Shore. She said there is no formal registration process to be a member.
Cambridge Indivisible Treasurer Ilia Johnson said she joined the chapter this year to get more representation for the Hispanic community in the area and to support her neighbors. She said she likes that Cambridge Indivisible is a group "for everybody."
"All we want to do is what's best for everybody," she said.
During a Cambridge Indivisible rally held along U.S. Route 50 in Cambridge on April 19, Gloria McVeigh said she joined the chapter after Harris was elected in November. She said it's a nice group that holds the same values as herself.
Although there have been disapproving shouts from people driving their cars past Cambridge Indivisible rallies these past few months, Fowle said the chapter hasn't faced much opposition other than from Harris.
In the past, Harris has shared his criticisms of and concerns with the Indivisible organization as a whole.
Following a Cambridge Indivisible rally held March 13 that called on Harris to hold an in-person town hall and questioned his allegiance to his constituents, Harris alleged those at the rally were "brought in by buses" and not his constituents. He said he heard from a Washington, D.C., organization's leader "who knows what's going on" that people at the rally were getting paid to be there.
"This is AstroTurf," Harris said about the organization in March. "This is not grassroots."
Fowle said the chapter does get internet trolls on its public page, and she deletes their comments and blocks them.
"It's like listen, when this hits you — and it will — I'll be there for you if you want," she said about the internet trolls.

title: Seafood odor dispute in Easton's 4th ward still simmering
author: Konner Metz
content:
Seafood odor dispute in Easton's 4th ward still simmering

 May 9, 2025 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: Konner Metz | Section: Local News 
 
 675
 Words 

 Read News Document

 EASTON — As summer nears, disagreement between a local seafood processor and neighboring residents over odor mitigation efforts is resurfacing.Residents in Ward 4 have long complained of odor emanating from Chesapeake Brand Seafood on Maryland Avenue during crab season.
It led to action by the Easton Town Council last December. The town passed an ordinance requiring seafood processing operations to install odor control technology "in such a manner that no odor" could be detected.
Per the ordinance, an odor control system must be installed by July 1. But Chesapeake Brand Seafood is now requesting an amendment to the ordinance, citing that industry experts say the "no odor" language is an unachievable goal.
Peter Maloney, who lives around 500 feet from the business, has been a vocal neighborhood leader for affected residents. He says the odor makes it hard for his kids to enjoy time outside.
"It's not something we signed up for," said Maloney, who moved to Easton around five years before the business opened in 2019.
He added that Chesapeake Brand Seafood isn't acting as a good neighbor with its attempt to amend the already-approved ordinance.
"They're kicking the can down the road," Maloney said.
At Monday's Town Council meeting, the amendment was introduced and referred to the Planning Commission for review at its May 15 meeting. Town Council will still have the final say.
If passed, the amendment will remove the requirement that odor control systems act "in such a manner that no odor from any product or by-product can be detected outside the building on the same property or on adjacent properties or public rights-of-way."
Replacing the deleted language is, in part, the requirement that engineers or industry experts confirm the installed odor control equipment uses "best control technologies and methods designed to mitigate odor before it leaves a building."
Owner Mitch Hughes says his business requested the amendment due to the "no odor" language. He's looking for clarity over whether that mandate would be based on odor detection or resident complaints.
"Zero odor means I'm done completely," Hughes said. "It's just not possible."
Hughes is ready to install the odor control technology, but he's holding off since he doesn't want to begin footing the $800 monthly cost if it won't end up meeting the ordinance.
"They all said we can install a system and get your odor down," he said. "But there's no way you can reach zero odor."
Maloney and other residents spoke in opposition to the proposed amendment Monday.
"I feel like I've earned my right to retire, and I don't want to have to do it inside my household," Carla Howell said.
"We are organized, and we are all very angry about this as you can hear," Emily Stone said. "And we will not be quiet until something is done."
Ward 4 Councilmember the Rev. Elmer Davis, who pushed for the ordinance to be passed last year, said he's against any amendment.
"I think the ordinance as it stands is an excellent ordinance," Davis said. "And the crab industry hasn't been a good neighbor."
Ward 1's Maureen Curry said Monday that Chesapeake Brand Seafood gave the council a "flat-out no" on the prospect of moving to a new location, likely one not in a residential area. Hughes, whose business was legally permitted by the town to locate on that property, says he's only against moving if he has to foot the full bill.
Hughes said the business has taken steps as requested by town code enforcement to reduce odor. Remaining complaints, he said, are due to the steaming process.
"It's kind of hard to fix the smell of steamed crabs," Hughes said. "That's just part of the process. That is our process."
But Maloney and other residents said Monday the proposed amendment feels like a stall tactic from Chesapeake Brand Seafood as the July 1 deadline nears.
Maloney said in an interview that the neighbors aren't looking to hurt a business. They are, however, fighting for what he calls a "well-worded" and effective ordinance to stand as originally approved.
"To loosen this at the expense of all property owners who have dealt with this for five years is unfair," Maloney said.

title: Cambridge, Hurlock speak out against Dorchester tax differential cut
author: Maggie Trovato
content:
Cambridge, Hurlock speak out against Dorchester tax differential cut

 May 9, 2025 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: Maggie Trovato | Section: Local News 
 
 655
 Words 

 Read News Document

 CAMBRIDGE — Leading into the first public budget hearing for Dorchester County's proposed fiscal year 2026 budget, Cambridge and Hurlock leaders made their appeals for a reinstatement of tax differentials."We beg you to pull out a pencil and make some changes," Hurlock Council President Earl Murphy Jr. said at the Dorchester County Council meeting May 6.
During the standing-room-only meeting, the council heard from municipal leaders as well as residents about their concerns with the state of the draft budget.
Concerns largely centered on a proposal in the county's draft budget to remove tax differentials, or lower property tax rates, for Cambridge and Hurlock residents. The proposal was one of multiple tax increases suggested in an effort to address a $6.2 million deficit.
The differentials aim to address services paid for by the municipalities instead of the county.
In the current fiscal year, Cambridge residents pay the county 92.67 cents per $100 of assessed valuation of property. Hurlock residents pay 91.79 cents per $100 of assessed value. If the differential is removed, these residents will pay the county's proposed rate of $1.03 per $100 of assessed value.
At the meeting May 6, Cambridge Mayor Lajan Cephas said the removal of the tax differential would only be acceptable if the county planned to provide the services to Cambridge and Hurlock residents that the municipalities currently provide.
"Let's be real, the county does not have the capacity to fulfill these necessary service needs," she said. "Therefore, why remove the differential?"
Cephas proposed the county should instead take out a loan on its reserve fund and pave three less miles of roads in fiscal year 2026. She said doing this would save the county enough money to keep the differentials.
Hurlock Town Manager John Avery suggested keeping the tax differentials in place and imposing a higher tax across the county. He said that would be more equitable.
Cephas also mentioned an idea to create a Dorchester County Revenue Options Task Force. She said those in the task force would be charged with locating potential additional revenue streams. She said she would sign up to be on the task force if it was created.
"A loss for Dorchester County is a loss for Cambridge," she said. "And we're in this battle with you."
In an interview May 7, Hurlock Mayor the Rev. Charles Cephas said the duty of elected officials is to make life better for their constituents. He said with other financial concerns like inflation, the removal of the tax differential could be devastating for residents.
Charles Cephas said after the county meeting, he is still "very concerned" and "very wary" the county's budget difficulties will be an annual issue. "And the residents are unable to financially support this type of increase," he said.
In recent months, the county's budget woes have created an atmosphere of concern, frustration and, at times, despair during meetings. The council has said its budget problems have largely been brought on by cost shifts from the state.
Former Cambridge Mayor Cleveland Rippons argued the county is doing the same thing to its residents that the state is doing to the county with cost shifts.
"Is that not the same?" he asked.
At the end of the meeting, Dorchester County Council President Lenny Pfeffer said the council hears what everyone is saying and understands this is hard for residents.
"We lose sleep over this," he said. "Everybody says that we don't care. We do care."
Pfeffer said the council has made efforts to address budget problems without raising taxes, but those efforts have not been fruitful.
"If we don't pay the bills, they'll withhold our income tax," he said about the state. "That is why this is so hard for us to deal with."
The Dorchester County Council will hold its next budget public hearing May 13 at 6 p.m. The final budget hearing and budget adoption is slated for May 20. Pfeffer said the council cannot make any changes to the draft budget until after the next public hearing on May 13.

title: Character, truth, civility matter
author: Staff Writer
content:
Character, truth, civility matter

 May 10, 2025 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: Staff Writer | Section: Editors Inbox 
 
 345
 Words 

 Read News Document

 The voters of Easton made a clear statement on May 6: Character, truth and civility matter.As chair of TalbotDems, we do not typically engage in nonpartisan municipal races. But there are moments when silence becomes complicity. This election was one of those moments.
In the race for Easton Town Council president, Don Abbatiello's victory is a rebuke of disturbing tactics. What should have been a thoughtful campaign about Easton's future devolved into a smear operation.
Residents's mailboxes were flooded with campaign mailers riddled with distortions, personal attacks and fabricated attributions.
This wasn't a fluke. It's part of a broader pattern, including in the last mayoral race and in Talbot's last Board of Education election, where similar mis- and disinformation tactics were deployed.
Let's be clear: This is not how we build trust in our institutions or inspire faith in local government.
We must recognize what this climate costs us. Running for office is hard. It takes courage, vulnerability and a willingness to serve.
When elections are defined by deceit and personal destruction, we risk deterring good people from stepping forward. Toxic tactics don't just harm their intended targets — they corrode our civic culture and discourage participation at every level. Do we want to be a community where fewer of our neighbors are willing to put their name on the ballot?
That's why Don Abbatiello's candidacy — and his win — matter so deeply. He chose a different path. He ran a campaign grounded in service, not slander. He listened, engaged and refused to stoop to the politics of fear. His leadership style reflects the best of Easton: respectful, thoughtful, inclusive and committed to all residents — not just those aligned with one political view.
In electing Don, the people of Easton showed that they value honesty over artifice and unity over division. They showed that even when misinformation floods, truth still has the power to rise above it.
Let's take heart in this result and the historic turnout for this election. It shows that voters are paying attention. It reminds us that integrity still wins. And it proves that voting matters.

title: Andy Harris, local Republicans take aim at Moore, talk '26 election cycle
author: Konner Metz
content:
Andy Harris, local Republicans take aim at Moore, talk '26 election cycle

 May 13, 2025 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: Konner Metz | Section: News 
 
 874
 Words 

 Read News Document

 DENTON — During the Caroline County GOP's annual Lincoln Reagan Dinner last week, U.S. Rep. Andy Harris and state Sen. Steve Hershey took aim at Gov. Wes Moore amid speculations he will make a 2028 presidential bid.Speaking to a room full of locally elected Republicans and Republican voters in Denton on Thursday evening, Harris (R-Md., 1st) acknowledged Moore's (D) frequent visits to the Eastern Shore.
"He's smooth. The guy's smooth," Harris said, pausing briefly. "The guy's as liberal as the day is long," he added. "The guy's a socialist."
Rumors of a potential Moore presidential run, though denied by the governor himself, have emerged amid his weeklong trip to Japan and South Korea last month and his slot as the guest speaker for a high-profile South Carolina Democratic fundraiser later in May.
Hershey (R-Kent, Queen Anne's, Cecil, Caroline) tackled the Moore speculations head-on, stating that the governor wouldn't make an appearance on ABC's "The View" just to remain governor. In Moore's May 1 spot on the daytime talk show, the governor repeatedly stated he is "not running" in 2028.
Following his appearance on "The View," Moore told CNN that he's focused on Maryland when asked whether he's ruling out a 2028 presidential campaign.
"I think anybody who is positioning themselves in 2025 for 2028 is not taking 2025 seriously," he said.
But Hershey was adamant that Moore will run for the presidential seat.
"It's going to end here in Maryland," Hershey said Thursday. "That thing is going to go away, because we have done such a great job of holding him accountable for what has gone wrong in Maryland."
Moore is up for reelection to his gubernatorial seat in 2026. He will face at least one Democratic primary challenger in the form of retired businessman Ed Hale.
Hershey was less confident about the Republican Party's chances to defeat Moore in the 2026 gubernatorial race, but maintained his hardline stance.
"They are going to spend more money on Wes Moore than any governor race probably in the country," Hershey said. "Because people do think he's going to be the next president. And he cannot possibly lose a governor race in Maryland. But we're going to fight that. We're going to put a great candidate out."
Hershey proclaimed the 2025 General Assembly as the "worst session" he's experienced and said it is "at the hands" of Moore. He said that House and Senate Republicans will hold the governor accountable as next year's gubernatorial election nears.
LOCAL ELECTIONS
While Hershey emphasized that Republicans will focus on flipping a handful of seats in Maryland's General Assembly in 2026, other Republican leaders spoke to the importance of campaigning at an even more local level.
Nicole Harris, Andy Harris' wife and chairwoman of the Maryland Republican Party, said she and Executive Director Adam Wood have kept the party's efforts in town and county elections quiet.
"We didn't want the Democrats to catch on," she said. "The Democrats have caught on over the last few weeks.
"So now we need all hands on deck. But we have flipped more seats in municipal elections than the Democrats have so far this year."
Nicole Harris said the state party is celebrating a sweep in last week's election in La Plata, a town in Charles County that is welcoming an entirely new council.
Julie Quick, chair of the Caroline County Republican Central Committee, noted Preston's election of a new town commissioner as a recent Republican loss. In a race where only 36 residents voted, newcomer Scott Messick defeated incumbent Nelson Anderson in the non-partisan race.
"Had we gotten out the vote, we could've taken that election," Quick said.
Republican-endorsed candidates in the race for Easton Town Council went 0-for-3 in last week's election, a campaign cycle which sparked questions of whether political party influence is appropriate in nonpartisan local races.
Quick acknowledged that some local candidates may not want endorsement from a political party. But she said the committee still needs to "recruit good candidates" and create a foundation to support the party's state delegates and senators.
"They're the bench, and we need a bench," Quick said of municipal candidates.
HARRIS TALKS 2026
Thursday, Rep. Harris briefly made mention of Jake Day, the Department of Housing and Community Development secretary who's rumored to be considering a challenge of Harris for the 1st district seat that stretches the length of the Eastern Shore.
Day confirmed to Maryland Matters earlier this month that he's raising money for an "exploratory effort."
"Tax them till you leave office Jake Day," Harris told the crowd Thursday, likely referencing Day's time as mayor in Salisbury.
When asked of Day's potential congressional bid in an interview with The Star Democrat after the event, Harris said, "This is America. Anybody can explore."
"He's just not going to have any luck because he has a record."
Harris added that he's focused on carrying out President Donald Trump's agenda — not his run for reelection next year.
The congressman did note that as chair of the far-right House Freedom Caucus, he offers a unique level of access that can benefit the residents he represents.
"It's an incredibly important role because it gives me access — immediate access to the president, to the White House, to leadership, to chairmen of committees," Harris said. "All of whom will be able to influence what the federal government does that's good or bad for the 1st congressional district."
