title: Residents frustrated with Dorchester budget proposal
author: Lily Tierney
content:
Residents frustrated with Dorchester budget proposal

 May 15, 2025 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: Lily Tierney | Section: News 
 
 611
 Words 

 Read News Document

 CAMBRIDGE — The sign-in sheet to speak was as full as the room at Tuesday's public hearing on Dorchester County's proposed budget for fiscal year 2026.In the packed council chambers, residents brought concerns over the looming possibility of losing their tax differentials.
Cambridge Mayor Lejan Cephas walked up, shook each council member's hand and stepped to the podium. She encouraged the council to think about the ramifications of this decision and pleaded to keep the tax differential for city residents.
Cephas then read a letter from the Mid-Shore Board of Realtors.
"In Dorchester County, 33% of homeowners and 30% of renters are already cost burdened, spending more than 30% of their income on housing," she said. "Increasing property taxes would further strain these households potentially leading to displacement or severe financial hardship."
In the letter, the board articulated that getting rid of the tax differential will disproportionately affect senior citizens and low-income households while simultaneously unfairly burdening Cambridge and Hurlock residents.
Concerns largely centered on a proposal in the county's draft budget to remove tax differentials, a move suggested among multiple tax increases in an effort to address a $6.2 million deficit.
The tax differentials, introduced in Dorchester County in 2007, lower property taxes in Cambridge and Hurlock to offset the cost of providing duplicate services like zoning and policing in the surrounding municipalities.
The county raised its overall tax rate by 3 cents in its budget proposal, a 3% increase. That increase would be more steep for Cambridge and Hurlock residents if the differentials are removed.
In the current fiscal year, Cambridge residents pay the county 92.67 cents per $100 of assessed valuation of property. Hurlock residents pay 91.79 cents per $100 of assessed value. If the differential is removed, these residents will pay the county's proposed rate of $1.03 per $100 of assessed value.
Some residents, such as Tom Hannon, advocated for a more equitable tax increase. Hannon noted that higher taxes are inevitable but do not have to be inequitable. Seated residents nodded their heads and echoed his sentiments with a "mhm" and "that's true."
Several more county residents came up to speak. A majority remained on theme, condemning the council for the proposed budget plan and begging for their voices not to fall on deaf ears. The room was tense. Residents and council members alike hung their heads and let out frustrated sighs throughout the 45 minutes of open session.
Council member Ricky Travers was the first to comment. He insisted the council give staff direction on changing the budget to better reflect the residents' voices before signing it on May 20.
"That would mean, you know, we're talking, everyone in the county is taxed the same," he said. The room erupted in applause.
Council Vice President Mike Detmer appeared visibly frustrated throughout the evening. When asked if he had a comment, he said, "I have a lot to say actually."
Detmer expressed that this is painful for him for two reasons: the first being that he dislikes taxes and the second being that this is not his doing.
"This entire imbalance was foisted upon us by a supermajority from somewhere else," he continued.
"It's extremely painful to have any implication on things originating in this county. This is all from the state," he said. As Detmer concluded, a few residents walked out in frustration.
At prior meetings, Dorchester County officials have placed some blame for the $6.2 million deficit with state mandates for education funding and cost shifts from the state for things like teacher pensions.
Council member Rob Kramer did not make a comment and council member William Nichols stated he is waiting until the budget vote next week to comment. That meeting will be held on May 20 at 6 p.m.

title: Eastern Shore legislators push for Gov. Moore to veto solar bill
author: Konner Metz
content:
Eastern Shore legislators push for Gov. Moore to veto solar bill

 May 15, 2025 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: Konner Metz | Section: Local News 
 
 626
 Words 

 Read News Document

 EASTON — Eastern Shore legislators, House Republicans and agricultural advocacy groups in Maryland are making one last effort to nix controversial solar energy legislation by asking for a veto from Gov. Wes Moore.Senate Bill 931, the Renewable Energy Certainty Act, was passed by the General Assembly in April. It aims to increase the state's solar generation by streamlining the regulatory process for solar projects. Fencing, setback and vegetation requirements would be standardized.
House Republicans and the Eastern Shore Delegation both wrote letters to the governor urging him to veto the bill. While Moore (D) hasn't publicly signaled whether or not he's considering a veto, some believe it could be in play given he hasn't yet signed the legislation.
"I've heard it is possible," said Sen. Johnny Mautz (R-Caroline, Dorchester, Talbot, Wicomico) in an interview Wednesday. "I'm hopeful that he would see the opportunity and the wisdom and just say, 'No, not yet.'"
Qualms with the solar legislation largely relate to a reduction in the control local governments would have over solar project approvals, and the increase in Public Service Commission authority.
The legislation outlines a cap on how much land the Maryland Public Service Commission can grant to solar projects in each county — 5% of land designated for agriculture and forests.
Republicans attempted but failed during session to lower that cap.
Del. Chris Adams (R-Caroline, Dorchester, Talbot, Wicomico) said Thursday that Eastern Shore counties could have thousands of acres up for solar development even with the 5% cap.
At a legislative wrap-up discussion in Easton Wednesday, Mautz said solar interests came into Annapolis and "cleared the decks."
"They wanted to set up their own regulatory system, they wanted to set up their own siting system," he said. "And they wanted to run this through the Public Service Commission."
"It puts an X on the Eastern Shore," Mautz added. "We are the prime target for solar investment."
The Chesapeake Climate Action Network, an environmental nonprofit that's one of the bill's many advocate groups, encouraged supporters to contact Moore's office and lobby for no veto. Brittany Baker, the organization's Maryland director, said rumors of a veto were floating.
"The rumor mill was churning, and no one had a concrete answer here or there," Baker said.
Baker said in addition to streamlining processes that otherwise vary greatly across the state, the bill is set to codify best practices. And it could help local farmers who are looking to remain economically viable, she said.
"It provides another way for people to be able to stay on their farms and make revenue," Baker said.
PUSH TO VETO
The governor's office didn't comment specifically on whether Moore is considering a veto, but did provide a statement.
"As Governor Moore reviews the hundreds of bills put forward this session, he will continue to work with the State Legislature, local leaders, and all partners involved to ensure that we are signing legislation that will make Maryland safer, more affordable, more competitive, and the state that serves," the statement read.
Baker said despite rumors, the Chesapeake Climate Action Network believes Senate Bill 931 will become law.
"We're pretty sure at this point that the governor will not be vetoing this bill," she said.
Mautz acknowledged a veto is a tricky, party-line situation. He said it would be messy, but "less messy" than what happens down the line if the bill becomes law.
"For the governor to veto it, he's going to cross his own party," Mautz said. "He's going to cross some of his own advocates. It's going to be extremely controversial."
Adams acknowledged that vetoes are rare. But he said the bill not yet being signed may signal "at the minimum, that the governor's paying attention."
If Moore doesn't sign the Renewable Energy Certainty Act by May 27, it automatically becomes law. The governor's next slate of bill signings is scheduled for May 20.

title: St. Michaels presents budget with surplus, water rates may rise in the future
author: AHMAD GARNETT agarnett@chespub.com
content:
St. Michaels presents budget with surplus, water rates may rise in the future

 May 15, 2025 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: AHMAD GARNETT agarnett@chespub.com | Section: News 
 
 455
 Words 

 Read News Document

 ST. MICHAELS — Multiple municipalities on the Mid-Shore have struggled during this budget season to balance their budgets, but St. Michaels has presented its fiscal year 2026 budget with a surplus for the second year in a row.At the Commissioners of St. Michaels working session on Wednesday, town officials announced that the $156,000 surplus would be added to the reserve fund for future use and offsets.
"We actually had a surplus last year and then we continue to have a surplus this year, and it's just being fiscally responsible, and the best thing about this — we didn't have to raise our taxes," Commission Vice President Katrina Whittington said. "So it's just governing well and staying within our means. We really run a close knit as far as expenditures, and anything where we can save, we do that."
According to fiscal year 2026 documents, the town's revenue went up almost $1.5 million compared to fiscal year 2025.
According to St. Michaels Town Manager Don Richardson, the general fund expenditures are estimated at $5,477,915 with the revenues at $5,644,493, resulting in a surplus of revenues of $166,580.
The surplus will drop to $156,580 after the town makes changes to the St. Michaels fireworks funds.
Within the water enterprise fund, the town is projected to have another surplus. In the fund, the expenditures are $855,838, with revenues at $946,900 — a surplus of revenues of $91,062.
The real property tax rate will stay the same at 47 cents per $100 of assessed value. This would mean the owner of a $300,000 home will pay $1,410 to the town.
While the the town plans to put surplus funds into reserve, St. Michaels officials will meet next week to go over their five-year strategic plan, which could alter the 2026 budget allocations, Whittington said.
Within that strategic plan, the town will likely decide to bring in a third water well, which would cause the town water rate to rise. A portion of the surplus funds may go to cover the cost of building the new well.
"We have to bring a third well on, so we have to look at how we're going to pay for this third well," Whittington said. "We're conducting a water study rate. We may have to increase the water rate.
"A lot of the grants that were available with the new administration, those grants have been taken away. So, we're going to have to look for ways to generate additional revenue for our town to get our projects done that we need as far as the infrastructure."
The commissioners thanked town staff for their work on the budget.
"Thank you all the staff for this budget of 2026. Thank you for all your hard work putting this together. Very well done," Commissioner David Wojciechowski said.

author: Konner Metz

District 37 legislators reflect on this year's session, wins and losses

 May 17, 2025 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: Konner Metz | Section: Local News 
 
 459

 EASTON — Reflecting on this year's legislative session Wednesday, Sen. Johnny Mautz and Dels. Chris Adams and Tom Hutchinson discussed some wins and some losses for Eastern Shore constituents.The three Republicans — who represent Talbot and parts of neighboring counties — spoke to residents and officials at a Talbot County Chamber of Commerce event hosted at Easton VFW Post 5118 Wednesday. They emphasized their objections to the state's budget.
Adams and Hutchinson said the legislature didn't address key areas hindering the state's financial outlook, such as high spending in Medicaid and education. Well over $1 billion in tax and fee increases did not please the Republican legislators.
"The amount of fees and increases is going to affect every single one of us here in this room," Hutchinson said.
During the event, Mautz delivered the news that Maryland lost its triple-A bond rating from Moody's, an agency which had offered its highest rating to Maryland since 1973.
Mautz said this year's budget, which he voted against along with Adams and Hutchinson, "didn't help."
"It's not a partisan issue," Mautz said. "It's either fiscally in control or it's fiscally questionable. And the experts are now saying what we're doing in Maryland is fiscally questionable."
Gov. Wes Moore (D) and Democratic state officials blamed the Moody's downgrade on Republican President Donald Trump.
"To put it bluntly, this is a Trump downgrade," they wrote in a joint statement. "Over the last one hundred days, the federal administration's decisions have wreaked havoc on the entire region, including Maryland. Washington, D.C. received a credit downgrade. Thousands of federal workers are losing their jobs. Actual and proposed cuts to everything from health care to education will continue to exact an incalculable toll on Maryland and states across the country."
Friday, Fitch Ratings, one of the three main credit rating agencies, retained its triple-A assessment for Maryland. S&P Global Ratings had not released its rating as of Friday.
WINS
While the local legislators came away unsatisfied with budget and energy bills largely passed by the Democratic majorities in the House and Senate, they did touch on what they view as important victories.
Hutchinson said multiple bills to address health care workforce shortage issues were passed. One of those was House Bill 602, which requires the State Board of Nursing to pursue reciprocal agreements with neighboring states for advanced practice nurses.
The delegate added that the failure of some bills can be deemed as a success.
He noted bills on surgary drink taxes, bottle taxes, unhoused individuals and police traffic stops all failed, among others.
Hutchinson emphasized the importance of in-person testimony by local leaders, officials and advocates during bill hearings this past session in Annapolis.
"Those voices are really heard," he said. "They make a difference. They can really change the outcome or just change the dynamics of a bill incredibly."

title: Planning Commission recommends against seafood odor amendment
author: Konner Metz
content:
Planning Commission recommends against seafood odor amendment

 May 17, 2025 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: Konner Metz | Section: Local News 
 
 613
 Words 

 Read News Document

 EASTON — The Planning Commission Thursday provided an unfavorable recommendation on a recently proposed amendment to a seafood odor ordinance.The ordinance, which came after a multi-year push from Ward 4 residents, aims to address complaints of odor emanating from Chesapeake Brand Seafood, a facility located on Maryland Avenue near many homes. The legislation was passed in December, but a final resolution hasn't been reached.
The business recently requested an amendment to the already-approved ordinance, citing that industry experts consider legislation's requirements unachievable.
It requires the business to install odor control technology so "that no odor ... can be detected outside the building on the same property or on adjacent properties or public rights-of-way." The deadline to install is July 1.
Owner Mitch Hughes, attorney Zach Smith and the vendor of an odor control system explained Thursday that the ordinance isn't feasible as written.
Their amendment proposes a new standard — that engineers or industry experts confirm odor control equipment uses "best control technologies and methods designed to mitigate odor before it leaves a building."
Commission members agreed the proposed change was too vague. But they also acknowledged that the original ordinance doesn't create a clear path to compliance.
"I feel like we're trying to put a round peg in a square hole here," member Tom Klein said.
Chairperson Philip Toussaint said the business, which was legally permitted to operate by the town beginning in 2019, should've never been OK'd at that site.
"That's tough to hear when we, again, followed the town zoning codes," Smith said. "It's tough to hear that position from the Planning Commission."
Smith said the amendment is not an attempt by Hughes to avoid addressing the odor complaints. Hughes noted he's fully willing to install the odor control system, but he doesn't want to foot the cost if his efforts won't meet the ordinance.
Smith said if the "no odor" requirement isn't changed, it leaves only two options: Chesapeake Brand goes out of business or involves the town in "some sort of protracted legal battle."
Commission members, along with some residents, criticized the business for proposing the amendment so soon before the July 1 deadline.
"If we had another month or two, it could've been doable," said William Ryall, the commission's chair pro tem.
The commission voted 4-0 to advise the Town Council to reject the amendment. But in that same motion, the commission directed the council to incorporate an "enforceable standard" into the already-approved legislation. Despite much discussion Thursday, it's not yet clear exactly what that standard might be.
The Town Council will still review the proposed amendment, likely considering the commission's advice to find a middle ground on a standard that can be met and enforced.
PUBLIC INPUT
Public comment was mixed Thursday, with many of the residents affected by the odor in attendance to oppose Chesapeake Brand's amendment. Some suggested alternative ways to reach a compromise.
Shawn Nuthall said the amended wording has "no teeth, no data, no standards."
"We've been going through this for years and years and years," he said. "It's way, way too long. They should've done something before now."
Others, including some fellow business owners and seafood processors, spoke in support of Hughes and Chesapeake Brand Seafood.
"Mitch got a permit," Donna Bramble said. "He did not hide what kind of business he was having. He told you what it was going to be. It's a signed, legal document, and now the town is trying to take that away."
Joe Spurry, owner of Chesapeake Landing Seafood in St. Michaels, said Hughes has good intent and that the town should be wary of not driving the business away.
"He started a business that nobody starts," Spurry said. "Processing seafood is a dying business. I'm one of the last in Talbot County. He's the newest."

title: The big pour: Cambridge Waterfront Development Inc. promenade makes progress
author: Lily Tierney
content:
The big pour: Cambridge Waterfront Development Inc. promenade makes progress

 May 19, 2025 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: Lily Tierney | Section: News 
 
 429
 Words 

 Read News Document

 CAMBRIDGE — Last week, Cambridge Waterfront Development Inc. did its first "big pour," according to Treasurer Frank Narr.The concrete base for CWDI's promenade was poured May 10, a visible sign for the community that progress is underway. The project aims to develop the waterfront similarly to Baltimore's Inner Harbor.
Progress has been slower than many hoped as CWDI has faced significant headwinds.
Tensions between the developer and the City of Cambridge came to a head when the city filed a lawsuit in May of 2024 over a transfer agreement. The lawsuit was dismissed without prejudice a few months later, and the city and CWDI entered a memorandum of understanding to address issues that were not included in the lawsuit settlement.
"And, you know, honestly, that has actually kind of been a blessing in disguise," said CWDI Board President Angie Hengst about the lawsuit. "It has allowed us to open up those doors of communication with the county and city even more," Hengst said.
The city and county managers now sit on the board of CWDI, which has helped bridge divides between the development project with the community. "It is really great to have their constant input," Hengst said.
Narr has been with the project for over 30 years and cares deeply about making sure it is done right. For Narr, it isn't about finding partners who can simply fund the project, but finding partners who care about the mission.
That mission aims to foster community engagement, economic growth and further development projects in Cambridge. "It really needs to be a place where everyone in our community feels there's a place for them," Narr said. "And so continuous access to the waterfront, public open space, no gates, no walls, nothing that would say you're not welcome."
Narr acknowledges that the negative backlash CWDI has received from the public has been tough, but he chooses to focus on what is in his control. "There's times when people question, 'Why are you still doing this? You must be getting a benefit from this,' and I'm thinking, 'No it's my commitment to my community to make sure we get what we deserve and we get what will make us all proud,'" Narr said.
Now that they've overcome the litigation hurdle, the main challenge CWDI faces, like many nonprofit organizations at the moment, is funding. "I think that's really our biggest challenge right now," Hengst said.
The promenade is slated to be finished by the end of summer and CWDI is holding a meeting on May 20 to deliver updates to the County and City Council and is open to the public.

title: Abbatiello, Rankin, Davis sworn in as Easton's new council sets off
author: Konner Metz
content:
Abbatiello, Rankin, Davis sworn in as Easton's new council sets off

 May 20, 2025 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: Konner Metz | Section: Local News 
 
 505
 Words 

 Read News Document

 EASTON — Family, friends and residents packed the council chambers Monday to watch three Easton Town Council members take the oath of office, including new president Don Abbatiello.Abbatiello, newly-elected Ward 2 representative Robert Rankin and returning Ward 4 representative the Rev. Elmer Davis were sworn in by Mayor Megan Cook, marking the start of council's first meeting with its new makeup.
Abbatiello defeated outgoing president Frank Gunsallus in a heated election on May 6. But all was cordial Monday night as Abbatiello shifted from his Ward 2 chair to the center seat on the dais.
The new council president thanked his wife and two kids, mother and sister, and town residents for their support during the campaign.
"We're facing a lot of challenges as a community," Abbatiello said. "Growth, housing, access to medical care, traffic — these are just some of the things that we heard during the campaign that people are really concerned about. We do have some challenges ahead of us. And I'm looking forward to working toward solutions to those challenges."
Abbatiello added of Gunsallus, "Even though we disagreed and were at odds during the election, I want to thank Mr. Gunsallus for his service to the community over the last two years."
Gunsallus, whose term as president began in 2023, provided remarks before shaking hands with the rest of the council at the start of Monday's meeting.
"We haven't always agreed, but we've always shared the same goal: to do what's best for Easton," Gunsallus said. "And for that, I am proud."
"To the new council, I wish you nothing but success as you take on the important work ahead," he added. "May you lead with wisdom, listen with compassion and help Easton grow in a way that honors its past and embraces its future. I have every confidence that this town is in good hands."
Easton residents came out in droves to vote on election day, with over 3,200 ballots cast, a town record for a municipal election. All three races were contested, but Abbatiello and Rankin secured decisive victories (69% of votes each) in two-person races while Davis won comfortably (54%) in a three-person race.
After the swearing-in ceremony, Cook said she believes voters "sent a clear message."
"They want to see respect and civility restored," Cook said. "They want their local leaders focused and working together collaboratively to address the needs of our community."
Following the meeting, council members shared excitement for the work ahead of them.
"I applaud all three of you for how you ran your campaigns, and I am delightful at the outcome," said Ward 1 representative Maureen Curry, who endorsed Abbatiello. "And I am so looking forward to working with all of you."
Ward 3's David Montgomery, who made a somewhat surprising endorsement of Abbatiello during the campaign, said voters demonstrated a want for "integrity, openness (and) clarity."
"I am looking forward very much to the next two years of working on this council and working together cooperatively, in a friendly manner, with respect for each other, even when we don't necessarily agree on everything," Montgomery said.

title: Greensboro Historical Society building decision to be made June 5
author: AHMAD GARNETT agarnett@chespub.com
content:
Greensboro Historical Society building decision to be made June 5

 May 20, 2025 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: AHMAD GARNETT agarnett@chespub.com | Section: News 
 
 471
 Words 

 Read News Document

 GREENSBORO — At the Greensboro Town Council Meeting Thursday, the council decided that on June 5, they will make a decision on whether or not the historical society would keep its space.Town officials began discussing potentially moving the Greensboro Historical Society out of the Weaver Building in March. The move would free up space for other organizations and town agencies, but it would leave the historical society without a permanent home.
Though no decision was made Thursday, Councilman Joe Noon made it clear he feels the council and the town should make a decision very soon because the town needs the building.
"Mayor, council, this was already discussed," Noon said. "We said that we were going to ask them to leave at one meeting, then we come back, then we say, 'we don't know if we want them to leave or not.' We need our building back.
"Let's stop playing with the historic society, please. You already know that we all need the building back. Let's just come up with the date."
The council members elected to hold a public hearing at the June 5 meeting, then make a decision on the historical society after the public hearing.
Councilwoman Christina Robinson and Councilman Pete Brelia said they had met with Greensboro Historical Society President Charles Dean and discussed multiple relocation options for the historical society.
While Dean couldn't make it in person to Thursday's meeting, he told the Star Democrat that the he had a "pleasant exchange" with the council members.
"We had a pleasant exchange of ideas when we did meet," Dean said. "It was not adversarial at all, nor did I think it would be, so I just look forward to the June 5 hearing and hope that the public would turn out to support the Greensboro Historical Society."
Robinson and Brelia made points on different locations, but no location has been solidified and no final decision was made. The council members say they plan to continue to work towards a solution that would be best for both parties.
"We all value the historical society," Robinson said. "We are trying to keep it within the town limits. No final decision has been made, but we're all aware that something needs to be done, and we are working to try and work out a solution that works out for everybody."
Dean assures residents that the Greensboro Historical Society will not be dissolved and will work to find a location if moved.
"If they vote to remove us from the Weaver building, they're not dissolving the historical society," Dean said. "The Greensboro Historical Society will continue to exist. We will find a place for the collection even if the museum has to go dormant for some time, things will be in storage and eventually we'll find a better place and we will to continue to celebrate Greensboro's history at that point."

title: Dorchester County Council approves 2026 budget
author: Lily Tierney
content:
Dorchester County Council approves 2026 budget

 May 21, 2025 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: Lily Tierney | Section: Dorchester 
 
 434
 Words 

 Read News Document

 DORCHESTER — After receiving community feedback over removing the tax differentials for Cambridge and Hurlock, the Dorchester County Council worked with each other, County Manager Jerry Jones and county staff to modify the proposed county budget.The differentials, which lower tax rates in the municipalities to account for duplicated services, remain intact in the fiscal year 2026 budget passed by the County Council Tuesday.
Rather than removing the differentials, the county made adjustments to its budget including deferring all nonprofit funding to a later time.
The county's real property tax rate will increase by 3 cents across the board, bringing the overall tax rate to $1.03 per $100 of assessed value. Cambridge residents will pay 95.67 cents per $100 of assessed value, and Hurlock residents will pay 94.79 cents per $100 of assessed value.
"We came up with a product. Is it the best product in the world? Heck no. But it will suit the needs of the people in the county," said council member William Nichols in reference to the budget.
As Nichols voted in favor of the budget bill, he made a point to explain to the community that this was the worst budget he has seen in the 30 years he's sat on the council. Nichols said that there have been no hidden agendas and that he appreciates all the feedback.
Council President Lenny Pfeffer is concerned the council will end up in the same position next year, with the state of Maryland expecting to reach a $6 billion deficit in the next two years if there are no significant changes.
Council member Rob Kramer agreed with Nichols, saying this was the worst budget he's seen in the 20 years in his seat, but "we made lemons out of lemonade."
Contention between the state capital and rural Maryland was brought up often. Kramer said he doesn't think Annapolis has any hope in rural Maryland, but at the same time, he doesn't have any hope in Annapolis.
Maryland Del. Tom Hutchinson (R-Caroline, Dorchester, Talbot, Wicomico) attended the meeting Tuesday, assuring residents they have a voice in Annapolis. Hutchinson echoed the sentiments of the council members, saying there's a major disconnect between what happens in the capital and what happens in the community.
"I just ask you, please, when you hear us talking about this stuff next year, please, I ask you to write letters, please make phone calls, please be as active as possible in your community to relay to Annapolis that Dorchester County cannot continue to take the economic hits it has been," Pfeffer said before opening up the floor for comments.
The budget bill will take effect on July 1.

 GREENSBORO — The town of Greensboro has officially sold the former town hall building that sits at 113 Main St.The town sold the building to 410 holdings for $165,000 in cash.
Town Hall has been empty since October, when asbestos and mold were found in a second-floor office.
"Laboratory results showed elevated levels of mold throughout the 2nd floor of the building and confirmed there was a risk of exposure and contamination," the town said in a Facebook post on Oct. 17.
Town officials have since been working out of the Town Meeting Hall on 115 Main St.
Interim Town Manager Jamie Fowler presented a timeline of the sale in a phone conversation with The Star Democrat Friday.
"We paid $115,000 for the house back in 2014, then we decided to sell it because of the issues," Fowler said. "They had introduced a bid for $191,000 contention on the buyers then the buyers backed out.
"So then there was a cash offer later on and they could only do $165,000 because if they to pay more they would have to get lending, which would involve inspections, which could make or break a sale."
At the town's most recent meeting, resident Kim Ernest brought questions and records about what the money from the sale of town hall will be used for.
Ernest stated that at the March 6 meeting, former Town Manager Tammy Kelledes said some of the money will be used for water/sewer reserves and debt reduction. Ernest then questioned whether this was where the money from the sale ended up.
"I don't know that that money's been spent yet. I don't have a direct answer for that right now," Mayor David Spencer said.
Ernest then asked if that was still the plan for the money. Spencer answered, "I can't say it is going to be or not. It depends on what the new budget says."

title: Stakeholders meet to discuss Cambridge waterfront
author: Lily Tierney
content:
Stakeholders meet to discuss Cambridge waterfront

 May 23, 2025 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: Lily Tierney | Section: News 
 
 363
 Words 

 Read News Document

 CAMBRIDGE — The Cambridge Waterfront Development, Inc. board, the Dorchester County Council and Cambridge City Council convened at their first quarterly stakeholder meetings Tuesday.The parties agreed to hold the quarterly meetings after convening in April. The meetings aim to repair relations between CWDI and the governments after years of contention including a lawsuit between CWDI and the city last summer.
Tuesday, county officials officials expressed lingering concerns CWDI won't attract a developer if it doesn't come up with a concrete project design soon.
During the open meeting, CWDI board members and Treasurer Frank Narr presented updates and working documents regarding the development of Cambridge's waterfront.
The team shared a revised version of the master plan introduced in 2023. The $3 million proposal laid out in the master plan includes a promenade (which is already under construction), two waterfront restaurants, townhomes, retail space, condominiums or a hotel, a facility for boat restoration and construction, two football fields' worth of public open space, and a fishing pier.
CWDI board member Tim Crosby said the goal is to create a vital, multipurpose space for the community that continues to honor Cambridge's maritime heritage.
According to County Council President Lenny Pfeffer, there have been multiple iterations of the design plan over the six years he's been on the council.
County Council Vice President Mike Detmer questioned the necessity of such a large amount of open space, saying residents have raised similar concerns.
Pfeffer, referencing CWDI's financial challenges without a secured developer. He said, "I'm real apprehensive about going forward without a buyer."
During the April meeting, Cambridge's Ward 1 Commissioner Brett Summers encouraged the board to hire a broker to support further development. Summers said a broker would offer valuable market expertise, assist with financial forecasting and modeling, and manage marketing and other critical functions.
During Tuesday's meeting, Narr expressed hesitation about hiring a broker due to previous legal issues with the city regarding a 2022 transfer agreement. However, Summers assured attendees that hiring a broker would not violate the agreement.
A decision on whether or not CWDI will hire a broker will be made at the next stakeholder meeting, which has not yet been set. Pfeffer hopes it will happen within the next three months.

title: Legacy Bricks honor military veterans, memorialize the fallen
author: Carl Hamilton cahamilton@chespub.com
content:
Legacy Bricks honor military veterans, memorialize the fallen

 May 23, 2025 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: Carl Hamilton cahamilton@chespub.com | Section: News 
 
 961
 Words 

 Read News Document

 Memorial Day remembers U.S. servicemen and servicewomen who lost their lives defending this country's freedom and, as is the tradition, they will be honored during ceremonies at American Legions, VFWs, churches and so forth.At the North East Community Park, however, fallen servicemen and servicewomen are memorialized every day of the year — not just on Memorial Day. A spotlight also shines there on U.S. military veterans in general. That's because there is a flag-court-style monument comprised of bricks bearing the engraved names of those who made the supreme sacrifice, as well as of those who are veterans.
Dedicated last July 3 during the town's Salute to Cecil County Veterans ceremony and fireworks show, the monument at the base of a tall pole holding the U.S. flag and the MIA-POW banner is known as the Legacy Bricks Veterans Memorial.
"North East town leaders understand the importance of memorializing those who paid the ultimate price and of honoring those who served. Many of those bricks out there are in memory of those who lost their lives defending the United States. Other bricks honor those who served in the military. Every person who ever served in the military took an oath — I will risk my life defending this country," emphasized Gene Daley, who is commander of the North East Veterans of Foreign Wars (VFW) Post 6027.
Daley, who served in the U.S. Army from 1986 through 1995, when he received his honorable discharge at the rank of staff sergeant, noted that North East VFW contributed one of the engraved bricks that make up the memorial.
"We have a brick out there for POWs-MIAs. They never returned from war and it's likely that most, if not all, are dead," said Daley, who is a 1985 North East High School graduate.
Of the more than 500 bricks cobbled together to create that special 320-square-foot area in the park, about 200 bricks already have been inscribed with names and other information about those servicemen and servicewomen who died while defending this country or about the military veterans. Each brick was bought for $75 by relatives of veterans and of those who lost their lives in service. They were purchased between November 2023 and January 2024 — the first ordering period.
About 40 engraved bricks were added recently, reflecting purchases made by families between November 2024 and January 2025, marking the second wave. Every year, during a two-month period that starts on Veterans Day in November and ends on New Year's Day in January, relatives of servicemen and servicewoman who paid the ultimate price or of military veterans can purchase legacy bricks to honor their loved ones.
There are approximately 250 blank bricks right now, and they serve as placeholders for future Legacy Brick purchases. Once ordered, the company engraves the requested message on a brick and ships it to North East. Then a blank, placeholder brick is removed from the monument and the inscribed brick is put in its place.
"This installation provides a lasting tribute to the men and women who have contributed to our nation's freedom. It covers every single major military conflict, dating back to World War I. Anytime we, as a town, can honor a legacy, it's a powerful thing," said North East Assistant Town Administrator Grant Handley.
North East Mayor Kelly Benson commented, "These Legacy Bricks honor those in our community who have made the most selfless sacrifice of servicing our country. It is a privilege to have this memorial in our community park."
Some of the inscribed bricks honor or memorialize servicemen and servicewoman who are or were Cecil County natives. Common information engraved on the bricks include name, branch of military, rank and duration of service and, when applicable, the conflict in which he or she served or in which he or she perished while serving.
"There also are personal messages on the Legacy Bricks, like, 'We miss you'," Handley said. "Some include cool nicknames, like 'Hell on Wheels', and the nicknames typically have something to do with the units that they served with."
The idea for a central monument in the park came about after Gold Star families had submitted plaques honoring their loved ones and asked the town to display them. Steve Riley, who works for Entech Engineering and is the town's contracted engineer, designed the Legacy Bricks Veterans Memorial.
"He did it for free, which was awesome. It was his way of contributing," Handley said.
The construction of the Legacy Bricks Veterans Memorial was included in a series of North East Community Park upgrades that totaled $343,828 and was covered by a combination of grants and other sources, such as the American Rescue Plan Act (ARPA). The overall project included two sand volleyball courts, a horseshoe pit, renovation of public bathrooms, new playground equipment, exercise stations along the walking trail, new handicap-accessible sidewalks and ramps to easily access park pavilions.
Daley is thankful that he served in the Army, explaining, "It gave me the confidence to do things that I didn't think I could ever do. It gave discipline. The military gives you a way to conduct yourself in your life."
One of the bricks in that town park memorial bears the name of Daley's late father, Felix Daley, who served in the U.S. Navy for about 20 years, starting during World War II. That brick, reflecting Felix Daley's service to his country, is a point of pride for his son and for his other surviving relatives.
As for Memorial Day, Daley commented, "It is important that we remember those who gave their lives for our country. The surviving parents, husbands, wives, brothers, sisters and children will always feel that loss. Memorial Day is akin to the day when someone important to you dies. We must always remember them."
For more information on how to order a Legacy Brick, call 410-287-5801, ext 7106.

title: Greensboro Town Council votes to fight solar appeal case
author: AHMAD GARNETT agarnett@chespub.com
content:
Greensboro Town Council votes to fight solar appeal case

 May 23, 2025 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: AHMAD GARNETT agarnett@chespub.com | Section: News 
 
 554
 Words 

 Read News Document

 GREENSBORO — With the mayor acting as the tiebreaker vote, the Greensboro Town Council voted to support the Board of Appeals in its fight against Halo Greensboro Property LLC, a proposed solar facility on Sunset Avenue.The Town of Greensboro Board of Appeals held a public hearing March 10, during which it consider an application filed by Halo Greensboro Property LLC for special exception approval to permit a private utility facility and major utility facility with capacity to produce 1.2 megawatts AC power with related equipment, transmission lines, utility poles, access areas, fencing and similar features.
The application was denied by the board. As a result, Halo Greensboro filed an appeal to the Caroline County Circuit Court. The Board of Appeals will be fighting the solar appeal.
Lindsey Ryan, town attorney, brought forward to the town council the option to support the Board of Appeals in the case or allow the court proceed with the case at hand.
Councilmember Joe Noon, who voted for the courts to proceed with the case without the council's support, emailed his decision to Ryan earlier in the week but wanted the public to know why he decided to make that decision.
"Just so the public knows, I do care about the solar panels, don't get me wrong. But I'm looking at everything else. I'm looking at the big picture too," Noon said. "Like the sale of the house, what we're going to use the money for... I'm looking at the big picture also. I'm not against fighting for the solar panels, but I'm looking at our bank. So, I'm not against fighting for our town to keep the solar panels out. I'm just trying to look at how we're going to pay for everything."
Councilmember Bob Harrison, who also voted in favor of letting the court make a decision without council input, agreed with Noon about saving money for the town.
"I agree with Joe," Harrison said. "Just let it go. How much money do we want to spend? If it's going to cost us more money, just let the judge make the decision."
Councilmembers Pete Brelia and Christina Robinson both voted to support the Board of Appeals in the fight. Brelia's explanation for support brought applause from the residents in attendance of the meeting.
"The Board of Appeals had a hearing, and they opposed it. These people are filing an an appeal, and I think we should do whatever takes to back our Board of Appeals," Brelia said. "... To have the Board of Appeals have to hearing, go through this and then all of a sudden us just say, 'Well, let's just see what the courts do. Just sit here and tread water waiting.' That's not very supportive. Those people come out of out of their homes, they took a lot of time, they listened to everything, and they're acting in our best interest. I think that we should support them."
Brelia made the motion to support the Board of Appeals, which Robinson seconded. Harrison and Noon opposed the motion, which meant the decision needed to be made by the mayor.
"Let's vote to fight it," Mayor David Spencer said.
According to a press release, a virtual public hearing for Halo Solar case will take place on Tuesday, June 10, at 6:30 p.m. To sign up to speak on the public hearing, residents can go to psc.state.md.us.

title: Claims misleading, false
author: Staff Writer
content:
Claims misleading, false

 May 24, 2025 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: Staff Writer | Section: Editors Inbox 
 
 386
 Words 

 Read News Document

 Last weekend, you published an article under the headline of "Legislators reflect on this year's wins and losses." The legislators were all three local Republicans (Messrs. Mautz, Adams, Hutchinson) and they spoke before what was probably a friendly audience, a local Chamber of Commerce.Your article quoted them making extraordinary claims that were misleading and patently false.
For starters, they ignored context. Mr. Mautz announced Moody dropped their rating of Maryland's general obligation debt for the first time since 1973. I'm certainly not going to argue that is good. But Mautz apparently did not say that the other major national rating service, Fitch, reaffirmed Maryland's GO rating as AAA. (Your article included that, but not as a quote from the speakers.) One out of two rating agencies lowered it. Not good, but not a financial disaster.
To put it in a greater context, a few days after these legislators blamed Democrats for the rating downgrade, Moody downgraded the U.S. government's credit rating. This makes the U.S. the first major economy in history to lose its top credit rating from all three major rating agencies. A unique accomplishment under Trump and Republicans. I'd guess these legislators like Trump and Congress despite crashing credit ratings.
Mr. Mautz also made a statement that is astonishing false. He said that a budget is not a partisan issue; it is either fiscally in control or fiscally questionable. If these three legislators produced a budget for Maryland, it must be balanced. Just as the budget passed by the state legislature.
What would be the difference between these balanced budgets? As a thought experiment, consider if the representatives' budget abolishes public education and the Democrats' budget does not. Which budget is in control and which is questionable? Good luck answering that without being partisan.
I'd love to go into the entire history of government budgeting that began in Mesopotamia in 2300 BCE. I'd bet in the 4,300 years since, no one has said with a straight face that budget issues are nonpartisan.
I would like to see these three gentlemen team up with Andy Harris and hold an open town hall where anyone, in person, can ask questions. All four share Trump's values and eagerness to impose them on Marylanders. I think that would be far more enlightening than a cozy chat with a Chamber of Commerce.
MICHAEL K. DAVIS
Easton

title: Eastern Shore Veterans Cemetery decked out with flag display to honor soldiers
author: Konner Metz
content:
Eastern Shore Veterans Cemetery decked out with flag display to honor soldiers

 May 27, 2025 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: Konner Metz | Section: Local News 
 
 414
 Words 

 Read News Document

 HURLOCK — Around 100 volunteers placed thousands of flags on graves at the Eastern Shore Veterans Cemetery Saturday morning just outside Hurlock.When the gates opened at 8 a.m., volunteers made quick work of the flag display, cemetery Superintendent Dean Arcoraci said. American flags whipped in the wind along with many Military Order of the Purple Heart flags honoring those killed or wounded in action.
"There's a lot of tradition here," Arcoraci said of the annual flag display.
The Eastern Shore Veterans Cemetery is one of five official veterans cemeteries in the state and the only one on the Eastern Shore. Arcoraci noted it was the first ever Maryland Department of Veterans and Military Families cemetery, opening in 1976.
Civil War veteran John Henry Blades was the first person to be buried at the cemetery. Today, there are around 8,000 burials and there's room for thousands more, Arcoraci said. He said the state also recently relaxed its residency requirements, allowing some families from nearby Delaware to place veterans at the Hurlock cemetery.
The cemetery features a unique design, with the burial sites forming curves facing the American flag in the middle of the cemetery.
Once the flags were placed, Mary Alice Jones and her son Bill Jones took some time to visit the graves of relatives, including Korean War U.S. Army veteran Joseph Horenstein.
Mary Alice Jones said it's important to remember and honor veterans no matter the time of year.
While Memorial Day was widely celebrated Monday, the Eastern Shore Veterans Cemetery commemorates Memorial Day later this week with an annual program.
At 1:30 p.m. Friday, the cemetery will host a Memorial Day program open to the public. It will include remarks from American Legion members and guest speaker Ross Cohen, acting secretary of the Maryland Department of Veterans and Military Families.
Memorial Day was originally observed on May 30 in the years after the Civil War. That tradition continued through much of the 20th century before a federal act moved it to the last Monday in May.
Arcoraci said the cemetery and its committee continues the May 30 program because of tradition. "I'm expecting quite a crowd," he added.
The Eastern Shore Veterans Cemetery partners with a number of local veteran groups and organizations, including local American Legions.
"This cemetery's about community involvement," he said.
The Eastern Shore Veterans Cemetery is located at 6827 E New Market Ellwood Road, Hurlock, MD, 21643.

title: Talbot County OKs $161 million budget
author: Konner Metz
content:
Talbot County OKs $161 million budget

 May 28, 2025 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: Konner Metz | Section: Local News 
 
 685
 Words 

 Read News Document

 EASTON — Talbot County made good on its promise to deliver a flat, conservative budget for fiscal year 2026. The County Council unanimously passed a $161.1 million spending plan Tuesday.It comes in at nearly $3 million under last year's budget amid what County Manager Clay Stamp calls "uncharted waters."
"The economic landscape out there is a bumpy ride right now," Stamp said. "This year, we knew that we needed to flatten the budget out, we needed to live within our means."
Stamp and other officials have emphasized Talbot County's continued financial commitments toward public safety, whether through capital projects such as an EMS station in Cordova or support for correctional officers.
In a draft version of the budget that only received a few adjustments Tuesday, the council is expected to allocate the following funds for public safety:
$11.5 million for emergency medical services.$10.5 million for the Talbot County Sheriff's Office.$7.6 million for the Department of Corrections.$5.4 million for emergency management.$3.3 million for volunteer fire departments.
Council members thanked Stamp, Finance Director Martha Sparks and Assistant Finance Director Kaitlin Foster-Clark for their work during the budget process.
"This was the most challenging budget that I've ever sat through," council member Keasha Haythe said. "The decisions were very hard on some items."
"It was definitely a heavy lift this year, but everyone bucked down, and we made it happen here," council member Dave Stepp said.
The county's property tax rate will remain largely steady at 79 cents per $100 of assessed value, though residents will see a supplemental tax of just over 1 cent per $100 of value on their tax bills.
EDUCATION FUNDING
That supplement stems from education funding OK'd by the county. While most line items were ironed out through deliberations, workshops and meetings, Tuesday's discussion centered on funding amendments for Talbot County Public Schools.
The budget already included $55 million in education funding as required by The Blueprint for Maryland's Future, the state's initiative to fund and improve education. County Council members were left to consider how much the county would contribute above that mark.
In a 4-1 vote Tuesday, the council approved an additional $600,000 in funding for schools, aimed at filling nine positions, including multilingual and special education roles. Council member Lynn Mielke was the sole no vote.
The approved budget change came after an amendment to fulfill the district's entire $1.1 million request — which had been scaled back from $5.5 million earlier this budget cycle — failed narrowly. Vice President Pete Lesher and Haythe favored the $1.1 million, but President Chuck Callahan, Stepp and Mielke did not.
Lesher argued it is "short-sighted" to not fund the full request. He said it'd be prudent for the county to gradually increase its education funding as even higher Blueprint projections loom in future fiscal years.
"This would be a small step in that direction," Lesher said. "And frankly, it will make next year, an election year, a lot easier for all of us up here."
"I think we should be going farther," he said of the $600,000 mark. "But this goes some distance."
Callahan sponsored the amendment to partially OK the district's request, citing the significant need for teachers. The $500,000 not approved by the council was requested by the district to increase teacher and instructional assistant salaries.
"I would ask that the school board use the money that we give you for (hiring) teachers," Callahan said. "I would like to see that, and not for something else."
Mielke said she was initially on board with Callahan's amendment. But she said she needs "more security" that the district will put the $600,000 toward the nine positions.
"I'm not advised that it necessarily would be," Mielke said. "So for that reason I couldn't support it."
A spokesperson for Talbot County Public Schools said in a statement to The Star Democrat that the district stands behind the $1.1 million request but understands the "challenges faced by council and staff in meeting the funding needs of Talbot County in these uncertain times."
"We are grateful for their support for educators' pensions and for the additional staff needed to serve our students," the statement read.
This story has been updated to include a statement from Talbot County Public Schools.

title: Idlewild Park's tile wall to be removed Monday
author: Konner Metz
content:
Idlewild Park's tile wall to be removed Monday

 May 28, 2025 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: Konner Metz | Section: Local News 
 
 296
 Words 

 Read News Document

 EASTON — Residents only have a few more days to visit a cherished tile wall at Idlewild Park before the town removes the collection on Monday.Hundreds of hand-painted tiles create a winding wall next to the playground at Idlewild Park. The tile display is as old as the park itself, which opened in the summer of 2007.
Many of the nearly two-decade-old tiles include handprints, names or school classes. However, they are significantly worn and at the end of their lifespan, town officials say.
Easton officials delayed the initial plan to remove the walkway in October following substantial community feedback. In a Facebook post last week announcing the June 2 removal date, the town stated it will remove the tiles and resurface and paint the wall. Tiles will not be retrievable.
"As there is no way to remove the tiles without damaging them and neighboring tiles, individual tiles can not be salvaged from this process," the town wrote.
Last fall, community members spoke of memories they had from the tiles and the park overall. Many suggested a community art project replace the wall.
Easton resident Michael McCormack said last fall he remembered painting his tile when he was 8 years old.
"You can see the weather, you can see the time has taken its toll on those things for sure," McCormack said at the time. "So you can see why they need to be taken down. It's just one of those things that I don't think people in the town really appreciated until they realized it was going to be gone."
The town has posted a gallery of the Idlewild Park tile wall on its website. The town's parks and recreation department is open to hearing suggestions on how the space should be used in the future.
To reach the town, email parksrec@eastonmd.gov.

title: Oxford commissioners approve budget items
author: Lily Tierney
content:
Oxford commissioners approve budget items

 May 29, 2025 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: Lily Tierney | Section: Local News 
 
 441
 Words 

 Read News Document

 OXFORD — Town commissioners approved eight budget requests during Tuesday evening's meeting, including employment posting for a new police officer position in Oxford.Before the approvals, resident Jim Wilcox began the open session by expressing concerns over hiring a new police officer. "I wanted the commissioners to seriously consider whether we could exist with two police officers rather than three," he said.
Wilcox said he's concerned it's expensive to hire a third officer and said there's no need to because there's no crime in Oxford other than the occasional speeding incident.
Town commissioner Tom Costigan said in an interview that it's true that there is very little crime in Oxford and hiring a third police officer will make sure it stays that way. "Or even even improve it, you know, if we can get to zero (crimes), then we're doing great," he said.
The other seven approvals included:
Awarding the Gordon Graves Community Service scholarship(s) of $1,000.Authorization for the town manager to submit an application to the Department of Natural Resources to license offshore blinds within municipal limits.Approval to contract with Capital Coatings to refinish the exterior of Town Hall.Approval of the purchase and installation of a ultraviolet index sensor at the water reclamation treatment plant, requiring a budget amendment.Approval of the purchase of a Wapro 14-inch valve for the causeway inlet check valve to improve wastewater management.Approval of the purchase of an emergency water reclamation treatment plant pump.Approval of the Avery Hall auto-renewal for employee health care benefits effective June 1 through May 31, 2026.
The meeting agenda also proposed an authorization to transfer more than $1 million from a maturing Bay Vanguard Bank Certificate of Deposit account to the Maryland Local Government Investment Pool for potentially higher returns. The Bay Vanguard account offers a fixed-term investment with a fixed interest rate, while the investment pool is designed to grow local government investments at a competitive rate.
Commissioner Katrina Greer proposed amending this item to include funds currently in Shore United Bank that are no longer maturing.
Commission President Norm Bell and Costigan asked to table this item to speak about it in a closed session among themselves. Residents began to murmur and did not seem pleased with this response.
"Didn't we go through this with a bank a couple of years ago about keeping the bank here and if we took the money out?" said Oxford resident Deborah Pulzone. Bell and Greer confirmed there have been several iterations of the same conversation over the past couple of years.
The current budget proposal for fiscal year 2026 is balanced, leaving little wiggle room. The budget will be adopted during the commissioners' next meeting on June 10 at 6 p.m.

title: Memorial Day parade remembers vets, America's 'forgotten war'
author: WILL BONTRAGER
content:
Memorial Day parade remembers vets, America's 'forgotten war'

 May 30, 2025 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: WILL BONTRAGER | Section: Life 
 
 560
 Words 

 Read News Document

 High Street in Chestertown was clear Memorial Day of many tourists following a successful Tea Party weekend, but the streets remained filled with locals honoring veterans during an annual parade, a longstanding tradition in the area.First responders from all Kent municipalities, local businesses, organizations, vintage vehicles and marching bands, symbolized the community's appreciation to the fallen. A crowd of approximately 500 lined the sunny streets, shouting well-wishes and flag waving.
After the festive Memorial Day parade, keynote speaker, veteran and board member of Sumner Hall, Aubrey Sarvis, spoke about his time serving during the Korean War, a conflict that started on June 25, 1950 — July 27, 1953.
Sarvis' message was simple yet strong — to never forget.
As a member of the U.S. Army 32nd Infantry Regiment, 7th Infantry Division from 1961-1962, he talked about that war, dubbed the "forgotten war" because it was overshadowed from World War II and Vietnam.
But for those who experienced the conflict, there was no way of forgetting it.
Sarvis said while on guard duty in the 38th parallel, separating North Korea and South Korea, he knew two things about his fellow soldiers: they were afraid and they did not want to die.
Surrounded by veterans, he provided sobering statistics of those who were killed in action or severely wounded, starting from World War I to the wars in the Middle East following Sept. 11, 2001.
He talked about those who died on the Western Front, France and Belgium, buried under poppy fields. He spoke of those 23,613 killed in action in Korea and the 58,220 who deployed in Vietnam and came home in a fresh casket with brand new American flags.
Thinking about his fallen comrades in every conflict, he recited the poem: "In Flanders Fields," by John McCrae, written in World War I. The poem beckons the hearers to remember the dead buried under poppy fields or those living would never be free.
President of Sumner Hall, Vanessa Isaacs Ringgold also remembers the sacrifices of these soldiers and stated how Sumner Hall is one of two existing African American Grand Army of the Republic (GAR) buildings still standing in the country.
She said that in 1868, founder of the Grand Army of the Republic Colonel John A. Logan issued a general order to 7,000 post members to decorate the graves of fallen comrades.
Sumner Hall aims to carry on that tradition of honoring and remembering. She said fraternity, charity and loyalty, is what they strive for, and will continue the legacy of the Parker White American Legion #143, formerly led by by the late Calvin Frasier. It was founded in 1919 and was the first Post in Kent County Maryland started by African Americans.
After the speakers, veterans gathered around the memorial and held a moment of silence for the lost, followed by "Taps" played by trumpeter Brad Holloman.
Ringgold said she was honored to be a part of this ceremony. She added whereas in former years, Sumner Hall has done something separate for Memorial Day, this year, two groups came together, and she hopes they will continue planning the Memorial Day Parade together.
She thanked Katy Weddell, Ellen Uzelac and everyone on the planning commission for their hard work, starting around February.
Sumner Hall encourages veterans to reach out to them, young and old. They hosts monthly events and meetings and is open to the community as an event venue. For information, visit sumnerhall.org.

title: Idlewild Park tile wall comes down
author: BROOKE ENSMINGER
content:
Idlewild Park tile wall comes down

 June 2, 2025 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: BROOKE ENSMINGER | Section: Local News 
 
 556
 Words 

 Read News Document

 EASTON — After months of delay, the tile wall at Idlewild Park has been taken down.The beloved wall has been covered with hundreds of hand-painted tiles since the park's construction in 2007. Some showcase artwork or footprints, while others display names or ages, unique designs representing the kids, families or town residents who painted them.
Tyrone Pinder, a maintenance worker from Easton, spent the day Monday taking down the tiles. Despite not growing up in Easton, Pinder was aware of the memories attached to the tiles.
"We got a couple of our bosses that had some on here," Pinder said. "We saw one of his, and it was all broken down and stuff."
Pinder said the removal of the tile wall was a part of the town's efforts to increase safety and make the park look neater. Gabriella Alvarez from Federalsburg said she understands the safety hazard after watching her daughter glide her hands against the chipped tiles.
"If it's gonna upgrade the park and for the children's safety, I'm okay with it," Alvarez said.
Despite the safety concern, Alvarez has appreciated the colorful presence of the tiles in the park.
"I thought it was really cute," Alvarez said. "While my daughter was playing, I would observe each one of them."
The construction of the park was a community effort, and the tiles helped represent that. The construction was completed with the help of around 500 volunteers, according to Mayor Megan Cook, who helped organize the creation of the park in 2006.
Cook said the tiles were created as part of a fundraising effort for the park's construction.
"Families could go in and paint a tile, and then the cost helped cover Kiln Born's or Clay Baker's portion, and then the rest went to help fund the construction," Cook said.
After nearly twenty years, the tiles were falling apart. While some only had minor chipping, others were almost entirely defaced, leaving little to see of the original artwork.
"Some of them have lasted the test of time, and a lot of them have succumbed to the weather and damage," Cook said. "It was time to kind of make a clean slate there."
After the town first announced in September that the tile wall would be removed, many residents wondered whether they would be able to retrieve their tiles. However, in a Facebook post last month, Easton officials shared that no tiles would be salvaged during the removal process as removing them would cause significant damage.
"I think it was definitely a memory," Alvarez said. "I feel bad for the kids if their art was displayed, and they can't refurbish it or come back and get it."
Adalea Ringgold from Caroline County is among the park visitors who were surprised to see the removed tiles.
"It was my favorite part," Ringgold said. "It is really cute to see all the little kids throughout the years and their beautiful little tile marks."
With the tile wall officially removed from the park, its memory will be commemorated on the town's website with a gallery of all the tiles.
Ringgold suggested that the tile wall could be replaced with handprints or an updated wall with art created by the new generation of kids. The town of Easton invites residents to submit their suggestions for replacing the wall and will come up with a plan moving forward, according to Cook.
Residents can reach the town by emailing parksrec@eastonmd.gov.

title: Easton council members hesitant to change seafood odor ordinance
author: Konner Metz
content:
Easton council members hesitant to change seafood odor ordinance

 June 3, 2025 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: Konner Metz | Section: Local News 
 
 642
 Words 

 Read News Document

 EASTON — Easton Town Council members indicated Monday that they were leaning toward rejecting a debated amendment to the town's seafood odor ordinance, though there was no vote to put the issue to bed.The council's final vote on the amendment could take place at its June 16 meeting, ending months of discussion on the matter.
Passed by the Easton Town Council in December, the ordinance came after repeated odor complaints from residents living near Chesapeake Brand Seafood, a wholesale crab processor on Maryland Avenue. The law is set to take effect July 1.
The legislation requires that the business install odor control technology and do so "in such a manner that no odor ... can be detected" — or, in other words, "effectively eliminate outdoor odors."
Chesapeake Brand Seafood owner Mitch Hughes and his attorney requested the amendment to the ordinance, citing the "no odor" requirement as unachievable per industry experts.
Last month, the Planning Commission voted against Chesapeake Brand's proposed amendment. But the commission wasn't sold on the council's original ordinance, either. In a formal recommendation, commission members advised the council to find a more enforceable and achievable standard.
On Monday, the Town Council discussed but didn't take official action on that recommendation. Council members largely leaned away from changing the soon-to-be effective ordinance.
"If we move this to something else, then we're not going to get anything resolved," said Ward 4 Councilmember the Rev. Elmer Davis.
Davis represents many of the neighboring residents and has consistently advocated for the placement of odor requirements on the business. He said Monday the issue "needs to be dealt with yesterday."
Ward 2 representative Robert Rankin said he understands Chesapeake Brand — which opened in 2019 under a town permit — is simply a business trying to operate. But he said it's "unclear" if the business is ready to address its odor issue.
"I don't see a reason to change what's in place at this point," Rankin said.
Hughes has said he's ready to install odor control technology but is holding off since he doesn't want to foot monthly costs if the odor system won't end up meeting the ordinance's requirements.
"They all said we can install a system and get your odor down," Hughes said in an interview last month. "But there's no way you can reach zero odor."
The Planning Commission specifically recommended the Town Council alter language in the ordinance so it requires the business to "effectively mitigate" odors instead of "effectively eliminate" them. Town planners say it's consistent with odor reduction language used by the Environmental Protection Agency.
Ward 3 Councilmember David Montgomery said he didn't like the proposed change to "mitigate."
"It simply introduces a more ambiguous word for a clear one," he said.
The ordinance has brought mixed public reaction. A handful of residents and some seafood industry leaders spoke at the recent Planning Commission meeting, urging the town not to drive Chesapeake Brand away.
"Mitch got a permit," Donna Bramble said May 15. "He did not hide what kind of business he was having. He told you what it was going to be. It's a signed, legal document, and now the town is trying to take that away."
Meanwhile, neighbors concerned with the odors appealed Monday for the council to retain the legislation as passed.
"This is law," Peter Maloney said, adding concerns about the proposed amendment. "Are we allowing businesses to write law for us? That whole piece of this irks me."
After public comment, Ward 1 representative Maureen Curry said the council won't leave residents hanging.
"You guys (are) worth a lot more to us than Chesapeake Brand," Curry said. "And you've been there longer, and all we want is for him to be a good neighbor. And we're going to hold his feet to the fire."
Though the Planning Commission recommended against the seafood odor amendment, the council still has final say. A public hearing will take place before the potential vote June 16.

title: Greensboro will not bring northern towns onto wastewater system
author: AHMAD GARNETT agarnett@chespub.com
content:
Greensboro will not bring northern towns onto wastewater system

 June 5, 2025 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: AHMAD GARNETT agarnett@chespub.com | Section: News 
 
 440
 Words 

 Read News Document

 GREENSBORO — Caroline County is creating a plan to address septic system concerns in Henderson, Marydel and Templeville by building a wastewater treatment facility, but there is still a long way to go, officials say.The county has been brainstorming ideas since the May 6 commissioners meeting, where Commission President Travis Breeding announced the town of Greensboro would not take the towns onto its wastewater treatment system.
Greensboro Mayor David Spencer said the Greensboro Town Council came to that decision because of the wear and tear the facility would take by adding three new towns.
"I don't know that the council had absolutely said that they didn't want to be involved in the process. I think that they preferred not to be because of the additional responsibilities and potential expenses that may incur on our residents," Spencer said in an interview with the Star Democrat on Monday.
"I know that they were going to come back and give some more numbers... I don't know that the door has been absolutely closed, but I don't think the council had any appetite to try to move forward at this time," Spencer said.
The discussion arises after multiple north county residents complained about problems with their septic tanks. One resident brought their concerns to the county commissioners in April.
"My mom's property started flooding with the rain, and she is on a septic, and it's been drained three weeks ago," Kia Pierce said at an April meeting. "But the flooding is causing her septic lines to back up to the point where we cannot flush the toilet, and it's coming through the sinks now."
The commissioners are working on a plan, Breeding said, but it all depends on government permits and funding.
"We're talking to Maryland Department of Environment about other options, whether it be individual plants for each town, which we don't think is feasible, or one new plant in a centralized location that all three towns, Templeville, Henderson and Marydale, could connect to," Breeding said.
"We are looking at options as far as locations of a potential plant and what kind of discharge permit MDE would be willing to give us... Then also we're looking at what kind of funding MDE or (U.S. Department of Agriculture) may have available to help us construct a new plant up there."
While the county is working with MDE and USDA, Breeding said there is no time table for when the county will have a solidified plan.
"It's all pretty much funding-dependent, and one thing I've learned in the two years I've been in the office, it takes a lot longer than you think it's going to take," Breeding said. "So, we're working through it."
