title: ICE outlines immigration enforcement as QA officials explore 287(g) agreement
author: ANDREA GRABENSTEIN and HANNAH COMBS
content:
ICE outlines immigration enforcement as QA officials explore 287(g) agreement

 August 3, 2025 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: ANDREA GRABENSTEIN and HANNAH COMBS | Section: Local News 
 
 790
 Words 

 Read News Document

 STEVENSVILLE — As Queen Anne's County leaders weigh the possibility of entering a formal partnership with U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement, community members and officials remain divided.U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement Agent James Brooks spoke to a full room July 30 during a Queen Anne's County Republican Central Committee informational session, offering a nonpartisan overview of ICE's operations, national enforcement protocols and local implications.
Brooks, the community relations officer for ICE's Washington and Baltimore field offices, outlined the agency's primary focus on enforcing immigration law as enacted by Congress. ICE is tasked with identifying, arresting, detaining and removing individuals unlawfully present in the United States.
Underscoring the complexity of the issue at hand after decades of interpretation and practice by several White House administrations. "Immigration law is the second most complex set of codes next to tax codes," Brooks said.
reviewing options
In separate interviews, Queen Anne's County Commissioner Chris Corchiarino and Sheriff Gary Hofmann said the county's intent is to "fully comply" with federal mandates. They noted that many components of the 287(g) program — through which local jurisdictions partner with ICE on immigration enforcement — are already being fulfilled within the scope of current capabilities.
For example, there is a designated desk for ICE agents at the county sheriff's office, and at least one recent transfer has been made from the county detention center to immigration officials, officials said.
In July, county leadership assembled a task force to study the 287(g) program. The group — composed of Corchiarino, Hofmann, legal counsel and a representative from the detention center — is evaluating the purpose of such an agreement, the potential fiscal impact and any legal liabilities.
Corchiarino said the county commissioners would be required to vote before entering into any agreement. That vote could take place as early as this fall. He added that any needed funding could be drawn from the existing budget.
"As a sheriff, my commitment is to foster a safe environment for all members of our community, regardless of their citizenship status," Hofmann said. "We recognize the complexities of immigration laws and the impact they can have on federal funding. Our priority is to protect our citizens from gangs, criminals and violent offenders while also showing compassion and support for our immigrant community."
Understanding ICE operations
Brooks explained that ICE's operational components include Enforcement and Removal Operations, which conducts arrests and removals, and Homeland Security Investigations, which investigates transnational crimes.
"We don't go out and see who we can arrest," Brooks said. "We already know who we are targeting when ICE is going out to effect arrests."
He stressed that ICE detention is meant to streamline the deportation process, not to punish.
However, due to Maryland's "Dignity Not Detention" law, ICE must seek out-of-state facilities for detainees, oftentimes in Pennsylvania or Virginia.
Maryland has no ICE detention centers, only field holding offices — meaning the Baltimore and Salisbury centers for ICE do not contain beds and are not designed to house detainees past a temporary hold. The goal aims to transfer individuals "within hours," Brooks said. But he could not confirm what current protocol and practices are at those offices.
At press time, ICE had not responded to follow-up inquiries about these procedures.
The removal process, he noted, is far more involved than simply returning an immigrant to their country of origin. It often includes considerations for asylum, travel documentation, legal proceedings before an immigration judge, and agreements with third-party countries.
Brooks said while ICE officers often face criticism, morale remains high within the Baltimore field office. "Officers are busy but good. They know they're making a difference in their communities by going after the worst of the worst," he said.
He added that some officers choose to wear masks when in public as a personal safety measure due to the agency's current public image.
Community perspectives
The presentation was meant to provide factual, nonpartisan information, according to QACRCC President Helen Bennett.
"I think it counter-balances the misinformation that is out there," Bennett said. "And really, knowledge is power and we need to get information that is real, viable and truthful."
Bennett said she was particularly surprised to learn about the lack of ICE detention centers in Maryland, calling out-of-state transfers "a pretty penny." She noted that many attendees expressed interest in learning more about forming a 287(g) agreement.
Committee member Rick Bowers voiced his personal belief that the county should "fully engage" with ICE to enhance public safety and federal resource access.
Conversely, Queen Anne's County Democratic Central Committee Chair Elaine McNeil said her committee opposes entering into a 287(g) agreement.
"They just want a new start. And we're all trying to enjoy that ourselves," McNeil said of immigrants. She expressed concern that individuals could be "unlawfully processed and treated in a manner like some kind of criminal."
The topic remains under discussion by the Democratic committee, she said.

title: Easton moves forward with campaign finance ordinance
author: Konner Metz
content:
Easton moves forward with campaign finance ordinance

 August 6, 2025 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: Konner Metz | Section: Local News 
 
 431
 Words 

 Read News Document

 EASTON — Three months after a heated municipal election, Easton leaders are advancing legislation to limit campaign contributions and add a number of new reporting measures for candidates.The Town Council has ironed out a drafted campaign finance ordinance. Council members wrapped up their proposed edits to the legislation Monday during the second of two workshops on the matter.
Ward 3 representative David Montgomery, who sponsored the ordinance alongside Mayor Megan Cook during the lead-up to May's election, says he's pleased with its status.
"I think there have been some very valuable comments," Montgomery said in an interview Tuesday. "So I'm very happy where the draft stands now."
Easton doesn't currently have any campaign finance-related laws in place, and financial disclosures submitted by candidates around the dates they file for candidacy don't offer specific details into campaign contributions. The matter raised debate during the election cycle in May, especially between current Council President Don Abbatiello and his predecessor, Frank Gunsallus.
The council is expected to decide on a public hearing date for the ordinance at its next meeting Aug. 18. That hearing will allow for more resident input before the legislation is eligible for a vote.
On Monday, Ward 4 representative the Rev. Elmer Davis asked for the council to take its time with the legislation.
"I don't want to rush into anything when we have time on our side," Davis said.
Here's a look at some of the specific rules candidates would have to follow if the ordinance passes:
Campaign contributions, except from spouses or domestic partners, would be limited to $1,000. Council increased the mark from $250 as originally proposed.Contributions from political committees and organizations would be prohibited. (Town elections are nonpartisan, though May's election raised questionsabout political party influence.)All candidates would need a treasurer.Treasurers would be required to submit regular campaign reports to the town office, beginning no later than two months prior to the election date.Campaign materials would have to include authority lines unless the town's election supervisor grants exemption.Candidates would not be allowed to accept more than $2,500 in loans during an election cycle.As drafted, the ordinance would also require persons, organizations and political committees to report election-related spending, even if independent of any candidates. Expenditures under $100 would not need to be reported to the town.On Monday, the council agreed to increase a 48-hour deadline for the reporting of independent expenditures to one week.Also at Monday's workshop, council amended the draft legislation to require that election winners pay any fines related to the campaign finance rules before being sworn in. A violation of the campaign finance ordinance would result in a $500 fine.

title: Planners send short-term rental regs to County Council with major revisions
author: Konner Metz
content:
Planners send short-term rental regs to County Council with major revisions

 August 8, 2025 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: Konner Metz | Section: Local News 
 
 360
 Words 

 Read News Document

 EASTON — New short-term rental rules proposed by two Talbot County Council members this spring will soon return to the council's desk, though the controversial draft legislation has been significantly changed by the county's Planning Commission.On Wednesday, commission members voted 3-0 to recommend a much different version of short-term rental rules originally introduced by council members Lynn Mielke and Pete Lesher.
Mielke and Lesher's proposals aimed to address what some say is a proliferation of rentals in the county, hurting small communities and villages. Rental owners and agents, though, have said the proposals are an unnecessary example of government overreach.
According to county data from June, there are about 185 short-term rentals in operation. That's largely even with the past two years.
As currently set up, property owners obtain short-term rental licenses from a review board. Once an initial license is approved, they must obtain renewal from the board one year later, then every two years. Thirteen new licenses had been approved in 2025 as of early June, per county data.
Initially, Mielke and Lesher's proposed restrictions included mandatory landlines, more detailed stay logs for license renewals, a seven-night minimum stay for lease holders in residential and village districts, and a split of licenses into two classes based on if the property is the applicant's primary residence.
The Planning Commission gutted most of that.
Landlines, seven-night minimum stays, a class split for licenses and most of the stay log requirements were struck through by the commission in its recommendation.
In some areas, such as with a 60-day deadline for rental license holders to submit a renewal application, the commission is suggesting reduced regulation.
County staff prepared the edits that were presented Wednesday based on a lengthy discussion at the commission's July meeting. Commission member Chip Councell said the update was an accurate reflection of that meeting.
The County Council, though, will have final say on the matter and whether or not language struck by the commission is plugged back in. As of Friday, the short-term rental legislation isn't on the council's agenda for its Tuesday meeting.
"Of course, the ball's in the County Council's court," Councell said. "This is our recommendation. Obviously, they can do whatever they see fit."

title: Code enforcement protects our neighborhoods
author: BARBARA KNEPP
content:
Code enforcement protects our neighborhoods

 August 9, 2025 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: BARBARA KNEPP | Section: Columns 
 
 799
 Words 

 Read News Document

 For years, the city of Cambridge has invested significant time, staff resources and taxpayer dollars responding to the same properties with the same code violations — season after season, year after year. These chronic offenders not only waste city resources but also damage neighborhood appearance, reduce property values and erode the morale of residents who follow the rules.Under the leadership of building safety specialist Sandra Wyatt, we've seen measurable improvements in enforcement, and she continues to work diligently. This persistent problem, however, is not the result of staff neglect. It is a systemic failure — one that demands stronger legislative tools and a modernized policy framework.
Sandra and her team need full support to make lasting change possible.
THE PATTERN
Each spring and summer, the cycle restarts. Lawns grow wild, sidewalks become overrun with weeds and trash piles up. Residents report the same properties again and again. In response, property owners often make only superficial fixes — cutting just the visible grass or doing the bare minimum to avoid penalties. Then, the neglect resumes. This isn't ignorance — it's manipulation of a system that relies too heavily on complaints and is too lenient with repeat offenders.
And it's no secret who the habitual offenders are. Year after year, it's the same absentee landlords at the top of the list — those who collect rent while allowing their properties to fall into disrepair. Their names are familiar to city staff and residents alike. Yet the current enforcement framework allows them to continue this cycle unchecked, undermining neighborhoods and exhausting public resources.
A small number of properties are monopolizing city time while dragging down entire neighborhoods.
The impact:
Blight: Unmaintained properties project abandonment and disinvestment.Burnout: Code enforcement officers are stretched thin, spending too much time on chronic violators.Frustration: Residents who follow the rules are left feeling ignored and disillusioned.
No enforcement team, regardless of their dedication, can solve this problem without the authority and tools to act decisively.
Cambridge is a city that values pride, beauty and order. But unless we stop rewarding neglect with repeated warnings, the same properties will continue to set us back. Chronic violators — often absentee landlords — exploit leniency and loopholes, knowing the consequences are minimal. This has created a cycle of neglect, decline and frustration.
To break this cycle, I respectfully ask that the City Manager work with City Council to implement the following reforms:
1. Escalate penalties for chronic violators
Why we need it: Current penalties are too low to serve as a deterrent. When fines are seen as just another cost of doing business, there's no incentive to comply.
Why it would work: Escalating fines — starting with a warning but increasing sharply for repeat offenses — send a clear message: Neglect will not be tolerated. Many cities have adopted this model successfully, using tiered penalties, court citations and liens to compel compliance.
2. Make rental licenses contingent on property maintenance
Why we need it: Many of the worst offenders are rental properties owned by absentee landlords who collect rent while ignoring basic maintenance.
Why it would work: Tying rental licenses to code compliance gives landlords a compelling reason to maintain their properties. License suspension or revocation for ongoing violations would ensure accountability, protect tenants, and uphold neighborhood standards.
3. Fund and staff neighborhood-based enforcement
Why we need it: Our centralized enforcement model is stretched too thin and largely reactive. Officers can't monitor every area effectively.
Why it would work: Neighborhood-based enforcement allows for localized monitoring, faster response times, and stronger community relationships. Cities like Durham, North Carolina; and Baltimore, Maryland; have seen significant improvements after adopting this model.
4. Automate abatement for repeat overgrowth violations
Why we need it: Overgrown yards are highly visible signs of neglect. They attract pests, present safety hazards and depress property values.
Why it would work: After a documented history of noncompliance and proper notice, the city should be empowered to cut the grass and bill the owner — placing unpaid fees as a lien if necessary. This shifts the burden of cost to the violator and allows for swift, consistent action.
5. Make code enforcement data public and accessible
Why we need it: Lack of transparency allows chronic violators to operate without scrutiny and leaves residents uncertain about whether their complaints are being addressed.
Why it would work: Public dashboards or searchable databases improve accountability and build trust. Cities like New Orleans, San Francisco and Philadelphia have seen success by making this information accessible to the public, enabling community oversight and targeted policy improvements.
These reforms are not about punishment — they are about restoring fairness, equity and dignity to our neighborhoods. They give the city the tools to act swiftly, consistently and effectively, and they support the dedicated staff who have been doing their best under inadequate conditions for far too long.
Let's make pride, order and beauty the norm — not the exception — in every part of Cambridge.

title: Greensboro Historical Society has new location with plans to move soon

content:
Greensboro Historical Society has new location with plans to move soon

 August 12, 2025 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: AHMAD GARNETT agarnett@chespub.com | Section: News 
 
 419
 Words 

 Read News Document

 GREENSBORO — The Greensboro Historical Society has found its new location just blocks away from its current location, where the town said in June that the historical society could not longer keep its offices and artifacts.After months of discussion, the Greensboro Town Council voted on June 5 to give the historical society 120 days to vacate the Weaver Building.
Longtime Caroline County resident William Satterfield will allow the historical society to rent his building on Sunset Avenue, which in the 1960s was a bar and a hardware store.
The historical society was first told about a potential move out of the Weaver Building in March, when officials raised the need for more space to house town agencies. The town determined the building could be used to house either the police department or the town employees' office, but the council has leaned toward moving the police department.
With the move on the horizon, historical society Acting President Robert Moser talked to society staff and members about what is needed to ensure a safe relocation.
While no official move date is set because of new location repairs, the historical society will create a packing committee; a new location cleaning and repair committee; a moving committee; and a building, management and security committee.
The committees will be made of historical society members and community members. The historical society is asking community members to donate boxes, bubble wrap and their time to help.
"We're going to reach out to people within the community, and hopefully word of mouth from friend, to friend to friend gets people out there an opportunity to come and help," Moser said.
"We've had quite a few people reach out to us in regards to letting us know when the move is going to happen or what they can do and how they can help us facilitate the move," he said.
In addition to the move, the historical society is set to hold its biggest fundraiser of the year on Sept. 19.
The 22nd annual Greater Greensboro Open golf tournament is low on sign-ups right now, Moser said, but the historical society hopes for good participation to help with costs at the new location.
"It is our largest fundraiser in the year, which is going to be very important for us now since we have different utilities, internet and all that stuff that was provided to us through the town for the past seven years is now going to be our responsibility to pay," Moser said.
If you are interested in helping the Historical Society with moving, contact Rdmoser60@gmail.com.

 CAMBRIDGE — The Cambridge City Council met Monday, Aug. 11, and the following actions were taken:Mayor Lajan Cephas opened the meeting with a moment of silence for members of Cambridge's immigrant community after a number of arrests by U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement last week. Cephas also honored former Cambridge Commissioner Gorton McWilliams, who died Monday, with a moment of silence.Commissioners heard a presentation from RTC Solutions and Dorchester County Public Schools Superintendent Jymil Thompson about programming targeting violence among students in Dorchester County Public Schools. The city agreed to discuss the violence prevention initiative further by setting up a meeting with stakeholders who could help fund the program.Commissioners heard a presentation from the Alpha Genesis Community Foundation about an event proposal from Blacks of the Chesapeake Foundation. title: Move-in date for Doverbrook Apartments uncertain due to snag with HUD
author: Konner Metz
content:
Move-in date for Doverbrook Apartments uncertain due to snag with HUD

 August 12, 2025 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: Konner Metz | Section: Local News 
 
 614
 Words 

 Read News Document

 EASTON — The Doverbrook Apartments, rebuilt and seemingly ready to welcome in residents, have spent all summer empty due to a snag between the Housing Commission of Talbot and the U.S. Department of Housing and Urban Development.Run by the housing commission, the 64-unit, voucher-based complex celebrated a renovation this spring, adding 14 apartments to accommodate more low-income tenants. It opened its doors to town, county and state officials for tours upon completion.
But move-in for residents has been delayed since May.
Easton Town Council members expressed concerns earlier this month about the delay, pointing out how it has and will continue to create confusion for residents.
"You're gonna have a lot of people who ride by those buildings, and say, 'What in the world is going on?'" said Councilmember the Rev. Elmer Davis, whose ward includes Doverbrook, at an Aug. 4 town meeting.
Don Bibb, the Housing Commission's executive director, fielded questions from the council on the matter.
Bibb said the mounting holdups stem from HUD's requirement that the complex's housing choice voucher plan undergo a 45-day public comment period and be advertised in a newspaper. The plan, available for public review in Easton's town office, outlines the complex's occupancy guidelines and priority and waitlist rules, among other things.
Bibb said the commission made slight changes to the plan, such as clarifying which residents are given priority. HUD determined the changes necessitated a reset of the 45-day comment period.
"We dispute that point," Bibb said at the Aug. 4 meeting. He said a waiver request has been submitted to the federal agency.
HUD did not respond to a request for comment Tuesday.
The apartments were closed in December 2023 for renovation. Returning residents, who have been temporarily housed by the commission in St. Michaels, will have priority. In April, 145 people applied to be put on the Doverbrook waitlist, Bibb said last week.
Davis said in an interview Tuesday that the situation is a "sad state of affairs."
The council member has spoken to residents who have sent in applications, and he said their excitement to move into the new apartments has dwindled with the significant delay.
Residents must meet income standards and qualify for the housing vouchers to have their applications approved for the voucher-based complex. Davis is concerned the holdup could put some at a disadvantage.
"What if a person was good in May and may not be good in August or September?" Davis said. "They won't be able to get an apartment, and I don't think that's fair."
Bibb said in an interview last month that rumors spurred by the delay, such as site contractors not getting paid, are false.
Amid swirling speculation, Bibb said the commission would like to get the ball rolling, but he maintained that the commission would continue to honor HUD's needs.
"We're losing revenue. That's not a good thing," Bibb said on July 25. "But it is what it is. Compliance with federal government is a critical point for any type of project like this."
At the time, Bibb said the hope was for most of the units to be occupied by the end of August. But at last week's Town Council meeting, it seemed that target would be moving back.
Bibb told the council that if the waiver request isn't approved, the updated housing choice voucher plan for Doverbrook Apartments was set to go live Aug. 7. That would make Sept. 21 or 22 the worst-case scenario dates for move-in to begin, he said.
Davis said he hopes such delays can be prevented in the future. He acknowledged that the renovated apartments themselves are impressive.
"I think (last week's) discussion brought a lot of enlightenment," Davis said on Tuesday. " ... There were still a lot of questions that were left on the table."

title: Talbot County's cannabis bill fails, goes 'back to the drawing board'
author: Konner Metz
content:
Talbot County's cannabis bill fails, goes 'back to the drawing board'

 August 13, 2025 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: Konner Metz | Section: Local News 
 
 802
 Words 

 Read News Document

 EASTON — A zoning bill for cannabis facilities in Talbot County failed to pass Tuesday after months of consideration, sending the County Council back to square one.Since recreational cannabis was legalized in Maryland in 2023, local jurisdictions have been tasked with creating zoning regulations for different types of cannabis operations. Talbot County planners have worked nearly a year on drafting a cannabis processing and growing bill, outlining rules on setbacks from homes, odor mitigation and more.
On Tuesday, council members voted down two proposed amendments to the cannabis bill and, eventually, the bill itself. Opposition from council President Chuck Callahan and member Lynn Mielke, along with abstentions from Keasha Haythe (and, in one instance, Dave Stepp), combined to defeat the legislation. Vice President Pete Lesher and Stepp supported the amendments, while Lesher was the sole yes vote on the unamended bill.
Lesher told The Star Democrat that he didn't expect the bill to fail. He believes without it, the county in a tricky spot.
"I think we find ourselves in an interesting position figuring out what the course forward is on regulating cannabis," Lesher said during the meeting. "The state has told us that we must do so, and we now don't have a plan."
As drafted, the legislation would have required processors and growers to locate at least 500 feet away from residential lots, mitigate cannabis odors so nothing is "detectible from adjacent properties" and obtain site plan approval from the county.
Multiple state cannabis license holders had advocated for a reduced setback and lessened odor mitigation requirements, citing that they may not be able to successfully open in Talbot County without those changes. But those edits didn't appear in legislation on the table Tuesday.
Stepp offered an amendment to harden the 500-foot setback so it couldn't be reduced by way of an agreement between affected neighbors, though that failed with only Lesher's support.
Lesher offered an amendment to make permits for processors available only through special exception, as well as increase minimum lot size for growers and processors from 20 to 40 acres. Those changes were recommended by the county's Planning Commission, but only Stepp joined the vice president in supporting them.
Council members who voted no on the legislation cited varying reasons.
Haythe said in an interview after the meeting that she needs more information and has concerns about the effects of odor on children.
"We're gonna have to go back to the drawing board and come up with something," Haythe said. On Wednesday, Haythe said she's working with council and County Attorney Patrick Thomas on drafting a new bill.
In an interview, Stepp said there were "too many moving parts" with the legislation for it to pass. The residential setback should be closer to 1,000 feet, he said.
"I feel like it wasn't the best product that we could've put forward yet," Stepp said. While he still has "a hard time believing" recreational cannabis passed statewide, he acknowledged the county is in a position where it must create some sort of local zoning law.
Many residents have weighed in on the legislation. The matter gained traction in Cordova after a license holder said she was in talks to buy the now-closed Triple Creek Winery. Property owners haven't confirmed or denied if that's still a consideration.
Some residents raised worries that a cannabis business could locate too close to Chapel District Elementary School. Haythe echoed that sentiment.
"Children are a huge concern as it relates to the odor that's smelled, the air that's breathed in the areas where the growing and processing will be done," she said. "We just don't want that to affect the children at that school."
Callahan wrote to The Star Democrat that his concern is land value. "The community doesn't want this," he wrote on Wednesday.
WHAT'S NEXT
It's unclear exactly how soon legislation may return to the council's desk. Any significant changes may necessitate a return to the Planning Commission and potentially a council-commission work session. The council already met with commission members in September to draft the now-failed bill.
In the meantime, the county will operate without clear zoning on cannabis processing and growing facilities. At Tuesday's meeting, Lesher asked how staff will deal with potential permit applications from cannabis license holders looking to locate in Talbot County.
Bryce Yelton said he believes the county "might have to hold it" based on the fact that zoning legislation is under consideration. He deferred to Thomas, the county attorney, for a firmer answer.
Thomas said state law requires cannabis operations to comply with local zoning. Prospective cannabis operators may not be able to make progress in this current limbo period, he said.
"If the county were to take the position that cannabis does not fall under existing agricultural use, then it wouldn't be permitted as such under the zoning code," Thomas said. "So without this (bill), they wouldn't be able to go forward under that position."

title: Talbot County approves senior task force
author: Konner Metz
content:
Talbot County approves senior task force

 August 13, 2025 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: Konner Metz | Section: Local News 
 
 329
 Words 

 Read News Document

 EASTON — The Talbot County Council passed a resolution to create a Senior Citizens Task Force amid calls to address a rise in senior homelessness.Council OK'd the task force 5-0 at its meeting Tuesday after hearing from senior care and housing experts at a work session last month. Council member Lynn Mielke originally brought forth the resolution earlier this summer.
Mielke said she's pleased the task force was established and looks forward to serving on the body. Council Vice President Pete Lesher thanked Mielke for leading the effort.
"I look forward to working with the folks that we'll be calling together for that," Lesher said.
The task force will make recommendations to the County Council on housing, health care, transportation and meal services for homeless seniors.
It will consist of representatives from the following entities, among others: Commission on Aging, Delmarva Community Services, Talbot Interfaith Shelter, Neighborhood Service Center, Talbot County Health Department, Easton Town Council and County Council.
At the July 29 work session, Talbot Interfaith Executive Director Julie Lowe cited an increase in calls from seniors as evidence that homelessness is growing.
In 2023, the shelter received 15 calls from men 55 and older and 14 calls from women 55 and older. One year later, those marks increased to 30 and 23, respectively.
This year, the Easton-based shelter has already received 19 calls from men and 13 calls from women in that age range, Lowe said.
Other nonprofit and health care leaders advocated for the task force's creation at that meeting. They said it's especially needed to help align local nonprofits, county boards and the health department.
"There isn't anybody who is behind all of these organizations pushing to keep everybody connected," said Rachel Smith, chair of the county's Commission on Aging. "And that's what we found is one of the biggest problems. We have all these organizations out here that are doing so much great work, but then we've got to figure out a way to connect so we can help all these people."

title: Easton task force narrows list of recommended housing solutions
author: Konner Metz
content:
Easton task force narrows list of recommended housing solutions

 August 14, 2025 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: Konner Metz | Section: Local News 
 
 650
 Words 

 Read News Document

 EASTON — An 18-member group tasked with identifying solutions to address the Easton's affordable housing stock is honing in on which specific recommendations to send to Town Council.Last Thursday, 11 members of the Attainable Housing Task Force met to review a draft version of the task force's final report prepared by Miguel Salinas, the town's planning and zoning director.
They agreed on five main recommendations, which will be spelled out in an edited version of the draft and eventually presented to the Town Council at a joint workshop. Those recommendations include:
Zoning reform suggestions including removing limits for "missing middle" units such as townhomes, increasing maximum densities for some residential districts and adjusting dimensional standards and lot size requirements.A public-private partnership with a housing organization to build an affordable housing project on public land. Potential sites to include the old Talbot County Health Department and vacant county land near Magnolia Drive.Community education to help residents better understand the affordable housing issue.Make some fee exemptions for developers. A main recommendation is to create a Payment in Lieu of Taxes, or PILOT, program, which could provide a property tax break to developers building affordable units.Inclusionary zoning.
Many at the meeting said the task force's job is to lay out potential solutions to improve Easton's affordable housing conundrum. There is no "silver bullet" fix, said task force co-chair Michael Ports, also a member of the Planning Commission.
"These are all just little pieces to the puzzle," said Susie Hayward, director of government affairs for Mid-Shore Board of Realtors. "Not one area is gonna solve the problem. These are all just pieces to make it better."
DEBATE
Ward 3 Councilmember David Montgomery — who serves on the task force alongside Ward 2's Robert Rankin — raised most of the concerns on the recommendations.
Montgomery said the community outreach recommendation went out of bounds for town government duties. He asked for a "more neutral tone." The draft report indicated that the Town Council should consider a housing webpage and a "media initative to 'put a face' to the housing crisis."
"The part that I could never, ever support on this is a media campaign to provide a human face" to the issue of affordable housing, Montgomery said. " … I just don't think that's the role of government."
Others responded that it's needed to educate people on what exactly affordable housing is.
"It's important to define it for people to understand it because nobody does," task force member and realtor Jim Bent said.
Hayward added that people need to understand that affordable housing matters for "the survival of our businesses."
"They're surviving now without them," Montgomery responded. Hayward disagreed, citing a Talbot County Chamber of Commerce survey of business owners where they expressed concerns that "employees are tentative when they're living in other counties," she said.
At one point, Montgomery said the task force didn't have the proper time "to discuss the pros and cons" of the recommendations. It met 10 times in 2024, though draft recommendations weren't specifically discussed until the final five meetings.
Rankin suggested that when editing the report, Salinas include drawbacks to the recommendations. Ports said the pros and cons aspect was already written especially well by Salinas in the section recommending inclusionary zoning, which Ports believed "strengthened" the argument for inclusionary zoning.
Inclusionary zoning was a hot topic during the town's last election. A draft town ordinance requiring residential developers to allocate 15% of their units as affordable stalled out this winter.
Montgomery, a vocal opponent of the measure, said at the task force meeting that the body's recommendation should be less focused on the old draft ordinance and take a more general stance on inclusionary zoning.
Even if passed, Montgomery said, inclusionary zoning wouldn't immediately bring affordable housing units to Easton.
"That's right, that's why we should've passed it three years ago," Hayward responded. "That's why we gotta pass it today, for all the developments that are coming up in the next five years, 10 years."

title: St. Michaels continues discussions of dog park
author: AHMAD GARNETT agarnett@chespub.com
content:
St. Michaels continues discussions of dog park

 August 14, 2025 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: AHMAD GARNETT agarnett@chespub.com | Section: News 
 
 305
 Words 

 Read News Document

 ST. MICHAELS — Dog park discussion continue in St. Michaels.At the Wednesday Commissioners of St. Michaels meeting, the commissioners announced that there will be special sessions in the future to discuss all things dog park and to pick a location that makes sense for all residents of the town.
While determining the master plan for San Domingo Creek Park construction, discussion arose about a dog park being included in the master plan. The commissioners decided not to include a dog park in the plan.
One of the reasons brought forward at the meeting Wednesday was that if dog park plans were added to the master plan, the grant received from the Maryland Department of Natural Resources could be pulled back.
"We have to identify what works best for the dog park, what works best for all stakeholders," Commissioners President Jay Hudson said. "So we have to take into accounts our DNR obligations and trying to find the best place that works. It's going to be community input, and that's really going to be what drives where it goes."
Residents voiced their opinions about where the dog park should or shouldn't be located.
The commissioners want to take into account multiple factors when decided the location of the dog park, including cost of building and maintenance, liability concerns, who is allowed to use the park and the less amount of people affected by the noise and traffic.
Town Manager Don Richardson, who started in the position earlier this year, has experience with creating a dog park in Easton.
"So I think we are actually a lot better off having somebody who has that experience and is able to ask the questions that we don't really know to ask quite yet," Hudson said.
While no date has been set, the commissioners will announce the dates for the special sessions about the potential dog park.

title: Autumn Block Party in Ridgely approved for second year
author: AHMAD GARNETT agarnett@chespub.com
content:
Autumn Block Party in Ridgely approved for second year

 August 14, 2025 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: AHMAD GARNETT agarnett@chespub.com | Section: News 
 
 444
 Words 

 Read News Document

 RIDGELY — The Autumn Block Party in Ridgely is back for another year, and committee members expect it to be better than last year.At their July meeting, the Ridgley Town Commissioners approved the block party for the second year.
The idea of the block party came from a conversation in a Facebook group last year started by committee member Anthony Duckery.
Committee member Holly Justice, commented on Duckery's post and they began conversations about creating an autumn block party for the youth in Caroline County.
After more conversations multiple members of the community Tina Hurley, Erin Wheeler and Chad Leister joined the committee.
At the end of the block party last year, the committee put out a poll to the community to see what could be better about the event. Extending the time was the biggest item the residents raised.
"People said that they would have liked it to be longer and a couple of other things, so we did decide this year to make it from 12 p.m. to 7 p.m. just to give people that weren't able to make it due to sports or whatever they had going on last year, they can maybe attend this year," Justice said.
Other changes include the amount of vendors and the resources those vendors provide for the community.
"We offer nonprofits the opportunity to set up information tables," Justice said. "We do not charge them a vendor fee because we get how difficult it is with for-profit. We wanted to give them a platform to tell people about their services."
Food and family fun will continue to be free at the event. The committee ensured the block party had many free components because they wanted children and families in the community to have something to enjoy without worrying about a price.
"This is something that we want to do, and we really are about trying to keep this a free event. That was key for us is making it free," Justice said. "... I didn't want for the block party to be something that people had to see if they could do. I wanted them to know they could do it and it not be finances that would keep them from it.
"I don't feel that children should be excluded from the fun things, and life in general, just because unfortunately this economy is crazy and everything is astronomically priced. I wanted to just be able to give them a day where no one had to worry."
The block party will include a DJ, bands, dance performances, free games, face paintings, sports tournaments, craft stations and more.
It will be held on Saturday, Sept. 13, from noon to 7 p.m. at Martin Sutton Park in Ridgely.

title: Community Engagement Resource Day brings information to residents
author: AHMAD GARNETT agarnett@chespub.com
content:
Community Engagement Resource Day brings information to residents

 August 14, 2025 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: AHMAD GARNETT agarnett@chespub.com | Section: News 
 
 279
 Words 

 Read News Document

 FEDERALSBURG — On Tuesday, the Caroline Human Service Council held its fourth annual Community Engagement Resource Day at Chambers Park in Federalsburg.Hundreds of community members came out to hear about resources and enjoy free family fun.
Executive Director of the Caroline Human Services Council Susan Runnels mentioned how important it is to have this event in Federalsburg. She said the event allows residents not only to connect with resources available to them, but allows community members to connect with each other.
"We call it the Resource Community Engagement Day because we want the community to come out and engage with each other. Not just for the resources, not just for the food, but to come out and engage with each other," Runnels said.
Ummu Thomas, CEO of Freddie Bell Jones Inc., an agency that helps organizations with grant writing and one of several vendors at the event, made points on how important it was to be at Resource Day.
"It's very important because it puts us right here with the folks that we want to serve," Thomas said. "We do soft skills training, so that's largely working with the children, but we also work with nonprofits to help them secure grants and funds."
In addition to the free resources, Aaron's Place food pantry provided free food items, and the Caroline Human Service Council provided waterslides and free food for children and families.
Federalsburg Mayor Kim Abner said Resource Day is very important to the community.
"Spread community awareness," Abner said. "Federalsburg is a great community, and there are a lot of resources here for people that need help, and we have it whether you need help or not. There's plenty of resources to get at."

title: Easton's food truck rules come under scrutiny
author: Konner Metz
content:
Easton's food truck rules come under scrutiny

 August 15, 2025 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: Konner Metz | Section: Local News 
 
 677
 Words 

 Read News Document

 EASTON — Residents and food truck owners are speaking out against Easton's rules on food trucks as the town has begun enforcing restrictions more closely.Trisha Wright and Daniel Reyes, owners of the Korean BBQ food truck T & D Fusions, say they had been setting up next to places like the Shore Medical Center and Kohl's before the crackdown this month.
Wright organized an online petition this week for the town to reconsider its limits on food trucks. As of Friday, it received over 3,000 signatures and widespread attention on social media.
"I just feel like we're being shafted because we're mobile," Wright said.
An ordinance on food trucks has been in effect since 2011. It states that mobile food businesses must operate in conjunction with an approved temporary use, such as a permitted festival or parade. Other town rules include:
Food trucks can operate on property owned by the food truck establishment itself, said Town Council President Don Abbatiello in an interview.Food trucks serving crews at active construction sites are exempt, per the 2011 ordinance.Food trucks can acquire a "transient business" license, per the
town charter
. Fees for the first two days are $500 each, and $150 for each day after up to a maximum 30 days.
Discourse online has especially centered on food trucks that had been setting up during lunch hours outside the hospital.
Food truck operators say they've heard from hospital employees who are upset the trucks are no longer there. Employees relied on them as an easy, accessible lunch option, said Mary Jo Flatten, owner of the lemonade bus Bravanson's Main Squeeze.
"They take care of us, so we should turn around and take care of them," Flatten said.
Shore Regional Health spokesperson Trena Williamson said in a statement the hospital complies with town zoning rules.
"We appreciate the interest from food truck vendors; the Town of Easton determines where they may operate and what zoning and permitting requirements they must follow," Williamson wrote.
The food truck debate is expected to come up at Monday's Town Council meeting. President Don Abbatiello said the council is considering both short- and long-term solutions.
"What we're gonna try to do is try to come up with something at the very least that would allow for food trucks to go back to the hospital area," Abbatiello said.
Further out, he believes there's a "desire on the council to have a real conversation" on the ordinance. Any major proposals will include ample time for public input, he said.
"We got to be fair to the restaurants and businesses that actually employ the folks that live here in town and pay taxes to help support town initiatives," Abbatiello said.
Abbatiello said he's unsure of exactly how consistently the town has enforced the 2011 ordinance. This summer, a restaurant raised the concern of food trucks operating in town limits, Abbatiello said. Town leaders declined to name the restaurant.
The recent enforcement has followed the "ordinance as it is written," Abbatiello said.
Wright said other areas have been more welcoming, such as Caroline County and Cambridge. But local food trucks are still pushing for change in Easton's regulations, she said.
"It does take effect on all of us, so we have to become one," Wright said. "We have to become stronger together."
As council members prepare to discuss the matter on Monday and food truck supporters organize to come out to the meeting, one local business is stepping in to fill the void.
KustomScapes & Pools owners Karen Glass and Jon Glass Sr. are scheduling a lineup of food trucks outside their business next week. The pool business sits off of Easton Parkway at the end of Route 662. Despite being surrounded by town land on all sides, the property itself is county land and not bound by Easton's food truck ordinance.
Karen Glass said they wanted to pull together as a community after hearing about the food truck controversy. They have trucks slated for almost every day next week and a coffee truck every other Friday, she said.
"This is what our community was built on," Jon Glass said. "The community supporting each other and small businesses supporting small businesses."

title: Grassroots lobbying derails Maglev train plans
author: DAVID REEL
content:
Grassroots lobbying derails Maglev train plans

 August 16, 2025 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: DAVID REEL | Section: Columns 
 
 772
 Words 

 Read News Document

 Until recently, Maglev trains were being considered for passenger service between Washington, D.C., and Baltimore and eventually between Washington, D.C., and New York City.Unlike traditional passenger trains with locomotives pulling steel wheeled cars on steel tracks, Maglev trains use a powerful combination of electromagnets and levitation.
As a result, Maglev trains can run at top speeds between 250 and 300 miles per hour. That is significantly faster than Amtrak's soon to be launched NextGen Acela, a high-speed passenger train between Washington, D.C., and Boston with top speeds of 160 miles per hour.
After seeing and riding Maglev trains on a trade trip to Japan, Gov. Moore expressed great enthusiasm and strong support for Maglev passenger trains in Maryland.
Despite Moore's enthusiasm and support, Maglev trains are not in Maryland's immediate future, and most likely never will be.
Recently, U.S. Department of Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy announced the Federal Railroad Administration is canceling more than $26 million in federal grants to study a Maryland Maglev project.
Duffy noted this project has seen nearly a decade of poor planning, significant public opposition, tremendous costs overruns and nothing to show for it. He noted the project would result in significant unresolvable impacts to federal agencies and federal property, including national security agencies and Fort Meade.
Some will say this decision is comparable to previous Trump administration decisions that negatively impact Maryland such as keeping the FBI headquarters in downtown Washington, D.C., instead of moving it to Maryland and recent news reports about relocating a U. S. Department of Agriculture research center from Maryland.
That is simply not the case with the Maglev decision.
The Maryland Coalition for Responsible Transit (MCRT) has strongly opposed Maglev trains running through Maryland for many years.
The all-volunteer MCRT was formed in January 2020 by a group from Prince George's County and Anne Arundel County to evaluate transportation proposals from a broad array of perspectives, then communicate their findings and recommendations to government decision-makers and also educate the public.
MCRT launched a grassroots lobbying effort with a concise message — stop the proposed Maglev service from being built and operating in Maryland.
Ultimately, their message was heard by and resonated with a wide range of current and previous Maryland Republican and Democratic local, state and national elected officials.
Gov. Hogan, a former and current resident of Anne Arundel County, originally supported the concept. After it generated widespread public opposition, he changed his stance to oppose it.
Members of the Prince George's County Council sent a letter to the Federal Railroad Administration urging rejection of the Maglev proposal.
Angela Alsobrooks, now one of Maryland's U.S. senators, signed that letter when she was a member of that council.
U.S. Sen. Chris Van Hollen has said: "Concerns about the project and its impact on Maryland communities were long running. While its potential was promising, the devil lay in the details, and those details were never fully fleshed out — including how the project would affect residents, our environment and nearby federal agencies."
Despite his enthusiasm for the Maglev project, even Gov. Moore has accepted the Federal Railroad Administration decision. His spokesperson recently said in part, "… this project had challenges that were insurmountable."
Following the decision, Susan McCutchen, a board member at MCRT said the decision brought her a mixture of excitement and surprise.
Her surprise was based in part on the MCRT prevailing despite an enormous amount of lobbying done on behalf of the company that planned to bring a Maglev project to Maryland.
According to media reviews of the company's disclosure reports filed with the Maryland State Ethics Commission, they spent $575,000 on lobbying in 2023 and $603,000 in 2024.
McCutchen has said humbly, "We worked very, very hard — and all volunteer — but it's for our communities, that's the bottom line."
Affirming that the MCRT effort was the result of "very, very, hard work, Maryland state Sen. Alonzo Washington and Maryland state Dels. Anne Healey, Ashanti Martinez and Nicole Williams issued a joint letter saying, "The outcome did not happen by accident. It is the result of relentless and unified opposition from our community and elected leaders — a coalition of residents, advocates, faith leaders, council members and state legislators who stood together to protect our neighborhoods, homes and environmental legacy. We made it clear: Our communities are not for sale, and infrastructure should uplift communities — not divide them."
MCRT's successful efforts are a case study of the awesome power and effectiveness of grassroots citizen lobbying.
Those efforts confirm that in the legislative arena a group of committed, energized, and mobilized citizens can prevail even when they are engaged in a dealing with an opponent who spends in excess of a million dollars to secure a win for their cause.

title: Potential bill on public nuisances workshopped at Caroline County meeting
author: AHMAD GARNETT agarnett@chespub.com

Potential bill on public nuisances workshopped at Caroline County meeting

 Author/Byline: AHMAD GARNETT agarnett@chespub.com | Section: News

 DENTON — The Caroline County Commissioners workshopped a potential legislative bill addressing public nuisances at their Tuesday meeting.The commissioners discussed a proposed amendment to the definitions section of chapter 137 of the county's code and a new section addressing public nuisances and their abatement in Caroline County.
As defined in the current legislation, a public nuisance affects an entire area or the public at large, unlike a private nuisance, which affects a single property.
Public nuisance properties can be properties that can cause harm to public health and safety or properties that have been abandoned or unkept. The main priorities for the commissioners with the potential bill are burning trash, temporary use of recreational vehicles and abandoned homes and properties.
The proposed ordinance provides framework for identifying the nuisances, which would include notifying landowners and tenants and providing due process hearings in case of disagreement.
"The county does have the power, as does the health department, the health officer and the secretary of the department of health, all have these powers under the state statutes to abate nuisance," County Attorney Stewart Barroll said.
"It doesn't give you a great deal of direction how you're supposed to do it, but you have the power," he said. "So the purpose of ordinances at county level is to give some framework to how public nuisance is identified by the director of planning and codes."
Inspections would be conducted by the county code enforcement office, and coordination with the health department would depend on the nature of the complaint.
Concerns were raised about the feasibility of incorporating appeal hearings into the regular County Commissioners schedule, given the potential for lengthy hearings, but county officials said most of the appeals would not reach the commissioners.
County officials and the county health department agreed to work on the commissioners' concerns within the proposed legislation.

title: Easton approves permit for 54th annual Waterfowl Festival

Easton approves permit for 54th annual Waterfowl Festival

 August 19, 2025 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: Konner Metz | Section: Local News 
 
 451

 EASTON — In less than three months, thousands will take to the streets of downtown Easton for the 54th annual Waterfowl Festival.On Monday, the Town Council unanimously approved the festival's permit, along with its transportation plan and food vendors list. This year's festival is slated for Nov. 13-16. Last year, over 25,000 attended, a record-breaking mark.
Waterfowl Festival Executive Director Deena Kilmon answered questions about the permit request on Monday.
Kilmon said a key change in this year's transportation plan is the addition of two bus stops, one at the festival building on the corner of South Harrison and South streets, and the other at the Framptom Funeral Home on the corner of North Harrison and Goldsborough streets.
The funeral home is a new venue for a festival art gallery, Kilmon noted.
According to the permit application, festival organizers expect there to be five buses on Friday, Nov. 14; 11 on Saturday, Nov. 15; and six on Sunday, Nov. 16.
Attendees will be encouraged to park at the Easton Elementary, Middle and High schools, along with other locations, including The Country School and Easton VFW Post 5118. Organizers reviewed the transportation plan with a bus charter service, police and economic development leaders.
"We have made every effort to minimize impact on local residents," the plan stated.
The approved food vendors list has 14 locations across town with around 22 total vendors. Kilmon said there are three fewer food trucks than last year.
"As our brick-and-mortar people can take over whatever they need to take over, we are backing down because we do not want to be in the food truck business," Kilmon said. " … We do it for the festival, because it's overwhelming for our local restaurants, especially with all our children."
Town Council President Don Abbatiello asked about an open-container alcohol concern that was noted by the Easton Police Department in its permit review.
"I know it was a concern that people would leave establishments with alcohol and walk around the streets," Abbatiello said. "Even though we don't allow that, it was still occurring. Has there been any reaching out to these different businesses to say, 'you need to do a little bit better tightening of that'?"
Kilmon said organizers, including newly appointed Festival Commission members, have been reaching out to businesses.
"We have expressed our concerns, too," Kilmon said. "We want our people, if you're buying our alcohol, to stay on our own property."
She said the Framptom Funeral Home parking lot will host the festival's tasting pavilion. There will be a fence and festival volunteers in the lot, who she hopes will prevent people from leaving the site with open alcohol containers.
"I think we're going to have better luck keeping our people where they're supposed to be," Kilmon said.

title: Easton council debates how to move forward with food trucks
author: Konner Metz
content:
Easton council debates how to move forward with food trucks

 August 19, 2025 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: Konner Metz | Section: Local News 
 
 632
 Words 

 Read News Document

 EASTON — After uproar from food truck owners and residents, the Easton Town Council is considering changes to its restrictions on food trucks.On Monday, the council discussed potentially revising a 2011 ordinance that limits food trucks to only operating during special events like festivals.
"I think that should be something we should take on as soon as we can," said Ward 4 Councilmember the Rev. Elmer Davis.
All five council members acknowledged they must keep in mind the town's existing restaurants when making any relaxations to food truck rules.
"2011 was a long time ago, and things change," Ward 1 Councilmember Maureen Curry said. "But we have to be mindful of our brick-and-mortar restaurants. We don't want to do anything unnecessarily to compete with them."
In the last two weeks, pushback against Easton's food truck rules has been widespread online. A petition garnered over 3,000 signatures.
The outcry came after town code enforcement began to more closely enforce the 2011 rules, prohibiting food trucks from operating in the parking lot of the town's hospital.
The council and attorney Sharon VanEmburgh agreed Monday to look at amending the ordinance by next spring. Then, they focused discussion on a short-term solution.
PILOT PROGRAM
Much of the food truck debate has centered on vendors that had been setting up outside the Shore Medical Center hospital on South Washington Street. Curry said the council received "tremendous" feedback from hospital employees who relied on the food trucks during lunch breaks.
"It's literally impossible to even go pick up a sandwich sometimes with the traffic in our wonderful, little town and get back to the desk within 30 minutes," Curry said.
Curry asked if the town could include the hospital in a short-term fix, such as a pilot program floated Monday. The program would likely be created through a resolution, VanEmburgh said, allowing certain businesses to invite food trucks to their properties.
Easton's program, if approved, would likely include a setback rule from nearby restaurants. VanEmburgh said the best mark may be around 300 feet.
Town Council members debated various provisions that could be included in a resolution to establish the pilot program.
Davis said any pilot program introduced would need to apply to other businesses in town.
"If we're gonna do it for the hospital, we got to be fair across the board to other people," Davis said. "I get the hospital has a need, but you can't just arbitrarily give them favor."
Ward 4's David Montgomery pushed back, saying a pilot program is meant to try out "in a specific time and place." He said the hospital should have "first crack" at a food truck pilot program.
Davis raised the concern that certain food trucks could be excluded from the pilot, providing an example.
"If there's a food truck that specializes in African American food that is not served at the hospital, what do we do in those instances to be fair?" Davis asked.
Montgomery replied, "It just seems to me that you're being obstructionist in these comments.
" ... The hospital has chosen in the past what food truck to invite on their private property," he added. "I think that's their right to do it."
The council also touched on transient license fees that food trucks pay when setting up at permitted festivals or events. Vendors pay $500 for the first two days and $150 for each day after up to 30 days.
"I would not be opposed to waiving that right now while we're in the pilot program," Curry said. "Because you can't expect a food truck to pay $500 to sit outside a hospital or a store or anywhere. Because they'll never recoup."
VanEmburgh said it makes sense to reduce that fee for the pilot program, though she said there probably should still be some fee.
The Town Council is expected to consider a pilot program proposal at a future meeting, potentially on Sept. 2.

 DENTON — Throughout the past two years, solar energy has been a major topic of discussion on the Eastern Shore.The conversation was raised again at the Caroline County Commissioners' bi-weekly meeting Tuesday, where the commissioners dissected a proposed legislative bill on solar.
The solar energy ordnance would bring the county in compliance with state law. The bill focuses on maintaining accessory solar, which is residential solar that is generating power for a property's electrical use.
After discussing several definitions they wanted to revise, the commissioners raised concerns about donating money to the Maryland Agricultural Land Preservation Foundation. The commissioners have no problem with donating to agricultural land preservation, they said, but they want to make sure the money is going back to farms in Caroline County.
The county contributes $20,000 per year to the land preservation foundation. On top of that, commissioners said, when solar projects come into Caroline County on agricultural land, the solar company has to pay an agricultural transfer fee, which the county also donates to MALPF.

"If we collect money in Caroline County, I want it to be used to preserve farmland in Caroline County," Porter said.
No official decision was made on donation of the funds, and the county will continue to discuss options at future meetings, the commissioners said.
The county officials will discuss some changes to the proposed bill and move the bill to an official legislative bill with the purpose of having the first reading at the next county commissioners meeting.

title: Oxford's loss of post office, bank impacts residents
author: Lily Tierney
content:
Oxford's loss of post office, bank impacts residents

 August 21, 2025 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: Lily Tierney | Section: Headlines 
 
 476
 Words 

 Read News Document

 OXFORD — Within the past two months, Oxford temporarily lost its post office and permanently closed the Bay Vanguard Bank.Residents are now having to drive to Easton for these services, and many are unhappy with the setup, according to a survey collected by Town Manager Holly Wahl.
Former Town Commissioner Jimmy Jaramillo said there is widespread frustration and disappointment among residents, which he's observed both online and in personal conversations during walks through town.
"As a former commissioner, I'm very concerned. With the post office, there's nothing you can do, that's a freak accident. I'm just glad everyone made it out safely," Jaramillo said. "But the fact that we no longer have a bank in town that local businesses depend on in order to make their business successful. It's very concerning."
A structural fire that occurred June 23 rendered the Oxford Post Office unusable until it's restored. The Commissioners of Oxford are looking for a temporary space in the meantime, but Commissioner Dave Donovan said it has been tricky due to the federal nature of postal mail.
Wahl said the delays in reopening the post office are due to insurance claims and adjuster processes, and the Oxford office may be closed into the new year.
"There is no set timeframe for a return to Oxford. In the interim, customers may continue to utilize neighboring post offices or usps.com for their mailing and shipping needs. We thank our customers for their patience during this time," said Mark Lawrence, strategic communications specialist for the United States Postal Service, in an email to the Star Democrat.
Many Oxford residents are unable to receive mail at home, since mailboxes are not permitted in the town's historic district, Donovan said.
"You know, having to drive all the way to Easton to pick up your mail is a big issue for a lot of people. Some folks get more and more of their stuff via email, but a lot of people don't," Donovan said.
The bank closed after town commissioners decided to take one of their funds out of the local bank and put it into an investment account that accrues more interest.
"But it came to a head in June, when the town had some financial instruments that needed to roll over into new terms as well as a debt facility that the town was negotiating, and the local bank just was not remotely competitive with what we could get from Short United," Donovan said, recounting a time before he was a commissioner. "I mean, it wasn't even competitive."
Wahl said after receiving surveys back from residents, the town is exploring options to restore some banking services.
"We are working with Shore United to see if we can bring a full service ATM into town, and they are looking at the feasibility of doing that and looking at a couple different locations that they could potentially provide that service," Wahl said.

Yost reported on audits of phone accounts showing the town paying for multiple inactive phone lines. The audit led to about $18,000-$20,000 in savings for the town.

The underbilling was due to an error with the flat rate on trash bills. The bill was divided by dumpster size. The town was not charging enough for the dumpsters including when dumpsters were full and over the trash line, resulting in an extra $100 charged by Republic.
The undercharges were deemed by council members to not be the apartment complexes' fault, so they decided to pay up to $24,000 in fees. The town notified the apartment complexes that trash service will end on Sept. 2, and Republic has been notified.
In addition to the issues with the dumpsters, the town discovered that the apartment complexes were being billed a flat rate for water and sewer services, which has been corrected for the next billing cycle.
Yost stated the cost could go up or down depending on residents' usage.
While the town is disappointed this has happened, they are thankful that Yost came in and discovered savings for the town and multiple undercharges.
"This all started looking at a phone bill," Mayor David Spencer said. "We're trying to be as transparent with the citizens as we can be to let you know where we are and where we're going and where we're headed to.
"There's been a lot of mistakes and as the mayor I have to own that. We can't go backward, we have to move forward. I think that we're doing a good job at doing that, and we owe it all to Cindy. She has uncovered a lot of money, a lot of savings for the community. In the end, I think it will turn out well. It's going to hurt for a little while hearing some of the things that have happened. It's going to hurt for some of you that haven't been billed properly, but we need to make it fair to everybody in the community."

title: Open primaries: Idea whose time may never come
author: DAVID REEL
content:
Open primaries: Idea whose time may never come

 August 23, 2025 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: DAVID REEL | Section: Columns 
 
 798
 Words 

 Read News Document

 More than 500 years ago, political observer and philosopher Niccolo Machiavelli wrote a timeless and thought-provoking message on resistance to change.He wrote: "It must be remembered that there is nothing more difficult to plan, more doubtful of success, nor more dangerous to manage, than introducing new ways of doing things. For the initiator has the enmity of all who would profit by the preservation of the old ways of doing things and merely lukewarm defenders in those who would gain by the new ones."
This observation is being tested by ongoing efforts in Maryland to change the rules relative to participation in and state funding of partisan primary elections.
This issue is driven in large part by the increasing number of individuals in Maryland who have chosen to register to vote as unaffiliated, often referred to as independents.
In April of this year, more than 22% of registered voters in Maryland are registered as unaffiliated. That number was less than 21% in 2023.
Another 2% of individuals in Maryland have chosen to register with a third party.
The bottom line is almost a quarter of the registered voters in Maryland are not registered as a Republican or Democratic voter and as a consequence, they cannot vote in primary elections.
One can assume this trend will not only continue but also accelerate.
In April of this year, more than 36% of new voter registrations, not changes to existing registrations, were unaffiliated.
In May of this year, five unaffiliated Maryland voters filed a lawsuit in Anne Arundel County District Court. They are working with an advocacy group — Open Primaries Education Fund (not to be confused with the Open Society Foundation funded by George Soros).
The plaintiffs in the suit acknowledge political parties may have the right to exclude citizens from their primary elections, but it is unconstitutional for the state of Maryland to organize and pay for those elections.
They claim the only way the state can be in compliance with the state constitution is if the state Democratic and Republican parties fund their respective primary elections or if both parties allow all qualified citizens, regardless of their party affiliation, to vote in primaries.
The defendant in the lawsuit is the Maryland State Board of Elections, the state agency that manages primary elections.
An assistant state attorney general representing the Board of Elections has requested the Anne Arundel County District Court dismiss the lawsuit based on four claims.
One claim is that a lawsuit filed by only five taxpayers is insufficient to establish standing for such a challenge.
Another claim is that the merits of the unaffiliated voters' challenge have already been considered and rejected in two previous court decisions — one handed down by a state court and one by a federal court.
The Supreme Court of Maryland issued a decision that "voters have no right under the state constitution to vote in the primary elections of a party to which they do not belong."
The U.S. Supreme Court has upheld closed primaries and a political party's First Amendment right "not to associate" and therefore cannot be required to allow unaffiliated voters to participate in their primary elections.
Complicating matters further on a judicial resolution on this matter is the opinion of a former senior voting rights attorney at the American Civil Liberties Union.
He has said the courts are often reluctant to depart from regular procedures on changing election laws and prefer to seek legislative consideration and action.
While pursuing changes in the Maryland General Assembly is always an option, recent history is that pursuing open primary legislation in that arena has failed to get traction.
In the 2023 General Assembly session, one bill was introduced in the Maryland Senate, and one was introduced Maryland House of Delegates, both on open primaries.
Each bill only had one sponsor which is a clear indication that neither bill had even minimal support in the General Assembly.
As a result, neither bill was voted from committee, an essential step on the always challenging process to enact a new law or revise an existing law in Maryland.
Also, no open primary legislation has been introduced in the General Assembly since then.
Going forward, I predict two outcomes on some form of open primaries in Maryland.
I predict, that in every court case, including any appeals to higher courts, eventually the definitive decisions will be that any changes to the election laws must be approved in the General Sssembly and signed by the governor.
I also predict, without widespread public demand for any election law changes in Maryland, they will never be approved in the General Assembly and by the governor.
If my predictions occur, it will affirm that Machiavelli's observation — "There is nothing more difficult to plan, more doubtful of success, nor more dangerous to manage, than introducing new ways of doing things" is as relevant today as it was when he wrote it in 1513.

title: Mobile competition is beneficial
author: Staff Writer
content:
Mobile competition is beneficial

 August 23, 2025 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: Staff Writer | Section: Editors Inbox 
 
 177
 Words 

 Read News Document

 I'm not clear why we differentiate between brick-and-mortar businesses and mobile businesses.As a previous owner of a brick-and-mortar business, I had mobile competitors. I took the approach that while I could offer a significantly larger array of products and services, there are customers that will opt for a less comprehensive menu.
I could have started a mobile service too, but the customer base I sought was not those needing or desiring limited mobile options.
So I would advise Easton council to treat mobile businesses like the brick-and-mortar ones. Charge them the same annual fee. Collect the taxes on their income. Collect taxes on the wages they pay their staff. And require the mobile businesses to adhere to the same OSHA, Department of Health, etc. laws and ordinances that all brick-and-mortar businesses are required to follow.
Restaurant owners aren't happy when another restaurant opens. Liquor stores aren't happy when another liquor store opens. But it's called competition.
Maybe … just maybe … mobile competition will get brick-and-mortar businesses to create competitive options rather than asking local governments to stifle them.
TERENCE JOHN
Easton
