title: Caroline County Commissioners advance solar ordinance with amendments
author: AHMAD GARNETT agarnett@chespub.com
content:
Caroline County Commissioners advance solar ordinance with amendments

 September 10, 2025 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: AHMAD GARNETT agarnett@chespub.com | Section: News 
 
 424
 Words 

 Read News Document

 DENTON — The Caroline County Commissioners have had multiple discussions about the future of solar energy in the county. Another discussion was on the agenda for the commissioners' meeting Tuesday.They discussed a solar energy ordinance designed to help bring the county's solar laws in compliance with state laws passed by Maryland General Assembly.
The ordinance would allow the county to put certain requirements for solar electric energy generating facilities in place.
Commissioner Larry Porter has had multiple safety questions about battery energy storage systems, which he feels were never answered by the state.
"I don't want to use the word lie, but I will because we've been lied to about this from day one," Porter said. "From the time this was brought up, we have been told by various agencies, various departments, that there were going to be safety provisions that were going to be introduced in this. There isn't anything in the Senate Bill 931. There was nothing in that bill, contrary to what I was told on record in that hearing that addresses self-contained fire suppression in these systems."
"Now, I was told down it when we were at MACO, I stopped and talked at one of the booths for the Maryland State Fireman's Association, and I was told it at that time, and that was August, that there had been some changes to the bill, but the guy didn't know what they were. So, until somebody can tell me that these things are going to be safe and they're not going to propose a hazard to our firefighters and first responders, I'm not going to agree to include them in this bill," Porter said.
Commissioners president Travis Breeding said he agrees with concerns for safety, but he said the county cannot completely remove battery energy storage systems from the law because it is against state law. Breeding suggested adding some safety precautions for the local fire departments in case of solar battery emergency.
While battery solar was the commissioners' main concern Tuesday, four amendments were suggested by the commissioners to take the legislative bill into second reading and public hearing.
The amendments were:
Increase the compensation fee from 50% to 100% of the fair market value for new solar arrays and battery solar storage systems.Add fire department equipment and training fee for battery energy solar systems and self-contained fire suppression systems within battery energy storage systems.Remove the county's 2,000-acre cap on solar development to bring the county in compliance with state law.Make changes to the zoning table to reflect permitted districts within the county where solar is allowed.

title: Easton leans away from annexing new land in comprehensive plan update
author: Konner Metz
content:
Easton leans away from annexing new land in comprehensive plan update

 September 10, 2025 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: Konner Metz | Section: Local News 
 
 728
 Words 

 Read News Document

 EASTON — As planners draft Easton's new comprehensive plan, the town's direction on annexing new land is becoming clear: slow down.At a workshop Monday, the Easton Planning Commission chose to retain language in the comprehensive plan update that discourages new annexations in the next 10 years.
As recently as last year, Easton annexed around 17 acres of county land east of U.S. Route 50 between the Royal Farms and Unitarian Universalist Fellowship. It's expected to become an affordable housing project, though the developer will still need town approval on an application.
Town Council members have indicated concerns about annexing additional land into town, especially as Easton deals with the question of whether it's maxing out on residential growth.
The comprehensive plan, last updated in 2010, is undergoing revisions before potential council approval later this year or early next year. It outlines how the town aims to grow in the next decade, touching on areas such as annexation, population growth and traffic.
On Monday and at a workshop last month, commission and council members noted that there may be exceptions to the no-annexation rule.
"I would have a hard time with being absolute about annexation, saying that that's not happening," Ward 2 Councilmember Robert Rankin said on Aug. 25. "Because there may be exceptions."
The main exception to completely halting annexation seems to be Easton Point, the development project that seeks to revitalize Port Street and the area around the Tred Avon River. The effort hasn't significantly progressed in recent years, council members say.
Ward 1 Councilmember Maureen Curry said at last month's meeting that Easton Point's redevelopment is "an enigma." She advocated that annexation of the county land in that area be excluded from any no-annexation directive in the new comprehensive plan.
"The Easton Point development project's been on the board for almost 20 years," Curry said. "We have to find a way to move that forward if we can."
Town leaders largely agreed that a project like Easton Point rises to the level of an "extraordinary" annexation that should be permitted under the comprehensive plan's guidance.
Still, the plan should emphasize that annexation generally is "not a priority for the town," said Planning Commission member Victoria McAndrews on Monday.
GROWTH RATE
Hesitation to approve future annexation requests stems, in part, from the town's growth. From 2000 to 2010, the town's population increased 36%, according to census data. In the next decade, growth slowed to 7%, bringing Easton's population from 15,945 to 17,101.
When commission and council members met for a joint workshop in August, the council maintained that the comprehensive plan should include a target growth rate for population. The 2010 version has a 1% annual growth rate, which for the most part hasn't been exceeded. Bumping it up to 1.75% was discussed.
Michael Ports, the commission's vice chair, said Monday that 1.75% "makes the most sense." But other commission members leaned toward a 1.14% annual growth rate, which is based off of historical trends.
Commission Chairperson Phil Toussaint agreed with the 1.14% rate, emphasizing that it needs to be at a mark so the Town Council feels comfortable approving the plan as a whole.
TRAFFIC
When housing projects come to the commission or Town Council for approval, they include traffic impact studies. Developers typically hire a traffic engineering firm to conduct the study of the development's potential impact on traffic backups.
Planning Commission members said moving forward, the comprehensive plan needs to demand more thorough traffic reviews. Klein said studies often choose a few intersections next to the project and ignore the town's main arteries, where traffic is already an issue.
Easton Planning and Zoning Director Miguel Salinas said the best way to expand the scope of a traffic impact study for a development is if town engineers or the State Highway Administration request a larger scope during meetings with the project's traffic engineer.
Town Engineer Rick Van Emburgh said he wants to continue requiring developers' traffic studies to include a percent change in traffic based on if the development were to be built.
Toussaint said he wants the studies to include more consideration on the impact to pedestrians, not just vehicles. He added that studies should be framed around the town's ongoing Complete Streets study, which is assessing Easton's roads on a large scale.
"What we've received in the past as a traffic impact study is going to be worthless for us going forward," Toussaint said. "It's propaganda at this point, prepared by the applicant's engineers."

title: Members of Oxford Historic District Commission removed
author: Lily Tierney
content:
Members of Oxford Historic District Commission removed

 September 11, 2025 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: Lily Tierney | Section: Local News 
 
 494
 Words

 OXFORD — With a unanimous vote last month, Oxford commissioners removed three of the the five members from the town's Historic District Commission.At the Aug. 19 town meeting, Commission President Katrina Greer announced that the Commissioners of Oxford unanimously voted in closed session to change the makeup of the commission. Greer said in a statement at the meeting that this decision reflects the best interest of the town.
Jennifer Stanley, Jim Wilcox and Justin Werner were removed from their roles on the commission. Their terms were not set to expire until 2026 and 2027. A fourth member of the commission, Terry Sullivan, whose term expires Saturday, has not been confirmed of a reappointment.
The commission's fifth and final member, Margaret Morris, is listed on the town's website as an "alternate member." Two new members were appointed at the August meeting.
The Oxford Town Historic Commission is a volunteer body appointed by town commissioners and has five members who have three year terms. The commission provides current and prospective property owners with guidance on how historical properties should be handled in the town.
Oxford Town Commissioner Dave Donovan said the commission will not discuss details of their decision beyond confirming unanimity of the vote and saying it was taken in the "best interest of the community."
"I think that's really all we're willing to discuss on that topic," Donovan said.
Stanley, one of the three Historic District Commissioners who was removed, said she was told about the decision in person prior to the meeting by a commissioner, who cited that she "wasn't efficient enough." Stanley did not disclose which commissioner gave her this news. She said she was never given advice on how to be more efficient.
Stanley, who has lived in the town for 45 years, said she had seen behavior like this before from town officials and expected something like this to happen. "I don't think this is an issue of transparency. I think this is an issue of control," she said.
Greer said that the decision was made in the best interest of the town, noting that the commissioners' top priority is serving all residents. She also expressed gratitude to the many volunteers on boards and commissions who help carry that commitment forward.
Stanley does not agree that this decision is in its best interest. "It's unfortunate for the town," she said.
Moving forward
Barbara Ranson and Will Cawley were appointed to the Historic District Commission at the Aug. 19 meeting. According to Town Manager Holly Wahl, there are two additional spots that need to be filled. She said town commissioners held interviews Sept. 2.
"Commissioners recently implemented a new process for the town where they are reviewing applicants for all boards and commissions in public so that there's a transparent review of how members are appointed," Wahl said. "And so after an interviewing process, members are now appointed to boards and commissions by a vote of all commissioners."
Appointments for the open two spots are planned for the Sept. 29 regular commission meeting.

title: Cambridge Planning Commission advances community garden ordinance
author: Lily Tierney
content:
Cambridge Planning Commission advances community garden ordinance

 September 11, 2025 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: Lily Tierney | Section: Dorchester 
 
 564
 Words 

 Read News Document

 CAMBRIDGE — After three Cambridge Planning Commission meetings with public hearings, Blackwater Rising, a nonprofit organization that promotes nutritious food through community gardens, and planning commissioners have finally come to an agreement.Community gardens were not previously included in the city's code, prompting the need for an ordinance after gardens began popping up and being organized without clear regulation, according to Cambridge Director of Planning and Zoning Brian Herrmann.
Herrmann said it took three public hearings to get the language of the ordinance right and to provide the proper conditions without overstepping. "I find these regulations utterly confusing," co-founder of Blackwater Rising David King said on the second iteration of the ordinance during the Sept. 2 meeting.
"The fact that we had to have three hearings on the issue was that we had listed a number of things that we felt like either should or shouldn't be allowed in a community garden, but should have some sort of permission or oversight," Hermann said.
Those permissions or oversights are called conditions, and in the originally drafted ordinance, there were nine conditions. Herrmann said those conditions are likely what caused the three hearings.
He said the gardens were a conditional use because "we wanted to make sure that each garden had what we call a 'garden coordinator,' someone to kind of oversee the garden. And so we had to write that language and sort of specify that," he said.
In addition, there were nine items the garden coordinator had to get approved by city staff, then oversee the installation and use of these items.
Members of Blackwater Rising were against these conditions and expressed such during the public hearing.
The conditional items were one garden shed, benches and picnic tables, raised and or accessible planting beds, compost and waste bins, fences, signs, garden art, rain barrel systems and bicycle racks.
"So what I think the controversy was, you know, let's let each garden decide whether or not they want those things. And if they want them, they should be allowed," Herrmann said.
The ordinance applies to all land, not just city-owned property. This broad application made the drafting process more complex, Herrmann said. But he said it was worth it.
"I think the Planning Commission was a little upset with me that I kind of inferred that we should reopen the last meeting for public hearing," Herrmann said. However, he said without the public engagement, they likely would not have approved the ordinance for the City Council's review.
King said there are already three community gardens in town. He said to the best of his knowledge, they have not received any complaints about the gardens other than a hose that crossed the street.
King said Blackwater Rising is funded entirely by corporate grants, donations, fundraising and in-kind contributions, and it is run by volunteers. He said they are only asking the city "to not get in our way."
King said 30 residents showed up to the Sept. 2 meeting to express their support for the less restrictive community guidelines. King said a good compromise ordinance was reached, more in line with other jurisdictions that encourage community gardens.
"I think the process worked the way it's supposed to, so that's a good thing," Herrmann said.
The Cambridge City Council will have final say on the ordinance. It will be raised for a first reading at an upcoming City Council meeting, but Herrmann is not certain as to which meeting it will be.

title: Claiborne residents, operating their own well, look for water supply solution
author: Konner Metz
content:
Claiborne residents, operating their own well, look for water supply solution

 September 13, 2025 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: Konner Metz | Section: Local News 
 
 819
 Words 

 Read News Document

 CLAIBORNE — When Rob Todd moved to Claiborne in 2013, he didn't expect to be partially responsible for the village's water services. But it's a role he and others have assumed.From 2015 to 2019, Todd was one of four volunteers for the resident-led Claiborne Water Company, a group that oversees a water system serving about 30 properties.
"I, for one, didn't envision my retirement years being a well operator," Todd said while taking a walk to the community's well on Thursday afternoon.
Todd, 77, volunteered for a relatively short stint. He credits longtime Claiborne resident Renny Johnson — the "water czar" — with the decades-long heavy lifting of maintaining Claiborne's water. Johnson handles the billing, fields questions from residents and arranges testing of the well system.
Johnson moved to his Claiborne house in 1979 and was handed the water company books just a few years later by the outgoing man in charge.
"We had a water company meeting where we invited the people that were on the system to talk about (it), and no one else would take it over," Johnson recalled. "So I said I would, not thinking that I would be doing it for this long."
Johnson, 77, and others are hoping to pass the duties off and find a long-term solution to what's become a multifaceted problem keeping the water system in line with state regulations.
As Claiborne's population ages, attracting volunteers is difficult, Johnson and Todd said. And now more than ever, the Maryland Department of the Environment is pushing Claiborne to meet standards for what the state considers "community water systems."
Community water systems aren't served by a municipal company. They are smaller-scale, like the Claiborne water well. However, MDE requires systems with over 15 properties hooked up to have a licensed operator, according to residents and county officials.
Four Claiborne residents — Johnson, Todd, Jim Richardson and Kirke Harper — explained the issue at a Talbot County Council work session on Sept. 9. While the county doesn't maintain the water system, County Engineer Ray Clarke is willing to help where he can.
"We're grateful that the county was willing to listen to our problem," Todd said.
'WE'RE AGING OUT'
Claiborne, an unincorporated village on the Chesapeake Bay, is a short detour on the drive from St. Michaels to Tilghman Island.
According to residents, a 19th-century railroad company drilled Claiborne's old water well, which was then turned over to the residents when the railroad closed in 1928.
Johnson and Richardson took over in the early 1980s, back when each household paid $18 annually to hook up and just before the railroad's well was replaced. Now, the yearly fee is $200. A second, separate water system serves 14 properties closer to the Bay and past the main Claiborne Road strip. It's not subject to all of the same MDE rules.
Claiborne Water Company's current building is a white structure housing a pressure tank and chlorine pump. It sits a handful of paces away from the well cap a few feet above ground level.
Residents say efforts to find a licensed operator in recent years have come up empty, which is why they're seeking county assistance.
MDE spokesman Jay Apperson said in an email that the state's increased rules on water system operators were implemented in 2001.
"Maryland regulations include requirements for certification, such as passing examinations and continuing education," Apperson wrote.
Claiborne's water company volunteers aren't overly concerned about water quality. MDE's most recent review of the Claiborne water system indicated that it meets state and federal requirements. Low levels of arsenic, while in compliance, was the leading worry.
MDE inspects the water system at least every three years, Apperson said.
Residents' core concern, instead, boils down to meeting MDE's certification requirements, which likely means passing the buck off to a qualified operator.
And for Johnson, who beat cancer a few years ago, juggling the billing, testing and upkeep responsibilities continues to take a toll. "I'm older now, and I don't have as much strength or wherewithal to carry on," he said.
"We're aging out," Johnson added. "Nobody who's retired wants to take on the responsibility of running the water company."
SOLUTIONS
At the county work session, officials agreed to explore options for the Claiborne Water Company through a preliminary engineering report, or feasibility study, which could be authorized at the council's next meeting on Sept. 23.
Clarke, the county engineer, explained that homeowners connected to the community system mostly can't drill individual wells because of necessary setbacks from private septic systems.
Extending sewer services down to the Claiborne village could be a longer-term solution to make private wells a possibility, officials said. But in the short-term, the residents are still seeking a fix.
County Council Vice President Pete Lesher, acting as a liaison to the Public Works Advisory Board, said he understands Claiborne residents have been "clamoring for some assistance" for a long time.
"I'm well aware that, in (this) process, you've already actually explored a lot of options and are coming to us because you've come up empty," Lesher said.

title: Dorchester council talks juvenile crime, other priorities with state legislators
author: Konner Metz
content:
Dorchester council talks juvenile crime, other priorities with state legislators

 September 17, 2025 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: Konner Metz | Section: Dorchester 
 
 643
 Words 

 Read News Document

 CAMBRIDGE — Dorchester County Council members provided a number of requests to local legislators on Tuesday in advance of the 2026 General Assembly, including an ask to tighten up on juvenile crime.During an annual meeting outlining the county's goals for statewide legislation this winter, Eastern Shore delegates and senators weighed in on the logistics of potential bills the county would like to see offered.
Del. Sheree Sample-Hughes (D-Dorchester, Wicomico) acknowledged the request for more stringent laws on juvenile crime. She noted that she and others are looking to see what comes out of the state's juvenile reform commission, which was created last year.
"I hear you loud and clear and know that there's something needs to be done," Sample-Hughes said. "But I think we're in the trenches of trying to figure out what is in this task force."
Youth crime in Cambridge has raised concerns in recent weeks, especially from Dorchester County Sheriff Jimmy Phillips. On the second day of school at Cambridge-South Dorchester High School, two students were arrested after assaulting the school safety monitor.
Sample-Hughes noted that last winter, a failed piece of legislation would have increased the age minimum from 14 to 16 for a juvenile to be tried as an adult. County Council Vice President Mike Detmer said it should go the other way, if anything.
That legislation even being proposed last year is a sign that "the well's gonna be poisoned" for any commission or task force recommendations, Detmer said.
"This is not hypothetical. This is reality that unfolds weekly in our town," Detmer said. "And it's a hazard to people around and it's a hazard to them."
Council Member Ricky Travers said state youth justice laws are "setting up a whole group of juveniles for failure."
Meanwhile, Council President Lenny Pfeffer said the county's warden has raised concern about separation requirements between juvenile and adult inmates.
"Our facility, being limited on staff, and size and logistics, sometimes finds it difficult to house a juvenile," Pfeffer said. "We have to sometimes bring in additional personnel above the normal shift size."
Pfeffer said it's a "one size fits all" conundrum, where the rural and small Dorchester County can't as easily comply with state regulations.
For his part, Detmer said he's "increasingly concerned about the legislature's encroachment on local control," noting he doesn't think the Eastern Shore legislators are responsible.
"We need to have something where there can be more nuance with blanket laws," Detmer said.
WORKERS' COMP
Pfeffer said the county is bound by state law to pay out equal workers' compensations to all fire service volunteers, whether they perform on-duty or administrative roles. He asked if there's a way for state law to be adjusted so those working in purely administrative roles, and with less risk of workplace injury, could be classified differently.
Del. Christopher T. Adams (R-Caroline, Dorchester, Talbot, Wicomico) addressed the council's request. He warned that a workers' comp bill won't be easy. He added that it's important the county doesn't get caught reducing workers' comp for someone who may switch between field service and office work.
"Don't get mixed up in these scenarios where you have an audit and/or you have a person that does clerical work on Monday through Wednesday, but then ends up on a fire call Thursday or Friday and then gets hurt," Adams said.
Sen. Johnny Mautz (R-Caroline, Dorchester, Talbot, Wicomico) asked council members to take a look at workers' compensation laws that other counties are bound by to see if there's something that could work.
Other potential legislation discussed by the County Council and state legislators on Tuesday included:
Outlawing the use of shoulders to pass vehicles in left-turn lanes. Dorchester County Sheriff's Office Sgt. Robbie Larimer said there's been accident concerns.Reducing or removing the requirements for the county to advertise leases in newspapers. Del. Tom Hutchinson (R-Caroline, Dorchester, Talbot, Wicomico) said he's tried to see through a bill on the matter multiple times, though it's never passed.

 ANNAPOLIS — The three Republican delegates representing Maryland's District 36 — Steve Arentz of Queen Anne's County, Jay Jacobs of Kent County and Jeff Ghrist of Caroline County — formally filed for reelection Wednesday."The District 36 team, which also includes Senate Minority Leader Steve Hershey, has long worked together to advance fiscal responsibility, economic growth, local infrastructure investment and policies that protect the values and livelihoods of the Shore's families and businesses," the incumbents said in a joint press release Wednesday. "Their record reflects years of collaboration and dedication to Caroline, Cecil, Kent and Queen Anne's counties."
Arentz, who has served as a District 36 representative since 2013, when he was appointed to fill the seat vacated by now Sen. Steve Hershey, underscored his focus on economic development and local business growth in the press release.
"The Eastern Shore deserves a team that knows how to deliver results," Arentz said. "From championing small business growth to securing investments in local infrastructure, I've been proud to stand shoulder to shoulder with my colleagues in serving this district. I am running for reelection because there is more work to do to strengthen our economy and preserve our way of life."
Jacobs was mayor of Rock Hall before being sworn in as a District 36 representative in 2010. In the press release, he emphasized his "commitment to protecting the Shore's values."
"Representing the people of District 36 is the honor of a lifetime," Jacobs said. "Our constituents expect us to fight for common sense, to push back against Annapolis overreach, and to ensure that rural Maryland is never forgotten. I am proud to run for reelection with my colleagues so we can continue to give the Upper Shore a strong and respected voice in the General Assembly."
Ghrist, who was elected to his seat in 2014, highlighted the importance of working families and education.
"As a lifelong resident of the Shore, I know the challenges and opportunities facing our families, schools and communities," Ghrist said. "I am committed to making sure our children have a quality education, our communities remain safe, and our families can thrive without being crushed by taxes and regulations. Running as part of this team ensures we will continue delivering results for the people who sent us to Annapolis."
Hershey, who serves alongside the three delegates, praised their record and offered his support for their reelection.
Earlier this month, Hershey, a Republican, announced that he had launched an exploratory committee to look into the viability for a gubernatorial campaign.
"Delegates Arentz, Jacobs and Ghrist have proven themselves to be tireless advocates for the Eastern Shore. title: Transportation officials tour Eastern Shore to discuss funding and project statuses
author: Lily Tierney
content:
Transportation officials tour Eastern Shore to discuss funding and project statuses

 September 17, 2025 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: Lily Tierney | Section: News 
 
 975
 Words 

 Read News Document

 Members of Maryland's Department of Transportation came to the Eastern Shore on Tuesday to meet with county and city officials and give updates on current projects.MDOT officials traveled through the Mid-Shore to discuss the agency's Draft Consolidated Transportation Program for fiscal years 2026 to 2031, which details a $21.5 billion, six-year capital budget investment in the state's transportation network.
Three separate meetings were held with MDOT officials Tuesday, one each in Talbot, Dorchester and Caroline counties. The meetings are part of the department's tour visiting every Maryland county.
TALBOT
Meeting with local officials at the Talbot County Community Center, acting Secretary of MDOT Samantha Biddle presented a draft of the Consolidated Transportation Program, emphasizing efforts to enhance safety, maintain systems and drive economic growth.
Biddle and other MDOT representatives shared status updates for several transportation projects in the county.
The Route 50 corridor project from Dutchman Lane to Lomax Street in Easton is in the final design stages, with construction expecting to begin in 2026, Biddle said. This project includes signalized pedestrian crossings at the Route 50 intersections with Dover and Matthewstown roads.
State Highway Administrator Will Pines reported that the State Highway Administration upgraded and improved 38 crosswalks across Talbot County in fiscal year 2025.
The county will receive a Kim Lanpheir Bikeways Grant for bike racks as part of the Easton Community Bicycle Parking Initiative. Director of Local Transit Support Travis Johnston said that MTA will provide Talbot County with $1 million in operating grants and preventative maintenance for local transit operations.
St. Michaels Town Manager Don Richardson requested the restoration of two crosswalks, which District Engineer Kenny Fender said would be completed in the next two weeks.
Sen. Johnny Mautz (R-Caroline, Dorchester, Talbot, Wicomico) raised concerns over a funding issue for the Oyster Recovery Program, which he said is designed to mitigate damage from port activities and has been the backbone of oyster restoration.
Biddle responded to Mautz's concerns with good news, saying funds are secured for this fiscal year to continue that work. But the conversation escalated at the Dorchester County meeting later Tuesday, when Mautz expressed he felt the secretary had presented conflicting answers throughout the day.
DORCHESTER
Mautz worried transportation officials weren't following through on the details of the contract between MDOT and the Department of Natural Resources. That contract outlines that the agencies together will provide $2 million in funding this fiscal year for the oyster program, Mautz said, among other specifics.
Biddle ensured that the departments would hit the $2 million "target," adding that she will "stay very close" on the matter as her agency works with DNR.
Meanwhile, transportation officials told the Dorchester County Council and residents on Tuesday that a long-awaited roundabout project in East New Market is moving forward.
During MDOT'S stop in Dorchester, Pines said the department's six-year capital funding plan fully supports the roundabout design for the intersection of Routes 392 and 14 in East New Market next to Dockins Service Station.
According to the draft plan, estimated cost is $4.65 million for the improvement. Pines said Tuesday the design should be completed in 2026.
Dawn Stanley, who was in an accident at the intersection two years ago and pushed transportation officials on the matter at last year's annual meeting, clapped when Pines spoke and thanked him.
"Knowing that that roundabout is coming is really essential," said Dorchester County Council Vice President Mike Detmer. "Talking with responders from Station 21, this has always, always been a problem. This is gonna be a triumph of making the roads safer."
SHA District Engineer Mark Crampton touched on efforts to fix culverts at Route 336 as it goes over Worlds End Creek. The road is one of limited access points for residents in southern Dorchester County.
Crampton said temporary improvements have been done and estimated a three-week construction timeframe to begin this summer once school is out. State transportation leaders will meet with the county next week to look at the detour route, Crampton said.
Other areas discussed included:
Warwick Elementary School. Biddle said officials have worked to improve safety on the roads in front of the school in Secretary.Route 392 sidewalks. Biddle said the sidewalks on the portion of the state road in Hurlock were completed this year.
CAROLINE
MDOT came to the Health and Public Service Building on Tuesday morning to hear Caroline County's requests for projects and answer questions from the County Commissioners.
The commissioners also listened to MDOT's plans to ensure federal funding possibilities are still available for the county.
"Our team specifically at the State Highway Administration is looking for opportunities to look where we can apply federal funds for critical safety and state of repair projects here in the county," Biddle told the Star Democrat in an interview after the meeting.
"So, as many projects as we can identify that are federally eligible, it allows us to stretch limited state resources even further to be able to do more projects such as, the intersection improvements referenced by the commissioners today or just safety and resurfacing project where those are helpful and necessary parts of keeping our system in a state of good repair," Biddle said.
Here are the current projects in the county under construction, in progress or requested:
Bridge replacement and rehabilitation at Maryland Route 16 and Harmony Road. The project is already under construction.Intersection capacity improvements from Maryland Route 16 and Harmony Road to Greenwood Road. A planning study is underway.Additional striping or re-striping at the intersection of Maryland Route 317 (Burrsville Road) and Maryland 313 (Greensboro Road). This was requested by the county.Signal change for the traffic lane at Maryland Route 16 (Harmony Road) and Maryland 404. This was requested by the county.Additional lighted intersection at Maryland 404 and Gay Street. This was requested by the county.Consideration of the 16 E school in Greenwood and 404 as a major breakout point. The commissioners requested this change, calling the road as a "major disaster."
Reporters Ahmad Garnett, Konner Metz and Lily Tierney contributed to this report.

title: On Constitution Day, U.S. district judge speaks on checks and balances in Oxford
author: Lily Tierney
content:
On Constitution Day, U.S. district judge speaks on checks and balances in Oxford

 September 18, 2025 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: Lily Tierney | Section: Local News 
 
 578
 Words 

 Read News Document

 OXFORD — Part-time Oxford resident and U.S. District of Maryland Judge James Breder spoke about judicial independence and the constitutional system of government at the Oxford Community Center on Constitution Day, Sept. 17.Breder explained the U.S. Constitution's division of federal government power among the three branches — legislative, executive and judicial — and the importance of checks and balances.
"This division of power was a central feature of the framers' plan for a representative and democratic government," he said. "Now, when I refer to the framers, I'm referencing the men, and they were all men, who met and conceived the Constitution and the Bill of Rights."
The framers wanted to prevent the concentration of power and subsequent tyranny they experienced under the British king, as noted by the founders in the Declaration of Independence.
They divided power as an intentional design to prevent any single person or group from amassing too much power. When describing this system of checks and balances, Breder quoted James Madison, who called it "essential to the preservation of liberty."
For Breder, friction between the branches of government is a predictable consequence and a sign that the system is working as intended, ensuring the government can control itself.
That's Breder's job as a U.S. district court judge. It is the judiciary's job and power to check the other branches, a process known as judicial review. Though this concept is not explicitly stated in the Constitution, Breder said the principle has been in practice since the early days of the country and was formally established through the benchmark case Marbury v. Madison.
"The Marbury decision established this power of judicial review as a part of our constitutional government, and it has endured for more than 200 years," Breder said.
In order for Breder to properly do his job, he said he must be independent from political influence.
"They must be free to decide cases according to the law. A judge under the control of the government will be reluctant to rule against the government even when the government acts improperly and even when citizens' constitutional rights are at stake," he said.
Breder cited the French Revolution "reign of terror" as a historic example of where the lack of an independent judiciary rendered a declaration of rights ineffective, leading to the imprisonment of 300,000 people and nearly 20,000 executions by guillotine through a revolutionary tribunal that denied rights like counsel and appeal.
Breder then outlined the constitutional grounds for impeaching a judge. "The Constitution provides that, 'the President, Vice President, and all civil officers of the United States shall be removed from office on impeachment for a conviction of treason, bribery, or other high crimes and misdemeanors.'"
The term "maladministration" was removed from early drafts of the Constitution to prevent impeachment based on political disagreement with a judge's rulings. The word was deemed too vague.
"Several thousand (individuals) have served as federal judges during the course of U.S. history, and yet, only 15 have been impeached by the House, and only eight of those have been convicted by the Senate," Breder said.
All eight impeachments were for reasons outside of the judges' rulings, such as habitual drunkenness, improper business relationships with litigants, perjury, bribery, and one Civil-War-era judge who was impeached for waging war against the United States.
In his closing remarks, Breder reiterated the importance of checks and balances within government.
"The framers did not make impeachment available for maladministration, and it should not be used to remove judges who make decisions viewed as erroneous or unpopular," Breder said.

 CENTREVILLE — Updates for popular sports and inclusive playgrounds are on the horizon for Queen Anne's County parks.Church Hill Park will be getting a upgrade with the construction of three pickleball courts.
According to the Town of Church Hill, a layout for tennis courts was initially included in the original park masterplan back in the 1980s, but due to a surge in pickle popularity, the town felt as though pickleball courts would be a better suited facility.
The Department of Parks and Recreation are contracting with ATC Corp to construct three pickleball courts and associated storm water management facility in an amount no more than $243,245.
ATC has developed all the other county pickleball courts and has a great relationship with the county, Parks and Recreation Director Steve Chandlee said.
The project is currently in the engineering phase and officials are hopeful to have to have the community playing ball by spring or summer, he said.
Chandlee also noted the complete replacement for a more inclusive playground is coming to Mowbray Park, with equipment delivery estimated in about 12 weeks.
While the current playground is still safe, the equipment is about 23 or 24 years old with pieces much more difficult to replace, Chandlee said. The playground will be closed beginning in October to give staff about a month to remove all materials and level the surface before construction is expected through the winter.
Excited for the inclusive playground project's prospect, a poster showcasing the intended playground with estimated dates for construction is expected to be installed around the vicinity as well, he said.
"Because of the popularity of that playground, we want to make sure we get the word out appropriately and to as many different avenues as possible," Chandlee said.
Initiatives to bring forth Mowbray Park as a more inclusive, accessible, and sensory-friendly space for all children were led by non-profit Noah's Perfect Playground.
Following a public hearing held Aug. 26, the Queen Anne's County Commissioners approved upgrading the sewer service designation of two neighboring Stevensville properties Sept. 9.
The Brennan and Prevoznik properties are both single-family dwellings at 233 and 235 Great Neck Road in Stevensville under the same ownership, according to the county.
With both properties currently served via a failing on-site sewage disposal system and the remaining soils on the site are deemed to be unsuitable for a replacement system, the commissioners approved amending the properties from "No Planned Service" to "Service on Demand" with a "Limited Development" designation which would require any intensification on this site, such as a subdivision, to be required to re-amend the Plan.
In other business, county property wetland mitigation moves forward as the commissioners awarded a contract to Martin's Excavation and Hauling, LLC of Centreville to establish approximately 16 acres of forested wetland on county-owned "Tanner" property in the amount of $1,115,152.
This construction project aims to satisfy the remaining wetland mitigation deficit for permitted wetland impacts in Bay City, Cloverfields and County projects presently totaling 15.4 acres, according to the county. A total of 11 bids were received.
The Solid Waste Division of the Public Works Department was approved the purchase of a Caterpillar 926 14A Wheel Loader with 2.25yd bucket and optional 12' plow, from Carter Machinery Company, of Felton, DE, in the amount of $264,844.

title: City of Cambridge outlines property owners' responsibilities
author: Lily Tierney
content:
City of Cambridge outlines property owners' responsibilities

 September 19, 2025 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: Lily Tierney | Section: Dorchester 
 
 424
 Words 

 Read News Document

 CAMBRIDGE — Cambridge officials have created a document outlining the responsibilities of residents to help clarify what property owners must take care of versus what falls to the city, a merchant or a utility company.Officials decided to create this document because of increasing code enforcement issues within the past year that caused city staff to spend more of their time handing out citations and going to look at properties.
At a meeting in June, City Manager Glenn Steckman said Cambridge was stepping up its code enforcement as trash cans are increasingly left on the sidewalk, grass is going uncut and cars are parked in the wrong direction.
"There seems to be a lack of lawnmowers in our community because the grass and grass height has been an ongoing issue in the town, and we're having to send violation notices out," Steckman said.
Per the document released this month, property owners are responsible for the following:
Maintaining the weatherhead, the cap where the service line meets the building.Maintaining wiring from the weatherhead to the meter, and from the meter into the building.Maintaining and marking privately owned underground lines such as pet fences, sprinklers and outbuildings.Maintaining all piping from the outlet side of the gas meter through the building.Performing annual checks of gas line connections.Maintaining clean access points for plumbers.Maintaining the sewer service line from property line to building.Maintaining all plumbing within the building.Preventing unauthorized stormwater connections like sump pumps and downspouts.Maintaining sidewalks, driveways, aprons, sod, and ensuring they are safe for public use.Removing snow from sidewalks within 36 hours after snowfall.Trimming trees and shrubs so they don't obstruct sidewalks. Must have seven-foot clearance on sidewalks or 12-foot clearance on streets.Immediately removing animal excrement from sidewalks, streets, parks or other public places unless physically unable.Maintaining the water service line from the curb stop to the building.Maintaining plumbing inside meter pits and within the building.Installing and maintaining a Pressure Reducing Valve (PRV) if required.Keeping the water pit visible and maintaining plumbing inside it.Keeping weeds, grass, and vegetation under 6 inches.Keeping property free of litter, refuse, and unsightly growth.
The city is responsible for the following:
Maintaining, repairing, operating public sewer mains under streets and public areas.Repairing and maintaining curbs, gutters, streets.Maintaining water mains.Maintaining service line up to curb stop.If a water meter is in an outdoor pit the city owns and maintains the meter and the pit.
The utility companies are responsible for the following:
Maintaining meters and transformers on property that are part of the utility system.Servicing lines from pole to weatherhead.Maintaining all equipment and piping up to and including the gas meter.

title: Chair of honor: Delaware Rotary honors POWs, MIA soldiers.
author: Josh Shannon jshannon@chespub.com
content:
Chair of honor: Delaware Rotary honors POWs, MIA soldiers.

 September 19, 2025 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: Josh Shannon jshannon@chespub.com | Section: News 
 
 537
 Words 

 Read News Document

 A new display outside of city hall ensures that prisoners of war and service members still missing in action will never be forgotten in Newark, Delaware.The Newark Morning Rotary Club unveiled a POW/MIA Chair of Honor during a brief ceremony Thursday evening, on the eve of National POW/MIA Recognition Day.
"The Chair of Honor will surely stand as a testament to our commitment to remembering and respecting the courage and dedication of the brave individuals who we honor today," club president Jamie Zingaro said. "It also reminds us of the horrors of war and the tremendous impact war has on our families. As Rotarians, we recognize the importance of service above self, and this memorial will continue to remind us of the service and sacrifices so many have made to keep us free."
Hundreds of POW/MIA Chairs of Honor can be found in public spaces around the country, ranging from professional sports stadiums to city halls, and even the U.S. Capitol Building. The perpetually empty chair is meant to help people remember that even though the soldiers are not here, there's always a place for them.
Newark already has a Chair of Honor that is used at the annual Memorial Day ceremony and displayed inside city hall. However, the new one is suitable for outdoor display.
The chair was installed in an area of the city hall parking lot that also includes flagpoles and a plaque honoring city employees who served in the military. It is surrounded by stanchions topped with symbols representing each of the branches of the military, and a bronze plaque explains the purpose of the chair and includes the words "You are not forgotten."
With the blessing of city council, the Rotary Club funded the project and committed to maintaining the display in the future.
Rosely Robinson, who has helped install dozens of Chairs of Honor throughout Delaware and surrounding states, noted that since World War II, there are still 81,000 service members unaccounted for.
"Outside of their families and friends, they have nearly been forgotten," Robinson said. "This chair serves as a constant reminder of those still missing and that we have a place for them when they come home."
Of those missing, 121 are from Delaware.
"It doesn't sound like a big number, but 121 families, brothers, sisters, moms and dads are still waiting, and they should never be forgotten," Robinson said.
Ralph Galati, an Air Force captain whose plane was shot down over North Vietnam, was a prisoner of war for 14 months.
"It was not heroic. It was not brave," Galati said. "But it was performing one's duty, hopefully with dignity and to be able to return with honor."
He said he and his fellow prisoners showed their resolve through resistance by having church services, singing the national anthem and reciting the Pledge of Allegiance.
"All of them were forbidden to be discussed and performed during captivity," he said. "Yet they were the very things that mattered the most to us, so we proudly recited them, regardless of the punishment or consequences. And today, none of these are taken lightly by me. It could be a flag flying gently overhead, or a song before a baseball game or a great rendition of the national anthem, the impact is still the same."

title: Maryland officials warned on bridge contracts
author: MARY BURKE, HOLLIDAY WOODARD and PETER RICCIO Capital News Service
content:
Maryland officials warned on bridge contracts

 September 22, 2025 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: MARY BURKE, HOLLIDAY WOODARD and PETER RICCIO Capital News Service | Section: State News 
 
 388

 WASHINGTON — The Trump administration on Friday warned Maryland officials not to award contracts based on sex and race in the reconstruction of Baltimore's Francis Scott Key Bridge."Any reliance on race- or sex-conscious factors in contracting decisions could introduce significant legal vulnerabilities and inefficiencies in the management of the project," Secretary of Transportation Sean Duffy said in a letter to Maryland Gov. Wes Moore on Friday.
The secretary criticized the project's work plan, arguing that Moore has "prioritized race and gender-based requirements ahead of project completion."
Democrats in the Maryland congressional delegation responded in a joint statement, noting the bridge project was approved by Congress.
"As we have with other major infrastructure disasters with nationwide implications, Congress came together on a bipartisan basis to provide the full resources necessary for reconstruction to ensure it can be rebuilt as quickly and efficiently as possible," the lawmakers said.
"The federal government's commitment to fund the rebuild is enacted into law, and the construction contract was awarded through a legal, competitive, transparent process," they added.
Moore did not address Duffy's comments about sex and race.
"We will continue to work with the Trump Administration to find ways to reduce costs and rebuild faster," Moore said in a statement. "The safety of the bridge and the sound stewardship of taxpayer dollars remain our top priority as we work to fully restore economic vitality — not only to the Port of Baltimore and the State of Maryland, but for the people across the country."
Along with concerns over hiring practices, Duffy questioned the reconstruction project's budget.
"DEI contracting practices and ballooning project costs are already threatening to delay this critical project," Duffy said. "We will leverage our oversight authorities to ensure this vital bridge is rebuilt the right way."
President Donald Trump last month said on social media he might have to "rethink" federal support for the Key Bridge. He called Baltimore "crime ridden" and "out of control" and has threatened to send federal troops into the city, as he has in Los Angeles, Washington and Memphis.
Trump's warning about the bridge funds followed Moore's invitation to Trump to visit Baltimore or "keep our name out of your mouth."
The bridge collapsed in March 2024 after it was struck by a ship. The demolition of the bridge began in July. Following reconstruction, the bridge is slated to open in the fall of 2028.

New Shelter Alliance aims for 24/7 support, year-round housing in Kent County

 CHESTERTOWN — Some 170 people representing a cross-section of Kent County gathered Monday for The Shelter Alliance's inaugural event, an evening focused on the root causes of homelessness, practical pathways to stability and self-sufficiency, and the organization's new leadership under Executive Director Kimrose Goodall.Chestertown resident and Maryland Planning Secretary Rebecca Flora opened the program by introducing Jake Day, Maryland's secretary of Housing and Community Development, noting their shared commitment to approaches that are data-driven and heart-led.
After touring Kent County earlier in the day, Day said the state is grappling with the compounding effects of not building sufficient affordable housing over the last 16 years. He said the Moore administration believes everyone deserves safe shelter and called for collaboration across all levels of government. Day highlighted the Maryland Shelter and Transitional Facilities Grant Program, which funds improvements to emergency shelters and creation of transitional housing, and said the department will partner with The Shelter Alliance to bring resources to Kent County.
Goodall brought the conversation local, noting Kent County ranks third in Maryland for adolescent homelessness. While single men comprise the largest group experiencing homelessness nationally and locally, she said, many single women, mothers with children and a growing number of older adults are also facing uncertain futures.
Goodall outlined The Shelter Alliance's mission to provide a shelter operating 24 hours a day, year-round, paired with individualized, wraparound support. The organization has an eight-member working board, an executive director and a case manager, and coordinates with partner agencies and community organizations to streamline intake and tailor services to each guest's needs. She said the board plans to expand and invited attendees to apply.
During a Q&A, attendees asked about Goodall's vision for a future facility. She said the ideal site would be an existing structure that can be safely adapted to meet diverse guest needs and is near public services, including substance use and mental health support, partner agencies and everyday amenities. Proximity matters, she said, because transportation challenges in Kent County can hinder access to vital programs and resources.
The evening concluded with a presentation honoring board president Carol Niemand for her role in founding The Shelter Alliance and steering the organization to early milestones.
An annual report summarizing The Shelter Alliance's accomplishments was available at the event and will be posted on Facebook and at shelteralliancemd.org, which is scheduled to launch on World Homeless Awareness Day, Oct. 10.

title: New plaques at Harmony Community Park honor Roger Layton, Sarah Mueller
author: Konner Metz
content:
New plaques at Harmony Community Park honor Roger Layton, Sarah Mueller

 September 23, 2025 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: Konner Metz | Section: Caroline 
 
 548

 HARMONY — Caroline County honored two respected leaders Saturday by unveiling plaques in their names at the Harmony Community Park.Families and friends of Roger Layton and Sarah Mueller gathered for a joint dedication at the park, which is on Route 16 north of Preston and south of Denton.
A fence for the park's ball field got a new addition: a plaque cementing it as Roger Layton Memorial Field, named after the former Caroline County commissioner and longtime youth softball and baseball coach.
In front of the park's pavilion, a large plaque set on brick dedicated the park to Sarah Mueller, a well-known community volunteer and former Character Counts coach at Preston Elementary School. Character Counts coaches teach trustworthiness, respect and fairness to school-age kids.
Current Caroline County commissioners and other officials attended and spoke to the expansive impacts both Layton and Mueller had on the local community.
Stacy Seward, one many local softball players coached by Layton, recalled fond memories of her former mentor.
"He created lasting memories for so many young athletes," said Seward, the county's grants coordinator. "For example, teaching us how to slide in the playground sand at Denton Elementary School, saying 'If I can get my old body down here, you girls can too.'"
Steward said he was key to creating the county's first ever softball travel team.
"He was the true backbone to girls' softball, not only in Caroline County, but to the entire Eastern Shore," Seward said.
Commission Vice President Larry Porter said Layton, a commissioner of eight years and former investigator for the State's Attorney's Office, always put Caroline County first.
Daughter Jaclyn Crawford said her father's "real gift was his deep commitment to young people."
"In each role, he was known for his competitive spirit, but above all, his determination to make life safer and better for the community," Crawford said.
In addition to Crawford, other family members of Roger Layton who attended Saturday's dedication included: wife Faye Layton, sister Rena Callahan, stepfather Ronald Sard, granddaughter Madison Weston, cousin Rick Davis and more.
After Layton's sign was unveiled, the curtain was removed off of a large plaque dedicated to Mueller. Husband John Mueller then reflected on his wife's knack for helping people.
"If she heard that you needed something, she'd be the one to offer," her husband said. " ... She was always there first."
He recalled not just her volunteer efforts as a character coach for elementary school kids, but also her assistance in collecting dog and cat food for the local Humane Society.
In addition to John Mueller, his four kids and six grandchildren attended Saturday's dedication, as well as Sarah's mom, Jessie Browne.
Around four years ago, the Mueller family donated $20,000 to the county for upkeep and improvements at Harmony Community Park, including to the pavilion, walking trails and playground.
County commissioners thanked the Mueller family for their donation to the park and spoke about Sarah Mueller's lasting legacy.
"Sarah was more than a neighbor," Porter said. "She was a friend, volunteer, mother and a mentor who gave so much of herself to this community, from her time as a Character Counts coach to her years with the Girl Scouts, where she poured her love into children and back.
"By placing her name here at Harmony Park, we make sure her kindness, spirit and her legacy will always be a part of this place."

title: Concerns over data centers voiced at public meeting
author: Ilana Williams iwilliams@somdnews.com
content:
Concerns over data centers voiced at public meeting

 September 24, 2025 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: Ilana Williams iwilliams@somdnews.com | Section: News 
 
 792
 Words 

 Read News Document

 Shouts against data centers were heard from the back of the room during a meeting earlier this month that addressed noise, water and electricity impacts but also stressed potential economic benefits.There is interest in building data centers in Charles County, Jim Chandler, director of economic development for county government, said during the Sept. 20 meeting at Mary B. Neal Elementary School.
There is a 432-acre proposed data center development located on Billingsley Road near the county landfill and recycling center, according to a presentation from NAI Michael.
Charles County is aware of the commercial development interest in the Piney Reach property for a data center, according to a statement from county government sent to Southern Maryland News.
Prince George's County had a protest against data centers because there are concerns about water, electricity and electronic waste, Carlos Childs, a Waldorf resident, said. The Charles County work group for data centers should also include members of the public and surrounding neighborhoods to provide insight, he said.
"They're saying that the Charles County government is supportive of a data center coming here," Childs said. "Which is weird that it wasn't said … or that they even mentioned the Piney Reach [data center] at all."
Childs was told about the proposed Piney Reach center and found the presentation on Google, he said.
So far, the county has not received any development plan submissions. The economic development department views this property "as an opportunity site for a number of industrial-type uses, one of which could be the future use of data centers."
"Data centers need to be carefully located and need regulation," Chandler said.
Phones, computers and GPS systems use data centers, Mark Thompson, chief of commercial development for Charles County, said. Data centers are large, one- to two-story buildings that have computer servers. They have high security to protect information and back up generators.
"For the longest time, you've heard people talking about the cloud … data centers are effectively the cloud," Thompson said.
Water impacts
Data centers require a lot of energy and get extremely hot, making the water use high to cool the systems, Thompson said. They use a closed-loop system, which keeps water in the system.
"We need to look at those things and think about them relative to other commercial uses," Thompson said.
Treated waste water is already being used for cooling at the CPV St. Charles Energy Station, which can be used for the same purpose as data centers, Jason Groth, director of planning and growth management, said.
"Our reclaimed, effluent water is ever-growing," Groth said. "As we grow, as new connections are made to the system, more water is produced. Therefore more reclaimed water is produced."
Economic benefits
Data centers can generate up to 5,000 construction jobs, and data center employees earn around $100,000 a year and generate billions of dollars in state and local taxes, Chandler said.
Data centers offer jobs for engineers, computer technicians, systems maintenance and security, Thompson said, as well as electricians, carpenters and plumbers while the center is being built.
Data centers also have a higher assessed value than homes and generate significant property taxes, Thompson said. The land sold for a data center in Frederick County generated $50 million in recreation taxes.
"That's a significant, significant revenue," Thompson said. "As we are all faced with revenue challenges throughout the state and the counties, we need to be thinking about that as a very important consideration."
The advocacy group Strong Towns Charles County is concerned about being able to support the infrastructure and impacts to wildlife, Maddie Kaba, co-leader of Strong Towns, said.
"We're talking about an initial construction boom now and all the revenue that it's going to bring in, but how are we being responsible with that money and making sure we save some of it," Kaba said.
Traffic, noise addressedData centers don't generate a lot of traffic because there are not a lot of people coming in and out, Thompson said. Cooling centers and generators generate around the same amount of noise as power plants and recycling centers.
Back up generators have to be run every 10 to 15 minutes and create noise, Groth said. To ease the noise, the generators will be built within the data center campus between two buildings.
"The further the building can be set back away from a property line or adjacent use is really key," Groth said.
While data centers should not be compared to the recycling center because it gets rid of harmful plastics and metals, Shelly Posey, a resident who lives outside La Plata, said she liked the idea of using wastewater.
"I won't say that I'm positive, but I'm in the middle," Posey said.
The county is working on a zoning text amendment that will include constraints on data centers if they were to be built, Groth said. It will move through the public process starting in October.

title: Cambridge ordinance proposes updating code on group housing
author: Lily Tierney
content:
Cambridge ordinance proposes updating code on group housing

 September 24, 2025 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: Lily Tierney | Section: Dorchester 
 
 502
 Words 

 Read News Document

 CAMBRIDGE — Cambridge's Unified Development Code is "outdated," according to City Planner Brian Herrmann, who has proposed a new ordinance to align the city's code on group housing with state and federal laws.But rumblings on social media express concern over the proposed ordinance, saying it will lead to a proliferation of these types of residences if passed. Herrmann said that will not be the case.
A group home is a residential facility that provides supervised housing and support services for individuals who require assistance.
In the current code, group homes can have no more than eight clients and are allowed in every district. The new ordinance sets out to clarify where and what type of group homes are allowed.
The code only defines two uses: a group home and a set of institutional residential uses like nursing care, intermediate care and child care institutions.
The proposed ordinance would eliminate these two uses and replace them with four new categories: large group homes/large halfway houses, recovery residences, small group homes/small halfway houses, and commercial properties like assisted living facilities, residential care homes and nursing facilities.
The large group homes/large halfway houses, recovery residences and small group homes/small halfway houses will be regulated on the state and federal level.
"So we don't really have much say in it other than we do give a zoning certificate to say that, yeah, you do meet the zoning requirements and we're going to sign off on that," Herrmann said.
Herrmann clarified that the large group homes/large halfway houses would be primarily allowed in institutional, commercial mixed use and maritime resort zones, meaning few are likely to be in typical residential neighborhoods.
On social media, residents have expressed concerns over the ordinance out of fear the group homes will change the makeup of residential neighborhoods.
"I understand all of the concerns. I think everyone would probably have them with their own property. The issue is that we have to follow the rules and we can't just make them up," Herrmann said on aligning the city's code with state and federal regulations.
According to Herrmann, passing the ordinance will enhance the city's ability to register, track and inspect certain facilities, add enforceable conditions, and require a Board of Appeals review for some uses.
"It's a little stricter," he said.
Herrmann said in the past few years, the city has received far less applications to create these types of homes. He said they used to get 12 to 14 applications, but in his time as city planner, they have only received two.
Because downtown Cambridge has a form-based code, which puts more emphasis on what the homes look like rather than their use, Herrmann said the area is less attractive to applicants.
"I guess we just haven't seen as many applicants in the last couple years as we did in the past, which, to me, tells you that we're moving in the right direction. And then if we can get our code up to what it needs to be, and it's a little stricter, I think we'll be even better off," Herrmann said.

title: MACo leaders meet with Talbot officials to discuss 2026 General Assembly
author: Konner Metz
content:
MACo leaders meet with Talbot officials to discuss 2026 General Assembly

 September 25, 2025 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: Konner Metz | Section: Local News 
 
 536
 Words 

 Read News Document

 EASTON — Leaders from the Maryland Association of Counties shared predictions for a calmer legislative session in 2026 during a meeting with the Talbot County Council on Tuesday.Michael Sanderson, MACo's executive director, and Jack Wilson, the association's president and current Queen Anne's County commissioner, met for an annual check-in with Talbot officials.
Sanderson reminded the council members of last year's volatile General Assembly session, during which legislators and Gov. Wes Moore (D) had to reckon with closing a $3 billion gap in the state's fiscal year 2026 budget.
Some savings came through cost shifts placing more burden on county governments, the MACo leaders said. But they added that the upcoming 2026 session, and the fiscal year 2027 budget that goes along with it, likely won't be as dire.
"Relatively calm, probably not a big crisis," Sanderson said of his projection for this year's session, which officially kicks off Jan. 14 in Annapolis.
He said the large budgetary concerns are likely to reappear in 2027 as legislators put together a plan for fiscal year 2028.
"The story from last year is gonna repeat itself, but with a year off," Sanderson predicted.
Specifically, the executive director said Maryland's expansive education funding formula, The Blueprint, will influence the 2027 session. And in the short-term, some counties are already coming to grips with increasing cost shares for education.
"Every county is either in the midst or a year or two away from seeing a year where the increase in school spending required under Blueprint requires all the money or even more money than your county's likely to gain in revenue for that year," Sanderson said. "It's an obvious squeeze at the local level."
Talbot County's fiscal year 2026 budget included $55 million in education funding required by The Blueprint's formulas. On top of that, the council approved an additional $600,000 in funding to fill new positions.
That mark had been scaled back twice from the original ask the Talbot Board of Education made of the council — first requesting $5.5 million in supplementary funds, then $1.1 million.
County Council Vice President Pete Lesher, who supported the district's $1.1 million request earlier this year, said it was "short-sighted" for the county to only fund the district's request partially, given that Blueprint requirements are only set to increase in future years. But other council members opted to hold back on dedicating the full request as the county aimed to even out its spending hikes seen in years prior.
Sanderson said on Tuesday that housing legislation will be at the forefront this winter. Recently, Moore signed an executive order that aims to speed up the permitting and building of affordable housing projects.
"I anticipate that being a big fight," Sanderson said. "Whether it's a big fight in the more rural jurisdictions is yet to be seen."
Council Member Lynn Mielke asked how Easton fits into state plans to tackle the housing issue.
Sanderson said there's an opportunity for MACo to advocate for provisions so a potential housing package doesn't "overwhelm" local jurisdictions. He said the association can help push for certain changes to help counties and towns that lack authority in certain areas, such as the variation of impact fees on developers.
"At the same time, we generally want to keep land use decisions local," he added.

title: St. Michaels Commissioners discuss sea level rise projects
author: AHMAD GARNETT agarnett@chespub.com
content:
St. Michaels Commissioners discuss sea level rise projects

 September 25, 2025 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: AHMAD GARNETT agarnett@chespub.com | Section: News 
 
 384
 Words 

 Read News Document

 ST. MICHAELS — On Wednesday, Roy Meyer of the Climate Change Sea Level Rise Commission and multiple engineers presented key sea-level rise mitigation projects to the St. Michaels commissioners.Meyer said the projects were for the wellbeing of the town of St. Michaels residents and tourists.
"If there's one thing that impacts the town and the Maritime Museum in the same way, it's sea level rise and flooding," Meyer said. "So I mean their campus is going to be flooded, our roads are going to be flooded."
The projects, which will be carried out in two phases, will potentially raise road elevations to five feet. An Advanced Systems grant with FEMA and a state grant will help the town cover the cost of the projects.
Phase one involves raising Mill Street, Burn Street, the Harbor walkway and the end of Cherry Street to an elevation of five feet. It also includes demolishing and rebuilding Honeymoon Bridge at a higher elevation and wider size, rebuilding piers at the Chesapeake Bay Maritime Museum, installing a larger culvert system where Mill Street meets the tidal area, and adding a north sidewalk along Mill Street.
The cost of Phase one would be more than $5.3 million.
Phase two will address Mulberry Street, Muskrat Park, and Church and Green streets. Phase two features two options, short-term and a long-term solutions.
The short-term would include modifying the parking lot and existing swale in the park to provide immediate relief from flooding by getting water off the streets faster. This solution is expected to be effective for daily high tides until 2050 and cost $708,366.
The long-term approach raises the roads, similar to phase one. It would also move the roads away from the pipe system and allow for overland flow, separating stormwater and tidewater.
Raising to elevation five feet is the ideal solution, but challenges exist with a wall along Church Street near a cemetery and columbarium, engineers said. The long-term approach would cost $896,724.
The commissioners elected to proceed with prioritizing the already advanced Phase one construction plans and will follow up with the Maritime Museum to discuss options.
The commissioners selected the short-term solution for phase two, saying the town will develop a detailed long-term plan for Muskrat Park. The commissioners also said they would defer action on Mulberry Street until more clarity emerges from private development plans.

title: Easton council members to host ward town halls for residents
author: Konner Metz
content:
Easton council members to host ward town halls for residents

 September 26, 2025 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: Konner Metz | Section: Local News 
 
 459

 EASTON — Beginning Monday, Easton council members will host ward-specific town halls in hopes of increasing transparency and engaging with constituents.Maureen Curry (Ward 1), Robert Rankin (Ward 2), David Montgomery (Ward 3) and the Rev. Elmer Davis (Ward 4) will each host town halls open to their constituents at the Easton Volunteer Fire Department in the coming weeks.
The town halls were mentioned during Easton's recent election, including by Don Abbatiello, now council president and then Ward 2 representative.
Abbatiello said he aims to attend all four town halls.
"We wanted to make sure that we left no stone unturned when it came to sharing information," Abbatiello said.
Rankin will kick off the meetings with Ward 2 residents on Monday. Montgomery will host Ward 3's discussion on Oct. 9. Davis will lead Ward 4's on Oct. 23, and Curry will wrap it up with Ward 1's meeting on Oct. 27. All four meetings will be held at the Easton fire hall from 7 to 8 p.m.
Abbatiello said the idea to host semi-regular ward town halls birthed from discussions on the campaign trail, with some residents feeling like they didn't have enough access to town information or couldn't attend town meetings, which are typically twice a month at 5:30 p.m.
The council president said the town's done a good job in improving its communication to residents since he joined the council in 2019, especially on its website and social media platforms. The new town halls are a continuation of that effort, he said.
Council members will provide brief presentations to residents at the meetings, updating them on recent projects in town and their respective wards. Then, the sessions will open up for feedback and questions from the public.
"We want residents to be informed and know what's going on," Rankin said. " ... The more we can hear from folks … that really helps us a lot."
Housing, growth and traffic are expected to be major points of discussion, council leaders said.
"The central topic, for me at least, will be growth," Montgomery said. "And I think that's a topic that concerns everybody of Ward 3 because of how residents have to tend to traffic."
Rankin said he expects his discussion to touch on recent development projects and the town's comprehensive plan, which is in the process of being updated for the first time since 2010 and will lay out a vision for the town's growth over the next decade.
Davis said that in addition to growth and development, he expects to field questions on the Easton Police Department and resident concerns about safety.
The Ward 4 representative highlighted the town halls as another avenue to be open with the public.
"Everybody can be included and get some questions answered," Davis said. "Our main goal is to show transparency to the community."

title: Welcoming fall with stories that matter
author: Staff Writer
content:
Welcoming fall with stories that matter

 September 27, 2025 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: Staff Writer | Section: Headlines 
 
 149

 Fall may be the busiest time of the year in the newsroom.With school is back in session, festivals in full swing and candidates preparing for local elections, there's no shortage of things to cover. Our reporters have been clocking overtime for the past few weeks to make sure they're bringing important stories to you.
The extra hours can be exhausting, but they give us a chance to reflect on why we cover the things that we do.
